en: A Brief Introduction to the Convergence of the *Laṅkāvatāra* and the *Śūraṃgama-samādhi* Those who discourse on the school of Nature (*xingzong*) often fall into the trap of abstract principle; those who discourse on the school of Characteristics (*xiangzong*) often fall into the trap of concrete phenomena.

They do not realize that characteristics are identical to nature, and that there are no characteristics apart from nature—just as waves are identical to water, and there is no water apart from waves. This is true emptiness (*zhēnkōng*).
The non-obstruction between principle and phenomena within wondrous existence is this Dharma-gate of non-duality.

Although the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* characterizes it according to the School of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇavāda*), Bodhidharma came from the West holding this as the transmission of the Buddha’s mind-seal. This is because the three realms are mind-only and all dharmas are consciousness-only;
if one can simply realize that the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is itself the Tathāgata-garbha, then one will know that what is manifested by one's own mind is illusory.

The characteristic of these [phenomena] is that they fundamentally lack intrinsic nature and are fundamentally unborn; thus, one immediately attains the realm of self-awakened noble wisdom (*svapratyātmāryajñāna*).
This direct pointing to the single mind (*ekacitta*) without falling into gradual stages constitutes the Sudden Teaching (*tongjiao*) of the Mahāyāna.

As for the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, it is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) concerning the cultivation and realization of the Tathāgata’s secret cause; it can truly encompass all scriptures. Regarding the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*) and the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) it indicates:

Do the seven elements, twelve bases, and eighteen realms not involve the realm of phenomena (*nimitta*)? Yet the Sūtra says: "All dharmas that arise are manifested solely by the mind, like flowers in the sky;
they ultimately have no substance. To realize that these are illusory and false is to immediately return to the Truth.

Once one abandons this mind of arising and ceasing, there is nothing further than the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*. Therefore it is said: "The faculties and their objects share the same source; bondage and liberation are without difference."
The second, the ultimate firmness of all phenomena, is the ultimate firmness of all principles; it does not mean that one must first destroy appearances before they become true.
One who penetrates this point will find that not only do these two sutras follow the same track, but the entire Great Canon of teachings emerges from a single path.
Chan Master Yiyu was in profound resonance with the True Exegesis and had attained a thorough penetration of the mirror of the mind; he ascended the dharma platform and preached.
The Dharma is not confined to a single assembly; wherever it appears, it can illuminate the nature of mind and enable people to open up right knowledge and vision.

This is by no means comparable to those contemporary teachers who merely string together trivialities and glean fragments to suit the demands of the examination hall. Recently, while he was staying at Tiantai Temple, monks and laypeople alike took refuge in him as their preeminent leader.

At the request of those from the Western Regions, he brought forth his commentaries on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* and the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra*, which follow the same path, and presented them for inspection.
I have examined this work closely and find it direct and unimpeded, its nature and characteristics perfectly harmonized, sweeping away all entanglements.

It is a compass for the ocean of true meaning and a bright lamp for the dark chamber. The Western Regions [India] has solicited various fellow practitioners to carve this into woodblocks to propagate its transmission widely, and they have requested that I, the unworthy one, compose a preface while joyfully contributing to the effort.
On the first day of the first month of winter in the first year of the Tianqi era, the Layman from Fudu, Wu Yongxian, bows in greeting and writes this preface for the *Lengyan Heye*.
Though orphaned at a young age and born into a poor neighborhood, I took refuge in a secluded temple; yet, while my refined inclinations favored the Buddha-dharma, my mind remained unsettled.
At that time, there was an elderly master named Ran in the mountains who was skilled in medicine, poetry, and the study of the *Śāsanavāha* (the Teachings of the Buddha).

He delighted in conversation with me, and during our discussions, he frequently cited and expounded upon the essential points of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* to inspire me; I, too, was able to silently grasp his meaning.
At that moment, my mind became intent upon the *Śūraṅgama*, and I privately studied the *Tianru Huikai* commentary even amidst the bitter cold.

During the humid heat of summer, he did not cease his textual investigations; whenever he caught even a partial glimpse [of the truth], he would become self-congratulatory, believing that the profound essence of this sutra was fully contained therein.
Thinking there was nothing further to aspire to, he remained secluded on the Western Mountain of Lake Tai.
In the year of Bingxu, it happened that the Huazang Monastery in Wuxi was inaugurating a lecture period on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, and the presiding master was the aforementioned...
The Great Master Xuelang, the Head Seat, was a venerable elder of the mountains;
his fellow practitioners, the elders Yuan and Ran, were both learned in the teachings and skilled in poetry, and they had also maintained a friendship with me. They sent a letter stating:
"Xuelang of Jinling is truly a great Dharma Master of our time; his insight is eminent and far-reaching, and the torrent of his discourse surges like rivers and streams pouring forth."
A bridge for those in the final age and an eye for the human and celestial realms, you currently reside at Huazang Temple, extensively expounding the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Yet, you remain secluded in a remote corner, staring at the Milky Way; why do you not emerge from the mountains to attend the lecture hall and partake in the flavor of the Dharma?
I reflected deeply on this: "The profound meaning of the *Śūraṅgama* has had its mysteries and subtleties fully revealed by the ten masters, and Tianru has further distilled their essentials."

The meaning is intended as a comprehensive interpretation; if it were merely a collection of various jewels, then the lecturer’s mouth would be like a cascading river, yet this would not exceed relying on clever knowledge and insight to gloss over the world—how could one establish new doctrines apart from this? [Kui]ji did not leave, and Gong again sent a letter saying:
"The subtle purport of the Tathāgata is vast and a deep abyss; how could it be exhausted by a single bit of knowledge or vision, or a single phrase or character?"

The meaning cannot be fully exhausted; it is like the great ocean: a mosquito or gadfly drinks from it and is satisfied, a mole drinks from it and is satisfied, and an asura drinks from it and is satisfied—each according to its own capacity.
How could one see anyone who can suck the waters of the sea dry in a single mouthful?
Come, sir, and I shall not fail you; do not be so conceited. Thereupon, I joyfully purchased a boat.

He proceeded directly to the Dharma assembly; at that time, his former master held a fly-whisk in his hand, looking left and right and coughing or stretching, displaying nothing but the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and completely sweeping away the fragmented habits of textual scholarship.
Among the audience present, some bit their fingers, some danced for joy, and some offered praise, all exclaiming: "How rare! This is truly great!"
To be a patriarch and yet also a great teacher—this is indeed so! I too was momentarily bewildered, yet ultimately attained a state of tranquil composure.
Thereupon, with palms joined in reverence, I thanked the Head Seat, saying: "Your exhortation to take up this office has not been in vain; my solitary coming here has not been in vain.

From that time on, I attended at his side daily to listen for instruction. Whenever I encountered passages that were cryptic, convoluted, or difficult to grasp, I would invariably seek clarification from the Master. The Master said: "This is the teaching of the Tathāgata."

The source and course of the Dharma are non-dual, yet its tributaries branch into a thousand variations; however, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* unifies all dharmas as its progeny and encompasses all scriptures as its kin.
Although it consists of ten fascicles, it is truly the general preface to the Great Canon.
Those who are resolved to serve the teachings must first read it, and they must read it with thorough mastery. Once mastered, it will permeate one’s eyes, mind, mouth, and teeth.
Within these depths, there is naturally a path of entry characterized by a subtle resonance; one need not borrow the jaws of others to pick up their tears and spittle.
If you first clarify the meaning of the sutra, then looking back at the various commentaries, the distinction between the pure and the turbid will become immediately apparent.

Otherwise, you will have your mind stolen by the commentaries, and the meaning of the sutra will instead grow obscure. Having first obtained the method for reading the sutras, since that time I have practiced it alone.
In my quiet dwelling, I placed nothing upon my desk but the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*; likewise, I kept nothing within my breast, at the corners of my eyes, or on the tips of my lips but the *Śūraṅgama*.
As I read and contemplated it, whenever I encountered a passage that did not satisfy my mind, I would immediately transcribe it and paste it upon the wall.

I constantly investigated these points, striving with all my might to achieve thorough penetration. Thus, through frequent moments of realization over the course of several years, I came to grasp the single thread that runs through the entire *Śūraṅgama*.

Every word of this treatise accords with the Buddha’s mind without the slightest discrepancy. Looking back upon my former methods, they were truly like trying to measure the heavens with a bamboo tube or scoop up the ocean with a ladle.
By reading the commentaries of various masters, the points of right and wrong, gain and loss, became clear within my breast, leaving me with no lingering doubts or obstructions.

Thereupon, I gathered together all the fragmentary insights I had acquired throughout my life from teachers and friends, as well as [my own lifelong... (Note: The source text appears to be incomplete at the end. The translation provided reflects the available portion.)

I had previously recorded my own realizations as a private memorandum and kept it in a chest to prevent forgetfulness. Not long after, I happened to see the *Lengyan Zhengmai* (The True Pulse of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra) on a friend’s desk;

upon unrolling it and reading it, I found that the points where it pointed out flaws and exposed errors coincided with my former private notes by a large margin—perhaps seven or eight parts out of ten.
Those that did not coincide accounted for three or four parts out of ten, yet when compared...
Although the commentaries and sub-commentaries of former masters have galloped side by side like horses on the same track, they have already long since surpassed them.
I rejoiced and congratulated myself, saying: "How could there be such a Dharma Master? We dwell in a remote corner, never having even heard his name;
how fortunate we are now to have obtained this unsurpassed and rare treasure! Is this not what is meant by 'seeking it not'?"
Since arriving here, I have intended to consult with various donors to carve woodblocks for dates and pears in order to propagate this work widely.

However, I learned that the printing blocks had already been transmitted to Jiaxing and Huzhou long ago. Nevertheless, Master Jian’s compassionate heart was so earnest that he wished for everyone to fully understand it;

thus, he provided detailed explanations for every scriptural meaning, whether easy or difficult. Because his explanations were so thorough, the language became prolix, and such verbosity is inconvenient.

Regarding beginners, they all look out at the vast ocean and retreat; therefore, I have again taken my private notes from ordinary days and compiled them into a single volume—those points which accord with the various characteristics of Buddha-nature as if they were of one track—to entrust to the carver for printing.

This is truly intended to entice those of like mind who prefer either complexity or simplicity, so that both may enter the Dharma-gate of Perfect Penetration. As for the great purport of the sutras, it has already been [addressed].
Since this has already been established by the prior definitive judgment, it is not recounted again; I shall merely set forth here the lineage and provenance of the Dharma in this manner.
Written by the monk Tongrun of Er-Leng-’an in the year of the Dragon’s Flight (1621), the eighth year of the Tianqi era, for the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra*:
The Definitive Meaning of the Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Cultivation, and Realization, and the [Realizations] of All Bodhisattvas.
The First Fascicle of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra:
A Concordance* Composed by Shi Tongrun of Erleṅ’ān, Ming Dynasty Part One: Explanation of the Title Part Two:
Explanation of the Names of the Translator, the Transcriber, and the Scribe [The text continues with the explanation of the title and the names of those involved in the translation process.]

Regarding the three characters "Dàfódǐng" (Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa): according to other scriptures, this refers to the mark of the invisible crown of the head (*anavalokitamūrdhatā*) among the thirty-two marks of a Buddha's body.
It is situated amidst the blue-spiraled hair (*nīlakuñcitakeśa*), appearing red all around like a spring mountain emitting the sun, yet its summit cannot be seen.
At the time of his initial birth, he should have been nursed by a Bodhisattva of the ninth stage as his wet nurse.
If one wishes to reach its summit, even after traversing Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it can never be seen; this is one of the three mysteries.

This sutra begins with the manifestation of light from the mark of the invisible crown and the recitation of mantras, yet the Tathāgata first designates that there is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Crown. According to the explicit meaning of the scripture, this refers to Bodhi.
"Nirvana" refers to the fundamentally pure essence, the Tathāgatagarbha, the Mind.

Because this mental essence encompasses and gives forth the ten voids and pervades the myriad phenomena, the five eyes cannot perceive its form and the four types of eloquence cannot describe its appearance;
only our Great Awakened One, upon beholding the morning star, opened the Buddha's knowledge and vision and gazed directly at its summit—therefore, it is so named.

The Dharma is the supreme and most excellent pinnacle-dharma of Great Enlightenment. That which is called "The Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, the Cultivation and Realization of the Definitive Meaning" is precisely the manifestation of this Dharma;
therefore, it is termed the "Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa. As for the term "Tathāgata," it is a specific designation for Great Enlightenment:
"Tathā" (Thus) refers to the unchanging name, while "Gata" (Come) refers to following conditions; in the Small Vehicle, there is "Tathā" (Thus) but no "Gata" (Come).
Ordinary beings come [into this world], yet they do not correspond to it; only I, the Great Awakened One, both correspond to it and have come, and for this reason am called the Tathāgata.
Regarding the term "secret cause" (*mi-yin*): "secret" refers to that which is known and seen by oneself alone; "cause" refers to the production of the holy fruit.

This means that the Great Awakened One takes this *uṣṇīṣa*-dharma as the cause and gives rise to the myriad practices. Regarding "cultivation and realization": it refers to refining, polishing, and treating [the mind].

To practice it is called cultivation; to forget the mind and attain silent resonance with it is called realization. This refers to the Great Awakening relying on this "Crown Dharma" (*uṣṇīṣa-dharma*) to sever delusions and realize the truth.

As for the term "definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*), "definitive" means that nothing remains uninvestigated or exhausted, and "meaning" means that which does not fall within the realm of words or discursive thought.
It is said that the Great Awakening appeared for the sake of this primary ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and this great causal condition.
Because it has now been thoroughly investigated and exhausted without remainder in this world, it is called "definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*).

This is because the karmic consciousness of sentient beings is vast and boundless, entirely devoid of awakening; they dwell perpetually in the long night, transmigrating through birth and death with no end in sight.
Some merely occupy the "transformed city," indulging in the bliss of quiescent extinction and halting midway, unable to press forward. Nor have they yet...

One who is able to understand [this] is a Bodhisattva; though there is a path ahead leading to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), they have not yet reached the ultimate perfection and their task is not yet complete.

Ultimately, this is still "not fully understood. Only when it is the Great Awakening—where obstructions are exhausted and delusions are empty, causes are exhausted and fruits are fulfilled, and all functional duties are completed—is there nothing further to be done.
Since every single meaning is fully understood and no further meanings remain, one thereby knows the Dharma.

The mountain of nature is high and steep; only the Tathāgata can ascend directly to its summit, for there is no further place above it. Only then is the attainment of unsurpassed enlightenment fully realized. As the subsequent text states:
"In this manner, through twelve layers of single and double [stages], one exhausts the wondrous enlightenment and achieves the unsurpassed path.
Therefore, it is called "The Definitive Meaning of the Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Cultivation, and Realization. This refers to the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas.
Śūraṅgama means that from the stage of Dry Wisdom (śuṣka-vijñāna) up to Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi),

one takes this "Crown Dharma" as the cause to cultivate the six perfections, gradually severing ignorance and partially realizing ultimate truth. By ascending through the various stages of the Bodhisattva,
one is able to tread the steps of the Buddha at every stride and achieve firm stability in every matter— what is called "analyzing the sandalwood."
Like sandalwood, every fragment is fragrant; like a broken jade arch, every particle is precious jade. Although one has not yet attained ultimate realization, one has already attained partial truth;
therefore it is said that for all Bodhisattvas, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* is the foremost among the myriad practices.
Thus we know that the originally pure essence, the *tathāgatagarbha*, can only be fully exhausted by Buddha after Buddha, which is called "ultimate awakening" (*atyanta-bodhi*). Only the Buddhas...
Because the Bodhisattvas' partial severance and partial realization is termed "partial awakening," the subsequent text states:
"The Tathāgatas of the past have already accomplished this gate; the Bodhisattvas of the present each now enter its perfect clarity.

Aside from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, other world-transcending ones who attain minor fruits, as well as the sages and worthies who govern the world, though they each possess their own insights and entries, are but dim and indistinct.
One may glimpse a partial view of it as if through a crack, yet for the most part, these remain seated within the realm of semblance-realization.

This is because they have been unable to empty the five aggregates (*skandha*), exhaust the six sense faculties (*indriya*), terminate the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*), transcend the two deaths (*dvividha-maraṇa*), and surpass the measure of the mind (*citta-mātra*);

thus, they have not yet reached the ultimate perfection. Only the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, having exhausted the heights and fathomed the depths, penetrating both essence (*svabhāva*) and appearance (*lakṣaṇa*), realize the Unsurpassed Dharma.
Because it is peerless, the Sūtra designates it as the "Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama King"; its purport is profound indeed.
A "Sūtra" (sūtra) means that which is constant; it establishes an eternal standard for all time and serves as the final radiance of the Buddha-lamp.

Therefore, if one follows the subsequent text, because the mind can be taken as a model and upheld, it is called a "Sūtra. Thus, the three categories and the seven elements are all [included therein].

This sutra takes the mind as its comprehensive inclusion of all phenomena (*dharma*). According to the *Miaofa lianhua jing xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), it sometimes emphasizes a single atom:
when the Buddha was in the world, he proclaimed the teaching with his golden mouth and listeners attained the Way; thus, sound constitutes the sutra.
After the Buddha passed away, it was transmitted through paper and ink; thus, form constitutes the sutra. If one says, "Those who cultivate my Dharma..."
Realization is self-knowing; thus, one takes the Dharma as the scripture. In this land, only the three objects [of smell, touch, and taste] are employed, while the other three faculties are dull.
When the nose smells paper and ink, there is no cognition; when the body touches a scroll, it cannot perceive it;
and when the tongue tastes paper and ink, it cannot understand them. In other lands, however, all six objects are fully employed, as the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra says: "In..."
Regarding "equal in food and so forth," they are also equal in regard to the dharmas; this refers to taking what is specifically encountered by the tongue-root as the primary sūtra.
In some lands, one attains the Way through celestial garments touching the body, which takes tactile sensation as the primary sūtra.
Or, one attains the Way upon seeing the Buddha’s radiance, which takes visible form as the primary sūtra. In the Land of Universal Fragrance, fragrance serves as the Buddha.
In this regard, some exclusively take fragrance as their scripture, while others attain the Way through silent, wordless contemplation of the mind;

these take intention as their scripture. Those in other lands have sharp faculties regarding the six sense organs and can take all six sense objects as their scripture, whereas those in this land have dull faculties regarding the three [upper] organs and thus take only the three [lower] objects as their scripture.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Paramiti.

"India" (Tianzhu) is the general name for the countries of the Western Regions; this is translated as "Moonland" (*Candradvīpa*), because while the great nations appear like stars among the multitude of small nations, this country is like the moon.
"Śramaṇa" means "diligent cessation"; it refers to one who diligently practices wholesome dharmas.
Because it brings about the cessation of unwholesome conduct, it is called *Paramārtha*; this is the name of the translator.
A translator transcribes Sanskrit characters into Chinese characters.
This sutra was recited from memory by the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna in the Dragon Palace and brought forth; it is the supreme [teaching] of the lords of the five regions of India.

That which was cherished as a treasure and kept secret, never transmitted before: formerly, when the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai heard that this sutra existed in the Western Regions, he gazed westward day and night, prostrating and praying to behold it, yet he did not succeed in seeing it.

Later, when Paramārtha wished to transmit it to China, he repeatedly brought it in secret, but each time he was captured and turned back. Finally, he wrote it down with exquisite, fine silk. It was then...
Śikṣānanda cut his own arm and hid it within his skin, sailing by sea to reach Guangzhou. There, he met the Chancellor Fang Rong, who was presiding over the southern selection office in Guangzhou;
Fang requested that the translation take place at Zhizhi Temple, where he served as the scribe (*pen-shou*). Once the scripture was completed, copies were transcribed and submitted to the throne.
However, as Emperor Zhongzong had recently ascended the throne and the state was beset by many affairs, there was no leisure to promulgate it. At that time, there was the Chan Master Shenxiu.
He entered the inner sanctum and saw the manuscript of the original text being presented; he transcribed it and returned to Du-men Temple in Jingzhou.
At that time, Dharma Master Hui-zhen constantly admired this scripture, and upon visiting Du-men Temple, he obtained it.

The scripture was first transmitted during the tenth year of the Tianbao era, when Dharma Master Wei-quo of Xingfu Temple in the Western Capital again obtained it from the former Chancellor Fang Rong’s residence.
The original text recorded by the scribe was first provided with a commentary and widely disseminated.
The śramaṇa Meghaśikṣa from the kingdom of Udyāna translated the words;
"Udyāna" means "Garden" (Yuán) in this language. This great kingdom is named after its gardens and groves, and it is located in Northern India.
Zhumi Jia Shijia (竺彌伽釋迦), which in this language means "Able to Subdue," was a translator of terminology—that is, one who translated words.
This refers to the act of weighing and judging the correct principles of both [languages] to translate Indic terms into Chinese.
Recorded by the Bodhisattva Precept Disciple, Former Minister of Justice and Concurrent Vice President of the Secretariat and Chancellery, Fang Rong.
Regarding "Bodhisattva Precepts," this refers to a secular official who has received the Bodhisattva precepts. Regarding "Disciple," this refers to one who [takes refuge] in the Triple Gem...

"To act as a Great Master" (*dàshī*) refers to his former position; it means that while he was currently serving as the Governor of Guangzhou and presiding over the Southern Examination (*nánquán*), he pointed out the names of subordinate officials who were actually his former subordinates.
As for "Righteous Counselor" (*zhèngyì*), historical records refer to him as a Righteous Admonisher (*zhèngjiàn*), a member of the censorial office.

"Grand Master" (*dàfū*) means one who greatly upholds the teachings of the world, rectifies social customs and transformation, promotes the upright, removes the crooked, and establishes talented individuals.

The term "concurrent" (*jian*) signifies that both the Secretariat (*Zhongshu*) and the Chancellery (*Menxia*) are internal ministries; these are, in fact, the palaces of the Left and Right Ministers.

However, since the Secretariat primarily manages imperial edicts while the Chancellery primarily issues administrative decrees, Li Rong concurrently held authority over both ministries and was therefore recorded as such.
As for the title "Pingzhangshi," the *Book of Documents* states: "He shall act as the 'Pingzhang' of the people," meaning he shall ensure the equitable distribution of the myriad things.
"Clarifying all affairs and making them manifest is his official duty. Fang Rong was the father of Fang Guan; both father and son served as ministers.

It is said that Rong’s translations were somewhat crude compared to those of Guan. Those who took up the pen to receive the dictation would refine and polish the text if it had become clumsy or unrefined following the oral interpretation.
Since Minister Fang held this dual office within the translation assembly, he [is mentioned] alongside him.
These two masters mutually manifest each other's merits.
Regarding the general principles of the sutra, regardless of its length, they are divided into three sections: first, the introduction; second, the main body;
and third, the dissemination. First, the introduction is explained, which includes both the general and the specific.

Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove Monastery together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, all of whom were great arhats free from outflows.

First, the general introduction is explained because it applies universally to all sūtras; it is also called the "Introduction of Certification and Faith" because it certifies that the Dharma has been transmitted and inspires faith in people.
Formerly, when the World-Honored One was about to enter nirvana, Ānanda asked the Buddha three questions:
first, after the Buddha’s nirvana, upon what should we rely? Second, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, who...
"One should act as the teacher; at the beginning of all sūtras, one should ask three times: 'What words should be placed at the head? The Buddha said:
'After my parinirvāṇa, you should rely upon the four foundations of mindfulness. From this day forward, the Prātimokṣa shall be your teacher.
At the beginning of all sūtras, you should place the words "Thus have I heard" and so forth. Furthermore, after the World-Honored One had passed into extinction, Ānanda ascended..."
While the Buddha sat preaching the Dharma, three doubts arose simultaneously: first, the doubt that the Buddha had been reborn; second, the doubt that a Buddha from another world-system had arrived;

and third, the doubt that Ānanda had transformed his body to become a Buddha. When Ānanda uttered the words "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) and so forth, these three doubts were instantly dispelled.
Therefore, the beginning of every sutra is invariably headed by this formula. "Thus" (*evam*) is a term referring to the Dharma; "I" (*mayā*) refers to the compiler.
These individuals refer to such teachings as having been personally heard from the Buddha and not being their own speculative fabrications;
the term "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) is used because the calendars and systems of reckoning differ between India and China.

Furthermore, "One Buddha" (*eka-buddha*) signifies awakening (*bodhi*), meaning that his own awakening and his awakening of others have brought the perfection of enlightened conduct. Śrāvastī is also known by other names.
Śrāvastī is translated here as "Abundant Virtue," for the kingdom abounds in four virtues, namely: wealth and treasures, the five objects of desire, extensive learning, and liberation.

Jetavana is fully called Jetṛvana; "Jetṛ" means "Victorious in Battle," which was the name given to the Crown Prince of King Prasenajit at birth because his father had defeated foreign nations in war, and thus this beautiful title was established. "Vana" means "grove. Sudatta purchased it by scattering gold.

The "Garden" refers to the Prince’s Forest of Giving (*Jetavana*), which is the *Anāthapiṇḍika-ārāma* monastery; it is also called a "monastic grove" (*vihāra*), as it was established by Anāthapiṇḍika as a place of tranquility.
The term "bhikṣu" (monk) contains three meanings: a mendicant (*bhikṣaka*), one who destroys evil (*bhedaka*), and one who terrifies Māra (*bhīṣaka*).
As for the "one thousand two hundred and fifty persons," these were first those whom he converted, such as the five disciples beginning with Kauṇḍinya, followed by the three... [etc.]
Kāśyapa and his brothers, together with their one thousand disciples, converted Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, each with their own hundred disciples;
they then converted the householder Yaśas and fifty others. Because the scripture cites a general figure, five persons are omitted from this count.
This assembly had previously served non-Buddhist teachers and practiced austerities for many kalpas without attaining anything; they encountered the Tathāgata only just now.

Because they have immediately attained the fruits of sainthood (*āryaphala*), they respond to the Buddha’s grace by constantly following the Buddha’s transformations as his "constant followers" (*anucara*).

"Outflows" (*āsrava*) refers to leaking; there are three such outflows: the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*). Since these three types of leakage are now absent, it is called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).
The term *arhat* contains three meanings: non-arising (*a-bhava*), slayer of thieves (*vīta-rāga*), and worthy of offerings (*dakṣiṇīya*).
The "Great" refers to those who are not of fixed nature, but have turned their minds toward the Buddha Vehicle. This above constitutes the sixfold accomplishment, namely:
faith, hearing, time, master, place, and assembly.

O Son of the Buddha, you abide in the maintenance [of the Dharma] and skillfully transcend all realms of existence; you are able to achieve majestic deportment within the lands and follow the Buddha in turning the wheel of Dharma.

"Wondrously worthy of receiving the final testament, he strictly purifies the *vinaya* and establishes a grand model for the three realms; his response-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) are infinite, delivering sentient beings and rescuing those of the future, transcending all worldly burdens.
This praises his virtues. First, it praises his virtues of self-benefit: "The dweller" refers to one who abides securely in the palace of the Tathāgata; thus says the Sūtra.
It is said that the Tathāgata’s palace is boundless, and the Self-Awakened One dwells within it; "to hold" means to grasp the Dharma-seal of the Tathāgata.
Thus, a sutra states: "By holding this dhāraṇī-heart, one is able to receive the empowerment of the touching of the crown and the bestowal of prophecy throughout the ten directions;

even before one's own fruition is perfected, one shall likewise receive the Buddha's bestowal of prophecy throughout the ten directions. By dwelling in this palace and grasping this seal, one is able [to achieve this].

Because they carry out the commands of the Dharma King and succeed to the throne of the Dharma King, they are called "Sons of the Buddha. Regarding the phrase "skillfully transcending all realms of existence" (*sarvabhava*):
this refers collectively to the places where one takes birth within the three realms—the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the realm of formlessness.

Since the humans and devas of these three realms do not escape the law of cause and effect, they are called "all realms of existence. In the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), transcending the three realms is considered "transcendence," but it is not termed "skillful."
Now, he emerges from the triple world while remaining within it; unlike in former days when he feared the triple world as if it were a prison, he is said to have "skillfully transcended" it.
To praise his merit of benefiting others, it is said that he "tames and matures" beings—this is called "accomplishment" (*siddhi*). To follow them accordingly, it is called "attainment" (*prāpti*).
He possesses a majestic presence that inspires awe and a dignified demeanor worthy of emulation, such as the three thousand modes of deportment and the eight hundred rules of conduct.
The myriad subtle practices can naturally achieve fulfillment for oneself and for others;

that is to say, one manifests various dignified demeanors while remaining in the samādhi of non-arising and cessation, unlike in former times when one was attached to quiescence and refused to bring sentient beings to fulfillment.
"Following the Buddha’s turning of the wheel" means assisting the Buddha in propagating the transformation and turning the Great Dharma Wheel, rather than as it was in former times—merely...
To contemplate emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness while not delighting in preaching the Dharma is what is meant by being "wondrously capable of receiving the final charge.
"Receiving the final charge" means that the Tathāgata entrusts his family legacy to one; "the final charge" means to be entrusted with future affairs.
Since you have now taken up this family legacy and can further make vows to uphold this sutra, it is said you are "wondrously capable," unlike your former inability.

Upon receiving this Dharma, not even a single thought of attachment or delight arises. Regarding "strictly purifying the *vinaya* to establish a grand model for the three realms": *vinaya* here is translated as "subduing.
It refers to the disciplining and training of body and mind to restrain and subdue transgressions and faults; it is precisely the Threefold Aggregate of Precepts (*tri-skandhaka-śīla*).
"Strict" refers to the body and "pure" refers to the mind. As for the ten eyes that look and the ten hands that point, how could one dare not to be strict?
If even a hair’s breadth of thought remains attached to the karmic causes for the three miserable realms, how could one dare claim that these are not impure?
Now, having fully perfected pure and white Brahma-conduct, your words serve as a model for the world and your deeds as a standard for the age;

you are no longer like those of old whose precepts were flawed and who were designated as "name-monks" (naming-ārhats), unable to act as Dharma-teachers within the triple world. Your manifested bodies are infinite, delivering and liberating beings.

Regarding "sentient beings," "delivering" means removing their suffering, and "liberating" means releasing them from their bonds. This means delivering beings according to their various types and liberating them according to their circumstances;
it is not like the practice of days past, which was like tuning a lute while its pegs were glued down—lacking skillful means.

To "rescue those of the future and transcend all worldly burdens" means to extract those who have fallen upon the thorns of false views and to ferry across those who are drowning in the mud of desire.
The roots of defilement drag one toward the dust, and the mind becomes burdened by attachments; now, I cause them all to transcend these states and not fall into the pitfalls.
This vision of compassion extends to the furthest reaches of the future, unlike the past when I acted for my own sake alone, like a gazelle leaping by itself.
Their names were Śāriputra of Great Wisdom, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākauṣṭhila,
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Subhūti, Upāli, and others, who served as the leaders.
This is the enumeration of their names. A name is the guest of reality; therefore, where there is reality, there must be a name. Śāriputra—Śāri meaning "Sparrow" (śārikā)—is his personal name.
His mother was named Śārī because her eyes were as distinct and clear, and as agile and fluid in movement, as a sparrow;
thus he was named after his mother. Maudgalyāyana means "Clan of the Mung Beans" (mudga). His name is Kauṣṭhila.
Lūṭa means "knotless tree" in this language; Mahākauṣṭhila means "Great Thigh.
He was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra, formerly known as the Brahmacārin Dīrghanakha. Pūrṇa means "Full"; his father’s name was Maitrāyaṇī, meaning "Compassionate Mother.
Because his name now combines those of both his parents, he is called Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra. Subhūti says:
When Śūnyatāputra was born, his storehouses were all empty; the diviners said, "This is the sign of one who has realized emptiness (*śūnyatā*);

it is both auspicious and favorable. He is thus named Subhūti (Good Appearance) and Subhūṣita (Good Fortune). Upānanda means "the nature of dust is empty," for he awakened to the nature of form (*rūpa*) among the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
As for the term "foremost" (*agra*), it means "surpassing others"; that is, a gentleman does not desire to surpass many people.
"Among these, 'foremost' means being the head that emerges above all other things; it refers to how each of the Arhats possesses superhuman abilities that place them at the pinnacle of men.
For example: Śāriputra is foremost in wisdom; Maudgalyāyana is foremost in supernatural powers; Kauṣṭhila is foremost in extensive learning;
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra is foremost in preaching the Dharma; and Subhūti is foremost in understanding [emptiness]."
Śūnyatā-agra and others— furthermore,
there were immeasurable Pratyekabuddhas who had attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), along with those at their initial resolve, all coming together at the Buddha’s dwelling;

together with the bhikṣus who had concluded their summer retreat and were performing the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, and the Bodhisattvas from the ten directions who sought to resolve their doubts and respectfully revere the Compassionate and Venerable One, intending to seek the profound meaning.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata prepared his seat and sat in tranquil ease, proclaiming the profound Dharma assembly for those gathered in the congregation.

The pure assembly attained what they had never experienced before. With the *kalaviṅka*-like voice of a seer, [the teaching] pervaded the worlds of the ten directions; Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges assembled at the site of enlightenment, with Mañjuśrī as their leader.
This describes the assembly that has gathered like clouds. *Pratyekabuddha* (辟支) is translated here as "Solitary Realizer" (*dokaku*) and also as "Conditionally Awakened" (*engaku*).
Those who appear in an age without a Buddha and, by observing the transformation of phenomena, personally realize non-arising, are called Solitary Realizers.

Those who appear in an age with a Buddha and, by observing the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*)—both their forward progression and reverse cessation—awaken to non-arising, are called Conditionally Awakened. Their faculties are compared to those of the *śrāvaka*.

"Having heard that [the assembly] was somewhat proficient because they were able to suppress and sever habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), those who have attained the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*)—having truly exhausted all delusions—and those who, from their first resolve, have investigated the truth and severed delusions, all came to the Buddha’s presence; this means they arrived without prior consultation and became close without being invited.
The following section clarifies the purpose of their coming. "Belonging to" (*shǔ*) means it is appropriate for them. "The summer retreat and the *pravāraṇā* ceremony."

When these bhikṣus reach the beginning of the summer retreat, they immediately enter the *varṣā* (the rainy season retreat) to observe the *kaṭhina* and remain secluded; they do not go out to beg for food.

This is called "concluding the summer" (*xiū xià*) and is also known as "sitting in wax" (*zuò lá*). The day for the *pravāraṇā* (the ceremony of self-examination at the end of the retreat) is the day when the period is completed and the restrictions are lifted—namely, the three days of the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth of the seventh month.
Because they have observed the ninety-day seclusion and had no opportunity to visit the Buddha, [they perform this ceremony]...

On the day of concluding the retreat (*pravarana*), if one knows of one's own transgressions, one may freely present them; if one does not know of one's transgressions, they are left to the discretion of the Sangha to raise them.
This is for the purpose of examining the virtue and practice of the ninety-day period. "The ten directions" means that Bodhisattvas do not reside in only one direction.

"Bodhisattva" is translated here as "one who awakens sentient beings. "To inquire" means to seek clarification and resolution, because the mind harbors doubts and obstructions; thus, one makes a request.

To "inquire" means to seek resolution and penetration; it is reverence and it is to receive with deference. To speak with compassion is to gather [the disciples], while to speak with severity is to subdue them;
this refers to the Tathāgata’s possession of these two gates of subduing and gathering, and thus one reverently receives his teachings.

Furthermore, those who seek the profound meaning state that the reason for such reverent reception is not merely to seek resolution of doubts and obstructions, but also to further seek the subtle cultivation and the subtle [realization].

"Realizing the definitive meaning" refers to preaching the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of beings at that very moment. "Spreading seats for peaceful dwelling" means unfolding the sitting mats (*kaṣāya*) and abiding in tranquil repose.
"Proclaiming the profound and abstruse" means expounding the teachings that are deep, secret, and mysterious.
"The Dharma feast" is synonymous with the "Dharma seat," and "the pure assembly" refers to the assembly of those who are pure. "Attaining what has never been attained before" means...
This is to hear what has never been heard before. *Kalinga* is translated here as "the bird of beautiful voice"; because the Buddha’s voice resembles it, he is compared to it.
As for its pervading the worlds of the ten directions: formerly, Maudgalyāyana exhausted his supernatural powers to trace the reach of the Buddha’s voice;

having traversed worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he reached a buddha-field where the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) was exceedingly vast, and the circumference of his alms bowl was as large as a major thoroughfare.
Even as he shook his mendicant’s staff while traveling upon it, the disciples of that Buddha asked their Buddha, "What kind of insect is this that has the appearance of a human?
That Buddha replied, "This is a high-ranking disciple of Śākyamuni from the Sahā world;
you must not underestimate him because of his small size. Thereupon they questioned Maudgalyāyana as to why he had come there, and Maudgalyāyana explained that he had done so to exhaust the Buddha.
The sound of his voice was continuous with the Buddha’s speech; it is said that the Buddha’s voice is inexhaustible and cannot be fathomed by you.

Because [the sound] is continuous, one knows that the Tathāgata’s voice pervades the worlds of the ten directions. That sandalwood-like bodhisattvas come to gather at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is because their minds penetrate the ten directions, and they assemble upon hearing the voice.
Mañjuśrī is here translated as "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode), signifying the fundamental [nature].
Because wisdom is the eye for discerning phenomena, it stands as the foremost.
At that time, King Prasenajit, on the anniversary of his father the king’s death, prepared a vegetarian feast and invited the Buddha to the inner palace;

he personally went out to welcome the Tathāgata and extensively provided rare delicacies and unsurpassed, exquisite flavors, while also personally extending invitations to the great Bodhisattvas within the city.
There were elder householders who simultaneously provided a meal for the Sangha, awaiting the Buddha’s arrival;
the Buddha then commanded Mañjuśrī to lead the Bodhisattvas and Arhats to attend to the various hosts of the feast.
This was the invitation for a meal offering by King Prasenajit—here called "Victorious Army"—the king of Śrāvastī.

His name day is his memorial day; because it is painful for a person’s child to speak of the day their parent passed away, they conceal it and do not dare to mention it, thus making the day of death the memorial day.
Those who prepare the vegetarian feast cultivate merit for the deceased to provide spiritual sustenance.
"The former kings" refers to the inner palace and the left and right wings of the royal residence. "Holding a fast within the inner court" signifies the height of reverence.
"Welcoming [the monks] in person" indicates that they revere the virtue of the Dharma King, setting aside their status as human kings.
"Rare delicacies" means that which is presented; it refers to the fact that the food served consists entirely of precious items from the world, none of which are ordinary.
"Pin" (品) means to invite; "yan" (延) also means to welcome. Having already welcomed the Buddha himself, one further welcomes the Sangha, showing respect for both the teacher and his disciples.
When merit and virtue flourish together, one is called a *changzhe* (elder); when one dwells in purity, one is called a *jushi* (lay devotee).

To provide meals for the Sangha at the same time is for the superior to lead by example so that those below follow. "Zhu" (竚) and "wei" (竢) mean to stand and wait. The Buddha’s instruction to distribute [the offerings] accordingly was to comfort the hearts of the multitude.
The King issued a decree, saying: "The decree of the former Dharma-kings is also called a 'decree. I ask the World-Honored One:
if your emanations are immeasurable, why do you not respond yourself, but instead command Mañjuśrī to lead the response to offerings? What is the meaning of this? The answer was:

"It is to demonstrate conformity with worldly laws, so that there is no mutual displacement of rank. If one were to say that the emanations are immeasurable, then Bodhisattvas and Arhats would each [be separate]."
"Everyone is capable [of this]; why must it necessarily be the World-Honored One?
Only Ānanda had previously accepted a separate invitation and was traveling far away; he had not yet returned and could not attend to the sequence of the Saṃgha.
Since there were neither elders nor preceptors with him, he was returning alone on the road. On that day, there was no alms-food provided, so immediately Ānanda took up his alms-bowl."
As he went on his alms-round through the city in sequence, he first sought out the final donor to serve as his host for the meal,

regardless of whether they were pure or impure, of noble Kṣatriya lineage or of the Caṇḍāla caste. He practiced universal compassion toward all, making no distinction between the lowly and the humble,
resolving to bring all sentient beings to the fulfillment of immeasurable merit.

This is the introductory prologue (*nidāna*), so called because it initiates the sequence of this sutra; it is also termed the "specific prologue" (*pratyeka-nidāna*) because each possesses its own causal conditions for its inception.
Since this sutra takes the accidental fall into a brothel as its point of departure, it first recounts the reasons for that accidental fall:
"Ānanda"—here translated as *Qingxi* (Joy)—was the son of King Droṇodana; he was born on the day the Buddha attained enlightenment and was named Śuddhodana.
When King Śuddhodana heard that the Prince had attained enlightenment, King Droṇodana further announced that a son had been born in the royal palace;

the entire kingdom rejoiced, and for this reason he was named Ānanda (Joyful). He was the younger brother of the Buddha’s paternal uncle. "Having previously accepted a separate invitation" means that before the day of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, one has already accepted an individual invitation from another quarter.
"Not having leisure" (*bùluáng*) means having no opportunity; as the poem says, "I have no leisure to escort my father."
The Arhats normally emerge in a regular sequence, but since Ānanda has now accepted a special invitation and has not yet returned, he is unable to take his place in the order of the Saṃgha.
As for those above him, there is no one; the "Upādhyāya" (Preceptor) is here called the *Ācārya*, meaning a teacher of discipline who is able to correct his disciples.
According to the Vinaya regulations, when monks travel to a distant place, these two teachers must accompany them.
The reason for such strict observance of conduct is to prevent errors and omissions. Now, because there is no second teacher, one returns alone;

because one does not rank among the monastic order, there is no formal offering. Immediately following this, the text describes the practice of impartial compassion regarding the alms bowl as a suitable vessel:
its size should correspond to the amount of food required for oneself. As for "begging in sequence," it means begging from door to door without making any distinctions or selections.
Furthermore, regarding the donor who has never yet fed the Sangha or practiced giving: the very first request for two characters is precisely where Ānanda went astray.
The Sūtra says, "One seeks the wisdom of all Buddhas, yet does not cling to that seeking.

If even seeking the Buddha’s wisdom is not permitted to give rise to greed and attachment, how much less so for one who has not fed the Sangha and yet makes a request without having made an offering? Moreover—
As soon as there is a seeking mind, there is discrimination; once there is discrimination, there is purity and impurity, and there is noble and base.

How could one then view all things with equal vision? The Kṣatriya royal family and the Caṇḍāla butcher family—since you speak of "just beginning to seek" and "only now practicing" universal compassion, it is evident that Ānanda originally had none at all.
This mind arises ultimately because there was no prior provision; the "arousing of the intention" (cittotpāda) is synonymous with "forming the intention" (manasikāra).

Only when one is harmonized, responsive, and attuned can one enter the marketplace and extend a helping hand, practicing compassion with equanimity. What is here called "forming the intention" refers to a state of deliberate effort;
it is not to be compared with a state that is neither thinking nor striving.
Ānanda already knew that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, had rebuked Subhūti and Mahākāśyapa for having minds that were not impartial as arhats,

and that he had praised the Tathāgata’s impartiality in expounding the Dharma without obstruction to dispel all doubts and slanders. Having passed through the moat of that city, he walked slowly toward the city gate,
maintaining a dignified and orderly demeanor, solemnly observing the rules of purity.
This passage describes the act of setting out to beg for alms as being in accordance with the Buddha’s words, rather than arising from personal inclination.

Subhūti abandoned the poor to follow the wealthy, while Mahākāśyapa abandoned the wealthy to follow the poor; one did so because the wealthy give easily, and the other because the poor plant the seeds of merit.
The Tathāgata rebuked their lack of impartiality, as they were motivated by the desire to go to some and not to others.
Because the distribution was equalized among both the poor and the wealthy, it was not equitable. Now, Ānanda, out of reverence for the Tathāgata’s words from the past, has conceived this thought:
first, to elucidate the compassion that is impartial, unobstructed, and free of hindrance;

and second, to prevent the mouths of the multitude from giving rise to doubt and slander. As for those who speak with doubt and slander: if [the alms] were directed exclusively toward poor households, then the wealthy...
Those who doubted him said, "This must be one who uses a deceptive name to beg for alms; he is not a disciple of the Buddha.
If he had gone exclusively to wealthy households, the poor would have slandered him, saying, "This man must be secretly coveting their prestige and power; he is not a disciple of the Buddha.
Ānanda, intending to resolve these doubts and slanders, went from door to door begging in sequence, even at high-ranking mansions where curtains were suspended.
The word "jing" (經) means "to traverse. A moat (*huang*) refers to a waterless area surrounding a city wall; a "guo-men" (郭門) is a city gate.
Those four lines of the verse describe the manner of walking with measured steps while begging for alms, precisely revealing a state where the mind has not yet been fully transformed.
Such conduct may lead one into purity but cannot lead one into impurity; it may lead one into the Buddha [nature] but cannot...
One may be a bhikṣu who has fallen under the influence of Māra, yet not a bodhisattva;
now, to act as a bodhisattva while appearing as a bhikṣu—what difference is there from seeking a roasted owl by shooting at its pellet?

That one does not go so far as to break the tripod legs and overturn the lord’s stew is due to the power of the Tathāgata’s divine mantra. This section explains the causes and conditions; simply read the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
At that time, when the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food, his every action was naturally measured and required no effort;
thus, the inner state of a sage is clearly distinguished, and it is evident that he could not possibly have been advancing like wax.
At that time, while Ānanda was on his almsround, he passed by a brothel where he encountered the great sorceress Matangi,
who, using the *sāvikāra* mantra of the ancient Brahmanic gods, drew him into her bedchamber; there she embraced and caressed him with her own body, nearly destroying his precept-body.
This describes the cause of his accidental fall into a brothel; "on account of begging for alms" refers to the sequence of begging for alms from house to house.
A "magician" (*māyākāra*) is one who transforms non-existence into existence and changes existence into non-existence, using illusory arts to delude the minds and eyes of people.
*Mātanga* means "one of natural disposition"; she was a prostitute. *Śāṇḍakalyāyaṇī* is [the name of] the Golden... (text fragmentary).
The spell transmitted by the non-Buddhist leader Śiva, known as the "Ancient Brahmā," was said to be a divine incantation bestowed by Brahmā in antiquity;
its doctrine was intended to move the hearts of men. As for the seduction of Sundarī into the chamber of lust:

because Ānanda possessed the twenty marks and secondary signs of a Buddha and his complexion was as beautiful as silver, Sundarī conceived a desire for him and subsequently used the power of this spell to capture him and bring him under her influence.
"Lecherous seat" refers to a lecherous body; "caressing and rubbing" refers to one who intends to destroy the essence of the precepts.

This means that by using a lecherous body to press against [Ānanda], he sought to destroy the pure essence of Ānanda’s precepts. Because the Venerable One’s seeking mind had not yet ceased and his mental attention was not yet forgotten, his mind was never at peace.
Seeing how it had never been equanimous, he intended to practice compassion with impartiality, yet in the end he fell into the hands of Māra. Thus it is said.
One who knows non-attainment cannot possibly enter the mud or the water to practice compassion with equanimity.
Zhenjing said: "In the unimpeded interpenetration of phenomena, one acts with sovereign ease: holding a pig's head in hand while reciting the pure precepts in the mouth;
chasing someone out of a brothel without yet having paid his wine debt; untieing the sack at the crossroads—such is it."
Only those whose conduct is upright are worthy of being received by extending a hand; practicing impartial compassion, they enter both the pure and the defiled without any hindrance.
Question: This sutra directly reveals the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama; for what reason does it take the error of falling through excessive learning as its introductory theme? Answer:
Generally speaking, those whose innate faculties are sharp and keen delight in extensive hearing and broad seeing. Once their hearing and seeing have become manifold, [they may fall into error].
Since one cannot attain this Great Samādhi if the mind is not concentrated and the will is not unified, a person of extensive learning was provisionally employed as an initiator.
However, that he inevitably fell into a brothel was because his outflow of desire had not yet been eliminated; even with much learning, it only nourishes the root of craving.
If the outflow of desire were once removed, then all extensive learning would become jewels of wisdom. Thus, the subsequent scripture states:
It is said that if one does not first eliminate the outflows of desire (*kāmāsrava*) while accumulating learning, it will result in error and delusion.

The former masters have also said that while understanding arising from hearing may appear beautiful before one's eyes, if it is harbored for long, it becomes a malady; thus, falling into error through excessive learning is cited as the catalyst [for this teaching].
Question: If this is so, then would all the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*) and twelve divisions (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*) taught by the Tathāgata be without merit?

For what reason does the Sūtra further state that those who hear even a single phrase or a single verse shall all attain Buddhahood, while those who do not understand it are called "Bhikṣus who have heard nothing"?
Answer: If one hears the Dharma and is willing to apply oneself to its cultivation, then even a single phrase or a single verse can lead to Bodhi.
However, if one possesses much learning but does not practice, then the three piṭakas and twelve divisions of the scriptures will merely flow on like surging waves.
Reading extensively only serves to nourish attachment and defilement; therefore, a Great Sūtra says: "It is like a person skilled in prescriptions and medicines who cannot cure his own illness.
Not practicing the Dharma while possessing much learning is just like this. Question: If this is so, then those who cultivate right concentration need not read the sūtras or study the teachings;
they should instead merely abandon the limbs, cast out their intelligence, and preserve their ignorance and simplicity.

Is it appropriate to take this as one's practice? It is said: "If one does not penetrate the teachings of the scriptures, their understanding of the rational nature will not be clear and they will not comprehend meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*).

If they do not even know the path, by what means can they enter? If one takes merely sitting like a log, 'piling up' dead stillness, as one's practice, the ancients condemned such a person as a 'dead man whose soul has not yet dispersed,' one who has fallen into emptiness and non-existence, and an outsider (*tīrthika*). Furthermore, it is said:

How could silent illumination or heterodox Chan ever be acceptable? Therefore, one knows that if the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*) is not yet clear, one must first investigate the scriptures and teachings.
Once the scriptures and teachings are clear, and the path of entry is known, one is then fit to advance in practice.

If the scriptures and teachings are already clear, the methods of Chan contemplation are understood, and the path of entry is known, yet one still clamors with mere words to vie for superiority, refusing to remain in quietude—this is unacceptable.
Venerable Sir, you have rightly established this as a standard for those who take extensive learning as the realization of truth,
not as a standard for those who are dull-witted and ignorant.

The Tathāgata knew that she had employed sorcery, and when the fast was concluded and he returned, the king, along with his ministers, elders, and lay devotees, all came to follow the Buddha, wishing to hear the essential points of the Dharma.
At that time, from the crown of the World-Honored One’s head, there issued forth a hundred-jeweled light of fearlessness;
from within this light, a thousand-petaled jeweled lotus emerged, upon which a transformation-body Buddha sat in the full-lotus posture and proclaimed a divine mantra.

The Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī to take the mantra and go to protect [them], so that the evil spell might be extinguished; he then exhorted Ānanda and Mātaṅgī to return to the place where the Buddha was.
This was the compassionate rescue of the Tathāgata.
It is the Tathāgata’s constant practice to preach the Dharma after the conclusion of the midday meal; since they have now returned so quickly, it must surely be...
Because there is a specific purpose, the king, his ministers, and the great assembly follow him. As for the emission of a hundred-jeweled light of fearlessness from the crown of his head:
this light demonstrates that it possesses every excellence of the most supreme Dharma; thus it is called "hundred-jeweled.
Because it destroys every evil, it is called "fearless light. That within this light a thousand-petaled jeweled lotus arises demonstrates this light of wisdom.
It is the foundation of the myriad practices. As for the manifestation of a Buddha sitting in the full lotus posture, it demonstrates that this light of wisdom is the mother of all Buddhas.
Since the Buddha did not himself recite the mantra but commanded a manifested Buddha to do so, it shows that this heart-mantra is the immovable wisdom;
it must have been spoken by the Immovable Buddha (Aksobhya). The Buddha then charged Mañjuśrī to take the mantra and depart.
Regarding the eradication of evil spells: demonic incantations fundamentally stem from the root of lust.
Since the Buddha has already spoken the spell and further commanded a person of great wisdom to go forth while upholding it, the spell is entirely the person and the person is entirely the spell.
When the power of this spell is applied to the root of lust, it is like hot water dissolving ice or light dispelling darkness; therefore, it causes the fire of lust in Mādrī to be extinguished.
Suddenly, Ānanda’s precept-body was restored to its original state; "urging him to return" means urging and encouraging him to return so that he might see the Buddha.
The Introduction section is concluded.
From here below is the Main Section (Zhengzongfen), which is divided into two major parts: first, the fundamental basis of Bodhi and Nirvana; second...
This is the root of the cycle of birth and death. The first section is further divided into four parts:

(1) the Section on the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*), (2) the Section on the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), (3) the Section on the Path of Realization (*sākṣātkriyāmārga*), and (4) the Section on the Conclusion of the Sūtra. Now, regarding the first, the Section on the Path of Vision:

When Ānanda saw the Buddha, he prostrated himself and wept with grief, lamenting that from the beginningless past he had been devoted solely to much hearing (*bahu-śruta*) without fully perfecting the power of the Way.
He earnestly entreated the Tathāgatas of the ten directions for the original expedient means by which they attained the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* of Bodhi.
At that time, there were also bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as great Arhats from the ten directions.
The Pratyekabuddhas and others, all wishing to hear [the teaching], withdrew to sit silently and awaited the Sage’s instructions.
This was because they had mistakenly fallen [into error] that they requested the Great Samādhi. An ancient attained the "finger-pointing Chan" and used it inexhaustibly throughout his life;
yet Ānanda, though he maintained the Tathāgata’s secret and wondrous adornments through kalpas, could not escape [suffering].

Because of the ordeal with the Mātanga woman, we know that even if one is extensively learned and widely erudite, if one does not truly cultivate and realize the truth, all will fall into the livelihood of a ghost;
and when the wind of external circumstances blows, they collapse at once.

This is entirely because their daily scholarly efforts were excessive while their power of the Way was insufficient, leading them to fall into error and then suddenly give rise to indignation—just like Su Qin’s tattered fur robe.
Upon returning to my hometown, I could not help but prick my thigh to contemplate the Way, aspiring to the rank of high minister;
this regret is the indignant and yearning intent that man cannot be without. This "hate" (regret) is the vanguard for attaining the Dharma-body;
after Ānanda attained enlightenment, he changed his vows because of this one regret. All subsequent weeping of sorrow and self-reproach flow from this very regret.
Regarding the phrase "one who has emerged from a state of exclusively extensive learning but whose power of the Way is not yet complete":

"exclusively" specifically refers to those who simultaneously resolved their minds for enlightenment with Śākyamuni and the Buddha King of Emptiness (*Śūnyarāja*). To enter from the outside is "extensive learning";

to emerge from within is "the power of the Way. An ancient worthy said: "The power of one who enters through language and written characters is shallow; [the power of one who enters from within is profound]."
That which flows forth from within one's own breast is what possesses such great power;
this refers to the earnest aspiration for the fruit of Buddhahood while seeking the causal mind. Bodhi is the fruit of awakening; śamatha and so forth are the causal minds.

If one follows the conventional path, *śamatha* is called "cessation" (*zhi*), *samādhi* is called "equipoise" (*dengzhi*), and *dhyāna* is called "meditative concentration" (*jinglü*). If one follows the Perfect [Teaching]...
Awakening to stillness means that the dissolution of illusions is the meaning of quiescence; if one follows this sutra, it means that the wondrously profound and total retention is immovability.
"Wondrously profound" refers to the essence of this mind, which is wondrously enlightened and limpid, being originally pure.
"Total retention" refers to the essence of this mind, which pervades all things without exception throughout the three categories and seven elements. "Immovable" [refers to its unshakeable nature].
This means that the essence of this mind is a sage when in a sage and an ordinary person when among ordinary people; it does not fall into the categories of sage or ordinary person.

Alternatively, *śamatha* signifies the meaning of immutability, *samādhi* signifies the meaning of following conditions, and *dhyāna* signifies the meaning of being both immutable while following conditions and following conditions while remaining immutable.
Alternatively, *śamatha* is the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, and *samādhi* is... [text fragment ends]
The "Samādhi of the Empty Tathāgatagarbha" refers to both the empty and non-empty Tathāgatagarbha.
This means that although I have long heard of this single mind and its threefold contemplation, I have never awakened to it, cultivated it, or realized it;
thus, failing to attain its function, I have been held captive by the power of Māra and had no way to liberate myself. Only now do I realize that mere erudition has been of no benefit to me.
"However, although I have received the Tathāgata’s prediction that I shall become a Buddha, if I do not cultivate the causes, it will ultimately be difficult to attain the fruit.

Since all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have attained perfect enlightenment by means of these three [practices], I do not know by what means the Tathāgata first attained awakening, nor by what means he attained realization.
Question: Since this sutra requests the exposition of the three contemplations, why [is this said]?"
Regarding these questions: where does this answer *śamatha*, where does it answer *samādhi*, and where does it answer *dhyāna*?
The answer is: if one is at the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), one first analyzes its meaning to bring about understanding.
Thus, from the refutation of the deluded mind and the karmic consciousness, up to the refutation of cause-and-condition, spontaneity, conjunction, and non-conjunction, [one proceeds directly].
To reveal that the nature of wondrous enlightenment is the primordially existent, ultimate, firm, and indestructible essence is the answer to the meaning of *śamatha*.
Furthermore, to clarify that each and every aggregate, sense-base, and element flows forth from within this wondrous enlightened nature and is entirely devoid of self-nature,
thereby revealing that all phenomena are ultimately firm and indestructible, is the answer to *samādhi*.
The meaning further clarifies that the seven great elements are fundamentally illusory in nature yet fundamentally true;
although they manifest according to karma and pervade the entire Dharma-realm, they are primordially pure and have never been moved from that state.

This demonstrates that phenomena are identical to principle, which is the answer to the meaning of *dhyāna*; thus, Ānanda attained awakening through this and praised that the Buddha’s Dharma-body is itself the wondrous.

Zhan is the Honored One of Total Retention and Immovability. Therefore, from the beginning of the fourth fascicle, he revives two questions to clarify the doubts regarding the three categories and the seven elements, concluding with the three Tathāgata-garbhas to manifest that the one mind’s perfect penetration fully contains these three meanings;
thus it is called "wondrous. It is like the *Awakening of Faith*, where the one mind fully contains essence, characteristics, and function.
Therefore, it is called "Great Ear. This means that this very *tathāgatagarbha* mind, when manifest alone apart from the myriad dharmas, is termed *śamatha*;
when present within the myriad dharmas without leaving a trace, it is termed *samādhi*;

and when being both present and apart, yet neither present nor apart, it is termed *dhyāna*. Although there are three names, they are collectively the one perfectly penetrating *tathāgatagarbha* mind.
If, during the stage of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), twenty-five sages each realized perfect penetration through one of the three categories or seven elements,
yet [the Buddha] uniquely selected the single gate of the ear-faculty for deep entry, it was because he took the ear-faculty as the gateway for entering the three *tathāgatagarbhas*.

If, however, this refers to the stage of the Path of Realization (*abhisamayamārga*), then the three *tathāgatagarbhas* themselves constitute the central core of the mind used as the causal ground (*hetubhūmi*).
Flowing into [the stages] until reaching wondrous enlightenment—this again takes the three Tathāgata-garbhas as the awakening of the ground of fruition.
Thus one knows that the path of seeing sees this, the path of cultivation cultivates this, and the path of realization realizes this; there is no other dharma. Question:
The general outline of the three contemplations is already known; as for the initial skillful means mentioned below, to what should it be pointed? Answer: If it is...
The stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) takes the shattering of the mind to reveal true seeing as its primary expedient;

the stage of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) takes the ear-faculty as the gateway as its primary expedient; and the stage of the Path of Realization (*sākṣātkriyā-mārga*) takes the causal mind of non-arising and non-ceasing as its primary expedient.
According to Ānanda’s single question, these constitute the general purport of this sutra regarding seeing and cultivation.

Since the realization of the Way can encompass everything, the subsequent text addresses the following: the portion concerning the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*) answers the subtle *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*;
the portion concerning the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) answers the ear-faculty as the primary expedient;
and the portion concerning the realization of the Way answers how the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attained Bodhi—the meaning being that one desires to obtain the fruit of Bodhi.
Awakening must first enter the subtle state of śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna—the Tathāgata-garbha mind—as the causal ground.
To enter this Tathāgata-garbha mind, one must take the faculty of hearing as the means of practice by turning the hearing inward.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "You and I share the same vital breath, our affection equal to that of siblings.
When you first resolved your mind, what superior signs did you perceive within my Dharma that caused you to suddenly renounce the deep and heavy bonds of worldly affection?"

This was the first instance of thorough examination and insight. Since Ānanda had requested that the three contemplations serve as the cause for attaining Buddhahood, the World-Honored One should have replied directly by asking, "What is śamatha? What is samādhi? What is dhyāna?
Instead of answering in this manner, He instead questioned him regarding where his initial aspiration for enlightenment resided; this was because it was subtle.
This single word "one" (*eka*) is the Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s self-realization, which must not be lightly disclosed to others.
Furthermore, as Ānanda was at the very beginning of his ardent resolve, it was also inappropriate to immediately administer the stern medicine of the Dharma;

therefore, [the Buddha] first probed the source of his illness and spoke gently, saying, "Those who are of the same breath as I, whose feelings are equal to those of the heavenly kin," in order to offer consolation.
In my heart, I thought that even when others inquire, I must disclose everything with full sincerity; how much more so in the case of you, who share the same root and branch as I?
If there were anything I asked about that I did not disclose to you with full sincerity, it would be contrary to the brotherly affection that overflows from my words.

However, regarding your question concerning the primary expedient for attaining enlightenment, I— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly. This translation reflects the complete sentence structure and intent up to that point.)
He then asked you: "If a carriage lacks its three-inch axle-pin, it cannot move;
if a door lacks its three-foot bolt, it cannot be closed. If one does not know the source of an illness, it is difficult to apply the medicine of the Dharma.
Thus, he questioned you back in response to your request. His intention was that in this world, there is no kindness or affection greater than [that of a parent].

"Parents, yet when you first resolved your mind [on awakening] within my Dharma, what did you perceive that you could suddenly renounce your profound kindness and heavy affection all at once to join me and leave the household life? An ancient worthy said:
'The final secure barrier is not separate from the first word. Thus Ānanda asked, and the World-Honored One likewise examined him in this way."
Ānanda said to the Buddha: "I see that the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks are supremely wonderful and peerless;
his physical form is translucent, like lapis lazuli. I have constantly reflected that these marks are not produced by desire and attachment. Why is this?

The vapor of desire is coarse and turbid, a mixture of stench and carnal union, a chaotic confusion of pus and blood; it cannot give rise to such supreme, pure, wondrous, and luminous purple [radiance]."

The *Jinguangji* (Collection of Golden Light) states that one who, out of longing and reverence, follows the Buddha to shave their hair and beard, first sets forth the knowledge and vision of sentient beings.
In my view, when one sees the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks, the act of seeing constitutes the "seeing-part" (*jian-fen*) and the marks themselves constitute the "marked-part" (*xiang-fen*).
These thirty-two [marks] begin with the mark of the invisible crown of the head (*an-wei-ding-xiang*) and end with the mark beneath the soles of the feet.
"Peaceful, secure, supreme, wondrous, and extraordinary" refers to recognizing the thirty-two marks as marvelous.
