To transcend all classes and emerge at the head is called "supreme"; to remain unstained amidst the five turbidities is called "wondrous";
to blend with the multitude of forms yet remain uniquely distinct is called "extraordinary"; to be preeminent among all sages is called "absolute. His physical form is translucent, like lapis lazuli.
That which has length, shortness, largeness, and smallness is called "form" (*rūpa*); the hundred bones, four limbs, and the body are called the "interior";

being transparent and luminous both inside and out is called "penetrating clarity. Therefore, *vaiḍūrya* (lapis lazuli) is used as a metaphor. Ānanda, having been questioned by the World-Honored One once, emptied his entire inner treasury;
yet he was suddenly deprived of his eyesight all at once by the thirty-two marks [of a Great Man]. How could he have known that which sees and that which is seen?
Seeing that all [perceptions] belong to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and are entirely false and illusory, one constantly reflects:

"Below this, from the aspect of perceived characteristics (*nimitta-lakṣaṇa*), the pure and the defiled arise, giving rise to love and hatred; this is adding further illusion upon illusion within what is already illusory.
This, then, is the arising of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) from the dependent nature. Therefore it is said: "These characteristics are not produced by desire and attachment."
Because the energy of desire is coarse and turbid, it cannot give rise to the supreme purity of the translucent lapis lazuli or the wondrous brilliance of the gathered purple-gold light;
thus, upon seeing the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks, they conceived a heart of thirsty longing, forming thoughts of the extraordinary and thoughts of the rare.
Thereupon, they immediately renounced their attachments and loved ones to shave their heads and follow the Buddha—this is the loathing of the coarse and turbid.
To delight in purity and clarity is entirely the mind of consciousness engaging in discrimination and calculation;
how could one know that because the signs of defilement are not forgotten, one is turned by Māra, and because the signs of purity are not forgotten, one is turned by the Buddha?

Although there is a difference between Buddhas and Māras and a distinction between the pure and the defiled, all of it is nothing but the establishment of cognition within knowledge and vision; this is, in total, turning toward objects and turning away from awakening. This is what is meant here by the "signs of seeing."
Among these three subtle states, the "evolving and manifesting" (pravṛtti-vijñāna) and "conceptualization" (manas) constitute the six coarse states; they serve as the initial pulse of this sutra.
Therefore, in the subsequent text, the six coarse states are first refuted, followed by the refutation of the three subtle states, and finally the Tathāgatagarbha-citta is revealed.
Only through this sequential unraveling can the profound purport be seen.

The Buddha said, "Excellent, Ānanda! You and all others should know that all sentient beings have, since beginningless time, experienced the continuous succession of birth and death because they do not understand the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature. By means of various false imaginings—and because these imaginings are not true—there is this cycle of transmigration."
This pair of headings—Reality and Delusion—constitutes the fundamental framework of this sutra. "Excellent! is an expletive of praise;
it means that since you were able to renounce worldly attachment and leave the home life upon seeing the thirty-two marks, was this not a truly decisive act of a great man in the world?
How could anything be more excellent than this? However, this single thought of loathing defilement and loving purity is precisely the "knowledge" of sentient beings.

Seeing that the continuous succession of birth and death arises from these two types of ignorance—namely, the ignorance of "arising" (*pravṛtti-avidyā*) and the ignorance of "moistening" (*āsrava-avidyā*)—and that all of this is rooted therein, [the Buddha] then directly addresses them, saying:
"You all... and so forth. This refers collectively to all sentient beings within the three realms who have not yet transcended the birth and death of the segmented realm (*paricchinna-janma-maraṇa*);
"not knowing" means "not being awakened" (*abodha*) to the eternally abiding true mind, the inherently pure and luminous essence.
It is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision: to remain unchanging amidst turmoil is called "permanence"; to be without coming or going amidst birth and extinction is called "abiding";
to be without decay amidst illusion and falsehood is called "truth"; to be unmoving amidst the myriad dharmas is called "nature";
to be unstained amidst defilement is called "purity"; and to be unclouded amidst the vapors of desire is called "clarity."
I say to you: You possess this essence of mind, supreme, pure, wondrous, and luminous, which is fundamentally coextensive with the Dharma-realm;

yet, instead of turning back toward it, you recognize only the reflected clarity of the Tathāgata’s supreme, pure, wondrous, and luminous physical form as something extraordinary, giving rise to thirsting admiration.
This is to abandon your own numinous tortoise and watch my dangling jaws—what is this if not deluded thought? It is because of you, day after day...
All that you employ daily is merely this deluded thought. This thought is not your eternally abiding true mind;
it is the very root of your birth and death. Because you have mistakenly employed this mind, taking a thief for your son, there is the cycle of birth, death, and transmigration.
Linji said: "The single moment of pure clarity in your mind is the Dharma within your own house."
The Buddha of the Body within a single thought-moment of non-differentiation is the Reward-body Buddha (Sambhogakāya) in your own home;

the light within a single thought-moment of non-differentiation is the Transformation-body Buddha (Nirmāṇakāya) in your own home. These three kinds of Buddhas are none other than you who are listening to the Dharma right now.
Venerable sir, if you do not turn back to reflect upon yourself but instead rush outward in pursuit, it can be said that your karmic consciousness is vast and wandering, without [a clear object].
This may indeed be relied upon.
Now, as you wish to investigate the true nature of the manifestation of unsurpassed bodhi, you should respond to my questions with a straightforward mind.

Because the Tathāgatas of the ten directions follow one and the same path, they all transcend birth and death by means of a straightforward mind; it is because both their minds and words are straightforward.
In this way, from beginning to end, throughout all stages, there shall forever be no trace of deviousness.
Fearing that the Venerable One might have something concealed or withheld in his words, I urge him to speak with a straightforward mind in answering my questions. I say:
since you wish to investigate supreme Bodhi and truly desire to illuminate your own nature, you ought to reveal it with a direct mind.

If you have doubts regarding me, ask directly; if there is a question, answer directly. You must not speak with half-swallowed words or conceal the head while showing only the tail, for to do so constitutes a state of deviousness.
As the former masters said: "The moment you conceive a thought to deliberate, you have already become crooked.
Without conceiving such thoughts, everything is authentically true, and everything is luminously wondrous. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The straightforward mind is the Way."
Because the field is direct, one can transcend birth and death; because it is direct, one can realize Bodhi.

All Buddhas of the ten directions take the direct mind and direct speech as the beginning of the path to enlightenment. When both mind and speech are direct, the internal and external are of one suchness;
thus, one may directly transcend birth and death and directly enter the Ocean of Wondrous Adornments. Therefore, at Mount Tai...

My son, whenever you see someone asking for directions, simply say, "Go straight ahead. If there is even the slightest detour, you fall into the cognitive views of ordinary beings and will encounter the byways of deviation.
As the text below says: "The deluded mind ceases of its own accord; when it ceases, that is bodhi. This is the direct path.
Failing to attain bodhi, one instead becomes a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, or a follower of external paths.

The celestial Māras all represent devious paths; now that you, Venerable One, have distinguished between the pure and the defiled, there are effectively two paths within a single mind, which already constitutes a detour—therefore, I urge you to strive with diligence.
"Ānanda, I now ask you: when you first resolved your mind upon the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks, what did you see that caused you to feel such love and delight?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha: 'World-Honored One, it was by means of my eyes and my mind that I felt such love and delight.
Because I observed these supreme marks of the Tathāgata with my eyes, love and delight arose in my heart; therefore, I resolved to cast off this life.'"

"Death. This is the subtle and discerning knowledge and vision of sentient beings. Since the Venerable Sauti was already in the hands of the World-Honored One, [the Buddha] pressed him firmly upon the mark of his vision.
He then caused him to resolve his mind and turn back to question the point again, seeking to have him himself search for the root of delusion.
"When you first saw the thirty-two marks, what was it that went to see them? When you felt a thirst of longing, who was it that went to love and delight in them?
"Venerable Sir, if one can recognize these two words 'who' and 'what' at this very point, the business of a lifetime of study is finished.
[The Master] asked again, "But how can you fail to distinguish between the monastic and the lay? He answered impulsively, "It is by means of the eyes that I see."

When the mind gives rise to affection and delight, the "eye" refers to the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) and the "mind" refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Seeing with the eye and knowing with the mind constitutes the cognitive vision of sentient beings;
how could they know that the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is called "mind," and that the essential radiance of this mind is "seeing"?
As will be shown extensively below, these teachings do nothing more than overturn the cognitive vision of sentient beings into the cognitive vision of the Buddha.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "What you have said is true; that which you truly love and delight in arises from the mind and the eyes.

If you do not know where the mind and the eyes are located, you will be unable to subdue the dust of worldly toil. It is like a king who, having been invaded by bandits, dispatches an army to eliminate them;
that army must first know the location of the bandits. It is the mind and the eyes that cause you to wander in saṃsāra—this is the fault."
"I now ask you: where do this mind and these eyes currently reside?
This subtle examination is for the sake of knowing the place from which the perceptions of sentient beings arise.

Because Ānanda identified the seer as the eye and the lover as the mind, failing to realize that birth and death and their inversions are fundamentally rooted in this, the World-Honored One accordingly [addressed him]."
Pressing him further on the origin of that [recognition], he said: "Since you have identified the one who delights in the thirty-two marks, that is the mind;
and since it is that which sees the thirty-two marks, that is the eye. You have already been captured by the thief.
For example, when a country is invaded by bandits and an army is dispatched to eliminate them, one must first know the place where the bandits rely, and then block their path of retreat."
If you cut off their provisions, raze their nests, and take their heads, then the borders will be cleared and the alarms of war will naturally cease.

Now, your cycling through birth and death does not depend on external things; it is fundamentally caused by the malevolent influence of your own kinsmen and the plundering of your own family treasures.
If you wish to eliminate them with the divine soldiers of the Three Contemplations, you must first know them.
He interrogated him regarding his location, saying: "Where now are this eye that can see and this mind that can know? Where do the eye and mind reside?

This was the second round of careful inquiry. Because the Venerable’s illness was deep-seated and profound, the World-Honored One thoroughly investigated the source of the ailment one by one until it was clearly understood; only then did he prescribe medicine according to the specific malady.
[Ānanda] said, “Yes. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, all ten types of ordinary beings in the world likewise maintain that the consciousness-mind resides within the body;
even when observing the Tathāgata’s blue-lotus eyes, they are seen to be on the Buddha’s face. Now, as I observe this floating [image]...”
The sense organs and the four sensory objects reside only upon my face, yet this consciousness-mind truly dwells within the body.
This is the Venerable One’s first presentation of the "spear method," asserting that the mind resides within.

As for the "ten types of ordinary beings," among the twelve classes of living beings, those who are dispersed in space or in the state of non-conception are excluded, because they lack the dual characteristics of both body and mind; thus, the term "consciousness-mind" is used here.
The consciousness refers to the "blue lotus eye" because the Tathāgata’s eyes are pure, refined, and broad like a blue lotus.

The "floating roots of the four objects"—that is, the coarse and superficial sense organs composed of visible form, odor, flavor, and tangibility—are called "floating-dust roots" in contrast to the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
This means that from ordinary beings up to the sages, none have the eyes outside while the mind remains inside.
"I would rather not know that the eye is outside while the mind truly dwells within the body.
Although you, Venerable Sir, possess such clever and sharp wit as if no one else existed, you do not realize that the crown of your head has already touched the ground.
If a child of only three feet were asked about the mind right now, they would immediately point to their chest with a finger and say, 'It is inside.'"
From the very beginning of receiving a physical form within the womb of one's parents, by absorbing the two drops of red and white, this attachment arises;
it exists spontaneously without waiting for instruction, and is thus called "innate ignorance" (*sahaja-avidyā*) or "solidified delusion.
Therefore, one firmly clings to this body as the dwelling place of the mind, like a goose in a jar or a frog in a well, never [realizing its true nature].
One can emerge from it, yet remains unaware that the body has returned to dwell within the mind—like a single bubble in the great ocean;
this is the great delusion of sentient beings. Thus, even the Venerable One shared this same calculation.
Had the Venerable One been asked where the mind and eyes reside, had he recognized the fundamental point (*di-tou*), he would have walked hand-in-hand with the World-Honored One as an equal.
Wandering in the ocean of awakening, how could there still be the various deluded attachments described in the subsequent passages?
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "You are now sitting here in the Tathāgata’s lecture hall looking at the Jeta Grove; where is it now? [Ānanda replied:
"World-Honored One, this great multi-storied pavilion and pure lecture hall is in Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden; the Jeta Grove is indeed right here."
“Ānanda, what did you first see within this hall just now? “World-Honored One, within the hall I first saw the Tathāgata, and next I observed the great assembly.
“Thus looking outward, I beheld the groves and gardens from afar. “Ānanda, by reason of what do you behold the groves and gardens?
“World-Honored One, because the doors and windows of this great lecture hall are wide open, I am able to see them from within the hall at a distance.”
Beholding him,
the Venerable One held his mind within with absolute certainty, like a strong man bracing his spirit as it surges upward toward the Ox and Dipper constellations;
the World-Honored One, being one of all-encompassing wisdom, perceives the innermost depths of the heart without needing to analyze phrases, dissect sentences, or elaborate upon the text.
The topical outline proceeds by using immediate, shallow, and easily understood matters to interrogate the student, forcing them to answer with their own mouth so they have no place to evade;
it then uses the "Dharma Cave" and "Dharma Claws" to capture them alive.
Thus, one first examines and determines internal and external objects, as when the Venerable One replied, "I am now in the hall," or "I am in the forest."

Since the forest is outside the hall, it was said, "This is great," and so forth. Next, he again examined the sequence of priority and saw that the Venerable One’s answer revealed seeing the interior first and then the exterior.
A third time, he examined the cause for seeing the exterior, and the Venerable One’s answer revealed that one sees the exterior because doors and windows are open.
The World-Honored One asked three times, and the Venerable One likewise responded three times in succession.
Each of the three turns of speech falls into the net of the World-Honored One’s own elaborations;
he then uses those very words to refute them—what is called "using your own spear to pierce your own shield."
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, extended his golden arm and stroked the crown of Ānanda’s head, informing Ānanda and the entire multitude:

"There is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which fully encompasses the myriad practices and serves as the wondrously adorned path through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend in a single gate. Listen attentively now! Ānanda prostrated himself in reverence.
I humbly accept your compassionate instruction.
This prior demonstration of the essence of the three contemplations serves as the foundation for opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
When Ānanda first asked about the initial expedient means of the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*, the World-Honored One instead questioned him regarding that very [foundation].
At the beginning of his resolve, [the Buddha] examined Ānanda’s understanding to see whether it was true or delusory;
yet Ānanda instead used his conscious mind to grasp at the Tathāgata as having visible marks, thereby becoming confused about his own True Buddha, which is formless and invisible.
The Tathāgata further interrogated him regarding the conditions for the thirty-two marks: "By what do you see them, and by what do you take delight in them?"
The Venerable One replied that he saw with his eyes and delighted with his mind; the Tathāgata then further interrogated him regarding the place from which the mind and eyes arise.
The Venerable One stubbornly insisted that this mind resides within the physical body.
At this point, Ānanda’s thieving person has been exposed and the thieving object remains present without concealment; now, wishing to advance and destroy it, [the Buddha] first...
He pointed it out to him, saying: "There is a samādhi... and so forth. The meaning is that this Great Buddha-Crown is all-pervasive and inclusive;
there is no dharma it does not contain and no practice it does not perfect. It cannot be known by wisdom, nor can it be seen by vision.
It is the father of the bodhisattvas and the mother of all Buddhas; even my thirty-two marks are all within this.
Since this reflected image is manifested externally, why do you instead recognize it as being within your physical body?
Now, if you wish to investigate supreme Bodhi and open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, you must first recognize this Unseen Summit (uṣṇīṣa).

Then, without practicing *śamatha*, *śamatha* will spontaneously arise; without practicing *samādhi*, *samādhi* will spontaneously arise; and without practicing *dhyāna*, *dhyāna* will spontaneously arise.
Dhyāna is called the Samādhi of True Suchness and is also named the Samādhi of Single Practice. When a Bodhisattva attains this samādhi, all myriad practices are perfected;
in every thought-moment they can realize the true and eternal, and in every encounter they can reach the ultimate.
It is also called the King of the Śūraṅgama, for the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend the wondrous through this single gate.

When the ocean of fruition is adorned, one does not encounter bypaths nor further deviousness; so how could one suffer from the fault of hoarding learning or the incompleteness of the power of the Way?
Thus, an ancient worthy said: "The source of the Way is not far, the ocean of nature is not distant;
simply seek it within yourself and do not look for it elsewhere. If you seek it, you will not find it; even if found, it would not be real. This being so, if one desires—
To investigate unexcelled Bodhi, this is the very first step to be taken.

If one wishes to accomplish this task, one must take a single gate as the initial expedient means, for this one gate is the great highway for entering the Sublime Adornment—what is called "the one path to Nirvana.
The seven successive refutations in the following text are all intended to reveal this.

I reveal this meaning, yet I regret that the Venerable One, by attempting to fathom the Tathāgata’s "Crown Dharma" with a mind of discursive thought, remains separated by the inner wall and ultimately fails to see it. Question:
Why is it that *śamatha* and *dhyāna* are not mentioned here, while only *samādhi* is singled out? Answer: This *samādhi* is precisely what is referred to below as the "Great Dharani Gate."
All samādhis are the sublime path of wondrous cultivation; through śamatha one awakens to them, and through dhyāna one realizes them.
Therefore it is said: "The samādhi that is like an illusion allows one to transcend the stage of no-more-learning in the snap of a finger.
Since there is no other path of cultivation apart from this single gate, the World-Honored One focused his attention upon samādhi, and thus [the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*] consists of twenty-five [chapters].
All sages enter by this very path; thus the ancient Avalokiteśvara Tathāgata was also said to have "entered samādhi through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation.
This is because within the Tathāgata-garbha lies the Great Dhāraṇī, for it is the Tathāgata-garbha itself.
Dinglin says: "Touching the crown of the head" is a caress to demonstrate affection; "prostrating at the feet" is a submission to demonstrate reverence. It is because the superior loves the inferior.
[The Buddha] stroked [Ānanda’s] head; because one shows respect to a superior, one bows at their feet.

The Buddha told Ānanda, "As you have said, while the body is in the lecture hall and the doors and windows are wide open so that one can look far out at the groves and gardens, there may also be sentient beings within this hall who do not see the Tathāgata but do see those outside the hall. Ānanda replied:
"It is impossible, World-Honored One, that one who does not see the Tathāgata within the hall could see the groves and springs outside; such a thing cannot be.

Ānanda, you are also like this. Your spiritual mind is all-encompassing and clearly aware. If the mind that is currently clear and aware were truly inside your body, then it should first perceive the interior of the body.
Is there any sentient being who first sees what is within the body and only afterwards observes what is outside?"

If external objects cannot be seen [by the mind], yet the liver, heart, spleen, and stomach are visible, and the nails grow, the hair lengthens, the tendons turn, and the pulses throb—all of which should be clearly perceived—how is it that you do not know them?
If you certainly do not know what is within, how can you know what is without?
Therefore, you should know that your claim that the perceiving, cognizing mind dwells inside the body is impossible.
This refutation of the deluded mind shows that it does not exist within. As in the passage "As you [said] below," he first restates the previous words;
then, with "There is also... below, he again examines what was seen. From "Ānanda" below, he falls into his own trap three times.

Below this, the World-Honored One does not set up a separate furnace or hearth, but rather borrows the staff already at hand to strike him. The meaning is that [the mind] is not seen within the hall, as if...

It is simply impossible that you could see the forests and springs; what you are currently calculating is merely like being inside a hall and not seeing the Tathāgata, yet claiming to see the forests and springs outside. Therefore it is said: "You are also like this.
If your numinous mind of knowing is at the gates of the six sense-faculties—vividly unclouded and clearly and constantly aware—then such clarity is manifest before you.

The consciousness that realizes this truly exists within the body; at that time, one should first perceive the internal viscera and organs, and only thereafter observe external objects, so that the dharma and the analogy may correspond.
Is there any sentient being who first sees their own viscera and only afterwards observes external objects?
Even if one cannot see its depths, one must at least see its surface; how could it be otherwise?
Do you not understand this at all? If within your spiritual mind you do not see the heart, liver, spleen, or stomach, and within your body you do not see nails growing,
hair lengthening, tendons moving, or pulses throbbing, yet you can still see forests and springs from the outside—
how does this differ from being inside a hall and not seeing the Tathāgata or the great assembly, yet being able to see forests and springs from the outside?
Why is it otherwise? Therefore, it is said: "One certainly does not know within. The two words "How can one know without?
are a rhetorical question intended to serve as the basis for what follows.
Ānanda’s method of inquiry had reached this point when he was completely overwhelmed by the World-Honored One. Thus, the conclusion below refutes that [cognition] does not reside within.
Ānanda bowed his head to the ground and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have heard such teachings from the Tathāgata and realized that my mind truly dwells outside the body. Why is this so? It is like a lamp burning within a room:

that lamp must first illuminate the interior of the room, and only after passing through the door of the room does it reach the courtyard. Yet all sentient beings do not see their own bodies from within."
If one perceives only that which is outside the body, like a lamp placed outdoors that cannot illuminate the interior of a room, this principle must be clear and free from delusion;
would it not be equivalent to the Buddha’s definitive meaning (nītārtha), and thus free from error?

This second [position] holds that the mind exists externally. This was taught by the World-Honored One as a conventional teaching for those who cling to the view that phenomena exist outside the mind, stating that "the three realms are mind-only" and that "sentient and insentient beings share the same dharma-nature. The Venerable [Xuanzang], being of sharp and keen intellect, understood immediately upon hearing this.

He realized that if one knows what is internal, how can one know what is external? These two statements—negating the former habit and shaking it loose—were intended to overturn his long-standing attachments.

Because one abandons the internal and grasps the external, it is said, "Thus have I heard," and so forth. Below, an analogy is cited to specifically establish that one sees the external but does not see the internal:
it is like the light of a lamp exiting from the door of a room and reaching the courtyard; thus, it can see the external.
Likewise, just as the light of a lamp outside cannot illuminate the interior of the room, one does not see the internal. This is the meaning.
Since this is decisively clear and free from doubt, it is identical to the definitive discourse (*nītārtha*) of the Tathāgata;
as it is necessarily without error, it is said that it is identical to the Buddha’s definitive teaching and is thus free from falsehood.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "These bhikṣus have just now returned from begging for alms-food in the city of Śrāvastī and have come back to the Jeta Grove.
I have already finished my meal; you observe whether when one bhikṣu eats, all these people become satiated.
Ānanda replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Although these bhikṣus possess the bodies of arhats..."
The destinies of beings differ; how can one person cause a multitude to be satiated?
The World-Honored One is a great master of skillful means: if one approaches from the left, he turns to the left; if from the right, he turns to the right.
Whether from this side or that, there is nothing he will not accept; whether within or without, everything may be swept away. He also provides a parable in response to this.
This refers to the principle of "plum for plum and pear for pear," or "returning a cow for a horse. Therefore it is said:
"All these types of edible food have physical form and can be grasped. "To dwell" means to stay overnight. When one person eats, do all people become satiated?
This is an inquiry as to whether by that person eating, others can be satiated; the answer is "no," referring to those Arhats.
Although the fetters of the individual (pudgala-bandhana) have been exhausted, the fetters of the fruit (phala-bandhana) still remain;

thus, one cannot merge with the multitude into a single body—how then could one person eat and cause the multitude to be satiated? Observing this response, the Venerable’s calculation is once again disjointed.

The Buddha said to Ānanda: "If the mind that perceives, knows, and sees were truly located outside the body, such that the body and mind existed externally to one another and were mutually unrelated, then what the mind knows the body could not perceive, and what the body perceives at its own boundary the mind could not know.
I shall now show you my hand of Tūlasi-cotton; when your eyes see it, does your mind discern it? Ānanda replied: [Yes.]
Thus the World-Honored One said to Ānanda: "If they were mutually cognizant, how could it be that [the object] is outside?
Therefore, you should know that your claim—that the mind capable of awakening and knowing resides outside the body—is impossible."
This directly refutes the notion that the mind does not abide within. If the body and mind were external to one another, then each would be entirely unrelated to the other;
thus, what the mind knows, the body could not perceive, and what the body perceives, the mind could not know.
Only when they are joined as a single entity do their functions differ. To verify this through an experiment, I shall now demonstrate the actual relationship between the body and the mind.
"Externally obstructed" means that *tūla*—here translated as "fine fragrant cotton"—is in color like hoarfrost, and the Buddha’s hand is like it.
This describes how the eyes see something and the mind immediately gives rise to discrimination; this is knowing through mutual correspondence rather than through external separation.
The Buddha says: "With one single push, it turns over; there is no need for further effort. Therefore, the conclusion is that the breaking [of delusion] does not reside in an external location.
Ānanda lit a paper lamp to see the World-Honored One, but it was suddenly extinguished by the World-Honored One’s single breath.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has said, because one does not see the internal, one does not dwell within the body."
"Because the mind and its objects are mutually dependent and inseparable, it does not exist outside the body. As I now contemplate, I know it must reside in one specific location.
The Buddha asked, "Where, then, is that location? Ānanda replied, "This cognizant mind does not know what is within, yet it can see what is without.
As I ponder this, it seems to be hidden within the sense organs, just as if someone were to take a crystal bowl and place it over both eyes."
Although objects may come together with them, they do not obstruct those faculties; as soon as one sees, one immediately discriminates.

Yet, when I am aware and able to know, this mind does not see within because it resides in the faculties; while it gazes clearly at the external without obstruction, it remains hidden within the faculties.

This third hypothesis concerns the latent root (*mūla*). This hypothesis also arises when the World-Honored One speaks of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), stating that consciousness arises from four conditions and that the sense organ (*indriya*) serves as the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).

Upon hearing the words, "Because these seeds exist, as soon as one hears or sees, the mind gives rise to discrimination," [the opponent] immediately leaps up and proposes this alternative theory of the latent root; thus it is said: "That root follows along with seeing."

This refers to discrimination (*vikalpa*) and latency (*saṃvṛti*). "Root" (*indriya*) refers to the ultimate sense-faculties (*paramārtha-indriya*), which are inferred as roots because they can give rise to consciousness;

one does not realize that this mind itself is the fundamental root from which all phenomena arise. One falsely imagines that the root gives rise to the mind, while the mind remains latent within the root.
This is like the following analogy used to establish one's own attachment: the *vaiḍūrya* gem is used as a metaphor for the eye.

The eye is further likened to the mind: just as a crystal placed over the eye does not obstruct the eye’s vision, so too the mind-root (cakṣur-indriya) joined with the mind does not obstruct the mind’s seeing.
Now, the following passage explains why one sees the external but not the internal, which is entirely due to the fact that the sense-organ is concealed.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "As you have said, that which is submerged within the roots [of the eyes] is like lapis lazuli;

that person should see mountains and rivers through eyes encased in lapis lazuli. "No, World-Honored One," Ānanda replied, "that person would not actually see lapis lazuli through eyes encased in lapis lazuli.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "If your mind were fused with the lapis lazuli in this manner..."

When you see mountains and rivers, why do you not see your own eyes? If you could see your eyes, the eye would be identical to its object, and the principle of "following" (the subject perceiving the object) could not be established.
If you cannot see them, how can you say that this cognizing mind resides hidden within the sense organs like glass?
Therefore, you should know that your claim that the awakened, cognizing mind dwells inside the roots like glass joined [to them] is untenable.

Trampling upon emptiness, the World-Honored One scrutinizes even the finest details to search out people's shortcomings, saying:
"In the analogy, the eye sees both the mountains and rivers and also sees the lapis lazuli. In the Dharma, since it is the mind that sees the mountains and rivers, it should also see the eye.
Why does it not see it? If the mind were able to see the eye, then the eye would instead become an object of perception for the mind."
If it is not the faculty that produces [cognition], then your reckoning—that the faculty follows the seeing and immediately performs discrimination—cannot be established;
this commits the fault of contradicting your own words. Furthermore, if the mind does not see the eye, you commit the fault of the example and the principle being inconsistent.
Thus, since both [positions] are untenable, how can you reckon that [the faculty] lies hidden within the root?
Just as when two pieces of lapis lazuli are joined, the point of contact is invisible; likewise, the conclusion here is that the "breaking" does not reside within the sense organ.
Furthermore, when Ānanda held out his lapis lazuli bowl to compete with the World-Honored One in a contest of wealth, it was again shattered by the World-Honored One into fine powder.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, I have now further reflected as follows:

within this sentient being’s body, the internal organs reside inside while the orifices are situated on the outside. Where there are organs, there is darkness; where there are orifices, there is light.
Now, when I face the Buddha and open my eyes to see light, I call this ‘seeing the external’; when I close my eyes and see darkness, I call this ‘seeing the internal. What is the meaning of this?”

This fourth pair of positions calculates both the internal and the external. This was also stated by the World-Honored One when discussing the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), because he said that the eye can see light and can also see darkness.
Upon hearing this, the Venerable One [Vasumitra] immediately concluded that the eye cannot be established as having a single object;
he then maintained the two-fold statement and calculated that the faculty (*indriya*) can see both light and darkness, thereby seeing the internal and seeing the external.

Wu Xing of the exterior [tradition] says: First, he calculates that [the faculty of sight] is within; however, because one cannot see the internal viscera, this is refuted. Next, he calculates it is outside;

yet this again invites the difficulty of the body and mind being separated. Furthermore, he calculates it is hidden within the roots [of the eyes]; but this contradicts the analogy of the crystal cage over the eyes.
This is truly because if there were a covering, there would be darkness. When one sees in the dark, it is called "seeing within"; it does not necessarily require [the organ] to be inside.
Because one perceives that the heart, liver, spleen, and stomach have apertures, one is clear; thus, when one perceives clarity, it is called "seeing the external.
There is no need to demand that the body and mind be outside [the eyes]. If internal and external were established in this way, then they would not be solely hidden within the roots.
If this were so, one might avoid the three aforementioned faults; however, since it is not known whether this principle is appropriate or not, it is said: "This is..."
As for the meaning: what is called "doubt in the center" results in rambling speech.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "When you close your eyes and see darkness, is this realm of darkness facing the eye or not facing the eye?
If it faces the eye, the darkness is in front of the eyes; how then could it be 'internal'? If it were internal,"
If you are in a dark room where there is no sun, moon, or lamp, this darkness within the room is entirely your own internal organs;
if you do not face it, how can seeing be established?
This destruction of the darkness of seeing is called "seeing internally. You should now simultaneously open both gates to examine and determine this for yourself.
The following section is the formal refutation: If this characteristic of darkness were to face the eye, then this characteristic of darkness would be in front of your eyes;
how could it then be established as "seeing darkness by closing the eyes" and called "seeing the internal"?

Even if you grant that the characteristic of darkness, though in front of the eyes, could still be established as being "internal," then for anyone dwelling in a dark room where there is no light—this...
If all dark rooms were to consist entirely of your three *jiao* and six *fu*, that would be illogical.
If this appearance of darkness does not face the eye, then this eye should not encounter the darkness; how then can one see darkness before the eyes?
Thus, whether the eye faces the darkness or does not face it, neither case is established internally.

If, apart from external views, one forms an internal correspondence such that with eyes closed one sees darkness—this is called seeing within the body—and with eyes open one sees light, why does one not see one's own face?
If one does not see one's face, an internal correspondence is not established.

If this were established, one would realize that the mind and the eye faculty, as well as even empty space, must exist within [the body]. Yet, if they were in empty space, they would not be your own body.
If it were so, then the Tathāgata seeing your face now would also be your own body; your eyes would already know the body, and the body would lack sensation.
If you insist that both the body and the eyes possess sensation, there must be two cognitions; thus, your single body would become two Buddhas.
Therefore, you should know that your claim that seeing darkness is called "seeing within" is impossible.
This is an example of granting [the opponent's premise] only to refute it: it demonstrates that seeing darkness does not constitute seeing the interior. To grant the point:

even if one allows that this appearance of darkness is not outside but within, and allows that when one sees darkness with eyes closed, it is called "looking back" (reversing the gaze) into the body—then by the same logic, when opening the eyes to see light, one should likewise be able to look back at one’s own face. If, when opening the eyes...
If one cannot turn back to observe one's own face, then even when the eyes are closed, one cannot turn back to observe within the body; therefore it is said:

"If you do not see the face, internal reflection is not established. If you claim that when the eyes are open and seeing light, you can also see the face, then your eyes and mind would both reside in empty space, and thus the notion of "internal" as being the turning back to observe within the body could not be established.
"It is so. If the mind-eye were already within empty space, then empty space itself would be your body, and your own physical body would, conversely, no longer belong to you.

If you claim that although the mind-eye is in space, one still sees one's own face and it is still one's own body, then when the Tathāgata now sees your face, would the Tathāgata’s body also be your body? Furthermore, you—"
If the mind-eye is already conscious within the void, then this body of yours ought to be without consciousness.

If you insist that the body itself possesses sensation while the eye in the void also possesses cognition, then your single body would have two cognitions—one in the void and one in your own person. Since there are two cognitions, you [would be] two.
Is it logical that the body should become two Buddhas? When one investigates and pursues this line of reasoning to its conclusion, such a "both-and" argument collapses like ice melting away.
Therefore, the final summary concludes that the refutation does not lie in either the internal or the external;

to calculate both the internal and external simultaneously further reveals Ānanda’s cleverness—what is called "cleverness entangling the principle and brilliance injuring the Way"—which the World-Honored One has now refuted.
Abiding like the butcher Ding who dissects an ox, moving with the hand without striking a single sharp edge;
thus it is said: "All manner of supports and standards require effort; when everything follows along naturally, skillfulness is achieved. As the former masters said:
"If you wish to know where the Buddha goes, it is simply this very sound. This being so, the knowing mind that is capable of this resides within the body and has never [departed].

It is not as if one were to say that heaven and earth share a single root and all things are of one substance, or that the three categories and seven elements are all *tathatā* (suchness), and thus reckon that what lies outside the body has never failed to be suchness. Rather, it is like saying: "Observe this assembly of noble ones;
as you survey them with your eyes, your gaze moves across them like reflections in a mirror, without any further differentiation. Your consciousness follows within this."

If one points to the finger and calculates that the hidden root has never not been thus, or says that seeing darkness and seeing light means the nature does not shift or change, then calculating both the internal and external is likewise never not correct.
Yet, because Ānanda clings to traces and gives rise to emotional attachments, every sentence of his questions becomes a sickness;
and because the World-Honored One unties bonds according to the situation, every sentence of his answers becomes medicine.
The Venerable Yaogude said: "If you can realize it, even dead words become living words; if you cannot realize it, even living words become dead words.
The miraculous and divine transforms into putrid decay, and putrid decay transforms back into the miraculous and divine. Truly, there is no fixed dharma.
These four preceding reckonings all stem from the World-Honored One’s single phrase, "How do you know the external? which acted as a hook that stirred Ānanda.
Therefore, the Venerable One abandoned one [view] and clung to another; that is to say, those who merely receive the words lose the meaning, while those who stagnate in the phrases become deluded.

Regarding the latter three calculations, once his knowledge and views were exhausted, he again drew upon the profound meanings of the nature and characteristics (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*) spoken by the World-Honored One, extending the vines and sprouting branches to recklessly produce conceptualizations.
He impudently presumed that if this were correct, it was all correct, and if this were incorrect, it was all incorrect.
"No, it is not so. Ānanda said, "I have often heard the Buddha reveal to the fourfold assembly that because the mind arises, all manner of dharmas arise;
and because dharmas arise, all manner of minds arise. Now, as I contemplate this very essence of contemplation, I realize it is truly my own mind-nature that follows along [with these states]."
Wherever the mind conjoins, it follows that it exists there; yet it does not reside in any of the three locations—internal, external, or in between.
This fifth hypothesis holds that the mind resides wherever it happens to conjoin.

Because Ānanda saw that the World-Honored One was successively refuting each position, he first cited what the World-Honored One had previously said as evidence, intending thereby to silence the Tathāgata.
How could one know that the Tathāgata’s entire body is a sword, such that to touch it is to die instantly, with no room for mercy?

That mental phenomena arise from the mind precisely means that both mind and objects arise through transformation from the *karmic consciousness* (*ālayavijñāna*), appearing simultaneously as delusions like two bundles of reeds leaning against one another.
It is not that the mind can produce objects; rather, there are no objects apart from the mind, and no mind apart from objects.
The Venerable One has erred in asserting that objects can produce the mind by claiming that the arising of mental phenomena must necessarily be so.
Therefore, I shall now set forth my own correct view. I reflect upon what the World-Honored One taught regarding the arising of mental phenomena from the mind:
that which is capable of this reflection is truly my own mind-nature; this mind, in accordance with [its conditions]...
If one phenomenon were to arise in conjunction with another, it would simply follow that specific phenomenon and would not be fixed in locations such as the internal or external;
this is for the Venerable One to measure the minds of others by his own mind, thereby turning the finest cream into poison.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "What you have just said—that because dharmas arise, various kinds of mind arise, and that wherever they meet, the mind follows—is based on the premise that this mind has no substance.

If it had no substance, then its meeting with anything would be impossible. If something could meet with another while lacking substance, then the nineteenth element would be formed by the meeting of the seven particles;
such a principle is not tenable. If, however, it does possess substance, then consider, for example, when you use your hand..."
"Strike your own body. As for this mind that you know, does it emerge from within, or does it enter from without? If it emerged from within, you would see what is inside your own body;
if it came from without, you should first have seen its face."
This is precisely to refute the mind’s failure to conform to conjunction. World-Honored One, it is like Jīvaka grasping grass;

there is nothing that is not medicine, for wherever his hand reaches, the illness is cured. Therefore, I refute [the notion of conjunction] by means of both having a substantial entity and lacking one.

As for conjunction, it is like a lid fitting a box; it must be that both possess a substantial entity before they can join. Now, the mind of which you reflect is fundamentally but a floating thought and is truly [unreal].
Since there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and because there is no intrinsic nature, there is no locus for conjunction.

If one were to claim that things lacking intrinsic nature can nevertheless conjoin, then the nineteen elements (*dhātu*) and the seven objects (*viṣaya*) should also possess conjunction; since this is not the case, it is said that [your position] is incorrect.
If something possesses intrinsic nature, it must necessarily have a point of origin; if it has a point of origin, it must necessarily involve entering and exiting. If...
"Coming and going must involve both the internal and the external; since there are already both internal and external, how could one avoid repeating the same error as before?

How could seeing arise in accordance with each [condition]? Ānanda said, "Seeing is the eye, while mental cognition is not the eye; therefore, it is illogical for seeing to be the eye. The Buddha said, "If the eye were able..."
If one could see you while you were inside the room from outside the door, then all those who have already died would still possess their eyes and should therefore all see objects;
if they do see objects, how can they be called dead?

Because the foolish Śrāvakas do not distinguish between the faculties (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), upon hearing the statement that "one sees internally," they instead give rise to doubts and objections, thinking:
"The mind may be called 'knowing,' but the eye may be called 'seeing. Now, to take the mind as 'seeing' seems inconsistent with the meaning. This is what is meant by the saying:
"A barbarian drinking milk, yet instead finding fault with the skilled physician. The World-Honored One, whether [the capacity] be short or long, accommodates it accordingly.
"High follows low; the samādhi of the mouth is brought forth. Thus he answers by citing two successive metaphors.

First, Ānanda is used as a metaphor for the mind, and the door as a metaphor for the eyes. Although the middle door is open and allows for seeing, seeing can only occur if there is someone inside the room.
If there is no one inside the room, how could the door itself see? Likewise, although the eyes in the Dharma are...
Generally speaking, for seeing to occur, there must first be consciousness; if there were no consciousness, how could the eye see?
This precisely demonstrates that the capacity to see resides in the mind. Next, it clarifies that the eye alone cannot see.
Ānanda, furthermore, as for this mind of yours that is capable of awareness and cognition, if it must have a substance, does it have a single substance or multiple substances?
Is it currently located within your body, or is it pervasive throughout the body?

If it were a single substance, then when you prick one limb with your hand, your other four limbs should feel it; if they all felt it, the pricking would have no specific location. If [it were]... [the pricking]... [then...]
If [the self] were a single entity, then your own body could not be established; if it were multiple entities, then you would be many people. Which entity among them would be "you"?
If it were a pervasive entity, it would be the same as what was previously pointed out. If it were not pervasive, then when you touch your head, you should also touch your feet;
yet your head has sensation while your feet should be without cognition. Since this is not the case for you, you should therefore know that [it is] according to where [the sensation occurs].
It is impossible for the mind to follow [objects] at the point of conjunction; such a thing cannot exist.
My meaning is that while dharmas have fixed characteristics, the mind has no fixed substance. It is just like a gourd on water: when pressed, it turns;
or like a jewel in the sun, whose color has no fixed form—how could it have a fixed substance? If it had a fixed substance, [it would be as you claim].
This concerns whether [the body] is a single entity, multiple entities, pervasive, or non-pervasive.

If it were a single entity, then plucking a single hair should cause all hairs to move, and touching one limb should cause the entire body to feel sensation. If the entire body feels sensation, there should be no spot that is not touched;
yet if there is a spot that is touched, it is certainly not a single entity—"touched" (chì) here meaning "contacted. If, on the other hand, it were multiple entities...
Then it would follow that many people exist, because a single person consists of only one body; yet since there are multiple bodies, they would likewise constitute many people.

Furthermore, among these many people, you do not know which specific body is yours. If [the self] pervades the entire body, then as before, when one limb is touched, all four limbs would simultaneously experience sensation.
If it does not pervade the body, then when you touch your head, you should also simultaneously touch your feet—or if you touch your head... [the rest of the sentence is truncated in the source].

If it were known [only] when touched by the head, it would be known as "knowing"; if unknown when touched by the feet, it could be called "not pervasive. Yet, since it is known when touched by the feet and known when touched by the head, it is not the case that it is not pervasive;
therefore, we say this is not so. Thus, one knows that the substance of the mind is neither one nor many, and neither pervasive nor non-pervasive.
Since the mind has no fixed substance, it does not conform to things that possess a fixed nature. This can be understood.
Knowing this, the final conclusion—that the breaking [of delusion] does not reside in whatever place it may correspond to—was revealed;
Ānanda, having merely dangled his "pumpkin seal" to show off his cleverness, was cast by the World-Honored One into the depths of the great ocean.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I have also heard the Buddha conversing with Mañjuśrī and other Dharma-princes regarding the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
At that time, the World-Honored One also said that the mind is neither within nor without.
As I reflect upon this, since there is nothing seen within, it cannot be established as being inside; and since the body and mind do not know one another, it cannot be established as being outside."
Since the external is not the object and they are now mutually known, and since there is no seeing within either, it must exist in between.
This sixth [position] again relies on the sacred teaching to maintain that it exists in between.

However, what the World-Honored One said—that it is neither internal nor external—was precisely to state that the mind has no fixed location; it did not mean that the mind exists in between. Yet the Venerable One persists in this attachment.

Because one does not know what is meant by "intermediate," as soon as one calls it "intermediate," it becomes fixed in a specific location; therefore, [the text] below examines whether this intermediate state resides in the body or in the external environment.

The Buddha said: "Regarding what you call 'intermediate,' that intermediate must certainly not be confused, for it cannot be without a location. Now, when you investigate this intermediate state, where is it?"

Does it exist as a location, or does it exist within a place, or should it be considered within the body? If it were within the body, would it be at the periphery or in the center? If it were in the center, it would be identical to the interior.

If it were in a place, would it be something indicated by a marker or something not so indicated? If it were unindicated, it would be identical to the non-indicated; and if it were thus non-indicated, there would be no fixed determination.
Why is this? It is like when a person uses a marker to designate a center: if one looks from the east, it is to the west; if one views it from the south, it becomes the north.
Since the external manifestation of the body is already confused, the mind should likewise be disordered.
First, one must examine whether the "middle" resides in the body or in the object; subsequently, both are refuted, as neither has a fixed location.
If it were located below, it would mean residing within the body; yet since the body possesses the two aspects of center and periphery, if it were at the periphery, it could not be the middle.
If it were in the middle, it would be the same as the previous case; if it were inside, one ought to perceive the interior;

and if it were below, it would mean that within its location there are two meanings—manifest and non-manifest—used to designate an object in order to reveal the middle. To say "manifest" implies that if there is no non-manifest, then there is no middle;
and if there is manifest, then the middle does not exist. Since the substance of the manifest itself lacks fixedness now, how could the mind possibly have a fixed middle?
"And yet, they are not confused.
Ānanda said, "Within what I have explained, it is neither of these two kinds, as the World-Honored One has said: 'With the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises.
When the eye possesses discrimination and the object of form is present, consciousness arises therein; thus, the mind is located there."
As soon as the Venerable One heard this, both body and mind were shattered within him, like fire reaching the crown of one's head;

he immediately extinguished it, which is why it is said that what I have taught is neither of these two types. Furthermore, because one would instead shift the blame onto others, it is said, "as the World-Honored One has spoken":
that eye-consciousness arises with the eye and form as conditions means it arises from the conjunction of the faculty and the object.

Because consciousness takes the eye as its dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and visible form as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it is said that "the eye possesses discrimination while the dust of form is without cognition.
This is a venerable one’s mistaken interpretation of the Buddha’s intent, adding unnecessary commentary;

for he fails to realize that while the eye can illuminate objects and consciousness can discriminate them, the eye itself is actually devoid of discrimination. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Its eyes are all-pervading..."
Viewing [objects] as merely like reflections in a mirror, without further analysis, and then sequentially identifying and pointing them out within that [mirror-like state]—this is the proof.
The intention of the World-Honored One is that the two factors of eye and form serve as the conditions for the arising of consciousness;

it does not mean that the eye and form themselves can produce consciousness, because consciousness possesses its own seeds capable of producing it. Furthermore, regarding the two dharmas of sense-faculty and object...

Since all these are seeds of form (*rūpa*), how could seeds of form give rise to the actual manifestation of the mind? Therefore, it is said that the seeds and manifestations of the sense faculties can only guide the seeds and manifestations of consciousness.
It is acceptable to say that the faculties serve as the conditions for the arising of consciousness, but it is not acceptable to say that they actually produce consciousness.
The Venerable [Master] did not realize that the three—faculty, object, and consciousness—each possess their own seeds, and thus he clung to this [erroneous view].
Since both the faculties and their objects can give rise to consciousness, it is said that "consciousness arises within them.
The Buddha said: "If your mind were located between the faculties and their objects, would this essence of the mind partake of both, or not partake of both?

If it partakes of both, then the nature of the object and the nature of the mind would be intermingled; the object would not be the knower, and they would stand as two opposing entities. How could this be?"

If one attempts to establish a middle that encompasses both [extremes], it cannot be established; for if there is neither knowing nor not-knowing, then there is no essential nature (svabhāva). What, then, could serve as its characteristic?
Therefore, one should know that it is impossible for such a "middle" to exist.
The World-Honored One refutes [the opponent] by means of both the "inclusive" and the "non-inclusive. To speak of the inclusive is like parents uniting to together produce a child;
to speak of the non-inclusive is like producing a child spontaneously without depending on parents. Regarding the refutation of the inclusive, there are two meanings below.
If one follows the World-Honored One’s approach of "taking what is mistaken and following it further" (*jiang cuo jiu cuo*) to accord with the [opponent's] intent...

If one were to refute this by means of calculation, then the object (*viṣaya*) should point to the dust-particle (*rajas*) and the substance (*dravya*) should point to the sense-organ (*indriya*). Therefore it is said:

"If the two were to combine and produce [cognition] together, then the sense-organ and the dust-particle would be intermingled in a single location; they should not stand as opposing entities established in duality.
Now, as for the nature of the dust-particle, it is not the same as the sense-organ's possession of cognition; furthermore, they cannot stand as opposing entities established in duality.
If both [object and consciousness] were combined, who could say that the two were combined? Rather, it is within them that cognition arises.

If we follow the Tathāgata’s own correct principle, the term "objects" (*wu*) should generally refer to the sense organs (*gen*) and their objects (*chen*), while the term "essence" (*ti*) should refer to the essence of the mind (*xin*). Therefore, it is said:
"If the two were combined to produce [cognition], then objects and essence would become confused; for the organs and objects are the 'objects,' while the conscious mind is the 'essence.'"
Since the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) arise together, these are material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) giving rise to mental phenomena; therefore, they are called "confused.

Because the organs and objects are insentient and differ from the sentient nature of the mind, the organs and objects belong to the *nimittabhāga* (image-part), while the nature of the mind belongs to the *darśanabhāga* (seeing-part).
These two parts, the seeing and the image, are relative phenomena that stand in opposition like enemies; since there is not even a middle position between them, how [could there be a true self]?

And yet you say that consciousness arises within it? If consciousness were to arise of itself without depending on both the sense organ and the object, then in the absence of the organ and the object, there would be no essence of mind. Since there is no capacity to produce, there can be nothing produced.

That being the case, what could possibly be defined as "within," such that you say consciousness arises therein? Therefore, Ānanda, the conclusion below refutes the notion that it does not reside within the middle.
This boundless, broken sand-pot was presented to the World-Honored One, yet he struck it into pieces once more.
The Venerable One clings to the internal, clings to the external, and clings to the middle—just like a snake of Changshan: strike its head and the tail responds;
strike its tail and the head responds; strike the middle and both ends respond. How could one know that what is called "the late night" does not face [any of these]?
"It is like the reed flowers at night: when the intermediate space between them and their two ends is severed, they vanish.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, in the past I saw the Buddha together with the four great disciples—Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, and Śāriputra—turning the wheel of Dharma, and you always spoke of awakening to and discerning the nature of the mind."

Since it is neither within nor without, nor in between— being nowhere at all— and since this state of being entirely without attachment is called "mind," is it not the case that my state of being without attachment is what is called "mind"?
This seventh point concerns non-attachment. When the World-Honored One was in the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, he expounded the true doctrine of non-attachment:
that it exists neither within, nor without, nor in between; he spoke directly of the mind having no location and no place where it dwells.

Since the mind has no such dwelling place, one should not have further attachments. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "If one dwells in all dharmas, one does not dwell in the *prajñā*; one does not dwell in one [dharma]."
Regarding the statement that "all dharmas abide [in emptiness]," the *Prajñā-pāramitā-śāstra* explains: "If one abides in dharmas, one does not see Prajñā;
if one abides in Prajñā, one does not see dharmas. This is because dharmas possess marks (*nimitta*) while Prajñā is markless (*animitta*).
Furthermore, it is not the case that a markless Prajñā is established separately from dharmas that possess marks, for marks are themselves non-marks and are entirely Prajñā. As the Sūtra says:
If one studies Prajñā, one should study all dharmas. Why is this? For Prajñā is the meaning of non-abiding;
the very arising of the mind is abiding and attachment. If one does not abide in or attach to any dharma, that is Prajñā.
Therefore it is said: the mind has no location; in the state of having no location, there is only the single mind. The essence of the single mind is from the beginning...
In the state of quiescent extinction, there is only the one who enters, which resides solely in the mind’s knowing. Yet the Venerable [Huangbo] misinterpreted the Buddha’s intent, saying:
"I shall now take this mind and not allow it to attach itself to any phenomena. Can such a thing truly be called "mind"?
He did not realize that "taking the mind and not allowing it to attach" is already an act of attachment. Therefore, the former masters said: "To call it 'suchness'..."
This is indeed a transformation; where wisdom does not reach, one must strictly avoid speaking of it.
To speak of it is to give rise to horns. The Buddha said to Ānanda: "You say that the nature of the mind which perceives and discriminates has no location whatsoever.
Yet, the world, empty space, water, land, flying creatures, and all such objects and phenomena are called 'all things. If you do not cling to them, do they exist or do they not?"

If there were nothing, it would be identical to a tortoise’s hair or a rabbit’s horns; how then could one not be attached? To say one is not attached while there is something existing cannot be called "nothingness.
If there are no marks, then it is not non-existent; if it is not non-existent, then there are marks. If marks exist, then they are present; how can there be non-attachment?
Therefore, one should know that the claim that all non-attachment consists in the awakening mind realizing that the mind does not exist is impossible.
The World-Honored One, confronting the point where words fail, pressed him further, saying:
"As for your non-attachment to all things, does this mean that your mind originally possesses a locus, yet now does not attach to any dharmas?
Or does it mean that your mind originally lacks a locus, such that it naturally does not attach to any dharmas? If your mind originally lacked a locus..."
If this mind is naturally unattached because it has no location, then it is fundamentally non-existent like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit;

how could one further speak of its being "unattached"? If your mind had a location from which it did not become attached to all phenomena, then that mind would already have a place of attachment—how could it be called "non-attachment"? Therefore, he restates and refutes it as follows:
If you truly have no mental characteristics (*citta-nimitta*), then you are truly without mind and certainly have no attachment;

if it is not true that you are without mind, then you must necessarily have mental characteristics. Since there are mental characteristics, there must necessarily be a locus, and there will certainly be attachment.
How then can you say that "all things are without attachment"? Thus, it is not merely that there are characteristics that cannot be called non-attachment; rather—
The signless (*animitta*) cannot even be called "non-attachment," for as soon as one speaks of the signless, one falls into the sign.
Thus, the former masters said: "Non-arising ultimately does not abide; the myriad phenomena merely flow on. If you form an understanding of non-arising, you will instead be fettered by non-arising.
If you realize that deluded thoughts are non-arising, this is the unmoving true mind. Formerly there was...

A student asked National Teacher Zhong: "When one does not apply intentional effort (*manasikāra*), is there still a state of quiescence? He replied: "If you perceive quiescence, that itself is intentional effort.
Therefore, it is difficult for the faculty of mind (*manas*) to escape; both movement and stillness fall into the dust of dharmas (*dharmarajas*).

Not only does the understanding of 'non-attachment and following conditions' lead to falling into perverse thoughts, but even the arising of a mind that seeks to 'mysteriously merge with quiescence' is likewise."

Furthermore, because views still persist, one knows that all of this is merely intellectual opinion. To take Chan as a teaching for the sick or to treat it as a formal doctrine is like trying to cook rice by steaming sand or seeking fish by climbing a tree;
it is a waste of effort and labor, and one will vainly pass through kalpas as numerous as dust motes. If the mind does not arise, then the myriad dharmas are unborn.
As soon as the mind arises, one immediately falls into attachment. Therefore, the conclusion below states that the refutation does not reside in a single point.

There is absolutely no place of attachment; Ānanda has brought this head of a dead cat—having nowhere to land—to present to the World-Honored One, yet it too has been cast by the World-Honored One into another world-system. The Dharma-body has no location, yet there is nowhere it is not.
At first, Ānanda reckoned that the mind was within or without; he secretly calculated both possibilities, following them until they converged in the middle.
Because they [the practitioners] thus conceive of the mind as having a location, the World-Honored One refutes this by means of "non-location.

When they reach the seventh stage, they again conceive of the mind as being without location; therefore, the World-Honored One refutes this by means of "location through the existence of characteristics.
Although this is a single period of refuting attachments to reveal the principle that there is truly neither location nor non-location, it is what the former masters called "existence."
"One should not abide where there is a Buddha, nor rush past where there is no Buddha; this is the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama King.
Herein, the three *tathāgatagarbhas* are fully revealed. Even though the subsequent passage—“being apart from all marks is precisely all dharmas;
being apart and yet not apart, being identical and yet not identical”—exerts its utmost effort to describe them, it still does not [fully capture them].
If a wise person can apply this beyond these seven points, they have already grasped more than half the great meaning of the entire sutra.

These seven rounds of question and answer serve only to dismantle the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*)—that mind which has no fixed location, whose coming and going occur at no set time, and whose origin is unknown;
it is that mind which bends and stretches across heaven and earth and again caresses the four seas.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One, seeing that Ānanda’s mind was deluded and stuck in appearances, adhering to them at every turn, interrogated him, saying:
"Where are this 'mind' and this 'eye' located now? This word "located" (*zai*) is derived from the character for "appearance" (*xiàng*) within the thirty-two marks of a Buddha;
thus, he did not conclude with the phrase "it exists," but rather with the single expression "it is located. Furthermore, it is said that he refuted [the location] in seven stages.

This merely refutes the theories of arising from self, arising from other, arising from both, and arising without cause: the internal calculation that it arises from self and the external calculation that it arises from other;

the latent root calculation that the mind arises following the sense organs—which is also arising from self—and the calculation that where the mind meets its object, it arises following the object—which is also arising from other; and the dual calculation of both internal and external.
Furthermore, there is the calculation of self-arising; in the interim, one calculation is that [the object] arises from both sense-faculty and object (root and realm), which is non-attachment;
one calculation is that it arises without cause. Moreover, wherever they conjoin, there is the grasping of all marks arising, which is non-attachment;

one calculation is the grasping of arising apart from all marks, which is the latent root; this is the grasping of the *lakṣaṇavāda* (mark-doctrine) regarding the predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), while the interim is the grasping.

In the *lakṣaṇa* (characteristics) school, the predominant object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is non-attachment; in the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) school, it is the profound meaning of signlessness (*animitta*).
Based on these seven questions, one can clearly see that the Venerable [Zhùtǔ] has his belly full of the Buddha-dharma.
Yet, the World-Honored One’s sevenfold refutations did nothing more than address his points of attachment to untie his knots and loosen his bonds for him. As the former masters said: "The Buddha..."
In the Dharma, how many people are led astray! In worldly affairs, how many people attain awakening! Thus we know that the Dharma has no fixed characteristics;
delusion and awakening depend upon the person. As the *I Ching* says: "To manifest it through spiritual intelligence depends upon the individual.

In these seven rounds of questioning, there is a progressive refinement at every stage. For instance, it says: "If one recognizes the mind in this way, it truly resides within the body"—this is the One Reality.
Master Zi’s demeanor was haughty and self-important, as if there were no one else around, like a three-day-old tiger possessing the spirit to devour an ox.
When the second round cited the analogy of the lamp-lighting, Master Zi said, "Is this not the definitive meaning of the Buddha, free from delusion?
Although he remained stubborn, even his expression of "observing" (guan-de) and "two characters" (er-zi) showed a slight yielding. Upon reaching the third round, he then said:

"As I contemplate, it seems to lurk within the roots; 'as I [perceive]' means to measure the principle with one's own mind—it may be so, yet his resolve has slightly declined. In the fourth instance, he says: "What is the meaning of this?
I do not know whether it is right or wrong; I do not dare to decide that it is necessarily so. Upon reaching the fifth instance, he then reflects.
"Considering that my own mind is grounded in reality, and because I take the authoritative scriptures (*āgama*) as proof, I claim there can be no error;
thus I again open my mouth with force and say it is 'real. When it comes to the sixth round, one should speak with moderation, saying:
'According to what I have seen, it may well be so. The word 'may' (*dang*) already implies a sense of precariousness; by the seventh round, however—"
"Is it not the case that I have no attachment which could be called 'mind'? "No, no"—these words express doubt and indecision, whereby one becomes dejected and lacks vigor.

As for what is called "the heroic mind first arising like the surging tide of a spring river, its keen resolve suddenly dissolving like withered leaves in autumn frost," this sutra is profound in its meaning and intent;
even considering the brushwork of the translator and the refinements of the editor, [it remains thus].
"The man of Ying wielding his axe and Cook Ding carving with ease—both have entered the realm of spiritual transformation; how profound and wondrous!

At that time, Ānanda, who was among the great assembly, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'I am the youngest brother of the Tathāgata, having received the Buddha's compassionate love.'"

Although I have now left the household life, I still rely on my former charm and affection; thus, despite my extensive learning, I have not attained the outflows-free state and am unable to subdue the spells of Śābala.
I have been turned by them and drowned in a house of debauchery, solely because I did not know the destination of the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
I only pray that the World-Honored One, in his great compassion and pity, will reveal to us the path of *śamatha*, so that those of the icchantika class may [attain liberation].

After Mleccha Huī had spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; the great assembly likewise waited expectantly with thirsty hearts, longing to hear his instructions.

Ānanda, having been subjected by the World-Honored One to seven rounds of release and capture, now reached this point where the bow was broken and the arrows exhausted, as he surrendered and offered his sincere devotion.
To reproach oneself is to seek instruction. The youngest brother refers to the natural order of kinship;
