speaking of compassion and affection means that the Tathāgata’s loving heart cherishes all beings, which is not mere emotional attachment. It is like those who rely on indulgence and pity—what is called "the pampering of a child in a wealthy family.
Because they are favored by love and rely on indulgence, they are unwilling to advance in cultivation, instead becoming attached to much [worldly distraction].
Hearing this, he took it as a factual realization, yet he did not know that the true mind’s ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) was the place where he ought to reach.
Thus, his failure to attain the state beyond outflows (*anāsrava*) was due to being turned by Māra; this too was caused by this very ignorance.

All these preceding instances arose from not knowing the eternally abiding true mind and instead employing various false thoughts (*vikalpa*); hence there are such statements as "there is cyclic existence" (*saṃsāra*).
Therefore, we repent and reproach ourselves for having relied on your love and compassion.

While this is the sincere sentiment of your venerable selves, it is also intended as an exhortation for those in the末法 (mofa) age who rely on the names and positions of their fathers and brothers yet refuse to advance in cultivation.

We only pray that you will graciously grant us instruction; for we, being ignorant and deluded, have always been indolent and negligent, relying on your affection and failing to practice even in the slightest degree.
Although those who lack actual realization are surely objects of great compassion, we find no path by which to reach this true limit (bhūtakoṭi).
Therefore, we pray that you point out the path for reaching the true limit; for śamatha is the great highway for reaching the true limit.
Icchantikas are said to be "lacking in faith," and Mlecchas are said to be "evil."

"Seeing" refers to those who do not believe that they themselves possess this Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, yet instead falsely recognize the thirty-two marks as marvelous and excellent, seeking them outwardly; such people all hold the evil views of an icchantika.
Now, having obtained this path and reached this limit, one is finally able to give rise to faith and destroy these evil views. With a devoted heart, one thirsts for it.
Those who stood with their heads upturned, waiting respectfully to hear his instructions, saw that he held both person and Dharma in high esteem, for they were not like those who listen casually.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted various rays of light from the gate of his face; the radiance was so brilliant as to be like a hundred thousand suns.
The Buddha-worlds throughout the ten directions shook in six ways; thus, lands as numerous as motes of dust in the ten directions were simultaneously revealed.
By the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, all these worlds were merged into a single realm.
Within those worlds, all the great Bodhisattvas remained in their respective native lands, joining their palms in reverent attention.
This silent demonstration of the emission of light is intended to reveal that fundamental luminosity (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*) is not separate from its present location;
therefore, he first silently indicates its essence at the gateway of the six sense faculties to inspire faith. Linji said:
"There is a True Man of No-Rank who emits light and shakes the earth at the gateway of your six sense faculties—look, you people who have not yet realized this!"
To say that "its light shines brilliantly like hundreds of thousands of suns" refers to the moment when the eye is engaged;
it is the state where, as with a thousand suns, the myriad phenomena cannot escape their shadows and substances.

To say that "the entire Buddha-world shakes in six ways" means that, intending to shatter the six consciousnesses to reveal the six sense organs, he first causes the earth to tremble to awaken them. "Micro-dust... [The text ends here.]
That the lands appear simultaneously means that delusory objects do not create a barrier, just as mustard seeds in a jar are all clearly manifested at once.
That the worlds of the ten directions merge into a single realm means that the sphere of wisdom manifests its perfect penetration as the single Buddha-land.
That the Bodhisattvas and the assembly all abide in their own original lands means that the measure of the mind is fundamentally pervasive and the hearing of the mind is fundamentally lucid.

Furthermore, because sentient beings possess this fundamental radiance yet remain obscured and unaware of it, they divide it into the three categories of sense organs (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Consequently, they are unable to transcend the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). If one can cause inner clarity to emit light, then the mind of the sense organs, objects, and consciousness will dissolve at that very moment.

Thus, seeing and hearing become interpenetrating, and through the union of opening and closing, perfection is achieved; for this reason, these auspicious signs are shown beforehand as a result. If one is able to...
To realize this auspicious radiance, one attains the fundamentally pure essence of *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* without moving a step.
As for the "six quakes," these refer to shaking, rising, surging, trembling, roaring, and striking.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have followed various inverted karmic seeds that naturally cluster like *akṣa* berries.

That practitioners of the Way are unable to achieve unexcelled bodhi—resulting instead in the attainment of the stages of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or even becoming followers of external paths, devas, māras, or the retinues of māras—is entirely due to their ignorance."
Practicing these two kinds of fundamental delusions is like boiling sand in the hope of producing fine food;
even if one passes through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, one will never obtain it. What are these two, Ānanda?

First, the root of beginningless birth and death, which is that very攀緣心 (pān-yuán-xīn—the mind of grasping at objects) that you and all sentient beings now take as your own nature. Second, the beginningless Bodhi.
The fundamental essence of Nirvana is originally pure and tranquil; it is this very consciousness-essence of yours that is fundamentally luminous and capable of giving rise to all conditions.

Yet, that which is lost amidst these conditions arises because sentient beings have neglected this original luminosity. Though they act throughout the day, they remain unaware of it, and thus they perversely enter the various realms of existence.

From here below, the previously mentioned essence of pure luminosity and its various delusive functions are further opened into two kinds of roots, which serve as the structural framework for this entire scripture.
"Various inverted karmic seeds naturally [forming] like an *akṣa* cluster" refers to the crown of the head (*mūrdhan*).
"Like hair on the crown" means that the various inversions refer to having the crown turned downward and the feet directed upward.
Therefore it is said that the inverted mind’s cognition of what the eye sees is the root of inversion; the various inversions mentioned below all proceed from this.
As for the term "karmic seeds," it refers to how, when one is deluded regarding this awakened mind, ignorance suddenly arises;
through this ignorance, the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) is transformed, whereby various kinds of karma are created and seeds are perfumed—this is called "karma."
The various [causes] must necessarily have fruits; when cause and fruit arise in succession, one revolves through birth and death without interruption.

Therefore, the three—afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering—necessarily share a single root, just as the *akṣa* fruit (the fruit of the *akṣa* poison tree) necessarily produces three [seeds] from a single stalk.
Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Due to the habitual tendencies of various karmas and the habitual tendencies of the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*), they coexist."

When one retribution has been exhausted, another retribution arises again; as explained below, individual karma, collective karma, karma that follows from prior karma, and karma that initiates future karma—all these fundamentally flow forth from karmic seeds.
This serves as the foundation for the subsequent detailed exposition of the seven destinies (*sapta-gati*).

Those Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who turn their backs on the Great Mind to realize the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle, as well as those outside the Way (*bāhya-mārga*), are those who have departed from the Correct Path.
Those who follow deviant paths include: the various devas who cultivate the ten wholesome actions and delight in their fruits;
Māra—here translated as "the Killer"—who is addicted to the realm of desire and disrupts correct cultivation.

All such cases result from failing to distinguish between the two paths of truth and falsehood, mistaking sand for rice, and practicing blindly and in vain until this state is reached. This shall be explained in detail in the subsequent text.
The Venerable Master [Wonhyo] provides the foundational context for discerning the realms of Māra by revealing to us the path of *śamatha*.
Regarding the Venerable Master’s direct pointing out of two paths: he states that the root of beginningless birth and death is precisely fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).
This arises from the initial delusion regarding the single *dharmadhātu*, whereby the non-enlightened mind (*abodha-citta*) is produced.

Because there is this mindfulness, it is said that [time] is beginningless. Like the appearance of flowers from eye-strain or the arising of dreams during deep sleep, they fundamentally lack a causal origin and have no fixed place of birth;
all are merely deluded thoughts and not produced by other external conditions.

From these, the subtle karmic consciousness arises first, followed by the "evolving aspect" (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*) which functions as the capacity for seeing, and subsequently the "manifesting aspect" (*nimitta-lakṣaṇa*) appears.

From these three kinds of subtle consciousnesses, external objects arise; furthermore, the four kinds of coarse consciousnesses—characterized by the manifestation of wisdom, continuity, grasping, and conceptualization of names—then emerge.
Thereupon, one clings to the internal and the external, reaching for this and grasping at that, with every thought-moment proceeding without ceasing and without even a moment’s rest.
Thus, one gives rise to delusions, creates karma, and revolves through birth and death. This very root of birth and death is your own present state.

To take this process of climbing eastward and leaning westward as one's own nature is precisely the root that separately establishes the realms of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, celestial māras, external paths, and the seven destinies.

That which is the beginningless essence of bodhi and nirvāṇa, the primordially pure body, refers to the fruition-awakening of bodhi and nirvāṇa; the primordially pure body is the causal mind. This purity—
The essence is precisely this eighth, subtle, and refined thought present before you, which is called the "consciousness-essence" (*vijñāna-śukra*).
It is primordially complete as the one true Dharma-realm of original luminosity—unborn and unmoving;
it is neither defiled by birth-and-death nor purified by nirvana; it is neither deluded by ignorance nor awakened to by bodhi. This is it. However...
Although this fundamentally bright and fundamentally pure essence does not correspond with deluded defilement, it fails to maintain its own nature and, following conditions,
gives rise to various delusive thoughts. As all sentient beings grasp at the east and pursue the west,
they take these various grasping and pursuing delusive thoughts to be their mind-nature, and conversely treat the fundamentally bright and fundamentally pure essence as...
"To cast it aside and disregard it"—this very act of casting it aside and disregarding it is the root of Bodhi and Nirvana.
The meaning is that if one wishes to realize the fruit-consciousness of Bodhi and Nirvana, one must take the unborn, undying, primordially pure essence as the causal mind;
and this causal mind must be sought from within the *vijñāna-śuddha* (the pure essence of consciousness). Therefore, [it is said in the] *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*:
The treatise states: "The pure dharma-realm is the true self-essence of all Tathāgatas, which has been naturally pure since beginningless time.
It is fully endowed with various qualities of nature and characteristics, numbering as many as the atoms in the worlds of the ten directions;
it is without birth or cessation, like space, pervading all phenomena, and is equally shared by all."

All phenomena are neither identical nor different, neither existent nor non-existent; they are free from all marks, all conceptual constructions, and all verbal designations, being utterly unapprehendable.
Their intrinsic nature is suchness, revealed by the two kinds of emptiness and the absence of self, which is realized solely by the pure, noble wisdom of the sages.
This purity is partially realized by the various sages and perfectly realized by the Buddhas.
The Dharma-realm is the wondrous mind of True Suchness; it is the source of the ocean of fruition for all Buddhas and the ground for the actual realization of all sentient beings.
Because sentient beings have neglected this innate luminosity, they remain in perfect enlightenment all day long without ever realizing it.

Thus, though the various realms of existence are fundamentally not places one should enter, to enter them is called "entering erroneously. This is due to neglecting [this luminosity] through the use of a攀緣心 (pān-yuán xīn—clinging and seeking mind).
To take one aspect of the fundamental luminosity while discarding the other is precisely the reality of delusion.
Ānanda, if you now wish to know the path of śamatha and desire to transcend birth and death, I shall now question you further.
At that moment, the Tathāgata raised his golden arm, bent his five fingers into a fist, and said to Ānanda, "Do you see this? "I do, World-Honored One," Ānanda replied.

When he spoke of seeing the Buddha, [the Buddha] asked, "What do you see? Ānanda replied, "I see the Tathāgata raising his arm and bending his fingers into a fist of radiant light that dazzles my mind and eyes.
The Buddha asked, "By means of what do you see? Ānanda replied, "Together with the great assembly, I see with my eyes."

This was a test of his insight. [The Master] said, "Since you asked me about the path of *śamatha* with the desire to transcend birth-and-death and reach the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), I have pointed out two great highways for you, each clearly distinguished. However, I do not know which path you are currently taking.
Therefore, he raised his fist to examine the locus of [the student's] vision, saying: "Do you see this now? This is what is meant by...
He extracts the priceless treasure of Central China, which differs from the jade of Zhao and the gold of Yan. Ānanda did not understand;
he should have realized it before the fist was even raised. Instead, he answered with factual precision, saying, "I see the World-Honored One," and pressed him further, asking, "What do you see?
To which [the Master] replied, "A thorn in soft mud. Ānanda missed the mark right before his eyes and instead said, "I see [the Buddha]."
The Tathāgata bent his fingers into a fist of radiance to illuminate my heart-mind and eyes. I merely recognized the fist;
yet the World-Honored One, with his heart laid bare in full view, struck me once more with a single blow, saying: "By what do you see? Ānanda’s eyes were dull and his head was muddled;
he repeatedly missed the mark, as he continued to say: "I and the great assembly all see with our eyes."
This means that because one has not moved even a single step from where one formerly practiced, Wénlǐng says: "When the golden fist is raised, one must directly recognize the fundamental luminosity;
if the manifestations of sensory objects (dust-phenomena) are not yet eliminated, one will continue to mistake the thief for the son."
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "Now answer me this: when the Tathāgata bends his fingers into a fist of light to illuminate your eyes and mind, your eyes can see it;
what do you take to be the mind when my fist shines upon you? Ānanda replied: "As the Tathāgata now investigates the location of the mind, I use my mind to investigate, pursue, and examine it.
That which is capable of such investigation—that, I shall take to be the mind. The Buddha [said]: "... (The text continues with the Buddha's refutation).
"Alas, Ānanda! This is not your mind.

This is a further inquiry that brings forth the deluded mind in order to refute it. Seeing that the Venerable One’s words did not accord with his own, the World-Honored One shifted the pivot of the dialogue and proceeded along a different path, saying: "Now you answer me: when the Tathāgata snaps his fingers..."
The Radiant Fist shines upon your eyes and mind; even if you grant that it may be seen by the eyes, with what object will you identify the mind to meet the radiance of my fist?

Though you may use yellow orpiment from within your mouth and a sharp sword from the tip of your tongue, alas, Venerable Sir, you remain as before—painting the face of Yan-yan and presumptuously comparing yourself to Xi-zi, yet still identifying the capacity for reasoning as the mind.

Because of its nature, it is called the Tathāgata manifesting now. This so-called "fine teacher" goes about in such a manner, yet he does not know that this mind is like a form within a bell—without substance and entirely dependent on external objects;
or like the moon in water—not real, yet appearing as a void manifestation. To take this empty wheel for the truth is the height of delusion, O World-Honored One!
Seeing that Ānanda did not realize it head-on, Huangbo manifested the majestic power of a crouching lion and let out a single shout, saying:
"Tsk! This is not your mind; it is what the *I Ching* calls 'striking the ignorant: it is advantageous to punish them so as to release them from their shackles.
At that moment, even if it were Huangbo, Deshan, Linji, or Yantou themselves, they would have been deaf for three days."
Therefore, the *Zongjing* says: "Because Ānanda clung to this deluded mind, the World-Honored One rebuked him;
because the Second Patriarch sought this deluded mind and found it utterly unobtainable, the First Patriarch then transmitted the robe.
The previous seven instances of refutation were the razing of the bandit’s nest; this present rebuke is the beheading of the bandit."
Ānanda was startled; he rose from his seat, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha: "This is not my mind. What should it be called?
The Buddha told Ānanda: "This is a false appearance and conceptualization of the external objects before you that deludes your true nature.
Because from time immemorial until this present life you have mistaken a thief for your own son, you have lost your original constancy and thus undergo the cycle of rebirth."
This refers to Ānanda being startled by the shout; "startled" describes his state of sudden fear. When the World-Honored One gave him a single shout, Ānanda was truly caught off guard;
he could not respond or match it, and was left utterly shattered and dissolved, as if falling apart like ice melting or a wall crumbling.
This is what is meant by the saying: "When a luminous gem is thrown at a person, few do not instinctively draw their swords"—yet Ānanda, in turn, failed to live up to this single shout. Therefore...

Ānanda said, "This is not my mind; what should it be called? Seeing that Ānanda was startled and uncertain, the World-Honored One withdrew his teaching and said, "This mind arises based on the false appearances of external objects; it is called 'delusive thought.
Because of this delusive thought, your true nature is confused and obscured. How could you recognize this as your mind? Thus he spoke.
From beginningless time until now, you have mistakenly identified the mind as if recognizing a thief as your own son;
consequently, you have cast aside the eternally abiding true mind and neglected it, thereby suffering in vain through the endless cycle of birth and death.
This is what is meant by "Hanshan lost his way, and Shide led him home."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I am the beloved younger brother of the Buddha; because my heart loves the Buddha, he caused me to leave the household life.

How could my heart alone provide offerings to the Tathāgata? Even as I have traveled through lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to serve various Buddhas and spiritual friends, and have with great courage performed all manner of difficult practices and dharmic deeds—it is all by means of this very mind."
It causes those who slander the Dharma to eternally lose their roots of goodness; this too is due to this mind.

If this manifestation were not the mind, I would be without a mind, identical to earth and wood. Apart from this awareness, there is nothing else. Why then does the Tathāgata say that this is not the mind?
I am truly terrified, and among this great assembly, there is no one who does not harbor doubt. I pray that you will extend your great compassion and reveal [the truth].
This indicates that one has not yet awakened;

it is a state of being startled and doubtful because one clings to delusion and does not let go. What the World-Honored One intended with his single heart of compassionate care has instead resulted in a state of stagnation.
An ancient said: "Not only can those who can merely speak not be found, but even those who can truly understand are likewise unattainable."
Indeed, as the Venerable Xiangxia recounted his own life, he observed that all the many functions of performing good and evil deeds were carried out by this mind;
apart from this mind, there is no other mind, which would otherwise result in total annihilation, making him no different from insentient objects such as wood or earth.
What he did not realize was that the agent of performing good and evil belongs to the category of "initiating karma" (*karmābhisamskāra*).
To clarify: what is called "delusive thought" (*vikalpa*) refers to neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil; this, however, is the Venerable One’s original face.

To abandon that which is inherently present without knowing how to cherish it, and to fail to relinquish delusive thoughts—this is what is meant by the saying, "One who was clever as a child may not necessarily be excellent as an adult.
My expression of "true alarm and fear" contains a vast disparity from [the Venerable One's view] and does not accord with common human sentiment; therefore, I have combined these points.
In this great assembly, there is not one who does not harbor doubt; it is like being in the same pit where the soil is no different.

As the former masters have said: "Suddenly, amidst a clear sky, the sound of a thunderclap; at the three-tiered waves of the Yu Gate, how many with horns and heads have gone off to become dragons, while the crabs remain as before, straining their eyes? Is this not what the Venerable One meant?

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to cause Ānanda and the great assembly to enter the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), rubbed the crown of Ānanda’s head while seated upon the lion throne and addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata has constantly taught that all dharmas that arise are manifested solely by the mind.
All causes and effects, as well as the subtle atoms of the world, take the mind as the substance of their formation. Ānanda, if all..."
Within all that exists in the world, down to the very roots of blades of grass, leaves, threads, and knots, each possesses its own substantial nature;
even empty space has a name and appearance—how much more so for the pure, wondrously pure, luminous mind-nature?
All minds are themselves devoid of inherent substance.
This verse demonstrates that the true mind has a substantial essence in order to dispel the doubt that it is as insentient as wood or earth.
The "Dharma-patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is precisely the essence of the mind that is neither good nor evil.

Because the World-Honored One saw that Ānanda clung to the delusory as real, he let out a thunderous shout to startle him into fear; he then comforted him by stroking his head. This is what is meant by the so-called "occasional iron."
Wrapping cotton balls in brocade or using a special stone to feign anger and feign joy allows one to both release and restrain;
thus the *Zongjing* says that by saying "four in the morning" and "three in the evening," one causes the monkeys to rejoice.

Just as one applies bitter ointment or washes with water to nourish an infant according to the occasion, the Tathāgata proceeds through the various dharmas that possess substance to manifest that the true mind must necessarily exist.

"Substance" (*tǐ*) refers to all causes and effects; "the ten realms" refers to the primary retributions (*zhèngbào*), while "the minute dusts of the world" refers to the secondary retributions (*yībào*).
Grass, leaves, threads, and knots are the finest among things with form, while empty space is the largest among things without form.
This precisely means that whether sentient or insentient, whether large or small, all things possess substance.

How much more so for the nature that is pure, wondrously pure, and luminous—the mind that is the beginning of heaven and earth, the mother of all things, and the fundamental nature of all good and evil minds—could it possibly lack substance? Formerly, when Dadian first visited Shitou, Shitou asked, "Which one is your mind?
Dadian replied, "The one that perceives words. Shitou then shouted at him and sent him out; he did not return for ten days.
The Master asked in return, "Since that which was previously described is not it, what else is this 'mind'?

The monk said, "Setting aside the raising of eyebrows and the twinkling of eyes, bring me the mind. The Master said, "There is no mind to bring. The monk said, "Originally there is mind; why do you say there is no mind?
To say there is no mind is nothing but slander. At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment. If one were like the Venerable One...
If you had known from the beginning that there is a mind, it would not have required the Tathāgata so many circuitous explanations.
If you insist that the nature perceived through discrimination, thought, and reflection must be the mind,
then this mind should exist as a distinct, complete entity apart from all objects— the spheres of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch— and apart from all activities, just as you do now.

To listen to my Dharma is to have discrimination based on sound. Even if you were to extinguish all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and inwardly maintain a state of profound stillness, this would still be a mere reflection of the discrimination of mental objects (*dharmaviṣaya*). I am not commanding you to hold that this is not the mind;
rather, you must subtly examine the mind itself. If there is a nature of discrimination that exists apart from these external objects, then that is the true [mind].
If your mind discriminates that which is devoid of substance and separated from external objects, then these are merely shadows of the discrimination of external objects.

Since external objects are not permanent, when they change and perish, this mind would likewise be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit; thus, your Dharma-body would be subject to annihilation.
Who then could cultivate and realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas?
This instructs the Venerable One to examine and discern that [the mind] is capable of inferring its own falsity, thereby removing the attachment to that false mind.

To grasp firmly and refuse to let go is called "clinging" (*parāmarśa*). "Discriminating through vitarka and vicāra" refers to *vitarka* (initial inquiry) and *vicāra* (sustained examination). It says:
"If you grasp at these presently active discriminations of the six sense-objects as being the true mind and are unwilling to relinquish them, then this very mind should be abandoned."
Only when one sets aside the six sense objects and possesses a distinct, non-infiltrating, and non-leaking, perfectly complete essence is that the true mind.
Now, as you sit here listening to my teaching, this mind that hears the Dharma arises because of the sounds of my preaching;
it is a mind of discrimination, a mind of infiltration and leakage, not the perfectly complete essence. How could it be the true mind? Not only for you now...
Furthermore, the six consciousnesses still engage in active discrimination and thus cannot be called "true.

Even if you were to extinguish all seeds and active manifestations of these six consciousnesses to become an Arhat, should you inwardly maintain a state of secluded tranquility and indulge in the bliss of cessation,
refusing to let go, then this very maintenance of seclusion still belongs to the mental faculty (manas) and remains but a shadow.
Since phenomena cannot be the true mantra, and the seeds currently manifesting have not yet been emptied, how can you claim this to be the truth?
You say, "Today I am not intentionally refuting what you grasp as being wrong;
it is simply that you take this discriminative observation and subtle deliberation—speculating whether it exists or does not exist, whether it is real or false—if..."
That which has a substantial nature apart from the external objects before one is truly apart from them; that which lacks such a nature is false.
Now, the conceptualizations, discernments, and reflections you cling to all exist because of those objects.

Since the objects that can produce them are fundamentally not permanent—changing and perishing in an instant—the mind produced by them likewise perishes along with the objects. Since the mind follows [the objects]...
If it were extinguished, your Dharma-body would likewise be reduced to ashes and severed;

what then would you have as the causal-ground mind to realize this patience of the non-arising of dharmas? Therefore, know that the mind fundamentally does not exist, but arises because of sense-objects;
apart from these sense-objects, no thought can be established, and apart from discrimination, no sense-object can be obtained.
At that moment, Ānanda and the great assembly were silent and overcome with despondency. The Buddha addressed Ānanda:

"All those practitioners in the world who have attained the nine successive meditative absorptions (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti) in this present life, yet fail to exhaust their outflows and become Arhats, do so because they cling to these deluded thoughts of birth and death, mistaking them for reality. Therefore, although you now possess much learning..."
They fail to achieve the fruits of sainthood;
through this teaching, they lose what they already possess. To "lose what one possesses" means that one lacks self-mastery:
one cannot desire to cling, yet one cannot bring oneself to let go. Seeing their entanglement and stagnation, the World-Honored One spoke with extreme urgency and pain.
To stimulate those practitioners who are training, he refers to the three preceding fruits of the path;
"the nine successive attainments" (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) refers to the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

Because these are entered in a sequence of nine stages, the first eight are mundane concentrations (*laukikasamādhi*), while the last one is a supramundane concentration (*lokottarasamādhi*); therefore, one who attains the ninth concentration transcends [the mundane].

Those who have realized nirvāṇa within saṃsāra and attained the fruit of arhatship are now said not to have exhausted their outflows and achieved arhatship because they are attached to the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) and refuse to relinquish it. This very absorption of cessation is but a shadow-like phenomenon;
this very attachment is likewise a false conceptualization (vikalpa). Because they grasp at this false conceptualization and mistakenly take it for a real dharma, they fail to attain the final goal.
Because of their inherent nature, although they practice, they do not attain the state of a true Arhat; thus it is said:

"The person sitting at the end of a hundred-foot pole—though they have gained entry, it is not yet true. How much more so for you, who have not yet mastered the extinction samādhi (nirodha-samāpatti) and have not maintained profound stillness;
you cling to the delusory appearances of external objects, mistaking them for reality and refusing to relinquish them. Therefore, though [you may reach] the one..."
Regarding those who have turned toward the path of much learning but have not yet attained the fruit of sainthood because their power is incomplete:
what was previously called "guarding" (*shou*) means to embrace and hold fast without shifting; what is here called "clinging" (*zhi*) means to adhere tenaciously without relinquishing.

The character for "guarding" is a sickness, and the character for "clinging" is likewise a sickness. If one discards the character for "guarding," it is no longer a shadowy affair; if one discards the character for "clinging," it is precisely [the Way].
The World-Honored One’s two instances of using harsh and piercing words were intended to probe deeply and strike home for the sake of the person,
seeking to cause the Venerable One to abandon deluded consciousness and seek the true mind.
Having heard this, Ānanda again shed tears of grief; prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he knelt for a long time with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Since I followed the Buddha to leave the household life and develop the mind of enlightenment, I have relied upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and have always thought to myself that there was no need for me to practice, believing that the Tathāgata would bestow samādhi upon me.
I did not realize that body and mind can never substitute for one another, and thus I have lost my original mind."
Although we have left the household life in body, our minds do not enter the Way; we are like destitute sons who abandon their father and flee, only today realizing he exists.
Though we possess much learning, if we do not practice, it is equal to having heard nothing at all; it is like a person speaking of food who can never be satiated by the talk alone.
World-Honored One, we are now entangled by the two obstacles precisely because we do not know the nature of the mind, which is quiescent and eternal. We only pray that...
The Tathāgata, out of compassion for my destitution and exposure, has brought forth his wondrous and luminous mind to open my eye of the Way.
Because he previously twice rebuked my perceptions and exhorted me to abandon them, I have now expressed my feelings and repented to beg for the eye of wisdom.
Since Ānanda responded by explaining the arising of appearances and the development of the mind, the World-Honored One already knew that Ānanda recognized the capacity for discernment.
As for their distinction: that which is capable of seeing objects is the mind, while that which sees them is the eye.
When asked where the mind and the eyes currently reside, one calculates that the eyes are outside and the mind is inside.

Yet, when the Tathāgata refuted the substantiality of the mind, Ānanda again raised the objection that the eyes see and the mind knows. This continued until [the Buddha] raised his fist and asked, "With what do you perceive this?"

When [the Buddha] saw him, he said, "I and the great assembly shall all see with our own eyes. When asked, "What constitutes the mind? Ānanda replied, "That which is capable of deliberation is the mind.
Therefore, the Tathāgata urgently refuted and shattered that which is capable of deliberation in order to reveal that the true mind possesses a substantial essence.
Only then did Ānanda believe that the deliberating mind was false; thus, he requested the true mind and simultaneously requested the eye of the Way.
That he wept again and again with sorrow—first out of self-reproach, then out of self-blame, and finally in tears—all these were points of genuine heartache for Ānanda.
For Ānanda and Śākyamuni had simultaneously resolved their minds toward enlightenment under the Buddha King of Emptiness;
yet while Śākyamuni had already attained Buddhahood after kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, Ānanda had remained [in the cycle] for immeasurable...
Even those who delight in extensive learning throughout kalpas do not yet know the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure clarity;

how could they not feel heartache when such a thought arises? Thus, with tears of compassion, he presents his plea. Previously it was said that one relies on the Buddha’s tender affection and does not practice;
here it is said that one relies on the Buddha’s supernatural powers and feels no need for me to correct them. This means that the Tathāgata is my lord.
Lunbi ranhui’s samādhi—how could he have known that father and son ascend the mountain each exerting their own effort, for one cannot substitute for the other?
Thus it is said: "One does not know that body and mind fundamentally cannot substitute for one another.
Upon hearing the reprimand, one realizes that the Tathāgata admits no sentimentality; this single heart of hope has fallen entirely into emptiness. Therefore, I...
Hitherto, although you have left the household life, you have never truly entered [the path];
how is this different from one who dwells in a place of rich fertility yet cannot nourish themselves, but instead rushes outward to beg for food from others?
Today I finally understand that "speaking ten feet is not as good as practicing one foot. Therefore, even if one has much learning, if one does not...

"Practicing without ever gaining benefit is because talking about cakes cannot satisfy hunger. Those "enveloped by the two obstacles" refer to the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obstacle to the known (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

One severs the obstacle of afflictions to realize the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), and severs the obstacle to the known to realize the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Now, I am enveloped by these two obstacles and am unable [to proceed].

That one fails to liberate oneself stems fundamentally from not knowing the nature of the mind, which is quiescent and eternal; by clinging to these deluded thoughts and mistaking them for reality, one remains bound.
As for "quiescent and eternal," it is called "quiescent" because it does not waver, and it is called "eternal" because it has no coming or going.

To say one is "destitute and exposed" means that because there is no flavor of the Dharma to nourish the spirit, one is destitute; and because there is no Dharma-robes to cover the body, one is exposed.
Therefore it is said: "To reveal the wondrously luminous mind" means that although I possess this wondrous mind, I have always kept it hidden and concealed;
failing to distinguish between good and evil, I mistakenly took my capacity for reasoning to be the ultimate reality, unaware that there exists separately the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*.
Thus I pray that the World-Honored One will lift the veil and bring it forth, opening my eye of the Way. This means that although I possess [it]...

My eye of the Way has been consistently obscured and blinded, unable to distinguish black from white; I have merely relied upon my fleshly eyes, believing them capable of seeing, unaware that there exists a separate Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.
Therefore, I pray that the World-Honored One will scrape away this cataract and open it for me—this is the formal request for the revelation of the Buddha’s knowledge and the Buddha’s vision.
At that moment, from the *svastika* on the Tathāgata’s chest, there surged forth precious light;

its radiance was brilliant and shimmering, possessing hundreds of thousands of colors, which simultaneously pervaded Buddha-worlds as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, universally bathing the crowns of all the Tathāgatas in all the precious lands of the ten directions.
The light then returned to Ānanda and the great assembly, whereupon the Tathāgata addressed Ānanda, saying: "I shall now, for your sake..."
He erects the great Dharma banner and causes all sentient beings throughout the ten directions to attain the wondrous, subtle, and secret nature of pure, luminous mind and obtain the eye of purity.
This was first indicated through the manifestation of light in silence, and only thereafter did he grant permission to speak. That light surging from his chest specifically reveals the Buddha.
Know that the Buddha’s vision emerges from within one's own breast; only then does it cover heaven and earth.

It is not a light emitted by attachment to delusion. "Radiant" (*huàngyù*) describes the shimmering quality of the light; "possessing hundreds of thousands of colors" means it is accomplished through myriad virtues.
Thus, the light pervades all dust-motes and lands, as well as the assembly of Tathāgatas—this is precisely [the point].
It is revealed that sentient beings, insentient things, and both the noble and the ordinary are all equally emanated from within the light of sameness;
therefore, regarding those who say, "I shall erect for you the great banner of Dharma," I declare: the banner of your own nature has already fallen to the ground long ago.
What I now establish for you is so that it shall never again collapse. Whether sought internally or externally, not a single object exists upon which to bestow [this teaching].

Because it is all-pervasive and yet utterly complete, it is called the wondrous, subtle, and secret nature. Within the dense array of the myriad phenomena, there is a single sphere of light that is neither internal nor external;
therefore, it is called the pure and luminous mind. It enters into all sensory objects without becoming mixed with them, and responds to all faculties without being defiled;
therefore, it is called the pure eye. The nature of the eye is spoken of in terms of stillness, the mind in terms of illumination, and the eye in terms of wisdom.
[The Buddha] said:
"Ānanda, you previously answered me that you saw my radiant fist. From what cause does this fist possess its radiance? How is it formed into a fist?
And who is it that sees it? Ānanda replied: "It is because the Buddha’s entire body is made of Jāmbūnada gold, blazing like a precious gem."

Because it arises from the purity of the mountain, it possesses radiance; because I truly observed with my own eyes the five fingers curled and clenched to show them to others, it possesses the mark of a fist.
Having previously refuted the mind that conditions objects as being false, I now wish to reveal that the seer is true; therefore, I am pointing to the nature of seeing mentioned before.
He raised three successive questions to examine the matter in detail, causing him to answer clearly;
thereafter, he used an illustration to elucidate the meaning of Jambūnada gold—translated as "superior gold. To the south of Mount Sumeru there is this *jambu* tree;
when its fruit juice enters the water, the sand and stones turn into gold. If a single grain of this gold is placed among ordinary gold, all the latter lose their color before it. [The Buddha’s...]
The color of the body is like that of a blazing red flame; "vermilion" (*kṣipta*) refers to that which is born of purity.
This means that the Tathāgata is not born from desire, but is born from immeasurable merit and wisdom; therefore, he possesses radiance like Jāmbūnada gold.
This answers the question of why such radiance exists. As for my actual visual perception, I formerly identified it as flesh.
"The eye is that which sees. To this he replied: "By means of what do you see? The Tathāgata’s fingertips all possess the mark of the wheel;
therefore they are called "wheel-fingers. As for "bending and clasping," one bends the five fingers to form a clasp, thereby creating the appearance of a fist.
To this he replied: "How is it that a fist is formed?"
The Buddha told Ānanda, "I now tell you these true words: those who possess wisdom must rely on parables to attain awakening.
Ānanda, it is like my fist: if there were no hand of mine, my fist would not exist; if there were no eyes of yours, your seeing would not exist.
If you take your faculty of sight as an analogy for the principle of my fist, is the meaning not the same? Ānanda replied, "It is so, World-Honored One."
He said, "Indeed, World-Honored One, since there is no 'my eye,' my seeing is not established; the matter of my eye-faculty is analogous to the Tathāgata’s fist.
The World-Honored One saw that the Venerable One still clung to the eye as being the act of seeing, so he took his bare hand and empty fist and made a point of it.
Using the dazzling mirror as an analogy, he asked: "For example, if I have hands, I have fists;
if you have eyes, you have seeing. Are these principles the same or different? Ānanda understood only how to push a boat downstream with the current, but not how to steer it against the wind.
Lacking skill in drawing analogies, he replied: "If one has eyes, then one sees."

If there are hands, there are fists; yet, while you use the eye as an analogy for the fist, the principle and the facts are of the same category, you fail to realize that you are using this quiescent and eternal mind-nature as an analogy to establish a view of annihilation.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Your statement that these two cases are analogous is not correct. Why is this?
For example, while the fist of a handless person is ultimately non-existent, the lack of sight in one who has no eyes does not mean that seeing is entirely absent. Why is this so?
You should try asking a blind person on the road, 'What do you see? Those blind people will surely answer you, 'At present, before my eyes, I only [see darkness]...'"
When one sees darkness, there is nothing else to behold; by this principle, observe that the external objects themselves are dark—how could the seeing itself be diminished?
If this reasoning were not correct, it would be like saying a cart does not travel crosswise or that logic does not allow for a crooked conclusion:

since there are no hands, there can be no fists, yet the absence of eyes does not mean there is no seeing. Because this analogy is inappropriate, it is said that [the opponent's position] is not so. This is why... [it is said below].
Furthermore, he cites the case of a blind man to provide proof: there was once a sightless mountain dweller who sold divinations.
After a heavy rain, he walked along the road wearing bright shoes, yet not a speck of mud adhered to them. When people asked him the reason, he said, "The tip of my staff has eyes; thus I know.
Therefore, although a blind person lacks physical eyes, they have never lacked the power of seeing; hence it is said that the external objects themselves are dark.

What loss is there in seeing this? This is the World-Honored One pointing out, upon the physical mass of an ordinary person, a pair of eyes that settle heaven and earth and illuminate the heavens and reflect the earth.
Thus we know that within the cave of ignorance exists the Great Treasury of Radiance;
what is called "the numinous light shining alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects" is not the same as a deluded mind that lacks substance when separated from its objects.
Ah! As an ancient proverb says: "The same flour and dough are made into different things by the hands of men.
Ānanda took this mind-nature, which is quiescent and eternal, and instead fashioned it into a view of annihilation; this can be called "turning gold into iron.
The World-Honored One, taking up this very view of annihilation, used it to reveal the mind-nature that is quiescent and eternal; this can be called "turning iron into gold."
Ānanda said, "The blind before my eyes perceive only darkness; how can this be called seeing?

The Buddha told Ānanda, "The blind, having no eyes, perceive only darkness, while a person with eyes situated in a dark room also perceives darkness. Is there a difference between these two kinds of darkness, or is there no difference?
[Ānanda replied,] "In this way, World-Honored One, when comparing the darkness perceived by the person in the dark with that of the group of blind people—"
There is no difference.
How profound it is that the faculties and consciousness are so difficult to distinguish! Ānanda has consistently treated the eyes and the mind as two separate things;
furthermore, he does not realize that the faculty, the light, and the darkness are all augmenting conditions for the nature of seeing, yet he has consistently identified them as such.
Because he had lost his way due to misunderstanding, upon hearing the words, "In one moment, when the sensory objects are present, you yourself see in darkness; what deficiency could there be?
he feigned ignorance and confusion, not daring to believe it, and instead raised an objection, saying: "World-Honored One, those who are blind see nothing before their eyes;
they perceive only darkness. How can this also be called 'seeing'? The World-Honored One then took the case of a person with sight who sees darkness.
The Venerable One answered that there was no difference in his intended meaning when he established an analogy between the vision of a person without eyes and the seeing of darkness,
by questioning whether they were the same or different. His point was that although those with eyes and those without eyes are indeed distinct,
there is no difference in the darkness they perceive.

Ānanda, if a person who has no eyes sees only the darkness before them, and suddenly regains the light of their eyes and perceives various forms within those external objects, this is called "seeing with the eyes.

If that were so, when a person in the dark sees only the darkness before them and suddenly obtains the light of a lamp and likewise perceives various forms within those external objects, it should be called "seeing with the lamp.
If it were seeing with the lamp, then the lamp would possess the capacity for vision; [yet] the lamp itself does not see.

The name "lamp" and the act of "observing with a lamp" have no concern with your own affairs; therefore, you should know that it is the lamp that can manifest color, while the one who sees thus is the eye, not the lamp.
It is the eye that can manifest color, while the nature that sees thus is the mind, not the eye.
Because Ānanda’s answer was unerring, the World-Honored One immediately used it as an illustration to clarify that the capacity to see belongs to the mind and not to the eye;
thus he said: "If a person without eyes were to obtain the light of a lamp in the darkness and thereby perceive forms, this would be called 'seeing with the eyes.
Then, if a person in the darkness were to obtain the light of a lantern in the darkness and thereby perceive forms, it should likewise be so."
Regarding the designation "lamp sees": if the lamp possessed seeing, then the lamp itself would be the seer and should not be called a "lamp.

If the eye possessed seeing, then the eye itself would be the seer and should not be called an "eye. One should know that the lamp acts as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) only insofar as it can manifest form;
it cannot see form. That which sees form is the eye, not the lamp. By this analogy, one should understand the nature of the eye.
"If it is merely a dominant condition that can manifest color but cannot itself see color, then this nature of seeing color must be the mind and not the eye.
Venerable sir, you have previously mistakenly treated these two as distinct;

today the World-Honored One has merged them into one—what is called 'separating them results in injury to both, while merging them results in beauty for both. [The Master] asked: 'What is the nature of seeing?'"
Question: What is the distinction regarding the mind? Answer: Herein, the nature of seeing is precisely the "seeing-division" (*darśana-bhāga*) of the *ālaya-vijñāna*;
because it is called "seeing" when located in the eye, it refers to the nature of seeing as being the mind itself.

One must understand that although this teaching by the World-Honored One brings the faculty of seeing back to the mind, it also implicitly bestows the illuminating path-eye of the wondrous mind, which is inseparable from it.
The realization of the nature of seeing arises because Ānanda had hitherto known only that the nature of seeing is the eye, and did not know that the nature of seeing is the mind;

therefore, [the Buddha] reverses this by saying, "This is the mind, not the eye. The two characters "mind" (心) correspond to the "not-mind" (非心) mentioned previously, precisely meaning that what was previously refuted as the "perceiving subject" (能緣) is not the mind, whereas that which is your ability to see is indeed the mind. Since you now know the perceiver...
To realize that "the seer is this mind" and thus know that it is the capacity to see, not the eye, settles at once the long-standing attachment to the notion that the mind knows while the eyes see;
it is what is called "a single drop of ink forming two dragons."
Although Ānanda had heard these words along with the great assembly, their mouths remained silent while their minds were not yet enlightened;
they still hoped that the Tathāgata would compassionately proclaim his instructions, so they joined their palms, purified their hearts, and waited expectantly for the Buddha’s merciful teaching.
This was because the interlocutor had not yet realized it; he waited for further elucidation.

Although the World-Honored One’s teaching was without deficiency and he pointed out that the nature of seeing is the mind—the tranquil and eternal nature of the mind—the interlocutor, despite his deep faith in the Buddha’s words, remained silent.
However, as the fetters of consciousness were not yet opened, he could not attain realization and thus still hoped for a further proclamation. First...
"Dechun, it is precisely because things are so extremely clear that what is attained is made to seem slow; this is indeed true.
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his hand, which was marked with webs of soft cotton-like light, and opened his five fingers as he instructed Ānanda and the great assembly:
"When I first attained the Way, in the Deer Park, for the sake of Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya and the other five bhikṣus..."
Furthermore, you and your fourfold assembly have said that all sentient beings fail to achieve Buddhahood or Arhatship solely because they are deluded by adventitious afflictions;
for what reason did you yourselves attain enlightenment at that time and now achieve the fruits of sainthood?
The Tathāgata, wishing to cause his disciples to assist from the side and provide verbal clarification for the sake of illumination, posed this question.

Although the World-Honored One used the analogy of a blind man gazing into darkness—whose vision remains unimpaired—to reveal to him the wondrous mind and the eye of the Way, Ānanda had long been entangled by the two obstacles; he remained submerged and sluggish, unable to attain awakening.

Having attained awakening, he skillfully employed expedient means to once again present the proven remedy from former times; feigning a question to his disciples, he caused those of like standing to understand through an indirect line of reasoning.
This was because he wished to spare himself while casting the calamity upon others; thus he said, "When I first attained the Way," and so forth.
The Deer Park was the place where the ancient kings used to graze deer. The five bhikṣus were [the disciples of] the Buddha.
When he was first a crown prince, the King commanded five men to attend upon him:

first, Aśvajit (translated here as Mashiáng), second, Bāṣpa (translated here as Xiáxián), third, Mahānāman (of his paternal clan), fourth, Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya (translated here as Jiěběnjiè), and fifth, Kāśyapa (translated here as Yìnguāng, of his maternal clan). Among these five bhikṣus...
Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya was the first to attain realization.
At that time, Kauṇḍinya rose and addressed the Buddha: "I am now the eldest among this great assembly and alone have earned the name 'Realized' (*ājñāta*).

This is because I attained the fruit of the path through my awakening to the two terms 'adventitious' (*āgantuka*) and 'dust' (*rajas*). World-Honored One, it is like a traveler who stops over at an inn or stays there for the night."
Or, having finished eating a meal, one packs for the journey ahead and does not remain settled; if the host truly has no intention of receiving them as guests, they will likewise not stay.
Reflecting thus, non-abiding is called "guest-staying" and staying is called "host. This is because that which does not abide is defined by the meaning of being a guest.
Furthermore, it is like when after a fresh clearing of the skies, the bright sun rises and its light enters through a crack in a wall, illuminating all that exists within the void of space.

"The appearance of dust and the substance of dust shake the void, yet the void remains tranquil. Contemplating in this way, that which is clear and still is called "void," and that which shakes is called "dust";
thus, that which shakes is defined as the meaning of "dust. The Buddha said, "It is so."

This is Dignāga’s own account of his realization. When the Tathāgata first attained the fruit [of Buddhahood], he turned the Wheel of the Four Truths for the five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya, and revealed the two characters of "adventitious dust" (*āgantuka-rajas*).

Because Dignāga was the first to understand this, it was as if a high monk on a wall responded immediately upon being called; thus, he declared his place of realization, which is known as "striking and singing" (*kua-chang*).
Together they follow and respond to the beat to form a rhythm; it is like first setting forth the realization that this illusory body is the Truth of Suffering.
The traveler is a metaphor for the physical body; the inn where he stays is a metaphor for lodging within the three realms.

Whether staying overnight or eating, it is a metaphor for the great and small years of life, having no leisure to dwell in peace—a metaphor for the transition when retribution ends. It is from this that the characteristics of the body undergo change.
Because they flow without ceasing, they are likened to traveling guests. An ancient poem says: "Human life within heaven and earth is like that of a traveler on a distant journey.
Li Bai, the Imperial Scribe, said: "Heaven and earth are the inn for all things; yin and yang are the overnight guests for a hundred-year span.
These can both be inferred by analogy. If one were truly the master, there would be no place to go; "syou" (攸) means "place" or "destination."
This means that the host always dwells in his place without coming or going.

Through such reflection and observation, once one has personally seen the host within this impermanent body, one knows that that which migrates and does not abide is called a guest, while that which does not migrate and remains eternally is called the host. Furthermore, it is as when one awakens to this delusion.

The mind is the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). The metaphor of a clear sky after a fresh rain, with the bright sun rising, illustrates the initial attainment of the sun of wisdom upon breaking through the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

The metaphor of light entering through a crack and illuminating the appearance of dust motes in the air illustrates that when the sun of wisdom has a single opening of clarity, it first attains the power to perceive the eighty-one grades of subtle afflictions of thought (*anuśaya*).
When the substance of dust moves while empty space remains tranquil, one perceives the movement of the dust and thereby realizes the immobility of space.
I have thus reflected and observed that within the midst of distracted thoughts, I have realized the principle of emptiness;
therefore, I know that that which wavers and moves is called "dust," and that which does not abide is called "space. However, this is not merely for Ānanda’s sake.
Since this thorough exposition of the great meaning also serves as a transmission of the World-Honored One’s own dharma-intent, the World-Honored One certified it, saying, "So it is.
Thereupon, in the midst of the great assembly, the Tathāgata bent his five fingers; having bent them, he opened them again; and having opened them, he bent them once more.
He said to Ānanda, "What do you see now? Ānanda replied, "I see the Tathāgata’s palms, adorned with a hundred jewels, opening and closing amidst the assembly.
The Buddha asked Ānanda, "Do you see my hands opening and closing amidst the assembly?
Is it my hands that open and close, or is it your vision that opens and closes? Ānanda replied, "World-Honored One, it is your jewel-adorned hands amidst the assembly..."
"The opening and closing of my hands is like the Tathāgata’s own hands opening and closing; it is not that the nature of my seeing has opening and closing.
The Buddha asked, "What moves and what is still? Ānanda replied, "The Buddha’s hands do not remain still, yet my nature of seeing is not even stillness;
what, then, could be 'not remaining'? The Buddha said, "It is so."

This was first verified through the examination of the hand. The World-Honored One, seeing that Cennapa had articulated the two meanings of adventitious dust and the primary space, intended to lead Ānanda to realize the primary through the adventitious and realize space through the dust.

To draw him toward the location where the hand was opened and closed so that he might discern it, the Buddha asked him about the opening and closing of the hand, saying: "What do you see? Ānanda responded in full detail.
Ananda answered truthfully, "I see the World-Honored One’s hand opening and closing among the assembly.
The World-Honored One pressed him further, saying, "Do you see my hand opening and closing among the assembly?
Is it my hand that has the opening and closing, or is it your vision that has the opening and closing? Ananda replied offhand, "I see the Tathagata’s hand opening and closing by itself."

"World-Honored One, the opening and closing of my visual nature do not correspond to the opening and closing of the eyes. Because the World-Honored One perceived the resonance within these words, he examined him and asked, "What moves and what is still?

The World-Honored One, with a heart of profound compassion and sincerity, sought to reach the very bottom of the matter for the sake of others; thus, he further examined who was moving and who was still.

Ānanda, having exhausted all attempts at evasion, now took full responsibility and answered anew that it was his head that moved while his vision remained unmoving—so-called, "even if there are a thousand ways."
Since the wind does not ultimately differ in its nature across different blades of grass, the World-Honored One further confirmed this, saying: "It is thus.
This means that if one knows the head moves while the seeing remains unmoving, this is the principle that adventitious defilements are distinct from the fundamental emptiness.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed the great assembly: "If sentient beings designate that which is in motion as 'dust' and that which does not abide as 'guest,' then consider this:
Ānanda, you observe your own head moving back and forth, yet your vision remains unmoved;
you observe my hand opening and closing, yet your vision neither expands nor contracts. How is it that you now take that which moves to be your body?"
Taking movement as their object, from beginning to end, they undergo birth and extinction in every thought-moment; thus they lose the true nature and act with inverted views.
Their fundamental nature and mind having become false, they mistake external objects for themselves, revolving within this cycle and taking upon themselves the process of wandering through saṃsāra.
Although this appears to be a reprimand directed at the great assembly, it is in fact intended to bring Ānanda to realization by means of the assembly.

Seeing that the Venerable One had mastered the meaning of the immovability of the emptiness of the subject, the World-Honored One stirred up the assembly—this being the intent of "beating the grass to startle the snake"—meaning:

The two aspects of manifestation—arising and ceasing, and non-arising and non-ceasing—both reveal the nature of the mind.

The Buddha said to the Great King: "Your body is present now; I ask you again: does this body of yours remain eternally like a diamond, indestructible, or will it eventually decay and perish?
"World-Honored One," [the King replied], "this body of mine will ultimately undergo transformation and perish. The Buddha said:

"Great King, you have never before been extinguished; how then do you know of extinction? "World-Honored One, although this impermanent and decaying body of mine has never before been extinguished, I observe that it changes and passes away from moment to moment before my eyes. It is ever-new and does not abide; like fire turning to ash, it gradually dissolves and perishes.
As this process of perishing continues without ceasing, I know for certain that this body must eventually reach total extinction. The Buddha said, "It is so."
Because I wish to demonstrate the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing, I first examine its arising and ceasing. I say: "You harbor doubts regarding the place where you will die in the future;
I shall question you based solely on the place where you are currently living. I require you to investigate this for yourself:

If one can know extinction, one can also know birth; yet you do not yet know birth—how then can you know death?

To this, I now provide my answer: this body will ultimately follow the path of transformation.

Hanging from a cliff amidst the dew, an old tree flashes like lightning in one's eyes; one must decisively realize that this body will ultimately perish and only then attain liberation.
When the Buddha spoke thus, he sealed [the disciple’s] realization that this body is a phenomenon of impermanence and rapid decay.

therefore, we know that this body will ultimately undergo transformation and extinction.
This further carefully examines the suddenness or gradualness of arising and ceasing. Your physical form likely does not decay all at once;

How could that which is fundamentally without arising or ceasing undergo birth and death for you? Yet you still cite the likes of Maskari Gośālīputra, who claimed that this body..."
Upon hearing these words, King Sarvamṛtyu understood with faith that after death one abandons this life to pass on to another;
together with his great assembly, he leaped for joy and experienced what he had never known before.
Furthermore, when he carefully examined the vision of the river, he saw those who were young and old, yet when he sought their answers, he saw neither the young nor the old.
The World-Honored One clearly pointed this out, meaning: although your face is wrinkled, the essence of seeing is not wrinkled.
That which is wrinkled changes, while that which is not wrinkled does not change; that which changes perishes, while that which does not change does not perish.

This very [essence] is the nature of non-arising and non-perishing within the body of arising and perishing. As the former sages said: "If you wish to recognize the immortal one within the hermitage..."
How could a person be separate from this present skin-bag? Though the countenance may appear youthful or aged, the seeing-nature remains undiminished;

though light and darkness come and go, the numinous light is never obscured. This is the treasure within the poor son’s garment, the jewel in the wheel-turning king’s topknot, and the gold in the poor woman’s chamber—it is the very substance within the Tathāgata-garbha. How can you look down upon it?

Pushing their understanding to its limit, they disparage themselves as mere commoners and seek exclusively outwardly, unable to reflect within. Having wasted many kalpas in this way, they turn their backs on their own numinous spirit;
with empty talk of annihilation, they lose their fundamental true nature. How can you say that within this state you undergo birth and death?
You say that this essence of seeing is neither wrinkled nor changing; how then can it follow your body into the present?

"Do they undergo birth and extinction simultaneously? Since you do not experience birth and extinction in the present, yet claim that this body will be completely extinguished after death—is this not even more erroneous?
Makkhali (translated here as "Not Seeing the Path")—King [Ajātaśatru] heard these words below and turned from the heterodox to the correct path.
"Abandoning birth and proceeding toward birth" means that one realizes the abandonment of this state and the transition to that; it refers to moving from one darkness to another.
Entering one dark chamber and exiting another, or emerging from one wheel of suffering and entering another wheel of suffering, there has never been a moment of cessation.
This chapter, however, achieves cessation through King Nimi’s contemplation upon the body;

the World-Honored One reveals non-arising and non-ceasing through his illumination upon vision—this is what is meant by "not leaving the path beneath the flowers, yet being led into the heavens within the cave. This.

Thus, this not only refutes King Prasenajit’s view of nihilism, but also answers Ānanda’s two-fold request. Question: Formerly, National Teacher Zhong asked a Zen practitioner, "From where have you come? The practitioner replied, "From the South. The Master asked, "How do the teachers (jñāna-sākṣin) of the South instruct people? He replied, "The teachers of that region directly point out [the nature] to the students. The Master said, "And what do they point out? The practitioner replied, "They point out that mind is Buddha. The Master said, "If so, then all sentient beings are already Buddhas; why must they seek it further? The practitioner was speechless. The Master then said, "I do not say that mind is Buddha; I say that the Buddha is mind. The practitioner again asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master replied, "The very one who asks is the Buddha. The practitioner was again speechless. The Master then said, "I do not say that mind is Buddha, nor do I say that the Buddha is mind; I simply say that mind is not mind, and no-mind is Buddha. The practitioner was again speechless. The Master then said, "You have come from the South; have you seen the Great Master Mazu? The practitioner replied, "I have seen him. The Master asked, "What did he say? The practitioner replied, "He said, 'Directly pointing at the human mind, seeing one's nature and becoming a Buddha. The Master laughed heartily and said, "That fellow has a mouth like a bowl! The mind is the Buddha, and the Buddha is the meaning of awakening. You now fully possess the nature of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing;
this nature is well able to raise the eyebrows, blink the eyes, come and go, and function throughout the body. When the head is touched, the head knows; when the foot is touched, the foot knows.
For this reason, it is called "Perfect Universal Knowledge" (Samyak-saṃbuddha). Apart from this, there is no other Buddha. This very body is—
The mind-nature undergoes neither birth nor death, while the body undergoes birth and death.
It is like a dragon shedding its bones, a snake sloughing its skin, or a person leaving an old house; the body is impermanent, but its nature is eternal. The Master said:
"If that were so, there would be no difference between this and the non-Buddhist heretic Śreṇika. He claimed: 'Within this body of mine, there is a spirit.'"

This nature is the capacity to perceive sensations; when the body perishes, the spirit departs, just as when a house is burning, the owner leaves and the house is impermanent while the owner is permanent. To examine it thus is to fail to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox.
Now, the Tathāgata reveals that what is wrinkled undergoes change, while what is not wrinkled does not undergo change; he has attained the state where there is neither "with" nor "half."
The principle that "half is arising, half is ceasing" and "neither arising nor ceasing" is identical to the answer given to the State [of Wu].

Both the refutation of the attachment to a single moment and the opening of the provisional teaching of a single moment are sublime eloquence. One should grasp this through the meaning; do not recklessly indulge in conjecture, for you will incur the censure of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated before the Buddha, joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha:

"World-Honored One, if this faculty of seeing and hearing is indeed neither produced nor extinguished, why does the World-Honored One say that we have lost our true nature and act in a state of delusion?
We pray that you will arouse your compassion and wash away our defilements."
This reason is given to answer the arising of doubt. Because King Ajātaśatru’s knowledge and insight were not extensive, his mind was illuminated by a single word and he proceeded directly to faith.
Ānanda, however, possessed great knowledge and vision; because he was prone to emotional attachment regarding encountered matters, he only believed after a time and then suddenly doubted.
This doubt arose from hearing the words "losing the true nature and acting in a perverted manner," leading him to think:
Because there exists a nature of non-arising and non-ceasing distinct from arising and ceasing, I request that you clarify the natures of arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-non-ceasing.

Furthermore, regarding the doubt concerning the essence of hearing and seeing—that it is unchanging yet subject to movement—I mean this: if one thinks that seeing and hearing must necessarily be subject to arising and ceasing, then they can be called "lost";
since these acts of seeing and hearing are necessarily neither arising nor ceasing, they are quiescent and eternal, and thus identical with all [phenomena].
Since there is no difference between Buddhas and ourselves, why does the World-Honored One say that we have lost our true nature and act with inverted minds,
while not saying the same of the Buddhas? It is as if one were to obtain the "reviving soul" incense and yet strike the "poisonous drum."
Immediately, the Tathāgata extended his golden arm and lowered his hand to point toward Ānanda, saying:
"Do you now see my *mudrā* hand as upright or inverted? Ānanda replied: "To the sentient beings of the world, this is considered inverted;
I do not know who is upright and who is inverted. The Buddha told Ānanda: "If people of the world consider this to be inverted, then..."
"What do people of the world take to be upright? Ānanda replied, "If the Tathāgata raises his arm—his hand being as soft as *tūla* cotton—and points it toward the sky, that is called 'upright.

The Buddha then raised his arm and said to Ānanda, 'If this inverted state were to exchange its head and tail, and people of the world were to gaze at it even more intently, then you would know that your own body and those of all the Tathāgatas are equally pure.'"
The Dharma-body is elucidated through analogy as the body of the Tathāgata, named the Truly All-Knowing One (*samyak-saṃbuddha*). Your own bodies are called "perverted in nature.
As you contemplate your own bodies with earnest attention, consider where the name "perversion" applies: in what sense is your body called the Buddha-body, and where is the name "perversion" applied?
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly gazed fixedly at the Buddha with unblinking eyes, their vision clouded and bewildered, not knowing [where the distinction lay].
The place where the body and mind are inverted:
here, the World-Honored One lowered his hand to verify their inverted state of mind. *Mudrā*—translated as "seal"—refers to the marks and signs of the hands.
Ānanda, having once suffered the poisoned hand [of Devadatta], did not dare take responsibility for it himself, but instead cast the blame upon another.
Because the sentient beings of the world provide answers, it is said, "The sentient beings of the world," and so forth. The World-Honored One pressed him further, saying:
"If people of the world consider this to be inverted, then what would they take as upright? Ānanda twisted the straight into a curve and replied:
"If the Tathāgata points upward with his hand, that is called upright. The World-Honored One took his error and used it.

Pointing directly at the error, he raised his arm and declared: "If you truly consider this upward-pointing finger to be correct, then this is precisely a case of placing the crown upon the shoes, turning the head into a tail and the tail into a head. Where else would you seek such inversion?
Furthermore, this single arm is inherently neither inverted nor correct; it is the entire world that, in relation to the arm, distinguishes between right and wrong."
Therefore it is said: "Twofold is this biased view. How could you know that looking downward is inverted? Indeed, looking downward is inversion;
looking upward is correct, yet even that is inversion. How can you take looking upward as correct and looking downward as inverted?
Because you all have given rise to this twofold view, whereas the Tathāgata does not hold such a view, I shall now show you your own body and the Tathāgata’s pure [body].
If one were to clarify the analogy of the Dharma-body, the body of the Tathāgata is titled the "Perfectly All-Knowing One" (Samyak-saṃbuddha).

Your own bodies, however, are called "inverted" because they deviate from their true nature (*dharmatā*). To claim that you are equal to the Buddha and without distinction, while not admitting this is an inversion, is an error.

Since you have already been shown to be inverted through this clarification, I shall further prick you with the needle of inquiry to compel you to seek the reality behind the name and examine yourselves.

Because there is a basis for this inversion, it is said: "Examine your own body with diligent scrutiny according to your own understanding, and by comparing it with the body of the Tathāgata, you shall realize that the body of the Tathāgata is called 'Rightly All-Knowing. Your own bodies, however, are called 'inverted' in accordance with their nature.
Since you already possess the name 'inversion,' there must necessarily be a reality to that inversion. From what actual basis does it arise?"
This is why Ānanda was given that name: when the World-Honored One questioned him once, he was like one who has eyes but is blind, or has a mouth but is mute;
