he found himself with no words to respond and no principles to defend. Thus it is said: "He did not know where his body and mind were inverted.
This is what is meant by the saying: "Before the face of a person of great wisdom, there is always a darkness three feet deep."
The Buddha, arising in compassion and pitying Ānanda and the great assembly, uttered a voice like the ocean tide to address all the good sons gathered there:
"I have often said that all conditions of form and mind, as well as the mental factors and all objects of cognition, are manifested solely by the mind.
Your body and your mind are both things manifested within this wondrously bright, true, and essential wondrous mind."
"How is it that you have lost your original, wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind, and your precious, bright, and wondrous nature, by mistaking awakening for delusion?
Hereafter, this section correctly reveals the actual locus of inversion; because one must not miss the proper time, it is called the 'sea tide.

'Form' refers to the eleven types of form-dharmas; 'mind' refers to the eight consciousnesses as the sovereign mind-kings; that which can perceive is the mental factors (*caitta*), and that which is perceived is the object."
Because they are objects, it is said that "the various conditions" refer to the fifty-one mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) that are employed by the mind;

"the various dharmas that serve as objects" refers to the dissociated phenomena (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). "Manifested solely by the mind" means exclusively;
"mind" here refers to the *tathāgatagarbha*-mind. This states that the five categories of form and mind all manifest within the *tathāgatagarbha*-mind.

Just as images appear in a clear mirror, since all phenomena arise as reflections from the storehouse-consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), it can be known that your body and mind are both objects manifested within the wondrous mind.
The body is identical to the sense-faculties. The body encompasses the sovereign [mind] which dispels the massed darkness and shines alone;
thus it is called "wondrously luminous. It mingles with the myriad things yet stands revealed alone; thus it is called "true essence."

To say that the body and mind are themselves the departure from body and mind is called the "wondrous mind. As for the phrase "how can it be below," this correctly clarifies the actual locus of inversion. Regarding "originally wondrous":
it is inherently wondrous from the beginning and does not depend on cultivation to be perfected. The "perfectly wondrous and luminous mind" is spoken of in terms of responsive communication;
the "precious, luminous, and wondrous nature" is spoken of in terms of immovability. The character "awakening" (wu) refers to the wondrous, luminous, true essence—the wondrous mind.
The character "delusion" (*mi*) refers to body and mind; this is because both the body and mind are phenomena that falsely manifest through the delusion of the wondrously luminous [nature].
Therefore, I mean that your body and mind are both objects manifested within the vast and wondrously luminous mind, exactly like reflections in a mirror or bubbles on the sea.
Yet you take this spirit-like clarity, which is expansive, penetrating, universal, and all-pervading—
To cast aside the wondrous mind and disregard it, while instead identifying this mere, trivial body and mind as one's fundamental nature—is this not to mistake delusion for awakening?
Obscured darkness becomes emptiness;
within the darkening of emptiness, the binding of darkness forms form; form mingles with false thoughts, and the conceptualization of these appearances constitutes the body.

Gathering conditions within, they waver; rushing outward, they flee in wild abandon. Taking this state of turbid confusion as their fundamental nature, they are once deluded into regarding it as the mind, and thus become certain that it resides within the physical body.
They do not know that from the physical body outward, including the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth, all are things within the wondrously luminous true mind.
It is like discarding a clear ocean hundreds of thousands of miles wide and instead recognizing only—
To take the substance of a single bubble as the entirety of the tide and to exhaustively fathom the vast oceans—to do so, you all are people who are doubly lost within delusion.
It is like my stretching out my hand; there is no difference between us. The Tathāgata calls such people those who are to be pitied.
The following clarifies why the body and mind constitute delusion within awakening. It is said that this perfectly luminous and wondrous mind originally possesses no characteristics of body or mind;
yet, due to the initial lack of awareness within the essence of this wondrously luminous mind, it suddenly gives rise to a stirring mind.
This causes the primary meaning of emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) to become obscured and darkened, resulting in a dull emptiness devoid of cognition or sentience.
This means that because ignorance and craving arise, giving rise to pervasive delusion, there is the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Due to this single delusion, and by accumulating delusion upon delusion, one condenses and solidifies within the stubborn void to form the colors of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
That is to say, as deluded transformation does not cease, worlds are born; once the four great elements exist, one again uses false views to grasp at a small portion.

The colors of the four great elements are divided and combined to form the five aggregates and the body of faculties; thus it is said that color is mixed with delusive thoughts, and these thoughts and their characteristics constitute the body.
This refers to how the essence of vision reflects color, and by binding with color, forms the faculty of sight, and so forth.

This is precisely why the body represents delusion within awakening. Since there is already a body of faculties composed of the four great elements, both internally and externally, they combine to produce a delusively existing "conditioned breath."
Within this, they accumulate [mental objects] based on internal reflected images, which stir without ceasing; they pursue external real forms, which they chase without end.

Thus, they remain in a state of dark confusion and agitation—neither clear nor pure—and yet they cling to this very state of dark confusion and agitation as being the true, subtle, wondrous mind and the precious, luminous, wondrous nature. This is precisely why the mind is [as it is].
To awaken within delusion is to be already lost; once deluded in this way, this state of murky confusion and agitation is itself the wondrously luminous nature of the mind.

Yet, one further confuses this wondrously luminous nature by seeking it within the physical body, failing to realize that not only is this body an object manifested within the wondrously luminous mind, but even the empty space and the vessel-world are all the wondrously luminous mind itself.

These are objects manifested within [the mind]. Now, you abandon this vast and wondrous mind to falsely identify the four elements as the characteristics of your own body and the reflected shadows of the six sense-objects as the characteristics of your own mind.
How is this different from abandoning the hundreds of thousands of clear and pure oceans and instead identifying a single floating bubble within them as the entirety of the tide in the sea?

This great ocean is also contained within this [body]; viewed in this way, one knows that when your body and the Tathāgata’s body are compared and illuminated, although they are of the same substance and fundamentally without distinction, the Tathāgata has fully realized that the ocean is the ocean and the bubble is the bubble.
Because he does not abandon the ocean to recognize the bubble, it is said that he possesses "correct knowledge" (*samyag-jñāna*), whereas you do not recognize the bubble as the ocean.
Therefore it is said: "You have universally known [the truth], yet you have abandoned the ocean to recognize a bubble, and further recognized that bubble as the ocean.
Thus it is called "inverted nature. This is why I say that you are people who have added a double layer of delusion upon delusion.

It is just like when I hang my hand down: in reality, there is no distinction between inversion and correctness, yet you take this downward hanging to be inverted and the upward [pointing] to be correct.
I point to this very thing as being the locus of your perversion; therefore, know that you originally had nothing lost.
It is due to perversion that you claim there is loss—this is precisely why the Tathāgata calls you "those to be pitied. The meaning is this:
if you had truly lost [something], it would not be so deeply pitiable; it is because of your perversion that you are thus [constantly deluded].
"To lose [this] is like a pearl-holder who becomes a beggar and suffers in poverty; it is for this reason that the Tathāgata feels such deep compassion.
Ānanda, receiving the Buddha’s compassionate salvation and profound instruction, wept, joined his palms, and said to the Buddha: "Although I have received the Buddha’s..."
"Thus, Wondrous Sound, you have awakened to the wondrously luminous mind—the fundamental ground of the heart that is originally perfect and eternally abiding.

Yet, as for my awakening to the Buddha’s present preaching of the Dharma, I currently rely on the conditioned mind to look up in reverence; I have merely obtained this mind and do not yet dare to recognize it as my original fundamental ground of the heart.
I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will proclaim his perfect voice to uproot my doubts and lead me back to the Unsurpassed Way."
This third instance concerns the present function and further identifies the perceiving subject.

Regarding the "compassionate rescue," it means that after ten thousand kalpas of being suspended upside down and a lifetime of delusion, one suddenly attains enlightenment; yet, because the mind still harbors doubt, he weeps once more and asks:
"Although I have received the Buddha’s words and realized that this wondrous, luminous mind is my very own self..."
Originally, the ground of the mind is fully endowed with perfection, unborn and undying, eternally abiding;
yet we have consistently neglected this vast and true nature, instead identifying this murky and turbulent state as the nature of the mind.
Therefore, it is only fitting that we are called "those whose nature is inverted. Nevertheless, my current seeing of the Buddha and hearing of the Dharma both rely upon conditions.
Although the World-Honored One does not wish for me to recognize this mind and instead rejects it as "not-mind," I dare not fail to recognize it because its function is obtained.

When the World-Honored One requires me to recognize it, he refers to the Perfectly Wondrous Mind; yet, although it is vast and great, its function is not currently manifest, and I merely possess it in vain.
For these reasons, I again dare not recognize it. This is precisely what the Venerable Master [Dōgen] intended.

When one is still unsteady in their practice and the provisional mind and the true mind are held simultaneously without resolution—like a person confused at a fork in the road, dazed and uncertain—one must request that the root of doubt be uprooted.
Only upon reaching the ground of non-doubt can one return to the Unsurpassed Way. As the Honored Ancestors said:
"It is easy to keep one's mouth open from beginning to end, but difficult to preserve a heart steadfast through the winter cold. Master Zongze.

From this point forward, one must proceed until each person individually knows that the mind pervades the ten directions and attains the original wondrous mind, which is eternally abiding and imperishable;
only then will they be willing to acknowledge it. This "acknowledgment" (認) corresponds to the "acknowledgment" (認) mentioned previously in the phrase "delusion within awakening."
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If you and the others still listen to the Dharma with a conditioned mind, this Dharma is also merely a condition and you do not attain the nature of the Dharma.
It is like a person pointing at the moon with their finger to show it to another; that person, because of the finger, ought to look at the moon.
If, however, they observe the finger and take it to be the substance of the moon, would this person not only lose sight of the lunar orb, but also lose the finger itself? Why is this?"
Since that which was pointed out was intended to be the bright moon, you have not only lost the finger, but moreover fail to recognize brightness and darkness. Why is this?
It is because you take the substance of the finger itself to be the nature of the moon's brightness; thus, the two natures of brightness and darkness remain entirely unapprehended.
You are just like this.
This rebukes him for recognizing the sense-object of sound while failing to realize the *dharmatā*. The character "shàng" (尚) is a term of reproach indicating a fault;
it means: "I have thus laid bare my heart and soul, lingering among the grasses to urge you to abandon delusive conditions and realize the *dharmatā*.
Yet, I did not expect that your understanding remains not a hair’s breadth different from what it was before. Furthermore, since you..."

If you listen with a conditioned mind to my teaching on the dharma-principle of the perfect and eternally abiding mind, then that perfect and eternally abiding mind will instead become an object of perception; how then could you possibly realize this nature of reality?
You should know that the one who preaches the Dharma is like a person pointing at the moon. If, after preaching the Dharma, you were to cut off all speech and cast away all cleverness—
Relinquish everything and silently investigate your own mind; this is like one who points at the moon and does not dwell on the finger.

If you continue as before, possessing much knowledge and many explanations while refusing to resolve them back into yourself, you are merely chasing words phrase by phrase—a person who mistakes the pointing finger for the moon.
If you mistake the finger for the moon, not only will you fail to recognize the moon, you will also fail to...
Pointing with a finger not only means failing to recognize the finger, but it also means failing to recognize light and darkness; for one points toward the dark using the moon’s light as a reference.

Now, you cling to the sound of the Dharma without penetrating the nature of the Dharma—how is this different from those who mistake the finger for the moon, who cannot distinguish black from white, and who remain unaware of the difference between dusk and dawn? Therefore, it is said: "You are also like this, O Mirror of the Source."

It is said: "If you wish to investigate the Buddha-vehicle and explore the precious treasury, you must bring every word back to yourself and cause each phrase to merge in silent accord with the true mind.
Do not cling to the literal meaning of the texts or allow your understanding to follow the words;
you must instead probe beneath the expressions to reach their underlying intent and harmonize with the fundamental source. In this way, the Way of innate truth will remain unclouded."

If the Master’s wisdom is manifest before you, yet you consistently turn your back on it to pursue the literal text, clinging to learning and giving rise to disputation, this is like addressing a wooden man to expect him to speak or waiting for a barren woman to give birth to a child;
you will pass through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in vain, never attaining the principle.

If you consider this mind that discriminates the sounds of my teaching as being your own mind, then this mind should inherently possess the nature of discrimination even apart from those discriminating sounds.
It would be like a traveler staying overnight at an inn who departs immediately after resting and never remains permanently;
yet the innkeeper, who stays there and goes nowhere, is called the master of the inn. This [mind] is just like that—if it were truly your mind.
If there is nowhere to go, how can one be free from the nature of non-discrimination regarding sound?

Is it not the case that this applies not only to sound, but that the discriminating mind may likewise be free from the nature of non-discrimination regarding the forms of the self and all other material phenomena (*rūpa*)?

In this way, until discrimination is entirely absent—neither form nor emptiness—the Kauśika and others take their ignorance for the "Dark Truth" (*tattva*), attaining a state of non-discrimination by being free from the conditions of all dharmas.
"Then your mind-nature has its own respective places of return; how can it be the master?
This rebukes the recognition of the deluded mind while failing to recognize the true mind. The deluded mind is like a guest, while the true mind is like the host;
the guest comes and goes, but the host remains unmoving. If you recognize this mind that discriminates the sounds of the Dharma—[it is merely a guest].
If you consider these to be real, then this mind should possess an essential nature independent of sound; why is it that upon the departure of sound, its nature vanishes?
Not only do I discriminate that my voice lacks nature when separated from sound, but I also discriminate that my appearance lacks nature when separated from my physical form (*rūpa*).
Since all of these belong to the discriminative function of the first six deluded consciousnesses, they are certainly not [real].

Even though the true mind (zhēn xīn) has no place for the six preceding types of discrimination (*vikalpa*) to exist as a separate self-nature (*svabhāva*), being neither material nor empty, it is precisely this seventh [consciousness] that takes the eighth as its object;
it is a "borderline" (*dai zhì*) object, which is both a form of discrimination and yet not a self-nature.
The Sāṃkhya teachers, being deluded and ignorant of this, consequently cling to it as the primordial self-nature (*prakṛti*).
Therefore, one should know that even though the eighth consciousness (the ālayavijñāna) is uninterrupted by its seven conditions, it is not yet the self-nature;

how much less so for the intermittent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which flows and shifts from moment to moment—how could one cling to it as the self-nature, reckoning it to have practical utility, and refuse to relinquish it?
Thus, auditory consciousness exists because of sound and is absent when separated from sound, and so on, up to mental consciousness, which exists because of dharmas.
If there is a dharma of departure, then such [a mind] does not exist; thus, both your mind and its nature would belong to the category of the adventitious, each having its own place of return.
Where, then, is your master? Will you remain forever a novice monk without a master?
Ānanda said: "If my mind-nature has various things to which it returns, then why does the Tathāgata say that this wondrous, luminous, original mind has nothing to which it returns?
I pray that you will deign to show compassion and explain this for me."

This question returns [the inquiry] to request why there is no returning. "Returning" is like borrowed goods that must necessarily be returned to their owner; if it were one's own house, there would be nowhere to return it. Therefore, he asks: while the conditioned mind has various things to which it returns, why is it that the wondrously luminous primordial mind has no place to return? The answer is: Formerly, Zhang Wugou visited Shanquan. Shanquan said: "If you wish to know the Buddha-nature, you must first understand the nature of the mind. What is the nature of the mind? It is like a mirror. When a mirror reflects an image, the image is not in the mirror, nor is it outside the mirror; it is neither inside nor outside. The nature of the mind is also like this. When the mind perceives objects, the objects are not in the mind, nor are they outside the mind; they are neither inside nor outside. This is called the 'unobstructed nature. Because it is unobstructed, it can manifest as all phenomena. Because it manifests as all phenomena, it is called the 'all-encompassing nature. Because it is all-encompassing, it is called the 'Buddha-nature. Zhang Wugou asked: "If the nature of the mind is like a mirror, when a person dies, the body decays and perishes, yet the consciousness does not perish. Since the body and consciousness are different, how can they be of the same substance? Furthermore, the body is material and obstructive, while consciousness is immaterial and unobstructed. How can the unobstructed become obstructed, and the obstructed become unobstructed? Shanquan replied: "The body and consciousness are not two separate things. They are like the waves and the water. The waves are the water, and the water is the waves. When the wind blows, the water stirs and forms waves; when the wind ceases, the waves subside and return to the water. The nature of the mind is also like this. When conditions arise, consciousness arises; when conditions cease, consciousness ceases. Consciousness is not different from the body; the body is not different from consciousness. They are one and the same substance, appearing differently according to conditions. This is why it is said that the obstructed is the unobstructed, and the unobstructed is the obstructed. Zhang Wugou asked: "If the nature of the mind is like a mirror, when a person looks at themselves in a mirror, the reflection appears clearly. But when a person looks at another person, the reflection is not as clear. Why is this so? Shanquan replied: "When looking at oneself, the distance is near, so the reflection is clear. When looking at another, the distance is far, so the reflection is not as clear. This is because the clarity of the reflection depends on the proximity of the object. The nature of the mind is also like this. When perceiving objects, the clarity of the perception depends on the proximity of the conditions. Therefore, the clarity of the mind is not fixed; it varies according to circumstances. Zhang Wugou asked: "If the nature of the mind is like a mirror, when a person dies, the mirror is broken. Since the mirror is broken, where does the reflection go? Shanquan replied: "The mirror is broken, but the nature of the mirror is not destroyed. The reflection returns to its source. The nature of the mind is also like this. When the body perishes, the consciousness returns to its original source. That source is the wondrously luminous primordial mind. Because that mind is originally without coming or going, it has no place to return. Zhang Wugou asked: "If the wondrously luminous primordial mind has no place to return, then what is the meaning of 'returning' in the context of the conditioned mind? Shanquan replied: "The conditioned mind is like a traveler who must return home. The primordial mind is like the home itself—it is the place of ultimate rest. Because the conditioned mind is subject to birth and death, it must return to its origin. The primordial mind, being eternal and unchanging, has no further destination to reach. This is why we say the conditioned mind has places to return, while the wondrously luminous primordial mind has no place to return. Zhang Wugou was greatly enlightened by these words. He prostrated himself and said: "I have now understood the principle of the mind. I shall never again doubt the teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. This is the answer to the question regarding the returning and non-returning of the mind.
Master Qing asked, "Is it not true that this matter is the share of every person and is fully accomplished by each and every one? Master Qing replied, "Indeed.
The official said, "If so, why is there no point of entry for me? Master Qing took a rosary from his sleeve and showed it to him, saying, "Whose is this?
The official lowered his head and had no reply. Master Qing then put the rosary back into his sleeve and said, "If it were yours..."
He immediately picked it up and took it away; as soon as there was any involvement of thought, it was no longer yours. Gong was struck with awe.
Thus one knows that as soon as there is discrimination, there is something that must be returned.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Furthermore, your seeing me—this is the fundamental essence of the clarity of seeing. Although this seeing is not the wondrous, clear, and pure mind,"
"Just as a second moon is not the reflection of the moon, you should listen attentively as I shall now show you the ground from which there is no returning.

From this point downward, he relies on the essence of seeing (*dṛṣṭi-sāra*) to demonstrate the true nature that does not return. As the proverb says, "When meeting a person, speak only three parts of the truth;
do not yet cast away your whole heart," he first uses the essence of seeing to demonstrate it, for it is truly subtle.
The pure, luminous mind, the wondrous nature of the precious jewel, possesses the three great aspects: essence, characteristics, and function.

Due to the non-awakening of ignorance, a single thought of deluded movement arises, whereby this fundamental essence is transformed into the *karmic consciousness* (*ālayavijñāna*). This wisdom-light is transformed into the "seeing portion" (*darśana-bhāga*), which is called the "transforming consciousness" (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
Furthermore, this true object is transformed into the "image portion" (*nimitta-bhāga*), which is called the "manifesting consciousness" (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*). Within this...

The essence of seeing is precisely the nature of the capacity to see; this nature of the capacity to see is the great light of wisdom that universally illumines the Dharma-realm, which is inherent within the substance of original enlightenment. Due to ignorance, this light of wisdom is transformed into the nature of seeing.
When it is now said, "Consider your own seeing and my seeing—the pure source of clarity," this specifically refers to Ānanda’s seeing.
At the time of the thirty-two marks, this point of luminosity is fundamentally inherent;

it is not borrowed from the light of the sun, moon, or lamps, and is therefore called the "source of luminosity. Because it responds to the eye-faculty to perceive objects without confusion, it is called the "seeing-essence" (*jien-jing*).
Although this seeing is a refined essence that is neither obscured nor confused, its substance still carries delusion, and the capacity for subjectivity still remains.

That which cannot be obtained through mutual interchange cannot be called "wondrous"; yet, because its essence is itself the Truth, it is like the second moon—it is not like the reflection of the moon in water, which is separated from the true moon by a single layer.

Because this wondrously luminous primordial mind fundamentally has no form or appearance, nor any location or direction, it is ultimately difficult to point out; therefore, one relies upon the visual essence (*dṛk-śuddha*) as a skillful means to reveal it.
This demonstrates that if one awakens to and perceives the seeing-essence (*darśana-vijñāna*), then the wondrously luminous primordial mind can be transcendentally realized.

There are three metaphors for this: first, the true moon represents the wondrously luminous primordial mind; second, the second moon represents the seeing-essence; third, the moon’s reflection represents the discrimination of conditioned objects.

These correspond to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) taught in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*: namely, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and [the imagined nature].
This is the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Ānanda, in this great lecture hall, when the eastern sky is opened wide and the sun rises, there is brilliant radiance;

at midnight during the dark fortnight, when clouds and mist shroud the light, it becomes obscure and dim; through the gaps of doors and windows, one perceives openness; yet within the walls and the roof, [one perceives obstruction].
In the intervals between them, one again observes the places where they are obstructed and differentiated; within the midst of the stubborn void, one again sees the pervasive nature of emptiness.
When the dense and turbid forms appear, the murky dust swirls; when it clears and the sky brightens, the miasma contracts.
Observe this, Ānanda: you have all witnessed these various changing phenomena; I shall now return each to its original source. What is that original cause?

Ānanda, these various transformations return to the sun for their illumination. Why is this? There is no light without the sun; illumination is dependent upon the sun, and therefore it returns to the sun.
Darkness returns to the blackness of night; openness returns to doors and windows; obstruction returns to walls and buildings;
conditions return to discrimination; the stubborn void returns to emptiness; density and turbidity return to dust; clarity and brightness return to a cloudless sky. Thus, all things in the world...

There is nothing that does not belong to this category. You perceive these eight kinds of objects; within the luminous clarity of your seeing-nature, toward what would you wish to return? Why is this?

If you were to return to light, then in the absence of light, you would no longer see darkness. Although there are various distinctions such as light and darkness, the seeing itself has no distinction.
Those things which can be returned to are naturally not you; as for that which cannot be returned to, if it is not you, then who is it?

Thus you know that your mind is fundamentally wondrous, luminous, and pure; yet you have become deluded and distressed, losing your original nature and undergoing the cycle of rebirth, constantly drifting and drowning within the source of birth.
For this reason, the Tathāgata calls you "one worthy of compassion."
In order to demonstrate that there is nothing to return, [the Buddha] first sets forth the eight objects that can be returned; their characteristics are eightfold.

"Ānanda, next" [is the section where] he reveals that each of the eight characteristics has something to which it returns—such as light following the sun when it comes and returning with the sun when it goes.

"Your seeing, below" [is the section where] he reveals three points showing that the nature of seeing does not return: for if it returned with light, one would not see darkness; if it returned with darkness...
When not seeing light, you see light now; when seeing light, you see darkness. Thus, you know that the nature of seeing does not come or go.
This nature of seeing is your own substance; it is the radiant sun of the Dharma-nature, functioning day after day and moment after moment without ever ceasing.
It is not like the seeing that discriminates sensory objects, which has coming and going. Therefore, he shows it by saying:
All things that can be returned exist because they are borrowed from external objects; they are naturally not one's own property.
As for that which you cannot return—since it is not something borrowed and is not your own property, whose property could it possibly be?
Simply by recognizing that this nature of seeing does not return, you will know that your mind is fundamentally wondrous, fundamentally luminous, and fundamentally pure.
Seeing the nature is the master among guests; the true mind is the master among masters.
It is for this reason that because you are deluded and do not awaken, you neither recognize the master among guests nor the master among masters.
Consequently, you have lost the true nature and suffer in vain through saṃsāra, emerging and submerging within birth and death with no time of escape. Therefore, I...
I say that you all are truly objects of compassion. Herein, the great lecture hall is a metaphor for the wondrously luminous primordial mind, the unmoving essence;
"light" is a metaphor for wisdom; "darkness" is a metaphor for ignorance; "pervasion" is a metaphor for the six sense faculties.

To be "penetrating," with all eight sides resonant and every place transparent, is to be unobstructed. To be "blocked," with the heart-mind choked like reeds, facing a wall or a barrier, is to be obstructed at every turn.
These obstructions of discrimination are like clouds; the stubborn void is like the indeterminate; the thick mists are like confusion; the clear and cloudless sky is like awakening.
This clearly demonstrates that all manner of illusory transformations arise from the Tathāgata’s wondrously bright, original mind;

yet this wondrously bright, original mind manifests brightness when brightness comes, manifests darkness when darkness comes, manifests penetration when penetration comes, and manifests obstruction when obstruction comes.
In reality, there is no characteristic of seeing, yet it is like a lecture hall where one perceives light, darkness, openness, and obstruction;

these all belong to the nature of seeing (*darśana-dhātu*). Therefore, the text first relies upon the nature of seeing to manifest that which does not return, and subsequently reveals the fundamental purity of the wondrously luminous original mind. Thus, the subsequent passage says: "When seeing sees, that seeing is not seeing; seeing is still..."

Because it is free from views, vision cannot reach its reality; since [the realization] is initiated from within this state, the three characters "Great Lecture Hall" (大講堂) in the analogy are of great significance and must not be treated with negligence.
Ānanda said, "Although I recognize that this nature of seeing has nothing from which it can return, how can I know that it is my true nature?
This arose because, upon hearing that the nature of seeing is itself the Truth, he presented his doubt and requested a definitive resolution;

for in the preceding text, the nature of seeing was first pointed out, and at the end of the second month, it was stated that the nature of seeing is the fundamentally wondrous and luminous mind—a statement that lacked a fixed standard of reference.
To prevent the arising of doubt, he said: "Although I recognize that this seeing-nature has nothing to return to, I do not know how this seeing-nature is precisely my own true nature.
It is said that 'the Great Way is right before one's eyes,' yet it is difficult to realize it right before one's eyes;
therefore, I request a definitive resolution."

The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "I now ask you this: although you have not yet attained the purity of the outflows-free state, by receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power, you see the First Dhyāna without obstruction;

yet Aniruddha sees Jambudvīpa as if looking at an *āmala* fruit in the palm of his hand, and the various Bodhisattvas see hundreds of thousands of worlds, while the Tathāgatas of the ten directions exhaustively perceive even the finest motes of dust."
In the pure land, there is nothing that is not entrusted; sentient beings see through with clarity, not exceeding a mere inch or two.
This refers to the point where the essence of vision encounters the objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) without giving rise to discrimination—this is the true nature.
Seeing the first dhyāna is the measure of the wisdom-eye of those in training (*śaikṣa*). Seeing Jambudvīpa should be understood as "seeing."
The vision of the Arhats and Śrāvakas within the Sahā world is the measure of the Human Eye; the vision of Bodhisattvas across hundreds of thousands of worlds is the measure of the Dharma Eye;
the vision of Buddhas across lands as numerous as motes of dust is the measure of the Buddha Eye;

and the vision that penetrates no more than a few inches of the sentient beings of this world is the measure of the Fleshly Eye. Thus, although the five eyes differ, their five measures are likewise distinct.

At the very moment of perceiving an object, there is likewise a distinction between broad and narrow; however, all such perceptions belong to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), where the essence of seeing illuminates its field without giving rise to conceptual discrimination.
Since we now wish to clarify the true nature right within this, I shall first set forth these five kinds of direct perception.
Wuxing said: *Amala* means "difficult to distinguish"; it resembles a peach but is not a peach, and resembles a crabapple but is not a crabapple.

Therefore, if one asks: since the objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the Buddha and of sentient beings differ as vastly as heaven and earth, how could their direct perceptions of the essence of seeing (*darśana-vidyā*) not be different?

The answer is: the essence of seeing in the direct perception of sentient beings is like a single spark of fire, whereas the essence of seeing in the direct perception of the Buddha is like a great conflagration across the earth; it cannot be said that a single spark is different from the great fire.
It is like fire: by expanding and filling the flame of a single star, it can burn the entire earth.
Thus, although the purity, responsibility, and harmony of the sage differ according to the time, the nature of the sage has never changed.

"Ānanda, furthermore, as you and I observe the palaces where the Four Heavenly Kings dwell, surveying everywhere across water, land, and air, we see various forms—some obscured and some luminous—all of which are nothing but the obstructions left behind by the discrimination of external objects.
You should, at this point, distinguish between self and other. Now, I shall lead you to select from within this faculty of seeing: who is my true essence, and who is..."
"Ānanda, exhaustively investigate the source of your vision regarding material objects. From the palaces of the sun and moon to the seven golden mountains, observe them all thoroughly;

though they consist of various kinds of light, they are material objects and not you. Gradually continue to observe the rising clouds, the flying birds, the moving winds, the stirring dust, the trees, the mountains, the rivers, the grasses, the weeds, humans, and livestock—all are material objects and not you, Ānanda. Thus it was said. These various...
Although the natures of all things, whether near or far, differ from one another, they are equally beheld by your faculty of seeing, which is pure and clear;

thus, while the various categories of objects possess their own distinctions, the nature of seeing remains without difference. This subtle, wondrous, and luminous essence is truly your own nature of seeing.
The following section elucidates how the essence of seeing perceived by direct cognition (*pratyakṣa*) and the objects of direct cognition are neither separate nor identical;

it requires Ānanda to examine and discern for himself amidst the myriad phenomena so as to reveal that that which has form and can be seen is a material object, whereas that which is formless and cannot be seen is the true nature. Therefore, it says: "Furthermore, you and I both see with our eyes."
The various forms and images mentioned previously are all nothing other than the lingering obstructions of the perceptions that differentiate external objects (*pūrvadhātu*).
If your nature of seeing were truly capable of differentiation, you should be able to distinguish self from other within these myriad phenomena.

The phrase "I shall take you" (*jāng nǐ zhě*)—the word *jiāng* here is used in the sense of "to request" or "to invite," as in the line "I shall invite Zhòngzǐ" (*Jiāng Zhòngzǐ xī*) from the *Shī Jīng*. Thus, I say "I [shall] take you."
I ask that you, amidst these myriad phenomena that appear before you, freely discern and choose: who is the nature that sees, and what are the objects that are seen?

Using direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) to illuminate the realm of direct perception—like tongs grasping an object or the eyes extending light to directly illuminate and hold it—you will realize there is no obstruction whatsoever; they are fundamentally one body, originally without self-nature.

He then proceeded step by step, examining each and every phenomenon to ascertain the precise location of the essence of seeing (*darśana-śuddha*), so that the disciple might know it for himself and realize it within himself.
Therefore, he instructed him, saying: "Right now, exhaust the full extent of your faculty of seeing;
first, from a high place, observe carefully everything from the sun and moon palaces downward. Is all that you see not composed of material objects, rather than being your own [seeing]?"
"Have you seen your nature? Next, from a distance, observe thoroughly and completely all around the Seven Golden Mountains.
Are the various lights and radiance you see not all objects, rather than your own seeing-nature?
You should further observe each and every thing in the places where clouds rise, birds fly, and the myriad phenomena of the universe appear. Is everything that you see not [an object]?"

"Are objects not your seeing-nature? Thus, by interrogating him one by one, I intended to cause Ānanda to recognize the Son of Heaven amidst the bustling crowd and to perceive the Old Monk atop the hundred grasses;
this is because seeing-nature is itself all dharmas. Having already caused him to investigate and examine, I further instructed him, saying: "Moreover, you..."
Whether objects seen by the eyes are distant or near, large or small, they all appear within the nature of seeing;

yet your seeing-nature pervades above all phenomena. Although things possess various differences, they are entirely what is illuminated by your pure direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the essence of seeing.
Thus, one knows that the distinctions belong to the objects, not to the seeing itself.
That which perceives nature is precisely this essence that is not mixed with external objects; it is the wondrous, pure, and luminous mind previously described.
This wondrous, pure, and luminous mind is truly your own seeing-nature and nothing else, because the seeing-nature is free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
Thus, the *Zongjing* says: "It is clearly verifiable, utterly beyond discursive thought, and directly realized without [conceptual] measure."

One may wonder who distinguishes between the preceding and the succeeding [moments of consciousness]. Because the first five consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness both take objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as their domain and apprehend the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena, they do not carry names and words and are devoid of conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

If the sixth and seventh consciousnesses were present, they would involve the two types of conceptualization—calculation (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*) and recollection (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*)—and would thus fall into the two valid cognitions of inference (*anumāna*) and non-perception (*abhāva*). Therefore, one knows that this is the nature of seeing.
All-pervasive and profoundly still, it is like a mirror that is ever-luminous, or like space that is unmoving;

while the myriad phenomena naturally emerge and subside, this single nature neither comes nor goes. Furthermore, when the characteristic of correct vision appears, who is it that sees the characteristic?

Because the six objects (ṣaḍ-viṣaya) are dull, they do not establish characteristics of themselves, nor do they bestow them upon others. Because the six faculties (ṣaḍ-indriya) are sharp, they forcibly establish them for themselves.
If, by means of conditions and objects, you can realize that the essence of the realm is fundamentally quiescent and that seeing does not arise of itself, you will enter the equal, true emptiness;
only then can it be called the ultimate realization of the nature of seeing.
If you see this as a thing, then you would also be able to see my seeing; if we were seeing the same thing, that could be called "seeing me."

"When I do not see, how is it that you do not see the place where I do not see? If you were to see this 'not seeing,' it would naturally be a phenomenon of seeing and thus not the mark of that 'not seeing.
If you do not see the ground of my non-seeing, then it is naturally not a thing; how could it be anything other than you?"
This was said because [the Buddha] feared that [Aniruddha] would mistake the object above for his own vision;
thus, he pointed to the very place where the object was seen to demonstrate the "mark of the invisible crown. Therefore it is said:

"If you see this as an object, then I and you both look together upon the Treasure Palace of the Four Heavenly Kings' Supreme Treasury, surveying all that moves on water, land, and through the air at that time; then you..."

One may also observe my own vision. If you claim that when you and I see an object together, you are able to see my seeing, then when I am apart from an object and not seeing it, you ought likewise to see me in that state of being apart from an object and not seeing; why do you not see me then?
If you say that even when one is apart from an object and not seeing an object, one can still see me while I am apart [from an object]...
In the place where objects are not seen, the very place you see as "not seeing" is naturally not that characteristic of non-seeing;
for that characteristic of non-seeing has no location and cannot be seen.
If you do not see the place of my non-seeing, this seeing is naturally not a thing possessing characteristics; since it is not a thing with characteristics, it is not a material entity.
Is this object not precisely your own *uṣṇīṣa* (unseen crown-mark)? This principle clearly demonstrates that the faculty of seeing can see objects, yet the object cannot see the faculty of seeing.
Because the object possesses form and location, it can be seen; because the faculty of seeing is without form and without location, it cannot be seen.
Therefore it is said: "Even if it were to pervade and fill all of space, when one looks for it, not even a speck is seen."
Regarding the characteristic of dust, the *Zongjing* says: "Furthermore, as for the seeing of nature, at the very moment it is seen, it is the self-nature itself.
Because this nature pervades all places, it is clearly manifest and revealed without the slightest obstruction. One cannot see nature by means of nature;
there is no mutual seeing between a 'this' and a 'that'."

Furthermore, when you now see an object, since you have seen the object, the object also sees you; thus, the natures of your bodies would become confused and intermingled, and you, I, and all the world would fail to be established as distinct entities. Ānanda, if it is you who see, then this seeing-nature is not me—it is yours.
This seeing-nature is all-pervasive; if it is not yours, whose is it? Why do you doubt your own true nature? Your very nature is this.
One does not falsely grasp at a self while seeking the real.
This further clarifies that if seeing were a substantial entity, it would result in confusion and intermixture;

for seeing and the object seen would each constitute two parts, standing opposed to one another as adversaries. Therefore, it is said: "If you say that when you now see an object, seeing must necessarily be the object, then [the object]..."

It would also follow that there must be seeing within you; if you see objects and objects also see you, then the natures of all sentient and insentient beings in the world would become confused and disordered, failing to establish their distinct identities.

Furthermore, below [the text] concludes by clarifying that the characteristics of seeing and being seen are distinct and do not become muddled; thus it says: "Now, when you see, this seeing belongs to you; it has nothing whatsoever to do with me."
If it is not mixed, you will know that the nature of seeing is free from all marks; yet, though it is not mixed, it can pervade all things, clearly illuminating them.
Thus, you will know that the nature of seeing is itself all dharmas.
In this way, those things you see—the palaces of the sun and moon, the seven golden mountains, the rising clouds, the flying birds, the moving winds, and the stirring dust—are all your own.
The true nature is all-pervasive and has nothing whatsoever to do with others;
why then do you lack self-confidence and instead harbor doubts? Furthermore, this true nature is something inherently possessed by you;
yet you doubt its authenticity and seek clarification from my lips, asking how one can know it is your own true nature—is this not delusion?
When one speaks of the correct teaching, one should immediately realize this true nature and not seek it elsewhere; thus the *Zongjing* says:

"If, at the moment of entering through faith, one naturally possesses clear and penetrating discernment, then even at the stage of complete and thorough understanding, one does not rely on mental conceptions—how much less would one go to others to seek one's own Dharma, taking their eyes as the basis for perfect penetration?"

Precious jewels can never relieve poverty, and speaking of food can never satisfy one's hunger; only by personally arriving at the gate of "sudden cessation" (*dunru*) and entering the path of non-learning (*wuxue*)—by illuminating this for oneself—can one finally reach the principle of non-action (*wuwei*).

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if this nature of seeing is necessarily 'me' and not anything else, then when I and the Tathāgata observe the Palace of Supreme Treasures of the Four Heavenly Kings and dwell in the Sun and Moon Palaces, this seeing is all-pervasive and circular, encompassing the entire Sahā world.
Yet when we return to the Vihāra, I see only the monastery; entering the hall of the pure mind, I behold only the eaves and corridors. World-Honored One, this seeing is thus..."
"The substance of this vision was originally all-pervasive throughout the entire realm; now that it is within this room, it fills only the room.
Does this vision contract from large to small, or is it severed by the walls and partitions? I do not know where the truth of this matter lies.
I pray that you will bestow your great compassion and explain this for me."

Because of the two preceding statements—"the nature you previously perceived is all-pervading" and "it is not you, so who else could it be?"—you have consequently identified the seeing as being the object.

Thus, there arises the doubt regarding its expansion and contraction, its largeness and smallness. This is truly because the essence of the fundamental clarity of the *vijñāna* (consciousness) possesses three aspects: first, the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*);
second, the seeing aspect (*darśanabhāga*); and third, the object-aspect (*nimittabhāga*). Although there are these three aspects, the seeing and object aspects together...
This belongs to the analogy of self-realization, which is like the two horns of a snail: when opened, they form a pair; when closed, they become one.
Therefore, the World-Honored One relied upon the omnipresence of the nature of seeing to reveal that the true nature is perfect and complete.

Yet Ānanda thought that if the nature of seeing were omnipresent and not mixed with external objects, it should remain unchanging in every location; why then, in the palace, does he see only [the interior]?
When one is in a room, one sees only the room; when on a veranda, one sees only the veranda.
Is it that this seeing was originally vast and has now shrunk to become small? Or is it that this seeing was originally pervasive, yet is obstructed and rendered non-pervasive by walls and buildings?
Now I do not know whether it ultimately exists within a single boundary, or whether it ultimately exists [beyond it].
Since that which is ultimately within the chamber must reside at the edge of the corridors, it is said: "I now do not know where this principle resides.
This principle refers to the seeing-nature (*darśana-svabhāva*). What is meant is that if one loses its efficacy in one place, it will be obstructed in both;
if it is obstructed in both, one will encounter stagnation wherever one goes.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "All worldly activities, whether great or small, internal or external, each belong to their respective objective fields (*viṣaya*).
One should not say that seeing expands or contracts. It is like seeing a square void within a square vessel. I ask you again:
Is this square void seen within the square vessel fixedly square, or is it not fixedly square? If it were fixedly square,"

If space were established separately within a round vessel, space itself would have to be round; if it were not fixed [to a specific shape], then when placed inside a square vessel, there would have to be no square space.
As for what you say regarding its location being unknown, such is the nature of its reality—how could it have a location?
This generally clarifies that expansion and contraction, as well as magnitude and minuteness, reside in the *nimitta* (phenomenal appearances) and not in the *darśana* (the faculty of seeing).

All activities—namely, the external objects such as large and small, internal and external, open and obstructed, bright and dark, and so forth—refer to the *bhāga* (divisions) of the sense organs, the body, and the vessel-world.

To clarify this, the following analogy is used: the vessel represents the *nimitta*, while space represents the *darśana*. This precisely means that it is the *nimitta* that possesses expansion and contraction.
The seeing has no fixed dimensions; it is like vessels that may be square or round, for emptiness has no determinate characteristics.
Therefore, it is said below: "Because the shapes of the vessels differ, one names the emptiness as different. The principle of the nature of seeing is thus. When you ask, "How can it exist? I say:
You see that the nature of seeing originally has no size; it appears large or small according to the capacity of the sense organ, just as empty space originally has no directionality.
The circle conforms to the vessel it occupies, whether square or round; thus, largeness, smallness, squareness, and roundness have no fixed location from the outset.

Why do you now insist on seeking their fixed location? This is what is called using directionless eloquence to drive away the attachment to fixity, employing non-attaining wisdom to subdue the limited mind.
Ānanda, if you wish to cause [the space] to enter into a state that is neither square nor round, you need only remove the squareness of the vessel; the essence of space itself has no squareness.
One should not say that there is a location where the square characteristics of empty space must be further removed.

Having already used a metaphor to clarify that [emptiness] is fundamentally neither square nor round, he again uses a metaphor to clarify the method of entering into that which is neither square nor round—namely, "shifting flowers to catch a butterfly" and "buying stones to gain more clouds.
The meaning is this: one should merely remove the vase or vessel, and the nature of emptiness will naturally be without squareness or roundness;
one should not, beyond removing the vase or vessel, further seek to remove the squareness or roundness of space itself, for space...

Because space exists within the square or round confines of a vessel, a sutra states: "If one does not attain the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), one cannot attain the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Since understanding that the mundane has no inherent nature is itself the reality, why do you chase after objects and follow your own emotions to arbitrarily give rise to divergent views?
You restrict the distance and proximity of spatial directions and fix the depth and shallowness of the vessel's capacity, like a caterpillar crawling along a branch.
Placing the front foot down while advancing the back foot is like a mad monkey who, having climbed a tree, lets go of a high branch to grasp a low one.

If one can eliminate the perception of objects and contemplate emptiness, there will naturally be no squareness or roundness, nor length or shortness. Once one knows that the mind is itself the objective realm, how could there be high or low, right or wrong?
If it were as you ask— that when entering a room, the visual faculty contracts and becomes small so that one looks up at the sun and sky,
or that when building walls and houses, the visual faculty is severed and interrupted, yet no trace of this remains when a small aperture is pierced—
this principle is not tenable.

This directly refutes the inappropriateness of his question: if you claim that when this vision enters a room it can be contracted and made small, then when looking up at the sun or moon, it should certainly be able to be raised upward;
if you claim that where it meets a wall it can be pinched and severed, then where it passes through a hole, it should certainly be able to be drawn through and made continuous.
Now that one cannot pull it upward to make it secure, how can one contract it to make it small?
Since one cannot draw it back to make it continuous, how could one further clamp it to cause it to break? Therefore, it is said that this interpretation is not correct.
All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been deluded regarding themselves and taken them to be external objects; they have lost their original mind and are turned about by these objects.

Therefore, within this state, one may perceive the great as small. If one can turn objects [back upon oneself], then one is identical to the Tathāgata, with body and mind perfectly luminous and unmoving within the site of enlightenment, able to universally contain the lands of the ten directions within a single hair-tip.
This uses the Dharma to correspond with the analogy, reiterating and clarifying the point:

because from time immemorial one has been deluded regarding this own self-originated, vast, perfect, and luminous wondrous nature, one clings to stillness within that wondrous perfection to form the faculty of sight;

grasping at forms, one forms the sense organs; relying upon these organs, one rushes toward external objects. Thus, one is internally fettered by the floating roots and externally bound by the vessel-world.
Because one is constrained within the sphere of activity and held by the *karmic consciousness*, unable to transcend it, one perceives large or small objects upon the various external sensory realms;
this does not mean that the nature of seeing itself has magnitude or minuteness.

It is just as empty space originally possesses neither squareness nor roundness, yet manifests squareness or roundness according to the vessel it occupies. If one can internally detach from body and mind and externally cast off...
When the world is overturned through the transformative consciousness of karma, the wondrous nature becomes perfectly pervasive and the six sense organs function interchangeably.

Thus, these ephemeral objects and the realms of the world may, by a mere thought, be transformed into supreme enlightened awareness. Then the body becomes the Dharma-nature body and the land becomes the Dharma-nature land;
the entirety of the worlds throughout the ten directions becomes a single eye, and the entirety of the worlds throughout the ten directions becomes...
When one Buddha-land is perceived by such an eye as being such a land, numerical distinctions are extinguished because of this perfect and clear understanding;

thus, while the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) cannot be moved, the body pervades the ten directions. Within a single hair-tip, one can contain entire lands—what expansion or contraction, what large or small, could there be?
It is said that when the vessel is removed, the space remains; the essence of emptiness has no [spatial] dimensions.
The square canopy was just like this.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if this essence of vision is necessarily my wondrous nature, then this wondrous nature is now present before me.
If what I see is necessarily my true self, then what are my current body and mind? And as for my current body and mind, they are divided..."

If there were a separate, real self that he saw, then why does he distinguish my body as not being that self? If my mind were truly the self, then it would cause me now to see the nature of seeing as the real self;
yet the body is not the self. How does this differ from what the Tathāgata previously refuted, namely, that an object can see the self?
I only pray that you will bestow great compassion and reveal the truth for one who has not yet awakened.
Furthermore, because this [view] takes the characteristic for the seer, there arises the doubt as to whether it is "self" or "not-self"—what is called resolving one doubt by means of another.
If this seeing-nature were necessarily your wondrous nature, [the text] would have taken up the previous statement:
"This subtle, wonderful, bright, and sincere is your seeing-nature. Now, [the phrase] "this wondrous nature is currently before me" takes up the previous [point that] the seeing-nature is pervasive.
If it is not you who pervades all, then who is it that sees? This necessarily brings forth the intention of resolving doubt; the meaning is this:
if the essence of seeing were to pervade all things, it would surely be my true nature manifesting upon external objects before me.
Yet, what is this thing within my present body that is capable of discernment? Now then—

The mind within the body discriminates that external objects truly possess functional activity, yet the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*) which pervades those external objects actually lacks such activity.
To discriminate that my own body is the locus where this nature of seeing pervades would mean that the nature of seeing should not be said to pervade all phenomena;
this is the same as the previous passage stating that while the causal mind has utility, the wondrous mind does not.

Because of its functional utility, one dares not yet acknowledge that the intent is sufficient; thus we know that Ānanda’s previous realization was merely a matter of verbal conduct and worldly affairs, as he had not yet been able to relinquish his attachment to conditions. How then could he have been willing to acknowledge that the nature of seeing is all-pervasive?
If it were said that that which pervades all phenomena is truly my mind, acting as the sovereign within my body to command me...
Now, when you see various objects, you perceive the nature of seeing as residing within external things;
yet those external things are actually my own body, which in turn is able to see me. If this were so, then this body would not be "I.
In that case, it would be no different from the objection raised by the Tathāgata—that objects are able to see me—resulting in a circular argument.
I have thoroughly investigated this matter, yet it remains beyond my comprehension; therefore, I pray that you will deign to show me compassion and further enlighten me.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "What you have now said—that the seeing is before you—is not the true meaning.

If it were truly real and located before you, and if you truly saw it, then this essence of seeing would have a specific location and could be pointed out. Furthermore, as for what is now before you..."
Seated in the Jeta Grove, you surveyed the groves, the channels, and the halls; looking upward, you saw the sun and moon, and facing forward, you saw the Ganges River.
Now, before my lion throne, you have pointed with your finger and described these various phenomena:

that which is dark is the grove, that which is bright is the sun, that which obstructs is the wall, and that which is unimpeded is space; and so on, down to the blades of grass, the trees, and even the finest hairs.
Although they differ in size, all possess form; there is nothing that cannot be pointed out.
If you must see it before you at this moment, you should use your hand to point with certainty and state: "Which of these is seeing? Ānanda, you should know:

if empty space were seeing, then since it has already become seeing, what would be empty space? If material objects were seeing, then since they have already become seeing, what would be material objects?

"You may minutely peel away and analyze the myriad phenomena to extract the pure, bright, and wondrous fundamental essence of seeing, and point it out to me so that it is as distinct and free from doubt as those other objects.

Ānanda said, "In this lecture hall on the upper terrace, reaching as far as the Ganges River below, looking up at the sun and moon, pointing with my hand, or gazing wherever my eyes turn—all that I point to are merely objects; there is nothing else."
"World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, how much less could I— a defiled beginner śrāvaka, or even a bodhisattva—
extract the essential seeing from before the manifestations of all phenomena, such that it exists separately from all things with its own distinct nature?
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is."

Below this, the text directly reveals that the seeing and the object are of one essence, transcending both "is" and "is not" to manifest that fundamentally there is no self or other, nor any objective entity.
My former masters have said: "If this were so, it would be like adding a head atop a head; if this were not so, it would be like cutting off the head to seek life.
When the World-Honored One saw Ānanda taking this nature of seeing and dividing it into its own part and another's part, its large part and its small part...

This division was not intended to require the Venerable One to personally point out, from among the myriad phenomena, what constitutes "seeing" and what does not, before then illuminating for him the principle that there is neither right nor wrong, that heaven and earth share a single root, and that all things are one body;
therefore, he specifically showed it to him, saying: "That which you now speak of as 'seeing' is present before you."
If these false and delusive words were entirely devoid of truth, and if this essence of vision truly existed before you, then you would certainly have some visible form or characteristic.

Since there is a visible form, it must necessarily occupy a specific location; since it occupies a specific location, it must certainly be possible to point it out, saying, "It is here" or "It is there.
Furthermore, when you look all around at objects possessing form that appear before you—
"Everything here can be pointed out with the hand. If this seeing-nature must necessarily be before you, you should also use your hand to point out with certainty which part is the seeing.
Ānanda, I now command you to look at the myriad phenomena while observing my pointing finger;
which among them is the seeing? You may then further command [others] to examine and analyze the myriad phenomena."
"The essence of seeing is identical to all objects, yet it clearly manifests itself to me. Ānanda, in response to these two points below, you were unable to speak.
If the seeing were identical to the object, why then, when I point my finger for you to observe, are you unable to identify which part is the seeing?
Furthermore, it is likewise impossible to separate the essence of seeing from the objects and manifest it clearly as something distinct from them. It is just so, it is just so.
The Buddha sealed this by stating that among the myriad phenomena, there is not a single thing that is "seeing," because the nature of seeing is free from all marks.
The Buddha further told Ānanda: "As you have said, there is no essence of seeing that exists apart from all objects as a separate self-nature."
"By nature, that which you have pointed to among these objects contains no such faculty of seeing. Now I shall further inform you:

as you and the Tathāgata sit in the Jeta Grove, look again at the gardens and groves, even up to the sun and moon; amidst these various distinct forms, there must certainly be no essence of seeing that can be subject to your pointing.
Furthermore, discern among these various objects which one is not the faculty of seeing. Ānanda said:
I truly see everywhere; in my Jeta Grove, I do not know what it is that is not seen.
Why is this? If the trees are not the seeing, how can one see the trees? If the trees are themselves the seeing, then how can they be trees?
This applies even unto space: if space is not the seeing, how can one see space? If space itself is the seeing, then how can it be space? I further reflected upon this:
"Among the myriad phenomena, even the subtlest manifestations are none other than seeing. The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is.
First, he confirmed that Ānanda was certainly unable to point out before the myriad phenomena which is his nature of seeing;
then, he further commanded him to point out among the myriad phenomena which is not his [nature of seeing].
"Seeing-nature, Ānanda! Below, the answer is given: "Among the ten thousand phenomena, there is not a single thing that is not seeing.
Thus it is, thus it is; this seals the fact that among the ten thousand phenomena, there is not a single thing that is not seeing, because the nature of seeing pervades all things.
Formerly, Kṣitigarbha asked Master Xiu: "The mountains, rivers, and the great earth—[are they] with you, O Venerable One?"

Regarding "same" and "different": when the fingers are held horizontally, it is called "separate storage"; when the two fingers are held vertically, it is called "identical storage. Now, since one cannot say they are identical nor that they are separate, can one also say they are "is" or "is not"? A former master said: "For one who has attained this, to say 'it is' is a path of transcendence; to say 'it is not' is also a path of transcendence. What is the meaning of this? It is because the Way is originally not a matter of being or non-being. If you can understand this point, then you will know that the Buddhas and patriarchs have never been absent from the world. If you do not understand, then even if you were to meet a Buddha or a patriarch, you would still be unable to avoid being deceived by them. Therefore, it is said: "If you wish to see the Buddha, look at the Buddha; if you wish to see the Dharma, look at the Dharma. This is what is meant by "the same" and "the different. If you can grasp this, you will naturally understand the meaning of "is" and "is not. If you cannot grasp it, you must continue to investigate until you reach a place where there is no longer any doubt. Only then will you be able to enter the gate of the Buddhas and patriarchs. Do not merely seek for it in words and phrases; if you seek it in words and phrases, you will fall into the pit of views. If you can cast away all such views, then you will be free from the net of the Buddhas and patriarchs. This is what is called the "path of transcendence. If you can attain this, then you will be able to manifest yourself freely in all places. If you cannot attain this, then even if you travel through the three realms, you will still be bound by the net of views. Therefore, it is said: "The Way is not a matter of being or non-being; it is simply that people’s minds are deluded. If you can awaken to this, then you will naturally be free from the net of views. If you do not awaken, then you must continue to investigate until you reach a place where there is no longer any doubt. Only then will you be able to enter the gate of the Buddhas and patriarchs.
