Because the World-Honored One neither holds the view that "it is" nor the view that "it is not," but approves of both, Master Chou said:
"All external conditions originally lack fixed characteristics; right and wrong, arising and ceasing, all proceed from the mind. If the mind itself does not arise, who can speak of right and wrong?
When subject and object are both absent, all phenomena are eternally quiescent. Therefore it is said: 'This pillar does not see the pillar.'"
"Not to see the pillar when it is not a pillar" means to realize this within the midst of right and wrong, rather than seeking it outside of right and wrong.
At this, the assembly—those who were not yet free from learning—heard these words of the Buddha and were utterly bewildered, unable to grasp the beginning or end of their meaning;
for a moment they were struck with terror and lost their composure. The Tathāgata, perceiving that their spirits were trembling with fear, felt compassion arise in his heart.
He comforted Ānanda and the great assembly, saying: "O sons of good family, this Unsurpassed Dharma King speaks words of truth;
he teaches according to reality, without deception or falsehood. This is not the fourfold confused and evasive discourse on 'immortality' of Makkhali Gosāla.
Contemplate this carefully, and do not fail in your grief and longing."
Because he had heard these two successive confirmations, the entire assembly was left in a state of bewilderment.

Since Ānanda first inquired about the nature of the mind as quiescent and eternal, there have been several further instructions, such as: "The external objects are naturally dark, but what deficiency does this cause the seeing?

and "When the hand opens and closes of its own accord, the seeing neither expands nor contracts. And again: "That which wrinkles is subject to change; that which does not wrinkle is not subject to change."
Furthermore, it says: "Your body and your mind are both objects manifested within the wondrously luminous true mind.
It also says: "If it were truly your mind, then there would be nowhere for it to go. And: "All things that can be returned to their source are naturally not you;
as for that which cannot be returned, if it is not you, who else could it be? It further says: "While the categories of material objects differ, the nature of seeing is no different. And: "Great..."

It was easy to understand that by using a mote of dust as a test, one could see that there is no expansion or contraction, and thus discern the seeing-nature apart from the dust and free from appearances;
yet, when it came to making Ānanda extract the essence of seeing from the myriad phenomena, he could not do so.
Furthermore, when asked to point out that which is not the nature of seeing within the myriad phenomena, he again failed. Thus, the Tathāgata [proceeded] in both ways.
It was fitting that at this single assembly everyone was utterly bewildered, not knowing where it had landed.

From beginning to end—meaning from start to finish—they were all struck with awe. Those who were dazed by his words lost their own footing; those who had fallen away from their original practice lost their former steps.
This was truly a case of inferior views being shaken and terrified, which he then comforted. He said, "Both of my two previous seal-approvals..."

These are words consistent with principle and truthful speech; they are neither delusory talk nor false speech, nor are they the doctrines of external paths that claim "existence is non-existence" or "non-existence is not existence"—the theory set between the two pillars.

It is only because your minds are coarse and your reflections shallow that you do not contemplate this with earnest attention. If you were willing to contemplate it earnestly, there would surely be a path for entry; you would certainly not fail me, whom I pity.
This was a manifestation of their sincere devotion.

At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, out of compassion for the fourfold assembly, rose from his seat amidst the great multitude, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet with palms joined in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, this great assembly..."
I have realized that the Tathāgata has clarified the meaning of these two kinds of refined vision—the seeing of form and emptiness, and what is or is not that vision.

World-Honored One, if the preceding conditions such as form and emptiness were themselves the vision, there should be something pointed out; if they were not the vision, there should be something upon which it rests.
Yet now I do not know where this principle leads, and thus I am filled with alarm and fear; it is not that my past roots of goodness are slight.
I earnestly pray that the Tathāgata, out of his compassionate wisdom, will clarify and reveal what these various objects and this seeing-essence fundamentally are,
so that within them there may be neither "is" nor "is not."
Because the great assembly was thus bewildered, he had a person of great wisdom act as their proxy to request a resolution of their doubts. His intention was this:
if form and emptiness were indeed the seeing, one should be able to point out its characteristics within the myriad phenomena;
why then is it impossible? If form and emptiness were not the seeing, one should see nothing at all within the myriad phenomena; why then is it so?

At the very moment of this single glance, there is nowhere that is not the present; yet it is precisely because this great assembly has heard these profound teachings whose meaning and intent are so remote and transcendental—having no place of attachment and being difficult to comprehend—that they experience alarm, doubt, and fear.

This is not like those in the past at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, whose roots of goodness were light and meager, such that they would not be willing to take up the Great Dharma upon hearing it.
Truly there is cause for alarm; I only pray that you will deign to provide a definitive explanation to resolve my doubts.
I do not know what kind of entities these two parts of the perceived object (nimitta) fundamentally are, such that between the two, it is neither existent nor non-existent.
This is similar to the account in the *Liezi* concerning the debate between two children over the sun.

The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī and the great assembly: "The Tathāgatas and great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, within their own abiding samādhi, perceive that both the seer and the objects of perception, as well as all conceptualized forms, are like flowers in the sky—fundamentally non-existent.
This seeing and these objects are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi. How could there be 'is' or 'is not' within this?"
Meeting one another in this assembly and returning to True Suchness (tathatā) serves to clarify the principle that there is neither right nor wrong.
To abide spontaneously in samādhi is the self-realization of the Tathāgata and Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage and above within the Śūraṅgama-samādhi;
as for other Bodhisattvas, although they possess samādhi, because their conceptualizing mind has not yet been forgotten, they merely rely on [external conditions].

Because other objects do not abide within one's own stage, the seeing itself is capable of seeing; that is, the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) sees the object-condition, which is the seen-part (*nimitta-bhāga*).
The aspect of what is conceived is precisely the aspect conceived by the six coarse consciousnesses mentioned previously. This is because the previous question asked:
"What are these various objects and images, and what is this essence of seeing fundamentally? Between them, there is neither 'is' nor 'is-not'."

Therefore, I tell you: because that great assembly has not yet attained the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama, they differentiate among the myriad phenomena, distinguishing between "thing" and "self," or "this" and "not-this.

However, when Buddhas and Bodhisattvas abide in this samādhi, whatever they perceive is fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi. Thus, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "The dharma-nature is like space."
All Buddhas dwell within emptiness; even while dwelling in this *dharmatā*, they do not perceive the existence of form-emptiness.
How could there be "is" or "is not" within it? This is the World-Honored One laying out the entire matter plainly, with no further concealment.
One should formulate the syllogism as follows: "The seer, the object of seeing, and the perceived characteristics are existent."
That phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent is the thesis; the reason is that they are fundamentally non-existent, being originally the wondrously pure and luminous essence of Bodhi;

the analogy is like flowers in the sky. Since the sky is fundamentally devoid of flowers, one knows that the wondrously pure and luminous essence is fundamentally devoid of the two divisions of perceived characteristics (*nimitta*) and seeing (*darśana*), for these characteristics and seeing are but false manifestations of the karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*). Furthermore, as for characteristics and seeing...
Since even that [the self] cannot be apprehended, how could there be "is" or "is not"?
Mañjuśrī, I now ask you: if there were another Mañjuśrī like you, Mañjuśrī, would that other Mañjuśrī be the true Mañjuśrī, or would he be without the quality of being Mañjuśrī?
Thus, World-Honored One, I am the true Mañjuśrī, yet I am without this [conceptualized] Mañjuśrī. Why is this? If there were such a thing as...
"Those two Mañjuśrīs are indeed such, yet today I am not without a Mañjuśrī; within this, there is truly neither the mark of 'is' nor 'is not. The Buddha said:
This wondrous clarity of vision and all empty objects are likewise thus. Originally, they are the wondrously luminous, unsurpassed Bodhi—the pure, perfect, true mind.
Through delusion, they become form and emptiness, as well as hearing and seeing, like a second moon. Who [could create it]?"
"Regarding this moon, who then is not the moon? Mañjuśrī replied, "There is but one true moon; within it, there is naturally neither 'this is the moon' nor 'this is not the moon.

Since the World-Honored One has already clarified this for me, yet fearing that I might still be unable to believe and understand, he has required Mañjuśrī to provide further elucidation from the side."
The Commentary: Since this is an elucidation based on the essential substance, it asks: "Is this very body of yours the true Mañjuśrī?
Would you allow that, outside of this Mañjuśrī, one could further add another Mañjuśrī and call him 'Mañjuśrī'?
Would you allow that, outside of this Mañjuśrī, one could subtract another Mañjuśrī and call it 'the absence of Mañjuśrī'? The text continues: "No."
It is precisely because those of great wisdom have a natural affinity of character that they spontaneously respond to one another in harmony;
thus it is said: "I myself am the one true Mañjuśrī. Beyond this, one cannot add another who is Mañjuśrī.
If one were to add another who is Mañjuśrī, then I would have two Mañjuśrīs. Yet, I do have one.
There is one true Mañjuśrī here, yet one must not call him "non-existent. This metaphor speaks precisely to the point:
apart from this one true Mañjuśrī, one cannot add another, nor can one subtract one.
This is because the essence of True Suchness (tathatā) neither exceeds nor lacks a single dharma; it is perfectly identical to the great void, without deficiency and without surplus.

The Buddha said: "Since you know that in the lower dharmas, the union of phenomena is ultimately without right or wrong, you should know that in the true essence, there is likewise fundamentally no right or wrong.
Because that very form-and-emptiness, hearing-and-seeing, is originally the unsurpassed, pure, and perfect true mind, yet through non-enlightenment the mind arises and possesses thought;
thus one becomes deluded into the karmic consciousness, which then transforms into the perceived and the perceiver."
The false existence of form and emptiness is precisely due to the essence of seeing; for form and emptiness arise based on the True (the *tathatā*), just as a second moon arises from the first.

Since it is like a second moon, one knows it is originally non-existent. How could one falsely give rise to conjectures upon that second moon, thinking "this is the true moon" or "this is not the true moon"?
One does not realize that whether [one thinks] this [second moon] is real or unreal, both are merely states of not having seen [the truth].
This refers to the True Moon; if one beholds the True Moon, one will no longer falsely establish distinctions of right and wrong. Thus, the *Yuanji jing* (Sūtra on Perfect Quiescence) states:

"All phenomena are but mind, without opposition; this is liberation through self-nature. It further states: "All phenomena do not confront the eye. Why? Because phenomena do not see phenomena, and phenomena do not know phenomena."

Therefore, when you now observe and discern between the self and external objects through various manifestations, this is called delusive thought (*vikalpa*); you cannot escape from within it by means of affirming or denying.
It is because of this true, essential, wondrously enlightened, and luminous nature that you are able to transcend such designations as "this" and "not-this."
This further uses the analogy to accord with the Dharma in order to clarify and illuminate the point:

because you have never dwelled in this Śūraṅgama Samādhi and your eye of wisdom is not clear, you give rise to various kinds of pervasive conceptualizations (*parikalpita*) upon the dependent nature (*paratantra*), which are called deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*).
Therefore, you cannot transcend these notions of "is" and "is not," just as a person with a visual disorder might speculate about a second moon.

The moon is neither "moon" nor "not-moon. If one attains the wondrous emergence of true *samādhi*, then the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses become a single, perfectly integrated, pure, and precious awakening.
Through realizing this wondrous awakening, one no longer falls into the extremes of "is" or "is not.

It is like a person with clear vision who, upon seeing the true moon, would never point to it and say, "This moon is the moon" or "This moon is not the moon. Thus, we know that [the distinction between] delusion and... [is merely a conceptual construct].
Direct perception is free from confusion; when one awakens to the true nature, it is empty, luminous, vast, and penetrating.
Ānanda said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, it is truly as the Dharma King has taught: that which perceives conditions throughout the ten directions is profoundly still and eternally abiding;
its nature is neither arising nor ceasing. This is different from the 'Dark Ultimate' (Tattva) discussed by the former Brahmin Śāṇakavāsa, and—"
What difference is there between the various non-Buddhist schools, such as those who throw themselves into ashes, who claim that a true self exists pervading the ten directions, and [the Buddha]?
World-Honored One, you have also previously expounded this meaning on Mount Laṅkā for Mahāmati and others.

Those non-Buddhists always speak of spontaneity (*svabhāva*), whereas I speak of causes and conditions; it is not within their realm of experience. Now, when I contemplate this nature of awakening, it is spontaneous and not...
How can you instruct those who are born and not subject to extinction, who have distanced themselves from all false and inverted views, and who resemble that which is neither caused nor spontaneous,
so that they may avoid entering among the heterodox and attain the true mind— the wondrously enlightened nature of clarity?

Below this, there is again the error of mistaking the conditions of perception for the wondrously enlightened nature of clarity, and further reckoning that wondrously enlightened nature of clarity as something spontaneous.
Although the World-Honored One initially elucidated the eternally abiding ground of the mind, Ānanda was unwilling to accept it;
thus, he did not dare to recognize it, but instead recognized the presently active mind of conditions as being functional. This continued until the vision itself was elucidated.

Because his nature had not yet reached the state of universal pervasiveness, and because he had not yet scrutinized the provenance of the seeing-nature, he further mistook the seeing for its object and the object for the seeing.

Only when this was clarified—that the essence of both form and emptiness is fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous substance of Bodhi—did he finally attain the realization of the statement that the seeing-nature is universally pervasive; hence it is said: "Truly as the Dharma King has taught," and so forth.
Furthermore, fearing that [the teaching] might be confused with external paths or contradict one's own school, he again requested a resolution of his doubts.
The phrase "it is truly so" is a word of pure faith, meaning that the Tathāgata’s fruit is indeed true speech and not deceptive or false. Regarding "awakened to conditions":
because the seeing-nature can see light, see darkness, see openness, and see obstruction, pervading all conditions, it is thus designated.
This being the condition for awakening, this very condition for awakening is indeed all-pervasive, indeed eternally abiding, and indeed neither arising nor ceasing.
It is not confused with the "first descending" or "first exiting" [theories] of non-Buddhist outsiders;

the Brahmin Saṃkhyā, here translated as "Pure Conduct" or "Golden Head," refers to the non-Buddhist outsider who posits the *tattva* (ultimate principle), specifically that which is among his reckoned twenty-five *tattvas*.

The first truth concerns the ash-throwing ascetics, who are non-Buddhist practitioners of austerities such as plucking out their hair, fumigating their noses, cauterizing their bodies, and lying upon pestles.
They postulate three types of *ātman* (self) regarding its size—large, small, and indefinite; this refers specifically to their calculation of a "vast self.
The World-Honored One has previously stated that this *ātman* is a false conceptualization (*parikalpita*), yet what is being taught here is the realization (*bodha*) of it.

What difference is there between this "all-pervasive realm" (*pratyaya-vyāpin*) and that which you postulate—the *prakṛti* (primordial essence) and the *puruṣa* (spiritual self)—which are both all-pervasive throughout the ten directions?
This is no different from mistaking fish eyes for bright pearls or mistaking a mountain pheasant for a colorful phoenix.
World-Honored One, [the Buddha] next points out the contradiction with his own school; "Laṅkā" here means "inaccessible," reachable only by supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Because that which can be attained is thus reached, this meaning points to causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

"Spontaneity" (*svabhāva*) refers to the fact that internal and external phenomena do not require laborious creation nor depend upon cultivation for completion; they are all fundamentally without cause, existing spontaneously.

It is as if one were to ask: who opens the rivers and seas? Who piles up the mountains and peaks? Who trims the thorns and brambles? Who paints birds and beasts? There is nothing in the world that has a creator.

Therefore, all phenomena are eternally natural; yet because they do not know that the *ālayavijñāna* contains seeds which, moistened by afflictions, lead to rebirth as the basis for the course of existence, they consequently conceive of a permanent, indestructible "self" (*ātman*) within the body that takes birth everywhere throughout the ten directions.
Regarding these causes and conditions: "cause" refers to the seeds, and "condition" refers to...
To assist in the expression [of this truth]: internal and external phenomena must necessarily be accomplished through a multitude of conditions (*pratyaya*) before they can produce a result.

This means that while those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) of the past constantly asserted spontaneity (*svabhāva*), the World-Honored One, while at Mount Laṅkā, constantly refuted the spontaneity of the non-Buddhists by means of the profound meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). The realm realized by me is not a realm realized by them.
Because of the realms (*dhātu*). I now observe that this nature of awareness is fundamentally innate; it does not come from borrowing elsewhere.
Amidst a thousand differences, it is perfectly realized everywhere; within the myriad phenomena, it stands far beyond each and every one.

Thus, not only does this contradict the *hetu-pratyaya* (causes and conditions) taught by the Tathāgata, but it also accords with the "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*) of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). I do not know how the world...
"World-Honored One, what further skillful means do you have to reveal that what the Tathāgata has taught differs in every respect from what those heterodox teachers calculate?
Only then may we refrain from entering among the various heresies, and only then may we attain the true mind and the nature of wondrous enlightenment."
The Buddha told Ānanda, "I have now thus revealed the skillful means and spoken the truth to you;

yet you still do not understand and are deluded into thinking it is 'spontaneous nature' (svabhāva). Ānanda, if this were necessarily spontaneous, you ought to clearly discern what constitutes its spontaneous substance.
For now, observe within this wondrously luminous seeing: what do you take as its self? Is this seeing itself by virtue of light, or by virtue of darkness?"
If you take emptiness as your self, or if you take obstruction as your self, Ānanda—if light were your self, you should not see darkness;

if, moreover, you take emptiness as your own essence, you should not see obstruction. Thus, even if you take various characteristics such as darkness as your self, then at the time of light, your seeing-nature would be annihilated; how then could you see the light?
This refutation of the essence of awareness shows that it does not arise spontaneously, because it fails to maintain its own nature and instead follows conditions.
First, I shall now sternly rebuke you and then proceed with the refutation: "I see that you do not penetrate the Dharma-nature;
therefore, I first refute your deluded mind to reveal the seeing-nature, and subsequently, I further borrow the seeing-nature to reveal the awareness-nature—how much effort this has cost!"

Through these various turns, I have revealed how many skillful means and truths for your sake; yet you still do not awaken, and instead continue to be deluded by the notion of "spontaneity" (*ziran*).
If you take this profoundly serene nature, free from arising and ceasing, to be spontaneity, you must clearly discern and distinguish it:
that you yourself possess a substantial essence that does not migrate or change—only then is it true spontaneity. Furthermore, as for you...
Contemplate this nature of seeing within the midst of light, darkness, emptiness, and obstruction: specifically, which phenomenon among these can be designated as its inherent essence?
If light were the inherent essence, then this nature of seeing would only be able to see light and could not see darkness.
If emptiness were the inherent essence, then this nature of seeing would only be able to see emptiness and should not see [obstruction].

Since you now clearly perceive light when it comes and darkness when it comes, and your perception changes according to what is encountered, you know that the nature of awareness is certainly not something natural.
Why, then, do you cling to it as being natural? Thus, Xue Jian asked the Sixth Patriarch:
"The Master speaks of 'neither arising nor ceasing'; how does this differ from the non-Buddhists? The Patriarch replied: "What the non-Buddhists speak of as 'neither arising nor ceasing'..."

This means that [the Tathāgata] brings cessation to what is about to perish and manifests cessation through arising; yet, although cessation occurs, it is not truly extinguished, and although arising is spoken of, it is non-arising.

When I speak of non-arising and non-cessation, it is because there was originally no arising from the beginning, and now there is likewise no cessation. This is precisely why my teaching differs from that of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
This is the intended meaning.
Ānanda said, "If this wondrous nature of seeing is not spontaneous, and I have now explained that it arises from causes and conditions, my mind is still not clear regarding this matter;
I ask the Tathāgata: how does this accord with the nature of causes and conditions?
The Buddha said, "Regarding what you call 'causes and conditions,' I shall question you further: Now, because of seeing, seeing arises before you. Does this seeing exist because of light?"
Seeing exists because of darkness; seeing exists because of emptiness; seeing exists because of obstruction. Ānanda, if seeing existed because of light, one should not see darkness;
if it existed because of darkness, one should not see light. This applies likewise to emptiness and obstruction, which are the same as light and darkness.
Furthermore, Ānanda, this seeing also conditions light to exist, conditions darkness to exist, and conditions...

If one perceives emptiness as an object, one obstructs the perception of existence; Ānanda, if one takes empty space as an object, one should not see obstructions, and if one takes obstructions as an object, one should not see empty space.
This applies even to perceiving light or darkness, which are identical in nature to empty space and obstructions.

This, moreover, identifies the wondrous enlightened nature as having the character of cause and condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). "Providing the beginning" is taken as the cause, while "assisting the cause" is taken as the condition;
the intention is that since it is not spontaneous, it must necessarily belong to the category of borrowed [conditions], such as the four conditions that give rise to consciousness.
However, this enlightened nature is fundamentally pervasive and eternal, and its nature is not subject to arising or ceasing—how, then, can it possibly accord with cause and condition?
The essential point is thus stated: "What is the meaning of this? How does it accord with the nature of causes and conditions? The Buddha said:
"First, I shall refute the view that the nature of seeing arises from a cause—'cause' here refers to the seed.

If you say that the nature of seeing manifests only after you perceive light and darkness, or penetration and obstruction, then from what among these light, darkness, penetration, and obstruction does this nature of seeing emerge?"
If it were produced with light as its seed, one should not perceive darkness; if it were produced with darkness as its seed, one should not perceive light.
Since it now perceives both light and darkness, we know that its essential nature is unchanging and does not arise following the causes of light.
Thus, the subsequent examples refute [the opponent's position]. Furthermore, the following section provides a refutation.
That the seeing-nature does not arise from conditions can be known by referring to the *Yujia lun* (Treatise on the Union), which says:
"In the world there is a precious mirror, its fundamental nature clear and limpid. When it is covered with a film, wiped clean, opened, or closed—when it is covered, it is not darkened for its sake;

when it is wiped, it is not brightened for its sake; when it is opened, it is not made empty for its sake; and when it is closed, it is not blocked for its sake. It is not that one bestows darkness or brightness upon it."
While opening and closing are not constant, their fundamental nature remains constant;

therefore, when the World-Honored One points to the nature of the clarity and precision of seeing, its capacity to accommodate the four kinds of objective conditions—light, darkness, penetration, and obstruction—is like that of a precious mirror.
You should know that this subtle, wondrous, and brilliant awareness is neither caused nor conditioned, neither self-caused nor spontaneous;
it is not non-existent, yet not existent, and not non-existent, yet not existent. It is free from all marks, yet identical with all phenomena.
How can you now attempt to direct your mind toward it, using the conceptual names and signs of worldly sophistry to make distinctions? It would be like trying to grasp it with your palm.
To grasp at empty space only increases one's own toil; how can empty space ever be caught by your grasping?
Herein, the traces are repeatedly swept away to reveal that the nature of awakening is both unchanging while following conditions and follows conditions while remaining unchanging.

This is because those who cling to spontaneity do not understand following conditions, and those who cling to following conditions do not know its unchanging nature. Therefore, [this teaching exists].

Regarding the distinctions between the non-Buddhists and the Hīnayāna: that which is "unchanging while following conditions" and "following conditions while remaining unchanging" is the grand paradigm for the World-Honored One’s teaching of the Dharma and the profound discourse on entering into principle. Therefore, he concludes by showing:
"One should know that such subtle, wondrous, and luminous awareness does not belong to causes and conditions, nor does it belong to spontaneity, nor does it belong to neither-causes-nor-conditions."

Naturally, this essence of subtle awakening and wondrous clarity is the primordially pure substance, fundamentally devoid of both "not right" and "not wrong," and likewise devoid of "right" and "wrong.
This is because it is apart from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and yet identical with all phenomena (*dharma*). Thus, it is not something to be understood through deliberation or discrimination;
for as soon as the mind attempts to conceive of it, it errs, and as soon as a thought stirs, it is separated from it. Therefore—

In this state, even a single thought-moment is not permitted; how then can you, while within the wondrous enlightenment, apply your mind and form intentions, using worldly conceptual proliferations and names and marks—such as "spontaneity" or "causes and conditions"—to fathom the Tathāgata’s wondrously enlightened luminous nature?
How is this different from grasping at empty space with your hands? How could empty space ever conform to you?
Because it is grasped erroneously, the *Zhengjingshi* states: "Causes and conditions, as well as spontaneity, are all worldly discourses;

existence and non-existence, the ultimate and the conventional, are all merely the discriminating consciousness of the mind. One must personally arrive at [realization] without waiting for further words. It is like a mirror reflecting a face:
one must have the eye-mind correspond exactly to it, just as a fish drinking water knows its temperature by itself. If this is not so...

To directly perceive this reality while attempting to resolve it through intellectual speculation and emotional seeking is like trying to shoot Mount Sumeru with a bow made of rabbit horns and arrows made of tortoise hair by a person without hands;

it is like pouring hot sand oil into a leaking cup without a lamp, or attempting to shatter the Iron Ring Mountains in vain toil and madness—such things can never come to pass. Furthermore, the former masters said:

It is said that it is neither through causes and conditions nor through spontaneity—the most wondrous among wonders, the most profound among profundities. The myriad phenomena of the universe manifest within its radiance;
yet though one seeks them, no root or source can be found. Thus, they mutually unfold and reveal one another.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if the nature of wondrous enlightenment is neither caused by conditions nor produced by causes, why does the World-Honored One constantly teach the bhikṣus that the nature of seeing possesses four kinds of conditions—namely, space as a cause, light as a cause, the mind as a cause, and the eyes as a cause?
What is the meaning of this?"
This passage cites past teachings to demonstrate that the wondrously enlightened and luminous nature serves as the cause and condition.

From the "Chapter on the Eight Returns," which relies upon the essence of seeing to reveal the wondrous enlightened nature, up until the "Chapter of Mañjuśrī’s Inquiry," it is clarified that both seeing and the objects of seeing are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous substance of Bodhi; yet Ānanda mistakenly took the cry of a crane for [the sound of a bell].

Because he mistook the essence of seeing for the wondrously enlightened nature upon hearing the warbling of the oriole, he said: "Truly, as you have said, this perceiving faculty pervades the ten directions;

it is a tranquil, eternally abiding nature, not subject to birth or extinction. Furthermore, because he clung to this nature as being either spontaneous (*svabhāva*) or caused by conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), the World-Honored One eliminated each of these views one by one, and only then directly revealed the wondrous luminosity of the essential awareness.
Is it not the case that one cannot apply the mind to that which is neither non-being nor being, neither is nor not-is, and which is both free from and identical to all characteristics?

How then could one falsely deliberate upon it through the lens of natural causality? Therefore, Ānanda, having heard these words, cited past teachings to prove that the nature of wondrous enlightenment must belong to causes and conditions;
thus he said: "It must be that the nature of wondrous enlightenment is neither cause nor condition."

"How is it that the World-Honored One, in his ordinary discourse, speaks of the nature of seeing as being endowed with four conditions—namely, space, light, the mind, and the eyes—and among these, the mind is the causal condition while space, light, and the eyes are the dominant conditions?

Within the Dharma-characteristics school (Dharmalakṣaṇa), it is taught only that consciousness arises from the four conditions; it has never been said that the wondrous enlightened nature arises from the four conditions."
Because the wondrous enlightened nature is not produced by productive causes, Ānanda has already committed an error by identifying the wondrous enlightened nature with the nature of seeing;
he has now committed an even greater error by further asserting that the wondrous enlightened nature arises from causes and conditions.
Therefore, the subsequent text first refutes that the nature of seeing belongs to causes and conditions, thereby revealing the true nature of the wondrous enlightenment.
That which is beyond the reach of the nature of seeing certainly does not belong to causes and conditions; these subtle words and wondrous principles are best contemplated with deep reflection.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda, what I have spoken regarding the various characteristics of worldly causes and conditions is not the ultimate truth (paramārtha). Ānanda, I further..."
Question: You worldly people say, "I can see. What do you mean by "seeing," and what do you mean by "not seeing"? Ānanda replied:
"Worldly people rely upon the light of the sun, the moon, or a lamp to perceive various forms; this is called 'seeing.
If these three kinds of light were absent, one would be unable to see. [The Buddha said: "Ānanda, if the absence of light is called 'not seeing,' then it should follow that..."
If you do not see darkness, yet must necessarily see darkness, this is merely ignorance; how can it be called "not seeing"?
Ānanda, if when in darkness you do not see light, it is called "not seeing"; now, when in light you do not see the characteristic of darkness, it is likewise called "not seeing.
Thus, both of these characteristics are equally termed "not seeing. Furthermore, if these two characteristics were to mutually cancel one another out, that would not be your seeing.
Since the nature [of seeing] is temporarily absent within these states, one knows that both are called "seeing.
How could it be that there is no seeing? Therefore, Ānanda, you should now know: when seeing light, the seeing is not the light; when seeing darkness, the seeing is not the darkness;
when seeing emptiness, the seeing is not the emptiness; when seeing obstruction, the seeing is not the obstruction. These four meanings are established.
Furthermore, you should know that when the seeing sees, that seeing is not [itself] seeing; even seeing is already apart from seeing, for seeing cannot reach it.
Why, then, do you speak of causes and conditions, spontaneity, and the characteristics of their conjunction?
You śrāvakas are narrow-minded, inferior, and lacking in wisdom, unable to penetrate the pure true reality. I now instruct you: reflect well upon this and do not grow weary.
This neglects the wondrous path to Bodhi.

This passage clearly elucidates that the nature of seeing does not belong to causes and conditions, using this as an analogy to demonstrate that the wondrous enlightened nature is certainly not produced by causes and conditions.
When I previously said that consciousness arises from the four conditions, it was precisely because non-Buddhists falsely cling to [the self]...
However, I merely borrow the concept of causes and conditions to break the attachment to spontaneity;
this is like using one wedge to extract another, which is a secondary matter and not the time for discussing the wondrous enlightened nature (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) as the primary truth.

Is it not then a mistake to misidentify the wondrous enlightened nature as a phenomenon of causes and conditions? Furthermore, it is not only the wondrous enlightened nature that does not belong to causes [and conditions].
If seeing-nature itself is the condition, how could it ever belong to causes and conditions?
If you claim that seeing-nature arises from causes and conditions, then it would be as when people each say, "I am the one who sees. By what means is this seeing accomplished?
Once seeing has already been accomplished, by what further means would it fail to see? Ānanda replied, "It is because of external objects, World-Honored One."
"Because of the light of the sun, moon, and lamps, one sees; because of the absence of the light of the sun, moon, and lamps, one does not see.
Thus, both seeing and not seeing belong to causes and conditions; therefore, we know that the nature of seeing arises from causes and conditions.
The World-Honored One borrowed these words to refute them, saying: "If this nature of seeing is called 'not seeing' when these three kinds of light are absent, then it should..."
If one does not see darkness, yet claims that although one does not see light, one must necessarily be able to see darkness, then this is merely the absence of light;

how can it be called "not seeing"? If one claims that being in the dark and not seeing light is what constitutes "not seeing," then one should also be called "not seeing" when not seeing darkness during the bright day. If this were so, then...
Is there any principle by which seeing darkness and seeing light are both called "not seeing"?

If you say that when light comes, darkness departs, and when darkness comes, light departs—such that these two characteristics of light and darkness merely contend with and displace one another, while the nature of seeing itself has nothing to do with it, being neither temporarily present nor temporarily absent—then seeing darkness and seeing light are both named "seeing. Why, then, would it be called "not seeing" at the time of seeing darkness?
This is called "not seeing. Once you understand this meaning, you will know that this seeing sees light but is not light;
it sees darkness but is not darkness; it sees emptiness but is not emptiness; it sees obstruction but is not obstruction. Thus, the nature of seeing does not arise dependent on conditions;

it stands forth alone and clearly revealed. Nevertheless, although this nature of seeing does not belong to the arising of conditions, it still belongs to one's own karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*).
Because the manifested [nature] and the wondrous enlightened nature still stand at a remove from one another, he takes this opportunity to refute it, saying:
"Although these four meanings of the seeing-nature have been established, you should further understand that when this wondrous enlightened wisdom illuminates and perceives this seeing-nature,
this wondrous enlightened wisdom is not itself the seeing-nature, for it is by means of the wondrous enlightened wisdom that this seeing-nature is illuminated and perceived."
At that time, because it does not combine with the nature of seeing, it is beyond the reach of the nature of seeing; for when light comes and darkness departs, wisdom arises and delusion perishes.
You should know that this wondrous enlightened nature resides at the locus of seeing and hearing, yet is beyond the reach of seeing and hearing;
it lies within the sphere of thought and deliberation, yet is beyond the reach of thought and deliberation. How then could one wish to—
Is one falsely conjecturing based on worldly causes and conditions, spontaneity, or the characteristics of combination?

This was the World-Honored One leading the Venerable Xiang toward a precipice ten thousand fathoms high and giving him another push, intending only that he would let go and take responsibility for himself.
In the two characters "seeing-seeing," the upper "seeing" refers to the wondrous enlightened nature (*miaojue xing*), while the lower "seeing" refers to the nature of seeing (*jianxing*).

Question: What is the difference between this nature of seeing and the nature of wondrous enlightenment (miao-jue-xing) when both take the nature of objects as their condition, such that you say the former does not equal the latter?

Answer: Although the essence of seeing conditions the objects of direct perception (xian-liang), they do not intermingle; yet, because the subject-object duality still persists, Ānanda designated it as "the awareness-conditioned.
If the wisdom of wondrous enlightenment conditions the realm of True Suchness (tathatā), then wisdom and principle are of one suchness.

This is precisely because there is neither subject nor object, which is beyond the reach of this essence of seeing. Therefore, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says that dharmas transcend seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
Because Ānanda’s perception was hazy and not true, vague and merely resembling reality, he confused them into one;
whereas the World-Honored One’s entire body is eyes, clearly discerning even the finest hair, thus distinguishing them into two—namely, their unification.

Thus, they are both impaired; if separated, they are both perfected. You disciples of inferior capacity have exhorted yourselves with words of encouragement, yet your resolve is narrow and inferior, and your aspiration is coarse and unstable.
Therefore, you do not recognize that this essence of seeing is the gateway between the mundane and the sagely.
Being obstructed by that [delusion], the Buddha’s knowledge and the Buddha’s vision do not open up; thus, you are unable to penetrate through the essence of seeing immediately.

I have now already instructed you regarding the realization of the true nature (*dharmatā*), and you have heard it; you should contemplate it more deeply, examine it minutely, and practice with diligent effort.
You must directly shatter the essence of views (*dṛṣṭi-sāra*) and enter into wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*);
do not be lax or negligent, nor stop halfway through. Therefore, the *Zongjing lu* says: "One must overcome oneself to accomplish the task, forgetting fatigue day and night. If...
It is like asking the way only to find one's hometown growing ever more distant; it is like seeing a treasure but failing to take it, thereby suffering poverty in vain.
It is exactly as when Sudhana ascended the pavilion or the Dragon Girl offered her pearl—at such a moment, one naturally perceives directly without waiting for deliberation.
What is called the "wondrous path to Bodhi" means that if one wishes to reach Bodhi, this alone is the essential clarity of vision.
To follow this path alone is most excellent. From the first fascicle, when the World-Honored One asked the Venerable One, "When you see the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks, what do you see?
Who is it that feels love and delight? He replied, "It is as if my eyes behold the Tathāgata’s supreme marks, and my mind gives rise to love and delight.
This, then, is to mistake the floating sense organs for seeing, and to mistake the mental consciousness for [the true seer].
To recognize both [the body and the mind] as the self is an error, for one has entirely fallen into the cognitive views of sentient beings.
Therefore, the World-Honored One first refuted that the consciousness-mind has no location, and next refuted that the consciousness-mind has no substance, saying, "This is not your mind.

Yet Ānanda had consistently clung to this conscious intellect as the root of birth and death; thus, upon hearing this censure and refutation, he was startled and rose from his seat. Consequently, there occurred—

Free from the doubt that [the mind] is as insentient as earth or wood, the World-Honored One enumerated everything in the world, down to blades of grass and knots of thread, interrogating their origins;
each has its own essential nature. How much more so for the nature of all minds, which are themselves without substance?
Only then did he realize that the "conditioned mind" he had identified was illusory, and thus he asked about the "quiescent and eternal mind-nature," begging for instruction on the mind.

At Venerable Ānanda’s request, the World-Honored One took up the case of a blind man staring into darkness; he then revealed the luminous, quiescent, and eternal nature of the mind, immediately pointing out that "this seeing-nature is the mind, not the eye.
This directly reveals that the seeing-nature is the mind, while conversely demonstrating that what the Venerable had previously clung to was not the mind.
At that moment, the World-Honored One feared that the Venerable might still be unwilling to accept this.
Because it is said that this seeing-nature is the mind, [the Buddha] used the flying light to manifest its immobility,

the river-watching to verify its unchanging nature, the hanging hand to clarify its non-loss, the eight directions to manifest its non-returning, and the successive observations to demonstrate its omnipresence;
he further revealed that this seeing has no expansion or contraction, no union or separation, and no right or wrong.

Originally, this is the wondrously pure and luminous essence of bodhi; through these successive and layered instructions, Ānanda consequently identified this seeing-nature as being identical to the wondrous enlightened nature.
Therefore, the World-Honored One struck him with a needle at the crown of his head and told him:
"When the seeing sees, that seeing is not seeing. As the former masters said: "As soon as it is thus, it is already not so."
This means that this seeing-nature is still one layer removed from the wondrous enlightened nature;
one should not immediately take this seeing-nature to be the wondrous enlightened nature, because this seeing-nature is a transformation of the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*).
If this karmic consciousness is shattered, then this seeing-nature is precisely the wondrous enlightened nature. Therefore, the following passage provides a distinction.
As for karma, it is said that all are produced by the disease of beginningless views; when referring to a single nation, it is said that all are produced by the delusions of beginningless views;

when referring to the great trichiliocosm, it is said that they are all alike the pure, untainted, wondrous mind of enlightenment, wherein seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing arise as false through the conjunction of the conditions of the disease of delusion, and die as false through that same conjunction. Thus one knows these two kinds.
The root of birth and death all arises from the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*); only by shattering this karmic consciousness does one attain wondrous enlightenment.

Thus, we know that the karmic consciousness is the universal gateway between delusion and awakening, and the common path shared by the holy and the ordinary. It is not related to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Only then will one understand that the two statements in the preceding text—"This is not your mind" and "Seeing nature is the mind"—constitute the essential gateways for entering the Way.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, although the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has for our sakes expounded upon the characteristics of causal conditions and spontaneity, as well as those of conjunction and non-conjunction, my mind has still not been opened; yet now I hear and see further."

Seeing what is not to be seen, our confusion and distress increase ever more; we pray that Your Great Compassion bestow the eye of great wisdom, revealing to us the clarity and purity of the awakened mind.
Having spoken these words, they prostrated with tears of sorrow and received the Sage’s decree.
Because this [passage] arises from the destruction of the view of the essence of seeing (*darśana-śāra*) and the subsequent birth of doubt, he requests a further clarification.

"As the Buddha... and below, he sets forth what he has already understood; "the various followers... and below, he sets forth what he has not yet understood; and now, with "now," he explicitly states the nature of his doubt. His intention is as follows:

since the World-Honored One has stated that the nature of seeing is immovable and indestructible, neither expanding nor contracting, and so on, up to saying "seeing and the object of seeing... [the doubt arises].
Since the fundamental source is the wondrously pure and luminous essence of Bodhi, it is clear that this refined visual consciousness is none other than the nature of wondrous enlightenment.
Yet, you suddenly say that when one perceives this perception, "perception is not perception," and that the nature of seeing is one. Why do you speak of the true and the false?
Furthermore, I only know that this nature of seeing does not belong to causes and conditions or to spontaneity; I have not yet understood [the rest].
This nature of seeing is a combination; it is not a non-combination. Your mind has not yet opened, and you are already bewildered and distressed.
Now, hearing further that "seeing-seeing is not seeing," you do not understand why this is so, and thus your bewilderment and distress increase all the more.
Previously, you were startled because I refuted the conditioned mind as being false; now you are bewildered and distressed because I refute the nature of seeing as being unreal.
I humbly pray that you will, in response to my earnest entreaty, manifest the Great Wisdom-Eye, which is the wondrous enlightened intelligence (*prajñā-jñāna*).

It is because of delusion regarding this [intelligence] that the "essence of vision" (*darśana-śuddhi*) is formed; yet when the awakened mind is clear and pure, it is the wondrous enlightened nature (*tathatā-svabhāva*), which resides within the essence of vision but does not belong to the essence of vision.
This is precisely the distinction between the initial awakening and the fundamental awakening. Please, for my sake, manifest the wondrously luminous mind and open my [understanding].
"O World-Honored One, when you spoke of the 'Eye of the Way,' you immediately pointed to this seeing-nature and showed it to me;

previously, I took this seeing-nature to be the Eye of Great Wisdom and the Nature of Sublime Enlightenment. Yet, the World-Honored One has now rejected this seeing-nature as not being definitive, [asserting] that there is another great wisdom-light, the True Dharma-Eye, and a bright, pure awakened mind to be bestowed upon me. I therefore humbly entreat you to reveal it."

This is shown below: the World-Honored One clarifies for them that the nature of seeing is fundamentally the "seeing-division" (*darśana-bhāga*) among the three subtleties, which, together with the "object-division" (*nimitta-bhāga*), both manifest from the *karmic consciousness* (*karma-vijñāna*). Therefore, one must eliminate the *karmic consciousness* and shatter the [deluded] nature of seeing;
only then is it the wondrous enlightened nature, and only then is it the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda and the great assembly, and wishing to expound the sublime path of practice for the various *samādhis* of the Great *Dhāraṇī*, addressed Ānanda, saying: "Although you possess a powerful memory, it merely increases your learning;
yet regarding the subtle and secret contemplation of *śamatha*, your mind has not yet fully understood it. Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you."
This detailed exposition is intended so that all future beings subject to outflows may attain the fruit of Bodhi.
Regarding the phrase "about to expound" (*jiang yu fuyan*): when one intends to speak but has not yet spoken, it is called "about to.

*Dhāraṇī*—translated here as "total retention" (*zongchi*)—refers specifically to the nature of wondrous enlightenment. The phrase "the various paths of sublime cultivation for the *samādhis*" is a general reference to the three sections of the text that follow.
The seven great elements are categorized into three groups; these three groups and seven great elements are all the points where one begins practice and applies effort.

They constitute the great path for realizing Bodhi. As the text below states: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, by practicing within each of the eighteen realms, have all attained the perfect and unsurpassed Bodhi. Although you have raised this objection below...
In his bewilderment, he said: "I have previously, for your sake, shattered your mind and rejected your views to open up the Great Dharani Gate.
Having already opened it, I intended to discuss with you the path of sublime practice so that you might enter this dharani gate.

Little did I know that although you possess a powerful memory, you merely increase your learning through hearsay; you do not engage in skillful reflection and thus do not penetrate the true nature of reality."

However, because subtle and secret contemplation within *śamatha* has not yet been clarified, I shall first elucidate subtle and secret contemplation for you, and thereafter discuss the path of wondrous cultivation.
"Subtle and secret" is said in contrast to the coarse; for it is through the discernment of vitarka and vicāra that something is considered coarse.

The wisdom of turning back to observe is subtle and profound contemplation. Using this to perceive darkness and perceive light is called the function of *vitarka* (initial application) and *vicāra* (sustained application).
Using this to turn back and observe the nature, thereby breaking through the *karmic consciousness* and directly perceiving the awakened nature, is what is termed subtle and profound contemplation;
it is not two separate things. Now you only know that the seeing-nature is true, yet you do not know...

That which you take to be real is in fact delusion, yet you do not know the reason for its being delusive; it is only natural that upon hearing this, your confusion and distress should increase all the more.
How could you know that the nature of seeing is the medicine that prevents hands from cracking when exposed to cold? It depends entirely on whether one uses it skillfully or unskillfully.
If one uses it skillfully, one will attain the wondrous, subtle, and profound nature of pure, bright mind, and achieve a state of complete purity.
Since the eye is within the palm of one's hand, what difficulty could there be? Therefore, I shall analyze and reveal it for you;
if one enters through this single gate, one can directly transcend to the stage of No-more-learning and ascend to the wondrous enlightenment without expending further effort.
Thus it is said: "I also cause all future beings with outflows to obtain the fruit of Bodhi. Furthermore, the subsequent text also says:
Through the Samādhi of Illusion, one can transcend the stage of No-More-Learning with a mere snap of the fingers.
Ānanda, all sentient beings revolve in the world due to two inverted, deluded views arising from discrimination;

they manifest in their respective places and revolve according to their karma. What are these two views? First, the deluded view of individual karma among sentient beings; second, [the deluded view of common karma].
The deluded vision of the commonality (*sabhāgatā*) of sentient beings:

from here below, this nature of vision will be developed into two kinds of deluded visions, which serve as the root of the two deaths—of分段 (*pariccheda*, limited segmentation) and 變易 (*pariṇāma*, transformation)—and also as the root of the two fruits of *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*; for both of these visions...
This is because they manifest from the karmic consciousness of ignorance. As for all sentient beings revolving in the world:
if we speak in terms of the realms within this world, these beings consist of ordinary people, those of the Two Vehicles, and the twelve classes of living beings.

Because they possess the deluded views of dualistic discrimination based on the two inversions, they turn their backs on the nature of awakening and unite with ignorance; therefore, they are called "inverted. This is due to the existence [of these conditions].
Because it discriminates the root-body and the vessel-world through subtle, continuous flows, distinguishing between what is proximate and remote, it is called "discriminative false seeing.

As stated in the following passage: "To establish knowledge within knowing-and-seeing is the very root of ignorance. That which "arises in its own place" refers to the *Awakening of Faith*, which says:
"Because one does not understand the single dharma-realm, the unawakened mind arises, and thus there are thoughts; yet these thoughts are non-existent."

The self-nature is not separate from original enlightenment; this clearly demonstrates that the two delusions are intimately close to the truth and serve as the basis for both bodhi-nirvana and samsaric karma.
Regarding those who undergo the cycle of rebirth, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "Because it relies on non-enlightenment, the mind moves; this movement is called 'karma.

When there is movement, there is the fruit of suffering, for it does not depart from its cause. Furthermore, this clarifies that the two delusions are themselves the karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*).

These constitute the root of the two types of death. Because Ānanda previously took the six consciousnesses and the three poisons to be the root of birth-and-death and nirvana, and did not realize that the karmic consciousness is the true root, [the Buddha] first sets forth these two phrases to reveal that the two kinds of delusive views—whether delusive or true—pervade both.
Regarding the terms "distinct karma" (*bieye*) and "common lot" (*tongfen*), there are two interpretations; if one relies on...
The Dharmalakṣaṇa school states that the "distinctive karma" (bīja) refers to the sense-faculties and the physical body produced by non-common karma;
these arise from the non-common seeds within the ālayavijñāna. Because they are produced by one's own karma and are experienced by oneself, they are called "distinctive.
As for "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā), it refers to the receptacle world produced by common karma, as it arises from the common seeds of the ālayavijñāna.
Because all beings have a share in what is induced by common karma (*sādhāraṇa-karman*), it is called "common.

If one relies on this sutra, the sense organs, the body, and the environment perceived by the single consciousness of a single person are considered the deluded perceptions of individual karma (*asādhāraṇa-karman*). Therefore, the text below states:
"Take, for example, your own present observation with your eyes of mountains, rivers, lands, and all sentient beings; these are all from time immemorial..."
Seeing what is produced by delusion, if it is so for one person, it is likewise so for all others;

therefore, with reference to the many people and the many consciousnesses that perceive the sense organs, bodies, and the physical world, these are termed "common delusive vision," because they equally delude the essence of awakening.
Thus, the text below states: "All are equally the pure, luminous, untainted, wondrous mind; seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are but the conditions for illusory sickness."
"Through the conjunction [of conditions], there is delusive birth; through the conjunction [of conditions], there is delusive death. Question:

Since Ānanda has already doubted that the "seeing of seeing" is not true seeing, why does the World-Honored One not answer directly, but instead extensively clarifies these two kinds of delusive seeing? Answer:

If one does not extensively demonstrate that there is "seeing" within delusive seeing, one cannot manifest the True Seeing that is "without seeing. Therefore, in the following text, many [distinctions] are extensively applied to a single person.

One should know that as long as a person has not yet abandoned the eye-disease of ignorance, whether they be an ordinary person, a follower of the Small Vehicle, or even a Bodhisattva at the stage of Equal Enlightenment, their vision is called delusive.
Only the Buddha alone has completely eliminated the eye-disease; his vision of the pure essence of true nature is free from disease, and thus he alone is said to possess true vision.
What is meant by "illusory vision caused by individual karma"? Ānanda, it is like a person in this world whose eyes have a red catarar;
at night, when looking at a lamp, they see a circular halo with five overlapping colors appearing distinct from the light. What do you think?

Is this circular radiance manifested by the lamp's light the color of the lamp, or is it the color of the seeing? Ānanda, if this were the color of the lamp, then it would not be seen by one who has the catarar.
Why is it that, while their views differ, this circular shadow is seen only by those with cataracts?
If seeing color were itself the manifestation of color, then what would you call the person with cataracts who sees the circular shadow?

Furthermore, Ānanda, if this circular shadow existed separately from the lamp, then a circular shadow should also appear when looking at a screen, a curtain, a table, or a bench; yet it does not exist apart from the vision [of the one with cataracts].

It should not be something visible to the eye; how then can a person with cataracts see a circular shadow? This analogy is established to clarify the deluded perception of individual karma (*bipakya-viparyāsa*). The eye is a metaphor for the noble wisdom of self-realization (*svasaṃvedana-āryajñāna*); the lamp is a metaphor for the truth of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi-tattva*); the red cataract is a metaphor for the ignorance of the karmic consciousness (*avidyā-karma-vijñāna*); and the circular shadow is a metaphor for the body-faculties and the vessel-world (*deha-bhājana-loka*). The intended meaning is as follows: ... [The text continues with the explanation of the analogy. ... Thus, although the light of the lamp is originally pure and free from defilement, because it is obstructed by the cataract, one perceives a circular shadow. This is entirely due to the fault of the cataract; it is not that the light itself has become obscured. In this way, the noble wisdom of self-realization is inherently luminous and free from all afflictions, yet because it is obstructed by the ignorance of the karmic consciousness, one perceives the various forms of the body-faculties and the vessel-world. This is entirely due to the fault of ignorance; it is not that the noble wisdom of self-realization has become obscured. Therefore, it is known that the body-faculties and the vessel-world are merely false appearances produced by the deluded perceptions of individual karma. They are not real dharmas, nor are they non-dharmas; they are neither existent nor non-existent, and they transcend all conceptual categories. They are like the circular shadow seen by a person with cataracts, which is neither the light itself nor something other than the light. It is merely a false appearance produced by the deluded perception of individual karma.
