When intelligence and principle are as they originally were, there is neither subject nor object; when ignorance stirs for the first time, subject and object are divided, and thus the sense organs, the physical body, and the objective world manifest.

Regarding the "intention" (yi) below, two gates are opened simultaneously to distinguish that the circular reflection does not exist as being identical to the lamp or the seeing, yet it does not exist apart from the lamp or the seeing. If this circular reflection were identical to the lamp...
"If there is [an eye disease], there is no impairment; why do people not see the same?

This is a metaphor for the Tathāgata abiding in *samādhi*, wherein seeing and the objects of seeing are fundamentally non-existent, being originally the wondrously pure and luminous essence of *bodhi*.

Yet, this circular image is seen only by one who has the eye disease; this is a metaphor for when ignorance and the karmic consciousness exist, one then perceives the existence of the root-body and the vessel-world.

It is just like this: if this circular reflection exists because of seeing, then once this seeing has already become the circular reflection, what further thing could there be that is able to see that circular reflection?
To use this as a metaphor for the body, the faculties, and the vessel-world: if these were produced from seeing, then this nature of seeing would have already become the body and the vessel-world;
what further thing could there be that sees the body, the faculties, and the vessel-world? Therefore, one knows the nature of the faculties.
The physical body and the vessel-world arise from the transformation of karmic consciousness; they do not pertain to the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*).
If this circular reflection existed apart from the lamp, then one should likewise observe circular reflections appearing on the surrounding screens, curtains, tables, and mats.

This serves as a metaphor for how these root-bodies and the vessel-world would—if they were separated from pure *tathatā* (suchness)—be produced without cause, which is untenable. Therefore, it is said that they "arise in their own place."
Just as this circular reflection exists apart from the seeing [faculty], it should not be something gazed upon by the eyes;

likewise, if this body, its faculties, and the vessel-world existed apart from seeing, there would have to be one who possesses false seeing. Since no one fails to see the body, its faculties, and the vessel-world, how could there be such a thing as false seeing?
There must necessarily be the seeing of the body, its faculties, and the vessel-world.

Therefore, you should know that while form actually resides in the lamp, the seeing-illness constitutes the shadow; both the shadow and the seeing are defects. To see these defects is not itself an illness.
One should never say that this is the lamp or that this is the seeing, nor that within them there is something that is neither lamp nor seeing.
It is like a second moon, which is neither a real substance nor a reflection. Why? Because the perception of a second moon is produced by pressing [the eye]. No person of wisdom would...
One should say that this pressed root of the sense organ is neither form nor non-form, neither seeing nor non-seeing; it is likewise produced by a cataract of the eye.
Now, whom could one name as being the lamp or the seeing? How much more so when distinguishing between what is not the lamp and what is not the seeing?

This explains the origin from which the circular shadow arises. It means that since this circular shadow neither arises from the lamp or the seeing itself, nor exists apart from the lamp or the seeing, from where does it then arise? Therefore, it is shown: "Upon the lamp there is only radiance;
upon the eye there has never been a circular shadow. It is solely because the pure eye has a cataract that this [shadow] is produced."

The circular shadow is formed by the light; thus, this circular shadow arises from the red cataract. Therefore it is said that while the color actually resides in the lamp, the visual ailment constitutes the shadow.
Not only is the perceived circular shadow produced by the red cataract, but the one who perceives the circular shadow is likewise constituted by the red cataract.
This is because the eye is not the cataract and thus is not diseased, and the lamp is not the cataract and thus is not diseased.

Because there is no shadow, it is said that the seeing of the shadow is both a cataract; yet the essence of the vision that perceives the cataract has never fallen into the affliction of the cataract, and thus it is said that "seeing the cataract is not itself the disease.
Therefore, this circular shadow arises from the red cataract and has no relation to the lamp or the seeing;

one should not cling to the idea that this circular shadow is produced by the lamp or the seeing. Since it exists apart from the lamp and the seeing, one knows that it is like [the reflection in water].

When wisdom accords with suchness and is resolved according to the principle of suchness, one does not perceive the existence of the sense organs, the body, or the vessel-world (the external environment).
It is like a lamp: when it illuminates, no circular shadow exists inherently. Yet, due to a single moment of non-awakening, ignorance stirs delusively;

this awakened nature then transforms into the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*). Because there is a seeing-part, there arises a "characterized-part" (*nimitta-bhāga*), which constitutes the circular shadow. Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* says:
Because it relies on movement, one is able to see; because it relies on the capacity to see, objects falsely appear.

What is called "seeing the illness as a shadow" means that not only are the perceived objects—the body, the sense organs, and the physical world—arisen from ignorance, but the perceiver itself is also arisen from ignorance.
This is what is meant by "the shadow and the seeing are both cataracts. Nevertheless, the capacity to illuminate...
The division of the two aspects of the destruction of appearances, which arises from ignorance, is called "subtle and secret contemplation" and is also named "the noble wisdom of self-awakening.
This is the solitary brilliance of the numinous light, utterly detached from the sense organs and their objects;

it has never been afflicted from the beginning, for what is called "seeing a cataract" is not itself an affliction. Thus one knows that the sense organs, the body, and the vessel-world arise from the karmic consciousness of ignorance.
One must never cling to this root-body and the vessel-world as being identical to the nature of enlightenment, nor as arising from it or existing apart from it.
This is just like a second moon, which is neither the true substance of the moon nor a reflection of the moon, for it is produced by pressing upon the eye.

Since it arises from such pressing, how could one possibly cling to it as being the substance of the moon, or as being produced from that which is not the substance of the moon? It exists apart [from both].
Seeing arises not apart from the arising of seeing; since the second moon arises from the pressing of one [eye], one knows that the nature of seeing arises from a single movement.
This analogy precisely corresponds to the preceding passage: "Although this seeing is not the wondrous, brilliant, and pure mind, it is like the second moon, which is not the shadow of the moon.
Furthermore, below this, it again uses the circular reflection to correspond with the second moon.
The Moon.
What is meant by "common deluded vision"? Ānanda, in this Jambudvīpa, excluding the great oceans, there are three thousand islands among the level lands;
the largest of these central continents, encompassing its great nations from east to west, contains two thousand countries in total.
Beyond these three hundred [great continents], there are other minor islands within the various seas;
among them, some contain two or three hundred nations, while others have only one or two, up to thirty, forty, fifty, or even sixty.

Ānanda, if within this range there is a single minor island that has only two nations, and the people of only one nation collectively experience adverse conditions, then for the sentient beings of that land on that minor island—
They beheld all manner of inauspicious omens, such as seeing two suns or two moons;
therein appeared halos, solar spots, crescent rings, comets, meteors, flying stars, "burdened ears," rainbows, and halcyon bows—all kinds of evil signs.
These were seen only in this country, while the sentient beings of other lands neither saw nor even heard of them.
This clarifies the deluded vision of those with equal fortune (*sabhāgatā*). "This Jambudvīpa" below refers generally to the continent on the southern face of Mount Sumeru.
"Sea water" refers to the salt-water ocean outside the seven golden mountains. "Level land" refers to flat ground. A "continent" (*dvīpa*) is a landmass habitable within the waters.
Among these, the central continent consists of two thousand three hundred great nations; the remaining two thousand [are smaller].
Among the nine hundred and ninety-nine continents, regardless of the number of kingdoms they contain, we shall consider only the smallest continent, which has but two nations.
In one of these nations, all experience adverse conditions and witness various omens of ill fortune, such as halos, rings, pendants, and jade ornaments;
when evil vapors encircle them, it is called a "halo" (*huì*), and when there is a partial or total eclipse, it is called a "dimming" (*bó*).

It is said: when the jade pendants and rings appear in their proper places, it is an auspicious sign; when the baleful vapors approach the sun like star-like rays pointing in all directions, it is called a "sweeping star" (*ketu*);

when the radiant vapors radiate out in all four directions, it is called a "star of calamity" (*bō*); when they move crosswise, it is called "flying"; when they descend and pour down, it is called "flowing vapors";

when they flank the sun like a back or an ear, it is called "back-ear" (*fù'ěr*); and when the vapors reflect the sun, appearing sometimes bright and sometimes dark, they form rainbows and halos (*nǐ*). All of these are shared by all sentient beings.
Because all those who are moved by karma possess a share in it, they are able to see the same thing; as for why those in that land do not see it, it is because they lack the shared karma.
Ānanda, I now use these two matters to clarify the point through both affirmation and negation.

Regarding "advancing and retreating": first, advancing the analogy of individual karma (*bipakṣa*) serves to clarify the principle of individual karma, thereby revealing that the deluded vision of a single person constitutes "individual" [karma].
Next, retreating from the principle of individual karma and advancing again the analogy of individual karma serves as an illustration for the principle of shared karma (*sabhāga*).
Finally, retreating from the analogy of a single person’s individual karma and advancing the analogy of a nation’s shared karma [establishes the distinction between the two].
The "Dharma-Example" (dharmadṛṣṭānta) uses the commonality of the great trichiliocosm to reveal that the false views of many people are identical.
What is called "combined illumination" (saṃyuktaprakāśana) refers to the elucidation through the analogy of the identity or difference between the Dharma and the example.

By observing the examples—"you as the example," "that as the example," and "Jambudvīpa as the example"—the subsequent text states, "all are," which cites the example to illustrate the Dharma; thus, the Dharma and the example are each distinct.
The first is called "all" because they are distinct; the second is called "together" because it clarifies the matter by combining the same and the distinct;
the third is called "identical" because one country serves as an analogy for the great trichiliocosm. Thus, it is called "identical."

Ānanda, it is like the deluded vision of individual karma among sentient beings: the circular shadow that appears within the light of a lamp, though it seems to be an external object, is ultimately produced by the cataract in the eye of the observer.
This cataract is simply the exhaustion of seeing and is not created by the color itself; yet, the one who perceives the cataract never incurs the fault of seeing.
Take this as an analogy for you today, as you observe with your eyes the mountains, rivers, nations, lands, and all other things.
All sentient beings are formed by the disease of views that have existed since beginningless time. The view and its conditions appear as if they were present objects;

fundamentally, this is the clarity of my own awareness. The view that takes these conditions as its object is the cataract; the fundamental, enlightened mind of awareness is not the cataract when it perceives those conditions.

This section explains the analogy of individual karma by applying it to the specific dharma. First, the analogy is restated: "Although it resembles the external object, it is produced by an eye-disease.
This means that although this circular shadow appears with distinct characteristics, it is produced by a red eye-disease and is not substantially real;
therefore, it is said to "resemble" the object. "The disease is merely the fatigue of vision, not something created by form" means that this eye-disease arises from...
The fatigue causes the vision to arise, yet it does not actually originate from the lamp-light; however, one who perceives this optical aberration ultimately incurs no fault of vision.
If one can see that this red aberration arises from the fatigue of vision, then this vision is ultimately not the delusion of having an optical disease.
Following this example, apply the analogy to the principle: when the eyes observe the lands, this is the aspect of seeing.
Sentient beings are like the combined circular shadows of the objective aspect; they are all produced by the disease of vision that has existed since beginningless time.

This "disease of vision" is precisely the mark of karma arising from ignorance (*avidyā*). Because this mark of karmic ignorance perfumes [the consciousness] incessantly, it eventually gives rise to the subject that sees and thereby constitutes the object that is seen.
Therefore, it is said they are "produced by the disease of vision. This corresponds to the previous statement: "That seer is the cataract of the eye."

That which is established arises from the aspect of karma associated with ignorance, manifesting as the two divisions of appearance (*nimitta*) and seeing (*darśana*), just as one with cataracts in the eyes perceives circular halos.
That "the seeing and its object appear as if they were present before one" means that the evolving karma-consciousness manifests as these two divisions;
both appearance and seeing arise based upon self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*), because the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is not substantially real.
It is said: "Though this semblance appears to be the external object before one, it is fundamentally a cataract within my own luminous awareness that perceives what is conditioned.

This means that these two divisions—the seeing and the perceived—are originally the wondrously luminous essence of my fundamental awareness. Suddenly, a single thought arises and becomes a cataract of delusion;
thus, there come to be the 'seer' and the 'perceived. It is not that the luminous essence of awareness inherently possesses them from the beginning."
Furthermore, this confluence of the cataract constitutes the perception of fatigue; it is not something created by external forms.
If the awakened perception itself were the cataract, then the fundamentally awakened, luminous mind—which perceives conditions—would not be the cataract.

If one considers that this luminous, fundamentally awakened mind perceives this essence of vision as arising from the red cataract, then although this luminous, fundamentally awakened mind is present in daily life and universally perceives all conditions, it is in truth free of any cataract.
This false vision may be compared to the aforementioned case; however, one who perceives the cataract ultimately incurs no fault for seeing.

When one awakens to the cataract of that which is perceived, such awakening is not itself within the cataract; this is truly the seeing of seeing. How, then, could it again be called "awakening," "hearing," "knowing," or "seeing"?
Therefore, what you now see—myself, yourself, and all the ten classes of sentient beings in the world—is precisely the seeing of a cataract.
One who does not see the cataract sees the true essence of seeing; because this essence is not a cataract, it is not called "seeing.
This passage restates the answer to the doubt that "seeing seeing" further increases confusion and distress.

If one uses the luminous mind of original enlightenment to awaken to this perceived nature of seeing as arising from the delusion of a cataract, then this awakening mind does not belong to the cataract.
"Delusion" refers precisely to the meaning previously explained: when one observes the observing, that observation is not [itself] the seeing.
Since you now know that the nature of wondrous enlightenment is thus, you should understand that the essence of seeing belongs to delusive seeing; this is clear.
Why then do you equate and list this wondrously enlightened nature alongside seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing? How is this different from...?"
Is it not a great error to value the jade of Mount Jing equally with common stones? Huangbo said: "People of the world do not awaken;
they merely take seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing to be the mind. Because they are shrouded by these very faculties, they fail to perceive the luminous, essential body.
If one simply lets go of the mind right now, the essential body manifests of itself, like the great sun rising."

Because it illuminates the void and pervades the Dharma-realm without further obstruction, those who study the Way must not identify with seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, nor with purposeful actions and movements.
By emptying out seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, the path of the mind is cut off and there is no place of entry;
rather, one should recognize the fundamental mind within the very locus of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, for the fundamental mind does not belong to seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing.
Furthermore, it does not depart from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.

Therefore, you should know that your current seeing of me and your seeing of the twelve classes of beings—this seeing which possesses both the capacity to see and the objects seen—is precisely the seeing of eyes affected by a cataract.
It is like a diseased eye seeing circular shadows; it is not a seeing that illuminates the cataract itself, but is merely a false seeing.
He clearly perceives that the eye ailment is a false vision; it sees the truth without being mixed with delusion, and its essence is pure without being mixed with the ailment.
It responds to colors like a mani jewel and manifests forms like a clear mirror; though one looks at it all day, there is no perception of worldly phenomena.
Therefore, it cannot be designated by the term "vision" when accompanied by an ailment; thus it is said: "Even seeing..."
Being free from seeing, it cannot be reached by seeing; thus the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states:

"If one is free from the *karmic consciousness*, then there are no marks of seeing, for the Dharma-body of all Buddhas has no marks of form or color such that they might see one another. The *Ratnaketuparivarta-sūtra* (Renwang jing) states:
"All knowledge and views prior to the Vajra-samādhi are not called 'seeing'; only the Buddha’s sudden realization possesses all [knowledges]."
Because that which is known and seen by wisdom is called "seeing," it is termed false knowledge; yet where there is knowledge, there is something not known.
True knowledge is non-knowledge, wherein there is nothing unknown. False seeing is having a view, wherein there is something not seen. True seeing is non-seeing, wherein there is nothing unseen.
Thus, it is only when the knowledge and vision of sentient beings have been exhausted that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision manifest.
Ānanda, just as those sentient beings shared a common delusive vision, so too does this delusive vision of a single individual with a distinct karmic lot;
just as one person with an eye disease sees a circular shadow produced by a cataract,
so too do these inauspicious sights seen by a collective multitude arise from the miasmic evils within their shared karma— all of which are produced by beginningless delusive vision.
This section on the dharma of the distinct karma of regression further employs the analogy of the distinct karma of progression to clarify the dharma of the common lot (*sabhāgatā*).

Why is this example given? It is because the false perceptions of distinct karma are illusory and easy to understand, whereas the false perceptions of the common lot appear real and are difficult to believe;
the intention is to show that all things which appear real are likewise illusory. This is what is manifested by a single person with diseased eyes.
The example of the circular shadow belonging to the eye disease illustrates how the inauspicious sights seen by the people of a single country arise from evil conditions;
although there is a difference between the unreal and the real regarding what is seen, they are both produced by the delusions of seeing.
For example, within the three thousand continents of Jambudvīpa, including the four great oceans, as well as the Sahā world and all the realms of outflows throughout the ten directions,
along with all sentient beings therein, are equally this enlightened, luminous, and untainted wondrous mind. Through the conditions of the illusory maladies of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing,
they falsely arise through conjunction and falsely die through conjunction.

This uses the analogy of individual karma—which pertains to retrogression—to illustrate the principle of the commonality of the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneous class) as it applies to the great trichiliocosm. Question:

Why does the analogy of individual karma not likewise apply to the great trichiliocosm? Answer: Because the great trichiliocosm and a single nation are both subsumed within the deluded vision of the same *sabhāgatā*.
However, fearing that [the audience] might not grasp this all at once, the analogy is employed to clarify the shared nature of a single nation.
To take the commonality (*sabhāgatā*) of a single country as an analogy for the commonality of a great trichiliocosm:
if the inauspicious sights perceived within one country arise from pestilence and evil, then it is the same for all countries within the three thousand continents of Jambudvīpa in the south.
If it is so for the countries of Jambudvīpa, it is likewise so for the countries of the other three continents within the domain of a single sun and moon.
Since it is thus for the worlds under his governance, so too is it for the billion-fold world-system of a thousand million suns and moons governed by Śākyamuni;
and since it is thus for the great trichiliocosm, so too are all the conditioned realms of impurity governed by the various Buddhas who are the emanations of Śākyamuni throughout the ten directions.
Therefore, it is said that they are all equally the primordial, pure, and wondrous mind of enlightened awareness, free from outflows.
A single thought-moment of deluded movement transforms into seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing; through these illusory conditions of affliction, birth and death arise.
Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "That which is manifested before the eye is called 'the seen'; that which is heard from others is called 'the heard';
that which is constructed by the movement of one's own mind is called 'the sensed'; and that which is internally experienced by oneself..."

That which is realized is called the "knowable" (*jñeya*). From among these four kinds of faculties, the accumulated and produced habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from beginningless time—even down to the specific counts and divisions of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing—converge in a single place to form the conditions for illusory sickness. They arise simultaneously and perish simultaneously;
the very root of birth and death is truly based upon this. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states that "arising and ceasing" and "non-arising and non-ceasing..."
The conjunction of arising and ceasing, which is neither identical nor different, is called the *ālaya-vijñāna*, serving as the cause for the transmigration of birth and death.
If one can distance oneself from all conditions of conjunction as well as non-conjunction, then the causes of birth and death will further be extinguished and eliminated.
The perfect nature of Bodhi, the non-arising and non-ceasing quality of the pure fundamental mind, is the eternally abiding original enlightenment.
Hereafter, it is revealed that by transforming two kinds of deluded views, one realizes Nirvana and Bodhi as the fundamentally pure essence.

As for "all harmonious conditions," these refer to the two kinds of ignorance—namely, the ignorance of arising and the ignorance of moisture—which act as conditions in conjunction with objective realms.
That which arises through conjunction is the six coarse consciousnesses; their characteristics serve as the cause for birth-and-death in segments (*paricchinna-saṃsāra*).
That which does not arise through conjunction is fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*); because it suddenly arises from turning one's back on pure awakening, it is called "non-conjunction.

Its characteristics are the three kinds of subtle consciousnesses; they serve as the cause for birth-and-death through transformation (*pariṇāma-saṃsāra*). This is what is referred to in the *Awakening of Faith* as "correspondence" (*saṃprayukta*).
This is the mind that is non-associated with mental factors (*citta-viprayukta*).

If one employs this subtle and secret contemplation to illuminate and shatter the two kinds of ignorance, then the causes of the two deaths will be forever abandoned and the fruits of the two deaths will be eternally severed. Reaching this point, it may be called the perfected Bodhi;
it may be called the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing; it may be called the pure fundamental mind; and it may be called original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*).
"O Constant Abiding One, you still have not eliminated these two kinds of false views, nor have you emerged from the two deaths.

Your karmic consciousness is vast and boundless, with no fundamental basis to rely upon; yet you wish to take this very root of birth and death for the nature of wondrous enlightenment—is this not too premature a calculation?
If you would contemplate well and employ subtle, secret observation and illumination to perceive the root of birth and death, [you will find it]..."
Only when the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is severed completely by a single, fierce, and powerful stroke of the sword will it correspond to the designation of the pure and wondrous awakening.
From the first fascicle up to this point constitutes a major conclusion;

it is precisely what is meant by saying that when the root of beginningless birth and death is exhausted, the beginningless bodhi and nirvāṇa finally attain perfection. As the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* verse says: "Like..."
The coming-to-be of the pure storehouse (viśuddhagarbha) within the worldly *ālaya* is like gold and a finger-ring; they are mutually indistinguishable.
While the Buddhas realize it as the pure storehouse, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) grasp it as the *ālaya*.

Just as the same fine gold receives different names—such as "finger-ring"—depending on the conditions of the furnace fire, so too does the true mind receive [different designations] according to its defilement or purity.

The distinctions between ordinary beings and sages arise from conditions; by clinging to provisional names, the two views suddenly emerge, yet by awakening to the true essence, the one mind is perfectly realized.
Ānanda, although you previously awakened to the wondrously luminous nature of original enlightenment—which is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it a spontaneous nature—you still...

"You have not yet understood that this source of awakening is produced neither through combination nor through non-combination. Ānanda, I shall now question you again regarding the external objects before you.

You still harbor doubts based on the nature of all worldly delusive thoughts and their combined causes and conditions, thinking that the mind of Bodhi is realized through such combination. If that were so, then as for your own wondrous, pure essence of seeing—"
Is it in harmony with light, in harmony with darkness, in harmony with openness, or in harmony with obstruction?
If it were in harmony with light, then observe this light as it appears before you: where would it blend with seeing? The characteristics of seeing can be distinguished;
what form would the blending take? If it were not seeing, how could it see the light? If it were identical to seeing, how could it see seeing itself? Seeing must be complete and pervasive.

In what way could light and clarity be unified? If they were to unite, clarity would not be seen; if they were to see, they would necessarily be distinct from clarity. If they were mixed, the nature of that clarity would be lost;
if their names were mixed, the nature of clarity and its harmony would be lost. Thus, "clarity" and "harmony" do not constitute a meaningful sense.
It is the same for darkness, openness, and all various obstructions. Furthermore, Ānanda, does your currently wondrously pure essence of seeing now unite with light?

Does it unite with darkness, or does it unite with openness, or does it unite with obstruction? If it unites with light, then when one reaches a place of darkness, the characteristic of light has already ceased;
this vision would thus not unite with the various forms of darkness. How, then, could it see darkness?
If, when seeing darkness, it does not unite with darkness but unites with light, then it should not be seeing light. Since it does not see light, how can it be said to unite with light?
"Clear understanding is not darkness; that darkness, as well as openness and all manner of obstructions, is likewise so.
Hereafter follows the refutation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Conjunction means to blend the myriad things into one. If there were truly no conjunction, there would be no Bodhi;
for it was previously stated that the untainted, wondrous mind conjoins with seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.

Because they are unified in one place, there is birth and death; furthermore, fearing that he might misunderstand, [the Buddha] did not wait for him to ask again, but immediately cited his words to refute them.
The reason for this refutation is that arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-non-ceasing do not share the same characteristic.
Although [the Buddha] first concedes that [Ananda] has attained some understanding, he subsequently demonstrates that [Ananda] has not yet fully comprehended by stating, "The source of awakening..."
This refers to the fundamentally pure essence of awakening. Ānanda, [the Buddha] below this point examines and determines the locus of conjunction, saying:
"I have previously provided such instruction, yet you have not yet attained awakening;

you still harbor doubts based on worldly deluded thoughts regarding the nature of various causes and conditions, and you cling to the notion that this pure essence of awakening also arises through conjunction."
If that is so, with whom does your wondrous, pure essence of vision harmonize within the realms of light and darkness, penetration and obstruction?
"Realization" refers precisely to the realization of grasping. Now, as for what is called "harmony," it means being blended like water and soil until they cannot be distinguished.
If you claim that the essence of vision harmonizes with light, then when you raise your eyes to see light, it should coincide exactly with the appearance of light.
At the moment of manifestation, from what location does this essence of vision mix with it to become blended?

Furthermore, since clarity and vision do not intermingle, they can be distinguished clearly and distinctly. If the two were intermingled, clarity would lose its clarity and vision would lose its vision;
how then could one perceive their forms, or know that vision and clarity have been blended? If you say...
If the appearance of light is present yet not seen, then the characteristic of light exists in the locus of the characteristic and the seeing exists in the locus of seeing;
since they would not know one another, there should be no seeing. How then is it that one sees light immediately upon opening the eyes?
If you claim that the appearance of light is itself seeing, then when you see light, how is this different from seeing the seeing itself? It must be called the nature of seeing.
If [the light] were perfectly full, there would be no empty space for it to harmonize with clarity.
If one says that the marks of clarity are perfectly full, then there is no gap to accommodate the nature of seeing.

If you claim that seeing must be seeing and clarity must be clarity, such that they are each distinct from one another, yet now they are mixed and blended—then seeing loses its name and clarity loses its designation. When even names and designations no longer exist, how can one speak [of them]?
There is absolutely no such principle as the union of seeing and light;

Since the essence has already merged with light, when it reaches the time of darkness, the characteristic of light has already ceased; this vision likewise follows the light in ceasing.
It certainly cannot merge again with darkness. How then can it see darkness when darkness arrives?
