Furthermore, Ānanda, how is it that the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous true nature of suchness?
The following passage reveals that the Tathāgatagarbha is not separate from the six faculties. The Sanskrit term *praveśa* is translated here as "entry" (*ru*, 入) rather than "faculty" (*gen*, 根);
it is called "entry" because it encompasses both the capacity to enter and the objects entered, just as the visual faculty flows [into its object].

The faculties of the eye and ear, which respectively flow outward toward forms and sounds, act as the "enterers" (the subjects); the empty capacities of the eye to receive forms and the ear to receive sounds, etc., act as the "entered" (the objects).
Furthermore, because those who are deluded regarding internal forms are distinguished separately, the eleven types of form-dharmas are collectively termed "internal forms.
Among these, the six sense-objects belong to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), while the five sense-faculties belong to inference (*anumāna*).
Because one can infer the existence of these faculties by means of the arising of consciousness, the "original Tathāgatagarbha" refers to the fact that all Tathāgatas flow forth from this;
the "wondrous True Suchness-nature" refers to the fact that Bodhi is present at every point of contact through the gates of the six faculties.
As the Mahāyāna Sūtra says: "The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, mind, and all the sense-faculties—through these, there is constant transmigration."

Furthermore, it is said that there is nothing capable of turning [the eye]; to know that the eye is unarisen, lacks self-nature, and is described as empty, quiescent, and non-existent—this is precisely the purport of the wondrous nature of True Suchness (Tathatā).

Ānanda, that very act of staring with the eyes until they become fatigued, as well as the eyes themselves and the fatigue, are all equally the appearance of exhaustion produced by staring within Bodhi.
Because of the two kinds of false objects—light and darkness—the faculty of sight arises in the midst of them; it draws in these objective images, which is called the "nature of seeing.
Yet this seeing has no ultimate substance apart from those two objects, light and darkness.

This is the point where Aniruddha exchanged a cluster of grapes for the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). First, he cites a factual occurrence to demonstrate that the visual faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) is illusory:

looking straight ahead with fixed eyes is called "staring with fatigue" (*deng-lao*); because it arises from staring with the eyes, it is called the "sign of fatigue arising from staring. As the preceding text states:
"For example, when one stares with clear eyes, fatigue arises, and one perceives illusory flowers (*vikṣiptapuṣpa*). Therefore, [the divine eye is likewise a product of such exertion].

The pupils of the eyes are used as a metaphor for true nature (*tathatā*); the act of staring is used as a metaphor for exhaustion; and the floating flowers are used as a metaphor for the signs of that exhaustion.

This statement implies that it is not only the floating flowers that are the signs of exhaustion, but the pupils themselves are also the signs of exhaustion produced by the act of staring, because both the perceived object (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiving faculty (*darśana-bhāga*) belong entirely to the karma-consciousness of ignorance (*avidyā-karma-vijñāna*). Therefore, in the following section, the text explains how this staring gives rise to [the signs].

Regarding the meaning of the characteristic of fatigue (*klamatha-lakṣaṇa*): due to the two objects of light and darkness adhering to the profound stillness, the faculty of vision (*darśana*) arises and immediately resides within the field of vision.
The essence of vision reflects the forms, thereby absorbing these objective images to constitute the nature of seeing.

Since this seeing arises from the objects and has no substance apart from them, one knows that the nature of seeing is likewise a characteristic of fatigue produced by staring within the *bodhi*-mind.
Question: Previously, it was stated that the mind which takes objects as its condition has no substance in order to reveal that the nature of seeing does have substance;

yet now you say that the nature of seeing, when separated from objects, ultimately has no substance. Why is this? Answer: Previously, because Ānanda insisted on identifying with the mind that takes objects as its condition and refused to let it go, the World-Honored One wished him to abandon that conditioned mind and recognize the nature of seeing; therefore, he relied upon the nature of seeing [to make his point].
Having already demonstrated that it possesses substance, [the teaching] now intends for one to directly perceive the nature and recognize it as the wondrous true *tathatā*;

therefore, it further states that the perceived nature is without substance, which is also a state produced by staring into the *bodhicitta* until weariness arises— this being the method of "using a wedge to remove a wedge."
Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this seeing does not come from light nor darkness, it does not emerge from the sense organ, and it is not born from space.
Why is this? If it came from light, it would cease when darkness follows; thus one should not see darkness. If it came from darkness, it would cease when light follows;
thus there would be no seeing of light. If it were born from the sense organ, it would necessarily be independent of light and darkness. Thus, this essence of seeing is fundamentally...

If that which lacks intrinsic nature appears as objective forms before emptiness, then upon returning [to the source], one should see the sense organs themselves. Furthermore, since emptiness observes itself, what concern is it to your sense bases?
Therefore, you should know that the eye-base is false and illusory; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
The first three phrases first indicate non-arising. From "If it comes from light" onwards, it refutes that [seeing] does not arise from the object, because light and darkness are mutually exclusive;
if it were produced by light, one should not see darkness, for when it is dark there is no light, and seeing ceases along with the light.
The opposite applies to darkness. From "If it arises from the faculty" onwards, it refutes that it does not emerge from the faculty.
Because it is detached from dust and lacks a root, if one emerges into space and advances while observing the elephant, one may likewise observe the root upon retreating.

Furthermore, since space itself is capable of seeing, what concern does this have with your faculty? Therefore, the conclusion below—that the false is immediately the true—indicates that the three categories and seven elements are all to be sought by Ānanda within the sphere of daily life, in the very places of seeing forms, hearing sounds, putting on clothes, and eating food.
The patriarchs of the Chan school taught people to contemplate the "critical phrase" (huatou), which is precisely this method.

However, the patriarchs were unwilling to easily reveal the secret to others, instead requiring them to conjecture for themselves, harbor doubt within themselves, and seek and investigate for themselves.

Ultimately, they must investigate until they reach the point where this view arises from nowhere. After long persistence and intense pressure, when one’s practice reaches maturity, one suddenly [awakens] from within a state of cold indifference.
However, having personally witnessed this and attained a hundred-percent certainty, I would never lightly utter the four characters "the eye-faculty enters into falsehood.
Thus, Xiangyan said: "I do not value my former teacher’s Buddha-dharma;
I only value his refusal to break the seal for me—how great was the Buddha's compassion! He truly pushed his sincere heart into my belly. Therefore, he opened [his mouth].
I shall now explain for you this Tathāgata-dhyāna, which distinguishes it from the Zen of the Patriarchs.
Ānanda, suppose there were a person who blocked their ears tightly with two fingers; because the faculty of hearing is strained, sounds arise within the head.
Both the ear and the strain are but manifestations of the *bodhi* mind produced by staring into exhaustion. This occurs due to the two states of movement and stillness.
False sensory objects arise; when the faculty of hearing abides in their midst and draws in these objective images, it is called the nature of hearing.

This hearing, apart from those two objects—motion and stillness—is ultimately without substance. Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this hearing does not come from motion or stillness, nor does it emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from space.
Why is this? If it came from stillness, it would cease as soon as there is motion, and thus it would not be hearing.

Movement. If [hearing] came from movement to reach stillness, it would perish along with that movement, and there would be no awareness of stillness. If it were produced from the sense organ itself, there could be neither movement nor stillness.
Thus, the essence of hearing originally has no self-nature. If hearing emerged from empty space and thereby established a nature, then it would not be empty space.
Furthermore, if empty space heard by itself, what concern would that have for your auditory faculty? Therefore, you should know that the auditory faculty is illusory and fundamentally lacks a cause.
"Conditions do not possess an inherent nature.

This is where Avalokiteśvara exchanges the new rolled leaf for the faculty of the ear as the locus of perfect penetration (*āyatana*). First, he uses this matter to reveal the falsity of the ear-faculty;
the "fatigue" (*lao*) of the ear-faculty is synonymous with the "fatigue" produced by staring into space, and it encompasses both the sense organ and its affliction.
"Fatigue" (*láo*) refers to the sounds that manifest from the faculty of hearing due to its exhaustion. "Staring with fixed eyes" is the exhaustion of the eye-faculty;

"obstructing the ears" is the exhaustion of the ear-faculty. Just as with the appearance of floating flowers (*māndāraka-puṣpa*), if sounds are produced, they all belong to the manifestations of fatigue;
therefore, they are called "signs of fatigue. Because of staring with fixed eyes, one sees floating flowers; because of obstructing the ears, sounds are produced within the ears.
Sound. When the eye-faculty is fatigued, form arises as fatigue; when the ear-faculty is fatigued, sound arises as fatigue.

That which can cause fatigue and that which is fatigued are both the Bodhicitta manifesting as fatigue; therefore, it is said that they are all equally the "fatigue-phase manifested by staring" of Bodhicitta.

From "Because of... below, the fatigue-phase is explained and established. From "In this way... below, the place of non-arising is indicated. Why is this? From "If... below, [the opponent's view] is refuted.
If this hearing arises from a quiet environment, then when a moving environment appears, this hearing should immediately cease along with the quiet;
it should not hear the movement. Who then is it that hears the roaring of the myriad apertures?

If you claim that this hearing arises from a moving environment, then when a quiet environment appears, this hearing should immediately cease along with the movement; yet one still perceives the silence and the absence of sound.
Who is it? If it were produced from the sense organ, it would not depend on movement or stillness, and there would likewise be no hearing.
If it emerged from space, then that space must be able to hear and should be called the "ear," rather than empty space. Furthermore, if space hears by itself, what concern is that for the ear?
When the Great Being Avalokiteśvara realized perfect penetration, his initial point of departure was also this hearing, not movement.
"Quietude arises; it does not emerge from the sense faculties. Ultimately, where does it reside? By contemplating in this way and practicing thus, one gains entry into this gate.

Therefore, the subsequent text says: "The two characteristics of movement and stillness clearly do not arise. In this manner, as [the practice] gradually increases, that which is heard and that by which one hears are both exhausted, and so forth.
Ānanda, it is like a person who forcefully pinches their nose; after pinching it for a long time, they become fatigued and perceive a sensation of cold within the nose.
Because of that sensation, they distinguish between openness and obstruction, emptiness and solidity, and so on, even up to various fragrant and foul odors.

Both the nose and the fatigue are equally the signs of exhaustion produced by the staring of Bodhi. It is because of these two kinds of false objects—openness and obstruction—that the faculty of hearing arises.

Abiding in the center, inhaling these sensory objects of dust and phenomena is called the nature of olfactory-cum-auditory perception. This hearing is devoid of those two sensory objects of openness and obstruction;
ultimately, it has no inherent substance. You should know that this hearing does not come from openness or obstruction, nor does it emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from space.

Why is this? If it came from openness, then upon obstruction it would cease; how then could one perceive obstruction? If it were to exist because of obstruction, then when there is openness, it would not exist.

[Ananda] heard [the teaching]. [The Buddha asked: "How can you distinguish between fragrant and foul odors and other tactile sensations? If this faculty of hearing were produced from the sense organ itself, it would necessarily be subject to obstruction or penetration;
such a 'hearing mechanism' would have no inherent nature of its own. If it were produced from space, then that hearing would naturally turn back to smell your own nose.

Space itself would possess the power of hearing—what connection would it have with your sensory faculty? Therefore, you should know that the olfactory faculty is illusory; fundamentally, it is neither born of causes and conditions nor is it spontaneous."
Nature. This is Pāṇṭaka. He exchanged his double-hanging claws for the nostrils of Liao Tian. "Holding" refers to the retention of breath.
To hold it urgently is the toil of the nose; the sensation of cold is the sign of that toil. An ancient said, "There is some breath."
The breath is also a sickness. Therefore, it is said that both the nose and labor share the same characteristic of being labor. Master Zhi said:
"Throughout the day one adds incense and changes the water, yet does not realize that the body itself is the *dōjō* (place of practice).

If one can truly, at the very moment of smelling fragrance or stench, strike away the nostrils, then one will breathe through the same nostrils as all the Buddhas of the three periods of time. For this reason, the world...
When a person is hurried, their livestock becomes exhausted; when Tiṣya regulated his breath, he attained the Way.

Ānanda, it is like a person who licks their lips with their tongue; by licking repeatedly until they become fatigued, if that person were ill, there would be a bitter taste, whereas for a healthy person, there is a slight sensation of sweetness.
Through this contrast between sweetness and bitterness, the immobility of the tongue-root is revealed.
At that time, the nature of blandness remains constant. Furthermore, the tongue and its fatigue are both manifestations of the state of *bodhi* arising from the exhaustion of staring.
Because the two kinds of false objects—sweetness and bitterness—arise, the faculty of cognition emerges between them to absorb these objective images; this is called the nature of knowing taste.
This nature of knowing taste has no ultimate substance apart from those three objects: sweet, bitter, and bland. Thus, Ānanda, you should know this.

Thus, when experiencing bitterness or blandness, one knows that sweetness has ceased; this knowledge does not arise because of the blandness. Furthermore, it does not emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from space. Why is this?
If the cessation of sweetness occurs upon the arrival of bitterness, how can one know the blandness? If it emerged from the blandness, then sweetness would have already perished;
how then could one know the two characteristics of sweetness and bitterness? If it were produced from the tongue, there would necessarily be no sweetness.

Regarding the flavors of blandness and bitterness, one perceives these as the fundamental nature of taste; yet they have no inherent self-nature. If emptiness were to produce its own flavor within space, it would not be known by your mouth.
Furthermore, if emptiness knew itself, what would that have to do with your sense faculty? Therefore, you should know that the tongue-faculty is false and illusory;
fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
This is the Dharma-gate realized by Kauṇḍinya at the place where he was chewing his rice. To lick an object with the tongue is called "licking";

to do so incessantly is called "repeated licking. This repeated licking is the toil of the tongue; sweetness and bitterness are the characteristics of the toil of the tongue. It is through this faculty of the tongue that one knows sweetness and bitterness;

this is called the nature of knowing taste. This nature of knowing taste— *Note: The source text appears to be a commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, specifically the section concerning the faculties of Kauṇḍinya (憍梵鉢提). The term "mature" (*shú* 熟) likely refers to the habitual, repetitive action of licking.*
Apart from that sweetness and bitterness, there is ultimately no substance. Tell me, then, with what do you drink tea and eat rice?

If you can find the place where the tongue falls within this, you will know that the broad and long tongue-mark, which covers the three thousand great thousandfold worlds, has never been separate from the very spot where it licks the lips and chews the rice.
Ānanda, it is like a person who touches one warm hand with a cold hand. If the power of the cold is greater, the warm hand follows the cold;
if the efficacy of the warmth prevails over the cold, it becomes warm. In this way, through the touch of this union, the cognition of separation is revealed as it engages with these forces.
If this is established, it arises from the touch of fatigue, involving both the body and its exhaustion; all are equally the *bodhi* (awakening) manifested by staring into the void.

The characteristic of toil: based upon the two kinds of false objects—the separated and the joined—one awakens within this state and draws in these objective images; this is what is called the nature of cognitive awareness.
This essence of cognitive awareness is ultimately without substance apart from those two objects of separation and joining, or opposition and compliance.

Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this awareness does not come from separation or joining, nor does it exist because of opposition or compliance; it does not emerge from the sense organs, nor is it...

"Śūnyatā-born. Why is this? If [the sense organ] comes together when there is union and departs when there is separation, how can it perceive separation? The same applies to the two characteristics of opposition and compliance.
If [perception] were to emerge from the sense organ, there would necessarily be no four characteristics of union, separation, opposition, or compliance;

thus, the cognition within your body would fundamentally lack self-nature. It must then emerge from space, and space itself would possess cognition—what connection would that have to your sense faculties? Therefore, it should be understood..."
One knows that the body-sense field is empty and false, fundamentally lacking causes and conditions and possessing no nature of spontaneity.
This is the Dharma-gate realized by Pilindavatsa while in a state of enduring pain. "Tactile sensation" (*spraṣṭavya*) is the object-field corresponding to the body;
here, the coldness and heat of the two hands constitute the tactile object-field, and the tactile sensation manifested through their contact becomes apparent.
Regarding the perception that arises apart from a cognizer, this is precisely the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).

It is said that this body-faculty necessarily perceives through the conjunction of the two tactile objects—cold and heat—and likewise perceives through their separation. Thus, one correctly sees that the body-faculty is known by means of these two sensory objects;
it perceives both union and separation. When their momentum is engaged as a cause, it results from the tactile sensation of exertion.

"Engaging with conditions" (*sheshi*) carries the meaning of victory and defeat; that is, by engaging heat with cold, one causes the cold to become hot, and by engaging cold with heat, one causes the heat to become cold, thereby giving rise to perception and cognition. "Engaging with conditions" refers to the physical body's exhaustion from cold and heat, which are the phenomena manifested through such exertion.
As for "contrariety and conformity": it is like seeing heavy furs when it is hot, or obtaining fine linen when it is cold.
To encounter cool breezes when it is hot and warm fires when it is cold is to act in accordance with nature.
If, when reaching out your hand, you happen to scratch an itch, or when putting on your shoes, you happen to tread upon your own heels, then you will meet Vatsa face-to-face.
Ānanda, it is like a person who, when weary, falls asleep; when the sleep is deep, he awakens; when encountering sensory objects, he remembers them; and when he fails to remember, he forgets.
These states of inversion, arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, along with inhalation, exhalation, and the internal return [of consciousness], do not transcend one another.

The faculty of cognition that accords with the mind, together with the mind itself and its weariness, are all but the appearance of fatigue produced by the fixed gaze of Bodhi, caused by these two types of arising and ceasing.

The false objects gather, and consciousness abides in the center, drawing inward the internal dust; seeing and hearing flow against the current, and where the flow does not reach is called the nature of awakened cognition.
This nature of awakened cognition is ultimately without substance apart from those two objects of waking and sleeping, and arising and ceasing.
This is the place where Śūnyatā-ja (Empty-born) enters the ocean of jewel-luminous emptiness from the faculty of mental cognition (*manovijñāna-indriya*).

This "faculty of mental cognition" refers to the essence of the eighth consciousness; because it is able to give rise to the mind, it is called the root of the mind, and thus named the faculty of mental cognition.
As for the saying, "When weary, one sleeps; when fully matured, one awakens," it is because this conscious essence grasps this root-body and experiences it through it.

Because they arise as objects to produce sensations of security or peril in common with the mind, "waking" and "sleeping" are used to reveal that the sense organs and the body are their own direct *nimitta-bhāga* (objective images).
As for "recollection" and "forgetting"—wherein one recalls upon perceiving an object and forgets when one fails to recall—it is like seeing a wondrous thing and then remembering it;

yet there are cases where one forgets entirely, such that although one did not clearly perceive the extraordinary object before, it is vividly retained without loss. Thus, "recollection" and "forgetting" are so named.
To manifest the vessel-world as its coarse *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) is what constitutes its inverted arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.
This means that the essence of this consciousness is fundamentally the wondrously perfect, truly pure, and wondrous mind; yet, due to non-awakening, it gives rise to deluded thoughts.
Consequently, this wondrously perfect, truly pure, and wondrous mind transforms this nature of non-arising and non-ceasing into the karma of arising and ceasing.
Because consciousness can take as its objects the sense organs, the body, and the vessel-world (the environment), there arise waking and sleeping, as well as recollection and forgetfulness;
this is precisely the arising and ceasing of inversion. Regarding "sucking in and habituating [them] within so that they do not exceed one another":

this means it is able to contain and store the seeds of both the aspect of the perceived (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the aspect of perception (*darśana-bhāga*). Since all seeds return to this [consciousness], they are perfumed moment by moment without interruption.
Because it possesses these three meanings and takes these three objects as its conditions, it is called the faculty of mental cognition (*manovijñānendriya*).
As for the statement that both the mind and the fatigue are equally the "fatigue-induced manifestation" (*deng-fa-lao-xiang*) of Bodhi:

this means that not only are the three types of objective realms manifested by the *karmic-consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*) manifestations of fatigue, but the *karmic-consciousness* itself is also a fatigue-induced manifestation within the heart of Bodhi. This is the collection of cognitions.
Regarding the one situated in the center, the first five faculties are all said to "arouse seeing," "arouse hearing," and so forth; only this [sixth faculty] is said to "arouse cognition.

"Arouse" refers to their manifestation (*samudācāra*), while "collect" (*saṃcita*) refers to their seeds (*bīja*), because the manifestations of the first five faculties all arise from these seeds within.
As for "sucking up and gathering internal objects": "sucking" (*āsvādana*) means to absorb habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and "gathering" (*grahaṇa*) means to seize and take hold of them.
The "internal dust" refers to internal form (*rūpa*), which denotes the three categories of objective realms (*viṣaya*).
This means that the nature of cognition (*vijñāna-svabhāva*) incessantly absorbs these three types of objects and is, from time to time, perfumed by them.

Regarding the statement that "seeing and hearing flow against the current, and where the current does not reach, that is called the nature of cognition": this indicates that the first five sense organs can only perceive their own respective domains (*sva-bhāga*).
Because the objects of direct perception cannot each be reflexively cognized, the five sense organs do not see, hear, smell, taste, or touch;
this is the locus where the mental faculty (*manas*) can perceive and know.
This mental faculty is ultimately without substance apart from those states of waking and sleeping, arising and ceasing; for [apart from] waking...
Sleeping belongs to the body and arising-and-ceasing belongs to the mind; the body is its *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) and the mind is its *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect).
Therefore, apart from these two aspects—the seen and the seeing—it has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this faculty of cognition does not come from waking nor does it come from sleeping; it is neither born nor does it perish.
It does not emerge from the sense-faculties, nor is it produced from space. Why is this? If it came from waking, it would cease immediately upon sleep—what then would there be to sleep?
If it must exist at the time of birth, yet it perishes, it is then the same as non-existence; who then would experience its cessation? If it were born from its own cessation...

If it ceases immediately upon extinction, who knows that which arises? If it emerges from the sense organs, then its two states of waking and sleeping would correspond to the body’s opening and closing;

yet apart from these two physical forms, this cognizer is like a flower in the sky—ultimately devoid of intrinsic nature. If it were born from space, it would simply be the cognition of space itself; what concern would it have with your sense-faculties?
Therefore, you should know that the mental faculty (*manāyatana*) is illusory; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it unconditioned.
The nature of spontaneity.

First it was designated as "unborn," and next [the notion that] this nature of awareness arises from waking was refuted. If one were to claim that this nature of awareness comes from waking, then at the time of sleep it would perish along with the waking state;
who then would be the one experiencing the profound, heavy sleep? Thus, whether in the waking state or the sleeping state, [it remains].
Have you ever for a moment departed from what is called "embracing the Buddha in sleep night after night, arising together with him morning after morning"?

If you say that this nature of awareness exists at the time of its arising and perishes at the time of its cessation, then as soon as it arises, it has already perished; who then is it that experiences this cessation?
If it were to arise again from that which has ceased, then it would be the same as having nothing once it has perished; who then is it that knows this arising?
"What character is one? What character is two? These were all teachings intended for Ānanda to contemplate and thereby cause him to reflect upon and awaken to himself.
If you claim that this nature of awareness arises solely from the sense organ, you do not understand how the two conditions of waking and sleeping open and close along with the movement of the body:
when weary, the form joins and one sleeps; when in deep sleep, the form opens and one awakens. If it were separate [from the body]...
Regarding the two objects of waking and sleeping, this nature of awakening and knowing ultimately has no substance, for it does not arise from the single sense-faculty alone.

Little do you realize that this faculty of mental cognition is not only the root of heaven and earth, but the root of all phenomena, the root of ignorance, the root of all consciousnesses, and the root of birth and death; yet it is also the root of nirvana and the root of bodhi.

The transformation of the ordinary into the holy through the extraction of the root lies precisely here. If one breaks through this barrier, it is called Perfectly Complete Knowledge (*samyak-saṃbuddha*);
it is called Initial Enlightenment, Original Enlightenment, Perfect Enlightenment, Wondrous Enlightenment, Unsurpassed Enlightenment, All-encompassing Enlightenment, and Ultimate Enlightenment.
This is the great pivotal point for opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; it is a pity that the World-Honored One spoke of it without cause.
The *Pojing* (Sutra on Breaking) states: "The six sovereign kings are eternally pure. Thus, the eye-faculty spontaneously contemplates forms with sovereign unimpededness;
furthermore, it is eternally present as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), its fundamental nature never shifting. Is this not like a king who always attains sovereignty? Therefore it is said:
"The light emitted from the gate of the eye shines forth, breaking through mountains, rivers, and the great earth," extending even to a single thought-moment of the mind-faculty.
A thousand *li* appear like clouds when responding to the mind; at such times, discernment ceases, yet the illumination of the myriad phenomena never halts.

Even as one penetrates through mountains, rivers, and stone walls, that which illuminates remains eternally quiescent. Therefore it is said: "Whatever is encountered by the six sense faculties is none other than the Buddha-dharma.
It is like Jīvaka grasping herbs—none of them are not medicine—or like Mahānāman holding a clod of earth or a pebble.
Because there is nothing that is not this treasure, the subsequent passage states: "Transmigrating through birth and death, you realize wondrous permanence;
it is none other than your six sense faculties. Thus, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra says: "The Dharma-nature is originally without arising, yet it manifests as having arising.
Within this, there is neither a subject that manifests nor an object that is manifested. The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, mind, and all the various faculties of perception—[are one].
All things are empty and devoid of intrinsic nature; it is only through the false mind that they are discriminated as existing. Thus one should observe that all things are without intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, Ānanda, how is it that the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous true nature of Suchness?
First, this [section] generally challenges the premise that these twelve bases (*āyatana*) are established as distinct categories for those who are deluded regarding form but not regarding mind.

"Base" (*āyatana*) refers to the locus or site; the eleven material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are all the sites where the mind cogitates and rests, while the single phenomenon of the mental faculty (*manas*) is the site from which those eleven material phenomena manifest and arise. These twelve bases are fundamentally one.

The perfectly interfused, pure, and precious awakening is separated by the various defilements, resulting in a state of chaotic differentiation where each part is divided into distinct boundaries like those of the six states.
Consequently, they cannot be merged into a unified whole; thus, Ānanda must attack it everywhere.
If one location is broken through, then the other eleven locations will submit of their own accord without waiting for a call to surrender. Therefore, he attacks them.
In all these locations, no clever stratagems were employed nor any scaling ladders set up; rather, they simply took the present staffs and drove [the enemy] straight out.
In the first fascicle, the seven locations were used to break the notion that the mind has no location; these twelve locations are used to break the notion that the sense bases have no location.
"Ānanda, you should now observe this Jeta Grove and its various springs and ponds; what do you think?

Do these forms arise first and are then seen by the eye, or does the eye arise first and then perceive the characteristics of form? Ānanda, if it were the visual faculty that produced the characteristics of form, then when looking at empty space—which is not form—the nature of form would have to be extinguished.

If that nature were extinguished, then everything would be revealed as utterly devoid of the characteristics of form. Yet, since the characteristics of form are not absent [in the objects], [the faculty cannot be their producer]."

Who clarifies the nature of emptiness? Emptiness is also like this. If visual consciousness were to arise from the dust of form to see, then when one contemplates emptiness as being non-form, that seeing would immediately perish.

Once it has perished, it is entirely non-existent; who then could clarify the distinction between emptiness and form? Therefore, you should know that both seeing and the emptiness of form have no location.
Thus, both form and seeing are dual locations that are illusory; fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.

This is the point of entry for Upānanda’s realization. In the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school (Dharmalakṣaṇavāda), the two aspects—the perceived (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing (*darśana-bhāga*)—are compared to the two horns of a snail:
when extended, they form a pair; when retracted, they become one. This is because both arise as manifestations from the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*).
Therefore, the World-Honored One questioned him regarding the immediate perception of forms, saying: "Now, you search..."
I have always taught that all phenomena arise by relying on causes and depending on conditions. Consider this:
when you open your eyes now and see the Jeta Grove, does your visual perception within your eyes arise because of the Jeta Grove so that you see it?
Or does the Jeta Grove arise because of your visual perception within your eyes so that you are able to see it? Which is it?
These two phrases constitute the Vajra Ring and the Shrub of Thorns; even the Buddhas of the three periods cannot provide an explanation for them.

If you claim that it is your visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) that produces this Jetavana Grove and that you thereby perceive it, then when your visual faculty perceives empty space, it would not see the Jetavana Grove, and the Jetavana Grove should consequently cease to exist. If [the grove] were produced by...
Once the nature of form has dissolved, the seeing-nature that produces it also ceases.
When seeing has perished and there is no longer any appearance of form, what further thing could manifest its empty essence? This emptiness is also refuted by the same logic as below.
If you claim that this Jeta Grove arises within your visual faculty and causes you to see the Jeta Grove, then when your eye looks—
When space is empty, it is not a matter of observing form; since there is no form capable of being produced, there is likewise no vision that can be produced.
Once vision has vanished, what further thing could there be that sees emptiness or sees form?

One fails to realize that form does not arise from the eye—the eye is itself quiescent—and the eye does not produce form—form is itself quiescent. Therefore, the *Zongjing* says: "Outside the mind..."
There is not even a hair’s breadth of a dharma that possesses a substantial nature such that they would mutually know one another or mutually reach one another.
Why? Because it is a single dharma; there is no dharma that can be known or reached by another.
If there were two dharmas, they would indeed interact with one another. Master Zhao said: "If these various natures abide within a single world-period, what thing could possibly [exist]?"
The reason this phenomenon is called "non-transmigration" while its affairs are termed "ultimately firm and solid" is because of its coming and going.
Ānanda, listen further:
in this Jeta Grove, when the meal is prepared, the drum is struck for the assembly to gather, and the bell is tolled. The bell and the drum—
Regarding the continuous succession of sounds before and after, what do you think? Do these sounds come to the ear, or does the ear go to the place where the sound is?
Ānanda, if this sound were to come to the ear, then while I am begging for food in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, I would not exist there;
yet this sound must surely come to the location of Ānanda’s ear, [just as] Maudgalyāyana and Kāśyapa [are present elsewhere].

One should not hear [all sounds] simultaneously, much less the one thousand two hundred and fifty śramaṇas within that assembly, who all come to the place of eating upon hearing the sound of the bell.
Furthermore, if your ear travels to the location of the sound, then just as I am here in Jeta’s Grove, there would be no "I" remaining in Śrāvastī;
yet when you hear the sound of a drum, your ear has already gone to the place where the drum is being struck.
When the sounds of bells ring out all at once, they cannot be heard simultaneously; how much less so the various sounds of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep within them?
If there were no coming or going, there would likewise be no hearing. Therefore, you should know that both hearing and sound have no location;
thus, these two—hearing and sound—are both empty and false, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor arising spontaneously.
This is the point where Kauṇḍinya attained realization. Previously it was said: "Form arises and the eye sees; the eye arises and the form appears. Now it is said:

"Sound comes to the side of the ear, and the ear goes to the place of the sound. Although this is like looking for a wedge through a hole, it is merely a matter of failing to apply it at the right time.
If one had directed [the mind] toward Ānanda’s first response—when he said, "I see the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks"—[the truth would have been realized].
When the feeling of joy arose, the World-Honored One ought to have asked: "Is it that the eye arises from the appearance of form, or does the eye arise from form to see?
Ānanda remained silent with his mouth closed, not daring to present his method;

since that opportunity had already been missed, the World-Honored One ought likewise to have asked during the second inquiry regarding the place where he realized the Buddha’s manifested sound of the Dharma.
As for the saying, "The sound comes to the ear, or the ear goes to the place of the sound," Ānanda should have plugged his own throat and sought a way to turn himself around.
The World-Honored One let him off twice, causing the Venerable One to guess eastward and westward. This is what is meant by:
"If one does not cut when it should be cut, one instead invites chaos. To wait until this point to bring it out is also [a failure].
It is like drawing one's bow after the bandits have already passed. If you claim that the sound comes to Ānanda’s ear, then there should be no sound at all at the ears of others;
this would contradict the fact that everyone hears it simultaneously. If you claim that the ear goes to the place of the drum, then there would be no ear at the place of the bell;
this would contradict the fact that one can still hear the bell. Therefore, we know that the sense-object of sound—its arising and ceasing, its movement and stillness—is entirely empty.
Sound does not reach the ear-faculty, nor does the faculty go to the locus of sound. Since there is no coming or going, both mind and object are empty;
being ultimately ungraspable, from where do your capacity to hear and that which is heard finally emerge?
Because many people in the world pass by in error at the gateway of sound and form, the World-Honored One questioned them closely.

This is also not like ordinary things; if you can gain realization at the point of these two questions, only then will you believe that all forms are the Buddha’s forms and all sounds are the Buddha’s sounds.
You will also understand the ancient saying: "This very seeing and hearing is not seeing and hearing. There are no other sounds or forms to present to you.
If you understand this, there is fundamentally nothing to do; how could essence and function hinder one another?

Whether [the fragrance] is distributed or not is a statement of truth. Ānanda, you should again smell this sandalwood in the incense burner. If even one *zhu* of this incense were burned, its scent would be smelled simultaneously throughout the forty *li* of Śrāvastī; what do you think? Does this fragrance arise from the sandalwood, or does it arise from the wood? Or does it arise from the burning, or does it arise from the rubbing? Or does it arise from the person who burns it, or does it arise from the person who smells it? Or does it arise from the wind, or does it arise from the space? Or does it arise from the nose, or does it arise from the consciousness? Or does it arise from all these conditions combined? Or does it arise from none of these conditions? Or does it arise from something else entirely? Or does it arise from no cause at all? Or does it arise from the mind? Or does it arise from the body? Or does it arise from both body and mind? Or does it arise from neither body nor mind? Or does it arise from the past, or does it arise from the future, or does it arise from the present? Or does it arise from the three times collectively? Or does it arise from the three times individually? Or does it arise from the three times together? Or does it arise from the three times separately? Or does it arise from the three realms? Or does it arise from the twelve sense bases? Or does it arise from the eighteen elements? Or does it arise from the five aggregates? Or does it arise from the six sense objects? Or does it arise from the four great elements? Or does it arise from the twenty-two faculties? Or does it arise from the twenty-four secondary factors? Or does it arise from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment? Or does it arise from the eighty-four thousand dharmas? Or does it arise from the eighty-four thousand afflictions? Or does it arise from the eighty-four thousand practices? Or does it arise from the eighty-four thousand Buddhas? Or does it arise from the eighty-four thousand Dharma-treasuries? Or does it arise from the eighty-four thousand monasteries? Or does it arise from the eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas? Or does it arise from the eighty-four thousand śrāvakas? Or does it arise from the eighty-four thousand pratyekabuddhas? Or does it arise from the eighty-four thousand sentient beings? Or does it arise from the eighty-four thousand worlds? Does the sandalwood incense arise from your nose, or does it arise from space? Ānanda, if this fragrance arises from your nose, then as something produced by the nose, it ought to emerge from the nose;
yet the nose is not sandalwood—how, then, can there be the scent of sandalwood within the nose? If you say that you "smell" the fragrance, then the fragrance must enter the nose;
to say that one "smells" when fragrance emerges from within the nose is logically untenable. If, on the other hand, it arises from space...
If fragrance were eternal and constant, it should always be present; why then must one rely on burning this withered wood in an incense burner?
If the fragrance were produced from the wood, then the substance of that fragrance would turn into smoke upon being burned. If the nose could perceive it, it ought to be affected by the smoke itself;

yet before the smoke has even risen far into the air, how is it already smelled within forty *li*? Therefore, one should know that fragrance, the nose, and the act of smelling are not [inherently connected].

Since both have no location—that is, the two locations of smelling and fragrance are illusory and fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously—this is the place where Xiangyan attains the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body.

Because he has smelled fragrance all day long yet does not know the source from which the fragrance comes, he is made to investigate in detail from where it emerges; thus it is said: "Does it arise from the wood, or from space?"
It arises from the nose; for if one were to say that this fragrance comes from the nose, then since the nose is not sandalwood, how could there be fragrance within it?
To say that the nose "smells" fragrance implies that one must take up the fragrance and have it enter the nose before it can be called smelling.
If it were the case that fragrance issues from within the nose and is yet called "smelling," it would not accord with reason. If one were to say that this fragrance...

If this fragrance were produced from emptiness, then emptiness would be permanent and the fragrance would likewise exist eternally; why then would it depend upon being burned within an incense burner before it could exist?
If it were produced from wood, then this fragrance would arise as smoke through burning, and the nose would perceive it;
if the nose perceives it, it ought to be enveloped by that smoke, yet how is it that within forty *li*—where the smoke has not yet reached—the fragrance is already present?

Having heard this, you know that this fragrance is neither from the wood, nor from space, nor does it issue from the nose; thus you know that the nature of fragrance is fundamentally all-pervasive—what need is there to wait for their meeting?
Ānanda, when you regularly hold your almsbowl among the assembly during the two meal times, you may encounter therein ghee, curd, or clarified butter (ghṛta), which are called...
"What do you think, Ānanda, regarding this supreme flavor? Does this flavor arise in empty space, does it arise within the tongue, or does it arise within the food?
If this flavor were to arise on your tongue—since there is but one tongue in your mouth—then that tongue would have already become the flavor of ghee;
when encountering black rock sugar, it should not change. If it does not change, [how can it perceive other flavors]?"
If the knowledge of taste were not distinct from the changing flavors themselves, then since the tongue is not manifold in substance, how could it perceive many flavors?
If this knowledge of taste arises within the food, the food itself is insentient; how could it know itself? Furthermore, if the food knew itself, it would be the same as someone else’s food;
what concern would that have for you? If the knowledge of taste arises in space, then when you eat empty space, what flavor would it have?
If space were to possess the quality of saltiness, then since your tongue is salty, your face would also be salty.

In that case, the people of this world would be like sea fish, constantly experiencing saltiness and never knowing what it is to be fresh. If they did not recognize freshness, they could not perceive saltiness;
being entirely without knowledge, how could it be called "taste"? Therefore, you should know that taste, the tongue, and the act of tasting are all without a fixed location.
Thus, both the tasting and the flavor are equally empty and false; fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of spontaneous nature.
This is the place where King of Medicine attained the meditation of the single flavor.
Since all people eat and drink yet few know the true flavor, he was made to seek the source and emergence of that taste at the edge of his alms bowl; hence it is said: "Does this flavor arise..."
Whether in the air, on the tongue, or within the food—if you claim that this taste arises from your tongue, then your single tongue should perceive only a single taste;
it should not shift so as to perceive other tastes. If it does not shift and perceives only one taste, it cannot be called "knowing taste. If it shifts and perceives other tastes, how can it be one?
If you know many flavors with the tongue, then it is clear that these flavors do not arise within the tongue itself.
If you claim that these flavors arise from within the food, since food lacks consciousness, how could it know of itself whether it is sweet or bitter?
Even if food could know of itself whether it is sweet or bitter, that food would be just like another person; it would have no concern for you. Why, then, do you say [it is yours]?
To call one who knows flavor "a knower of taste" clearly demonstrates that this flavor does not arise from the food itself.

If you claim that this food arises from empty space, then when you eat empty space, what flavor do you experience? If it were salty, then all people in this realm would experience that saltiness and be identical to sea fish;
since they constantly experience saltiness, they would certainly never know what sweetness is, and if they do not know it, [how could they perceive flavor]?
If the bland does not recognize the salty, and since the two do not recognize one another, one cannot be called a person who knows taste;
thus, it would not arise from the clarity of emptiness. Since it is not in these three places, know that this taste is not separate from the present location.
If you truly recognize this fundamental ground, there is no need for chewing; the hundred flavors are fully present.
Ānanda, you habitually rub your head with your hand every morning; what do you think? Regarding this sensation known through rubbing, who is it that can touch?

Is the capacity to touch in the hand, or is it in the head? If it were in the hand, then the head would have no cognition; how then could there be contact? If it were in the head, then the hand would have no function;

how then could it be called contact? If each possessed its own [capacity], then you— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The full passage from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* continues: "...would be two selves. One self would perceive, and one self would not perceive. How could this be possible?"
Ānanda, there must be two bodies. If the head and the hand arise from the same single contact, then the hand and the head should be one entity.

If they were one entity, contact could not be established. If they were two entities, then as for contact—who would be the locus? That which is the locus cannot be the agent; that which is the agent cannot be the locus.
It should not be that empty space enters into contact with you. Therefore, you should know that it is the faculty of awareness that contacts.
That which is co-existent with the body has no location; thus, both the body and contact are equally illusory, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor arising spontaneously.
This is where Bhadrapāla touched his heel while at the bathing place; the World-Honored One then—
I have always exhorted my disciples to rub their heads three times a day, reciting these words themselves: "Guard the mouth, restrain the mind, and let not the body transgress.
Those who practice in this way shall attain liberation from the world; therefore, my disciples must follow this method entirely.
Although you now rely upon my Dharma and rub your heads three times a day, you do not even know where the places for rubbing are located, nor do you avoid rubbing them incorrectly.
Setting aside for a moment how much time has passed: when you are actually rubbing your head with your hand, the hand knows there is a head, and the head knows there is a hand.
Who is it that acts as the agent of contact and gives rise to this cognition? Is it the hand touching the head such that the hand is the agent of contact giving rise to this cognition?
Or is it the head touching the hand such that the head is the agent of contact giving rise to this cognition?
If this cognition arises because the hand is capable of touching, then the cognition of touch resides in the hand, and the head would become an insentient object;
how then could the head know that the hand has touched it and thus experience the sensation of touch?
If this cognition arises because the head is capable of touching, then the cognition of touch resides in the head, and the hand would become useless.

Regarding these objects, how can one know that the head touches my hand and call it "contact"? If the head and the hand each possessed a separate consciousness, then you, Ānanda, would have two bodies.
If the head and the hand possess only a single consciousness, then the hand and the head should constitute a single entity.
If they were a single entity, contact could not occur; yet if they were two distinct entities, [the same problem would arise].
To which does this contact belong? Does it belong to the subject that touches, or to the object that is touched?
If contact belonged to the subject, then wherever there is a hand or a head, all would become the subject that touches while there would be no object to be touched.

Since there would be no object to be touched, how could empty space possibly become the object touched by you? If contact belonged to the object, then wherever there is a hand or a head, all would become the object.
There is contact, yet there is no one who contacts; since there is no one who contacts, how could empty space become the one who contacts you?
Thus we know that if even that which is most superficial and immediate in our daily lives cannot be known, how can we know that which is profound and remote?
If, while rubbing your head, you happen to encounter a fellow traveler on the Way, then every point of contact is Bodhi.
There is no need for further deliberation.
Ānanda, regarding the rules that govern the arising of the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—which you constantly take as objects within your mind:
does this dharma arise from the mind itself, or does it exist separately from the mind in some other location? Ānanda, if it were identical to the mind...

If dharmas are neither objects of the senses nor objects of the mind, how can they constitute sense-bases (*āyatana*)? If they existed apart from the mind as having a separate location, then the self-nature of dharmas would have to be either consciousness or non-consciousness.
If it were consciousness, it would be called "mind" and would differ from you; it would not be an object, but rather identical to the mental objects of others.

Thus, you are yourself the mind. How could your mind further be divided into two in relation to you? If it were non-consciousness, then these objects, being neither... [the sentence is incomplete in the source].
The characteristics of form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, cold, warmth, and space—where do they reside now? Within form and space, there is no indication whatsoever;
nor can there be another space outside of the human realm. Since the mind has no object of perception other than these, from whom could such [characteristics] be established?
Therefore, you should know that dharmas and the mind both lack a location; thus, both the mind and dharmas are equally empty and false.
This is neither caused by conditions nor is it of spontaneous nature;

this is the point of entry for Kāśyapa’s realization. That which constitutes the laws of generation refers to the shadows manifested through the falling away of the active functioning of the three natures as apprehended by the five sense-faculties; each possesses its own rule and serves as the object of the mental faculty.

The realm [of objects] is called *dharmāyatana* (dharma-dust). Since this dharma is neither identical to nor separate from the mind, one must examine whether it is identical to the mind or separate from it.
If this dharma-dust were identical to the mind, then this dharma would not be dust;
it would not be an object perceived by the mental faculty (*manas*). How, then, could it constitute the objective sphere of the mental faculty? If this...
If mental objects (*dharmas*) exist apart from the mind and have a separate location, then does the self-nature of these mental objects possess cognition or not?
If you consider them to possess cognition, they should be called the "mind" and not "mental objects.
If these cognitive mental objects are not your own mind, then they would be like the mental scope of another person, with which you have no concern.
The cognitive objects (*dharmas*) that are known are themselves your mind; how could one person possess two minds?

Therefore, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* says: "In this way, are the mind and its objects different or not different? If the mind were different from the object, then within a single moment there would have to be two minds.
If the mind were identical to the object, it would be unable to observe itself, just as a finger cannot point to itself."
The tip cannot touch itself; if this dharma-object (*dharmāyatana*) were insentient, then since it is already apart from the five sense-objects which are insentient, where would it be located?
Now, between form and emptiness, there is no indication of its presence.
Could there be another space outside the human realm to accommodate this dharma-object? Even if...
If it abides outside of emptiness yet is not within, and is certainly not an object of perception for the mental faculty (*manas*), then from whom does this "dharma-object" (*dharmāyatana*) arise?
Thus, when one raises the mind or stirs a thought, one still does not know its point of descent; could it be that it is forever a masterless, solitary ghost?
Therefore, know that the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*), being without opposition, are all dharma-gates of non-contention (*araṇā-dharmamukha*). All objects are likewise so.
The Way of non-duality, which encompasses the void and exhausts the profound darkness, is precisely the realm of sentient beings right now;
it is truly inconceivable. Why then do you seek the activities of the sages from afar and disparage yourself as inferior? The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"For example, sunflowers turn toward the sun; yet these sunflowers have no heart of reverence, no consciousness, and no karma."
Because they are different from the nature of the phenomenon, they turn back on themselves; just as the *kadalī* tree grows because of thunder, yet that tree has neither ears nor consciousness.
Because one phenomenon exists, another phenomenon grows; because one phenomenon is absent, another phenomenon perishes.
Just as when a woman touches the flower of the *akāśa* tree, its fruit emerges, yet that tree has no mind.
Furthermore, because there is no distinct phenomenon that possesses the sensation of touch, one phenomenon arises from another;
because there is no distinct phenomenon [to possess it], one phenomenon perishes. It is the same with the magnet attracting iron: because there is a distinct phenomenon, one phenomenon arises;
because there is no distinct phenomenon, one phenomenon perishes. The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this: it cannot be extracted.
In *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, O son of good family, ignorance (*avidyā*) cannot absorb the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), nor can the formative forces absorb consciousness (*vijñāna*);
this may also be called "conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces" and "conditioned by the formative forces is consciousness.
Whether a Buddha appears or not, the *dharmadhātu* remains eternally constant. This World-Honored One has clearly expounded that all phenomena are non-arising. If so...
Furthermore, Ānanda, as for what are called the eighteen *dhātus*— the fundamental *tathāgatagarbha*, the wondrous nature of *tathatā*—
these eighteen realms are taught for those who are deluded regarding both form and mind, opening up the categories of form and mind for their sake. (In Sanskrit, *dhātu*).
Regarding this term *dhātu* (界): it carries the meanings of cause (*hetu*), genus (*gotra*), and boundary (*sīmā*). Here, we take the sense of "boundary" in the sense that they do not intermingle.

When contrasted with objects (*viṣaya*), there are the sense faculties (*indriya*); when contrasted with the faculties, there are the objects; and that which performs the discernment (*vijñapti*) between them is consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Because each has its own distinct boundary, the three groups of six combine to form the eighteen *dhātus*. Although there are three groups of six *dhātus*, [they are so designated].
Because its essence is one, it is called the fundamental Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous true nature of Suchness.
Ānanda, according to your understanding, the visual consciousness arises with the eye and form as conditions.

Does this consciousness arise because of the eye, taking the eye as its constituent element (*dhātu*), or does it arise because of form, taking form as its constituent element? Ānanda, if it were to arise because of the eye...

Since space is formless and devoid of anything that can be differentiated, even if you possess consciousness, what would you have it serve? Furthermore, your vision is not blue, yellow, red, or white;

as it has no representation, from what could a boundary be established? If [consciousness] were produced because of form, then when there is no form—such as in empty space—your consciousness should cease;
how then could you cognize the nature of emptiness? Moreover, if form undergoes change, you likewise cognize it.

The physical forms and appearances undergo change and transformation, yet your consciousness does not; from what, then, could a "realm" (dhātu) be established? If it follows change, then the characteristics of the realm would themselves be non-existent;
if it does not change, it is eternal. Since it arises from form, you should not be able to perceive the location of empty space.

If it were produced by both [form and consciousness] together, such that eye and form arise in conjunction, then if they were combined, there would be a separation in the middle; if they were separated, the two would be joined. Their essential natures would thus be in chaotic confusion; how, then, could a "realm" be formed?
Therefore, one should know that with the eye and forms as conditions, the eye-consciousness element arises;
yet since these three locations are all non-existent, the eye, forms, and the form-element are fundamentally neither causes and conditions nor of spontaneous nature.
This is precisely the point of entry for Śāriputra’s awakening. As you have clarified, I shall guide you by means of that very clarity.
Having previously provided various instructions, I feared you might not yet have attained full understanding;
therefore, I speak to you once more based on what you already clearly understand—namely, that which you ordinarily comprehend regarding the eye and forms.

With respect to the visual consciousness that arises conditioned by [the eye], does this consciousness arise from the eye and is therefore called "consciousness produced by the eye," being delimited by the eye itself?
Or does it arise from visible forms and is therefore called "consciousness produced by visible forms," being delimited by visible forms themselves?
If one asserts that this consciousness arises from the visual faculty, then it is delimited by the visual faculty.
Consciousness exists to cognize objects; if there were no forms or emptiness, even if your consciousness were produced, what would it have to use?
Furthermore, the very root of your seeing cannot be seen, nor is there any form or characteristic by which it can be manifested;

from what, then, could you establish this "root of seeing" as the boundary of consciousness? If you claim that this consciousness arises from the object of form, then [it must be] by means of that form-object...
Regarding that which constitutes a boundary, the characteristic of emptiness manifests and consciousness perishes along with the form;

since consciousness does not conjoin with emptiness, how could consciousness cognize this nature of space? If you claim that although [consciousness] arises from form, you cognize the transformation of the form while consciousness itself remains unchanging—then, as the categories are fundamentally different, how could there be an unchanging consciousness arising from a transformable form?

If it is because of the elements (*dhātu*) that they are called "elements," from what are these elements established? If you say that when matter changes, consciousness also changes accordingly, then both the producer and the produced would lack intrinsic nature;
thus, the characteristic of the elements would inherently be non-existent, and it would be impossible to designate matter as an element.
If, however, you say that while matter changes, consciousness does not change accordingly, then the essence of consciousness must be permanent.

Since this consciousness arises from form, it should constantly cognize form and not be able to cognize space; yet now that it cognizes space, it certainly does not take form as its constituent element (*dhātu*).

If you claim that this consciousness is produced through the conjunction of these two factors—the sense organ and the object—then we observe that the organ and the object stand in a state of direct opposition, like two hostile nations. If they were to be in conjunction, they could not possibly reach one another.
In the interim, they are fundamentally separate; yet if one considers them as being separate, upon opening the eyes one immediately perceives them as conjoined.

Thus, the essential natures of the sense organ and the object become intermingled and confused, with neither having a fixed point of reference. From what, then, could this consciousness arise through their co-arising?
When investigated in this manner, it is clear that this visual consciousness is not self-born, not other-born, and not born from both together.

O Śāriputra, if the meaning you understand—that visual consciousness arises with the eye and forms as its conditions—is not established, then from where does this visual consciousness ultimately come? Please look for yourself.

Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have understood—that the ear and sound act as conditions to produce the ear-consciousness—does this consciousness arise because it takes the ear as its cause and the ear as its constituent element (*dhātu*), or does it arise because it takes sound as its cause and sound as its constituent element?

Ānanda, if it were produced by the ear, then since the two characteristics of motion and stillness are not present before it, the faculty would fail to constitute cognition; and if there is nothing known, then even cognition itself cannot be established.
What is the form and appearance of consciousness? If it is apprehended through hearing, there is neither movement nor stillness; thus, hearing is not established as a distinct entity.
How then can the ear’s form, along with various colors and tactile objects, be called the "consciousness-element"? Furthermore, from what is the "ear-consciousness-element" established?

If consciousness arises from sound and exists because of sound, then it has no relation to hearing. If there is no hearing, then the locus of the characteristics of sound perishes; yet consciousness is said to arise from sound. How can this be?

If sound exists because it has the cause of being heard, then the characteristic of sound should be heard by the auditory consciousness. If it is not heard, it is not a sense-element (*dhātu*). If it were heard, it would be identical to sound;

once the auditory consciousness has already been heard, who would know that auditory consciousness? If there were no knower, it would ultimately be like grass or wood. It should not be that sound and hearing are mixed to form a middle element (*madhyadhātu*).
If there is no middle position for an element, then from what could the characteristics of internal and external be established? Therefore, one should know this.

With the ear and sound as conditions, the auditory consciousness-element arises; yet when these three locations are entirely absent, then the ear, the sound, and the auditory consciousness-element—these three—are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature.
This is the point of entry for Samantabhadra’s realization. If the auditory consciousness were produced from the ear, then [the claim that] it does not arise from the superior would be untenable.
The sense-faculties arise from their respective objects; since the two characteristics of motion and stillness do not manifest before them, there is no object.

Since the faculties do not constitute cognition, there is no hearing. "There must be nothing known" means that if there is no object, there is no hearing. "Cognition itself cannot be established" reiterates the preceding two points:
if there is no object, there is no hearing. "What form or appearance would consciousness have? means that if there is no hearing, there is no consciousness. If... [the text continues].

The following section refutes the inability of the *pāśuvārtha-indriya* (the physical, sensory organ) to produce consciousness. The first three phrases reiterate that even the *paramārtha-indriya* (the ultimate, subtle faculty) cannot produce consciousness;

how much less so could this ear-shape—a mixture of colors and tactile objects, devoid of sentience—be considered the *vijñāna-dhātu* (consciousness-element) and expected to produce consciousness? Since neither the ultimate nor the physical organ can produce it, the matter remains indeterminate.
Auditory consciousness does not arise from the ear as its cause, nor does it take the ear as its constituent element (*dhātu*).
If one were to claim that consciousness arises from sound without depending on the faculty of hearing, how could one know that without hearing, the sound itself would not even exist?

From what, then, could consciousness arise? Even if one grants that consciousness arises from sound, one must also grant that it exists because of the auditory faculty; thus, at the time of hearing the sound—
Furthermore, one should also hear the consciousness, because consciousness arises from sound. If there were no hearing of consciousness, then sound would not be the element of consciousness.
If, however, there is indeed hearing of consciousness, then consciousness must likewise be identical to sound. Since consciousness is devoid of cognition, it has already been heard by the ear.

But what, then, is that which cognizes the hearing of consciousness? If you say there is yet another cognition that cognizes the hearing of consciousness, [that too would lead to an infinite regress].

If that were so, you would then be the same as grass and trees; since the single faculty does not emerge and the solitary object does not arise, the faculty and the object should not intersect to form a middle realm, yet consciousness arises between the faculty and the object?
Since there is neither a middle nor an inside or outside to this realm, from what, then, could this ear-consciousness be established? You should investigate this thoroughly.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand: with the nose and fragrance as conditions, the nose-consciousness arises.

Does this consciousness arise because of the nose, taking the nose as its constituent element (*dhātu*), or does it arise because of fragrance, taking fragrance as its constituent element? Ānanda, if it arises because of the nose, then within your mind, what do you take to be the nose?
Do you take it to be the physical form of the flesh and the two nostrils, or do you take it to be the act of smelling and knowing?
If you take the nature of movement to be the physical form and the physical substance, then the body knows; this is contact, and it is called the "body-element" (*kāyadhātu*), not the nose-element.

If the nose were called contact, then since the nose itself would have no name, how could a "realm" (*dhātu*) be established? If you take the act of smelling to be the knower, then within your mind, what constitutes that knowing?
If the flesh constitutes the knowing, then the knowing of the flesh is fundamentally contact and not the nose; if space constitutes the knowing, [then it is likewise not the nose].
If emptiness were itself aware, then flesh would naturally not be awareness. If this were so, then empty space would be you and your body would lack cognition;
today, Ānanda, you would have no place of existence. If you take fragrance to be awareness, then that awareness would belong to the fragrance—what concern would it have for you?
If fragrant and foul odors must arise from your nose, then those two kinds of flowing vapors—the fragrant and the foul—would not arise from the *eranda* tree.
Furthermore, regarding these two things—sandalwood and [the other substance]—they do not come to you; you must smell them yourself to determine whether they are fragrant or foul.

If it is foul, then it is not fragrant; if it is fragrant, then it should not be foul. If you were able to perceive both fragrance and foulness simultaneously, then you, as a single person, would have to possess two noses.
When I questioned you about this, Ānanda, there were two of you; which of the two was your true self? If the nose were one, then fragrance and foulness could not be two distinct things.

If stench becomes fragrance and fragrance again becomes stench, these two natures do not exist; from what, then, could the realms (dhātus) be established? If consciousness arises because of fragrance, then it must exist because of fragrance.
Just as the eye exists and yet cannot perceive itself, so too, because [consciousness] exists because of fragrance, it should not know fragrance.

If it knows it, it is not "arisen"; if it does not know it, it is not "consciousness. Since fragrance does not exist through being known, the fragrance-realm is not established; and since consciousness does not know fragrance, the fragrance-realm is not established.
Since the element of the nose is not established by means of fragrance, and as there is no intermediate space, neither "internal" nor "external" can be formed;
thus, the nature of that hearing is ultimately false and illusory. Therefore, you should know that the nose and fragrance serve as conditions to give rise to the element of nose-consciousness.
Since these three locations are all non-existent, the nose, the fragrance, and the element of fragrance are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
This is the point where Sundarananda attained realization. If [the nose] arises dependent on the nose, one should discern that olfactory consciousness does not arise from the nose.

The "physical form with twin claws" refers to the *audārika-indriya* (the physical sense organ); "knowing through smelling and being subject to movement" refers to the *paramārtha-indriya* (the ultimate sense organ).
If one takes the physical form as the basis, one should discern below that the physical organ has no substantiality, for its material substance is...
If "body" and "bodily cognition" are both identified as "contact," this doubly indicates that there is no actual entity called "nose";

if what is called "contact" is not the nose but rather the object, this doubly indicates that there is no name for a "nose. Since both name and reality are empty, from what could a sense-field (*dhātu*) be established?

If one takes olfactory cognition to be the basis, it will be demonstrated below that the ultimate sense-faculty (*paramārthendriya*) has no substance. If one considers flesh to be the nature of olfactory cognition, then it would be the flesh that cognizes.
If the cognition of the body were identical to the body itself, then what would the tactile objects (spraṣṭavya) have to do with the nose?

In that case, the nose would not possess the faculty of smelling. If you claim that space is the nature of the faculty of smelling, then if space were to possess cognition, your nasal faculty would be devoid of awareness;
this would mean that space is you, while Ānanda would have no location at all. By means of this...
"Regarding 'fragrance' (*gandha*)," [the text] clarifies that the fragrance perceived within the nose is also not the nature of olfactory cognition.
"If it were fragrance," [it would follow that] the two gases of fragrance and stench do not arise from the nose; they are not the nature of olfactory cognition.
*Elaṇḍa* is a stinking tree. Wuxing says: "The two things do not come [to the nose]"—this refutes the object by following the sense organ; since the objects are twofold...

If the sense organ were twofold, it would follow that the nose is one [organ] while the object below it is another; thus, by using the object to refute the organ, since the organ is already established as being only one, how could there be two objects?
Having thus successively refuted the notion that [consciousness] arises from the organ, we now argue that it does not arise from the object.

If you claim that seeing exists because of the eye, yet you cannot see the eye itself, then consciousness must likewise exist because of the fragrance, yet you likewise cannot perceive the fragrance itself.
One should not know fragrance; if one says one knows fragrance, then it is not the arising of fragrance. If one does not know fragrance, one should not be called "consciousness of fragrance.
