Since [fragrance] does not exist through knowing, how could it give rise to consciousness and thereby constitute the realm of fragrance? This turns back to explain that "knowing" is precisely non-arising.
If consciousness does not know fragrance, it likewise cannot be called "consciousness arising from fragrance. This turns back to explain.

"Not knowing" is not consciousness. What was previously called the "middle position" and what is here called the "intermediate" both refer to the middle between the sense faculty (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*), because consciousness arises therein.
Since "internal" and "external" refer to the faculty and the object, one should say: "Since there is neither internal nor external, an intermediate [position] is not established."
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding that which you understand: with the tongue and flavors as conditions, the tongue-consciousness arises.
Does this consciousness arise because of the tongue, taking the tongue as its constituent element (*dhātu*), or does it arise because of flavors, taking flavors as its constituent element?

Ānanda, if it arose because of the tongue, then all things in the world—sugarcane, *ume* plums, *hāridrā* (yellow myrobalan), rock salt, *śigru* (fine pepper), ginger, and cinnamon—would have no flavor at all.
Taste your own tongue: is it sweet or bitter? If the nature of the tongue were bitter, who would come to taste the tongue? The tongue does not taste itself; what, then, is the faculty of cognition?
Since the nature of the tongue is not bitter, flavor does not arise of its own accord; how, then, can the elements (dhātu) be established?

If consciousness arises because of flavor and flavor itself becomes the object of tasting, then it would be identical to the tongue-organ and should likewise not taste itself. How, then, could consciousness distinguish between what is flavor and what is not flavor?
Furthermore, all tastes do not arise from a single substance; since tastes are manifold, the consciousness that arises from them should likewise be manifold in substance.

If the substance of consciousness were a single entity, then when salty, bland, sweet, and pungent tastes arise together in combination and produce various distinct transformations, they would necessarily become a single taste.
If there were no differentiation, it could not be called "consciousness. How, then, could it be designated as the "tongue-taste-consciousness element"?
It is not possible for space to give rise to your mind-consciousness. When the tongue and flavors come together, there is fundamentally no self-nature within them;
how, then, could a realm arise? Therefore, you should know that with the tongue and flavors as conditions, the tongue-consciousness-realm arises; yet these three locations are all non-existent.
Thus, the tongue, flavors, and the tongue-realm—these three are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature.

This is the point at which Pūrṇa attained realization. If you claim that consciousness arises from the sense organ, then when the five flavors have not yet been combined, you yourself must taste your own tongue—is it sweet or bitter?

If you claim that the nature of the tongue is bitter, then since the nature of your tongue has already become the flavor of bitterness, who comes to taste the tongue? Since you cannot taste your own tongue, how can you know [its nature]?
Does the tongue produce the bitter taste? If you say the nature of the tongue is not bitter, then this tongue cannot even produce its own taste;
how then can it establish a sense-field (*dhātu*) to produce consciousness?

If you say that consciousness arises from the taste and that consciousness itself is the taste, then it would be unable to perceive the taste, just as the tongue-organ cannot taste itself. How, then, could one know [the taste]?
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "taste is not taste," if it is said that there are many tastes, then consciousness should also be manifold;
yet, since it is stated below that consciousness is one while taste is also one, one should not perceive the multiplicity of tastes.
If one does not perceive the multiplicity of tastes, it cannot be called consciousness. How, then, can taste be designated as the element of consciousness (vijñānadhātu)?—Wu.
Dharma Master Xing said: "Harmonization" refers to the blending of various flavors to form a single taste; "simultaneous arising" refers to the unchanging nature of the original substance;

and "transformation" refers to the altered flavors produced by boiling or roasting. It should not be argued below that [taste] arises without a cause; nor should it be argued below that [taste] arises from both [the tongue and the object].
Since the sense organ and the object have already merged into one, they lack even a self-nature—how could there be an empty space between them?

Can there be space within a gap sufficient for the arising of the realm of consciousness? Since it is not born from itself, nor from another, nor from both together, nor without cause, it is thus non-arising;
how could it be something produced by causes and conditions?
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand: body-contact serves as the condition for the arising of body-consciousness.
Does this consciousness arise because of the body and thus take the body as its constituent element (*dhātu*), or does it arise because of contact and thus take contact as its constituent element?

Ānanda, if it arises because of the body, there would necessarily be no dual conditions of conjunction and separation; what then would the body recognize? If it arises because of contact, there would necessarily be no such thing as your body.
Who is it that knows union and separation without being the body? Ānanda, objects do not know by touching; the body knows by having touch.
To know touch is the body; touch is the body. Thus, touch is not the body, and the body is not touch. These two characteristics—body and touch—originally have no location.
When united with the body, they constitute the very nature of the body itself; when separated from the body, they are identical to the characteristics of empty space, both internally and externally.

Since the middle cannot be established, how can the middle be posited? If the internal and external natures are not further established as empty, then from what could your consciousness arise to establish the sense-spheres (*dhātu*)?
Therefore, you should know that with body and touch as conditions, the body-consciousness-sphere arises; yet these three locations are entirely non-existent.
Thus, the body, touch, and the body-sphere—these three—are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

This is the point of entry for Upāli’s realization. If one examines the single faculty from the perspective of the body, neither *vitarka* (applied thought) nor *vicāra* (sustained thought) is established;

this is simply body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*). Body-consciousness necessarily arises through the two conditions of contact and separation, for it is through the sensation of contact that the cognition of separation becomes manifest.
If one examines the solitary object from the perspective of touch, [consciousness] does not arise independently, because only after there is a body [does consciousness follow].

Because one knows separation and knows conjunction, that which is generally called "contact" (spraṣṭavya) refers to an object touching the body such that the body perceives it as having names such as cold, warm, rough, or smooth.
If it has not yet reached the body, it is merely termed "form" (rūpa) and is not termed "contact.

Ānanda, I shall now refute the claim that [consciousness] arises from co-production. If you say that an object alone cannot produce cognition by touching itself, then it must necessarily arise in conjunction with [the sense organ].
One knows that there is contact only when the body and contact meet; does this consciousness arise only after the body and contact have conjoined?
However, if one knows that there is a body, that knowledge arises from contact and does not exist because of the body.

If one knows that there is contact, that knowledge arises from the body and does not emerge from contact. If this knowledge were produced solely by contact, it certainly would not emerge from the body.

If this cognition arises from the body itself, it certainly does not arise from contact; furthermore, while this cognition resides in the body, its location within the body is fundamentally indeterminate.
If it were to leave contact and unite with the body, then this cognition would be the very nature of the body itself.
If it were to leave the body and unite with contact, then this cognition would be a characteristic of space and so forth. Thus, this cognition of contact exists both internally and [externally].
Since the external [objects] have no fixed location, how can you say that the body and the object of touch meet in the middle?

Since there is no middle position, internal and external cannot be established; thus, from where could your consciousness arise to establish its boundaries? Therefore, it is clear that it arises right where it is.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand: with the mind and mental objects as conditions, the mental consciousness arises.
Does this consciousness arise because it takes the mind as its cause and the mind as its realm, or does it arise because it takes mental objects as its cause and mental objects as its realm?

Ānanda, if it were produced by the mind, then within your own mind there must be something being contemplated that brings forth your mind; if there were no preceding mental objects, the mind would have nothing from which to arise.

If separated from conditions, formless consciousness would have no purpose. Furthermore, is your conscious mind—the nature of deliberation combined with discernment—the same as or different from the mental faculty (*manas*)?

If they were the same, it would simply be the mental faculty; how then could anything be produced? If they were different, then since the mental faculty is not identical [to consciousness], there would be nothing for it to cognize.
If there is nothing to cognize, how can the mental faculty arise? If there is something to cognize, how can consciousness be distinct from the mental faculty? Is it merely the same or different?
If the two natures are unestablished, how can the realms be established? If the world arises from dharmas, then all worldly phenomena are not separate from the five sense objects.
Observe that the phenomena of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch have distinct characteristics;
they correspond to the five faculties and are not subsumed by the mind-faculty. Your consciousness definitely arises in dependence upon these dharmas. Now, observe this closely.

Regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharma-dharma*), what is their form? If they are apart from form and emptiness, movement and stillness, penetration and obstruction, union and separation, and arising and ceasing—transcending all such characteristics, ultimately nothing can be apprehended.
When there is arising, form, emptiness, and all phenomena arise together; when there is ceasing, form, emptiness, and all phenomena cease together.
Since the cause itself does not exist, what shape or appearance could the consciousness produced by that cause have? If characteristics and forms do not exist, how can the realms (*dhātu*) arise?

Therefore, one should know that with the mind and mental objects as conditions, the mental consciousness element arises; yet when these three locations are entirely absent, the mind, mental objects, and the mental consciousness element—these three—are fundamentally neither causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
This is the point of entry for Maudgalyāyana’s realization. First, let us examine the statement that [consciousness] does not arise from the sense-faculty:
in your mind, there must first be some object among the mental objects (*dharmas*) upon which you reflect, and only then do the characteristics of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) manifest.

If those prior objects did not exist, the mental faculty itself would not even exist; so how could consciousness arise? Furthermore, apart from mental objects, there is no distinct form or characteristic to be discerned. Even if one were to grant this...

If the mind (*manas*) is already capable of producing consciousness, what further use would there be for it? Furthermore, as you will argue below regarding the similarities and differences between the faculties and consciousness, the "consciousness-mind" is precisely the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*), because it arises from the mind-faculty (*mana-indriya*).

Since its function of deliberation (*santīraṇa*) is constant, and because it possesses the nature of discernment (*vijñapti*), it is said that both the mental consciousness and the mind-faculty take discernment as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Thus it is stated.

Furthermore, the underlying intention is this: since both the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) are capable of discerning objects, one must distinguish between that which is the productive faculty and that which is the produced consciousness.
Are these faculty and consciousness ultimately identical or distinct? Therefore, it is asked: "Are they the same or different?

If one were to claim that the consciousness is identical to the mind, then consciousness would simply be the mind; how then could the mind be designated as the producer and the consciousness as the produced?
If it is claimed that the consciousness produced is different from the mind (*manas*), then the consciousness thus produced would have nothing to cognize.

Since there would be nothing to cognize, it could not be called "produced from the mind. If, however, there is something to cognize, then cognition and the mind would share the same nature of discernment (*vijñapti*).
How then could one be "cognition" and the other the "mind-faculty"? The two entities of cognition and the sense-faculty would not even be distinct.
How can you distinguish the boundaries of consciousness as it arises?

If you claim it does not arise from the objects, yet you clearly perceive the five sensory objects vividly and distinctly in relation to the five sense organs—none of which are subsumed under the mental faculty (*manas*)—then if you say that mental consciousness does not arise from the mind but from the dharma-object (*dharmāyatana*), observe the nature of this dharma-object. What do you see it as being?
As for its shape: if one were to separate it from the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), no distinct shape could be found.

Thus, the arising and ceasing of the mental object (*dharma-āyatana*) is itself the arising and ceasing of the five sense-objects; apart from the five sense-objects, no separate arising or ceasing of a mental object can be found.

Furthermore, when seeking the essential nature and characteristics of the mental object upon which [consciousness] depends, even that cannot be found—how much less so the consciousness produced by that mental object?

What visible form or characteristic could this consciousness possibly have? Since even the characteristics of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) do not exist, how could one possibly establish a sense-field (*dhātu*) to produce consciousness?
Thus, we know that within the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), all are established by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
If the fundamental locus itself is empty, what existence can there be for the branches produced from it? Since the locus does not exist...
Furthermore, that which can be apprehended lacks any fixed boundaries; relying on deceptive phenomena and empty principles, one's sentiments are precarious and one's power is inferior.
Thus, the root-stocks of evil views are completely uprooted and the nesting holes of deluded consciousness are all overturned.

The solitary brilliance of the true mind pervades the entire Dharma-realm. Therefore, the *Zongjing* says: "If you can directly realize the internal mind, do not doubt external objects; if the mind is realized..."

When one realizes that all external objects are empty, then the solitary eye alone harbors its sentiments, and everything is nothing other than the wondrous nature; even mud, mire, tiles, and rubble are entirely household treasures.
The above may be taken as corresponding to the contemplation of "emptiness as identical with form" within the Contemplation of the Dharma Realm.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has often said that all the various transformations in the world arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, specifically through the manifestation of the four great elements in combination. Yet now, the Tathāgata seems to set aside both causes and conditions as well as spontaneity.
I do not yet understand to which category this meaning belongs; I only pray that you will take pity on us and reveal it for the sake of sentient beings."
The Dharma of the definitive meaning is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Having previously refuted that wondrous enlightenment does not belong to causes and conditions, [the Buddha] next refutes that the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*) do not belong to causes and conditions;
therefore, Ānanda again clings to causes and conditions to raise the question regarding the combination of the four great elements. His intention is to say that this wondrous...
"The nature of awakening is the dharma of quiescence; it is the primary meaning (paramārtha) and does not belong to causes and conditions—I have already heard your instruction on this.
The aggregates, elements, and sense bases are dharmas of arising and ceasing; they are the secondary meaning and certainly belong to causes and conditions.
Why, World-Honored One, do you categorically reject both? Furthermore, World-Honored One, you habitually speak of the various marks of transformation within the world."

If all things arise solely from the combination of the four great elements, then one should discard the concept of spontaneity (*svabhāva*) rather than discarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Why would one discard both dependent origination and spontaneity? If what was not discarded in the past is now discarded today, then that which was not discarded yesterday is incorrect today.
Conversely, if what is discarded today is correct, then what was not discarded yesterday must be incorrect.

This is not so. Furthermore, the failure to exclude [the view] in the past seems to fall into the view of existence (*bhāva-dṛṣṭi*), while the exclusion [of the view] today seems to fall into the view of non-existence (*abhāva-dṛṣṭi*).

Since both have fallen into one-sided extremes, they are certainly not the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). They appear to belong to mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and are not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Therefore, we do not know to which category this principle truly belongs; we pray that you will reveal for us the Middle Way and the definitive meaning. There is no other way.
Regarding the question on the Dharma of frivolous proliferation: "In this sutra, Ānanda three times grasped at causes and conditions, and the World-Honored One likewise three times refuted him;
is there any difference [in these instances]? The answer is: "Each of the three questions and three answers possesses its own profound purport;
this is also a major juncture within the sutra. This is because although Ānanda was present in the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and had previously heard [the teaching],..."

Having bestowed this prophecy, [the Buddha] considered those to whom he had long been accustomed and with whom he was well-acquainted—all of whom were followers of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) regarding the teachings on causes and conditions (hetu-pratyaya).

He realized that when the World-Honored One preached the Dharma of causes and conditions for those of initial capacity, his true intent was to lead them into the Great Matter of the Single Cause and Condition (ekakṛtya-ekakaranīya).
Therefore, when Ānanda requested the sublime śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna, the World-Honored One immediately took advantage of that moment.

Taking advantage of the situation, he gradually led him forward; beginning with Ānanda’s grasping of the nature of wondrous enlightenment as being caused and conditioned, the World-Honored One, seizing the opportunity, immediately clarified for him that the seeing of seeing is not seeing, and that seeing cannot reach [the object]. This was a borrowing of causes and conditions to lead him into the wondrous *śamatha*.

Furthermore, by means of the World-Honored One’s refutation of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and realms (*dhātu*), it was revealed that these are fundamentally not caused and conditioned.
Thereafter, Ānanda also seized the opportunity to pose a question, to which the World-Honored One replied that the seven elements pervading everywhere are the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha;
this was intended to lead him into the Great Dharani-gate of Samāpatti by means of causes and conditions.
When the subsequent text states, "Because the three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise," Ānanda again clung to the notion of causes and conditions.

When asked this of the World-Honored One, he answered: "It is neither inherently so nor not so; it is neither a union nor a non-union, yet it is both union and so-ness, while being entirely free from both union and non-union.
Only these words may be called the Dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). This employs causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) as a means to lead one into *dhyāna*.
Therefore it is said: "The dharmas produced by causes and conditions—I say they are empty; they are also called provisional names."
It is also called the meaning of the Middle Way; this is precisely the profound purport of the threefold contemplation within the single mind.
All of these are elucidated through causes and conditions. It is for this reason that the Tathāgata appeared in the world for the sake of the one great causal event.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "In the past, you were weary of and detached from the various Hinayana teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and you resolved to diligently seek unsurpassed Bodhi; therefore, I have now revealed the Ultimate Truth for you.
Why then do you again entangle yourself with worldly frivolous discourse and delusive conceptualizations? Although you are widely learned..."
"It is as when a man who knows medicine, upon seeing a genuine medicine before him, cannot discern it; the Tathāgata says such a person is truly pitiable.
Listen attentively now, and I shall analyze and reveal it for you, so that those in the future who practice the Mahāyāna may penetrate the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
Ānanda remained silent, accepting the Buddha’s holy command.
This first rebukes the ignorant and deluded before granting permission to speak, saying:

"Because you formerly delighted in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), I taught you the various teachings of the Lesser Vehicle regarding the harmony of causes and conditions—these being teachings of provisional meaning.
Now that you have grown weary of and renounced the various teachings of the Lesser Vehicle and earnestly entreat me for unsurpassed Bodhi, I shall therefore [speak] for you today."
I have revealed the supreme primary truth (paramārtha-satya) to you, yet you are unable to accept and uphold it;
instead, why do you continue to entangle and ensnare yourself with the worldly, frivolous, and delusory causes and conditions you heard in the past, refusing to abandon them?
Furthermore, all people in the world acclaim you as the foremost among the learned, yet when it comes to hearing the true truth, you are incapable.
Your faith and understanding are like those who have memorized the *Bencao* (Pharmacopoeia) by heart but do not recognize the actual medicinal herbs;
when presented with them, they cannot distinguish them and instead give rise to doubt—is this not truly pitiable?

Yet, this primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is free from the characteristics of verbal expression and free from the characteristics of mental objects; it is fundamentally undifferentiable and cannot be demonstrated. Now, you—
Since you are entangled by the causes and conditions of deluded minds and conceptual proliferation, I have likewise employed skillful means to analyze and reveal them for you.
However, this present revelation not only enables you to penetrate the true reality (*tattva*), but also enables those seeking the Mahāyāna in the future to penetrate the true reality.
What is called "true reality" refers precisely to the seven great elements, which are illusory and false.
This is the Tathāgatagarbha.
Ānanda, as you have said, the four great elements combine to manifest the various transformations of the world.
Ānanda, if the essence of those great elements were not itself a combination, it could not intermingle with the other elements, just like empty space.

If various forms that were not in harmony were to unite, they would be like magical transformations, where beginning and end mutually constitute one another and birth and cessation continue in succession;
life and death, death and life, follow one another like a whirling firebrand, never finding rest.
Ānanda, it is like water forming ice, and ice returning to become water again.

This is the dharma-gate realized by the Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara. First, one establishes a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) to establish the standard, and subsequently refutes it step by step so that there is no room for evasive speech.
"As for your [position]" below restates the previous question; next, the formal inference is established as follows:

"The great elements (*mahābhūta*) as a substantial entity (*dharmin*) have the thesis (*pakṣa*) that their nature is not a composite; the reason (*hetu*) is that they cannot then [function] together with the various great elements."

Because they are blended together, they are similar by analogy to space, which does not mix with various forms. As for the term "great nature" (*mahābhūtatva*), it refers to the nature of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
These "greats" are the substantial forms (*dravyarūpa*) of the four great elements. Furthermore, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:

Great nature is a property-possessor (*dharmin*) that is established through conjunction (*saṃghāta*), because its beginning and end are mutually constitutive and because its arising and ceasing are continuous; it is like a whirling firebrand (*alātacakra*).
The reason why the Wheel [of Dharma] first established these two measures of valid cognition was precisely for Ānanda’s sake;
for he had previously clung to the fixed notion that the various phenomenal transformations of the world all arise from the combination of the four great elements.

Upon hearing the World-Honored One say that the aggregates, bases, and elements are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously, he immediately gave rise to doubt and, conversely, pointed back at the World-Honored One’s own two [teachings].

If one expounds this as a partial teaching, their deluded attachments can be discerned; therefore, the World-Honored One first established the three branches [of dependent origination] to provide a definitive standard.

If one were to claim that the nature of the four great elements does not combine with the four great elements—just as empty space does not combine with various forms—this would be a biased adherence to spontaneity (*svabhāva*) and a fall into the eternalist view (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*), for such a person knows [the elements] to be unchanging while remaining ignorant of [their conditioned nature].

If, because of following conditions, one were to claim that the nature of the four great elements truly combines with the four great elements—like a whirling firebrand where beginning and end mutually constitute one another, being identical to a transformation—then this would be biased toward the view of causes and conditions and fall into the nihilistic view (uccheda-dṛṣṭi).
This is because such a person knows the following of conditions but does not know the unchanging; how could the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha be like this? And...
You may think this is partial; therefore, he again sets forth a similar example (*sapakṣa*) from the *Nyāya* school to demonstrate it, saying:

"Just as water becomes ice, and ice returns to become water. This continues until the refutation at the end of the passage, which shows that they can never be established through mutual production and thus are not a true synthesis.

Only after this does he establish the correct measure (*pramāṇa*) to prove his own thesis, thereby clarifying the two [positions] of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
To say that all [theories] are biased and not the Middle Way is a profound and mysterious principle; it is most fitting to examine this with great care.
Observe the nature of earth: when coarse, it is the great earth; when subtle, it is a minute particle.

Even down to the *paramāṇu* (neighboring-atom), if one analyzes that ultimate atom into its constituent parts, it is composed of seven such limits of form. If one further analyzes the *paramāṇu*, it is in truth the nature of emptiness, Ānanda, if it were thus.
When atoms are analyzed into space, you should know that space gives rise to the appearance of form.
As for your current question regarding how the various transformed phenomena of the world arise through combination: consider this—how many spaces must combine to constitute a single atom?
It cannot be that atoms are formed by the combination of atoms; furthermore, when an atom is analyzed and dissolved...

As for space, by how many material characteristics (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) is it composed? If it were composed of matter, then when combined with matter, it would be matter and not space; if it were combined with space, then when combined with space, it would be space and not matter.
Since matter can still be analyzed [into its constituent parts], how could space be combined [with anything]?
The following section correctly demonstrates that the beginning and the end cannot mutually establish one another, thereby refuting the theory of combination.

That which is subtle among objects is called "subtle" (*sūkṣma*); that which is more subtle than the subtle is called "extremely subtle" (*paramāṇu*); and that which is even more subtle than the extremely subtle is called "atomic" (*aṇu*).
Because the extremely subtle still possesses the characteristic of subtlety, it is termed the "limit of form" (*rūpa-paryanta-lakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, the extremely subtle is analyzed into...
When divided into seven parts, the subtle form is so slight as to be almost non-existent; therefore, it is called a *paramāṇu* (ultimate atom).
If one were to further analyze this *paramāṇu*, it would become empty space. This precisely demonstrates that the great earth can be analyzed until it becomes empty space.
If this *paramāṇu* can be analyzed into empty space, one should know that empty space must be able to give rise to material forms (*rūpa*). This may then be called the "beginning."
In the end, these would truly form a mark of harmonious union; yet now, this is hardly the case. You are currently attempting to refute empty space by claiming it cannot produce matter;
thus, you now ask: "By means of harmony and union, the various transformative marks of the world are produced.
Therefore, when you observe a single *paramāṇu* (infinitesimal atom), how much empty space must be combined with it for it to exist?

If one analyzes form down to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) and stops there, yet further analysis of the ultimate atom reveals it to be the nature of emptiness, then one must conclude that the synthesis of ultimate atoms necessarily begins with empty space.
Is it not the case that ultimate atoms are synthesized by means of empty space?
If one were to join an ultimate atom to another ultimate atom, would this not be so? If empty space cannot synthesize ultimate atoms, then one knows [the truth].
It is clear that empty space cannot give rise to the characteristics of form. Furthermore, the two subsequent lines directly refute the notion that the characteristics of form can merge with space.
If you claim that by analyzing those neighboring atoms (*paramāṇu*), one reaches the actual nature of space, then how many characteristics of form must combine to constitute this empty space?
Is it now that these characteristics of form are being analyzed away to become empty space? If [it is] form...
Since characteristics cannot combine to form space, it is clear that even when analyzing down to the level of atoms (*paramāṇu*), they cannot give rise to the nature of emptiness.
If one considers the second couplet regarding form (*rūpa*): form merely combines with form and cannot combine with space;
how then could the analysis of atoms produce space? If one considers the second couplet regarding space: space merely combines with space and cannot combine with form. How [could form arise from it]?
If space were to give rise to form, then it would be a case of beginning and end mutually forming one another—this being the analogy of disintegration like crumbling walls or melting ice.
Conversely, this becomes the counter-example of space not combining with various forms. Therefore, he refutes this by saying:
"If form could still be analyzed into space, yet space can never be joined together to become form."
In this way, not only is his analysis of form as being empty and provisional refuted,
but his previous calculation that form arises from emptiness is also defeated; for he does not understand that the arising of emptiness from Great Enlightenment is like a single bubble in the ocean.
You originally did not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, essential form is true emptiness and essential emptiness is true form; it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
It responds to the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of what they can know, appearing in accordance with their karma.
That which is known by the ignorant world as being caused by conditions or arising spontaneously is merely the conceptual calculation of the discriminating consciousness; it exists only as words.
There is no real meaning [in that].

This correctly establishes one's own position: that while both form (*rūpa*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) emerge from the *tathāgatagarbha*, form does not emerge from emptiness, and emptiness does not conjoin with form.
[The opponent] says: "In your ordinary view, you only know how to analyze form into emptiness, but you do not know..."

The nature is originally empty; it does not depend on the analysis of form to become empty. One merely knows that form is produced by uniting with emptiness, yet fails to realize that the nature is originally form itself and does not depend on uniting with emptiness to become form.

This is because the Dharma-nature body and the Dharma-nature land are fundamentally pure, fundamentally unmoving, and fundamentally all-pervasive. [This applies only] to the beings of the nine realms...

Because the arising of the mind involves defilement and purity, its magnitude varies, and karma is either wholesome or unwholesome, each [being] initiates its manifestation according to its own mind, responds according to its own measure, and follows according to its own karma. Thus, the *tathāgatagarbha* is transformed into the *ālayavijñāna*;
the *dharmatākāya* is transformed into the physical body (*indriyakāya*); and the *dharmatābhūmi* is transformed into the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
Those who are deluded regarding the fundamentally pure and all-pervading Dharma-realm mistake it for being produced by causes and conditions, thereby falling into the view of annihilationism;
those who are deluded regarding that which accords with the mind, responds to objects, and manifests according to karma cling to it as being spontaneous, thereby falling into the view of eternalism.
All of these arise from the conceptual calculations and discriminations of the mental consciousnesses of sentient beings; how could they know otherwise?

Is this not the True Doctrine (zhēnzōng) of "transformation according to conditions while remaining unchanging according to conditions"? One should formulate the syllogism as follows: **Thesis:** The nature of form is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true form;
this is the subject (*dharmin*). It is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it spontaneous (*svabhāva*); this is the proposition (*pakṣa*).

**Reason:** Because it is "unchanging while following conditions" and "following conditions while remaining unchanging. **Example:** Just as water becomes ice and ice becomes water. The *Zongjing lu* states:
For example, when the cold months arrive, water freezes into ice; when warmth returns, the ice melts back into water.
When sentient beings are deluded, they congeal their nature into mind; when sentient beings awaken, they dissolve the mind back into nature.
This not only demonstrates that one cannot break down atoms (*paramāṇu*) to produce empty space, nor can empty space give rise to material forms, but furthermore reveals the self-nature.
However, since clinging to causes and conditions is not [ultimately] real, the former two measures (direct perception and inference) are profoundly useful.

Thus, when the World-Honored One taught the Dharma, he never from the beginning departed from causes and conditions and spontaneity; he merely skillfully employed causes and conditions and spontaneity.
How could he have ever rejected them? Therefore, one should know that what was previously described as the aggregates, bases, elements, and sense-fields is in fact the Tathāgatagarbha.
All of these are for the purpose of revealing the great matter of causal conditions for you and demonstrating the definitive meaning of the Middle Way;
thus, you should know that what you have grasped are all but deluded thoughts and frivolous arguments—how could they be the discourse of definitive meaning? Question:

In the preceding passage, the *tathāgatagarbha* was already revealed through the aggregates (*skandhas*), bases (*āyatanas*), and elements (*dhātus*); is this *tathāgatagarbha* revealed here identical to that?

This is a specific answer: although the dharmas are the same, their meanings differ. To say that the dharmas are the same means that the five aggregates (*skandhas*) consist of the two dharmas of matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*);
the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*) consist of the three categories of faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Since the "great element of form" (*rūpa-mahābhūta*) is the object, the "great element of seeing" (*darśana-mahābhūta*) is the faculty, and the "great element of consciousness" (*vijñāna-mahābhūta*) is the consciousness, they are said to be the same in terms of dharma. However, the Tathāgatagarbha indicated within these three categories refers to—
Pointing to firewood is to indicate that it possesses fire; pointing to a well is to indicate that it possesses water;
pointing to a bellows is to indicate that it possesses wind; and pointing to the hollow of a mustard seed is to indicate that it possesses space.

The Tathāgatagarbha, which is fundamentally revealed by these seven elements, is as vast as the quantity of the firewood and fire, equal in measure to the great trichiliocosm, and fills the well-water.
The measure of these [oceans] is equal to the ocean of fragrant waters; the measure of the winds that fill them is equal to the Vairambha wind;

the measure of filling the pores of a mustard seed is equal to boundless space; and even the measure of filling all that moves, flies, and wriggles—knowing and seeing—all is equal and without distinction from the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Therefore, they are collectively designated as "Great" (Mahā). This is the meaning.
There is a difference here.
Ānanda, the nature of fire has no self; it depends upon various conditions. Observe those households in the city that have not yet eaten:

when they wish to cook their food, they hold a magnifying glass (*ādityamaṇi*) in their hands and seek fire from the sun. Ānanda, what is called "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) is like the relationship between me and you.
These one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus now constitute a single assembly.

Although they form one group, when their origins are examined, each has his own body, and each has a clan and a personal name from which he was born—such as Śāriputra of the Brahmin caste, Uruvilvākāśyapa of the Kāśyapa caste, and so on, down to Ānanda of the Gautama clan. Ānanda, it is thus.
The nature of fire exists through the combination of conditions. Suppose one holds a mirror in the hand and seeks fire from the sun;
does this fire emerge from within the mirror, does it come forth from the tinder, or does it arrive from the sun? Ānanda, if it came from the sun, it would naturally burn the tinder in your hand;
the forests from which it originated should likewise be consumed by fire. If it emerged from within the mirror, it should naturally [burn] within the mirror itself.
When fire arises from moxa, why does the mirror not melt? Though you hold it in your hand, it shows no sign of heat; how could it then be dissolved?
If the fire were produced in the moxa, why would it depend on the sun and the mirror? Only when their light meets can fire arise. Observe this again carefully:
the mirror is held by your hand, the sun comes from the sky, and the moxa grows in its own place; from what direction does the fire travel to reach here?
The sun and its reflection are far apart; they are neither joined nor conjoined, yet it is not that the fire-light arises from nowhere on its own.
You still do not understand that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of fire is true emptiness and the nature of emptiness is true fire—pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
It accords with the minds of sentient beings and responds to the measure of what they know. Ānanda, you should know that when people in the world hold a mirror in one place...
The fire arises pervading the Dharma-realm; grasping that it fills the world, it arises and arises throughout the world. How could it have a specific location? It manifests according to karma.
That the world is ignorant, taking delusion as its cause and condition, and that it possesses a nature of spontaneity—all these are merely calculations and discriminations of the conscious mind.
They are nothing but words and lack any real meaning.
This is the Dharma-gate realized by Ucchuṣma. First, it is established that the nature of fire is fundamentally without self;
it relies upon various conditions to appear as if having a self, yet it is not truly so. You should observe this, and below it is verified through experience that there is no self.
Observe how people of the world hold a magnifying lens (*ādityakānta*) in their hands and seek fire from the sun; when fire emerges, it is therefore called "fire."

That which arises through the conjunction of natures is just like the present assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus who, though gathered together in one place and called a "harmonious community," are in truth each distinct in their bodies, names, lineages, and clans when examined at their root;
this is true harmony. If your nature of fire were produced by such conjunction, then that—
If one holds a sun-mirror (*āditya-manthāna*) and moxa against the sun to seek fire, and fire emerges, one should interrogate each element regarding its fundamental source.
Each has its own point of origin: does this fire emerge from the mirror? Does it emerge from the moxa? Or does it come from the sun?

If one examines beneath the sun, it is not from the sun; if one examines beneath the mirror, it is not from the mirror; if one examines beneath the moxa... [it is not from the moxa]. Thus one investigates.
"It was not from the moxa that you produced this fire; furthermore, command him to examine closely where it originated.

He said, "These three things each have their own location. From which of these did this fire come? Having interrogated him regarding these three locations, [it was found] that there was no root at all.
"How could it have emerged of itself without a cause? Words must surely have a basis. You still cannot point out the fire below."
The place from which it comes is not within the mirror; the original source is within the *tathāgatagarbha*.
It manifests according to karma; it is not a product of combination. The previous statement that "the original" refers to its primordial unknowability;
the present statement that "it is still so" means that although I have already explained it for you, it remains thus unknown. Cui Bao’s *Gujin Zhu* states:
The *yángsuǐ* (sun-focusing mirror) is made of copper and shaped like a mirror; when it reflects objects, the image is inverted, and when directed toward the sun, fire emerges.
The *Huáinán Zǐ* states that the *yángsuǐ* is the same as the *huǒ fāngzhū* (fire *fāngzhū*).

The *Lúnhéng* states that on the day of the *bǐngwǔ* hexagram at noon on the fifth month, one melts and refines stones from the five directions into a circle like a mirror with a concave center; under clear skies, one directs it toward the sun.
Then fire emerges.
Ānanda, the nature of water is not fixed; its flowing and ceasing are without constancy.
For instance, in the city of Śrāvastī, there were the great illusionists Kapila Rishi, Kālakarṇi Rishi, Padma, Mahasattva, and others, who sought the essence of the moon to use in their mixtures.

Regarding the magical elixir, when masters and others on a day of the bright fortnight hold a *fangzhu* (a concave mirror) in their hands to receive the water from the moon, does this water emerge from within the pearl, arise spontaneously from the air, or come from the moon?

Ānanda, if it comes from the moon, then since it can cause the pearl to produce water even from such a great distance, all the trees and forests through which it passes should likewise discharge streams; if they were to flow, why wait for anything else?

The clear water produced by the *fangzhu* (concave mirror) does not flow from the moon; yet if it originates from the pearl, that pearl should constantly produce water—why then must one wait for the midnight hour to receive it under the white moon?
If it were born from space, since the nature of space is boundless, water would likewise be limitless;
if this were so, then from humans to devas, all would be submerged in a single deluge. How, then, could there still be those who travel by water, land, or air?

Examine this further with careful attention: the moon ascends from the heavens; the pearl is held in the hand; the water-dish was originally set out by a person. From what direction does the water flow here?
The moon and the pearl are far apart; they are neither blended nor joined. It cannot be that the crystal water exists of itself without a source.
You still do not understand that within the Tathāgata-garbha, the nature of water is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true water.
Pure and fundamentally such, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, it responds to the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of what they know.
If one person grasps at a pearl in one place, water appears in that place; if the entire Dharma-realm grasps at it, the whole Dharma-realm is filled with water. How could there be any fixed location?
It manifests according to karma. That the world lacks knowledge and is deluded by causes and conditions, as well as by the nature of spontaneity—all this is but the conscious mind.
Conceptualization and deliberation consist merely of verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever.
This is the Dharma-gate realized by the youth Candraprabha. Regarding "flowing and ceasing without constancy":
it flows when sought and does not flow when not sought. *Kapila* is translated as "yellowish-red"; *cakravāḍa* is translated as "wheel."
*Padma* is translated here as "red lotus. *Hrasvaka* is not clearly known [in meaning].
These non-Buddhists (tīrthika), while in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), may behold the orbs of the sun and moon, or see red lotuses and yellow or red colors; thus the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"For example, the forms of the sun and moon, the red lotus, the deep abyss, space, and ashes—these are the paths of the non-Buddhists, which lead to dhyāna."
This is the essence of the Yin, the water of the moon. Before the full moon it appears white; when the moon is at its zenith, it is called "day.
The *Fangzhu* (the Yin-conduit) is a water-crystal bead. The *Huainanzi* states: "When the *fangzhu* beholds the moon, it exudes moisture that becomes water.
If one examines the source of this water, Ānanda, it is clear that it does not come from the moon, nor does it issue from the bead.
The following section distinguishes that it does not emerge from the pearl; if it were to arise from space, the following section distinguishes that it does not arise from space.

You further command him to examine and discern its place of origin—*zhé* meaning "to ascend. If you still do not know, it means that although I have already explained it to you twice, you remain unaware.
Ānanda, the nature of wind has no substance; its movement and stillness are not constant.
When you regularly adjust your robes upon entering the great assembly, the corner of your saṃghāṭī robe moves and reaches a person nearby, causing a slight breeze to brush that person’s face.
Does this wind emerge from the corner of the *kāṣāya*, arise from empty space, or is it produced on that person’s face? Ānanda, if this wind were to emerge from the corner of the *kāṣāya*...

When you are wearing this robe, its fabric flutters and should therefore be separated from your body. Now that I am preaching the Dharma within this assembly, my robe hangs down; look at my robe—where is the wind?
It cannot be that there is a place for the wind to be hidden within the robe. If it were produced from empty space, then even when your robe does not move, why is there no brushing against it?
Since the nature of space is eternally present, the wind should be constantly arising; yet when there is no wind, where has it gone?
If space were to be extinguished, the extinction of wind could be perceived; what would be the appearance of space being extinguished?

If there were arising and ceasing, it would not be called "space. Being called "space," how could wind emerge from it? If wind arose of itself, then when you are brushed by it, the wind would have to arise from that very face brushing you;
it should then brush you yourself. When you straighten your robe, why do you instead brush against it? Observe carefully: it is you who are straightening your robe.
The face belongs to that person, while space is quiescent and does not participate in movement; from which direction, then, does the wind come to stir here?
Wind and space are distinct in nature, neither blending nor uniting; it cannot be that the nature of wind exists of itself without a source.
You simply do not realize that within the Tathāgata-garbha, the nature of wind is true emptiness and the nature of emptiness is true wind—pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
It accords with the minds of sentient beings and corresponds to the measure of what they know. Ānanda, it is like when you alone slightly move your robe, a subtle breeze arises;
it sweeps throughout the Dharma-realm and fills the lands, pervading the entire world. How could it have a fixed location? It manifests according to karma.
That the ignorant of the world deludedly take this to be caused by conditions or to possess a nature of spontaneity is entirely due to the discrimination of the conscious mind.
Such conceptual deliberations consist merely of words and possess no real meaning;
this is the dharma-gate realized by Vairocana-prabha. Regarding the phrase "movement and stillness are not constant," it is like a fan: it moves when shaken and remains still when not shaken.
*Saṃghāṭī* refers to the great outer robe. This [passage] below interrogates the source from which this wind arises. *Kāṣāya*...

"Kāṣāya" here translates as "dyed-garment. If [you claim] that Ānanda’s lower robe is not produced from cloth, yet it is not produced from emptiness, then since the nature of emptiness is eternally abiding, wind should be constantly produced; this means that while emptiness is eternal, wind is likewise eternal.

If when there is no wind, empty space should perish, then with the extinction of wind, emptiness would also perish; if emptiness were to perish, then wind could be perceived [as existing independently].

Regarding the question of what the appearance of the extinction of emptiness (*ākāśa*) is like: when the wind subsides, all the apertures become void, and thus their forms can be seen. If emptiness were to be extinguished, it should likewise have no visible form or appearance. Yet, this azure color is ever-present. If it were subject to arising and ceasing, it would be a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and could not be called emptiness. Since it is named "emptiness," one knows that the wind is not itself emptiness. Why is this so? Because the wind is merely a movement within emptiness; it is not emptiness itself. Furthermore, if the wind were emptiness, then when the wind arises, emptiness would arise, and when the wind ceases, emptiness would cease. If emptiness were to arise and cease, it would be a created thing and could not be called emptiness. Since it is named "emptiness," one knows that the wind is not emptiness. Why is this so?
