Because the wind is a conditioned phenomenon, whereas emptiness is unconditioned. Therefore, one knows that the wind is not emptiness. Furthermore, if the wind were emptiness, then when the wind arises, emptiness would arise, and when the wind ceases, emptiness would cease. If emptiness were to arise and cease, it would be a created thing and could not be called emptiness. Since it is named "emptiness," one knows that the wind is not emptiness. Why is this so? Because the wind is a conditioned phenomenon, whereas emptiness is unconditioned. Therefore, one knows that the wind is not emptiness. Furthermore, if the wind were emptiness, then when the wind arises, emptiness would arise, and when the wind ceases, emptiness would cease. If emptiness were to arise and cease, it would be a created thing and could not be called emptiness. Since it is named "emptiness," one knows that the wind is not emptiness. Why is this so? Because the wind is a conditioned phenomenon, whereas emptiness is unconditioned. Therefore, one knows that the wind is not emptiness. Furthermore, if the wind were emptiness, then when the wind arises, emptiness would arise, and when the wind ceases, emptiness would cease. If emptiness were to arise and cease, it would be a created thing and could not be called emptiness. Since it is named "emptiness," one knows that the wind is not emptiness. Why is this so? Because the wind is a conditioned phenomenon, whereas emptiness is unconditioned. Therefore, one knows that the wind is not emptiness. Furthermore, if the wind were emptiness, then when the wind arises, emptiness would arise, and when the wind ceases, emptiness would cease. If emptiness were to arise and cease, it would be a created thing and could not be called emptiness. Since it is named "emptiness," one knows that the wind is not emptiness. Why is this so? Because the wind is a conditioned phenomenon
Why do you insist on saying that the wind comes from empty space? This clearly demonstrates that the name and the reality do not correspond.

That "wind arises from space" is a common misconception held by ordinary people and those of the Lesser Vehicle; therefore, it is examined in detail here. If the wind were produced below, it would not arise from one's own face.
If you claim that this wind does not arise from one's own face while adjusting one's robe, but rather arises from the face of the person being brushed by it—[this is untenable].
Since it is that face which has already arisen, it should come and wipe you; since it is you who have adjusted your robe, you should wipe that face.
Why then do you say that the wind arises from that face and wipes you upside down?

If you truly do not understand this, my threefold exposition will be no different for you than if you had never heard it at all. Thus, know that the wind is fundamentally motionless, yet it is capable of moving.
If all things possessed motion from the outset, they would lose their own essential nature and could no longer move again. Now, this nature of wind pervades the entire Dharma-realm;
it is profoundly still and unmoving, quiescent and formless. When one investigates this motion, it is seen that it arises entirely from conditions.
For instance, within a sealed room, if one says there is wind, why does the wind not move? If one says there is no wind, yet when encountering...
Since movement arises precisely because of conditions, we know that the wind-element itself is not moving; rather, movement belongs to the various conditions.

If one were to maintain that it arises spontaneously (*svabhāva*), it would necessarily arise constantly; how could its speed be uncertain or its motion and stillness inconsistent? Therefore, we know that all things arise from conditions.

Furthermore, when investigating how various conditions combine to form a phenomenon, each individual condition does not exist [independently], nor does their combination exist [as a separate entity]. Within these conditions and their objects...
Both lack self-nature and are merely the movement of the mind; yet when one turns back to examine the mind itself, the mind is also unmoving.
Since the mind has no form, its place of origin cannot be found; thus one knows that all arise from true nature (*dharmatā*).

If true nature does not arise, only then does one see true nature pervading the ten directions. Because this nature is united with the true void, it is said: "The nature-wind is the true void; the nature-void is [the true void]."
According to the True Dharma, Nāgārjuna said: "If earth possesses the characteristic of solidity, it should not abandon that characteristic.
Just as when clarified butter, beeswax, honey, or resin melts, they abandon their solid characteristics and fall into the characteristic of moisture; gold, silver, copper, and iron are likewise so.
As water has the characteristic of moisture, when it becomes cold, it transforms into the characteristic of solidity. Such are the various kinds [of examples].
All such types are characterized by total relinquishment. Furthermore, it is said: "If fire truly possessed the nature of heat, why would some people enter fire without being burned?
Why does the fire within the human body not burn the body itself? And why can the water in clouds not extinguish fire? It is because fire lacks a fixed nature of heat;
because of the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*), fire cannot burn the body; and because of the causal conditions of karma."
The five viscera do not become hot because of the power of the divine dragon; water cannot extinguish them. If the nature of heat were distinct from fire, then fire would not be hot.
If the nature of heat were identical to fire, how could one say that "heat is like the nature of fire"? Other natures are likewise so.

Thus, because the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and the specific characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) do not exist, they are called "emptiness of nature" (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). The *Saṃyukta-ābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states: "If earth..."
If a nature were real, it could not be changed. A Dharma-body Bodhisattva can transform the great earth into golden ground;
if the seeds of gold were suddenly lost, how could they be real? If the nature of water were real, it could not be changed.
When devas and humans see water, they call it lapis lazuli; when hungry ghosts see water, they call it fire; when fish see it, they call it their dwellings. How, then, could it be real fire?
If a nature were real, it could not be changed; yet Śrīgupta was born from within fire.

Furthermore, in the Western lands there is cloth that is brightened by being washed in fire, known as "fire-washed cloth" (*agnika-vastra*); how then could this be real? If the nature of wind were real, it could not be changed;
yet Li Zǐ rode upon it to travel, and boatmen take advantage of it to steer their vessels—how then could these be real?
Because [these elements] are real, Nāgārjuna poses the question: "What are earth, water, fire, and wind? Are they substantial dharmas, or are they merely names? He answers:
"The ignorant person regards dharmas such as earth as real; however, when the sage observes them with the eye of wisdom, they are all seen to be deceptive.
For example, it is like a child who sees a reflection in a mirror and, taking it to be real, joyfully desires to grasp it."
A Great Being observes that this merely deceives the eyes of ordinary worldlings; when they see it formed through combination, they take it to be real earth.

Those with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) can disperse this earth, seeing it as nothing but subtle particles. Even when analyzed by the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*), though this earth is dispersed, it is ultimately unobtainable.
Thus one knows there is no real earth, and that water, fire, and wind likewise do not exist in reality and cannot be seen by the eye.
In reality, earth, water, fire, and wind are such that Panshan said: "In the Three Realms there is no dharma; where can one seek the mind?
The four great elements are fundamentally empty—upon what does the Buddha rely to dwell? The celestial sphere is unmoving, silent and wordless;
face-to-face presentation leaves nothing further to be done as a commentary upon this."

Ānanda, emptiness has no form; it is manifested through matter. For example, in the city of Śrāvastī, at a place far from the river, there are various kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, śūdras, as well as pahlavas and caṇḍālas, who have recently established a dwelling and dug a well to seek water.
When they have excavated one foot of earth, there is one foot of empty space within it; it is just like this.
Even when one digs out a cubit of earth, one recovers a cubit of empty space within; the depth of this emptiness corresponds exactly to the amount excavated.
Does this space arise because of the earth being removed, or does it exist because of the digging? Or does it arise spontaneously without a cause?
Ānanda, if this space arose spontaneously without a cause, why was there no obstruction before the earth had been dug? Why did one see only the great earth?
It is utterly devoid of penetration. If it emerged because of the earth, then at the time the earth emerges, one should see the void enter.

If the earth emerges first and there is no entry of the void, how can empty space emerge because of the earth? If there is neither entering nor exiting, then space and earth must originally have no different cause;
if they have no difference, they are identical. Thus, when the earth emerges, why does space not emerge as well? If it emerges because of digging, [then...]
If the empty space emerges from the boring, it would not have emerged from the earth; if it did not emerge because of the boring, then the boring itself must have emerged from the earth.

How then can you see the empty space? Examine this again with utmost precision and observe carefully: the boring follows the hand as it moves in various directions, and the earth shifts according to the ground.
Thus, from what source does this empty space emerge? The boring tool and the empty space—whether void or solid—do not function for one another; they are neither blended nor conjoined.

Space cannot emerge from nowhere on its own; since the nature of space is perfect, pervasive, and fundamentally unmoving, you should know that the earth, water, fire, and wind manifest before you are likewise called the five great elements.
Their natures are truly interfused and perfectly harmonious, all being the Tathāgata-garbha, fundamentally without arising or ceasing.
Ānanda, your mind is deluded and confused; you do not realize that the four elements are originally the Tathāgata-garbha. You should contemplate this.

"Whether space emerges or enters, or whether it neither emerges nor enters—you know nothing at all of this. Within the *tathāgatagarbha*, the nature of awareness is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true awareness;
it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. It accords with the minds of sentient beings and responds to the measure of what they know.
Ānanda, it is like a single well: when a well is dug, space arises within that well; the same is true for the empty space of the ten directions."
The fulfillment of the ten directions—how could it have a fixed location? It manifests according to karma;

that the world lacks knowledge and takes delusion as its cause and condition, or that it possesses a nature of spontaneity, is entirely the result of the discerning and calculating of the conscious mind. These are merely words and possess no real meaning whatsoever.
This is the Dharma-gate realized by Ākāśagarbha. "Emptiness is formless" means that it lacks the dimensions of size, shape, or circumference.

*Kṣatriya* refers to the royal caste. *Brāhmaṇa*—translated here as "Pure Conduct"—refers to those who dwell at home while guarding the Way and maintaining pure integrity in their conduct. *Vaiśya* refers to merchants. *Śūdra* refers to farmers.
Regarding these four castes of India: the *purohita* (translated here as "sharp-witted") refers to those of keen faculties;

the *caṇḍāla* (translated here as "butcher") refers to those who slaughter humans and livestock. Because in India, sexual misconduct and killing are equally held in contempt, the *caṇḍālas* are specifically regarded as the most wicked of men.
The laws of the land require them to ring bells and carry banners to warn others to take a different path, so that they do not travel together with virtuous citizens.
It is also translated as "adorned banner. Below this, [the text] interrogates the place of origin of this space. Under "Ānanda," it distinguishes that it does not arise without a cause.
Under "if it emerged from the earth," it distinguishes that it does not emerge from the earth. Under "if it emerged from the excavation," it distinguishes that it does not emerge from the excavation.
If one claims that this space emerges because of the excavation, then it should follow the hand as it excavates the void, and there would be no need for the earth to be removed.
If you say that space does not arise because of digging, but rather that space emerges from the earth itself, how then could one see space within a well?

You should further descend [into the well] and apply your mind to observe with thorough scrutiny. "Thorough scrutiny" (shen) means to examine its reality; "thorough examination" (di-shen) means not to observe superficially;
"thorough observation" (di-guan) means a determination to see its very core. If one proceeds in this manner, it will result in five [points].

"Great one, your mind is deluded and darkened"—this is a severe reprimand. It means that because you are obscured, confused, and ignorant of what is good and evil, you cling to the combination of the four great elements and refuse to abandon your old habits; you do not realize that the four great elements are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.
You should simply examine the element of space (ākāśa-mahābhūta) to investigate whether it has coming and going or no coming and going. If you awaken to this...
The element of space is great, immovable, and all-pervasive; it neither issues forth nor enters, nor does it neither issue forth nor enter.
This is precisely the awakening that the four great elements are neither blended nor joined, yet neither are they not blended and not joined.

If you do not understand this at all, it will mean that the more it is explained, the more you will grow dark, like a person who is entirely incapable of understanding the matter. "The nature of awareness is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true awareness" means that—
Seeing emptiness give rise to great awakening is not that it lacks a fundamental source; it is as the Perfect Awakening Sutra says:
"Boundless empty space is manifested by awakening.
Ānanda saw that awakening has no cognition, yet because of form and emptiness, there exists one such as you here in the Jeta Grove at the break of dawn.

At dusk it is obscured, and at midnight, when the white moon shines or the black moon is dark, it is likewise clear or dim. Thus, through the perception of light and darkness, this vision is analyzed.
Furthermore, is this vision combined with light and darkness? Is it of the same substance as the great void, or is it not of one substance?
Is it both the same and not the same, or different and not different? Ānanda, if this vision were again combined with light and darkness...

If light and space were originally of one essence, then light and darkness—these two essences—would mutually negate one another; when it is dark, there would be no light, and when it is light, there would be no darkness.

If light were identical with darkness, then seeing would cease to exist; if they were necessarily one, then when it is dark, seeing should perish. If seeing perishes, how could one see light or see darkness?
If light and darkness are distinct from seeing, then seeing would be subject to arising and ceasing. How, then, could it be established as a single unity?

If this essence of seeing were not of one substance with darkness and light, then when you separate it from light, darkness, and empty space to analyze its fundamental nature, what form or appearance would it have?
If this fundamental seeing were separated from light, separated from darkness, and separated from empty space, it would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.
Since light, darkness, and empty space—these three things—are all distinct from one another, from what could seeing be established? Light and darkness are mutually opposed.

How could it be that they are identical and yet both depart from the three elements? How could it be that they are distinct? Since space is fundamentally without boundaries, how could it be not identical?
Since you see darkness and see light, and their nature does not undergo change, how could it be not distinct?

You should examine this further with extreme subtlety, scrutinizing it with precision and clarity: does light arise from the sun, does darkness follow the dark moon, or do they both belong to empty space?
When it returns to the great earth, from what source does this essence of seeing arise? Seeing is aware while emptiness is inert; they are neither a harmonious blend nor a composite.

It cannot be that the essence of seeing arises spontaneously without a cause. If the nature of seeing, hearing, and knowing is perfectly pervasive and fundamentally unmoving, you should know that boundless, unmoving empty space, along with the shifting elements of earth, water, fire, and wind, are all equally called the six great elements.
The nature of reality is truly perfect and harmonious; all are the Tathāgata-garbha, fundamentally free from arising and ceasing.

Ānanda, your nature has sunk into delusion, yet your very faculties of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha. You should now observe these faculties of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing:
do they arise or cease? Are they identical or different? Are they neither arising nor ceasing, or neither identical nor different? You have never known this, O Tathāgata.
Within the storehouse-consciousness, the nature of seeing is luminous awareness; this luminous awareness is pure and essential, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

It accords with the minds of sentient beings and responds to the measure of what they know. Just as the faculty of seeing is all-pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, so too are hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the cognitive awareness of touch—these wondrous virtues are brilliantly clear and pervade the entire Dharma-realm, filling the ten voids. How could they have any fixed location? They follow the course of karma.
One discovers that ignorance and delusion in the world, whether as causes and conditions or as inherent natures, are all merely the conceptual constructions and calculations of the discerning mind;
they consist only of verbal expressions and possess no actual reality.
This is the place where Mahāsthāmaprāpta realized perfect penetration. To see the awareness is to see the nature;

because it constantly abides in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and does not give rise to discrimination, it is called "non-knowing. Yet, it must manifest through form and emptiness—this is what is meant by "the unchanging following conditions.
[The passage] beginning with "As for you" interrogates the origin of this seeing; that beginning with "This seeing" distinguishes how the nature of seeing is not [subject to arising].
The three phenomena are one essence because the two characteristics of light and darkness mutually supplant one another, yet the nature of seeing remains undifferentiated.

The passage beginning with "If it were like this" distinguishes that the nature of seeing is not a separate entity from the three phenomena, because the nature of seeing has no substance apart from its objects.

The passage beginning with "Light and darkness are opposed" distinguishes that they are neither identical nor different; the section on "dividing space and dividing seeing" distinguishes that they are not non-identical.

"Since it is neither the same nor different, you must further command him to investigate thoroughly from where this seeing-nature ultimately comes. First he was told to examine minutely; next, not merely minutely but with subtle minuteness; not merely examining but with detailed scrutiny; next, having already observed closely, he was further told to investigate secretly and then to examine with profound clarity. As for this "thorough examination and observation": [The text continues: ...its nature is such that it cannot be grasped by the mind, nor can it be perceived by the eyes. It is not something that can be sought through the faculties of hearing, smelling, tasting, or touch. It is not something that can be reached by the intellect or the consciousness. It is not something that can be attained through the six sense bases. It is not something that can be found within the four elements. It is not something that can be located in the five aggregates. It is not something that can be produced by causes and conditions. It is not something that can be extinguished. It is not something that can be born. It is not something that can be destroyed. It is not something that can be increased. It is not something that can be diminished. It is not something that can be obtained. It is not something that can be lost. It is not something that can be defiled. It is not something that can be purified. It is not something that can be old. It is not something that can be new. It is not something that can be past. It is not something that can be future. It is not something that can be present. It is not something that can be seen as a thing. It is not something that can be seen as a non-thing. It is not something that can be seen as existence. It is not something that can be seen as non-existence. It is not something that can be seen as coming. It is not something that can be seen as going. It is not something that can be seen as staying. It is not something that can be seen as changing. It is not something that can be seen as arising. It is not something that can be seen as ceasing. It is not something that can be seen as a self. It is not something that can be seen as a person. It is not something that can be seen as a sentient being. It is not something that can be seen as a life-force. It is not something that can be seen as a nourisher. It is not something that can be seen as a knower. It is not something that can be seen as a seer. It is not something that can be seen as a doer. It is not something that can be seen as an experiencer. It is not something that can be seen as a thinker. It is not something that can be seen as a perceiver. It is not something that can be seen as a speaker. It is not something that can be seen as a hearer. It is not something that can be seen as a smeller. It is not something that can be seen as a taster. It is not something that can be seen as a toucher. It is not something that can be seen as a cognizer. It is not something that can be seen as a mind. It is not something that can be seen as a consciousness. It is not something that can be seen as a thought. It is not something that can be seen as a perception. It is not something that can be seen as a feeling. It is not something that can be seen as a volition. It is not something that can be seen as a contact. It is not something that can be seen as a name-and-form. It is not something that can be seen as a realm. It is not something that can be seen as a field. It is not something that can be seen as a body. It is not something that can be seen as a head. It is not something that can be seen as a face. It is not something that can be seen as an eye. It is not something that can be seen as an ear. It is not something that can be seen as a nose. It is not something that can be seen as a tongue. It is not something that can be seen as a body. It is not something that can be seen as a mind. It is not something that can be seen as a color. It is not something that can be seen as a sound. It is not something that can be seen as a smell. It is not something that can be seen as a taste. It is not something that can be seen as a touch. It is not something that can be seen as a dharma. It is not something that can be seen as a form. It is not something that can be seen as a shape. It is not something that can be seen as a direction. It is not something that can be seen as a location. It is not something that can be seen as a time. It is not something that can be seen as a season. It is not something that can be seen as a year. It is not something that can be seen as a month. It is not something that can be seen as a day. It is not something that can be seen as a night. It is not something that can be seen as a moment. It is not something that can be seen as an instant. It is not something that can be seen as a second. It is not something that can be seen as a minute. It is not something that can be seen as an hour. It is not something that can be seen as a morning. It is not something that can be seen as an afternoon. It is not something that can be seen as a noon. It is not something that can be seen as a dawn. It is not something that can be seen as a dusk. It is not something that can be seen as a twilight. It is not something that can be seen as a morning star. It is not something that can be seen as a moon. It is not something that can be seen as a sun. It is not something that can be seen as a fire. It is not something that can be seen as a lamp. It is not something that can be seen as a candle. It is not something that can be seen as a torch. It is not something that can be seen as a lightning bolt. It is not something that can be seen as a cloud. It is not something that can be seen as a rain. It is not something that can be seen as a wind. It is not something that can be seen as a dust. It is not something that can be seen as a smoke. It is not something that can be seen as a mist. It is not something that can be seen as a fog. It is not something that can be seen as a dew. It is not something that can be seen as a frost. It is not something that can be seen as a snow. It is not something that can be seen as a hail. It is not something that can be seen as a thunder. It is not something that can be seen as a lightning. It is not something that can be seen as a dragon. It is not something that can be seen as a phoenix. It is not something that can be seen as a crane. It is not something that can be seen as a parrot. It is not something that can be seen as a peacock. It is not something that can be seen as a crane. It is not something that can be seen as a hawk. It is not something that can be seen as a falcon. It is not something that can be seen as a crow. It is not something that can be seen as a magpie. It is not something that can be seen as a sparrow. It is not something that can be seen as a dove. It is not something that can be seen as a pigeon. It is not something that can be seen as a goose. It is not something that can be seen as a duck. It is not something that can be seen as a fish. It is not something that can be seen as a bird. It is not something that can be seen as an insect. It is not something that can be seen as a worm. It is not something that can be seen as a plant. It is not something that can be seen as a tree. It is not something that can be seen as a flower. It is not something that can be seen as a fruit. It is not something that can be seen as a leaf. It is not something that can be seen as a branch. It is not something that can be seen as a root. It is not something that can be seen as a stem. It is not something that can be seen as a bud. It is not something that can be seen as a petal. It is not something that can be seen as a stamen. It is not something that can be seen as a pistil. It is not something that can be seen as a seed. It is not something that can be seen as a grain. It is not something that can be seen as a stalk. It is not something that can be seen as a sheath. It is not something that can be seen as a husk. It is not something that can be seen as a shell. It is not something that can be seen as a skin. It is not something that can be seen as a membrane. It is not something that can be seen as a bone. It is not something that can be seen as a muscle. It is not something that can be seen as a vein. It is not something that can be seen as a tendon. It is not something that can be seen as a joint. It is not something that can be seen as a limb. It is not something that can be seen as a finger. It is not something that can be seen
My intention is nothing more than to cause you to examine and scrutinize until you clearly perceive the point of its arising;

it does not mean that upon seeing the lower assembly as the six great elements, you must necessarily attempt to perform this assembly. This is because the two divisions of "seeing" and "form" are fundamentally one body.
Therefore, for those whose nature is submerged in samsara, I reprimand them for being drowned in causes and conditions and unable to emerge on their own.
Furthermore, you have not realized that the two words "already" (yù) and "should" (dāng) correspond to one another.
You were unaware that when I previously refuted the substantiality of the seeing-nature, you became even more confused and distressed.
Although I have elucidated this for you until now, you still do not know that this essence of seeing is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, and is inherently the Tathāgata.
"Zang also [says]: 'The seeing within the nature is the luminosity of fundamental awakening; the luminosity of fundamental awakening is the seeing of the clarity of the nature.
How could this mean that you previously took the eye to be seeing? This is like [the passage] where one root is used to unify the six roots:
when there is contact with taste, it is the tongue-root that perceives it only upon its union with flavor."
Therefore, discernment is the sensation of touch, and awareness is the faculty of body and mind.

That "wondrous virtue is brilliantly pure" means that these six faculties are the very marks of the virtues inherent in the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*), for they are the light of great wisdom. Thus, they are constantly radiant day and night;
their spiritual clarity is never obscured, and they are all-pervasive and perfect. Since their characteristic is such as this, how could they have a specific location?
Do you hold that they expand and contract according to size? You do not realize that all these are manifestations arising in accordance with karma;
how could they be true seeing or true hearing?
Ānanda, the nature of consciousness has no source; it emerges falsely from the six kinds of sense organs and their objects. Now, survey this assembly as a whole.
The noble assembly uses their eyes to survey them; as they look around, it is just like [seeing reflections] in a mirror, without any further differentiation or analysis.
Within this, your consciousness sequentially identifies and points out: "This is Mañjuśrī," "This is Pūrṇa," "This is Maudgalyāyana," "This is Subhūti," and "This is Śāriputra.
Does this consciousness that cognizes arise from seeing, or does it arise from signs, or does it arise from...?

Space arises suddenly without any cause. Ānanda, if the nature of your consciousness were born from within seeing, then in the absence of darkness, light, form, and emptiness—these four conditions—it would necessarily not exist;
since it would originally not exist, your seeing would be absent, and if the nature of seeing itself does not exist, from what could consciousness arise?
If the nature of your consciousness were born from the objective phenomena and not from seeing, then since you would not see light...

Furthermore, one does not perceive darkness or light; since darkness does not illuminate, there is no form or emptiness. When even those characteristics do not exist, from what could consciousness arise?

If it were to arise in emptiness, it would be neither characteristic nor seeing. Without seeing, there is no discernment, and thus one cannot know for oneself. Since light, darkness, form, and emptiness are not characteristics, the conditions for their cessation are absent.
Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing have no place to be established. If these two—characteristic and seeing—are not empty, then they are the same as non-existence.

If there were no external objects, even if you were to activate your consciousness, what would you have to discern? If it arises suddenly without any cause, why do you not perceive the bright moon at midday as distinct from other objects?
Examine this more closely; scrutinize it minutely: the act of seeing relies upon your pupils, while the forms being inferred belong to the external realm.
These forms may be characterized as existing or, if they cannot be so characterized, as non-existent. Given this, by what cause does such consciousness arise?
The movement of consciousness makes seeing clear; they are neither blended nor joined. Hearing, listening, sensing, and knowing are likewise so.

It cannot be that consciousness arises from conditions, nor can it emerge from nowhere on its own. If this conscious mind originally has no source from which it comes, you should know that the faculty of discernment—seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—is perfect and profoundly still;
its nature does not arise from any external locus. Furthermore, space, earth, water, fire, and wind are all equally termed the "Seven Great Elements."
The nature is truly perfect and harmonious; all are the Tathāgata-garbha, fundamentally without birth or extinction. Ānanda, your mind is coarse and floating;
you do not realize that seeing, hearing, and the resulting clear awareness are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha. You should contemplate these six consciousnesses of the sense bases:
are they the same or different? Are they empty or existent? Are they neither the same nor different, or neither empty nor existent? You originally do not know this, O Tathāgata.

Within the storehouse consciousness, the nature-consciousness is luminous and aware; this true consciousness and wondrous awakening are profoundly still and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, encompassing and expelling the ten voids.

How could it have a fixed location? It manifests according to karma. That the world lacks knowledge and is deluded by causes, conditions, and the nature of spontaneity—all these are merely the discriminations and calculations of the consciousness-mind; they are nothing but words and lack any real meaning.
This is the gateway to perfect penetration realized by Maitreya. That which has no source arises falsely due to the faculties and their objects;

therefore, you should now examine below how they arise falsely from no source. As for the observation: the holy assembly is the faculty and the environment is the object. The "pointer" refers to consciousness.
When it is said that the eye-faculty is all-pervasive and its vision is like a reflection in a mirror, yet devoid of discrimination—this refers to the eye.
Consciousness still includes the simultaneous, clear mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
When visual consciousness perceives a nature-object (*svabhāva-viṣaya*), it possesses natural discrimination (*svabhāva-vikalpa*) but does not yet carry names or engage in deliberative thought;

however, by means of that simultaneous mental consciousness, a second moment of apprehension arises regarding that nature-object, grasping at names such as "so-and-so" and so forth, which constitutes the discrimination of recollection and deliberation (*nāma-anuvyavahāra-vikalpa*).

"Furthermore, Ānanda, below I shall distinguish that the single faculty does not give rise [to consciousness]; if you [say it arises from the object], below I shall distinguish that the single object does not give rise [to it];
if you say it arises from space, below I shall distinguish that it does not arise from space.

If you claim that this consciousness does not arise from the faculty of sight nor from the visual form, but rather arises from space—if it were not the faculty of sight, then color and space could not be distinguished; if it were not the visual form, then the faculty would have no object."
Since from the outset there is no mutual perception of forms and they are merely a single emptiness, consciousness likewise must be non-existent.
If consciousness were necessarily present, yet did not couple with the sense organs and their objects, then even if your consciousness were to arise, what could it possibly discern?
Thus, to claim that consciousness arises from emptiness apart from the sense organs and their objects is even more untenable. [The following section] refutes the notion that it is not causeless.

"Give birth to you again and command him to observe closely; see how [the perception] relies upon two phrases that point to the sense organs and their objects, and two phrases that refer to form and emptiness.
These four are distinct and clear; from where does your consciousness emerge? When consciousness moves, seeing is still.
This means that because consciousness possesses discrimination, it is "moving," whereas because seeing is without discrimination, it is "still. Thus, there is movement and stillness.

Since they are not identical and are fundamentally distinct, each being fixed and without a place of arising, should consciousness not emerge spontaneously from its conditions, rather than having no source?
Below this, in the section establishing the seven elements, one should know that "discrimination" refers to consciousness, while "seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing" refer to the faculties;
that is to say, it refers to the seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing produced by discrimination.

These, together with the previous five great elements, are collectively termed the seven great elements; whereas the former [five] involve the convergence of characteristics into the faculty of seeing, these [seven] involve the convergence of both characteristics and seeing, which are all ultimately subsumed within consciousness.
As for your mind being coarse and floating, I sternly rebuke you for its superficial and frivolous application, for it refuses to penetrate deeply;
because it does not penetrate deeply, you do not realize that the consciousnesses produced by the six sense organs are [empty].

Tathāgata-garbha, you should observe whether the six sense bases, consciousness, and mind are the same or different, empty or existent, neither the same nor different, neither empty nor existent. If they were the same, they should not oppose one another within;
if they were different, they should not be mutually cognizant within their nature; if they were empty, they should not manifest present discrimination; if they were existent...
One should not understand this as being traceless or as conforming to the four propositions; rather, one should know it is the opposite of these.

As for your previous statement that you did not originally know—claiming that I previously refuted the absence of substance while you were startled and ignorant—I have now repeatedly revealed this to you, yet you still do not understand your original nature.
This is the height of your ignorance. That which is clearly known by the nature-consciousness is the true consciousness of enlightened clarity.
To speak of the treasury of original nature is precisely this wondrously luminous awareness; the clarity of fundamental enlightenment is precisely this consciousness of the true nature.
That which you previously identified as the enlightened nature—tranquil, pervasive throughout the ten directions, and not subject to arising or ceasing—is this very thing.
How could it be the mind-consciousness that you previously took to be the knowing heart? It is that which contains and exhales the ten voids.
"Containing" has the meaning of "receiving," and "emitting" has the meaning of "pervading everywhere. The "ten voids" refer to the empty space of the ten directions.
Since its essence is such as this, how could it have a specific location? Yet you, on the contrary, cling to the idea that it exists within the physical body;
you do not realize that what exists within the physical body is the essence manifested according to karma, and not the true essence. (Volume One, Section Seven)

In the section on "The Locations of the Mind," each paragraph concludes by stating, "There is no such possibility. In the fourfold classification of phenomena, each paragraph concludes by stating, "There is no location.
In the text on the seven elements, every paragraph asks, "How could there be a specific place?

All of these are branches and leaves that have issued forth from the single fundamental root: the phrase "the locus of the mind and eyes. This is because Ānanda had been identifying [the self] in every single instance.

Because there is a location, the World-Honored One’s Dharma involves the refutation of dharmas; subsequently, the World-Honored One spoke of the establishment of a locus through the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*), so that one may know the place where that which is established resides.
Once the locus has flowed away and been lost, one then knows the method for removing what is established.
The single word "locus" (*so*) is truly the great pivot between delusion and enlightenment.

At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the subtle and wondrous instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata, found their bodies and minds completely cleared away, attaining freedom from all obstructions.
Each member of the assembly realized for themselves that the mind pervades the ten directions;
they perceived the emptiness of the ten directions as clearly as looking at a leaf held in one’s hand, and saw that all things existing throughout every world are themselves Bodhi.
The wondrously luminous original mind is the essence of the mind, all-pervasive and perfect, encompassing the ten directions.
When you turn back to observe the body born of your parents, it is like a single mote of dust blown into the void of those ten directions—its existence and disappearance uncertain;

or like a single bubble floating upon a vast, tranquil ocean, arising and ceasing without trace. Thus, with clear self-knowledge, you attain the fundamental wondrous mind, which is eternally abiding and imperishable.
Prostrating to the Buddha with palms joined, he attained what he had never experienced before and spoke verses in the presence of the Tathāgata to praise the Buddha.
This describes his awakening. Regarding the "subtle and wondrous revelation": after the World-Honored One had broken through Ānanda’s mind, Ānanda asked, "What is my true nature?
The World-Honored One then used the "seeing-essence" (*jien-jing*) as a basis to provide illumination; thus, this marks the starting point of the journey.
At the very beginning, it was said: "The nature you see is all-pervasive; if it is not you, then who is?

Because of this single statement, some have mistaken the physical form for the seeing, while others have mistaken the seeing for the form; thus, various confusions and delusions arose, leaving them unsettled.
Therefore, the World-Honored One showed them, saying: "This seeing and its objects are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi. Ānanda, by means of this...
He then proceeded to identify this nature of seeing as the wondrous enlightened nature, and thus realized:
"Truly, as the Dharma King has said, the awareness that pervades the ten directions is a tranquil, eternally abiding nature, not subject to arising or ceasing.
When the World-Honored One saw that he had identified it as the true [nature], He further said: "At the moment of seeing the seeing, that seeing is not seeing. The former sages...
"What I mean is: if you have a staff, I give you a staff; if you have no staff, I take away your staff.
Because Ānanda was thereby even more deeply bewildered and distressed, the World-Honored One further showed him, saying:
"This vision still belongs to the karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*). If, amidst the revolving wheel of karma, one can distance oneself from the conjunction [of conditions], then..."

When the conditions for conjunction cease, the causes of birth and death are further eliminated, and the nature of Bodhi—which is beyond arising and ceasing—the pure fundamental mind, and original enlightenment, abide eternally.
At this point, Ānanda already knows that the nature of seeing is false and that wondrous enlightenment is true; yet he does not know where this nature of wondrous enlightenment ultimately resides.

The World-Honored One, fearing that [the assembly] might abandon the water to seek the waves or discard the image to search for the mirror, did not wait for their request but further instructed them, saying:
"Do you suppose that the seeing-essence (*darśana-tattva*) which I previously refuted is unreal, while the wondrous enlightened nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* is real?
Yet, if you wish to recognize this wondrous enlightened nature, you must not abandon seeing and hearing."

Because he has realized the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus), [the Buddha] further points out that each and every one of these aggregates, bases, and elements is the Tathāgatagarbha and each pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
Thus, from the manifestation of the earth element up to the consciousness element, the wondrous enlightenment is profoundly still and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm;
it was at this point that Ānanda suddenly attained awakening. Therefore, one knows that Ānanda—

The realization of this difficulty truly originated from the single phrase "the Tathāgata’s vision of nature is all-pervasive," which served as the catalyst for the sincere conviction that "awareness-conditions pervade the ten directions.

Because of this one conviction, the World-Honored One employed various indirect methods—striking here and there—to pry open the gateway to enlightenment; thus, one arrives at the state of wondrous enlightenment, serene and all-pervasive.
Suddenly, while discussing with Ānanda, the old master’s grasp of the essential pivot caused him to start up in a leap without even realizing it;

was this not a subtle and profound revelation? Although the second fascicle describes the state of awakening as one where body and mind are "vastly serene" (tài rán) and free from obstruction, there still remain many doubts and hindrances; therefore, [the Master] explains each point in detail until—
This means that one attains great non-obstruction throughout all points of contact. The following section correctly describes the locus of awakening;

each person individually knows that their own mind pervades the ten directions. This is a summary statement indicating that the wondrous enlightenment is profoundly still and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, encompassing and expelling the ten voids.
The phrase "knows by oneself" is intended to reveal that until now, one has merely relied upon the Buddha’s words.
Knowing is not knowing by itself; only now does one personally accept and have self-confidence, no longer shifting according to the verbal influence of others.
Previously, the scope of vision was limited to the first dhyāna; now, the emptiness of the ten directions is seen as clearly as looking at a leaf in the palm of one's hand.
Previously, one was turned by objects, distinguishing large from small, seeing expansion and contraction, and identifying with what was seen.
Formerly, you took objects for yourself and mistook those objects for your vision, remaining in a state of confusion and instability;
now, you see that all things in the world are fundamentally one perfectly integrated, pure, and enlightened jewel-awareness, with not a single thing acting as an obstruction or a barrier.
Previously, you took this dark and turbulent state to be the nature of your mind, and were certain that it was located within the physical body. Now...
Thus, you have already realized that the essence of mind is all-pervasive and perfect, encompassing and enveloping the ten directions.

Looking back at the body born of your parents, it is like a single speck of dust in space or a single bubble in the ocean; you no longer abandon the ocean to identify with the bubble, nor do you mistake the bubble for the ocean.
Previously, you did not know the destination of the true limit, you did not know the nature of the quiescent and eternal mind, and you did not know the relationship between body and mind.
"In my state of perversion, I did not know that the nature of seeing is the mind; I did not know that the aggregates, bases, and elements are the Tathāgatagarbha;
and I did not know that the seven elements pervade the entire Dharma-realm. Now, I know each of these for myself, without the slightest doubt.
Previously, the World-Honored One revealed to me the precious, luminous, and wondrous nature, which is fundamentally perfect, eternal, and abiding."

"In the past, I merely obtained this mind but did not dare to recognize it; now, having obtained the fundamental, wondrous mind that is eternally abiding and imperishable, there is no need for recognition.
This is precisely the moment when Ānanda let out a cry of exertion (*ālaṃbha*)—the point where one lets go from the precipice.
It is what is called: 'When the scale-weights reach the very tip of the branch, suddenly they are driven down and perform a somersault.'"
Therefore, in the following passage, he immediately speaks a verse in praise of the Buddha based on what he has seen and realized:
"O Wondrous, Profound, All-Holding, Immovable Honored One, King of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, rare in the world!

Eradicate my inverted thoughts of billions of kalpas, And grant that I may attain the Dharma-body without passing through the aeons of saṃgha. May I now attain the fruit and become a Treasure King, Returning to deliver as many beings as there are sands in the Ganges."

We, the assembly of śrāvakas, with this profound resolve, shall serve every land as numerous as atoms; this is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness. We humbly entreat the World-Honored One to bear witness:
we vow to enter first into the evil world of the five turbidities; until not even a single sentient being has attained Buddhahood, we shall never enter nirvāṇa here.

O Great Hero, of Great Power and Great Compassion, we pray that you will further examine and eliminate our subtle delusions, so as to enable us— (The text continues: ...to attain the supreme fruit of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.)

"May you swiftly ascend to unsurpassed enlightenment and sit at the site of awakening throughout the worlds of the ten directions. Though the nature of *śūnyatā* (voidness) may perish, the *śaṅkha-śilā* (adamantine) mind shall never waver.
Thus, Ānanda, having realized that the seven elements are all-pervasive, he consequently awakened to the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa shown by the Tathāgata.
The Śūraṅgama King is precisely the three contemplations within the one mind. To abide amidst all phenomena without being defiled is called "wondrously profound" (*miao-zhan*);
to abide amidst all phenomena without losing them is called "total retention" (*zongchi*).

To remain unchanging while following conditions among all phenomena, and to follow conditions while remaining unchanging, is called "immovable. Because it is wondrously profound, it is called "pure"; because it is all-pervasive, it is called "total."

Because it is maintained through its original nature, it is called "immovable. That which is called "pure" is precisely the luminous essence of intrinsic purity mentioned in the preceding text—the fundamentally pure essence of Bodhi and Nirvana, which is originally the wondrously pure and luminous essence of Bodhi.
As stated in the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra*: "When one body is pure, many bodies are pure; even unto all sentient beings throughout the ten directions."
The purity of Perfect Enlightenment (Vimala-bodhi) is precisely this; it corresponds to the meaning of *śamatha*.
That which is called "total retention" (*dhāraṇī*) is the wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind mentioned in the preceding text;

it is the Great *Dhāraṇī*, the Tathāgatagarbha, and what is termed Perfect Enlightenment—the sense organs, objects, and the four great elements, extending even to the *dhāraṇī* that pervades the entire Dharma-realm.

This corresponds to the meaning of *samāpatti* (meditative attainment), specifically that which is called "original suchness. This refers to the "ever-abiding true mind" mentioned in the preceding text;
it is unshakable true *tathatā*, it is the true mark (*dharmatā*), and it is perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). It is like space—thus equal and unshakable.
One should know that this is the equality and immovability of the nature of awakening (*bodhi-svabhāva*). This corresponds to *dhyāna* (meditation).

Because the Tathāgata has realized the nature of these seven great elements and the essence of the three contemplations, the world designates him as the "Wondrously Profound, Total-Holding, Immovable Honored One";
this does not mean he is called "Honored One" merely on account of his thirty-two marks.
Furthermore, because he attains a body of ultimate solidity precisely through the illusory and false, he is also designated as "Śūraṅgama."
King Bimbisāra is not renowned as a king merely for his conquest of worldly realms; rather, this is the most supreme, rare, and extraordinary matter of both the mundane and supramundane worlds.
Previously, I did not understand it, yet upon seeing the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks and his radiant physical form, I conceived thoughts of wonder and thoughts of rarity.
Today, I finally realize the rarity and extraordinariness of the World-Honored One.

It does not reside in the thirty-two marks. Previously, you took that which discriminates objects through conditions—arising and perishing moment by moment—to be the pure mind, without knowing that the wondrously profound essence is the pure mind.

Previously, you took the body to be the locus of total retention and held that the mind dwells within the body, without knowing that the essence of the mind is all-pervasive and perfect, encompassing and enveloping the ten directions.

This is what constitutes dhāraṇī. Previously, you took the aggregates, sense bases, and elements to be the nature of arising and ceasing, and the earth, water, fire, and wind to be the nature of transformation;
you did not know that these are in fact the immovable, all-pervading, wondrous nature of True Suchness.
All of this was formerly your inverted, deluded thoughts, which the Tathāgata today reveals to you one by one in minute detail.

To eliminate at once these deluded thoughts of inverted views accumulated over billions of kalpas, so that I need not laboriously pass through three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas to behold the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Dharmakāya of equality—how fortunate I am!
This is what is meant by "having crossed the bridge and walking upon the bank, one suddenly realizes one's entire body is soaked in mud and water. [He] asked Pó.

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that after practicing the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) for three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and planting the causes for the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) during one hundred kalpas,

one subsequently attains the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcadharmakāya*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Consciousness-Only) school maintains that one passes through one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* from the stages prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*),

another *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* from the first ground (*prathamabhūmi*) to the eighth ground (*aṣṭamabhūmi*), and yet another *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* from the ninth ground (*navamabhūmi*) to the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*), after which one attains the ultimate state.
Question: Why is it said here that the Dharmakāya does not pass through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*? Answer: That [teaching] concerns gradual cultivation, whereas this concerns sudden enlightenment.

Speaking in terms of gradual cultivation, one proceeds from the minute to the manifest, passing through the stages of confidence (*adhimukti*), abiding (*sthiti*), practice (*caryā*), and direction (*pratipatti*), until reaching Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) before finally realizing the ultimate fruit.
Speaking in terms of the sudden, however, in a single thought-moment there is no arising, and the boundaries of past and future are severed.
To be named "Buddha" immediately means that one does not even enter the gradations of stages and positions, let alone traverse the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

Long ago, the butcher Pāṇḍaraka went before the Buddha’s seat, and his ignorance was instantly extinguished; he then set down his knife and said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, I am counted among the thousand Buddhas.
The Buddha then confirmed this for him. Indeed, by the butcher Pāṇḍaraka laying down his butcher's blade, his ignorance—
Suddenly ceasing [the cycle of rebirth], you are now numbered among the thousand Buddhas; that your joy is such and your Dharma-eye is clear and bright is indeed worthy of the words [of the Buddha].

However, although your awakening is that of a Buddha, your meritorious practice has not yet reached the ultimate fruit; therefore, it is not mentioned that you possess the fivefold body or have attained finality.
I pray that you will now descend once more and make great vows, so that when I have not yet seen the Great Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa...

In times past, when I perceived the Dharma-body as something impartial, I thought to myself that only the Buddha alone had attained the nature of awakening, while all sentient beings were entirely excluded from it;
thus, I did not seek the path of Buddhahood above nor did I deliver sentient beings below.
Today I have come to know that Buddhas and sentient beings are equal and non-dual; therefore, I vow to seek the fruit of Buddhahood and I also vow to deliver all beings.
Since the World-Honored One has already used various skillful means to explain this in detail and with precision,
enabling me to perceive this Dharma of equality, such profound kindness is truly difficult to repay. Now, by preparing these two kinds of deep resolve—

to serve Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field above, and to deliver sentient beings as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field below— I am thus able to repay that which is difficult to repay.
To repay this profound kindness is what is called a true dragon finding water, which immediately knows how to stir up waves and create billows.

I humbly entreat you to further clarify your vow to deliver sentient beings: because Ānanda was fearful of these five turbidities during the assembly at the Lotus Sūtra and his heart harbored flattery and crookedness, making him unfit for transformation, he made a vow to uphold the sūtra in a foreign land; now that we see [the time has come]... [he has returned].
Because he re-awakens the great vows of the Dharmakāya, he pledges to enter first into this world of the five turbidities and deliver all sentient beings before entering parinirvāṇa;
this also carries the meaning of "changing the jade and changing the steps. *Nirvāṇa* (泥洹) here means "extinction and transcendence" (滅度).
Below, the Great Hero clarifies his vow to seek Buddhahood, stating that he shall cast off the heavy obstructions of ignorance; thus it is called "Great" (大).
To uproot the deep-seated roots of delusion and karma is called "Great Power"; to bestow upon sentient beings the bliss of the two types of cessation is called "Great Loving-kindness";
and to extract from sentient beings the suffering of the two types of death is called "Great Compassion. Regarding the request to further examine and eliminate subtle delusions, it means:

although my coarse delusions have been removed, there remain the accumulated latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) from beginningless lifetimes within the root-consciousness, as well as various forms of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Since the enumeration of these portions has not yet been exhaustive, I hope that the World-Honored One, who possesses great heroism, great power, and great compassion, will secretly bestow his protection to thoroughly eliminate subtle delusions, so that my five stages of dwelling may be fully exhausted and the two deaths forever extinguished.

Only when I have quickly attained perfect enlightenment and universally sat upon the site of awakening shall I finally achieve complete mastery. [This concludes the section on Śunyata. Below, the summary is completed.
*Śūnyatā* (śunyata) is translated here as "emptiness" (*kōng*); *akṣara* (śuokajia-lo) is translated as "indestructible" (*jiāngù*), which refers to the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*).
This means that while emptiness has no substance and cannot perish—or even if it could perish—my adamantine and indestructible mind shall never be turned back.
This expresses the sense that while empty space may come to an end, my vow shall be inexhaustible.
The above may be considered equivalent to the "Contemplation of the Non-obstruction between Emptiness and Form" within the *Dharmadhātu-āloka* (Contemplation of the Dharma-realm).
