At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra rose from his seat amidst the great assembly;
he bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue, you have skillfully expounded for the sake of sentient beings the Tathāgata’s ultimate truth. World-Honored One, among those who preach the Dharma, you have always commended me."

I am now foremost among those who have heard the Tathāgata’s subtle and wondrous Dharma-sound, yet it is like a deaf person standing more than a hundred paces away listening for the sound of a mosquito;

what they cannot even see, how much less can they hear? Although the Buddha has proclaimed this clearly to remove my delusions, I still do not fully comprehend the ultimate meaning of these principles and have not yet reached the ground of freedom from doubt. World-Honored One, although those such as Ānanda have been enlightened...
Although we who have awakened to the practice and eliminated the outflows have attained the state of being free from outflows within this assembly, and though we have exhausted all taints,
we still harbor lingering doubts and regrets upon hearing the Dharma-sound preached by the Tathāgata. World-Honored One, if all the world’s sense organs,
objects, aggregates, bases, and elements are the Tathāgata-garbha, pure and fundamental from the beginning, how could mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
The characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) succeed one another in a continuous flow, ending and beginning again.

Furthermore, as the Tathāgata has taught, the essential natures of earth, water, fire, and wind are perfectly interfused, pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*, tranquil and eternally abiding. World-Honored One, if the nature of earth were all-pervasive, how could it accommodate water?
If the nature of water were all-pervasive, fire would not arise. Moreover, how can it be explained that the two natures of water and fire both pervade empty space?
"World-Honored One, space does not obstruct or extinguish the earth-nature, yet the nature of the earth is obstructive while space-nature is void and pervasive.

How is it that both are equally omnipresent throughout the Dharma-realm, yet I do not know the meaning of their mutual course? I only pray that the Tathāgata will flow forth his great compassion, dispel the clouds of delusion from me and this great assembly.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, thirsting for the Tathāgata’s [teaching].
The above is the compassionate instruction.

Below this, Pūrṇa-maitrāyaṇīputra, having heard that the three categories and the seven elements are all the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha, clung to the nature as being difficult to reconcile with its manifestations, thereby raising two questions.
Pūrṇa’s rank had already reached that of an Arhat; he had already severed the afflictions of views and thoughts and had already shattered [the obstacles].
Although he had already realized the emptiness of persons through the destruction of self-grasping, his ignorance regarding the grasping of dharmas remained;

he did not yet understand that total phenomena are nature, nor did he know the source from which the myriad dharmas arise. He was unaware that total nature is form, and thus failed to comprehend why the seven elements are all-pervasive.

Therefore, he raised these questions according to his capacity. Yet, it was necessary to wait for Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, for Ānanda— (Note: The final sentence appears to be an incomplete thought or commentary on the role of Ānanda, suggesting he required the guidance of another to fully realize the teaching.)

That Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra stands foremost in extensive learning and Śāriputra precedes all in preaching the Dharma is because both are renowned as "Tigers of Meaning" (*arthavyākaraṇa-vyāghra*) for their prowess.
As for "Great Majestic Virtue" (*mahātejas*), it is called "majesty" (*tejas*) because he possesses great heroism and power to uproot the deluded roots of others;

it is called "virtue" (*guṇa*) because he possesses great kindness and compassion to guide others toward the gateway of awakening. He skillfully expounds [the Dharma] for the sake of sentient beings...

Those who come to the primary truth (paramārtha-satya) correctly comprehend that the three categories are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, and that the seven elements pervade the entire Dharma-realm;
these are all the Dharma-gates of the Tathāgata’s self-realization, which are extremely difficult to express in words.

Yet, the Tathāgata, out of compassion for human sentiments, has revealed them clearly at every turn, enabling sentient beings to skillfully employ their own minds and thereby attain awakening and entry. Therefore it is said:
It is well said; yet this principle of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is exceedingly profound and subtle, making it extremely difficult to conceive or realize.

Even though the World-Honored One has designated me as the foremost among those who preach the Dharma, now that I hear the Tathāgata’s subtle and wondrous sound of the Dharma, it is like a deaf person trying to listen for the sound of a mosquito from over a hundred paces away—what is more, it is something I have never seen before. How could I possibly [comprehend it]?
"Can one hear its sound? That 'not seeing' and 'not hearing' merely describe the subtle and wondrous nature of the Dharma-sound.
As Liezi said: "Between the banks of the Yangtze River there lives a small insect called the *jiaoming*. It flies in swarms and alights upon the eyelashes of a mosquito;
whether it settles, stays, or departs, the mosquito is not aware of it. Even Li Zhu, when he wiped away the film from his eyes and gazed at it, could not see it."
As for its form, even when Shi Kuang bowed his head and listened, he could not hear its sound;

yet when the Yellow Emperor dwelt with Rongchengzi atop Mount Kongtong, their minds were extinguished and their bodies stilled. Slowly, through the vision of the spirit, he saw it as a solid mass like the form of Mount Tai;
slowly, through the hearing of the vital breath, he heard it as a roar like the sound of thunder. It was thus.
"Venerable Sir, although the Buddha has clearly proclaimed this Dharma for us, enabling us to eliminate our doubts, we are ultimately unable to enter the state beyond doubt.
Furthermore, although Ānanda and the others have attained awakening, the habitual tendencies accumulated since beginningless time within their faculties remain entirely intact;
their doubts are still as they were. This is certainly the case even for those among us who are already in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*)."

"If even those who have realized that all outflows (*āsrava*) are eliminated still harbor lingering doubts and regrets, how much more so for those who have not yet attained the state of being without outflows?
Below this, the World-Honored One first restates the three categories [of phenomena] to present the doubt: since it is said that they are "pure," they should not suddenly give rise to defilement;
and since the realms of the vessel-world, the faculties of the body, and the fruits of karma are said to be "primordial" (*banyan*), they should not have continued in succession from kalpas past.

The severance [of delusion] is like the world undergoing formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness, or sentient beings undergoing birth, aging, sickness, death, and the cyclical recurrence of karmic fruition.
Furthermore, as will be detailed below when citing the seven elements to raise a doubt:

if it is claimed that the natures of the seven elements are each perfectly interfused and pervade the Dharma-realm, then earth should be able to overcome water, and earth and water would not be in harmony.
Water and fire are mutually incompatible; how could water and fire coexist? Their natures as pervasive or obstructive are each distinct;
how then could earth and space encompass one another? Therefore, I do not know where this principle leads.

These two questions constitute, respectively, a challenge based on contradiction with the sacred teachings and a challenge based on contradiction with worldly consensus. I only pray that you will graciously remove [this doubt].
The phrase "clouds of doubt" is used because these two types of doubt can obstruct the sky of the *dharmatā*.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇa and all the Arhats in the assembly whose outflows were exhausted and who were beyond training:
"Today, for the sake of this entire assembly, the Tathāgata shall proclaim the true ultimate nature within the ultimate truth, so that you in this assembly..."

“Those śrāvakas of fixed nature, as well as all those arhats who have not yet attained the two kinds of emptiness and have turned toward the Mahāyāna, shall all obtain the ground of the cessation of the One Vehicle—the true araṇya, the place of correct practice.
Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you. Pūrṇa and the others, revering the Buddha’s voice of Dharma, listened in silence.

This is the position of the proponents [of this school]. Regarding the nature of the ultimate truth within the ultimate sense, the Dharmalakṣaṇa school (Yogācāra) asserts that there are four types of ultimate truth:
first, the aggregates, bases, and elements as the conventional ultimate; second, the Four Noble Truths as the logical ultimate;
third, emptiness and suchness as the ultimate of realization; and fourth, the single true dharma-realm as the ultimate of ultimates. Among these...

The "Manifest" refers to the ultimate ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Those with the faculty of intermediate capacity who have exhausted the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*) and attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) are [the Manifest].

Those Śrāvakas of fixed nature with inferior capacity are [also the Manifest]. Those of superior capacity who, though not yet having attained the two emptinesses (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), turn toward the Mahāyāna are [the Manifest].

As for the two emptinesses, they are the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*): one who attains the emptiness of persons knows that sentient beings lack intrinsic nature; one who attains the emptiness of phenomena knows all dharmas [to be empty].
There is no inherent nature; the One Vehicle is precisely the Buddha-vehicle. The site of quiescent extinction is precisely the Great Ocean of Quiescent Extinction.
Āraṇya is also called araṇya; this is translated as "free from clamor and contention," or "a place of leisure and stillness.

Because both person and phenomena are empty, it is named the "true freedom from clamor and contention" and the "true place of leisure and stillness," which refers specifically to the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
Quiescent concentration is the ground for the practitioner to settle the mind and the place of true cultivation.
Apart from this One Vehicle, all else are merely bypaths and detours, not called true cultivation.

The provisional teachings state that śrāvakas of fixed nature and icchantikas who lack the seed-nature cannot attain Buddhahood, being like scorched sprouts or withered seeds; now, they all return to the One.
Only when one rides upon ultimate *nirvāṇa* and shall become a Buddha will the discourse on the supreme pinnacle of the Mahāyāna be fully exhausted;
therefore, it is called "correct cultivation. As the *Dharmarāja-sūtra* states: "If one determines the faculties [of a person] to be those of the Hīnayāna, one preaches the Hīnayāna Dharma for them;
if they are *icchantikas*, one preaches the dharma of the *icchantika*. This is to sever the Buddha-nature and to destroy the Buddha-body; such is the preaching of the Dharma."
A person may pass through hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas and fall into various hells. Why is this?

Because the nature of sentient beings is itself the Dharma-nature (dharmatā), which from the very beginning has neither increase nor decrease. Therefore, one should know that all phenomena (dharmas) are the Buddha-dharma, and all natures are the Buddha-nature (buddhadhātu).
The Buddha said, “Pūrṇa, as you have said, it is pure and fundamental by nature; how could mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
Have you not always heard the Tathāgata proclaim that the nature of awakening is wondrously luminous, and that fundamental awakening is luminously wondrous?
Pūrṇa replied, “Indeed, World-Honored One, I have always heard the Buddha proclaim this meaning. The Buddha said, “You refer to the luminosity of awakening as—”
"Furthermore, the clarity of the nature is called 'Awakening' (*bodhi*); when this awakening is not clear, it is called 'luminous awakening' (*prabhāsvara-bodhi*.
Pūrṇa said, "If this lack of clarity is what is called 'awakening,' then there would be nothing that is luminous. The Buddha said, "If there were nothing luminous, then there would be no awakening.

That which has something [to illuminate] is not awakening; that which has nothing [to illuminate] is not luminosity. Furthermore, this lack of luminosity is not the nature of profound clarity. This nature is necessarily awakened."

Taking delusion as clarity is what constitutes enlightened awareness; yet this awareness is not something that can be made clear. Because there is clarity, an object is established; once that object has been falsely established, your false subjectivity arises.
Within that which is neither identical nor different, a blazing diversity is formed. Based on that diversity of objects, identity is established;
and based on the manifestation of both identity and difference, one further establishes neither-identity-nor-difference.

From here below, the text elucidates how the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) of persons manifest according to their karma, such that the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*) fully constitutes phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*);
this serves as the answer to the question regarding the sudden arising of mountains, rivers, and the great earth.

The Venerable One has established this point of inquiry like one who has pulled out a sticky lacquer pot from the midst of a thicket of brambles, leaving people unable to move or turn; the World-Honored One is all-encompassing.
The wise man knew that the Venerable One still clung to causes and conditions and had not yet forgotten his attachment to dharmas;

thus, being unable to penetrate the principle that "inherent nature is the awakening to true emptiness, and inherent emptiness is the awakening to true nature," he took the previously spoken Dharma as a mere shadow on a deep pole and questioned him, saying:
"According to what you have asked, it is originally pure and tranquil; how then did the mountains suddenly arise?"

"Rivers, the great earth, and so forth—have you not always heard what I have previously taught in this Dharma assembly regarding the wondrous clarity of the nature-awakening (*prakṛti-bodhi*) and the luminous wonder of fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*)?
When I speak of the 'wondrous clarity of the nature-awakening,' I mean that the substance of the nature-awakening is fundamentally wondrous and eternally luminous;
it does not possess its wondrousness by virtue of being illuminated. This is what is meant by the 'luminous wonder of fundamental awakening.'"
This refers to the function of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), which is inherently luminous and eternally wondrous—not something that becomes luminous by virtue of being wondrous.

When Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra was caught on the World-Honored One’s single hook, he immediately responded, saying, "I have often heard the Buddha proclaim this meaning," for he did not realize his nostrils were already in the World-Honored One's hand;
thus, the Master again opened both gates simultaneously to examine him further.
He said: "Since you have heard that this nature-awareness is wondrously luminous and that fundamental awareness is luminously wondrous, how do you understand this in your mind?

Is it that the essence of nature-awareness's wondrous luminosity is like a bright mirror, which is luminous from the beginning and does not require external illumination to be luminous, and is therefore called 'nature-awareness wondrously luminous'? Or is it that the essence of awareness is fundamentally not luminous..."
A mirror having dust and grime must rely upon brightness to illuminate it; is this therefore called the "awareness that is illuminated"?

One [aspect] is the meaning of the fundamental nature (*tathatā*), while the other is the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Venerable sir, you find it difficult to forget what you are accustomed to;

thus, you remain entirely fallen into the pit of causal conditions and intellectual views (*jñāna-dṛṣṭi*). Unconsciously, you recognize brightness as the subject and fall into the realm of the object. Therefore, it is said: "If one..."
If one defines "awakening" (jue) as that which is luminous without depending on illumination, then there would be no awakening that lacks something to be illuminated.
The implication is that one must depend on illumination to illuminate, and only when there is something to be illuminated can it be called awakening;

thus, it is certainly not the case that one is called awakened while lacking anything to be illuminated—it must be that one is called awakened because there is something to be illuminated. How could one know that as soon as one posits an object...
If one understands this as falling into the causal conditions of arising and ceasing, then that cognitive vision is no longer the fundamentally pure and original awakened nature.

Therefore, the World-Honored One said to him: "If you say that when there is nothing, there is no ignorance, then must the wondrously luminous nature of awakening necessarily exist only when there is something, and only when there is illumination, does the wondrously luminous nature of awakening exist? Thus it is said: "If there is no illumination..."
How could the awakening of ignorance know the nature of awakening? This wondrous clarity of the nature of awakening can neither be designated as "having" nor can it be designated as "not having.
If it were "having," it would not be the nature of awakening;
if it were "not having," it would not be wondrously clear. Therefore, it can neither be designated as "not having" nor can it be designated as "having."
Because of non-illumination, one falls into a state of dark confusion and silent oblivion; because of illumination, one falls into a state of brilliant clarity and spiritual alertness.

Therefore, if you now identify this faculty of awareness as being necessarily "bright," then by this very thought, you will obscure the essence of the wondrous clarity of the nature-awareness, the fundamental clarity and wondrousness of original enlightenment, and the pure, original substance, thereby producing ignorance and the karmic consciousness of delusion.
Because that which is fundamentally not the object of illumination is forcibly established as an object of illumination, one falsely creates a conscious awareness.
As the former masters have said, "One who wishes to clarify the affairs of today darkens the person of original nature.
Therefore, it is shown that the essence of the wondrously clear and inherently pure awakened nature does not belong to any "so" (that which it is); thus, it is nowhere yet is everywhere.
Therefore, it does not belong to clarity, for while there is ignorance, there is no lack of clarity; thus it is said that awakening is not something to be clarified.
Now, within the state of pure nature-awakening, you recognize this nature-awakening as necessarily being clarity.

This very thought-moment of "necessarily being clarity" immediately transforms the nature-awakening—which has no location—into the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), just like [the reflection of] a jar within [a mirror].
Because emptiness would otherwise fall into spatial location, it is said that "by relying on clarity, a locus is established.

Once it has fallen into spatial location, it further transforms this great light of wisdom into the "seeing-portion" (darśana-bhāga), which is the faculty of seeing; thus it is said that "once the locus is falsely established, your false capacity arises.
Since the seeing-portion already exists, it further takes the ultimate reality of the principle—neither identical nor different—and transforms it into the "object-portion" (nimitta-bhāga).

Consequently, various distinctions arise; thus it is said that within the absence of identity or difference, differentiation is fiercely established. Therefore, the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) states:
"The initial lack of awakening suddenly stirs the mind, becoming the cause for the formation of the *karmic consciousness*. This is due to the fault of 'awakened clarity.

Because of this clarity, an objective realm is established, and the 'perceiving portion' (*darśana-bhāga*) suddenly arises. Following this perception, the 'object-portion' (*nimitta-bhāga*) is established and arrayed. This refers to such differentiation.
Regarding "that which is different" (*so-yi*), the first character "different" (*yi*) refers to the "difference" (*yi*) in the phrase "blazingly becoming different" (*chi-ran ch'eng-yi*);
"that which is different" (*so-yi*) refers to the character "different" (*so*) in the phrase "establishing the locus through cause-and-reasoning" (*yin-ming li-so*).

This means that this "difference" in "blazingly becoming different" is further different from that "different" in "establishing the locus through cause-and-reasoning. This is because the difference in "establishing the locus" is explained in terms of a single thought-moment.
The blazing intensity encompasses a vast range of differences; because difference is established based on identity, identity itself is also difference.
Because identity-and-difference are established based on identity and difference, the absence of both identity and difference is itself a form of difference.
This is because the karmic fruits of the world and its sentient beings are all contained within this character for "difference" (yi), and thus it differs from the "differences" previously mentioned.
Thus, through mutual disturbance and opposition, weariness arises; as this weariness persists for a long time, dust is stirred up, and their own characteristics become turbid.
From this, worldly toil and affliction are incited. What arises becomes the world, while stillness forms empty space. Is empty space the same as the world, or is it different?
There is no truly existent dharma of conditioned arising that is either identical to or different from that [mind].
This restates the preceding reason—that the three subtle states arise from ignorance—and further points out that the three subtle states give rise to the six coarse states.
That is to say, all these various disturbances mentioned above stem from the pure awakened mind due to its engagement with illumination.
In a single thought-moment, it arises as the evolving consciousness (*karmavijñāna*), transforms into the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), and splits into the perceived-object-part (*nimitta-bhāga*).

Therefore, it is said that they arise in mutual dependence and give rise to weariness. When this weariness persists for a long time, it gives rise to the dust of affliction; the "seeing" is the seeing-part, and the "dust" is the perceived-object-part.
All such things are the turbidity of its own characteristics; they are not made turbid by external objects. Thus, he concludes.
It says: "From this, the dust-labor of afflictions is aroused. The two characters "from this" (yousi) refer to the initial single thought of ignorance (*avidyā*).
"Dust-labor" (*chenlao*) refers to the two divisions of the perceived aspect (*xiangfen*) and the perceiving aspect (*jianfen*). "Afflictions" (*fan'nao*) refers to the six coarse states (*liuchu*).

This clarifies that through the principle of cause-and-effect, this single thought not only arouses the three subtle states (*sanshi*), but the various marks of the six coarse afflictions likewise arise from it.
Because it arises, he brings forth the two characters "afflictions" (*kleśa*) to highlight them, and in the subsequent text, he explicitly demonstrates this, saying:
"When you previously asked me how the various conditioned phenomena of mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise, they do not exist within your pure mind;
rather, they abruptly emerge from a single moment of recognition. This very moment of recognition is the sudden arising of the world."—Master Yuan.
This refers to how a single atom, when encountering the realm of motion, manifests the appearance of this collapsing mountain;
it is just as when you, in a single thought-moment, recognize [the mind] as "bright," causing the pure, awakened mind to suddenly become dark and obscured—this is stillness becoming empty space.
Regarding what was previously stated about establishing the "same" based on the "different": the "different" is the world, and the "same" is empty space, for empty space is non-dual.
Therefore, it is said that they are "the same" because they share the world; it is said that they are "different" because of their distinctions.
What was previously described as being "neither the same nor different" refers to the nature of neither sameness nor difference which is primordially non-existent. This realization is the void.

Once the world has already been formed, that which is subsequently established—namely, the karmic fruits of sentient beings and the six coarse aspects of all conditioned phenomena—is what is meant here.
The reason why the karmic fruits of sentient beings are neither identical nor different is that there are no sentient beings apart from karmic fruits, and no karmic fruits apart from sentient beings;

thus they are not different. Yet, because sentient beings are the agents who create and experience karmic fruits, while karmic fruits are that which is created and experienced, they are not identical.
Therefore, one should know that as soon as a single thought arises, ten thousand [phenomena] follow.
When all dharmas are complete, one knows that within a single thought-moment there is no arising, yet the myriad practices are fully present.
Formerly, a monk asked Master Langya Huijue, "The fundamental nature is pure and still; how is it that mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
Huijue replied with a stern voice, "The fundamental nature is pure and still; how is it that mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? Furthermore, another monk asked Master Xuan...

Chan Master Ting asked, "What is dependent origination within the true nature? The Master replied, "Virtuous One, the very moment you give rise to a single thought is dependent origination within the true nature.
This further reveals how the Tathāgatas and the Patriarchs each employ their own skillful means to guide and save sentient beings.
The clarity of awareness and the dullness of emptiness interact to produce agitation; thus, there is a wind-circle that sustains the world.

From emptiness arises agitation, and from the firmness of clarity arises obstruction. As for those precious metals, they arise because the clarity of awareness establishes solidity; thus, there is a gold-circle that maintains the lands.
When solid awareness forms the metal and agitated clarity produces the wind, the wind and metal rub against each other, giving rise to the fire-element, which serves as the nature of transformation.
Because the brilliance of the jewels produces moisture and the fiery light steams upward, there is a water-circle that contains the worlds of the ten directions.
The previous [explanation] answered the sudden arising based on the initial moment of ignorance; this answers the continuity based on the two types of ignorance—arousing and moistening.
First, the cause for the continuity of the world-system is clarified; as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The three thousand great..."

A thousandfold world-system is formed through immeasurable causes and conditions; for instance, the great earth rests upon the water-circle, the water-circle rests upon the wind-circle, the wind-circle rests upon the space-circle, and the space-circle has no further support. Yet, through the karmic resonance of sentient beings, the world remains securely established.
This case is likewise so; therefore, we first explain the wind-circle, precisely because it is the foundation of the true Dharma-nature land.
Coming from the immovable, through the sudden emergence of cognition and vision, one turns this wondrously bright essence of wisdom into "awakened clarity" (*jue-ming*).

This, in turn, turns the true emptiness of the nature of awakening into the dull emptiness of obscurity. What is called "establishing knowledge within cognition and vision" is the very root of ignorance (*avidyā*).
From this, cognition and vision, together with the wind of ignorance, suddenly begin to stir, filling and pervading all space.
Because space is empty, above the wheel of space there is a wind-wheel that sustains the world-system.
This arises from the initial single thought of false discernment, which, being deluded regarding fundamental enlightenment, constitutes the seed of the wind-wheel as ignorance.
Therefore, the solidification of the receptacle-world is entirely due to the sustaining power of the wind of ignorance, by which it is held so as not to disperse; this occurs below space.
Next, it is explained that since the wind of ignorance already exists, depending upon space it stirs;

and because this cognitive awareness and vision cling and grasp with increasing firmness, it further forms the Golden Wheel (*kāñcanacakravāḍa*) from within the dark and obscure space, maintaining the lands.
Thus, the four treasures form Mount Sumeru, and pure gold forms the seven mountain ranges. These golden mountains and treasure mountains are all [composed of gold].

"Clear awareness establishes solidity," which refers to how the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) is grasped and bound together by means of the subjective aspect (darśana-bhāga) to form the solid element of earth.
Next, "solid awareness of fire is accomplished through jewels" takes up the aforementioned gold and jewels produced by clear awareness establishing solidity.
Finally, "shaking clear awareness produces wind" takes up the aforementioned state where ignorance causes the movement of cognition and vision.
The wind element is that which issues forth; its awakening and illumination constitute cognition and vision (*jñāna-darśana*).

This cognition and vision, stirred internally by ignorance (*avidyā*) and dazzled externally by the metal of objective forms (*nimitta-kāñcana*), results from the friction between wind and metal, whereby the fire element (*tejas-mahābhūta*) is produced.
Thus, there is the light of fire, which has transformation as its nature. By "transformation" is meant the changing of the raw into the cooked, and the transforming of existence into non-existence.
This arises from ignorance; as the bell and drum of appearances produce increasingly intense perceptions, they ignite the fire of hatred, which acts as the element of fire.
From the brilliance of the jewels below, the four elements of water are drawn upward by the heat of the fire.
Consequently, both the perceived gold and jewels and the perceiving conscious clarity become ever more lustrous and moistened, leading to a persistent attachment that one is unwilling to relinquish.
Because the relinquishing [of objects] subsequently gives rise to the water of craving, there is a water-wheel that contains the worlds of the ten directions.

"Containing" means seeing that the entire world is enveloped by this water of craving. This arises from the mutual perception [of subject and object] which triggers the moisture-generating ignorance (*avidyā*) as the primary element of water.
Thus, one knows that the seeds of the four great elements are rooted in delusion and craving, continuing in an uninterrupted succession. (From the *Ancient Manuscript*).
It is said that because of the movement of deluded views, the external wind-circle is manifested; because of the firmness of grasping thoughts, the external gold-circle is manifested;
because of the dryness of investigative seeking, the external fire-circle is manifested; and because of the depth of affectionate attachment, the external water-circle is manifested.
Fire ascends and water descends; their interaction gives rise to solidity. That which is moist becomes the vast ocean, and that which is dry becomes the continents and sandbars.

By this principle, within those great oceans, flames constantly arise, and within those continents and sandbars, rivers and streams constantly flow. Where the power of water is inferior to fire, it solidifies into high mountains;
therefore, when mountain rocks are struck, they emit sparks, and when melted, they become water and soil. Where the power of water is inferior to fire, [it likewise solidifies].
When extracted, they become grasses and trees; thus, forests and thickets turn into soil when burned and become water when squeezed.
Through the mutual arising of delusions, they serve as seeds for one another; by these causes and conditions, the world continues in succession.
Previously, based on ignorance, the single development and transformation resulted in the formation of the seeds of the four great elements;

these causes—the seeds of the two great elements of fire and water—successively combined to form the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*). "Fire ascends" means that because the nature of fire is to move upward, it is called "ascending.
"Water descends" means that because the nature of water is to moisten and flow downward, it is called "descending. "Interacting and producing solidity" refers to fire and water...

Through their mutual generation, the vessel-worlds (bhājanaloka) arise: that which is moist becomes the great oceans—namely, the Sea of Sweet Water and the Sea of Salt Water—which are established by the descent of water as the vessel-world for aquatic sentient beings;
that which is dry becomes the continents and islands—namely, the four great continents—which are established by the ascent of fire as the vessel-world for land-dwelling sentient beings. It is thus.

By principle, the great ocean is originally a place of moisture; it should not have fire, yet where there is fire, it is because it has received a portion of the fiery element, and thus the flames constantly arise. A sandbank is originally a place of dryness;
it should not have water, yet where there is water, it is because it has received a portion of the watery element, and thus the rivers and streams constantly pour forth. Such is the power of water.
Furthermore, below [the realm of fire], land-mountains, forests, and marshes arise from the three elements of water, fire, and earth.
When the power of water is inferior to that of fire, because water can overcome fire, if the nature of water does not descend to join with fire, its power will surely extinguish the fire;
how then could it produce things? Now, however, water descends its own nature and joins with fire.

Therefore, when water and fire combine, they form high mountains; thus, when mountain rocks are struck, they produce flames because they have received a portion of the fire-element, and when they melt, they become water because they have received a portion of the water-element.
Earth is inferior to water in its power because earth can overcome water; yet if the nature of earth does not descend to conform to water, its power will necessarily [be overwhelmed].
How could extinguished water produce things? Now, it descends from the nature of earth to conform to water; thus, when earth and water combine, they draw forth grasses and trees.
Therefore, when forests and thickets encounter fire and become soil, they receive the portion of the earth's qi;
when they are squeezed and become water, they receive the portion of the water's qi. Through the mutual entanglement of delusion, these form the underlying knots of phenomenal characteristics.
Furthermore, ignorance serves as the seed for the wind-circle; the mind of grasping serves as the seed for the gold-circle; the mind of hatred serves as the seed for the fire-element;

and the mind of attachment serves as the seed for the water-circle. Through these four circles, delusions arise in mutual interaction, serving as seeds for one another and further generating the four great elements, whereby the receptacle world is established.
Thus, the world undergoes its phases of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness in a continuous cycle from beginning to end.
Furthermore, if ignorance is shattered, the wind-wheel ceases; if rigid attachment dissolves, the gold-wheel collapses;

if anger subsides, the fire-wheel becomes void; and if craving is exhausted, the water-wheel dries up. Thus, the vessel-world (the physical universe) would, at the very thought, transform into supreme enlightened awareness.

(Guan Yin said: "The movement of the five elements proceeds because of essence there is spirit; because of spirit there is consciousness; because of consciousness there is intention; because of intention there is the numinous; because of the numinous there is essence.")

The movement of circulation is unceasing: the essence (*jing*) is water, the numen (*po*) is metal, the spirit (*shen*) is fire, the soul (*hun*) is wood, and the intention (*yi*) is earth. That which ascends is fire; that which descends is water. That which desires to ascend but cannot ascend is wood;

that which desires to descend but cannot descend is metal. Metal and wood are the intersection of water and fire. Thus, the five phases (*wuxing*) all exist because of my thoughts and calculations; therefore, when the myriad things come, I respond to them with my nature (*xing*) rather than responding to them with my mind-nature (*xinxing*).

Nature is the state before the mind has sprouted. Without spirit, there is no intention; for without fire, there is no earth. Without intention, there is no numen; for without earth, there is no metal. If one is not present, all five are absent.

Those who reject the worldly discourse on the five elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*) all fail to trace them back to their origin; Guan Yin (Guanzi), however, was skilled at tracing back to the origin. Yet, the four great elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*) and the five elements are in reality not different; therefore, they are recorded together. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"By the sovereign power of the karma of sentient beings, first, based upon the lowest support in space, a wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) arises.
Such a wind-circle is solid and impenetrable, such that even if Mount Sumeru were to fall upon it..."
A man of great strength, brandishing a vajra with fierce power, strikes it down; yet while the vajra might shatter, the wind-wheel remains unharmed.

Furthermore, through the sovereign power of the karma of sentient beings, great clouds and rain arise above the wind-wheel; the drops are as large as axle-trees, and the accumulated water forms a wheel.
By the karmic power of sentient beings, the water does not flow away or disperse, just as food that has not yet been digested does not fall from consciousness.
The ocean is like a granary storing rice; the water-circle is likewise supported by wind so that it does not flow away or disperse.
Through the karma of sentient beings, a distinct wind arises which strikes this water, causing a golden circle (*kāñcanamaṇḍala*) to form upon it.

Just as when boiled milk cools, a film forms on the surface and solidifies, so the water-circle diminishes until it is only eight hundred thousand *lakṣas* thick, while the remainder transforms into gold. Upon this gold...
Upon the wheel [of the world-system] are nine great mountains; Mount Sumeru stands at the center, while the other eight surround it in a circle.
Among these eight mountains, the first seven are called the "inner" mountains. Outside the seventh mountain lie the four continents.
Beyond the continents, there is again the Iron Rim Mountain (Cakravāḍa), which encircles the entire world-system like a wheel. The seven mountains, beginning with Yugandhara, consist solely of gold.
The King of High Mountains, Sumeru, is composed of four jewels; its four sides, proceeding from the north, east, south, and west respectively, consist of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
Because of the majestic power of these jewels, their colors manifest in the sky; thus, the sky over Jambudvīpa appears like lapis lazuli.
These jewels and so forth are likewise accomplished through the sovereign karmic power of sentient beings.
Furthermore, great clouds arise and rain upon the golden wheel; the drops are as thick as axle-trees, and the rushing waves of accumulated water become a treasury of seeds for various jewels.
Through the impact of the fierce winds driven by its majestic power, these transform into various jewels.
Thus, when the water transforms into various jewels, the cause ceases and the effect arises; their essences do not coexist. In this manner, gold is transformed and produced.
Furthermore, by the power of karma, distinct winds are produced that separate the various jewels and gather them together to form mountains and continents;
they also differentiate the waters into sweet and salt, establishing the inner oceans and the outer ocean. Thus, the nine mountains rest upon the golden wheel (*kāñcanamaṇḍala*);
of the eight seas situated between them, the first seven are called the "inner" seas, all of which possess the eight qualities.
The eighth [great ocean] is the Virtuous Water, also known as the Outer Salt Water, which fills the outer seas. Within it are four great continents, each facing Mount Sumeru:
Jambudvīpa in the south, which is broad in the north and narrow in the south, with its three sides being equal in measure and shaped like a chariot;
and the other continents. Only within this continent is there a vajra-seat that reaches to the very limit of the earth below and rests upon the golden wheel. All bodhisattvas...

When all those who are about to attain perfect enlightenment sit upon this seat and arise from the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), it is because it possesses the power of firmness through its lack of remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*).
The eastern continent, Pūrvavideha, is shaped like a half-moon; the western continent, Aparagoyānī, is shaped like a full moon;
and the northern continent, Uttarakuru, is shaped like a square seat. The faces of the people in these continents correspond to the shapes of their respective lands.
It is likewise so; this refers to a single world-system governed by one Mount Sumeru and one sun and moon. Question:
Why does this sutra present the gold wheel first and the water wheel second, whereas the *Abhidharmakośa* presents the water wheel first and the gold wheel later? Answer:
That [text] establishes the order based on the formation of the world from the bottom up; this [sutra] establishes the order based on the arising of the world.
Their arising depends on internal conditions stimulating external objects to establish their sequence;

therefore, they are not the same. Furthermore, Pūrṇa, the delusion is not caused by another; the fault lies in the cognitive clarity (*jñāna*) itself. Once that which is deluded has been established, the principle of clarity does not transcend it.
For this reason, hearing does not go beyond sound, and seeing does not surpass form. Thus, the six delusions of form, smell, taste, touch, and so forth are formed.
From this, there is the separation of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and knowing; bound by common karma, they unite and separate, forming transformations.

Seeing clarity gives rise to the perception of form; seeing clarity gives rise to the perception of difference; seeing clarity gives rise to aversion; and shared perceptions give rise to craving. Craving flows as the seed, and the grasping of perceptions forms the womb.
Through their union, birth occurs, and by attracting one another through common karma, there is the causal condition for the arising of the *kalala* and *arbuda*.

According to their respective conditions, there are the womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born; the egg-born arise solely from thought, the womb-born are caused by emotion, the moisture-born result from contact, and the transformation-born respond to separation.

Through the mutual transformations of emotion, thought, contact, and separation, all karmic experiences follow their ascent or descent, and by these causes and conditions, sentient beings continue in succession.
This answers the cause for the continuity of sentient beings. For the Dharma-nature body is originally all-pervasive and truly possesses no physical body;
even this very physical body, when its original source is traced back, is likewise formed by the delusion of clarity.
This "delusion of clarity" is truly nothing other than the wondrously luminous awakened mind itself, which initially gave rise to a single thought that turned into [delusion].

Awakened clarity becomes that which is falsely imagined; once that which is falsely imagined is established, the profoundly still, perfect, wondrous, and luminous nature of awareness is divided into six locations.

Thus, when it resides in the eye it is called "seeing," and when it resides in the ear it is able to "hear. Consequently, localized obstructions arise, and it no longer remains all-pervasive and universally penetrating.
For this reason, one cannot transcend the physical world of the vessel; therefore, hearing does not extend beyond it.

To hear sound while not transcending form is nothing other than this: it is accomplished through the six delusions of form, fragrance, taste, and touch, which defile the six faculties and constitute the objects (*viṣaya*).
It is also accomplished through the six delusions of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, which grasp the six objects and constitute the faculties (*indriya*).
Thus, the six faculties and six objects each have their fixed locations; the union and separation of feelings and perceptions each have their respective [conditions].
In the realms of womb-birth, egg-birth, moisture-birth, and transformation-birth, those with fixed karma likewise each have their fixed retribution.
Those with identical karma are entwined together in one place; those with different karma may either separate or remain joined. Wēnlíng says:

"Identical karma" refers to the classes of womb- and egg-birth, because the three—the parents and the individual—possess identical karma and thus are entwined and born together. "Separation and joining" refers to moisture-birth.
Transformed beings (*nirmāṇakāya*) do not depend on parents but arise solely from their own karma; they may form through union with moisture or manifest through detachment and transformation.
This refers to the fundamental body (*mūlakāya*), which, due to inverted attachments, brings about the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

When entering the womb, it is likewise so. "Seeing light" and below explains the causes for entering the womb in the intermediate state, referring to the two types of birth: the womb-born and the egg-born.
When the intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) is about to enter a womb, all places for which it lacks a karmic affinity appear as a great earth black as ink;
only at the place where it has a karmic affinity with its parents does a single point of bright color appear.

Once this intermediate state being sees that bright color, it hastens toward that location, and its perception is thereby fulfilled. Therefore it is said: "Seeing the appearance of bright color gives rise to the perception of light."
Guishan Cheng says: "Diverse views" refers to perceiving the father as an object of aversion; "identical perception" refers to perceiving the mother as an object of affection.
For a female, it is the reverse. This section clarifies the cause for entering the womb, which is the ignorance that moistens rebirth (*upapatti-bhava-avidyā*).
It states that once this intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) perceives a desirable object, it immediately directs its craving toward the father.
The mother’s two drops of red and white serve as the seed; these two drops, through the application of this mental visualization, form the embryo.

Although this visualization arises from the union of the parents, it is actually due to the correspondence of one's own karma that it is drawn in and retained without being discarded, just as a magnet attracts iron. Thus, the three—father, mother, and self—are the causes.
Due to these conditions, one enters the womb and forms a body composed of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*);

because there are the characteristics of the *kalala* and so forth, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that there are generally five stages within the womb: first, for seven days it is called *kalala*, which means "congealed mucus";
second, for seven days it is called *arbuda*, which means "bubble," resembling a boil; third, for seven days it is called *peśī*, which means...
The fourth week is called *ghanā*, which means "solid flesh"; the fifth week is called *praśākhā*, which means "stage of limbs.

Since only these two are mentioned here, the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) is used. (The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "That which is called 'intermediate existence' (*antarābhava*) refers to the body of sentient beings belonging to the five destinies that exists between the state of birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) and death-existence (*maraṇabhava*).

It is also termed 'intermediate existence' because its substance consists of the five aggregates of maturation (*vipākapañcaskandha*), as it is summoned by karma. Thus, the bodies of those in the intermediate state of the womb or egg are like their future birth-existences; for instance, the form of one in the intermediate state of the human destiny resembles a human.")

The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of other realms is likewise; its body is the size of a child of five or six years. Although its physical dimensions are small, its sense faculties are sharp and keen, enabling it to perform various actions as if it were in its original birth-state (*pūrvakālabhava*).

It conceives perverted perceptions toward its parents: it sees either only the male or only the female. As it gradually approaches that location, it eventually ceases to see the parents and perceives only the sexual organs of the man and woman.

If it is a male intermediate being, it feels desire for the mother, giving rise to a lustful mind; if it is a female intermediate being, it feels desire for the father, giving rise to a lustful mind. Through the arising of these two kinds of affectionate desire, it unites with the object of its love. The emitted impurity flows into the womb, which it identifies as its own body, and thus it experiences joy.

Because this mind rejoices in the passing away from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and taking up birth in the state of existence (*upapattibhava*), it is said that "those of similar karma are entangled. Regarding those born by moisture or transformation, due to the power of prior karma, they do not distinguish between near and far;

through passionate attachment to a corresponding object, they immediately take birth upon encountering the scent of that place of defilement. Vibhīṣaṇa asked the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, once beings have died and received the intermediate body, but before they have received a new body, how do they abide?

The Buddha said: "It is like a seed producing a sprout. Does the seed perish first and then the sprout arise? Or does the sprout arise first and then the seed perish? Or does the sprout arise only after the seed has perished for a long time? Vibhīṣaṇa said: "World-Honored One, it is not that the sprout arises only after the seed has already perished, nor is it that the seed has already perished while the sprout has already arisen."

The cessation of the seed and the arising of birth occur simultaneously, without before or after. The Buddha said, "It is so, Lord of Laṅkā. It is not that the final consciousness of the old body ceases and then the initial consciousness of the new body arises; nor is it that the initial consciousness of the new body has arisen and then the final consciousness of the old body ceases.

Arising and cessation are simultaneous, without before or after. It is like the movement of a *kṛmi* worm: wherever the worm goes, its entire body follows along; one part does not remain stationary while the steps are shifted and it departs. In this way, the prior consciousness entrusts itself to a body, and the consciousness follows as a whole;

once entrusted, it does not leave until death, when it is then transferred and abandoned. Vibhāṣā said, "If it is thus, is there an intermediate state (*antarābhava*)? The Buddha said, "It is like sentient beings born from eggs: having abandoned their bodies and entrusted themselves to an egg, they remain there by the power of the winds of karma."

Within an egg, there is a congealed mass devoid of consciousness; it is only when the egg matures that consciousness first becomes aware. Why is this so? Because the nature of karma is such that, by the power of karma, sentient beings born from eggs have no perception until the time of maturation has arrived.

Furthermore, because of their meritorious karma, when a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) and his sons receive a body, they are not defiled by the impurities of the womb, nor are they mixed with such impurities; since they are untainted by the womb’s filth, they are mostly born through transformation (*upapāduka*). One should understand the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) by means of these examples.

Regarding the statement "womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born according to what is appropriate," this means that each of the four modes of birth is brought about by the mutual resonance of their respective determinate karma.

Therefore, in accordance with their responses, they are met with the fixed retributions of the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*). That which is called "perception" (*saṃjñā*) refers to unsettled and disordered thoughts;

that which is called "emotion" (*bhāva*) refers to the concentration of affection that one cannot relinquish; that which is called "union" (*saṃyoga*) refers to being closely attached without change; and that which is called "separation" (*viyoga*) refers to moving away from this and heading toward that.
It is through the invocation of these four mental states that the four modes of birth respond according to their kind. The following clarifies the inferiority of emotion and perception.
This is the fruit brought about by determinate karma (*niyata-karma*). It is said that because the mind or emotions may transform into perception (*saṃjñā*), or perception may transform into emotion;

or because union may transform into separation, or separation may transform into union, the retribution one receives may change from flying to sinking—such as a sparrow transforming into a clam—or from sinking to flying—such as a fish transforming into a dragon—and so forth. This is also not [the case].

This is also [the case for] the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*). (For example, even among humans, all four modes of birth (*yoni*) are present: as with Viśākhā Mīramātṛ, who had thirty-two sons born from eggs; Maṇḍhātṛ, the Wheel-Turning Sage King, who was born from moisture;

Ābhā, the Bhikṣuṇī, who was born by transformation from within the earth; and furthermore, Zhigong, who was born in a hawk’s nest; the Fifth Patriarch, who was born in a temple; Yi Yin, who was born from empty mulberry wood; and Hou Ji, who was born from a giant footprint. Even more extreme cases exist:

those who were exceedingly violent transformed into fierce tigers, and those who were excessively lustful transformed into women. Thus we know that good and evil arise from the mind, and since the mind undergoes transformations, it cannot help but transform. This concludes the section below.

Continuity. Pūrṇa, when conceptualization and craving are bound together as one, and craving cannot be abandoned, then the succession of parents and children in all the worlds arises without interruption;
these are rooted in sensual desire. When craving and attachment nourish each other and greed cannot be stilled, then—
In all worlds, those born from eggs, from moisture, from transformation, or from wombs, devour one another according to their relative strength and weakness;
these beings take the greed for killing as their root. Humans eat sheep, and when the sheep dies it becomes a human, and when the human dies they become a sheep;
thus it continues through ten types of births, dying and being reborn, mutually devouring one another, with such evil karma arising together and persisting until the end of the future.
These are rooted in theft and greed. You owe me my life, and I shall repay you for your debt;
by this causal condition, we remain constantly within birth and death for hundreds of thousands of kalpas. You love my mind, and I cherish your form;

by this causal condition, we remain constantly bound in entanglement for hundreds of thousands of kalpas. Only killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct serve as the three roots; by these causal conditions, karma [is produced].
"Continuity of the fruit.

This clarifies the cause for the continuity of karmic results. Regarding "craving and attachment bind together like glue," it means that the mutual affection between them is as solid as lacquer, firmly binding so that it cannot be untied; thus, at the time of rebirth, craving flows forth.
The various conceptions serve as the womb, through which parents, children, and grandchildren are born in an unbroken succession;
all of these take sexual desire as the basis for establishing their nature and life. Therefore it is said that "desire and greed are the root.

Regarding the phrase "greed and craving nourish one another," this means that they crave me, they nourish me, and they love my flesh and blood; all of these are nourished by the aspect of greed and craving, and thus they act according to their power.
The strong and the weak prey upon one another, just as it is said that half a catty is still eight *liang*.
This applies the case of humans to all other beings; it does not mean that only humans and sheep eat one another.

"Born together with evil karma" means that because they possess this evil karma, they are born together in the same place in every lifetime to meet one another and repay their debts. This refers to the greed of theft.

This refers to taking what is not given and taking by stealth; both constitute theft. For example, when people feed sheep, the sheep have never been fed by those people, yet the people take them by force to eat.

When the sheep die, they become humans who come to devour one another, yet they do not realize the reason for their being taken and eaten. This is "taking what is not given" and "stealthy taking," even though it involves killing.

Theft, sexual misconduct, and the three types of [false speech] differ in their forms, yet they all have greed as their root. Thus, one knows that the wandering through the three realms is caused solely by craving;
if this craving is severed, one will emerge from the three realms. Your two lines are elliptical and should be stated as:
"You owe me my life; you must return my life" and "I owe you your life; I shall return your life. This belongs to...
"Kill greed! I owe you a debt; I shall repay your debt. You owe me a debt; you shall repay my debt.
This belongs to the category of theft-greed (*steya-rāga*). Because these words regarding the debt of life are not resolved, the mutual entanglement of birth and death is likewise not resolved.
The two lines beginning with "You love" are also elliptical; they should be stated fully as: "You love my heart, and I love your heart; I pity you."
"O Rūpa, you cherish me; because the cherishing born of craving is not severed, the mutual entanglement of birth and death is likewise not severed.
Only by killing the lower fetters is the continuity [of existence] brought to an end. The *Saṃyukta-āgama* says:

'For example, when people of the world bury their ancestors in an auspicious location, they receive blessings for generations; otherwise, there is misfortune. People have relatives and kin, but the earth has no consciousness.'"

The response of blessings and calamities is as swift as a shadow following a form or an echo following a sound. For all sentient beings, the karmic fruits produced by the power of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and false conceptualization are likewise so.
Pūrṇa, these three kinds of inverted continuities are all the nature of the luminous clarity of awareness, which is clearly and fully cognizant. Because of this nature, [the cycle continues].
To understand how these characteristics arise from deluded vision: the various conditioned phenomena of mountains, rivers, and the great earth undergo a sequential flow;
because of this delusion, they end and then begin again.
This concludes that the continuous manifestation of these three types of succession all originates from that first sudden thought.

Regarding the seeds of birth: although these three types of continuity differ from one another, if one traces their origin, they all arise because the wondrously luminous essence of the mind-body initially lacked awareness and suddenly gave rise to a single thought;

thus it transformed into the *karmic consciousness* (*ālayavijñāna*), which is termed "awakened clarity" (*jue-ming*). Because there is this awakened clarity, it subsequently further transforms into the nature of clear cognition.
Because the faculty of cognition subsequently transforms into the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga), it is said that "from cognition arises the appearance.
Due to this false vision, the various conditioned phenomena of mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise;
they thus undergo successive flux and transition, ending and beginning again because of this. It is for this reason that all manner of illusory transformations are born from the Tathāgata.
This is the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment.

Pūrṇa said: "If this wondrous enlightenment is fundamentally a wondrously enlightened clarity, and is no more and no less than the Tathāgata’s mind, how is it that, without apparent cause, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena suddenly arose? Now that the Tathāgata has attained this wondrous, empty, and luminous enlightenment—"
When will the conditioned habitual outflows of the mountains, rivers, and great earth ever arise again?
This [objection] uses the nature of the cause to challenge the nature of the fruit, cross-examining the Tathāgata as to when they might ever again manifest according to karma.
The underlying intent is that the nature of sentient beings—the wondrous clarity of awakening, the essence of original enlightenment’s wondrous clarity—is identical to that of all Tathāgatas.
In equality there is no duality; yet sentient beings have suddenly arisen, without apparent cause, from within the essence that is fundamentally pure.
Once the Tathāgata has attained the essence of pure awakening, when could he ever again suddenly arise without apparent cause?
Conditioned phenomena are precisely the habitual outflows of sentient beings, which are the fruits of karma.
The Buddha told Pūrṇa: "Suppose, for example, a person who is lost mistakes south for north in a certain village.
Does this delusion arise because of delusion, or does it emerge through awakening? Pūrṇa replied: 'Such a lost person arises neither because of delusion nor because of awakening.
Why is this? Delusion has no fundamental root; how could it arise because of delusion? Awakening does not produce delusion.'"

"How is it that through awakening one understands the Buddha’s words? When those deluded people are in the midst of their delusion, suddenly there appears an awakened person who points them out and causes them to awaken.
Pūrṇa, what do you think? Would this person, though still deluded, give rise to further delusion within this village?
"No, World-Honored One. "Pūrṇa, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are likewise so. This delusion has no fundamental basis."

The nature is ultimately empty; from the beginning it was fundamentally without delusion, yet there appeared to be delusion. Through awakening, delusion is extinguished; once awakening arises, delusion does not occur.
This reveals that the awakened nature is immovable and fundamentally devoid of both delusion and enlightenment. First, an analogy is presented to examine the source from which delusion emerges;
subsequently, the answer explains that the cause of delusion comes from nowhere, stating that this ignorance originally arises from...
The pure awakened mind suddenly arises because it has no root; thus, it does not exist because of delusion.
If a deluded person were to suddenly awaken, awakening would mean the absence of delusion, yet this is not because of awakening.

Since this deluded person does not depend on either delusion or awakening, one knows that the nature of awareness is fundamentally unmoving, while both delusion and awakening belong to the gate of birth and death.
The Buddha said, "To summarize: I shall again employ an analogy and pose a counter-question.

Although you know that delusion and awakening have no root, suppose at the very moment someone is confused and mistakes south for north, there suddenly appears a person who points it out and causes them to awaken.
Even if this person was previously deluded, now that they have awakened, would they become deluded once more regarding this village? [He replied: "No."

This means that once one has awakened, there will certainly be no further delusion. Regarding the passage "The ten directions below," the principle of the Dharma dictates that this state is devoid of clarity and lacks any fundamental basis;
it is fundamentally and primordially empty (*ādikṣaya-śūnya*). It is just like the delusion of being lost in a direction, which has no further cause.
Because this pure enlightened nature was originally non-existent as delusion from the beginning, it suddenly gave rise to a single thought, which appeared to be deluded.
The essence of pure awakening is not true delusion; if it were true delusion, then once deluded, it would have a root, so how could it ever awaken again?
Since delusion fundamentally has no root, it is said to be "as if existent. It is just like being confused about south as being north—the direction has not actually changed.
Now that one has awakened to this delusion, the delusion immediately ceases; once ceased, how could it ever arise again?
Formerly, National Teacher Zhong asked Attendant Zilin, "What is the meaning of 'Buddha'? He replied, "The meaning of awakening. The Master said, "Has the Buddha ever been deluded?
He replied, "He has never been deluded. The Master said, "If so, what use is there for awakening? Thus one knows that since there is not even awakening, how could there be delusion?
Therefore it is said: "In the past, delusion and awakening were like delusion; today, awakening and delusion are like awakening."
"It is not awakening.
It is like a person with cataracts who sees flowers in the sky; once the disease of the cataracts is removed, the flowers vanish from the sky.
Suppose a foolish person were to stand upon that spot where the sky-flowers had vanished, waiting for them to be born again. Do you consider such a person to be foolish or wise?"

Pūrṇa said, "Space originally has no flowers; it is through deluded vision that they arise and perish. To see the extinction of the flowers and thereby take space itself to be extinguished is already an inversion.
To command them to appear again is truly madness and folly. Why do you call such a madman wise or foolish?
The Buddha said, "According to what you understand, why do you ask when the wondrous, enlightened, luminous emptiness of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas will [appear]?"
Furthermore, mountains, rivers, and the great earth emerge once more.
Again, a metaphor is raised to clarify that when the cataract is removed and the flowers vanish, the Tathāgata uses himself as a metaphor for the waiting;

the metaphor of the flowers arising again represents Pūrṇa being examined to determine whether he is foolish or wise; and the subsequent metaphor of the void’s source illustrates that the fundamentally pure awakened mind is originally [so].

"There is neither delusion nor awakening. This already implies that to speak of "awakening" is to fall into the secondary stage; how much more so to seek out one's "delusion" after having already awakened!
This is truly the height of worldly folly—how can you ask about the difference between folly and wisdom?
The Buddha spoke these words and, with a light flick of his hand, turned him away, saying: "You understand this clear sky; wait for the flowers to fall again."
Those born as humans are foolish and lack wisdom, yet you seek mountains, rivers, and the great earth within the pure awakened mind;
how does this differ from such a fool? As these two metaphors above demonstrate, even while deluded, one has never truly been deluded;
how much less could there be delusion again after awakening?
Furthermore, just as gold ore mixed with refined gold becomes pure gold once more and cannot be made impure again,
and just as wood turned to ash cannot become wood again, so too are the bodhi and nirvāṇa of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Regarding "gold ore mixed with refined gold": the ore is a metaphor for ignorance (*avidyā*), and the gold is a metaphor for the enlightened nature (*bodhi-svabhāva*);
this speaks of the union of ignorance and the enlightened nature. "That gold being entirely pure" is a metaphor for the exhaustion of ignorance and the state of pure enlightenment.

"Not becoming ore again" is a metaphor for the fact that the fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) of all Buddhas has already manifested, and thus the characteristics of ignorance and the mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*) do not arise again.
Thus, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) says: "Once the essence of pure gold is realized, it never again becomes ore.

The metaphor of wood represents afflictions (*kleśa*), while the metaphor of ash represents nirvāṇa. "Not becoming wood" signifies that having already realized nirvāṇa, one no longer gives rise to afflictions.
These two metaphors state that one who has already awakened does not again produce delusion; how much more so after awakening, when one further applies the four [practices]?
Having attained Great Nirvana through the perfection of the twelvefold refinement and realized Right and Equal Enlightenment, could one fall back into delusion?
Furthermore, Pūrṇa, you have asked: "Do the natures of earth, water, fire, and wind fundamentally interpenetrate and pervade the Dharma-realm? Regarding this doubt:

The natures of water and fire do not mutually overcome or extinguish one another; furthermore, it is proven that empty space and the great earth both pervade the entire Dharma-realm, yet they cannot coexist within one another.
Pūrṇa, it is like empty space: its essence is not composed of various phenomena, yet it does not obstruct the manifestation of those phenomena.
Why is this so? Pūrṇa, when the sun shines upon that great empty space, it becomes bright; when clouds gather, it becomes...
When stirred by dark winds, it moves; when clear and bright after a rain, it is pure; when the vapors congeal, it becomes turbid; when soil accumulates, it forms a haze (*māya*);

when water settles, it forms reflections. What do you think? Regarding these various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) in different regions, are they produced because of those [conditions], or do they exist independently of them?
If they were produced by those [conditions], Pūrṇa, consider this: when the sun shines, since it is the light of the sun, throughout the worlds of the ten directions—
Since it is the same solar radiance, why is a round sun seen again within the sky? If the sky were luminous, the sky itself should illuminate;

why then does it fail to produce such brilliance during the midnight hours when shrouded by clouds and mist? One should know that this light is neither the sun nor the sky, yet it is not distinct from the sky and the sun.
This clarifies that all seven elements arise from the Tathāgata-garbha mind according to karma; their entire manifestation is the nature itself.

This answers the question regarding how the seven elements can be both omnipresent and yet not mutually inclusive. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Moreover, you... first restates the previous doubt, while the passage beginning with "For example...
provides a parallel illustration to clarify that the substance of empty space is not identical to its manifold attributes—this serves as a metaphor for the Tathāgata.

The *ālayavijñāna* (the storehouse consciousness) is pure and fundamental by nature, pervading the entire dharma-realm. Its "not refusing to manifest various phenomena" is a metaphor for the seven elements (*dhātu*) appearing according to karma.

Because the profound stillness of true emptiness becomes obscured, when stirred by wind it moves; this is a metaphor for the wind-element (*vāyu-mahābhūta*), as a sudden gust of wind causes the great void to tremble. When the rain clears and the sky is serene, it is pure;
this is a metaphor for the space-element (*ākāśa-mahābhūta*), as ten thousand *li* are free of clouds and the azure sky is as if washed clean.

When the vapors coalesce, it becomes turbid; this is a metaphor for the element of perception (*darśana-mahābhūta*), as the distinction between space and perception is lost and the two aspects become muddled. From the accumulation of earth, it becomes solid.

The metaphor of "haze" refers to the earth element; when thick mists fly through the clear sky during the day, they obstruct and block it. Therefore, the metaphor of "water being clear so as to form reflections" refers to the water element;

when the water and sky become one color, the clear sky is reflected and manifested therein. Thus, the following section presents a dual inquiry regarding the source from which the seven elements emerge.
