Throughout the void, wherever there is clarity, it is all from the single sun. How could one see another round sun within the sky like a basin or a bowl?
If there were yet another round sun visible in the sky, then everything outside of that sun would simply be empty clarity;
how then could one say that it is illuminated *because* of the sun? If you claim that this is not clarity—

Because it depends on the sun, and because it depends on space—since space is eternally present, light should likewise be eternally present. Why is it that when darkness arrives, there is no radiance?
One should know that this light is neither identical to space nor the sun, yet it is not separate from space or the sun.
Since it is neither identical nor separate, one knows that it is pure and fundamental by nature, manifesting according to karma.
The fundamental falsity of perceived characteristics cannot be pointed out or described; it is like inviting a flower in the sky to produce a fruit in the sky.

How can one question the meaning of their mutual subversion and extinction? The fundamental reality of the nature is solely the wondrously enlightened clarity. Since this mind of wondrously enlightened clarity was originally neither water nor fire, how can you further ask why they are not mutually compatible?
This misplaced passage should follow the text below "There is no basis for reliance," as it cites the aforementioned unreality to answer the preceding question.
It simply means: "Observe carefully the characteristics of the seven elements; if they were truly real, they could indeed be pointed out.
For example, the reflection of the moon in water is originally unreal, such that one cannot even determine it to be a single entity."

To claim that they are two, or that one is west and the other east, and thus seek to refute their mutual sublation and extinction, is like attempting to gather empty flowers to form empty fruit—how could this possibly succeed?
If you carefully observe the nature of the seven elements, you will see that they are fundamentally the essence of true, eternal, wondrous enlightenment and clarity, and nothing else.
Thus, within the nature of wondrous enlightenment, there is originally neither water nor fire.
If water and fire do not even exist [simultaneously], how can you ask about their mutual incompatibility?
True, wondrous, enlightened clarity is also like this. If you clarify it through space, then space appears;
if you clarify earth, water, fire, and wind individually, then each appears individually; if you clarify them all together, then they all appear together. How do they appear together?
Pūrṇa, it is like the reflection of the sun appearing in a body of water.

When two people view this sun in the water together and each walks away—one to the east and one to the west—the sun appears to follow each of them. Since there was originally no fixed standard, one should not raise the objection:
"This sun is but one; how can it go in different directions? If the sun is indeed double, why does it appear as one? It is truly perplexing.
To turn toward the false is to have nothing upon which to rely;
this is the application of the Dharma to the analogy. One should formulate the syllogism as follows: "The wondrous clarity of true awakening" is the subject (*dharmin*);

"it is neither different from nor identical to [the seven elements]" is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because its essence is not the seven great elements, yet it does not obstruct the manifestation of those seven great elements.
The common analogy is like empty space. When you clarify space through your mind, then space appears;
this is precisely the manifestation of the characteristic of space following the activity of its arousal, just as when one digs a well, emptiness emerges.

"Each clarifies it, and each manifests it" means that if each follows their own karma, then their respective objects manifest accordingly—just as if one seeks fire in one place, fire appears in that very place.
"Emerging from one place while water emerges from another" refers to this. "Both are clear and both appear" means that as they follow their respective karma together, the objects appear identically;
for example, when the entire *dharmadhātu* is grasped, it arises filling the world. As for the phrase "How so? and below, he cites a metaphor to clarify the falsity of simultaneous appearance.
The fact that each appears individually is still insufficient to reveal the emptiness of collective karma (*sādhāraṇa-karma*), and thus [the text speaks of] their simultaneous...
The present manifestation is sufficient to reveal the falsity of collective karma; therefore, following the simultaneous appearance, it is further clarified by means of an analogy.
The reflection of the sun in water is one, yet as people move to the east or west, each perceives a sun [reflection] according to their own direction.

That the sun-reflection follows those to the east is because it conforms to the karma of the people in the east; that the sun-reflection follows those to the west is because it conforms to the karma of the people in the west.
When one faces west, the reflection of the sun in the water never actually follows the person east or west.

From this, one should know that all manifestations arise according to karma and are fundamentally illusory and without basis; it is generally like this. How then can one seek to challenge whether they are one or two, or whether they are east or west?
This is no different from the principle that "it is neither the sun nor the sky, yet the sky and the sun are one in their emptiness. Both are equally empty.
It is merely delusion.
Pūrṇa, you take the characteristics of form and emptiness to oppose and displace one another within the Tathāgatagarbha;

yet the Tathāgatagarbha accordingly manifests as form and emptiness, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. Therefore, within it, there is the movement of wind, the clarity of space, the brightness of the sun, and the darkness of clouds.

Because they give rise to delusion and confusion by turning their backs on awakening and uniting with the objects of the senses, they produce worldly toil and manifest the characteristics of the mundane world.
I, however, unite my wondrous clarity—which is neither extinguished nor born—with the Tathāgata-garbha;

and since this Tathāgata-garbha is solely wondrous, enlightened clarity that perfectly illuminates the Dharma-realm, within it one becomes infinite and the infinite becomes one. Within the small, the large appears; within the large, the small appears. It is not so.

The moving site of enlightenment pervades the worlds of the ten directions; his body contains the inexhaustible voids of the ten directions, manifesting jewel-king lands upon a single hair-tip and turning the Great Dharma Wheel within a mote of dust.
Because he extinguishes the dust of delusion and merges with awakening, he gives rise to the wondrously enlightened luminous nature of True Suchness.

This explanation clarifies the two meanings of the preceding passage: since the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the seven elements (*mahābhūta*) are thus, one cannot challenge the sense that their characteristics mutually suppress one another;
and since the nature (*svabhāva*) of the seven elements is likewise thus, one cannot question why they are not mutually compatible.

If so, for what reason do the seven elements exist? It is because your *karmic-consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*) is not empty and the perception of characteristics (*nimittadarśana*) has not yet been destroyed.
Following the karma of form and emptiness, they mutually compete and seize within the *tathāgatagarbha*;
yet the *tathāgatagarbha* itself manifests as emptiness or form according to your own karma. Thus, you perceive form and emptiness as pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*.

Consequently, when you open your eyes therein, you see only a dense array of material objects and a profusion of worldly afflictions before you, such that you do not realize it has become entirely a defiled land.

Phenomenal appearances are fundamentally empty and devoid of any basis for reliance; this is truly because sentient beings are internally obscured by ignorance and driven by the power of karma, such that their minds are naturally deluded and distressed, failing to realize the truth.
This is entirely due to turning one's back on pure awakening and uniting with false objects, whereby the dust of worldly toil arises;
thus they perceive the appearances of the mundane world but fail to see the wondrous, luminous nature of true suchness and sublime awakening.
While others establish characteristics based on the complete nature, I do not do so.
With ignorance already exhausted and the karmic consciousness already empty, there remains only the essence of pure, wondrous, and luminous wisdom, wherein nothing else exists.

By uniting this essence of wondrous, luminous wisdom with the Tathāgatagarbha, one perceives within the Tathāgatagarbha only the wondrously awakened, luminous mind pervading the ten directions, without a single thing existing apart from it.

Because they act as obstructions and hindrances, therein all phenomena are unimpeded; for the entirety of their characteristics constitutes their nature, one knows that while the mind exists, the objects of the Sahā world do not exist within the mind.
The Flower Treasury World contains space—these two phrases signify the mutual inclusion of the one and the many.
The two phrases regarding the "small" signify the non-obstruction of the broad and the narrow. The two phrases regarding "immovability" are as follows:
"One becoming immeasurable" means that without arising one ascends, and without moving one pervades; the body containing these two phrases is "immeasurable becoming one.
Regarding "a world-system appearing on the tip of a hair," this is the appearance of the support (the environment) within the center (the sentient being);

regarding "turning wheels upon motes of dust," this is the appearance of the center (the sentient being) within the support (the environment), which is the manifestation of the great within the small. All of these appear as such within the wisdom of suchness.
If the object of cognition merely realizes the principle of suchness (*tathatā*), the great function of Samantabhadra cannot manifest;

if one practices only the school of phenomenal reality (*yāvadbhāvikajñāna*), Mañjuśrī’s correct wisdom cannot reach its ultimate consummation. Only by possessing these two types of wisdom can one attain perfection.

The subsequent section on "extinguishing dust" is the inverse of the preceding and may be understood accordingly. Thus, one knows that if the karmic consciousness is not empty, every single thing becomes an obstruction.
When the consciousness of karma is empty, all things are mutually unimpeded. The *Zongjing* says: "The nature of the mind pervades all places;
therefore, the four modes of birth and the nine categories of beings all manifest within the self-nature body (*svabhāva-kāya*).
Because the true mind of the self serves as the nature of all phenomena, it manifests as form or emptiness, pervading the Dharma-realm, and appears as karmic retribution according to one's actions."
When ordinary beings are in different places, they float and sink within the ocean of karma, with birth and death continuing in succession;
when among the noble ones, the Dharma-body is perfected and its wondrous function is inexhaustible. Although their concealment and manifestation differ, their single nature remains unmoving.
The Tathāgatagarbha is the fundamentally wondrous, perfect, and complete mind; it is neither mind nor emptiness; it is not earth, water, fire, wind, or fire;

it is not the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; it is not form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or phenomena; it is not the realm of eye-consciousness, and so on, up to the realm of mind-consciousness;
it is not ignorance, nor the end of ignorance, nor the exhaustion of ignorance, and so on, up to...
It is not aging, not death, not the exhaustion of aging and death; it is not suffering, not its origin, not its cessation, not the path;
it is not knowledge, not attainment, not dāna, not śīla, not vīrya, not kṣānti, not dhyāna, not prajñā, nor the pāramitās;
and so on, up to: it is not the Tathāgata, nor the Arhat, nor the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The three types of bodhi are not the Great Nirvana; they are neither permanent, nor blissful, nor self, nor pure.
Because they are both mundane and supramundane, they are the Tathāgatagarbha—the primordial luminosity of the wondrous mind. This very mind is emptiness; it is earth, water, wind, and fire;
it is the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; it is form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects; it is the eye.
The consciousness element is thus, and so on, up to: the mental consciousness element itself is ignorance, ignorance itself is the exhaustion of ignorance;
and so on, up to: aging and death themselves are the exhaustion of aging and death; suffering itself, its origin itself, its cessation itself, and the path itself;
knowledge itself, attainment itself; generosity itself, ethical discipline itself, vigor itself, patience itself, meditative concentration itself, and wisdom itself.
The *rāga* (passion) is itself the *pāramitā*; and so on, up to:
it is itself the *tathāgata*, the *arhat*, the *samyaksambuddha*, the Great *Nirvāṇa*, the Permanent, the Blissful, the Self, and the Pure.

Because these are all identical as both mundane and supramundane, they are the *Tathāgatagarbha*, the wondrously luminous source of the mind, which is beyond both identity and difference, and neither identical nor non-identical.
This [passage] generally takes the quiescent single mind—which is neither identical to nor separate from [phenomena]—to reveal its wondrous nature as the substance of the three contemplations;
it is what the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* refers to when it says, "That which is called quiescence is named the single mind, and the single mind is named the Tathāgatagarbha.
First, it clarifies the departure from all phenomena to reveal the empty Tathāgatagarbha, for the substance of the Tathāgatagarbha is not [composed of] the multitude [of phenomena].
Because the marks are inherently pure, they are not the seven elements, nor the six faculties, nor the six objects, nor the six consciousnesses;
this is not a mundane dharma. It is not the dharma of pratyekabuddhas, nor the dharma of śrāvakas, nor the dharma of bodhisattvas;
this is not a supramundane dharma. It is not the three titles of the Tathāgata, nor the four virtues of nirvāṇa; this is not supramundane.
This is the supreme among intermediate teachings. Next, it clarifies how the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha is revealed through the myriad phenomena;
because the Tathāgatagarbha pervades the Dharma-realm and manifests according to karma, this constitutes the third [point]:

the simultaneous negation and illumination that reveals the empty and non-empty Tathāgatagarbha, for the Tathāgatagarbha transcends thought, mind, and verbal discourse. This follows from the preceding...
The World-Honored One initially elucidated that the three categories and seven elements are all the Tathāgata-garbha.

Because Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra did not yet understand this meaning, he raised two difficulties. His first difficulty was: "If it is pure and fundamental by nature, how could the mountains, rivers, and great earth suddenly arise?
This was due to his confusion regarding the principle of following karma; therefore, the World-Honored One first answered by establishing the objective realm through the logic of causality.

This shows that all things arise through the manifestation of karma; it reveals that while the nature of the myriad dharmas is true, their appearances are fundamentally illusory, such that appearances are entirely formed from this nature.
Second, regarding the question that the seven elements pervade everywhere yet cannot coexist:

this stems from not understanding that the seven elements are fundamentally based on the awakened nature (*prakṛti-vijñāna*). The World-Honored One first stated that the substance of space is not among the various appearances.
Yet I do not reject those various manifestations; rather, I employ them as metaphors to show that the seven elements are all the wondrously enlightened nature of clarity.
This reveals that although the characteristics of the myriad dharmas are illusory, their nature is fundamentally true, for the entirety of these characteristics is itself the nature.

It is because you turn your back on enlightenment and unite with the dust that you perceive characteristics but do not perceive the nature; it is because I turn my back on the dust and unite with... [enlightenment].

Because of awakening, one perceives the nature and does not perceive marks; having reached this point, the seven elements following karma have been clarified, and the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is also manifest.
Yet, while it may still be conceivable, its wondrousness has not yet been revealed.
Little do they realize that the Tathāgatagarbha cannot be discussed in terms of identity, nor can it be discussed in terms of non-identity; it cannot be discussed in terms of separation, nor...

If one argues that the Tathāgatagarbha is not distinct from earth, water, fire, and wind, then the vision of the noble ones should be identical to the deluded vision of ordinary people, and ordinary people should see reality as the noble ones do; thus, there would be no two truths.

Conversely, if one argues that the Tathāgatagarbha is not identical to earth, water, fire, and wind, then the ordinary and the noble would be eternally separate, and ordinary beings would be incapable of attaining realization.

If the Noble One were to discourse on the Tathāgatagarbha by means of what is not earth, water, fire, or wind, then when ordinary people perceive form, their vision would be identical to the Noble Wisdom’s perception of emptiness, and there would be no distinction between the two truths.

If, however, he were to discourse on the Tathāgatagarbha by means of what is not non-earth, non-water, non-fire, and non-wind, then ordinary people’s perception of form would remain eternally separated from true emptiness, and they would never attain sainthood. It is only at this point [that the distinction is resolved].
This reveals that the wondrous mind of the Tathāgatagarbha cannot be described as sound, yet it constitutes the essence of wondrous śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna;
this corresponds to the "Contemplation of the Total Extinction and Non-Reliance" within the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*. Therefore, it is said:
"Regarding this contemplated true emptiness, one cannot say it is identical to form, nor can one say it is not identical to form; furthermore, one cannot say it is identical to emptiness."
Not immediately [identifying with] emptiness, all dharmas are neither negatable nor non-negatable; this very statement cannot be accepted.
It is utterly extinguished and has no locus of reliance; it is beyond the reach of words and beyond the attainment of intellectual understanding. This is the sphere of practice. Why is this?
Because the moment the mind arises or a thought moves, one immediately deviates from the essence of the Dharma and loses right mindfulness.

How can the sentient beings of the three realms of existence in the world, as well as the world-transcending śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, use their minds of limited knowledge to fathom the unsurpassed bodhi of the Tathāgata, or employ worldly language to enter the Buddha’s wisdom and vision?
It is like the lute, the zither, the harp, and the lute: though they possess exquisite sounds, if there are no skillful fingers, they can never produce them—just so with you and all sentient beings.
It is likewise so with the precious, awakened true mind, which is perfectly complete in each and every being.

Just as when I press my finger, the Ocean-Seal manifests its radiance, yet when you briefly stir your minds, the afflictions of worldly toil arise first; this is because you do not diligently seek the unsurpassed path of enlightenment, but instead cherish the Lesser Vehicle and consider a little attainment to be sufficient.
This rebuke of Pūrṇa charges him with failing to practice diligently and instead engaging merely in verbal disputation to spur his progress.
It states that while the Tathāgatagarbha— the wondrously luminous source of the mind— is thus, worldly sentient beings nonetheless use their limited,
finite minds to measure the Tathāgata’s infinite realm, further employing the worldly five elements and their principles of birth and overcoming (sheng-ke).
If one speaks with the desire to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) states:

"The spheres of realization attained by the śrāvakas—in which body, mind, and speech are all utterly extinguished—can ultimately never reach that direct realization of the nirvāṇa manifested by the Tathāgata;
how much less can they fathom the Tathāgata’s sphere of complete enlightenment with a mind of discursive thought?"
Even if one were to take fireflies to burn Mount Sumeru, they could never set it ablaze;
likewise, if one gives rise to the mind of saṃsāra and views of saṃsāra while entering the Tathāgata’s great ocean of tranquil extinction, one can never reach it.

Thus, we know that what is called the "Buddha’s knowledge and vision" in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* possesses only its name but has not yet realized its actual substance; it is only in this sutra that the Buddha’s [knowledge and vision] is clearly elucidated.
To know and see that these three contemplations are perfectly interfused and quiescent within the single mind, the *tathāgatagarbha* nature, is as follows:
below, another analogy is raised to encourage this. "You and the dharma" corresponds to the precious, awakened true mind being fully perfected in each instance;

"the lutes, harps, and so forth all possess wondrous sounds" corresponds to the fact that while they all possess wondrous sounds, there is a distinction between those that emit sound and those that do not. This is because [the latter] lack the wondrous [mind].

The fingers and the marvelous fingers are merely names; when I say that I have attained this in my mind and respond with it in my hands, it is because a single press of the finger causes light to radiate brilliantly, illuminating heaven and earth so that all become marvelous functions—this is a metaphor for having marvelous fingers that produce marvelous sounds.
You, however, raise your mind but find only the dust of afflictions filling your eyes, and the myriad phenomena [obstructing you].
That the myriad phenomena do not manifest their wondrous function is like having no wondrous finger that can produce a wondrous sound.
The reason they do not manifest this wondrous function is none other than this: you have obtained only the price of a single day’s worth of nirvana and consider it a great gain;
because you are unwilling to advance in the cultivation of the unsurpassed path of enlightenment, they do not manifest. If you were willing to advance in cultivation...

He walked hand-in-hand with the Tathāgata so that they would never deceive one another; thus the *Zongjing* says: "When joy gathers into extraordinary tones, pressing a finger causes the notes of *gong* and *shang* to accord with the rhythm.
Humans possess the nature of awakening; when their wisdom and skill are refined, their function accords mysteriously with the Way.
Gain and loss rest with the person; refinement and coarseness depend on oneself. Therefore, when the Sugata pressed his finger, he emitted the light of the Ocean-Seal Samādhi."
When sentient beings raise their minds, they manifest the signs of affliction. Nāgārjuna said: "The nature of the mind of sentient beings is like a sharp blade used only to cut mud;
the mud is not formed, yet the blade is worn away by the sun. The principle of its substance is eternally wondrous, yet sentient beings themselves are coarse.
If one uses it skillfully, it immediately accords with its original wondrousness."
Pūrṇa said: "I and the Tathāgata’s jewel-like awakening—perfectly luminous, truly wondrous, and pure mind—are non-dual and complete.
Yet, though I have long been in saṃsāra due to beginningless delusion, I have now attained the Noble Vehicle and am still not yet ultimate.
World-Honored One, since all my delusions are now completely extinguished and I alone possess the wondrous, true, and eternal, I venture to ask the Tathāgata: regarding all sentient beings..."
For what reason do they have delusions that obscure their own wondrous clarity, causing them to undergo this drowning?

This is an exhaustive search for the cause of delusion, intended to sever it. From the words "I and" (*wǒ yǔ*) below, it refers to the Treasure-Awareness True Mind (*pǎojué zhēn xīn*), which is perfectly complete in each and every being;
yet in the past, I encountered beginningless false conceptualization, and suddenly, from the preceding state, [delusion] arose, and I have long been in saṃsāra.

The phrase "This person" refers back to the preceding continuity. "Now he has attained" refers below to the love and attachment for the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), where one considers a small attainment to be sufficient.
"World-Honored One" refers below to the analogies of gold ore, wood, and ashes. "I venture to ask" is the formal request regarding the cause of delusion.

He says that although his views and afflictions (*kleśa*) are exhausted, ignorance (*avidyā*) still remains; since he does not know the cause from which delusion arises, it is only fitting that the World-Honored One [explain it]. Five.

Abiding in the exhaustion [of all phenomena], while the two types of death have ceased, one alone is wondrous, true, and eternal; this is called Great Enlightenment. It must be that its knowledge of the cause of delusion is certain.
I venture to ask: by what cause do all sentient beings exist? Why does delusion arise? My previous question was:

"How can that which is fundamentally pure suddenly give rise to the world? The World-Honored One answered that it arises because of ignorance (*avidyā*). Now I ask: as for this ignorance, furthermore...
For what reason do you say that one must "directly exhaust the matter to its very bottom"?
The Buddha told Pūrṇa: "Although you have removed your doubts, other delusions remain.
I shall now question you again regarding various matters currently manifest in the world. Have you not heard of Yaśoda in the city of Śrāvastī, who suddenly, at dawn—"

In the morning, one looks at one's face in a mirror; one loves the head, eyebrows, and eyes visible within the mirror, yet one becomes angry and reproaches one's own head for not seeing its own face and eyes, thinking it is a shapeless *chimei* (demon) and runs about wildly. What do you think? For what reason does this person run about wildly without cause?
Pūrṇa said, "This person’s mind is deranged; there is no other reason. The Buddha said, "The wondrous enlightenment and perfect clarity are fundamentally..."

Since the perfect, luminous, and wondrous [nature] is designated as delusion, how can it have a cause? If it had a cause, how could it be called delusion? From these various deluded thoughts, they mutually condition one another;
accumulating delusion upon delusion, they have passed through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust. Even though the Buddhas have revealed this, they still cannot turn them back.
Such a cause of delusion exists inherently within delusion itself. When one recognizes that delusion has no cause and that delusion has nothing to rely upon—[this is the end of delusion].
Since there is no arising, what is there to extinguish? Those who attain Bodhi are like people at dawn recounting the events of their dreams;

though the mind may be sharp and clear, for what cause or condition could one take hold of things within a dream? How much more so when there is no cause and they have never existed from the beginning?

It is like that person in the city, Yan-rda-da-da (Śaṇḍha), who ran away in fear of his own head—what cause or condition was there? Yet, when his madness suddenly ceased, his head was [already there].
It is not obtained from without; even if one does not cease their madness, what has been lost? Pūrṇa’s deluded nature is thus:
for what reason would it exist?
Hereafter, by means of an illustration, it is revealed that delusion originally has no cause and arises abruptly. It says: "You already know."
The continuity of existence arises from causes and conditions; the seven elements are governed by the following of karma.

The Tathāgata’s wondrous enlightenment does not give rise to mountains, rivers, or the great earth, yet you do not realize that these are fundamentally illusory and without cause, and thus you vainly seek their cause. Therefore it is said:
"Although you have removed your doubts, other delusions remain. Right now, should there happen to be a single matter before your eyes, I shall immediately take this as an occasion to [instruct you].
When you have clarified this, you will thereby know its falsity.
Have you not heard of the story of Yanjadatta, who, losing his head in confusion, mistook a reflection for a goblin and ran about wildly?
Indeed, this Datta had never lost his head; he was no goblin himself, yet he suddenly imagined himself to be one and ran about in a state of frantic madness.
As for this madness, from what cause does it arise? "Yajñadatta" (演若達多) means "Sacrifice-Granted" (*Cisou*), as he was obtained by praying to a deity.
When Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra was questioned by the World-Honored One, he immediately answered clearly:
"This man merely developed a derangement of mind and ran away; there is no other cause. The Buddha’s words below clarify the matter by illustrating it through a concrete event.
Because Pūrṇa understands the phenomena but is deluded regarding the principle, I shall guide him by means of what he clearly perceives.

Because it transcends all else, it is called "unsurpassed"; and since Great Compassion is the foremost among all the Buddha’s merits, it is mentioned alone.
The stainless maṇi jewel produces whatever is desired and bestows it inexhaustibly; the Buddha is likewise thus, and is therefore called the "Pure Jewel King.
Regarding the phrase "well opening my mind": it means that previously, due to the weeds of causal conditions, my mind was blocked and unable to attain awakening;
now, through the World-Honored One’s threefold instruction, my mind has attained clarity and illumination, and is thus said to be "well opened" by various causes and conditions.
"Zhe" (者) is like using the head to infer its lack of cause, and using madness to infer its lack of conditions. "Ti" (提) means to rouse and awaken to alert one against deluded attachments;
"jiang" (獎) means to encourage and exhort to shake off weariness and indolence; "yin" (引) means to guide and support; "chen" (沉) means to sink into or be submerged by;
"ming" (冥) means to be obscured by darkness; "ku" (苦) refers to hatred and love. Below this, the World-Honored One specifically requested [the assembly] to enter.
This is the gateway to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. "Knowledge" refers to the "knowledge of clearly knowing for oneself" mentioned in the preceding text;

"containing and nurturing" means encompassing and giving birth to. The Tathāgata is the primary retribution (*vipāka*), and the *kṣetra* (land) is the environmental retribution (*niśraya*). [The text] says:
"I have long possessed this vast nature of enlightenment, which is inherently pure and pervades the Dharma-realm, containing and nurturing the ten directions, yet I was unaware of it."
I did not realize that the World-Honored One was using various skillful means to guide, encourage, and lead me toward awakening.
Compared to my former state, I have already undergone a transformation; I am exceedingly fortunate.

Thinking that by understanding this single matter, all matters would be resolved and I would have nothing further to attend to, I was unaware that the Tathāgata would still rebuke me for having no merit in my extensive learning.
It is not as good as practicing untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) for a single day. This *tathāgatagarbha* nature has no walls in the ten directions and no gates on the four sides;
there is no way to enter it. It is just like a traveler who, though granted a house by the Heavenly King, cannot enter it at all because he cannot find the door.
Therefore, one seeks instruction on the place where one enters. Muzhou said: "You all..."
Have you all yet found a point of entry? If you have not yet found a point of entry, you must seek one.
Once you have found a point of entry, you must not fail the old monk; therefore it is said:
"To find its gate is to equal all Buddhas in a single morning. If you do not find its gate, you will not see its inner chamber.

Because of my fondness for this family [of the Dharma], after awakening to the mind that conceals within, I have again requested to enter the gate. When asked, "How does one gain faith and entry into this Mirror of the School?

the answer was: "Simply by not moving the single mind and not dwelling in any phenomena, such that there is no realization of subject and object and the mind of intellectual understanding is extinguished—this is the faith of non-faith and the entry of non-entry."

When both person and phenomena are empty, subject and object are simultaneously quiescent. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Binding one's缘 (ālambana) to the dharma-dhātu, in a single thought-moment [one knows] the dharma-dhātu;
knowing the true dharma-dhātu, one should not waver. If one says, "I have entered the dharma-dhātu," one has already moved from the dharma-dhātu.
When both subject and object are forgotten and the very aspect of "entering" is quiescent, then non-movement within the dharma-dhātu is itself the entry into the dharma-dhātu.
Therefore, if there is one who can realize, there is a person; if there is something realized, there is a dharma.

Since there is no dharma outside the single true *dharmadhātu*, one cannot use the *dharmadhātu* to further realize the *dharmadhātu*. The "entrance" (*praveśa*) explained in the following text is intended to demonstrate this.
[The phrase] "I beseech you below" is the formal request to arouse the bodhicitta. Regarding the term "obscuration" (*āvaraṇa*), it is said to be "enveloped."
"Coma" refers to the "darkness" of mind, meaning those who have already realized the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* of the Hīnayāna;
it causes them to abandon the Hīnayāna and attain the Great Fruit (*mahāphala*). It is not known what kind of mind should be generated as the path of entry.

Furthermore, it instructs those below to request the severance of delusions, meaning those like us who have not yet realized the four fruits (*catur-phala*), whose mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) still persists in the world.
Since the World-Honored One does not permit the use of the mental consciousness to observe and subdue [the mind], by what means, then, are those past objects of attachment restrained,
so that one may subsequently attain the dhāraṇī and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision?
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas in the assembly who were not yet masterful regarding the bodhicitta,
and for the sake of sentient beings in the future age of the Dharma’s decline who shall resolve to attain bodhicitta after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
proclaimed the path of wondrous cultivation of the Unsurpassed Vehicle to Ānanda and the great multitude, declaring: "You all must resolutely resolve to attain bodhicitta."
Regarding the wondrous samādhi of the Buddha-Tathāgata, one should not give rise to weariness; rather, one should first clarify the two definitive meanings of the initial awakening of the bodhicitta.
First, the two meanings are briefly indicated: for those whose bodhicitta is not yet autonomous, whether they have already awakened the mind in the present time or...
Whether advancing or retreating without yet having reached a decision refers to the Unsurpassed Vehicle, which is the Buddha Vehicle.

The "wondrous path of practice" means that by means of this path, one proceeds directly to the Buddha Vehicle. "Not giving rise to weariness" means that upon attaining this path, one does not linger at the illusory city.
"That which ought to be" indicates what must necessarily be employed. "Arousing the initial resolve for enlightenment" [is the beginning].
This awakening is itself bodhi; it means that from the very first desire to give rise to the bodhicitta, one must never abandon these two meanings.
If the first meaning—the mind of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-citta*) as the *tathāgatagarbha*—is absent as the cause, there will be no way to realize the supreme fruit.
If one does not know the second meaning—the mind of the flowing consciousness of present karma—as the root of karma, there will be no place [for realization].
Because the mind must be subdued, it is essential to decisively examine the cause of the mind and to decisively examine the fundamental nature of karma.
How are the two meanings of the initial mind determined? Ānanda, as for the first meaning:

if you wish to cast aside the vehicle of the Śrāvakas, cultivate the Bodhisattva vehicle, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, you should carefully observe the mind that gives rise to the causal ground and its relation to the fruition.

Are the stages of realization identical or different? Ānanda, if one takes a mind subject to arising and ceasing as the fundamental practice while seeking the Buddha-vehicle of non-arising and non-ceasing, such a thing is impossible.

For this reason, you should clearly observe that all conditioned phenomena within the vessel-world are subject to transformation and extinction. Ānanda, consider the various things in the world that can be made...
Among all phenomena, what is there that does not decay? Yet, one never hears of empty space decaying or rotting. Why is this? Because space is not something created;

therefore, from beginning to end, it is without destruction. Thus, within your own body, that which is solid is earth, that which is moist is water, that which is warm to the touch is fire, and that which moves is wind.
By means of these four entanglements, they divide your profoundly still, perfect, wondrous awareness and clarity.
The mind functions as seeing, hearing, sensing, and discerning; from beginning to end, these five aggregates are turbid. Why are they turbid?
Ānanda, it is like clear water, which is pure and pristine by nature, while dust, soil, ash, and sand are by their very substance obstructive and solid.
These two entities are such that their natures do not accord with one another. Suppose there were a person in the world who took some of that earth and dust and threw it into [the water].
In pure water, when its capacity to retain [impurities] is lost and its clarity is gone, its appearance becomes turbid; this is what is called "turbidity.
Your five layers of turbidity are likewise thus.
This is the answer to the first question by means of the primary truth (*paramārtha*). The primary truth is that which was previously explained as the first...
The single ultimate truth is the *tathāgatagarbha*-mind; as it is called in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* the "nature-as-such, the ultimate mind," it is said:
"In this assembly of dharma, among the dragons and elephants, you should contemplate the ultimate truth. It says:
"If you all truly desire to abandon the Lesser Vehicle and cultivate the Bodhisattva practice to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, you should employ this subtle and esoteric [teaching]."
Contemplate and examine in detail whether this mind at the stage of the cause and the awakening at the stage of the fruition are the same or different;
because the final secure barrier is not separate from the very first thought-moment, you are made to contemplate them with scrutiny.
This is because all that Ānanda has previously employed has been the mind of causal conditions and birth-and-death, never having used the mind that is neither born nor extinguished.
The mind of the first principle arises and perishes, like quicksilver or silver ore; when subjected to smelting, it flows away.

The mind that is neither arising nor perishing is like refined gold, possessing real functional efficacy. Now, because you wish to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, you must first cause them to examine this:
only by taking the mind of the ultimate truth as the primary cause and condition can one enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata appears in the world for the sake of one great cause and condition. This refers precisely to this point.
As for what is called "arousing the mind" (*cittotpāda*), it means that this awakened mind is fundamentally pure and pervades the entire Dharma-realm;
however, because it is entangled and suppressed by the two obstacles, it does not arise. If this mind is brought to full development, then regarding the fruit of Bodhi—
What must be awakened to? The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "There is a great sutra scroll, equal in measure to the three thousandfold world system, contained within a single mote of dust;
it is so for all motes of dust as well. There is a person of wisdom whose eye of insight is entirely clear and pure;
they break open the dust and bring forth the sutra scroll, extensively benefiting sentient beings. If one develops this mind within the causal stage and realizes it directly, [this is it].

If you take this very mind and extensively cultivate the myriad practices, then every instance will reach ultimate realization and every affair will become firm and solid, flowing into the ocean of wondrous adornment;
it will be like water poured into water, perfectly harmonizing and merging.
If you do not take this as the causal-ground mind, but instead employ the birth-and-death consciousness produced by the karmic seeds perfumed by former names and words, [you will fail].
To seek the fruit of Buddhahood while taking [deluded] causes as one's foundation is like striking ice to find fire or digging the earth to find heaven;

how could such things ever be obtained? Therefore, those who seek the Buddha Vehicle must carefully examine the causal mind. The *Zongjing* says: "If one encompasses the preceding, one encompasses the subsequent;
it is like taking the first step that one immediately reaches the destination of a thousand-li journey. If one attains the One, all else is attained."
It is like observing the moon in the sky and thereby comprehending all its reflections in the water. The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"If one is separated from the initial arousal of the thought [of enlightenment], then the unsurpassed path will not be accomplished. Therefore, it is said that all merits reside within the initial mind.

For this reason, it instructs one to carefully observe whether things within the vessel-world (the physical universe) undergo destruction or remain indestructible, using this as an analogy for whether the mind undergoes arising and ceasing.
"You should contemplate everywhere the meaning of non-arising and non-ceasing: all conditioned phenomena in the world are subject to change and decay;

only empty space is indestructible because it is without fabrication. Thus you shall know that by taking the mind of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) as the cause, one attains the ultimately indestructible diamond body;
whereas if one takes arising and ceasing as the cause, even after many kalpas, [it will not be attained]."
Because it is subject to formation and destruction, those who seek the Buddha Vehicle must carefully examine the causal mind.

However, this nature of non-arising and non-extinction is not separate from the present consciousness of arising and extinction; it is simply because it is clouded by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*) that it cannot be seen.

Therefore, one is instructed to observe it with detailed scrutiny. The "four entanglements" (*catvāraḥ paryavasthānāḥ*) refer to the four great elements, for one is bound and constrained by these four elements.
Because one cannot attain mastery over them, they are called "entanglements" (*paryavasthāna*). That which is primordially pure and free from turbidity is called "tranquil" (*zhan*);
that which is primordially pervasive and without partition is called "perfect" (*yuan*). "Subtle and wondrous awakening" (*miaojue*) is the essence; "luminous mind" (*mingxin*) is the function.

You possess this tranquil, perfect, subtle, and wondrous awakening—the luminous mind that is primordially pure and naturally pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm. One [awakening] constitutes four [attributes].
When greatly entangled, it is not all-pervasive; when split into the six sense organs, it is no longer its original state; when transformed into the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), it is not pure.

Thus, from beginning to end, it constitutes the five turbidities. As for the beginning and the end: the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) is the beginning, and the turbidity of life-span (*āyuṣ-kaṣāya*) is the end.
How does the following metaphor clarify the characteristics of these turbidities? Clear water is a metaphor for pure awakening, while silt and dust represent the turbidities.

The analogy of the four great elements and the six sense organs refers to their respective categories; "obstructive" means having physical form and mass; "dharmatā" means naturalness or spontaneity; "following and conforming" means compliance.

"Gul-ming-gul" (汩湣汩) indicates the state of being turbid. This clearly demonstrates that the fundamentally pure awakened mind originally has no interaction whatsoever with the four great elements and the six sense organs;
it was only because that first thought suddenly arose at the beginning that the distinction between subject and object was created.
Because the pure awakened mind is obscured by turbidity and thus not seen, it is said: "Your turbidity [is such that] the five layers are likewise so.
As the subsequent passage states: "The self-mind grasps at the self-mind; through what is not illusory, illusory dharmas are formed. The character *qu* (to grasp) is the root of this turbidity.

Ānanda, do you see how empty space pervades the worlds of the ten directions? When the perception of emptiness is not distinguished, there is "emptiness" which lacks substance and "perception" which lacks awareness;
these interweave to form delusion. This is the first layer, called the *kalpa-turbidity* (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). Your body currently manifests as a composite of the four great elements as its substance;
seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are congested and obstructed, while water, fire, wind, and earth rotate to produce sensory awareness. These interweave.

The false formation of this constitutes the second layer, called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). Furthermore, within your mind, the recollection, cognition, chanting, and study of natures give rise to knowledge and vision, which appear as the six sense objects;

yet when separated from the objects there is no form, and when separated from awareness there is no nature. These characteristics interweave through falsehood to form the third layer, called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
Moreover, morning and evening, your births and deaths ceaselessly continue, and your knowledge and vision constantly desire to remain fixed upon...
The karmic fortunes of the world constantly shift within the realms of the land, which are falsely constituted through interweaving;

this is the fourth layer, called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). You who see and hear [these things] originally possess no different natures; yet, separated by the various sensory dusts, you manifest as distinct beings without cause.

Within your fundamental nature you recognize one another, yet in your functions you turn away from one another. Having lost the standard for identity and difference, they interweave and falsely constitute [this state]; this is the fifth layer, called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).

The turbidity of life (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*). This specifically clarifies the characteristics of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*). All five aspects of these turbidities are explained here based on the present moment;
first, the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). The Sanskrit term *kalpa* is translated here as "time period" (*shifen*). It refers to the moment when you raise your head and look once at the sky.
The two have no boundaries and each pervades everywhere; they cannot be analyzed apart.

Space originally has no substance, yet because of your single act of seeing, you perceive the vast and boundless expanse as "space. Seeing originally has no cognition; yet because space enters the eye, you know that which is bright and clear as "seeing.
Thus, that which has no substance acquires substance because of seeing, while that which has no seeing remains without substance.
Because the knower has awareness by virtue of emptiness, when one perceives emptiness, it becomes a continuous, dense mass;
this is precisely what is meant by turbidity, and because it is a state of temporal impurity, it is called the *kalpa-turbidity*.

As it is with the perception of emptiness, so it is with the perception of form. "Your body," and so forth, clarifies the turbidity of perception through grasping. This means that when you entered the womb...

Absorbing the essence of the father and the blood of the mother, you have formed this body of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are originally a single, pure brilliance, fundamentally free from obstruction.
Because of the blockages caused by your four great elements, you are unable to transcend them; thus, that which was unobstructed has become obstructed.
Earth, water, fire, and wind are originally not a single thing and fundamentally lack sentience, yet they are permeated by this essence.
The clarity takes possession of the objects to give rise to perceptions; where there was no cognition, there now arises awareness.
Thus, the six sense organs and the four great elements interweave delusive appearances to form a turbid mixture that obscures the true nature—this is called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*).
When the six organs are mentioned individually as "view," one is cited to encompass the rest. Furthermore, from "Moreover, you... onwards, he explains the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kāṣāya*).
It is precisely this mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that recollects, recognizes, recites, and practices, capable of taking the objects of the three periods of time as its domain.

This nature of mental consciousness arises from the six sense-faculties (*indriya*); because the faculties can give rise to consciousness, the characteristics of this mental consciousness manifest within the six sense-objects (*viṣaya*).

Since consciousness can cognize objects, it follows that apart from objects there are no characteristics of mental consciousness, and apart from the faculties there is no nature of mental consciousness; therefore, one knows [the existence of] the faculties.

When the dust-sensations and consciousnesses are mixed together as one, giving rise to greed, anger, and so forth, which turbidify the true nature, this is called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kāṣāya*).
Furthermore, from "Moreover, you... onwards, it clarifies the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kāṣāya*). Knowledge and vision are the master; karmic destiny refers to good and evil karma.
It means that although this physical body is the master that appropriates [existence], it is concerned with every step; yet, there is nothing one can do against the power of karma.
Because change does not permit one to act as its master, those who wish to remain cannot stay forever due to the shifting power of karma;
those who wish to depart cannot leave immediately because they are retained by their host. Thus, departure and remaining become intermingled in a single place, turbidifying the true nature;
this is called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). Because this karmic movement is the common lot (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of these sentient beings, it arises.
The basis is named the turbidity of sentient beings. [The phrase] "You all" and below explains the turbidity of lifespan:

it is because your six sense-faculties are originally one body; they are divided into six locations by these four entanglements. Since they are like members of the same household, they cannot be called different;

yet since each opens its own gateway from within their nature, they cannot be called the same. Thus, while they turn away from one another in their functioning, they are identical only in their being.
Because the distinction between the two cannot be fixed, it is called "loss of standard. Thus, oneness and difference are like warp and woof woven so densely that they cannot be separated;
lacking autonomy, they turbidify the true nature—this is called the turbidity of life-span (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*).
These five turbidities have been unclarified since the single thought-moment when [the mind] became obscured and turned into emptiness; therefore, their characteristics are shown.
Below, he further imparts the method for clarifying turbidity:
"Ānanda, if you now wish to cause seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition to reach far back in accord with the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity,
you should first select the root of birth and death and rely upon the nature of the unarisen and undying, perfect and tranquil essence, to revolve that tranquility against its own delusions."

By extinguishing birth and subduing it, one returns to the source and awakens to the fact that the fundamental luminous awareness possesses a nature free from arising and ceasing; this serves as the mind for the ground of practice.
Only then does one fully realize the cultivation and realization of the ground of fruition. It is like settling turbid water by storing it in a still vessel;

when the water is deep and motionless, the sand and silt naturally sink, and the clear water appears before one—this is called the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions. When the mud has been removed and only pure water remains, this is called...

Having eternally severed the root of ignorance, its characteristics are pure and refined; all manifestations do not become afflictions, but are entirely in accord with the pure and wondrous virtues of nirvāṇa.
Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are themselves the profound, perfect, and wondrous awakening—the luminous mind that differentiates. That which is differentiated is the causal mind.
The four virtues—constancy, bliss, self, and purity—are the contemplation of the fruit;
these four virtues now serve as the basis for cultivating the causes according to one's root-nature, and thus they are first established here as the standard.

It is said that when you are in a state where clarity and turbidity are not yet distinguished, you wish to use these four virtues within the causal stage to remotely accord with the four virtues of the Tathāgata’s fruition; there is a specific method for doing so.
One should first resolve the fundamental cause of birth and death. Previously, Ānanda took the six consciousnesses and the three poisons to be the root of birth and death;
he did not realize that this was merely the Tathāgata’s skillful means for leading those of inferior faculties out of the triple world, and not the ultimate reality.
Now, because Ānanda seeks unsurpassed bodhi, [the Buddha] causes him to first discern the nature of death.
The root of birth and death does not depend on the six consciousnesses of arising and ceasing;
it is fundamentally formed by the nature of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍāyatana*), which are originally unarisen, undying, perfect, and tranquil.

This nature of being unarisen and undying, perfect and tranquil, is precisely that which you have hitherto neglected, yet which the World-Honored One has declared to be "this mind. As for this root of birth and death, it is that which you have hitherto employed.
The World-Honored One rebuked them as being "not the mind," yet these six consciousnesses that arise and perish are in truth not other than this;

they originally proceed from the perfectly湛 (zhàn) and pure nature. Therefore, by means of this perfectly湛 and non-arising, non-perishing nature, one turns back the two kinds of false arising and ceasing—those within and those without the boundaries—causing them to turn their minds back so that they do not leap about in restlessness, but instead submit and return to purity.

The Awakened One takes this pure awakened mind as the causal ground of the mind; just as when gold is fashioned into vessels, every vessel is gold, so too can one perfectly fulfill the cultivation and realization of the ground of fruition.

This causal mind corresponds precisely to what follows in the text: from the first stage, the Stage of Generating the Mind (*cittotpāda-vihāra*), up to Equal Enlightenment (*samaya-jñāna*), it is called the "cultivation of wondrous awakening," and its realization is called "attestation. This is like the analogy of clarifying water below, where the stillness of the vessel corresponds to the perfection [of the fruit].

The profound root-nature is like sand and soil; when combined with adventitious dust, it constitutes the ignorance within the realm (*dhātu*), and when combined with fundamental ignorance, it constitutes the ignorance beyond the realm.
If these two types of ignorance are both exhausted, then the characteristic of clarity becomes pure and refined, entirely free from even the slightest obscuration.
Consequently, whether one feels anger or joy, acting as one pleases, there are no further afflictions, and everything is in accord with Suchness.

[The Master said: "This accords with the characteristics of the eternal, blissful, self, and pure. [The disciple] asked: 'If we examine the causal mind, why must it necessarily involve seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing?

[The Master] answered: 'It is because these four entanglements divide your profoundly still, perfect, wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind into the functions of seeing, hearing, sensing, and observing.
Thus, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are entirely the wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind. This being so, since they arise through seeing...'"
Turbidity is produced through hearing, cognition, and awareness; clarity is likewise achieved through hearing, cognition, and awareness. This is what is meant by:
"Having fallen from the ground, one must rise back up from that very ground. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"For example, if a wild elephant enters a pure pool of water, it will cause the water to become turbid. If a 'water-clearing jewel' is placed in the water, it immediately becomes clear and pure; one cannot say [that the water was originally impure]."
Outside of water there is neither the elephant nor the pearl; the mind is also like this. When afflictions enter the mind, they can cause the mind to become turbid;

when various wholesome dharmas such as compassion enter the mind, they can cause the mind to become pure. Thus, defilement and purity are not fixed, and truth and falsehood arise according to conditions.
If one is deluded by them, then moment after moment one revolves in saṃsāra and loses the true nature. If one illuminates them, then thought after thought [one realizes it].
The quiescent and perfect realization of *nirvāṇa* is like using one wedge to extract another, or using the coarse to meet the coarse;
if one does not cling to delusion, even "emptiness" need not be spoken of, for illusory shadows will subtly vanish and the flames of wisdom will subside.

Regarding the second meaning: if you all truly desire to give rise to the bodhicitta and generate great courage and resolve within the Bodhisattva Vehicle, you must thoroughly examine the root of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Since beginningless time, who has created these karmic actions that moisten rebirth, and who receives them? Ānanda, if you cultivate bodhi without carefully observing the afflictions...
Fundamentally, one cannot know the false roots and objects; since one does not even know where the inversion lies, how can one subdue it to attain the stage of Tathāgata?
Ānanda, observe those in the world who untie knots: if they do not see what was knotted, how could they know how to untie it?
You have not heard of empty space being torn asunder by you. Why is this? Because emptiness has no form or characteristics.
Because of the binding and the unbinding, your present eyes, ears, nose, tongue, as well as body and mind—these six acting as thieves and intermediaries—plunder the family treasure from within.
Due to this, since beginningless time, the world of sentient beings has been entangled in fetters; therefore, they are unable to transcend the vessel-world.
Previously, because the mind of the causal ground was defined as non-arising and non-ceasing, the primary meaning (the first sense) was indicated;
here, because the consciousness-stream of present karma is taken as the root of death, the secondary meaning is indicated to answer the second question.
The intent is that one who wishes to enter the mind of the primary meaning of non-arising and non-ceasing must resolutely turn toward the "second head" to see forms and hear sounds.
To directly apprehend the sphere of sound and thereby practice in reliance upon the six sense organs is the matter of the "second head";
thus it is compared to the second moon. As the former masters have said: "The first phrase refers to one who, through direct apprehension, is fit to be a teacher of all Buddhas;

the second phrase refers to one who, through direct apprehension, is fit to be a teacher of humans and devas. All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) are precisely these "old" [conditioned] things.
At that time, the causal dharmas being cultivated are based on the grasping consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as the root of the afflictions that initiate and moisten karma;
they do not realize that the flowing consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) is the root of the afflictions that initiate and moisten karma.

This is because where karma does not initiate is precisely where the mind is truly initiated, and when the mind does not moisten is precisely when there is true non-arising; therefore, cause them to examine this closely.

To examine in detail who performs the karma that moistens rebirth and who undergoes its results: the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) constitute the substance of the eight consciousnesses (*aṣṭa-vijñāna*).

These six organs induce the arising of the six consciousnesses and various afflictions (*kleśa*), acting as the cause of suffering. The six consciousnesses then create karma, which invites birth and death as the fruit of suffering.
While a coarse analysis suggests that only the six consciousnesses create karma, a subtle investigation reveals that it is actually the six sense organs that do so.
One's own actions manifest as retribution experienced by what appears to be only the six consciousnesses, yet the six perishing aggregates are likewise received by only the six sense organs;
thus, for those who seek clarity, it is made evident that the eight consciousnesses act and receive their own retribution, rather than the six consciousnesses alone.

Once one understands that the *ālayavijñāna* (karmic consciousness) creates karma and receives retribution, one will know that it is only by transforming this *ālayavijñāna* that one can give rise to the bodhicitta and realize the fruit of enlightenment.
Therefore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The seven consciousnesses do not transmigrate; they do not experience suffering or pleasure, nor are they the cause of nirvāṇa.

As for the Tathāgatagarbha, it experiences suffering and pleasure, and is accompanied by their causes; it arises and ceases. Thus, we know that the root of birth and death is not the six consciousnesses.
Ānanda, the following passage uses a reductio ad absurdum to show that those who wish to practice cultivation must certainly understand these afflictions.
If one does not know the root, then one will not know from where the body, the environment, and the world arise through delusion;
if one cannot even know the place from which delusion arises, how can one subdue the habitual攀缘 (pān-yuan) of the past in order to seek the fruit of the Tathāgata’s wondrous enlightenment?
For the One True Dharma-realm is fundamentally non-existent [in terms of arising].
The faculties and their objects arise from a single moment of non-awakening, whereby the false duality of subject and object is produced, leading to perversion.
Because of this perversion, the six consciousnesses are induced, arising and ceasing in an endless cycle of transmigration.

Therefore, if one desires to attain wondrous enlightenment, one must first know the place where perversion originates. Below, an analogy is used to clarify that without recognizing perversion, one does not know how to subdue it.
This is of the same intent as the following passage: "If one does not know the knot, then one does not know its untying.

That the knots can be untied yet are ultimately empty of both knotting and untying is a metaphor for the fact that while the knots of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) can be untied, the wondrous nature of awakening is fundamentally devoid of both knotting and untying.
Thus, the subsequent section correctly identifies the six sense-faculties as the knots and the locus of inversion; these "six" refer to the six [sense-faculties].
The essence descends into the two faculties—the ultimate and the phenomenal—and, confronting the six objects, forms the substance of the knots;

this is precisely the locus of perversion. With these six faculties acting as intermediaries, they summon internal thieves who plunder the treasures within the Tathāgatagarbha, scattering them abroad so that they have no place of return. People perceive only the six consciousnesses.

They are robbed of their family treasures by internal thieves, yet they do not realize it is these internal thieves who rob them of their family treasures. In truth, these are the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).

Thus one knows that the arising of delusion is created by the six sense faculties, the commission of karma is created by the six sense faculties, and the receiving of retribution is created by the six sense faculties;
even the robbing of the family treasures is likewise performed by the six sense faculties. These six sense faculties are, in fact, the very knot of birth and death. Therefore, it was said previously:
"Who creates and who receives? This refers to the "self-robbed" state, which is the locus of response.
The world of sentient beings is the *indriya-kāya* (the body of the faculties), while the vessel-world is the *bhājana-loka* (the physical environment).

It is said that these six faculties form knots because they all arise from the four entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), which divide your profoundly still, perfect, and wondrous awareness into seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing; thus, vision does not transcend form.

Because hearing does not produce sound and so forth, they become interwoven and form a knot; thus we know that when the faculties are bound, one cannot transcend the world, but when the faculties are liberated, one can then transcend the sensory objects.
Ānanda, what are called the "sentient beings" and the "world"? "World" refers to the constant flux of change, and "realm" refers to spatial orientation. You now—
One should know that east, west, south, north, southeast, southwest, northeast, northwest, above, and below constitute the directions;
past, future, and present constitute the time periods. Thus, there are ten spatial positions and three temporal flows.

All sentient beings, through the interweaving of their delusive thoughts, construct their bodies and exchange within these worlds, interacting with one another; yet, although the nature of these realms is established as fixed positions throughout the ten directions, [it remains fundamentally non-dual].
It should be understood that in the world, there are merely the directions of east, west, south, north, above, and below; there is no fixed position in between and no intermediate points.

These four numbers must be clearly understood as interacting with the world: three times four and four times three result in twelve, which, through successive transformations and tripled iterations, become one thousand, two hundred, and ten—comprehensively encompassing the beginning and the end.
Thus, within each of the six sense faculties, there are individually one thousand two hundred merits.
This is stated in terms of the world of sentient beings to reveal the number of the six sense organs. Since the mind is fundamentally without time, it is also without spatial location;
therefore it is said that "the ten ages of past and present are not separate from the present thought-moment, and the boundless ocean of lands is not divided from the tip of a hair.

However, as soon as one engages in conceptualization, there is spatial location; once there is spatial location, there is a fixed measure. Once there is a fixed measure, there is... [the limitation of the six organs].
Because there is a definite measure, there is movement and flux; thus, the *dhātus* have the ten directions and the *adhvan* (time) has the three periods.
The directions have limits, while time has flux, like warp and woof. All sentient beings are formed by the interweaving of the world and its phenomena to constitute this body;
therefore, the world and the *dhātus* exist within the body, their exchange and flux never ceasing for a moment.
Those who dwell therein simply do not know it themselves; it is like a strong man carrying another on his back while running, whom the one in the dark does not perceive.
Within the ten directions of the realms, only the four cardinal directions are taken as primary, while the four intermediate corners are not taken because they are not primary.
The zenith and nadir are not taken because they lack fixed positions, and the central position is not taken because it lacks a definite location.
Therefore, we take only the three periods of time and the four directions as they intersect;
since the three periods and the four directions intersect, their number is twelve, and the four directions and the three periods intersecting likewise number twelve.
"Flowing change in three layers" means that through the process of shifting and transforming, one becomes three layers. "One, ten, hundred, thousand" refers to [the progression of numbers].

Wuxing said: "To speak of 'increasing by one' as ten, 'increasing by ten' as a hundred, and 'increasing by a hundred' as a thousand—let us now clarify these three layers of multiplication as they apply to the world.
First, regarding the four directions, each is discussed in terms of the three periods [past, present, and future], totaling twelve.
Second, within the three periods of the eastern direction, one is transformed into ten, resulting in thirty; this applies likewise to the south, west, and north."

It is likewise thus: thirty in each of the four directions make one hundred and twenty; thirdly, by transforming ten into a hundred within the thirty of the eastern direction, they become three hundred;
the same applies to the other three directions, so that there are three hundred in each of the four directions, totaling one thousand two hundred.
By applying this principle to the world’s engagement with the directions, the pattern can be understood; such is the natural determination of this world-system.

As for the numerical values, they are like the "fifty numbers of the Great Derivation" (*dàyǎ zhī shù wǔshí*): using ten to multiply five, or using five to multiply ten, these are likewise fixed numbers.
However, because the *Yì* condenses [the elements] into the five phases (*wǔxíng*), it uses fifty; whereas this [text], because it condenses [the elements] according to the world, uses twelve.

These three times and four directions are subsumed within the non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*) of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), as they depend upon the sense faculties (*indriya*).
Because the six sense organs are provisionally established as states of form and mind, their merits are all inherently complete within their own substance, with none lacking perfection.
Thus, by showing how they increase from few to many across the three periods of time and the four directions, their perfection is merely revealed.
Furthermore, these merits are discussed collectively as that which ordinary beings possess; they are not the supreme functions of true nature. It is just as follows:
The subsequent passage states that the three faculties of ear, tongue, and mind are each "thousandfold and twofold" more complete than the other faculties;

this merely indicates they are slightly more developed, for how could it mean they pervade the entire Dharma-realm? Thus, we know that for the True Sage, the merits of the six faculties are all immeasurable.
Ānanda, you should further determine the relative superiority or inferiority among these faculties. For instance, the eye perceives that what is behind is dark while what is before is bright;
the front is entirely illuminated while the back is entirely in shadow; when looking to the left and right, it perceives only two-thirds of the surroundings.

In summing up the meritorious functions performed, it is incomplete by one-third. Thus, when speaking of its efficacy, it possesses only one-third virtue. You should know that the eye possesses only eight hundred merits, just as the ear does.
Listening pervasively throughout the ten directions without omission, whether movement is near or far, in stillness there is no boundary.

You should know that the faculty of hearing possesses one thousand two hundred merits. As for the nose smelling odors, it passes through the inhalation and exhalation of breath; there is out-breath and in-breath, yet it lacks the intermediate junction.
When examined against the three parts of the nasal faculty, it lacks one part. You should know that the nose possesses only eight hundred merits. As for the tongue...
In proclaiming all mundane and supramundane wisdom, his words possess method and order, and their principles are inexhaustible.

You should know that the faculty of the tongue is perfected with twelve hundred merits. Just as the body perceives touch and recognizes whether it is adverse or favorable—distinguishing them when they meet, yet being unable to perceive "separation" when they are apart;
and how the single, the combined, and the dual are verified through the faculty of the body, lacking one of these three parts—you should know [the same applies here].
The body possesses eight hundred merits of adaptability, silently containing all mundane and supramundane phenomena of the ten directions and three periods of time;

whether saintly or ordinary, there is nothing it does not embrace, reaching to the very limits of existence. You should know that the faculty of mind possesses one thousand two hundred merits of perfection.
In the preceding section, superiority and inferiority were not distinguished because the discussion concerned the mutual interaction of worldly phenomena;

here, however, we discuss the functional capacities of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*) in order to facilitate the selection of faculties. Thus, the relative superiority and inferiority of the organs are determined by their completeness or deficiency. Regarding the "two-thirds" of the eye faculty, the Master says:

[the field of vision consists of] two hundred *li* in each of the four cardinal directions and one hundred *li* in each of the four intermediate corners; this is the extent currently perceived by the eye.
When one looks at the front and the three sides to the left and right, there are already six hundred [parts]; adding the two corners in front, they total eight hundred.
Because the rear side and the two corners behind are not seen, it is said to be "two-thirds. As for the statement that the faculty of hearing listens all around without omission:
when drums are struck in the ten directions, they are heard from all ten locations; thus, when hearing a sound, it seems as though it is near.
When distant objects are not heard, there is in reality neither near nor far; therefore, it is called a "perfect faculty. Regarding the deficiency in the middle of the nose-faculty, Wēnlíng says:

"The outgoing [breath] can grasp the fragrance, while the incoming [breath] can smell the fragrance; because there is no capacity in the interval between the outgoing and incoming, it is deficient in the middle.
Chángshuǐ says: "The outgoing, incoming, and the interval between them together constitute three parts. One part consists of four hundred [units], and it is deficient therein."
Because the middle and the tongue intersect, there are only eight hundred [faculties] of the tongue-root;

it is said that while the function is partial, the principle is inexhaustible, for a single phrase contains immeasurable meanings, and both coarse words and subtle speech possess ultimate truth. Mount Gu said:

"This refers to the capacity to speak and does not concern the tasting of flavors; if one were to take the tasting of flavors as the primary function, its efficacy would be inferior, as it is subsumed within the 'middle' cognition."

The body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is distinct from that which is "separated," "united," or "both"; for when separated, it does not know [objects], whereas when united, there is sensation, as well as opposition and compliance, thus possessing two parts.
As for the mental faculty (*manas*) being "silent and receptive" (*maurkha-sahana*):

this means that this mental faculty is able to receive perfuming, maintain seeds, and silently accommodate all phenomena of the ten directions and three periods of time, including both mundane and supramundane, whether pertaining to ordinary beings or sages.
There is nothing that does not include it, exhausting its very limits; therefore, it is perfect and complete.

Ānanda, if you now wish to go against the current of the flow of birth and death and trace it back to its source until you reach the state of non-arising and non-ceasing, you should examine these six faculties of sensory reception:
which are conjoined and which are separated? Which are deep and which are shallow? Which is the most perfectly penetrating (*pariṣphuṭa*) and which is not?
If you can, O Manjuśrī, awaken to this faculty of perfect penetration, you will be able to reverse that beginningless stream of deluded karmic activity and follow the path of perfect penetration;
