compared to those with imperfect faculties, your progress will increase by a factor of ten million times a hundred thousand years. I have now fully revealed the magnitude of the merits inherent in these six kinds of profound, perfect luminosity.
Choose from among them according to your own preference; once you have selected the one through which you may enter, I shall clarify it for you so that you may attain realization.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions have all attained the supreme enlightenment through the complete perfection of their cultivation within each of the eighteen realms;

in this regard, there is no superiority or inferiority among them. It is only because you, being of inferior capacity, have not yet attained the perfect wisdom of mastery therein that I proclaim this teaching to cause you to enter deeply through a single gate. Once you have entered one [gate] without delusion, those other six will follow.
The faculty of knowledge is pure all at once.

Having previously determined that the root of birth and death consists of the six faculties, and having subsequently revealed that the merits of these six faculties may be complete or deficient, this [section] now causes one to select which among the six faculties constitutes the "perfect faculty. (Reversed order)
The "Word" (or Name) is the wondrous function by which one turns from the mundane toward the sacred. By following these six sense faculties, birth and death begin;
by reversing them, saṃsāra ceases. To flow outward and rush toward forms is to follow; to turn back the flow and return to the One is to reverse.

Not following what preceded and not pursuing what follows both constitute the meaning of reversal—just as in the *Yījīng*, the trigram Earth over Heaven (*Dìtiān*) forms the hexagram *Tài* (Peace/Thoroughfare).

When Heaven and Earth form the hexagram Pi (Obstruction), Earth and Mountain form Qian (Humility), and Mountain and Earth form Biao (Stripping Away), these all represent contrary principles. Therefore it is said:
"The five elements flow in regular order, yet the great earth is a pit of fire; the five elements are inverted, yet the great earth is the Dharma-treasure.
One must know that in the practice of cultivation there is no other subtle artifice; this single word "contrary" encompasses everything without exception. Thus it is said: "You..."
Now, wishing to go against the current of the flow of birth and death, you seek to trace back to the very root of that flow in order to reach the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing.
Since there is fundamentally no manual for manual labor, you ought to examine these six sense faculties through which experience is received:
which perceives when in contact, and which perceives when at a distance; which is deep and difficult to fathom, and which is shallow?

It is easy to discern who possesses the necessary equipment and who lacks it. If you can examine and investigate within these six faculties of enjoyment to realize which one is the faculty of perfect penetration, then by tracing this perfect faculty back to its source, you will seek to enter the non-arising and non-ceasing state from the flow of birth and death;
thus, its merit shall be compared against that of the faculties which are neither detached, nor profound, nor perfect.

The measure of their virtues is like that of the sun, increasing tenfold with each successive kalpa; this meaning subtly reveals that the faculty of the ear is difficult to master, profound, and perfect.
While the eye is detached yet not perfect, and the tongue is perfect yet not detached, the mind is both detached and perfect, yet it is not pure in its detachment.

This is because, prior to the mind, the first five faculties—though detached—are not uniform in their conjunction, as they all take objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as their domain, whereas [the ear] takes the present as its object.

Regarding objects, when the mental faculty (*manas*) is able to perceive three types of objects—objects not accompanied by names or designations, objects perceived without deliberative thought, and objects that are the combination or separation of the five sense faculties—it is therefore not purely "detached" (*li*).
Now, since the ear faculty can both grasp objects from within detachment and hear all around without omission, it is both detached (*li*), pervasive (*yuan*), and profound (*shen*). Now, as for me...

I have fully revealed the six kinds of profound stillness and perfect luminosity—the merits originally possessed by you—which involve separation and union, depth and shallowness, completeness and deficiency;
each aspect has been clearly explained. You may now choose from among them according to your own inclination and preference.
Wherever you find a point of entry, I shall further elucidate it for you, so that you may proceed directly forward without falling back into decline. However—
I certainly wish for you to choose for yourself rather than having me choose for you; there is a reason for this.

The Dharma-eye of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions is perfectly clear and their sagely nature penetrates all phenomena—whether in accordance with or contrary to them, they all become skillful means.
In reality, there is no superiority or inferiority, nor is there anything to be selected or rejected. It is only because your faculties are dull that you have not yet attained perfect penetration.

Because sovereign wisdom is not exempt from obstruction at the gates of the six sense organs, I have directed you to select one gate alone among these six and enter deeply until you reach the state beyond birth and extinction.

If you enter deeply through one gate, the remaining five organs will be simultaneously uprooted, and you shall attain liberation without expending further effort. Thus far has been the secret instruction.
The section on the faculty of hearing is concluded; what follows provides further clarification in response to a question.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how is it that by flowing against the current and penetrating deeply through a single gate, one can cause all six faculties to become pure simultaneously?"
Because his understanding of these causes was not yet clear and penetrating, he followed upon the two preceding points to request further instruction. His intention was this:

wishing to turn back the current of desire within birth and death to reach the state of non-arising and non-extinction, he did not know what constitutes that current of desire in birth and death which he ought to reverse;
furthermore, since the merits of the six sense faculties possess degrees of superiority and inferiority, each faculty must be distinct.
"How is it that by entering deeply through a single gate, all six gates simultaneously attain purity? Only upon hearing these words of inquiry does one understand the intent of the answer.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "You have now attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* and have already extinguished the worldly existence of sentient beings within the three realms."

Even regarding the afflictions to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), which have accumulated through beginningless empty habituation within the faculty of "I do not yet know" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), their habitual tendencies must depend upon the abandonment of those [afflictions] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) for them to be eliminated;
how much more so, then, is this the case for the specific divisions and enumerations of arising, abiding, change, and cessation?

This first answers the characteristics of the stream that must be countered. *Srotāpanna* (須陀洹) is translated here as "Stream-enterer," meaning that in the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), one enters from the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) into the state of a noble one (*ārya*), attaining the first fruit and thus entering the stream of the noble ones.

The afflictions to be abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya-kleśa*), namely the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), are also called the "stream of views. This refers to the arising of discriminative views when the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) encounters mental objects (*dharma-viṣaya*).

Therefore, because the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) cause one to transmigrate through the three realms and prevent liberation, by severing these afflictions of view, one realizes the first fruit and enters the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Among the latent tendencies accumulated since beginningless time, those that are empty habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) consist of eighty-one grades of the afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*);

they are also called the flow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the flow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the flow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*). Regarding the "flow of desire," it refers to the five [desire realms].
The root craving for the five sense objects is called the "afflictions of volition" (*saṃskāra-kleśa*), namely greed, hatred, delusion, and pride.

Because one wanders through the desire realm due to these afflictions of volition and cannot escape it, they are called the "outflow of desire. As for the "outflow of existence" (*bhava-āsrava*), it refers to the non-extinction of cause and effect;
this denotes the afflictions of volition in the form and formless realms, namely greed and pride. It is because of these afflictions of volition that [one remains bound].
Because one wanders through the realms of form and formlessness and is unable to achieve liberation, it is called the "flow of existence" (*bhava-srotas*).
Because there is no clear understanding, it is called "ignorance" (*avidyā*); specifically, this refers to delusion (*moha*) among the afflictions of the three realms.
Because one wanders through birth and death due to this flow of ignorance and cannot achieve liberation, it is called the "flow of ignorance. By severing these three flows, one realizes [nirvana].

Since the four fruits—from the second fruit and the third fruit up to the stage of the candidate for arhatship (arhattva-pratipannaka)—are all termed the "path of cultivation" (bhāvanāmārga), the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation are so called;
how much more so those factors such as arising, abiding, change, and cessation, and their respective divisions and enumerations?

Here, "among them" refers to within the sense bases (*indriya*), because apart from the *ālayavijñāna*, the various afflictions would have no basis for existence. As for "arising, abiding, change, and cessation," these refer to the [four characteristics of conditioned phenomena].
This refers precisely to the afflictions (*kleśa*) severed by Bodhisattvas; Tiantai identified these as the "view-delusions and thought-delusions beyond the realms" (*jiewai jiansi*).

According to the *Awakening of Faith*, among the three subtle states (*sanxi*), the second—the mark of karma (*yesiang*)—is the mark of birth (*shengxiang*). Following the three subtle states, the latter two of the six coarse states (*liucuxiang*) constitute the mark of abiding (*zhuxiang*).
Among the six coarse states, the third and fourth constitute the mark of difference (*yixiang*), and the fifth constitutes the mark of destruction (*xiesiang*). And...

Sixth, regarding the allocation of the specific number of categories: this refers to the total of forty-two grades from the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) up to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*).

[The Buddha] says: "Although you have now severed the outflows of views and attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), you still have not yet exhausted the afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) within the realm of desire; how much more so for the views and thoughts outside that realm? All of these are yours..."

Regarding those points that should be reversed and turned back when exhausted: the three emptinesses and six knots established in the subsequent five fascicles all arise from this, and that which is severed by the stage of the realization of the Way (*prativedha-mārga*) is also this very thing.
"Now, observe for a moment these six faculties before you: are they one, or are they six?
Ānanda, if you say they are one, why does the ear not see, why does the eye not hear, why does the head not tread, and why do the feet not speak?
If these six faculties are definitively established as six, then as I now proclaim this subtle and wondrous Dharma-door to the assembly, which of your six faculties has come [to listen]?"
Ānanda accepted these words. The Buddha said, "I heard with my ears; you heard with your own ears—what concern is this for your body or mouth?
Your mouth came to inquire about the meaning, while your body rose to show reverence. Therefore, you should know that it is not one, yet it culminates in six; it is not six, yet it culminates in one.
It never ends as your sense-faculties, yet it is fundamentally one, which becomes six. Ānanda, you should know that this faculty is neither one nor six, because from time without beginning..."

Because you have come from amidst inversion and decline, the meanings of "one" and "six" arise within your perfectly湛 (zhan) and profound state. Although you, O Srotāpanna, have attained the dissolution of the six, you have not yet lost the "one.
It is like the great void of space which merges with all vessels; because the shapes of the vessels differ, the names given to the space within them differ.
When the vessels are removed and one contemplates the space, one speaks of the space as being "one. But how can that great void of space be made to become the same as you? No.
How much more so when one speaks of them as being either identical or non-identical? Thus, your understanding of the six faculties of reception is likewise so.
Hereafter, wishing to answer the question regarding the meaning of "one" and the "purity of the six," [the text] first distinguishes that fundamentally there is neither one nor six. It says:
Since you do not understand why one [root] resolves into six purities, you should carefully examine whether these six faculties present before you are ultimately one or ultimately six.
If they were one, then the ear could see and the eye could hear;
the head could tread and the feet could speak. But now, this is not so. If they were six, then as for the body and speech...
Since the ears are each independent of one another, why is it that at the time of inquiring about the Dharma, the ear can only hear after the body has paid homage and the mouth has asked?
Therefore, you should know: if it were not one, it must be six, because they are mutually exclusive in their functions;
if it were not six, it must be one, because they are interconnected in their nature. It is certain.
Your root-essence does not possess a fixed one, nor does it possess a fixed six.

Since there is neither a fixed one nor a fixed six, that which now appears as one or as six arises entirely from the beginningless, single moment of delusion, wherein [the mind] becomes firmly bound with the external six sense-objects, intermingling and alternating with them; thus do the ordinary beings of the five turbidities come to be.
Those who cling to them as the six latent roots of the seeker (śaikṣa) grasp them as but one.

Now, although you have realized the first fruit and do not enter the six sense-objects, and though you have attained the dissolution of the six, it is certain that you still cling to the empty habitual tendencies within the six faculties;
these have not yet been eliminated, and thus you have not yet transcended "one. This is because you cannot eliminate the seeds of the one and six faculties, each of which remains fully present.
It is only natural that you do not understand the meaning of "one essence" and the "purity of the six faculties.
Furthermore, the way the profound, perfect, and wondrous nature descends into the six sense organs is like the vast void accommodating various vessels;

because the vessels differ, one speaks of the void as being different, but if one removes the differences of the vessels, one speaks of the void as being one. Whether it is one or many depends entirely upon the shapes of the vessels; how could the vast void itself possess oneness?
One should know that when the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) meet, there is duality; when the organs and objects do not meet, they become one.

This oneness and duality depend entirely on whether the organs and objects meet or do not meet; it does not mean that your profoundly perfect and wondrous nature inherently possesses either one or six.
Therefore, know that when the organs and objects are bound together, they are bound together as one; when they are liberated, they are liberated as one.
Due to the two types of phenomena—light and darkness—interacting within the wondrous perfection, they adhere to the stillness and give rise to vision;

the essence of vision reflects forms, and by binding these forms, the sense organ is formed. The source of this organ is termed the "pure four great elements," and its substance is named the eye, resembling a cluster of grapes.
This floating root pursues the four sensory objects, rushing toward forms. Due to the two types of phenomena—motion and stillness—clashing within the wondrous perfection...
From the viscous stillness, hearing is activated; the essence of hearing reflects sound, and as sound rolls back, it forms the faculty.
The root of this faculty is termed the "pure four great elements. Its substance is like a freshly curled leaf. This floating faculty flows toward the four objects, rushing toward sound.

Through the two conditions of penetration and obstruction, it activates the wondrous perfection within. From the viscous stillness, smelling is activated; the essence of smelling reflects fragrance, and as it takes in fragrance, it forms the faculty.
The root source is designated as the pure four great elements; the substance of the nose is like a pair of hanging claws.

The floating faculties flow and rush toward fragrances, and through the intermingling of the two types of phenomena—tranquility and transformation—within the wondrously perfect [state], they adhere to the limpid clarity and give rise to tasting.
The essence of tasting reflects flavors, and by binding flavors, the faculty is formed. The root source is designated as the pure four great elements; the substance of the tongue is thus named.

Like the crescent moon at its first appearance, the floating faculties flow outward toward the four sense-objects, rushing in pursuit of flavors through the mutual friction of the two types of contact—separation and union.
Within the wondrously perfect sphere, this adhesion to stillness gives rise to cognition; the essence of cognition reflects upon contact, and by grasping that contact, the faculty is formed.

The source of this faculty is termed the "pure four great elements," which serve as the cause for the physical body, resembling the drumhead of a waist-drum. The floating faculties flow outward toward the four sense-objects, rushing in pursuit of touch.

Due to the two kinds of continuity—arising and ceasing—within the wondrous perfection, the clarity becomes adhered to, giving rise to cognition; this cognitive essence reflects phenomena and grasps them to form the sense organs.
The source of these organs is termed the "pure four great elements," which serve as their cause. This is called "mental intention" (*manas*), like seeing floating objects in a dark room;
the physical roots flow outward and rush toward phenomena.
This clarifies that the knots of the faculties arise from sense objects. Now, the profoundly still, perfect, and wondrous mind is fundamentally free from attachment;

it is like a bright mirror in which all images appear. When a single thought of deluded movement arises, it becomes adhered to the two objects of light and darkness, and this clinging to the profound nature triggers the manifestation of the seeing-nature. However, at this stage, the knots of the faculties have not yet been formed. Once—
Furthermore, the visual essence again interreflects with the two objects—light and darkness—and merges with them in a single place;

it then gathers and binds these two objects to form the sovereign sense organ (*indriya*). Since this organ is composed of the original pure four great elements (*mahābhūta*), it is called the "root-source" and designated as the "pure four great elements.
However, being subtle and difficult to manifest, it is perceivable only by the divine eye of a sage.
Only now can it be seen; therefore, its substance is manifested by the clusters of grapes, while the floating roots serve merely as the support for the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
"Flowing out and rushing toward forms" means that this essence of vision relies upon those two roots to flow outward. Thus, the *Zongjing* says:
"There are two kinds of roots: there are the pure five material roots (*pañca-rūpīndriya*) and there are the floating roots."
If the five material faculties (*rūpīndriya*) are pure, the five material faculties have as their essence pure matter that is invisible and resistant (*anidarśana-sapratigha-rūpa*).
They are capable of producing the five consciousnesses and possess the function of illuminating objects;

that is to say, there is a portion of pure matter within the eye, like clarified butter (*sarpis*). Because this matter exists, visual consciousness arises; if it does not exist, it does not arise. As the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
The atoms of the eye-faculty are distributed laterally upon the pupil and abide there, covered by a clear membrane like crystal (*sphaṭika*), such that they do not obstruct one another.
The atoms of the ear-faculty are situated within the ear-cavity, coiled around like a rolled birch-bark scroll.
The atoms of the nose-faculty are located inside the nasal bridge, with their backs upward and their faces downward, like a pair of fingernails. [The atoms of the tongue-faculty...]

The atoms of the sense-faculties (*indriya-paramāṇu*) are distributed across the tongue in the shape of a full moon; the atoms of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) dwell pervading the parts of the body according to the dimensions of the body’s form.
As for the five "dust-like" faculties (*rajas-indriya*), they are the supporting bases for the pure faculties (*viśuddhendriya*);

they illuminate objects as their own substance, yet they cannot themselves illuminate objects because these dust-like faculties are coarse, manifest matter that serves as the support for the pure faculties. By virtue of this...
"Dong" (movement) below explains the "ear-knot. "Ji" (striking) has the meaning of stirring; that which does not omit either the clear or the turbid is called "Juan" (rolling up).
"You" (thereby) below explains the "nose-knot. "Fa" (arousing) means to induce; that which both receives and permeates is called "Na" (receiving). "You" (thereby) below explains the "tongue-knot.
That the five flavors enter into one another is called "Can" (intermingling); chewing their flavor finely is called "Jiao" (twisting). "You" (thereby) below explains... [the body-knot].
The "body-knot" (*kāya-grantha*) refers to the intersection of cold and warmth, which is called *mā* (contact); *bha* means to grasp or seize.

The "waist-drum" (*kaṭaka-muraja*) is the small waist-drum, commonly called the *janggu* (staff-drum), consisting of the head and the body. This is explained according to the intent of the *Śrī-lalita-vistara-sūtra*.

Regarding the term "mental intention" (*manas*), since the nature of the mind (*manas*) is deliberation, the "floating root" of the mind is the physical heart-mass (*māṃsa-piṇḍa-citta*), as described in the *Saddharma-smṛty-upasthāna-sūtra*.
This refers to that which resembles a lotus flower opening and closing; within it there is a single aperture.

This occurs because at the very moment one first absorbs the semen and blood of the parents, the consciousness (manas) immediately attaches itself to the center and rushes toward the phenomena—namely, the shell of ignorance (*avidyā*).
However, because it cannot be seen by people while within the body, the character "thought" (*si*) is used to clarify that it possesses volition.
The "locus of cognition" (*pramāṇa-sthāna*) refers to its site of operation. For example, one who is in a dark chamber can see things, whereas one who is in the light cannot;

while one situated in darkness can see various objects within the light, it is the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*) that resides in this realm of profound obscurity and silent stillness, acting as the strategist and planner for the five preceding faculties. It is for this reason that its mode of knowing is described in these terms.
This is the essence; it refers to what was stated in the preceding text: "Because this world gives rise to fetters, one is unable to transcend the vessel-world (bhājana-loka).
What is called a "knot" is identical to a "fetter."

Ānanda, it is thus that these six faculties arise from that awakened clarity; because there was clarity within clarity, the clarity of awakening was lost, and its essential discernment became defiled by attachment to delusion, causing light to manifest.

Therefore, at this moment, when you are free from darkness and free from light, the essence of seeing does not exist; when you are free from motion and free from stillness, the substance of hearing fundamentally has no reality.
Without penetration and without obstruction, the nature of smelling is not produced; it is neither change nor tranquility, and the sense of tasting has no point of emergence—it does not depart.
It is not appropriate for sensation to arise, for fundamentally there is neither arising nor ceasing; thus one understands where peace may be found.
This restates the previous argument that because of sense-objects there is bondage, thereby clarifying that because of being free from sense-objects there is no bondage.

It states that these six faculties all result from the substance of the nature-awareness, which is profoundly luminous; through a single movement, it transforms into the "luminous awareness" that acts as the subject of illumination.

Consequently, one loses the essence of awakened clarity and precise discernment. From this, vision arises by adhering to light and darkness, and hearing is formed through the binding of movement and stillness;
"etcetera light" refers to the essential radiance of the six sense organs, such as the light of the eyes or the light of life.

This is precisely the formation of knots by grasping at sensory objects. Therefore, apart from light and darkness, there is no nature of seeing; apart from movement and stillness, [there is no nature of hearing].
Thus, when the essence of hearing and so forth are absent—meaning they are detached from their objects—there is no "knot.

These terms, such as the "substance of seeing" and the "materiality of hearing," refer to the substance of the knot itself and do not refer to the fundamental nature (dharmatā). Because Ānanda mistakenly identified them as such, he gave rise to the doubt expressed in the following passage regarding annihilation.

You need only not follow these twelve conditioned characteristics—movement and stillness, union and separation, tranquility and change, penetration and obstruction, birth and death, light and darkness—but by uprooting even one of them, you will detach from the clinging and settle within. Settling in the fundamental reality, you will give rise to the original radiance;
as this luminous nature shines forth, the remaining five types of clinging will be spontaneously uprooted and liberated, without depending on the perceptions and views arising from external objects.
"Clarity does not follow the sense organs, yet it manifests by relying upon them; thus the six organs function interchangeably for one another.

Below this, he teaches that when separated from their objects, the "one" dissolves and the "six" vanish, for fundamentally there is neither one nor six. "Not following" means not complying with [the senses].
This character "not" (bu) is precisely the bridle and rein that restrains the rushing toward forms and sounds. It is the same as [the teaching] mentioned previously.
The characters "ni" (inverse), "fan" (opposite), and "xuan" (revolving) carry the same meaning:

they tell you that if you wish to prevent the six faculties from flowing after the six objects, you should select one perfect faculty as your point of entry. Focus your mind on this, concentrating all your strength upon it, and extract it first.
If one faculty is thus made to detach externally while remaining subdued internally, so that the faculty and its object no longer couple together, then...

The familiarized gradually becomes the nascent, and the nascent gradually becomes the familiarized; naturally, one returns to subside into the essence of the primordial brightness and original enlightenment.
From this point on, there is no further clinging to delusions, and the radiance is emitted so that the originally possessed, eternal light is revealed in its solitary clarity.

If this one faculty is thus uprooted, then the remaining five faculties are simultaneously uprooted at that very moment; this is what is meant by "one faculty returning to the source, and all six faculties [returning] together."
When liberation reaches this point, externally one does not follow after objects and internally one does not trace the sense-faculties;
the constant light manifests before one, which is a state of reflective illumination. This is merely a provisional reliance upon those faculties to manifest the appearance of seeing and hearing.
Although this does not alter the functions of the ears and eyes, in reality, seeing and hearing do not actually employ the ears and eyes. Thus, with respect to a single faculty—
It is able to perform the functions of the various sense organs; this is precisely the entry into the one non-delusive state, wherein those six faculties of cognition are simultaneously purified.
Thus, the *Zongjing* says: "Constantly illuminating and eternally radiant, even the Iron Ring Mountains cannot conceal its brilliance;

pervading all realms and all of space, the vast heavens cannot cover its essence. How could it rely on external objects to trigger its illumination, or give rise to cognition in response to confronting objects?"
Spontaneously quiescent, numinous awareness is profoundly still and boundless.
Ānanda, do you not know that within this assembly, Aniruddha sees without eyes;
the Nāga Upananda hears without ears; the goddess of the Gaṅgā perceives fragrance without a nose; and Gavāmpati possesses a distinct tongue?
The Śūnyatā-deva named Jñānāsvāda has no body, yet he perceives touch when reflected within the light of the Tathāgata, appearing for a moment;

since his substance is that of wind, his form is fundamentally non-existent. Even for Śrāvakas who have attained the meditative absorption of total cessation and reached quiescence—such as Mahākāśyapa here in this assembly, whose mental faculties have long been extinguished—he possesses a perfect and clear understanding that does not depend on mental thought.
This is because it is feared that ordinary and inferior practitioners would not believe in the mutual functioning of the six sense organs; therefore, this is cited to prove [the point].
Aniruddha is translated here as "Free from Poverty"; Upananda is translated as "Worthy Joy";
Gaṅgā is the name of a river, translated as "Heavenly Descent," because it flows from Lake Anavatapta at the summit of the Snowy Mountains; Gavāmpati is translated as...
The ox-headed man was an ox-herder. Śunyata means "emptiness" and refers to the deity who presides over emptiness.
Kāśyapa means "Drinker of Light. Aniruddha perceived with his mind; the dragon heard with its horns;
Pāṭali knew flavors with its tongue; and the deity of emptiness perceives touch without a body, for this deity has remained bodiless for many kalpas.
When the Tathāgata for Suffering emits the light that uproots suffering, the body briefly manifests contact, and the bliss is beyond description;

the gods of the formless realm are likewise similar. For those who cultivate the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the discriminating and co-emergent forms of self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*) associated with the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are entirely severed;
thus, there is no mental activity. The *Lun* (Treatise) states: "It is like a snake hearing with its eyes; it is not necessarily [the case that]..."
One need not suspect that the dragon Bāḍananda is like a blind eel that can travel through water only by obtaining a shrimp;
nor need one suspect that Aniruddha is like an ant that uses its body as a nose;
nor need one suspect that the goddess Gaṅgādevī is like a bee that uses its thorax as a tongue. It is just as [the sūtra] says:
Wind has no form; when an object resists it, it becomes turbulent. One need not doubt that this is the *śūnyatā* (or *śunyata*) spirit. Alas!
Sentient beings contend over the mere few inches of their mouths, ears, noses, and tongues, regarding color, fragrance, flavor, and touch as distinct from one another—is this not to be pitied?
Gu Shan said: "The six individuals, such as Nanda and the others, are perhaps ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) experiencing the retribution of their karma."

These are the attainments of the Lesser Sages, all achieved through deluded power; they do not even rely upon their own sense faculties, let alone achieve perfect liberation. How could there not be mutual functioning?
Ānanda, if your various faculties were now completely uprooted, such that they shone with inner clarity, then these ephemeral objects and the physical world—
All the various manifested forms of the world are like ice melting in hot water; as soon as they are contemplated, they transform into supreme awakening.

This passage refers to the faculties and the body; since these have already transcended, the physical environment likewise transcends. Because the two dharmas of the faculties and their objects are understood through the same understanding, the six faculties are simultaneously uprooted.
When the inner clarity emits light and one attains the Dharma-nature body, then the ephemeral physical vessel [is transcended].
When mindfulness corresponding to the realms up to light and darkness, motion and stillness, and so forth, is fully realized as the Dharma-nature land,
one knows that as long as the six sense faculties have not been liberated, not only is the external vessel-world unable to attain mastery,

but the body of the faculties themselves is likewise unable to attain mastery. Once the six sense faculties are liberated, not only does the body of the faculties attain great mastery, but the vessel-world also attains it.
Because they possess mastery, practitioners need only understand that the sense organs (*indriya*) are empty; there is no need for the labor of exiting the realm of the world.
This mastery over worlds is like that of Avalokiteśvara, who attains the thirty-two transformations to enter the bodies of various lands.

Thus, within the realm of sentient beings, from time immemorial, they have been bound internally by the six sense organs and externally by the six sense objects, such that every path they encounter manifests as a sensory field.
The emotions arising from what one beholds are like those of a monkey, whose six sense-faculties are all sticky; they resemble insects and larvae, which settle upon every object of the senses.
Thus, vision does not transcend the realm of form, and hearing does not escape the dust of sound.
Like fish cast into a net or birds trapped in a cage, one is blocked in both advancing and retreating, like a ram butting against a fence—trembling with fear at once.
If one can regard the world as a nest of fledgling swallows upon a curtain, and know that dust is consciousness and that objects are the mind itself,

then one will not be constrained by the passage of time— neither prolongation nor brevity— and will not be turned by the distinctions of magnitude. Thus, one can respond to objects through manifested traces, accede to conditions according to their capacities,
remain unmoved within the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), and manifest emanations throughout the entire Dharma-realm.

Ānanda, it is like those worldly people who gather their vision upon the eyes; if one were to suddenly close them, the appearance of darkness would manifest before them, and the six sense organs would become dark and indistinct, yet the head and feet would still resemble each other.
If that person were to run their hand over the exterior of their body, although they do not see, they can distinguish the head from the feet;
thus, perception and awareness are identical. Since seeing depends on light, when darkness arises, seeing ceases; yet if there is no light, seeing manifests of itself. From this, you should know.
Since the characteristics of darkness can never again obscure the faculties and sense objects have already dissolved, how could the awakened clarity not become perfect and wondrous?

This passage cites how ordinary people obtain vision without depending on light, thereby proving that [the faculty of sight] does not follow the physical roots but is manifested through them by relying upon them.
As for "concentrating the seeing in the eye," it means that the nature is fundamentally all-pervasive, yet the deluded do not know this and merely say:

Vision arises because of light; apart from light, there is no seeing. Suppose that while people are properly relying on light for vision to occur in the eye, they suddenly and abruptly close their eyes:
then the appearance of darkness manifests before them, no different from the other sense faculties.
Furthermore, if someone were to stand directly in front of them, the six faculties would remain dark and one would no longer perceive anything.

As for the head and the feet, when a person with closed eyes uses their hand to trace and stroke the body of another, although they do not rely on their eyes, they distinguish the head and feet clearly and without confusion.
Thus, what is known in the dark is no different from what is seen in the light; therefore, we know that seeing relies upon light.
If one were apart from light, there would be no seeing. If seeing could arise spontaneously without relying on light, then this would be the characteristic of non-illumination;
yet, how could the natural, quiescent illumination of spiritual awareness ever be interrupted?
This is that which light cannot illuminate and darkness cannot obscure. Who, then, can say that seeing must rely upon light to exist? Therefore...
A student asked a former master, "What is great compassion with a thousand hands and eyes? He replied, "It is like a person at night who finds their pillow by touch.

He continued, "If even an ordinary person's faculties can perceive things without relying on light, how much more so for one whose sense-faculties and objects have been dissolved and whose true radiance is uniquely revealed?
Such a person cannot fail to attain perfect penetration and achieve great sovereign mastery."
"How extraordinary!

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: 'World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, if one seeks the permanently abiding mind within the causal ground, it must correspond in name and designation with the state of fruition.
World-Honored One, if within the state of fruition there are bodhi, nirvāṇa, true thusness, and the Buddha...'"

The nature of the *āmalaka*-consciousness, the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, and the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom—these seven designations are distinct in name, yet their pure and perfect essence is firm and solid like a diamond-king, eternally abiding and indestructible.

If one perceives this seeing and hearing as being devoid of light and darkness, motion and stillness, and penetration and obstruction, they ultimately have no substance; they are like the mind of recollection when separated from its objects.
Dust is fundamentally non-existent; how can one take this ultimate annihilation as a causal practice in order to obtain the fruit of the Tathāgata’s sevenfold eternal abiding?
World-Honored One, if one is separated from light and darkness, seeing is ultimately empty. Just as there are no external objects before one, the nature of thought itself is extinguished.
Whether advancing or retreating, through subtle investigation in a cycle of inquiry, one finds that fundamentally there is no self-mind nor any mental factors associated with a self.

Who would establish a cause to seek unexcelled enlightenment if the Tathāgata’s previous teachings of profound, pure, perfect, and eternal [nature] were to contradict his truthful words and ultimately result in mere sophistry?
How can the Tathāgata be said to speak with true words? I pray that you will deign to show great compassion and dispel my ignorance and hesitation.

This erroneous attachment takes the nature of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) as the nature of the essence, thereby giving rise to doubts regarding annihilation. First, the preceding text is restated and established:

"If, during the causal stage, one takes a mind subject to arising and ceasing as the fundamental cause of cultivation while seeking the Buddha-vehicle—which is neither born nor extinguished—there is no such possibility.
This serves as the root of doubt. From the words "World-Honored One" onwards, [the text] first infers that the awakened realization of the fruit is eternal.
"Bodhi" (Awakening) is that which is attained by severing the five stages of dwelling; "Nirvana" is that which is realized by severing the two types of death;
"Tathatā" (Suchness) is that which is formed through the smelting and refining of the sūtras; "Buddha-nature" is that which is manifested through the polishing of causes;
"the empty Tathāgatagarbha" is that which appears when all existents are emptied; and "Amalavijñāna"—herein called the "Pure White Consciousness"—is this Great [Mirror-like Wisdom].
The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is entirely formed by the transformation of the karmic consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Merely discerning all things without defiled attachment is called "pure white"; illuminating the myriad dharmas perfectly without discrimination is termed "Perfect Wisdom.
Although these seven types differ in name, they are all the Dharma-gates of the Tathāgata’s self-realization. Once attained, they are eternal; there is no further [attainment].
Because it undergoes transformation, it is likened to a diamond (*vajra*); its purity is wondrous stillness; its perfection is total retention (*dhāraṇī*);
its firm solidity is immovability; and its eternal, indestructible nature is the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*.

Following this, [the text] next refutes the notion that the causal mind is subject to annihilation, showing it is inconsistent with the resultant awakening. First, it restates that apart from light and apart from darkness, there is no seeing.

The text following the section on "the nature [of consciousness] and so forth" cites the passage: "If a single atom is not permanent, then when it undergoes transformation and ceases, this mind is likewise like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.

The meaning of this passage is that the nature of seeing, being devoid of objects and lacking substantiality, is identical to the preceding consciousness-mind, which is also devoid of objects and lacks substantiality.
How can you take this state of ultimate annihilation as the mind for the ground of cultivation (*nidāna-citta*), and yet desire—
To attain the seven fruits of the Tathāgata’s eternal abiding—how is this different from seeking the fruit of empty space by grasping at flowers in the sky?

[The passage] "World-Honored One" below further distinguishes that the faculties and consciousnesses are not different; it advances by investigating with the conscious mind and retreats by examining the nature of seeing.
The term "cycling" means that the investigation and examination do not stop at a single instance. As for the statement, "I have thus investigated and examined in minute detail": if...
Since there is absolutely no "I" nor any locus for the mind apart from the external objects before one, this would result in total annihilation;
with what, then, could one take as a cause to seek the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed wisdom?
Now that this seeing-nature has become annihilated, how can the Tathāgata have previously said that the seeing-nature is tranquil, subtle, perfect, and constant? This being so—
To transgress one’s sincere word also constitutes frivolous discourse. How is it that the Tathāgata calls himself a speaker of truthful words?
This is because some, out of dullness of perception, fail to understand; others, out of stinginess, do not abandon their doubts.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Though you have studied much and possess great learning, you have not yet exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*).

In your mind, you merely know the causes of inversion, but when true inversion actually manifests before you, you are truly unable to recognize it. I fear that despite your sincere heart, you have not yet attained full conviction.
I shall now test you with various mundane matters to remove your doubts."
This first rebukes his perversion by saying: "Though you are fond of learning and possess great erudition, you have no intention to exhaust the outflows;
therefore, what is in your mind is merely the memorization of the causes of perversion. In reality, you cannot even recognize the perversions manifesting before you.
Even if I were to provide further instruction, I fear that what you cling to as being most true would, for a moment, [obstruct your realization]."
"Because you do not understand, I shall now clarify this for you by using a matter from the mundane world that is easy to comprehend;
you will surely resolve your doubts through this.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata commanded Rāhula to strike the bell once and asked Ānanda, "Do you hear it now?"
Ānanda and the great assembly all said, "I heard it. When the bell had ceased and there was no sound, the Buddha asked again, "Do you hear it now?
Ānanda and the great assembly all said, "We do not hear it. Then Rāhula struck it once more. The Buddha asked again, "Do you hear it now?
Ānanda and the great assembly again said, "We all hear it. The Buddha asked Ānanda, "How did you hear it?"
Ānanda and the great assembly asked the Buddha together: "If the bell is struck, we hear it;
when the striking has ceased and the sound has faded until both resonance and echo are utterly extinguished, this is called 'no hearing'."
The World-Honored One initially replied to Ānanda’s words that [the city] was like a golden wall and a moat, possessing a defensive strength that could not be breached;
yet Ānanda was able to attack what others could not attack—truly a fine scaling ladder for those looking upward to scale it.
The World-Honored One did not wield a single bow nor expend a single arrow, but merely borrowed the sound of the bell to provide illumination for him. This too is so.
It is like the saying: "When the city gate catches fire, the calamity reaches the fish in the pond.
If it were anyone else, a single blow from Rāhu would have shattered the knot of doubt; there would have been no need for further examination.

Because the World-Honored One saw that Ānanda was a subtle spy, he had Rāhu strike again and examine once more, desiring to cause him to investigate the point where the sound falls within the realm of hearing.
Alas, how regrettable that Ānanda feigned ignorance when struck, yet instead of recognizing his error,

he turned a phrase in such a way that one wonders whether this eminent disciple of the Buddha has fallen into the same stream as the nihilistic heretics! Thus we know that failing to recognize one's own eternally constant nature of hearing,

and instead following the arising and ceasing of the auditory characteristics produced by external sounds, is nothing other than being deluded regarding fundamental hearing and flowing along with the stream of sound.
As the former masters said: "The countenance and appearance are exactly like those of a real person; when handled before one's eyes, its luster seems fresh and new.
Yet, once it enters the fire for further smelting and refinement, it ultimately turns out to be nothing but counterfeit silver. Is this not what the Venerable One meant?
The Tathāgata again commanded Rāhula to strike the bell and asked Ānanda, "Do you hear the sound now? Ānanda and the great assembly all replied, "There is a sound.
After a short while, when the sound had faded, the Buddha asked again, "Do you hear the sound now? Ānanda and the great assembly answered, "There is no sound.
A moment later, Rāhula came again to strike the bell; the Buddha asked once more, "Do you hear the sound now?"
Ānanda and the great assembly all said, "There is sound. The Buddha asked Ānanda, "In what way is there sound? In what way is there no sound?

Ānanda and the great assembly all replied to the Buddha, "If the bell is struck, it is called 'having sound. When the striking has ceased and the sound has faded, when both the resonance and the echo have utterly vanished, it is called 'no sound.'"
This was done again to strike the bell for a second test, intending to show that whether the sound exists or does not exist is irrelevant to the nature of hearing.
After a short while—meaning after a brief moment or instant—he spoke again.
The Buddha said to Ānanda and the great assembly, "How is it that you now speak with such evasive confusion?
The great assembly and Ānanda simultaneously asked the Buddha, "In what way do we now name this 'evasive confusion'? The Buddha said, "I ask you whether you hear, and you say 'I hear.
Again I ask you about the sound, and you say 'the sound. Since your answers regarding hearing and sound are not fixed in this manner, it is thus [called evasion]."
Why is this not called "evasive equivocation"?

This passage refutes such equivocation because it involves answering "I have heard" when asked "Have you heard?", or answering "sound" when asked about "sound," or speaking with words as unstable as a rudder tossed by the wind;
thus, it is termed "evasive equivocation."

Ānanda, when the sound has vanished and there is no resonance, you say that there is no hearing. If, in fact, there were no hearing and the nature of hearing had already ceased, it would be like a withered tree;
if the bell were struck again, how could you know it? To know "there is" or to know "there is not" is simply the presence or absence of the auditory object.
How could that nature of hearing itself be subject to existence or non-existence for you? If hearing were truly non-existent, who would know that it was non-existent? Therefore—

Ānanda, it is the sound that undergoes arising and ceasing within the faculty of hearing; it is not that your hearing arises when sound arises and ceases when sound ceases, thereby making your nature of hearing existent or non-existent.
You are already inverted and deluded, mistaking sound for hearing—how much more so to be confused and take the permanent to be intermittent?
Ultimately, you should never say that the nature of hearing is absent apart from movement and stillness, or closure and openness.
Since Śākyamuni, father and son, had already used the sound of the bell to preach the Dharma to Ānanda, he further added a commentary to that very sound, saying:
"At the moment the sound of the bell first ceases, it is simply that there is no resonance; it is not that there is no hearing.
If there were no hearing, then your faculty of hearing would have perished along with the sound, and you would be the same as one who is non-existent."
If you know that when a withered tree is struck like a bell, you should no longer hear it once the striking ceases;

yet if you still hear it even after further striking, then it is clear that your faculty of hearing does not perish along with the sound. Thus, the presence of sound and the absence of sound belong to the objective field of sound (*śabdaviṣaya*), which may exist or not exist;
how could that nature of hearing exist because sound exists, or cease to exist because sound is absent?
Furthermore, if the nature of hearing were truly to perish along with the sound, then when you perceive the absence of sound, who is it that perceives this absence?

Thus, while the sound exists, there is the perception of its existence; when the sound is absent, there is the perception of its absence. How could the nature of hearing ever be severed or extinguished?
Therefore, know that it is the sound that arises and perishes within the hearing, and not your own nature of hearing that is produced by the sound or caused to cease.
"You have heard that the nature of hearing exists when sound arises; you now claim that this nature of hearing becomes non-existent when sound ceases. Therefore, I reprove you:
if this were either annihilationism or eternalism, it might be difficult to understand. But since you are a śrāvaka, you ought to find this easy to comprehend;
yet even now you are still confused, mistaking sound for hearing. How can you not wonder at this? Why do you hold the view of annihilation regarding the truly eternal nature?"
"Since you have now understood this, you should no longer cling to the notion that there is no intrinsic nature apart from objects.
Ānanda, you have indeed sought out the weaknesses of others, and the World-Honored One has likewise seen through your vulnerabilities; truly, you are a master opponent!
Suppose there is a person in a deep sleep, resting soundly upon a bed and pillow. While he sleeps, someone in his house pounds silk or husks rice.
In his dream, he hears the sound of pounding and husking, yet perceives it as something else—perhaps the beating of a drum or the striking of a bell.
During the dream, he wonders at the sound of the bell, thinking it to be the resonance of wood or stone. Then, suddenly waking, he immediately recognizes the sound of the pestle.
He addressed his family members himself: "While I was in the midst of a dream, I was confused by the sound of this pestle and mistook it for the sound of a drum.

Ānanda, how could this person, while dreaming, recall whether things were still or moving, open or closed, or permeable or obstructed? Although his physical form was asleep, the nature of his hearing was not clouded.
Even if your physical form were to dissolve and the radiance of your life-force were to depart, how could this nature ever be extinguished within you?
This citation of a dream incident serves to verify that the nature of hearing is uninterrupted. "Heavy sleep" refers to deep slumber;
"the sound of pounding silk" is the noise of a pestle, and "the sound of husking rice" is the noise of a mortar. "Strange during the dream" refers to interpreting a dream while dreaming.

"Suddenly awakening and immediately knowing the sound of the pestle" means realizing it was a dream only after waking up. "Informing one's family" refers to recounting it upon regaining consciousness.
The events within a dream—when Ānanda begins to snore and sleep below—serve to clarify that the nature of hearing does not become darkened;
furthermore, when the light of the eyes falls to the ground below, it serves to clarify that the nature of hearing is not extinguished.
Because all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have followed after forms and sounds, flowing with every thought, they have never awakened to the nature that is pure, wondrous, and eternal;
instead of following what is constant, they pursue birth and death. Consequently, life after life they wander through defilement.
If one abandons birth and death and maintains the True Constant, the eternal light will manifest before them, and the faculties, objects, consciousness, and mind will dissolve at that very moment.
When you distance yourself from both the conceptualizations that act as dust and the conscious mind that acts as grime, your Dharma-eye will immediately become clear and bright;
how then could you fail to achieve unsurpassed enlightenment?

Hereafter, it is shown universally that by chasing after cessation one remains deluded regarding permanence, and thus there is saṃsāra; whereas by abandoning cessation and guarding permanence, one immediately achieves correctness.

To "awaken" means not to follow that which is habitually pursued—namely, the various states of arising and ceasing—which is to turn one's back on the fundamental nature of the sense organs and instead chase after sounds and forms.
"Abandoning" means to cast it aside and not approach it; "maintaining" means to employ it without separation from it.

To abandon arising and ceasing while maintaining the true permanence is to "shed the stickiness and settle within. For the constant light to manifest before one is for the fundamental luminosity to shine forth.
When the faculties, objects, consciousness, and mind dissolve simultaneously, a single faculty is liberated and the other five faculties are accordingly uprooted.
Conceptual appearances as objects are subtle mental objects (*dharmaraja*), and the habitual tendencies of consciousness are defilements;

these are subtle attachments to phenomena—both are like the undershirt clinging to one’s body. Once these two types are separated from, the visual faculty immediately becomes clear and bright. This is it.
The *Shōbōgenzō* asks: "How could [the Buddha] not have attained unsurpassed enlightenment? Therefore, a student asked Master Kōjō:
"Master, when there is no lamp after nightfall, what then? The Master said: "For one who has realized the Way, the constant light is ever-present;
what distinction is there between day and night? The student said: "Why do I not see the Master’s light? The Master said: [The constant light is ever-present.]
[The Master] asked, "What do you intend to see with your eyes? A student said, "Ordinary people of the present day all see with their eyes.
The Master snapped his fingers and said, "Excellent! Since beginningless time, the faculties and objects of all sentient beings have intermingled, leading them to mistake a thief for their own son.
To this very day, they remain bound by shackles and fetters. You take what you see with your eyes and attempt to seek [the truth] through the conceptual discrimination of the mental consciousness."
The Buddha-way is precisely to turn one's back on the fundamental mind and follow after thoughts in a cycle of transmigration; such a person, though face-to-face, is worlds apart.
