Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, although the Tathāgata has explained the second gateway of meaning, I observe those in the world who attempt to untie knots;
if they do not know the origin from which the knot was tied, I believe such people will ultimately never be able to untie it."
Venerable One, it is likewise for the śrāvakas in this assembly who are still in training: from beginningless time, they have been born and extinguished together with various forms of ignorance.
Although they have attained such roots of goodness through extensive learning and are called "those who have gone forth," they are like those suffering from quotidian malaria.
We pray that you, out of great compassion, take pity on us who are drowning; today, what are these fetters, and from what do they derive their name?
He further resolved that all sentient beings suffering in the future might escape saṃsāra and not fall into the three realms of existence.

Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground before the great assembly; shedding tears and raising his palms in sincere devotion, he awaited the unsurpassed instruction of the Buddha, the Tathāgata.
Because this separately seeks the root-source of the bonds of birth and death, it cites the second preceding section of meaning to make its request.

"That which perishes and arises together with all ignorance" refers to the accumulation of beginningless empty habits within the faculties (*indriya*) throughout successive births, as well as the specific measures and counts of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing; therefore, it says "all. These various ignorances emerge from a single source.

That which arises simultaneously with the fetus, capable of functioning spontaneously without awaiting instruction, is called "beginningless habitual tendency" (*anādikālika-vāsanā*) and is also termed "innate ignorance" (*sahaja-avidyā*).
It is like a newborn infant who rejoices upon seeing its parents but weeps upon seeing others. This is similar to a tertian fever:
when the teaching is explained, it seems one has attained realization, yet upon encountering objects, one returns to delusion. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
Because the poison of this mouse has been unleashed, Master Guan says: "Pity my mind; though its clarity and power are insufficient, the seeds manifest as active states from time to time.
It is like a person who becomes狂 (mad) after drinking wine, yet upon being warned against drinking, immediately encounters fine liquor again;
or like one who desires purity but is stained by it, or who loves what is upright yet remains stubbornly perverse. All of these are due to the power of innate ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*).

Having thus understood that this ignorance is the root of birth and death, I do not yet know where its binding origin lies, nor from what point one must begin to effect liberation; therefore it is asked:
"What is this binding? From what does liberation arise?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda and all those in the assembly who were still in training,

and also to serve as a cause for transcending the world and as eyes for the future for all sentient beings, stroked the crown of Mahāpraṇidhāna’s head with his hand, which was like Jambūnada purple-gold light; immediately,
the worlds of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions shook in six ways, and Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust appeared.
Those dwelling in the various worlds each had jewel-radiance issue from their crowns;
at that same moment, this radiance came from those worlds to the Jeta Grove and drenched the crown of the Tathāgata’s head. This great assembly attained what they had never experienced before.
Then Ānanda and the entire multitude heard the Tathāgatas, as numerous as the motes of dust in the ten directions, speaking with one voice and in unison to Ānanda:

Excellent, Ānanda! If you wish to recognize and understand the innate ignorance that causes you to revolve in birth and death—the very root of your bondage—it is none other than your six sense faculties;

there is no other thing. Furthermore, if you wish to know the unsurpassed Bodhi that enables you to swiftly realize peace, liberation, tranquility, and wondrous permanence, it is likewise your six sense faculties and nothing else.

These Buddhas together testify that the six sense organs are the very source of both bondage and liberation. The initial touching of the crown of the head is intended to reveal the Dharma of the Crown.
As for the sixfold quaking, it is because the six sense organs are the fundamental abode of ignorance;
now, wishing to uproot them, they first cause them to tremble. The light from the crowns of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions collectively pours down upon Śākyamuni.
As for the "Summit" (Mūrdhan), it is shown that this summit-dharma is the single path to nirvana for the Bhagavāns of the ten directions.
From the opening of the two kinds of roots in the first fascicle until the section on the Path of Cultivation, although Ānanda was instructed by the Tathāgata regarding the beginningless,
empty habitual tendencies accumulated within the roots, as well as the specific measures and enumerations of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, yet—
Ultimately, they do not know what the fundamental source of ignorance and birth-and-death is, nor what the origin of supreme bodhi and nirvana is.
For this reason, they inquire into the root of bondage and liberation, whereupon the Tathāgatas of the ten directions speak with one voice, declaring:
"The root of the bonds of birth-and-death and supreme bodhi are both the six sense faculties; there is nothing else."
Other former masters have said that seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are all causes of birth and death, yet seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are also the very foundation of liberation.
This is what is meant by "the one who unties the bell is the same person who tied it. That they speak with one voice is because their realization is identical;
thus, what they teach does not differ. When the two deaths are forever extinguished, this is called "Peaceful Bliss" (Anraku).
The exhaustive consummation of the five stages is called liberation; that which transcends words and transcends thought is called tranquility;
that which is without arising and without ceasing is called wondrous permanence—this is precisely the fruit of the unsurpassed Great Bodhi.
Although Ānanda had heard such a Dharma-sound, his mind was still not yet clear; he bowed his head to the Buddha and said:

"How is it that my cycle of birth and death and the wondrous, eternal bliss are both identical to these six faculties and nothing else? The Buddha told Ānanda: "The faculties and their objects share the same source;
bondage and liberation are non-dual. The nature of consciousness is false and illusory, like flowers in the sky. Ānanda, because of the objects...
The arising of cognition depends on the sense-faculties; yet both the perceived object and the perceiving subject lack inherent nature, being like two reeds leaning against one another.

Therefore, if you now establish cognition within your cognition and vision, this is the very root of ignorance. If you perceive neither cognition nor vision, this is *nirvāṇa*, the untainted, true purity.
How could any other thing be admitted therein?
This Śākyamuni Buddha has explained in detail that both bondage and liberation arise from the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*).

Ānanda had presumed that the root of birth-and-death and bondage exists apart from these six faculties; yet the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have all taught that birth-and-death and liberation consist solely of the six faculties.
However, because they had not yet explained the reason why this is so, it remained half-illuminated and half-obscured, leading Ānanda to harbor doubts.

The root-source of birth and death must consist of the three—sense organs (*indriya*), sense objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Now, you have mentioned only the sense organs without mentioning the objects or consciousness;

I do not know what the meaning of this is, and thus I ask again: how is it that both the wheeling through birth and death and the realization of wondrous permanence are entirely due to the six sense organs and nothing else?
Therefore, the World-Honored One has further elaborated upon this, drawing out the branches and extending the vines, providing an explanatory commentary.

The reason only the faculties (*indriya*) are mentioned while the objects (*viṣaya*) are not is that both the perceived characteristics (*nimitta*) and the seeing (*darśana*) depend upon the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), sharing a single source.
Because they share this same source, when bound they are bound together, and when liberated they are liberated together; thus it is said there is no duality.

Since there is only non-duality, by mentioning the faculty, the object is included therein. As for the reason why consciousness (*vijñāna*) is not mentioned, it is because the nature of consciousness...
Having no source, they also emerge falsely from the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*); they originally lack substantial reality, being like flowers in the sky (*ākāśa-puṣpa*).
Therefore, by mentioning the sense organs, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is also included therein. Thus, birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa are nothing other than the six sense organs;
there is no other entity. Hence, the *Tongxin lun* (Treatise on Penetrating the Mind) says: "Bondage arises from the mind; liberation arises from the mind. Liberation and bondage both arise from..."
Because the mind does not engage with other objects, one knows that it has no self-nature; dependent origination is itself emptiness.
Just as one who wishes to cut off a stream need only block its source, and one who wishes to avoid birth need only sever its root—no great effort is required, for this is most concise and essential.
Ānanda further explains the meaning above: "Cognition arises from objects" means that it arises because of the six sense-objects.
The cognitions of the six sense organs arise because there are objects corresponding to those organs; that is to say, the six objects arise in dependence upon the six organs.
Thus, these two factors—the organ and the object—arise through mutual reliance and lack inherent nature (*svabhāva*).

Apart from the object there is no organ, and apart from the organ there is no object; they are like two bundles of reeds standing by leaning against one another. Therefore, regarding that which is known...
When the locus of seeing perceives light and darkness, the false forms adhere to the profound stillness, causing the faculty of seeing to flow outward and rush toward forms;

this very knowing and seeing is the root of ignorance. If, regarding the objects known and seen, one does not follow after external dust, detaches from these adhesions, and subdues them within, such that the inner radiance shines forth, then this very knowing and seeing is the root of Nirvana. Thus, these six...
The sense-faculties (*indriya*) are truly the source of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. How could there be anything else as the source within saṃsāra and nirvāṇa apart from these six sense-faculties?
It is like water encountering freezing cold that solidifies into ice, or ice meeting warm sunshine that melts back into water;
thus, the freezing of the ice and the melting of the water depend upon the cold and the sun.
Warmth is the origin; how could it be separate from the freezing cold? Apart from warmth, is there not another entity that serves as the origin of ice and water?
Therefore, the *Zongjing* says: "Worldly birth-and-death and world-transcending nirvana are both established based on cognition, views, names, and words.
If these cognitions, views, names, and words did not exist, their essence and substance would be fundamentally empty within the wondrously luminous mind."
What further thing could serve as a condition or an obstruction? Thus the Sixth Patriarch said: "Bodhi originally has no tree; the bright mirror is also not a stand.
Originally there is not a single thing; where can dust be gathered? From this we know that when a single film is in the eye, empty flowers arise in confusion;
when a single delusion is in the mind, the sands of the Ganges are born and perish. If one can detach from discursive thought, then [one shall realize the truth].
Abiding in the site of enlightenment and turning the Great Dharma Wheel, all together attain the Buddha-way. Previously it was said that "by means of consciousness one establishes objects";
here it is said that "by means of knowledge and vision one establishes knowing. Since such establishment is so harmful, those who possess the Way see nothing to be seen and know nothing to be known.
When not a single dharma is established, then every place of establishment is the Truth.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse: "The true nature of conditioned phenomena is empty, for they arise through conditions and are thus like illusions.

Unconditioned phenomena have no arising or ceasing; they are as unreal as flowers in the sky. Words manifest the 'true' by means of the 'false,' yet both the false and the true are equally dualistic delusions.
Since even 'neither true nor false' is not ultimate reality, how can there be a seer and a seen? Between them, there is no substantial nature; therefore..."
If the binding and unbinding of the interlaced reeds share the same cause, then there is no second path for the noble and the ordinary;

you should observe that the nature of the interlacing is such that both existence and non-existence are absent—delusion and obscuration constitute ignorance, while illumination and clarity constitute liberation.
Having personally examined the causes of the mind and karma from their origin to their end, all are ultimately entrusted to the "second moon" as a means to reveal the "true moon.

This constitutes a major point of resolution; therefore, the true nature (*tathatā*) is specifically designated as the fundamental essence (*dharmakāya*) to demonstrate that although the six sense organs belong to the secondary level of meaning, they are nonetheless proximate to the primary ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and are thus capable of serving as the basis for both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
If one gives rise to faith, it is because within the "Gate of Arising and Ceasing" (shengmie men) there is contained the meaning of both awakening (jue) and non-awakening (bujue).
This is because within the "Gate of True Suchness" (zhēnrú men), neither birth-and-death nor nirvana is established. Therefore, it is said:

"If one turns back to contemplate within the true nature (zhēnxing), all conditioned dharmas of birth-and-death are entirely false and illusory; because they arise by relying on causes and depending on conditions, they are thus compared [to illusions]."

One should establish a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) as follows: Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are the subject (*dharmin*); their emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the thesis (*pakṣa*); the reason (*hetu*) is "because they are dependently originated" (*pratītyasamutpannatvāt*);

and the concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is "like an illusion. Not only should one contemplate that conditioned phenomena such as birth and death are illusory, but one should also contemplate that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) such as nirvāṇa are likewise illusory.
Because they are without arising and without cessation, they are like flowers in the sky (*ākāśapuṣpa*); thus, one should establish an inference.

To say that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is an existent phenomenon whose thesis is the absence of arising and ceasing, with the reason "because it is not real" and the concordant example "like a flower in the sky," implies that both the conditioned and the unconditioned belong to the realm of duality. Since saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are equally like a dream from yesterday, one knows that truth is spoken of in opposition to delusion;
yet if even truth is delusory, then one knows that the true nature (*tathatā*) does not even exist alongside non-existence.
Regarding the correspondence with phenomena (*dharmas*), how could it possibly correspond with the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) of birth-and-death consisting of the seer and the seen?

Furthermore, both these phenomena of appearance and seeing belong to dependent origination; in between them there is truly no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), just like two bundles of reeds leaning against one another.
They cannot be discussed in terms of existence or non-existence. If one were bound by the conditioned, then [one would take] those leaning reeds as [the basis].
If there is a nature that is not substantially existent yet binds one to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is like the "mutually supporting reeds" (*parasparāśraya*):
because its nature is not substantially non-existent, one knows that the locus of these reeds is the universal cause for both bondage and liberation.

It is the common path for the noble and the ordinary, the very source of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. You need only carefully observe the two aspects of "nature," "emptiness," and "existence" within this passage.
Is it not that what you call "emptiness" is fundamentally the wondrously pure and luminous essence of bodhi? Is it not that what you call "existence" is fundamentally nothing at all?
Are you, within this state, inverted, submerged, deluded, obscured, and unaware? This is precisely the root of ignorance.
Are you, within this state, detached from external clinging and inwardly settled, giving rise to the radiance of original illumination? This is precisely liberation.
The root of this matter is that the six sense organs serve as the general cause for the loosening of knots; thus, it is clear that the path shared by both the holy and the ordinary is evident.

Nevertheless, one must understand that although this is so, bondage and liberation are entirely unrelated to true nature (bhūtadhātu), just as when Śrīghana was deluded, he was merely deluded himself, and when he awakened, he merely awakened himself—neither having anything to do with his head. One should establish the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
The true nature is an existent dharma that is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is neither empty nor existent.
The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like a pure, bright mirror.

Regarding the method for unraveling the knots: it proceeds through six stages, yet when the one [knot] is unraveled, even the root [of the six] perishes. By selecting the perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-vyavaccheda*), one enters the stream and achieves perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
These four lines are a standalone verse that serves as a prologue for what follows; they are subtle words where, as the discourse was about to end, another thread is once again drawn forth:
"The subtle *ālayavijñāna* has its habitual tendencies forming a violent torrent; fearing that one might confuse the real with the unreal, I have never openly expounded it."

The self-mind grasps the self-mind; that which is not an illusion becomes an illusory dharma through grasping. Without grasping, there is no non-illusion; if even non-illusion does not arise, how can illusory dharmas be established?
This is called the Wondrous Lotus, the Vajra-King Jewel-Awakening, the Illusion-like Samādhi, by which one transcends the stage of No-More-Learning with a mere snap of the fingers.
This Abhidharma is the single path to Nirvana for the Bhagavāns of the ten directions.
The following points clarify why the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) serve as the causes for both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa: because the six faculties, in their very essence, are the *ādānavijñāna*.
It is only here that the text returns to the opening statement of the first fascicle, "This is mind, not the eye.

*Ādāna* is translated here as "grasping and maintaining" (*zhíchí*), so called because it grasps and maintains the three categories of objective realms (*viṣaya*). The followers of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) are unable [to perceive this].

Because its origin is known, it is called "subtle" (*mī*); because even the Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) has not yet exhausted its limits, it is called "fine habitual tendencies" (*sūkṣma-vāsanā*).

"Habitual tendencies" refers to the perfumed portions of habituation—namely, the beginningless afflictive false habituation within the faculties and the false habituation of ignorance regarding arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.
These are synonyms for seeds; it is because this consciousness carries those false habituations that [they are so termed].
There is a subtle, continuous flow of arising and ceasing that is like a violent torrent, capable of manifesting the waves of active mental formations (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).

The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "Like a violent current of water, many waves arise. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* also says: "Where the water flows, the waves of the evolving consciousnesses arise from the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Thus, these six sense faculties are precisely the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) manifested by this consciousness, while the six sense objects are its perceived-division (*nimitta-bhāga*).

This refers to the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) produced by this consciousness; through the interweaving of these two aspects, they falsely constitute one another, whereby the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha is transformed into the ālaya-vijñāna.
If one is separated from these two aspects, the ālaya-vijñāna is itself the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha.
Therefore, the preceding text metaphorically compares it to a second moon, for that second moon is produced by the pressing of the eyes, just as the ālaya is produced [by the conditions of delusion].

Because consciousness arises from the establishment of cognition, the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states that the union of the perishable and the imperishable—neither identical nor different—is called the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
However, this store-consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) is not ordinarily or easily explained to others;
it must await the explanation provided by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions. This is because this consciousness is precisely the sixth [consciousness].
The nature within the intersection of the faculties is likewise a name common to both the noble and the ordinary; it cannot be said to be true, nor can it be called false.
To take it as true is to mistake a thief for one’s own son; to take it as not true is to mistake an enemy’s son for a thief.
For this reason, I have long endured in silence, never revealing or expounding upon it. Below the section on "One's Own Mind," it further clarifies the transformation of consciousness into wisdom.

Regarding the dialectical terminology of wisdom: these two aspects—the perceived (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiving (*darśana-bhāga*)—both belong to the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of one's own mind.
Just as the two horns of a snail emerge as a pair yet form a single entity when joined, there is fundamentally no grasper (*grāhaka*) and no grasped (*grāhya*).

Now, through the establishment of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) as distinct entities, they mutually attract and entangle one another; thus, the sense-faculty is formed and subsequently becomes the grasper and the grasped.
To grasp this is to grasp at one's own mind; to grasp at one's own mind is to fail to realize that the *tathāgatagarbha* is truly eternal and fundamentally not illusory.
Yet, due to deluded views, the six sense-objects suddenly arise and manifest, thereby constituting illusory phenomena.
If one were not to give rise to grasping or attachment when facing these objects, they would not be illusory; since even their arising would not exist, how could there then be a seer or a seen?
This is indeed the illusory dharma! Thus, the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) says: "To grasp at 'self' is defilement; not grasping at 'self' is purity.

If there is neither the mind that grasps nor the object grasped, then there are likewise no dharmas of either illusion or non-illusion—what is called the "identity of the false and the true" is itself a duality of falsehood.
If one truly reaches the state where both the true and the false are forgotten, then one will know that this is the fundamental *ālayavijñāna*.

It is not some other thing; it is precisely that aforementioned *tathāgatagarbha*—the nature of reality which is pure and fundamental (*viśuddha-mūla-prakṛti*) and all-pervasive throughout the *dharmadhātu*.
To speak of the "wondrous lotus" refers to the meaning of purity; "vajra-king jewel-awareness" refers to the meaning of being fundamental and natural;
and "illusion-like *samādhi*" refers to the meaning of pervading the *dharmadhātu*. If one is indeed able to transform this *ālayavijñāna*, [one will realize this].
When the subtle consciousness becomes the Tathāgatagarbha, one can transcend the seat of an Arhat and advance toward wondrous enlightenment in the mere blink of an eye.
Since there are no stages to be established, what need is there for the arduous labor of cultivating and realizing through every fiber of one's being?
Therefore, know that the divine efficacy and wondrous power of this Dharma are beyond comparison; none of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have not attained it through this alone.
To ascend the path to perfect enlightenment and to enter nirvana, there is likewise no way other than through this single gate; how can you not exert yourselves?
At this point, the text finally provides a concluding summary that corresponds to the title in the first fascicle:
"The Samādhi Named the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Śūraṅgama, the Single Gate that Transcends the Path of Sublime Adornment. Thus, one knows that the preceding text...
That "one gate" and "one path" are all cryptic references to the *ālayavijñāna*;
furthermore, what the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* refers to as "this house has but one gate, and it is moreover narrow" is likewise a cryptic reference to the *ālayavijñāna*.

Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly, hearing the Buddha-Tathāgata’s unsurpassed compassionate instruction—its gāthās and verses intermingled, refined, pure, subtle, and lucid—felt their minds and eyes opened and enlightened.
Exclaiming that it was unprecedented, Ānanda joined his palms, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha:
“I have now heard from the Buddha these words of Dharma, which are unobstructed, characterized by great compassion, intrinsically pure, wondrously eternal, and true.”
My mind has not yet fully attained realization; the six knots have been untied, yet the single [knot] has not vanished.
Pray, out of great compassion, grant us once more your pity for this assembly and for those of the future, bestowing upon us the sound of the Dharma to wash away our deep-seated defilements.

This was requested again because, despite having understood it, there remained points that were not yet clear. *Geya* (祇夜) is translated as "Verses in Response" (*ying song*); it is so called because these verses correspond to and respond to the preceding prose (*gadya*).
*Gāthā* (伽陀) is translated as "Independent Verses" (*feng song*); it is so called because they do not correspond to prose but arise independently to praise and extol with beauty.
Regarding the phrase "intermingled and refined," this refers to the two types of verse being combined into clear text, like the pattern of a brocade; such is its meaning.

If one penetrates the beads of a rosary so that nothing is not thoroughly mastered, this is called "the principle being refined, clear, and penetrating," meaning that as truth and falsehood confront each other and the sense organs and their objects arise together, there is no principle that is not fully understood.

"The mind and eyes opening and becoming bright" means that in the past I mistook discursive攀缘 (pān-yuán) for the mind, failing to realize that the mind is the King of the Wondrous Lotus Flower; and I mistook the floating sense-roots for the eyes, failing to realize that the roots [are but delusions].
This subtle consciousness of *ādāna* has, from this moment, had its mind opened and enlightened; it knows its own location and is free from all further doubt.
As for the exclamation "unprecedented," it is because that which the Tathāgata had never before expounded is now being expounded for the first time.

Regarding "unobstructed great compassion," it means that the Tathāgata knows all things and does not fail to speak of them; he speaks with total clarity, leaving nothing out, even down to the finest detail.
These obstructions all flow forth from the heart of great compassion;

therefore, the pure, wondrous, eternal, and true phrases of the Dharma are merely the realization and unraveling [of delusion], which is nothing other than the six sense faculties—there is no other substance.
"The six are resolved and the one perishes" means that when the six knots are untied, even the "one" no longer exists. As for the sequence for loosening the knots:
This means that both liberation and bondage possess corresponding counterparts and proceed in a sequential order without skipping stages;

this refers back to the previous statement regarding the sequence of the causes of bondage and liberation—specifically the phrase "once the first is resolved, the second also perishes"—to pose a question.
"Sinking defilements" (chen-gou) refers to subtle delusions, which are the subtle clinging to phenomena (dharma-grāha).
Immediately, the Tathāgata, upon his lion throne, adjusted his *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* and gathered his *saṃghāṭī*.
He took up a seven-jeweled armrest, reached out his hand over the armrest, and took from it the flower-cloth (*puṣpa-paṭṭa*) offered by the deva Kāpila.
Before the great assembly, he tied it into a single knot and asked Ānanda, "What is this called? Ānanda and the great assembly together replied to the Buddha, "This is called..."
At this point, the Tathāgata again knotted the folded flower-cloth and asked Ānanda once more, "What is this called?
Ānanda and the great assembly again addressed the Buddha, saying, "This is also called a knot. In this manner, he successively knotted the folded flower-cloth until six knots were formed in total.
As each knot was completed, he took the knot formed in his hand and held it up to ask Ānanda.
Ānanda questioned this, saying, "What is this called? The great assembly likewise responded to the Buddha in succession: "This is called 'knotting.
First, the demonstration that knots have a sequential order is intended to reveal that because there are six kinds of deluded roots, a single cloth thus [becomes knotted]."
The formation of six knots is as follows: light and darkness stimulate the faculty of sight; movement and stillness stimulate the faculty of hearing, and so forth.
*Nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* means an inner robe; *saṃghāṭī* means a great robe (*mahāsaṃghāṭī*). *Kāpāla* means "time-period," referring to the Yāma Heaven.
It is like layered flowers or the silks of the Western Heavens, its value being immeasurable; that what is offered today is even more precious can be understood from this.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, “When I first tied this cloth, you called it a ‘knot. This folded flower-cloth was originally a single strip;

why then, for the second and third times, do you and the others again call them ‘knots’? Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, although this precious folded flower-cloth was woven into a scarf and was originally a single entity, as I contemplate it, the Tathāgata tied it once and obtained [the first knot].”
If tying a single knot were named "one," and after a hundred ties it were called "a hundred knots," how much more so this cloth, which has only six knots?
It will never reach seven, nor will it stop at five. Why, then, does the Tathāgata allow that only the first is called a knot, while the second and third are not?

The single cloth is a metaphor for the *karmic consciousness*, while the six knots are metaphors for the six sense faculties. The underlying meaning is this: since a single cloth ought to form only one knot, why do six arise?
By thus cross-examining why the second and third are not called "knots," [the Buddha] intends to elicit from Ānanda the realization that the substance of the cloth is one;
it is because of the knots that six are formed, thereby demonstrating that the six knots are entirely the same single cloth.
It is that which has been formed. The Buddha said to Ānanda: "Regarding this precious flowered cloth, you know that originally it was but a single strand.

"The first knot that was tied is called the first; and so on, up to the sixth knot. Now, I wish to designate the sixth knot as the first.

Even if I were to exhaust my eloquence through successive lifetimes, how could I cause these six knots to change their order?"
The Buddha said: "In this way, although these six knots are different, they all trace back to their original cause—being fashioned from a single piece of cloth.
To attempt to make them disordered will ultimately never succeed. Thus it is with your six sense faculties: they are ultimately identical in arising, yet you perceive them as ultimately distinct."
Furthermore, one must examine this: the substance of these [six organs] is one, yet they form six due to their binding.
If one intends to unify the six into one, how could it be possible? To unify the six into one would be like using the faculty of the mind (*manas*) as the faculty of the eye.
The World-Honored One, because they know each other within their nature (*svabhāva*), questioned whether this were possible; the Venerable One, because of their function (*vṛtti*).
Because they face away from one another, the answer is that the six knots cannot be confused; this is called "ultimate identity within difference.
That which is called "ultimate difference arising within identity" means that prior to being knotted, they were originally a single entity with no distinction between identity and difference.
Once knotted, each has its own boundaries and divisions; thus, the function of the mind cannot be used for the eye, and the function of the eye cannot be used for the mind.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "If you insist that these six knots cannot become one, and you wish to know how they might become one, what would you say?
Ānanda replied, "If these knots persist, then 'this' and 'that' arise in conflict; from within them, this knot arises as not being that, and that knot arises as not being this.
