If one faculty is detached from its adhesions and lies dormant within, the remaining five faculties should be uprooted so that they are all completely liberated.
Here, "one" and "six" refer to the entirety of the six faculties in relation to the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Because the entire body of the six faculties is this very essence of consciousness, it is called "seeing" when located in the eye and "hearing" when located in the ear; thus, the six faculties are resolved and [unified with] consciousness.

The emptiness of the essence of consciousness is like the disappearance of the single cloth once the six knots have been untied; therefore it is said, "If one cannot even name it 'one,' how can it be called 'six'?
[The questioner asks: "When the six sense organs are untied, the essence of consciousness becomes empty; when the six knots are untied, the single cloth remains.

Does this not incur the fault of the analogy being inconsistent with the Dharma? [The answer is: The six sense organs arise dependent upon the essence of consciousness, and the essence of consciousness depends upon...
If it arises from the nature of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), then one knows that the essence of consciousness is empty;
this is illustrated by the analogy of the six knots, which depend upon a single cloth, yet the single cloth itself depends upon the weaving of warp and woof. Thus, how could the single cloth be real?
Therefore, one knows that the essence of consciousness is a mere name, and the single cloth is likewise a mere name.
Because your mind-nature has been deluded since beginningless time, false perceptions have arisen; as this delusion continues without ceasing, the wearying faculty of sight gives rise to dust.
It is like when the eyes are strained, there appear illusory flowers in space. Within the pure, bright, and essential clarity, these arise without cause due to confusion.
All worlds—mountains, rivers, the great earth, birth and death, and even nirvana—are nothing but the inverted, illusory signs of such wearying delusion.
This demonstrates the sequence of the arising of the sense-faculties and their fetters by means of an analogy. "The nature of the mind" refers to the pure awakened mind;
"madness and confusion" means that within the pure mind, one fails to realize its true nature, and thoughts arise, thereby forming the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*).
This corresponds to the previous "single cloth. "The false emergence of cognition and vision" arises from the transformation of the karmic consciousness.
When the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) is fatigued and gives rise to dust-like appearances, it is because from the seeing-part there further arises the object-part (nimitta-bhāga);

these two merge into a single cloth to form six knots. To illustrate this with a metaphor, the staring of the eyes represents the fatigue of the seeing-part, while the wild flowers represent the object-part;
the clarity and brilliance of the essence is the karmic consciousness (karma-vijñāna), and the turbulence of the mind-nature constitutes the fatigue of the seeing.

The arising of dust-like phenomena from the profoundly clear and luminous essence is like the appearance of frantic flowers when one stares fixedly with the eyes; all that follows below further applies the Dharma to the metaphor.
All the mountains, rivers, and great earth of the world are the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect), while birth-and-death and nirvana are the *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect).
If one clings to the *nimitta-bhāga* as being real and thereby falls into the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), this constitutes birth-and-death; if [one realizes it] as empty...
Those who take the perceived aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) to be non-existent and thereby fall into the view of dharmas [regarding it as real] are told in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*:
"That which has contention is called saṃsāra; that which is without contention is called nirvāṇa.

Since both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are ultimately unattainable, they are said to be all merely delusory flowers and inverted floral appearances. These six knots all arise from the frantic toil of the *karma-vijñāna*.
"Because they arise, we know that the single cloth and its six knots are all but the appearance of fatigue produced by the Bodhi-mind’s fixed gaze;
they do not exist inherently within the pure essence of the Bodhi-mind from the very beginning.
Ānanda said, "This fatigue is the same as the knots; how can they be untied? The Tathāgata took the knotted cloth with his hand and tilted it to one side.

He pulled at the left side and asked Ānanda, "Is it untied like this? "No, World-Honored One. He then turned his hand and pulled at the right side, asking again, "Is it untied like this? "No, World-Honored One.

The Buddha told Ānanda, "I have now pulled at both the left and right sides with my hands, yet it remains untied. If you employ skillful means, how would you untie it? Ānanda replied, "It cannot be untied."
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, one should untie a knot at its very center, and it will immediately unravel. The Buddha told Ānanda, “So it is, so it is.
If you wish to remove a knot, you must do so at its very center.”
This further asks for the method of untying the knots and secretly reveals their essential point.
It means that this "toil of seeing" which gives rise to the toil of dust is simply a knot formed from a single cloth; yet one does not know what kind of effort is required to untie it.
The fact that one cannot untie them by pulling either the left or the right side is a metaphor for ordinary beings who cling to duality and those of the Two Vehicles who remain attached.
All these [methods] involve the removal of knots; yet as long as the knots are not exhausted, they remain partial and deviant, and none can truly resolve them.

One must apply oneself to the "knotting mind" (*jiexin*) in order to achieve liberation. By "knotting mind," one refers to the subtle consciousness of *ādāna-vijñāna*, for it is the very core of the knotted roots;
thus it is called the "knotting mind. As the ancients said: "If one strikes a single blow at the life-root (*jīvitendriya*), everything is resolved."

The hundred [disciples] must have been so; for the twenty-five sages who followed after them were all without exception those who began their practice by binding the heart, and only by destroying the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) did they realize perfect penetration. Therefore, one should regard the single phrase "binding the heart" as the most critical point.
As the *Vaipulya-prabhāsvara-viśuddha-sūtra* says: "The Free World-Leader speaks that which is unspeakable."
"Forming a knot in empty space and then untying it while it is empty. The commentary explains: "When the mind has [grasping], there is a knot;

when the mind is empty, there is release. If there is no mind, there is neither knot nor release. The *Zongjing* cites an ancient commentary which says: "Pulling to the left or right in a biased manner illustrates having views or being without views.
One should address the very center of the knot to clearly elucidate the Middle Way; therefore, it is said that one is deluded regarding true emptiness."

Yet, when views of existence and non-existence arise, one clings to the sense organs and their objects, and the meanings of "one" and "six" emerge. If you truly realize your own mind, both bondage and liberation will vanish together.
Ānanda, I say that the Buddha-dharma arises from causes and conditions; it does not grasp at the coarse appearances of worldly conjunctions as the Tathāgata does.

He has elucidated the mundane and supramundane dharmas, knowing their fundamental causes and how they emerge according to their conditions. Thus, even a single drop of rain beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he knows its number;
and all the various things appearing before him—the straightness of pines, the crookedness of thorns, the whiteness of cranes, and the blackness of crows—he fully understands their origins.
For this reason, Ānanda, you should choose from among these six faculties within your own mind that which constitutes the "knot" of the faculties.
If one eliminates the marks of dust, the various delusions will naturally extinguish themselves; what need is there to wait for them to perish?
Below this, he urges him to resolve his intention to eliminate the knots, for one must select a perfect faculty as the condition for awakening.
Since the mind that unties these knots must enter through conditions, the masters of old said: "Those who enter through conditions never regress."

The loss [of realization] was like Lingyun seeing the peach blossoms or Xiangyan striking the bamboo; the twenty-five sages each attained perfect penetration through one of the three categories or seven elements.
This was because they all shared a karmic affinity with the Dharma, such that upon contact, they immediately entered it.
As the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "The seed of the Buddha arises from conditions. Thus it is said: "I teach that the Buddha-dharma arises from causes and conditions. Furthermore, fearing that you...
Furthermore, because you were previously entangled by worldly causes and conditions, I spoke of causes and conditions as the four worldly conditions combining to produce consciousness,
the three conditions combining to produce a person, and the two conditions combining to produce the various classes of beings.
My current discourse on causes and conditions is intended to select and distinguish the profound single gateway of the perfect faculties.

This entry elucidates the causal conditions for the Great Matter. Thus, I have observed the six classes of ordinary beings and the four classes of sages, knowing that the fundamental cause of each arises from conditions.

For example, the six classes of ordinary beings take the karma of good, evil, or immovability as their cause, and the two objects of aversion and attraction encountered at the time of entering a rebirth as their condition.
The four classes of sages take the hearing of the Dharma throughout many lifetimes as their cause.
With the dharmas of similar outflow as the cause and the guidance of encountered spiritual friends as the condition,

[he understands] even those things most difficult to know— such as the number of raindrops falling within world-systems as numerous as the sands of the Ganges— and the fundamental reasons for all that appears before him,

such as the straightness of pines and the crookedness of thorns, or the whiteness of cranes and the blackness of crows; because he perceives these without the slightest error, what he speaks will certainly not be false.
"Profit and error: you should firmly believe that one must choose a faculty with perfect roots to enter.

'If the knots of the faculties are untied, the appearances of dust will naturally perish' means entering deeply through a single gate. 'All delusions are extinguished' means the five faculties are properly uprooted and one attains perfect liberation.
'What need is there for the unreal? means how could one fail to achieve unsurpassed enlightenment?"
"Ānanda, I now ask you: regarding this *karpāsa* cloth with six knots appearing before us, can they be untied and removed simultaneously?
No, World-Honored One. These knots were originally tied in succession; today they must likewise be untied in succession.
Since the six knots share the same substance but are not tied at the same time, how could they be removed simultaneously when they are untied? The Buddha said:
The liberation of the six sense organs is likewise thus: when this organ is first liberated, one first attains the emptiness of persons;

the nature of emptiness becomes perfectly luminous, achieving liberation from phenomena; once liberated from phenomena, both are empty and do not arise—this is called a Bodhisattva attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) from within samādhi.

This clarifies that there is a sequential order to understanding. First, he poses a counter-question regarding those who share the same understanding and the same removal [of afflictions], desiring that they demonstrate that while the knots have a sequence, the process of untying them likewise possesses a sequence.

That the knots have a sequence means that, initially, due to ignorance (*avidyā*), one becomes deluded regarding fundamental awareness (*mūla-bodhi*) and forms the karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*); based on this karma-consciousness, [the subsequent knots] are formed.
The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) arises from the seeing-part, which in turn gives rise to the object-part (*nimitta-bhāga*).
Upon this object-part, the two types of grasping—conceptual and innate clinging to a self and phenomena—are induced, thereby forming the six knots. Regarding the sequence of liberation:
it means that the faculties are first liberated, whereby one first realizes the emptiness of persons; this is precisely the emptiness of the two types of self-view, both conceptual and innate.
Furthermore, because one merely empties the view of a self, that emptiness is still limited and has not yet attained perfect clarity;

by subsequently emptying both the conceptual and innate views of phenomena (*dharma-dṛṣṭi*), one attains the perfect clarity of the nature of emptiness and achieves liberation through phenomena (*dharma-vimokṣa*).

By realizing the emptiness of persons, the two types of view of a self—conceptual and innate—do not arise; by realizing the emptiness of phenomena, the two types of [view of phenomena]—conceptual and innate—[likewise do not arise].

When the two kinds of dharmas arise, even the views [of them] vanish; though one realizes the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*), the marks of the two emptinesses still remain. Next, one again empties those two emptinesses;
hence it is said that "both are empty and do not arise," meaning that even the "sickness of emptiness" is emptied.
Thus, when the six knots are untied and the single cloth is no longer perceived, birth and cessation are exhausted, and only then does one attain the state of neither arising nor ceasing.
To enter the Abode of Initial Resolve by means of the mind that serves as the ground is called attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);

this refers to the sequential order of the causes for the binding and the untying of knots. Question: In the Chapter on Flowing Against the Stream, it was stated that the six knots refer only to the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
Why, then, are six successive layers explained here? Answer: These six layers are inherently present within the six knots; they are not established by force.
Did we not say previously that the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) share the same source? Thus, by mentioning the organ, the object is naturally included.

Since the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is illusory, by mentioning the organ, consciousness is naturally included. This is like a single cloth being knotted into six knots, each of which inherently possesses six layers.
Otherwise, within the organ itself, there are accumulated beginningless false habits (*vāsanā*) that coexist with the organ.
Regarding the question of how to explain the specific divisions of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing within the intermediate state:
we know that although only six knots are mentioned, the three factors of sense organ, object, and consciousness, along with beginningless habitual tendencies and so forth, are all fully present.
Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the Buddha’s instruction on the perfect penetration of wisdom and awakening, were freed from all doubt.
At once they joined their palms, prostrated at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Today our bodies and minds are radiant and clear; we have swiftly attained unimpeded understanding.
Although we have realized the meaning of the 'one' and the 'six' being non-existent, we have yet to reach the fundamental root of perfect penetration, World-Honored One."

We have drifted through the ages, orphaned and exposed for countless kalpas; what heart or concern could we have anticipated joining the Buddha’s celestial kin? We are like infants who have lost their mother’s milk, suddenly encountering a compassionate mother.

If, through this meeting, the Way is realized and the secret words obtained are identical to our original awakening, then there will be no difference between having heard them and not having heard them at all.
We pray only that you will bestow your great compassion upon us, granting us the secret adornment so that we may achieve the state of a Tathāgata.

Having finally revealed this teaching and spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground and withdrew to conceal his secret intent, hoping for the Buddha’s hidden transmission.
This follows the preceding text on the selection of the faculties and the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), which constitutes the request for the fundamental basis of perfect penetration.

"Wisdom-perfect-penetration" refers to the realization of the mutual functioning of the six sense-faculties and the meaning of the "six dissolutions and one disappearance"; although this has not yet been realized, [he seeks it].
The mind is already free from doubt; that body and mind are unimpeded is due to awakening to the six kinds of liberation. Because the one [body] has perished, the body is unimpeded;
because [the body] has perished, the mind is unimpeded. Although these two phrases describe what has already been awakened to, these two subsequent phrases describe what has not yet been awakened to.
"World-Honored One" and below express a humble plea, signifying being "alone" in the sense of lacking a teacher to guide one, and "without virtue."
To find shelter for one's person is called "exposure"; what heart could fail to rejoice inwardly when such a thing occurs beyond all expectation?
If, moreover, by virtue of this encounter I may attain the fruit of sainthood, I shall not have disgraced my status as the Tathāgata’s younger brother.

Although I have now received the Tathāgata’s revelation of secret words, these remain merely matters of extensive learning and memorization; they do not yet constitute the domain of my own wisdom, remaining instead like counting another’s treasures.

Since there has not been even a hair’s breadth of new realization that differs from when one had not yet heard [the teaching], I again entreat the Tathāgata to bestow upon me the secret adornment (*guhyavyūha*), so that I may enter it.

What is called "secret adornment" refers to the aforementioned gate of non-leaking *nirvāṇa*, which implicitly points to the perfect faculties (*paripūrṇendriya*). This final instruction is identical to the very first [instruction].
Since this single gate is the initial stage of practice, it is called the "initial expedient means.

However, one must wait until the threefold contemplation within a single mind is already clear, the fundamental nature of karma arising from the mind is thoroughly examined, and the sequence for unraveling the knots is already known;
only then can one point out entry through one of these six gates. This instruction is presented at the very end.

Therefore, it is further said that this final revelation is precisely the request for the fundamental root of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong ben-gen*), serving as the door for entering the "Flower Mansion.
As for those who "withdraw and conceal their secret mechanism," this means that once the prostrations to the Buddha are completed, they remain silent and say nothing more;
they withdraw into secrecy, not daring to hope for the Tathāgata’s own golden-mouthed pronouncement, intending instead to have the World-Honored One command his various [disciples].
The holy assembly each spoke, and because I was able to enter [the truth] by means of their words, it is called "secret transmission.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed all the great Bodhisattvas and the great Arhats whose outflows were exhausted within the assembly:
"You Bodhisattvas and Arhats, having been born into my Dharma and attained the state of no-more-learning, I now ask you:"
Regarding the initial arousal of the mind and the realization of the eighteen realms, who attained perfect penetration, and by what skillful means did they enter samādhi?
This [passage] causes the twenty-five sages to each describe their own perfect penetration, thereby fulfilling Ānanda’s aspiration.
When it says "the initial arousal of the mind," it asks from which single dharma one first arouses the bodhicitta to gain entry into this [state].

Regarding the mention of the eighteen *dhātus* but not the seven elements (*mahābhūtas*): this is because the five great elements are objects (*viṣaya*), the element of sight is the faculty (*indriya*), and the element of consciousness is cognition (*vijñāna*).
Thus, although the preceding text has revealed that the three categories and the seven elements are all the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha, there was as yet no corroborating evidence;
therefore, it causes the twenty-five persons to each state their respective points of entry (*praveśa-sthāna*) in order to manifest what is meant.
"What I have said is not erroneous.
The five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'In the Deer Park and at the Kukuṭārāma, we witnessed the Tathāgata’s initial attainment of enlightenment; through the Buddha’s voice, we attained clear understanding.'"
Regarding the Four Truths, the Buddha asked the bhikṣus, "I was the first to declare my understanding; the Tathāgata sealed me with the name Ajñāta.
My wondrous voice is subtle, secret, and perfect; through sound, I attained arhatship. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, sound is supreme.
This describes the realization through the sensory object of sound. The Deer Park (Mṛgadāva) and the Cock Garden (Kukkuṭārāma) were both sites where ancient emperors raised livestock.
Kauṇḍinya is translated here as "Fire-Vessel" (*Agnidatta*), because in his previous life he was a fire-worshipping heretic (*agnihotra-tīrthika*).

The five bhikṣus were those whom the Buddha first delivered. When the Buddha left the household life, King Śuddhodana commanded three members of his clan and [the mother of] the [Bodhisattva’s] mother...

Two members of the clan followed and protected [the Buddha] from behind, each practicing a different path; because they were the very first to be converted when the Buddha attained enlightenment, he is called "He Who Beheld the Tathāgata’s Initial Attainment of Enlightenment.
When the Buddha turned the Wheel of Dharma by expounding the Four Noble Truths three times for the sake of the five bhikṣus, Cunda was the very first to realize them;
therefore, he is called "He Who Awakened to the Four Noble Truths through the Buddha’s Voice. As for Ājñāta—this...
"Explaining through understanding" means that by first understanding the Tathāgata, one is certified by the name "Understanding.
"Sublime Sound, Secret and Perfect" means that one awakens to and enters the soundless samādhi through sound itself; thus it is called "Sublime Sound.
Since all sounds are the Buddha's sound, it is called "Perfect. Because it is heard only by Dharmapāla himself and not by others, it is called "Secret. Below...
The text states that all that is secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous enters therein; thus the *Zongjing* says:
"It is like rolling back the waves of the great ocean and condensing them into a single drop, or gathering the lands of the ten directions and pointing them out within a single speck of dust."
Upānanda rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha: “I, too, observed the Buddha when he first attained enlightenment;
observing the signs of impurity, I conceived a great sense of revulsion and realized the nature of all forms.

By proceeding from the impure through white bones to subtle dust, they returned to emptiness. With both form and emptiness being non-existent, I attained the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). The Tathāgata has thus certified me.”
"My name is Niṣadha. When all coarse forms have been exhausted, wondrous forms become subtle and perfect. I attained Arhatship through these characteristics of form.
When the Buddha asked about the most direct path to universal penetration, according to what I have realized, the causal factor of form is supreme."

This is the entry point for awakening through the sense-object of form (*rūpa*). Because there is much greed and desire, the Buddha instructed the practice of the nine contemplations (*navasaṃjñā*) to remedy it, so as to transform that [greedy] mind into one that perceives foulness. Regarding what is called "impurity":
it means contemplating that within this body there are thirty-six internal substances, while externally, filth constantly flows from the nine apertures; from birth until death, it is always thus.

There is not a single thing that is pure; from the impurity of the seed, the impurity of the dwelling place, the impurity of the place of birth, to the ultimate impurity—these are the nine contemplations (navasaṃjñā):

first, the contemplation of bloating (*vyādhmātaka-saṃjñā*); second, the contemplation of the livid-blue (*vinīlaka-saṃjñā*); third, the contemplation of decay (*vipūyaka-saṃjñā*); fourth, the contemplation of being smeared with blood (*vilohitaka-saṃjñā*); fifth, the contemplation of festering pus (*vipaḍumaka-saṃjñā*);

sixth, the contemplation of being devoured by worms (*vikhāditaka-saṃjñā*); seventh, the contemplation of scattering (*vikṣiptaka-saṃjñā*); eighth, the contemplation of bones (*asthi-saṃjñā*); ninth, the contemplation of burning (*vidagdhaka-saṃjñā*).
It is thought that by proceeding from below through these nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*), one gradually returns to emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
When both emptiness and form (*rūpa*) are non-existent, form is initially regarded as the disease and the nine perceptions and emptiness as the medicine;

having reached this point, both medicine and disease are eliminated, and one suddenly awakens and enters the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*). Upānisaṭha means "near" or "slight," and it is also called "form."
"Nature" refers to the subtle atom (*paramāṇu*), for it is a minute portion of form; thus, "wondrous form is subtle and perfect" means that all forms are the Buddha’s form.
Regarding "the cause of form being supreme," it was previously stated: "I say that the Buddha-dharma arises from causes and conditions.

This expresses the realization and entry into the principle of causes and conditions as it pertains to the sense-object of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*). For instance, when contemplating a single phenomenon of form, there are five teachings through which one attains realization.

The initial Hīnayāna view regards this as real form and does not speak of its emptiness of nature; the Initial Teaching (Śāstra) view sees that these dharmas of form arise from conditions and necessarily lack self-nature;

the Final Teaching (Sūtra) view sees the non-obstruction of form and emptiness, wherein true emptiness does not preserve its own nature but follows conditions to manifest as form—this being illusory form;
the Sudden Teaching holds that there is no dharma of form that is not the True Principle.
Because that which is gathered is this very form, it is the single flavor of ultimate truth; there is no other separate dharma to be explained.
Water and waves are both transcended, and in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), arising is the total inclusion. One and many mutually encompass one another, established simultaneously.
A single block of perfect luminosity—whatever is raised is form, whatever is raised is emptiness; its meaning and flavor are sovereign, to be employed according to wisdom.
Therefore, whichever door one enters, there is nothing that is not revealed.
The youth Gandhahastin rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha:

"I heard the Tathāgata instruct me to contemplate thoroughly the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena. At that time, having taken leave of the Buddha, I retired to a secluded and pure chamber. There I saw various bhikṣus..."

When I burn aloeswood incense, its fragrance comes silently into my nostrils. I observe that this scent is neither wood, nor space, nor smoke, nor fire; it departs without attachment and arrives from nowhere.
Through this, my conceptual mind dissolves and the untainted (*anāsrava*) is revealed. Thus, the Tathāgata conferred upon me the title "Aromatic Perfection.
In an instant, the dust-like scents vanished, and a wondrous fragrance became subtle and pervasive. From this state of Aromatic Perfection...
Having attained Arhatship, when the Buddha asked about the supreme means of perfect penetration, I replied that, according to my own realization, the "Auspiciousness of Fragrance" was foremost;

this was because I entered the Way through the sense-object of fragrance. "Sitting in tranquility" (*yan-hui*) refers to sitting in stillness and calming the breath; it refers to a pure fast and a quiet chamber.
As for my observation below regarding the ultimate source from which fragrance comes—it does not arise from wood, nor does it emerge from itself... [text continues].
The smoke and fire do not emerge from elsewhere, nor do they arise from emptiness, nor do they emerge without cause;

by this principle, the "dissolving the consumer" means the deluded mind naturally ceases. "Revealing the outflow-free" means that through this, one immediately perceives the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
"Sublime fragrance, dense and perfect" means that all fragrances are the fragrance of the Dharmakāya, just as Lu Zhi [Su Shi] smelled the osmanthus.
The old nun who smelled the plum all attained realization through the fragrance.

The two Dharma Princes, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, along with five hundred Brahmās present in the assembly, immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha:
"Since beginningless kalpas, we have been skilled physicians in the world; we have tasted these [medicines] with our own mouths."
In the Sahā world, there are one hundred and eight thousand species of plants, trees, grasses, metals, and stones; all such things he knows completely.

Furthermore, regarding tastes—bitter, sour, salty, bland, sweet, and pungent—as well as their various combinations, those produced simultaneously, and those that undergo transformation, whether they are cold or hot, poisonous or non-poisonous, he is able to know them all thoroughly.
Serving the Tathāgata, he understands that the nature of taste is neither empty nor existent.
"It is neither identical to body and mind, nor separate from body and mind. By discerning the cause of flavor, I attained awakening;
the Buddha-Tathāgata then conferred upon my brothers, the two Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, their names. Now, within this assembly, we serve as Dharma Princes.

Through the faculty of flavor, I have awakened to clarity and ascended to the rank of Bodhisattva. When the Buddha asked about the most perfect penetration, I replied that, according to what I have realized, the cause of flavor is supreme."
This is the entry into awakening through the sense-object of flavor (*rasa*). First, the past cause is recounted: serving as a physician who tastes medicines like Shen Nong and others.
Following this, it clarifies that his past habits were not forgotten; he immediately began to contemplate from the locus of flavor.

"Neither empty nor existent" means that the nature within the intersection of both is neither emptiness nor existence. "The body" refers to the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*), and "the mind" refers to...

When tongue-consciousness contemplates this nature of flavor, it does not arise from the sense-organ or consciousness, because various flavors do not arrive and the nature of neutrality is ever-present;
nor does it arise apart from the sense-organ and consciousness, because outside of the sense-organ and consciousness there is no flavor.
One who awakens by discerning the cause of flavor is said to observe precisely at the locus of flavor and thereby enter awakening through that very locus of flavor.
Furthermore, for those who clarify the sense of taste, one realizes the samādhi of a single flavor (*ekarasa-samādhi*) through worldly flavors;
that is to say, every flavor is purely the essence of *amṛta* (clarified butter). The staff of Deshan, the shout of Linji, and the finger of Guizong are all means of manifesting this very flavor.
Bhadrapāla, together with his sixteen companions, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In the past, under the Buddha King of Majestic Sound, we heard the Dharma and left the household life.

Once, while entering the bathhouse according to custom during the time for bathing the Sangha, we suddenly realized the cause of water: it neither washes away dust nor washes the body; in between these two, there is tranquil stillness.”

Having attained the state of non-existence, my past habitual tendencies were never forgotten, continuing until the present time when I left the household life under the Buddha and attained the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*).

That Buddha named me Bhadrapāla; through the manifestation of sublime touch, I dwell as a child of the Buddha. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties, I have realized that the faculty of touch is the most excellent cause for attainment.

This is the entry into awakening through the sense-object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*). Bhadrapāla—translated here as Xiànshǒu (Worthy Protector) or Xiànhù (Worthy Guardian)—is none other than that person who was formerly known as Chángbùqīng (Never-Disparaging).
We shall now set forth his past history, which arose from the stimulus of water through the sense of touch.
Touch is the consciousness that arises in the interval when the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) comes into contact with the sense-object of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*), perceiving its coldness.

Warmth, roughness, and smoothness are termed "tactile sensations" (*spraṣṭavya*). Now, while bathing, as the water and the body come into contact, one should investigate the tactile sensations produced therein:
from what do they arise? One might say that the washing agent is the water and the object washed is the dust;
yet, as for the tactile sensations of warmth, cold, roughness, and smoothness occurring between them, they can neither wash away the dust nor cleanse the body itself.

Since one has naturally and peacefully realized the absence of self-nature and entered into awakening from this point, one had already attained the vision of the Truth (satyadarśana) during the time of Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja;

now, through the Buddha’s transformation, one further attains the state of No-more-learning (aśaikṣa). Because a single touch from this point makes every place of contact a site of the Way (bodhimaṇḍa) and every sight an object of Bodhi, it is said: "Wondrous Touch Proclaims Clarity."
Mahākāśyapa, the Bhikṣuṇī Golden Light, and others immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In a past kalpa, within this world-system, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa.
I was able to draw near to him, hear the Dharma, and practice its study. After that Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, I made offerings to his relics and lit lamps to continue the light."

Because she anointed the image of the Buddha with purple-gold light, from that time forth, in birth after birth throughout successive lifetimes, her body has always been perfectly full and a mass of purple-gold light.
These bhikṣuṇīs of Purple-Gold Light and the others were my own kinsmen who simultaneously resolved their minds on enlightenment.

I observe that the six sense-objects of the world are subject to decay and transformation; only by cultivating extinction through emptiness and stillness can one bring both body and mind to cessation.
"Having passed through hundreds of thousands of kalpas as briefly as a finger-snap, I attained Arhatship through the dharma of emptiness.

The World-Honored One has declared me the foremost among those who practice dhūta austerities; I have clarified and extinguished all outflows. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, according to what I have realized, the causal factor of dharmas is supreme."
"This is the entry through awakening by means of the dharma-object (*dharmāyatana*). "I [recall] at the lower level" narrates the past causes; "I contemplate" and below narrate that which is entered.

All worldly eons arise from the false movement of the dharma-object; now, by practicing the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and emptying the dharma-object, mental conceptions do not move.
Thus, forgetting place and forgetting time, passing through hundreds of thousands of eons is like the snap of a finger.
Now, holding this golden-threaded *kāṣāya*, he has entered meditative absorption on Mount Kukkuṭapāda to await the descent of Maitreya;
this is the proof thereof. *Dhūta* is translated here as "shaking off," for it is able to shake off the dust of phenomena (*dharmarajas*).

Thus, those who have clarified the wondrous Dharma transform worldly dharmas into supramundane dharmas, as expressed in the so-called "this dharma abides in its own place" (*dharmasthititā*)—the characteristics of the world.
They are eternally abiding. As for why the six sense-objects are all called "wondrous," it is because they are not bound by the objects themselves;

thus one knows that the self-nature of the six sense-objects pervades all places, and every single thing is a path of entry. How could they be restricted to a single gate? Every movement and action is none other than the Buddha-work;
even the falling of petals or the jingling of bracelets can serve as a place to settle the spirit. This concludes the section on the Perfect Penetration of the Six Sense-Objects.
Aniruddha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “When I first left the household life, I was constantly fond of sleep.
The Tathāgata rebuked me, saying that I was of the same class as beasts. Hearing the Buddha’s rebuke, I wept and reproached myself;
for seven days I did not sleep, and thereby lost both my eyes. The World-Honored One then showed me the Vajra Samādhi of Joyful Vision and Radiant Illumination.”
"I do not perceive the ten directions through the eye; rather, the essence is pure and transparent, as clear as looking at a fruit in the palm of one's hand.

Thus, the Tathāgata certified me as an Arhat. When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, to revolve the faculty of sight and return to its source is the foremost method."
This is called the entry through the faculty of the eye. Aniruddha—translated here as "Free from Poverty"—was the younger brother of the Buddha, the son of King Śuklodana.
In the past, he offered a single meal to a Pratyekabuddha; as a result, he experienced wish-fulfilling happiness for ninety-one kalpas.
However, he was prone to excessive sleep, and the Tathāgata rebuked him, saying: "Alas! Alas! Why do you sleep? You are like a snail!"
"Shellfish and similar creatures sleep for a thousand years without hearing the name of the Buddha. Aniruddha, however, remained awake throughout the night and lost both his eyes;
he later cultivated the Vajra-samādhi and attained the divine eye (divya-cakṣus). This was because his physical eyes were exchanged for the divine eye.
When I say, 'I do not perceive the ten directions by means of the eyes,' it clarifies that I do not follow the sense-faculties."
It is said that when the faculties are entrusted and clarity emerges, even the "half-head" divine eye can see one Buddha-world;
yet here it is said that one contemplates and sees the ten directions. This reveals the actual realization of the Tathāgatagarbha nature.
To turn back that seeing in order to see the nature is called "revolving the seeing. To follow the root rather than the objects is called "following the source."

Cūḍapanthaka immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “I lacked the capacity for recitation and retention, and possessed no nature for extensive learning.
When I first encountered the Buddha, heard the Dharma, and left the household life, I sought to remember a single verse of the Tathāgata;

yet for one hundred days, I could only retain what preceded while losing what followed, or retain what followed while losing what preceded. Out of compassion for my folly, the Buddha taught me the method of ‘peaceful dwelling.’”

While dwelling in the practice of regulating the inhalation and exhalation, I at that time contemplated the breath until it became subtle and reached its ultimate limit; I observed the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) within each moment (*kṣaṇa*).
My mind suddenly opened up and attained great non-obstruction, until finally, with the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), I became an Arhat.

Seated beneath the Buddha’s seat, I was certified as one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, by reversing the breath and following the void, this is the second [method].

1. This is the entry through the perception of the nose. Pāṇṭaka—translated as "Snake-Slave" or "Successor of the Path" because he was born by the side of a road—was formerly a great Dharma-master who recited the *Bhikṣu-broom* [text] while being miserly with the Buddha-dharma.
Because they were unwilling to teach others due to the retribution of their past delusions and dullness, they encountered the Buddha and left the household life.

Although five hundred bhikṣus were taught the same single verse, they could not master it after ninety days. To remedy their mental distraction, the Buddha taught them the method of regulating the breath (*ānāpāna*).
I shall now describe below the practice of regulating the breath; because the mind and the breath rely upon one another, the mind...
As the breath gradually becomes faint, it also gradually becomes subtle; at the point where the breath is most subtle, one further investigates its arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.
One continues this investigation until even a single thought-moment is found to contain ninety kṣaṇas, and each kṣaṇa is further found to contain nine hundred instances of arising and ceasing.
When one has applied such focused effort for a long time, a single bean will suddenly burst within a bed of cold ashes, and thereby the mind is attained.
Cessation of both delusions results in great non-obstruction; this is what is meant by "in a single breath, the Way does not exist, yet it accords with the future.
To "reverse the breath and follow emptiness" means to trace back the breath to its ultimate subtlety, where it likewise returns to emptiness.
Formerly, when Minister Mo Jiang visited Chan Master Nantang Jing to inquire about the essentials for resolving his mind, Nantang instructed him to dwell in a state of excellence.
While attending to my duties, I happened to enter the latrine and, smelling a foul odor, quickly covered my nose with my hand; thereupon, I attained realization and presented this verse:
"From of old, I have cherished a refined and elegant air, Often laughing at those who seek outside themselves.

Though ten thousand variations and a thousand differences may be sought, The place where it is found is originally right at the tip of the nose. This, too, was a case of losing one's nostrils by following after the breath.
Kauṇḍinya immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “I have committed verbal karma;
in past kalpas, I habitually mocked śramaṇas, and as a result, in every successive birth, I suffered from the disease of rumination.
The Tathāgata showed me the Dharma-gate of the single-flavor, pure mind-ground; having attained this, I extinguished my discursive mind and entered samādhi, observing the cognition of taste.”

Neither substance nor entity, one should, through mindfulness, transcend all worldly outflows; internally liberated from body and mind, externally detached from the world, far removed from the three realms of existence like a bird escaping its cage.
Free from defilement and with dust extinguished, the Dharma-eye becomes pure, and one attains Arhatship.

The Tathāgata personally certified me as having ascended the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I testified that, according to my realization, it lies in returning to the flavor and revolving the faculty of cognition.
This is the first. This is entry through awakening by means of the tongue-faculty. Kātyāyanīputra—here translated as "Ox-chewer"—in a past life saw an old monk who had no teeth yet was eating;
he laughed at him for resembling an ox. Consequently, in life after life, he was reborn with an ox-tongue, always remaining like that of an ox.
The Buddha, in order to prevent slander, granted him a rosary so that he might constantly recollect the Buddha, sever all miscellaneous conditions, and maintain pure, single-minded mindfulness;

thus it is called the "Dharma-gate of the Single Flavor and Pure Mind-ground.
