thus I attained the patience of non-arising and fulfilled Bodhi—this is the foremost."
This is the entry into awakening through the water-element (*āpas-mahābhūta*). The Buddha named Varuṇa (Water-Heaven) also entered awakening through the water-element;

therefore, those who practice the meditation on water (*āpasmṛti*) demonstrate what they have realized to others. Regarding the observation of "the lower": this refers to entering the contemplation upon hearing the Dharma.
As for "the nature of water cannot be overcome": because the nature of water is identical, it cannot be displaced or usurped by one another. This accords with the *Huayan* [Avataṃsaka Sūtra].
Within the Flower Treasury Ocean of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, there is a great lotus flower;
within that lotus flower are immeasurable seas of fragrant water, and each sea of fragrant water has a single lotus flower as the seed for various Buddha-fields and worlds.

Because the Flower Treasury World (*Puṣpakaraṇḍa-lokadhātu*) resides within these seas of fragrant water, it is called the "King of Floating Banner" world-system. Thus, it is known as the Flower Treasury World.
There are twenty layers piled one upon another, as high as a banner and thus most towering;
therefore, when one now contemplates the water within the body and finds it equal to the seawater without distinction, this is the melting of the mind through contemplation.

Although the contemplative mind has been perfected, one has not yet attained the dissolution of the body because, while the perception of water has been accomplished, non-self has not yet been realized, and the characteristics of water still persist as the entirety of the water.
Because he still possessed the vision of the Dharma even while his body had not yet perished, Śāriputra encountered a malevolent spirit.

While Śāriputra was in meditative absorption on the banks of the Ganges, due to the power of a karmic enmity from a previous life, he was seized by the spirit; upon emerging from concentration, he suffered a headache.

The Buddha said, "If you had no body through meditative concentration, it would have been shattered. Because he now experienced pain upon emerging from concentration, he harbored doubts and fell back into regression. (4)
As for the fact that his physical body remained as it was before, it is because his mind did not suffer pain. When asked, "From where does this water in the room come?

he replied, "It is produced by the power of meditative concentration; it is a form resulting from concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*). One can thus understand that when non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) used their resolute minds to turn stone into stone, they were likewise transforming water through the power of meditative concentration.
This demonstrates that all phenomena are but mind. [The text then asks: "What of Moonlight entering into concentration?"
At that time, because the boy threw pebbles into the water, his heart pained him; later, when he had them remove the pebbles, the pain ceased. [The question was:
"Does this single pebble ultimately exist within the heart or outside the heart? If it were outside the heart, it should not cause pain;
if it were inside the heart, then from where did this pebble enter? [The answer was: "The pebbles..."
Setting aside for a moment the question of whether this water within the room is ultimately outside the body or inside the body:
if it were outside the body, from where would it emerge after one has entered meditative concentration? If it were inside the body, by what path would it enter upon emerging from concentration?
If one knows the entry and exit of the water, one will likewise know the interior and exterior of the earthenware shards.

Thus, one who has attained the state of "losing the self" (wang-shen) shatters attachments so that the aggregates (skandhas) become empty. Once this body is empty, the contemplation of water (*āp-kṛtsna*) is also empty;
it then merges as one with the true nature of water which is emptiness by nature, and with the true emptiness of water itself. This becomes a single piece pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
When looking back at this body, how could it be anything more than a single bubble on a great ocean? One who attains the name "Childlike Purity" (*kumāra-bhūta*) possesses the state of a youth.
The true virtue of this [teaching] allows those who participate in the assembly of Bodhisattvas to realize the dharma-emptiness of the Bodhisattva.
The Dharma Prince Vairocana then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I recall that in the past, after kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Immeasurable Sound (Amitaghoṣa), who revealed to Bodhisattvas their fundamental awakening."
With wondrous clarity, I observed that this world and the bodies of sentient beings are all turned by the power of delusive conditions and the force of wind.
At that time, I contemplated the establishment of the realms, the movement of the world, the motion and stillness of the body, and the stirring thoughts of the mind;
I saw that all these movements were non-dual and without distinction. I then realized that the nature of these manifold movements comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
In all the ten directions, the deluded sentient beings as numerous as motes of dust were of one and the same false nature;

likewise, within a single trichiliocosm, all sentient beings were like hundreds of mosquitoes and gnats contained in a single vessel, chirping and clamoring together, creating a frantic uproar within a mere fraction of space.
Not long after encountering the Buddha, they attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). At that time...
When my mind opened, I beheld the Land of Akṣobhya Buddha in the east and served as a Dharma Prince for the Buddhas of the ten directions;

my body and mind emitted light, penetrating all things without obstruction. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, I replied: "Through observing that the power of wind has no dependence, I awakened to the Bodhicitta and entered samādhi.
I have unified with the Buddhas of the ten directions to transmit this single wondrous mind; this is the foremost."

This is the entry into awakening through the wind-element (*vāyu-mahābhūta*). As for "Lapis Lazuli Light" (*Vaiḍūryaprabha*), after his awakening he was transparently penetrating and unobstructed, like lapis lazuli;
thus he received this name. The Buddha whom he took as his teacher, named Immeasurable Sound (*Amitaghoṣa*), likewise entered realization from the side of the roaring of ten thousand apertures.
That which is turned by the power of the wind is what *Zhuangzi* calls the "sighing of Heaven and Earth" (*tiāndì yī*).
The name for this vital energy is "wind," yet they do not know from whence the wind originates.

I observe that what follows in the narrative—entering contemplation and observing the establishment of the realms—means observing that the world is established only by being sustained by the power of the wind;
observing the movement of the world means observing that the three periods of time also exist through the transformation brought about by the power of the wind.
Regarding the movement and stillness of the body: observe that each movement and each stillness of this body is also driven by the power of wind (vāyu).

Regarding the movement of thoughts in the mind: observe that this mind flows and shifts from moment to moment, never remaining still even for an instant, and that its arising and ceasing are likewise produced by the power of wind.
Observing in this way, one finds that the world, the body, and the mind are each distinct; yet, when investigating their ultimate cause, they are found to be one.
All arise from the movement of the wind of a single thought of ignorance, being equal and without distinction.
At that time, I clearly understood that all movement is false speech; even a mote of dust or a sentient being is all turned by the power of the wind of delusive conditions.
From the sentient beings of a single world-system to those of the great trichiliocosm, it is likewise; therefore, it is said they share the same delusion.

Regarding those who say that the frantic clamor within the square inch of the heart is stirred up by these sentient beings—that it is all within one's own "fang cun" (the inner mind) and not outside—it was said by the Patriarch:
"It is not the banner that moves, nor is it the wind that moves; it is the mind of the worthy one that moves.
This follows the account of awakening and entry [into the Way] upon meeting the Buddha. East is the direction of Zhen (Thunder), the beginning of all movement; because it is located there...
To perceive the Immovable Buddha within the midst of all moving phenomena is precisely what enables one to succeed to and glorify the Buddha-position.

That the power of wind has no dependence means that it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; thus, the phrase "unifying the Buddhas of the ten directions to transmit the single wondrous mind" refers to the fact that there are no Buddhas of the ten directions who do not observe this wind of ignorance and thereby realize the essence of immovable awakening.
...Thus it was.
The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I and the Tathāgata obtained the body of boundless extent under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara; at that time, I held four great precious jewels in my hands, which illuminated the ten [directions]..."

The Buddha-lands, as numerous as atoms, were transformed into empty space. Furthermore, from within the Great Perfect Mirror manifested by his own mind, he emitted ten kinds of subtle and wondrous jewel-light that flowed and drenched all the way to the limits of space throughout the ten directions.

All the *dhvaja-rāja* (banner-king) lands entered into the mirror, merging with my body; my body became identical to empty space, without mutual obstruction, and was able to skillfully enter lands as numerous as atoms.
By extensively performing Buddha-works upon this earth, I have attained great accordance with the Dharma through this great spiritual power.

Through my contemplation, I have realized that the four elements have no basis, that they arise and perish as mere false imaginings, and that empty space is non-dual; thus, the Buddha-lands are fundamentally identical. By illuminating this identity, I attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied: "Through my observation of the boundlessness of empty space, I entered samādhi; its wondrous power is perfect."
This is explained as the first [stage].

This is the entry into awakening through the Great Element of Space (*ākāśa-mahābhūta*). First, regarding the description of the great function within the fruition—wherein one grasps the four great elements with the hand—it signifies that having already attained the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna*), one employs these wisdoms to perceive that all four great elements are the true emptiness of the nature of form (*prakṛti-rūpa-śūnyatā*).

This is to subsume function back into essence. Furthermore, regarding "within one's own mind" and so forth, it indicates that the ten dharma realms are all manifested within the equal light of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom of one's own mind;
this reveals that the true color of the nature-emptiness arises from essence as function.
Regarding "the various banners" and below, it shows that by entering the lands into the body, there is no body that is not a land; the body is able to...
Below, it is shown that when the body enters the lands, there is no land that is not the body. Qingliang says:

"In its function (*yòng*), it surges like boiling water, operating in accordance with the true essence (*zhēntǐ*); in its essence, it is as clear as a mirror or still as water, gathering and assembling in accordance with conditions (*suíyuán*).
It is like the mutual reflection of Qin mirrors, or like the interlocking nets of Indra. This is precisely the meaning of this passage. Below this, the greatness [of the dharmakāya] is revealed.
This was due to my mind. Through my earnest contemplation, I observed that the four great elements have no basis and originally arise from birth and extinction, ultimately returning to emptiness.
Furthermore, I observed that empty space is non-dual and that Buddha-lands are fundamentally the same. Thus, emptiness is not different from the land, and the land is not different from emptiness.
Consequently, within the very locus where form and emptiness coincide, I suddenly attained illumination and realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Therefore, there is such a great function. That "wondrous power is perfectly luminous" specifically refers to the non-obstruction between emptiness and form, and the mutual interpenetration of body and land.
Maitreya Bodhisattva then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I recall the past..."
Throughout kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa; from that Buddha I went forth into homelessness.

Yet my mind remained heavy with worldly fame, and I delighted in frequenting noble families. At that time, the World-Honored One taught me to cultivate the samādhi of "mind-only consciousness" and enter into *samādhi*.
Since those kalpas have passed, I have used this samādhi to serve Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, seeking only worldly renown.
When the mind ceased and was extinguished, and until the appearance of Dīpaṃkara Buddha in the world, I attained the supreme, wondrous, and perfect samādhi of the conscious mind.
Even unto the exhaustion of empty space, the lands of the Tathāgatas—whether pure or defiled, existent or non-existent—are all manifestations produced by the transformations of my own mind.
World-Honored One, because I have realized that all is but the mind and consciousness, the nature of consciousness flows forth as these [lands].

"O Tathāgata, I have now received the prediction that I shall next succeed you as Buddha. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, I replied: 'I have observed with clarity that the ten directions are nothing but consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*).

This conscious mind is perfectly luminous; by entering into the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), I am far removed from the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Thus I have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); this is the foremost method.'"
This is the cause for great awakening and entry through consciousness. Those whose minds value worldly fame strive for empty reputation rather than true reality.
Those who delight in frequenting noble families do not turn inward but rush outward in pursuit.
Those who cultivate the meditative concentration on consciousness-only are led to examine closely that all phenomena are transformations of the mind and consciousness, and are not truly existent.
Furthermore, when one seeks worldly fame and the mind ceases to exist, knowing that the illusory realm is unreal, the mind suddenly becomes empty; this is the single-minded internal contemplation.

Upon reaching the stage of "under Maitreya" (Dīpaṃkara), through the perfection of contemplation, one awakens to and enters the wondrously perfect nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is consciousness.
As for the passage beginning with "even unto," one realizes that the purity and defilement of the vessel-world (the physical universe) all arise from the transformations of consciousness.
"Coming from outside" means that, O World-Honored One, all Buddhas flow forth from the nature of consciousness; the world does not undergo transformation through anything else.
Next, regarding "filling the place of a Buddha": it is because what has been realized is already ultimate that one fills the position of a Buddha.

The *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) consists of the *karmic-consciousness* (*karma-vijñāna*) and the two divisions of appearance and perception manifested by that karmic-consciousness. The *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature)...
From the two divisions of appearance and seeing, there further arises pervasive conceptualization, namely the dual grasping at self and phenomena.

To distance oneself from the dependent and the pervasive-conceptualized is precisely the perfected nature; for while the pervasive-conceptualized has a name but no substance, and the dependent has appearances but no intrinsic nature, only the perfected nature is their true essence.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Dharma Prince, together with fifty-two bodhisattvas of his same rank, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that in the past, during kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Amitābha.
Twelve Tathāgatas succeeded one another for the duration of a single kalpa; the last of these Buddhas was named Sūryaprabhācandraprabhābhibhū."
That Buddha taught me the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha: "Suppose there are two people, one who is single-mindedly mindful of another, and one who is single-mindedly forgetful of that person.

Such a pair may meet and yet not meet, or see and yet not see. Because the two remember each other and their mutual mindfulness is deep, this continues from birth to birth, like a form and its shadow, never diverging. So it is with the Tathāgatas of the ten directions."
He compassionately regards all sentient beings as a mother remembers her child. Even if the child were to run away, what would it avail the mother’s remembrance?

But if the child remembers the mother as the mother remembers the child, then throughout successive lives, mother and child will never be far apart. If the minds of sentient beings remember the Buddha and recite his name, they will certainly see the Buddha in this present life or in the future;
they will not be far from the Buddha, and without relying on other expedient means, their own minds will naturally open.
"Just as the body of one who has been perfumed with incense bears its fragrance, this is what is called the Adornment of Fragrant Light.

In my original stage of practice, I entered the patience of non-arising through the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha. Now, in this realm, I gather those who mindfully recite the Buddha's name and lead them back to the Pure Land.

When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties, I made no selection; by fully gathering the six sense-faculties and maintaining a continuous flow of pure mindfulness, I attained samādhi."
This is the foremost.
This is because, through seeing [the Buddha], one attains great awakening and entry. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* states:

"By means of the light of wisdom, he universally illumines all beings, causing them to leave the three miserable realms and attain supreme power; thus he is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta. The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "In the past, during the causal stage..."
When Amitābha was a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), Avalokiteśvara was his eldest son and Mahāsthāmaprāpta was his second son;
they now reside in Sukhāvatī at the left and right sides of Amitābha. As for the twelve Tathāgatas, they are:
Immeasurable Light, Boundless Light, Unattached Light, Majestic Light, Loving Light, Joyful Light, Wondrous Light, Inconceivable Light, and Peerless [Light].
The light is immeasurable; it eclipses the light of the sun and eclipses the light of the moon, surpassing the radiance of both sun and moon.
The intent is that throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, one must not for even the duration of a finger-snap entertain thoughts of the five worldly desires.

This is called the succession of the pure mindfulness of the twelve Tathāgatas, which constitutes one kalpa. As for what is termed "recollection of the Buddha" (buddhānusmṛti), if one relies on the conceptual mind, then such recollection is merely conceptual.

The Buddha of initial awakening is identical to original awakening; the union of the initial and the original is what is called "Buddha-remembrance" (nianfo). If one speaks of it according to the phenomenal level:

"remembrance" refers to darkly recording [the Buddha] without forgetting, and "Buddha" refers to emitting light to welcome and guide. Thus, the one who remembers belongs to oneself, while the one remembered belongs to the Buddha.
One person who focuses exclusively on recollection is a metaphor for the Buddha remembering sentient beings; one person who focuses exclusively on forgetting is... [a metaphor for sentient beings].

This is a metaphor for sentient beings not recollecting the Buddha. "Meeting yet not meeting" and "seeing yet not seeing" means that because the Buddha is single-mindedly mindful of sentient beings, he is never absent from their presence;
yet, because sentient beings do not recollect the Buddha, although the Buddha is before them, they neither meet nor see him. It is truly like the relationship between a mother and her child.
If one recollects, there will be no separation forever. This is like when Wenhui first saw Mañjuśrī:
he passed him by face-to-face, which is what is meant by "not meeting, not seeing. Later, when Mañjuśrī appeared atop the rice pot, this was "meeting" and "seeing.
The three lines concerning the ten directions apply to one who is exclusively mindful; the two lines beginning with "like a child" apply to one who is exclusively forgetful.
If you can combine these four phrases and maintain mindfulness without departing from the Buddha, then the Buddha will not be far away;
He is right here in this very place. If you recollect the Buddha with single-minded devotion, you shall see Him face-to-face morning and evening.

There is no need for any other expedient means, for by focusing exclusively on the recollection of the Buddha, your mind will naturally open. It is solely through such focused mindfulness of the Buddha that one attains the opening of the mind.
The analogy of a person who has been perfumed with incense and thus possesses its fragrance illustrates that one who recollects the Buddha will inevitably see the Buddha.

"Adorned with the fragrance and light" means that one adorns the *dharmatā*-Buddha, which is the fundamental nature of reality, with the fragrance and light of mindfulness of the Buddha. The six lines beginning with "I was originally...
refer to using the Dharma realized within oneself to deliver others. "Comprehensively subduing the six sense faculties" means that when one recollects the Buddha with single-mindedness, then—

To fully restrain the six sense faculties is for all six bases to be entirely devoted to mindfulness of the Buddha. Thus, when the eye does not grasp at forms, it is the eye being mindful of the Buddha;

and so on, until when the mind does not dwell upon dharmas, it is the mind being mindful of the Buddha. Because the six sense faculties are thus fully restrained, pure mindfulness is attained in uninterrupted succession.
This is because single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha and the resolute determination to engage in Chan meditation are fundamentally no different from one another.

If one follows the practice of *nien-fo* (reciting the Buddha’s name) with the practice of *chan-ch'an* (investigating Zen), one will know that this land possesses only two gates as the swift paths for entering the Way.
For both Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta are ministers who assist Amitābha;

one receives people through *nien-fo*, while the other instructs the multitude through *chan-ch'an*. Each has opened a distinct method according to the specific capacities of beings within this realm.
Regarding this matter, people of the world generally regard Chan meditation as superior and look down upon the practice of Buddha-recitation (*nianfo*).
I know that such individuals not only fail to understand the profound secret of Buddha-recitation, but they also do not understand the sublime essence of Chan meditation.
If one does not employ the method of "single-mindedness without distraction" when practicing Chan, one will certainly never awaken to it. If not...
If one approaches the recitation of the Buddha's name with a mind like a cat stalking a mouse, one will certainly not be born in the Pure Land.
Do not say that reciting the Buddha’s name is easy while Zen meditation is difficult; you should know that if it is difficult, both are difficult, and if it is easy, both are easy.
This depends on the depth of one’s power of faith and the thinness or thickness of one’s habitual tendencies. Question: A practitioner of Zen not only cannot allow [thoughts] to arise...
The views of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span are identical to the view of a Buddha and the view of dharmas; even these must not arise.
Therefore, this sutra denounces the arousal of the mind through the perception of signs as a "vajra of birth and death," and it censures seeking form through sound as a deviant path.

As for those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, their resolve lies in the continuous succession of pure mindfulness appearing before them, so that they will certainly see the Buddha in the future.

Thus, the two gates of emptiness and existence are diametrically opposed and distinct; how could they possibly be discussed as being on the same footing? Those who practice Chan have their resolve set on dissolving all phenomena;

therefore, they cannot allow a single thought to arise, sweeping away both good and evil entirely. Those who practice Buddha-recitation have their resolve set on being welcomed and guided by the Buddha;
they must maintain pure mindfulness continuously so that the Buddha is seen in every instance. Only those who can exhaustively [fulfill this requirement]...
Only by sweeping away all [delusions] can one see one's nature; once one can see one's nature, how difficult would it be to see the Buddha?
Furthermore, if one maintains pure mindfulness in succession, one will certainly be able to see the Buddha; once one can see the Buddha, seeing one's nature will also be easy. Therefore it is said:

"Those who abide only in true emptiness realize wondrous existence; those who abide only in wondrous existence perceive true emptiness. Although there are two gates, how could their ultimate goal differ?
There are two [approaches]: first, those who practice Chan have their resolve set on seeing one's nature (*xìng*), yet they find it difficult to enter the stream;
second, those who practice Buddha-recitation (*niàn-fo*) have their resolve set on seeing the Buddha, yet they find it difficult to achieve single-mindedness without distraction.

It is precisely appropriate for each to excel in their own specialty rather than hanging their thoughts upon both. If one’s thoughts hang upon both, not only will one fail to see one's nature, but furthermore—
One cannot see the Buddha. This concludes the Seven Great Perfect Penetrations.
*The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Cultivation and Realization and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas*, Fascicle Five.
The Sixth Fascicle of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas.
Composed by Shi Tongrun of Erleṅ’ān.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I recall that in the past, incalculable kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Avalokiteśvara.
Under that Buddha, I resolved upon Bodhicitta; that Buddha taught me to enter through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation."

Samādhi. This refers to the Ear-organ Perfect Penetration (śrotra-indriya-pariśuddha-samyak-prativedha). If one were to follow the sequential order, it would correspond to the stage of Auditory Wisdom (Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa);
however, among all twenty-four sages, none possess this perfect penetration that accords with the faculties of those in this region. Only this single gate aligns both the faculty and the teaching.
The meaning of universal penetration (*pariṇāmanā*) should be fully realized, and thus these words of extensive celebration follow one another; for this reason, they are explained separately.

As for the name "Avalokiteśvara," it refers to one who perceives sound with the ear and form with the eye. Because people hear with the ears and observe with the eyes, the Buddha whom he takes as his teacher is likewise named Avalokiteśvara.
This is because the Dharma he has realized was transmitted to him, such that its source is distant and its flow is long-lasting; he enters [the path] through hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Regarding *samādhi*: in this tradition, the essence of the teaching lies solely in hearing through sound; it enters via the faculty of hearing.
Thus, the character "hearing" (*wen*) refers specifically to the nature of hearing—which is neither born nor extinguished—as verified by the striking of a bell. As for "contemplation" (*si*):
it is not the universal mental factor of volition, nor is it the volition that thinks of good or evil, for both thinking of good and thinking of evil belong to erroneous contemplation.
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Although Ānanda has a powerful memory, he cannot avoid falling into perverse thoughts.

This refers to the thought that neither contemplates good nor evil; it means that the practitioner employs this "right thought" of not thinking at all, focusing single-mindedly on the nature of hearing and investigating where this faculty comes from, thereby causing [the mind] to...
Hearing with inverted perception, the auditory faculty detaches from its object and recedes inward; this serves as the sharp tool for uprooting [delusion] and the vanguard for eliminating the knots.
By turning downward to enter the stream and cause the "what" to perish, one reaches the manifestation of ultimate quiescence—all of which relies upon this single thought to achieve deep penetration.
This is what is meant in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* by "directly advancing through mind-only to observe the continuous flow," and what was referred to in the preceding text as "if..."
If you wish to eliminate the fetters, you must rely on the power of this contemplation within the very mind of those fetters. Luoshan said, "The single thought prior to sound is known by all.
Miaoyan said, "By means of the wondrous state of 'thought without thinking,' reflect upon the inexhaustible brilliance of the numinous flame.
When thought is exhausted, one returns to the source; the nature and characteristics are eternally abiding, and phenomena and principle are non-dual—this is the Tathāgata."
Therefore it is said: "Think of it, think of it; the spirits and deities will penetrate it. This cultivation does not refer to the performance of various fabricated practices;
rather, it means to realize that all phenomena are like illusions, to understand that they have no fundamental basis, and to refrain from giving rise to grasping or attachment.
When all subtle defilements naturally dissolve and the nature of awakening manifests before one, this is called "right cultivation through reflection."
This shows that because one cultivates this detachment, it is as stated in the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*: "To know illusion is itself detachment; to detach from illusion is itself awakening.

As for "entering," it refers to the entire body having already arrived. "Samādhi" refers to the aforementioned Great Dharani Gate, meaning that by pulling out this single root, one immediately attains the entry of the entire body into this Great Dharani Gate. Question: At the beginning...
Having already refuted that this thought is false, why is it used again here?
The answer is that Ānanda has consistently identified this thought as real and refuses to let it go; this is like taking a thief for one's own son.
Therefore, it must be refuted and destroyed so that he may recognize the thief and seek out the true son. Now, once again...
To employ this thought is to recognize it as a thief; it is to borrow a thief to kill a thief, transforming calamity into merit.
If one mistakes the thief for a son, one robs oneself of the family treasure. If one borrows a thief to kill a thief, then that thief becomes a meritorious minister.
Furthermore, although the gates practiced by the twenty-four sages differ, the essential point of their mental application and observation is the same.
All of these rely upon this contemplation; without this contemplation, there is no place to begin.
Thus, the practical application of the twenty-four sages is all manifested through the single gateway of Avalokiteśvara. It is like a lamp made of oil and wax:

if it is not lit with fire, it will never become bright. If one claims that it does not depend on contemplation and that one should directly transcend the mind, intellect, and consciousness to practice, [this is a grave error].
Upon thorough investigation, it appears that this single gate was taught solely for those of the highest capacity;
yet this both contradicts the ancient teachings on Avalokiteśvara and violates the principle stated in the subsequent text that the Dharma is taught equally to those of shallow and deep capacities.

Furthermore, since even the single gate of Buddha-remembrance (*buddhānusmṛti*), which is the most simple and easy, is here made even simpler, one can know that this present gate is easier still than Buddha-remembrance. Alas!
Why is it that explaining the most difficult practice to perform is no different from leading someone through the gate only to reject them at the end?
Therefore, know that one who, upon hearing this Dharma for the first time, directly accepts it without falling into discursive thought, possesses the highest capacity.
Should their faculties be somewhat dull, they cannot avoid entering by means of conceptual thought. Once those of inferior capacity have attained it...

Since hearing and reflection must also be applied with full effort toward cultivation before one can enter [the realization], we know that those of superior faculties do not require reflection but see directly, while those of middling or inferior faculties must certainly employ reflection and cultivation.
Thus, hearing, reflection, and cultivation are taught as methods for both shallow and deep [capacities]; is this not perfectly clear? However, one must not employ distracted or erroneous reflection.
If one employs perverse or distracted thoughts, one can never enter; therefore it is said: "The faculty of knowing is muddled by confused thoughts;
only when the mind is clear and lucid will you finally see. It is also said: "Ānanda, even with a powerful memory, you cannot avoid falling into perverse thoughts.
Therefore, by employing the correct thought of not thinking at all, one observes and naturally attains entry. Question: If one practices Chan meditation, may one employ this "not thinking at all"?

If one employs the correct contemplation of "not thinking of anything" to contemplate the true mind that is without marks, and employs the correct mindfulness of "not recollecting anything" to recollect the true Buddha who is without marks, then practicing Chan is itself... [the same as reciting the Buddha's name]. Question: If one uses the correct contemplation of "not thinking of anything" to contemplate the true mind that is without marks, and uses the correct mindfulness of "not recollecting anything" to recollect the true Buddha who is without marks, then practicing Chan is itself [the same as reciting the Buddha's name]. Why, then, does the subsequent text also exclude it? To say "recite the Buddha's name" is precisely to engage in Chan meditation; this accords with the principle that "this very mind makes the Buddha" and "this very mind is the Buddha.

Why then would one exclude it? If one must recite the name of the Tathāgata with the mouth and must visualize the form of the Tathāgata with the mind, then this becomes a "mindful mindfulness," which falls into the trap of Chan meditation; therefore, it is excluded. Furthermore, as for Chan meditation...
Taking the mind’s constant letting go as the primary mode of reciting the Buddha’s name, and taking the moment-to-moment lifting up of the mind as the essential principle:

when one lets go, one sees the Buddha immediately upon standing; thus it is easy. When one lifts up the mind, there must be no interval between thoughts, continuing even across lifetimes until the Buddha comes to welcome one;
thus it is difficult. Therefore, Zen meditation is even easier than the recitation of the Buddha’s name; its simplicity is indeed appropriate.

Initially, within the realm of hearing, one enters the current and loses the object; once that which is entered has become still, the two characteristics of motion and stillness clearly cease to arise.

Thus gradually increasing, the hearing and the heard are both exhausted; with the exhaustion of hearing, one does not dwell therein; the awareness and the object of awareness are both empty; when the awareness of emptiness reaches its ultimate perfection, both the emptiness and the object of emptiness are extinguished.
With the extinction of birth and death, quiescent extinction manifests before one.
This describes the beginning and end of entering contemplation. "Initially, within hearing" refers to the nature of hearing itself;
it means that I initially took the nature of hearing as the object of contemplation, and ultimately took the nature of hearing as the gateway for entry.
"Entering the flow" means following the flow is called "going out," while reversing the flow is called "entering. As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Not entering..."
Form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and phenomena are called the "entrances"; for one who practices within these streams, this is the initial application of effort.

Relying on the power of this entry into the stream serves as the instrument for uprooting [delusion]. However, the method of flowing against the stream must rely upon the right reflection that is free from the hundred [delusive] thoughts.
The *Abhiṣeka Sūtra* says: "The meditating bhikṣu has no other mental conceptions; he maintains only..."

Only after contemplating this single dharma will you see the truth. This is because the two sensory objects of movement and stillness adhere to the profound stillness (*zhan*), giving rise to hearing.
The essence of hearing reflects sound; as sound rolls away, it forms the faculty. Thus, the faculties and their objects become entangled and cannot be disentangled.
Now, if you wish to disentangle them, you must first employ this "right-thought" that is beyond all thinking to observe from where this hearing arises. It is this.
To observe that movement arises from stillness and stillness emerges from movement in this manner allows one to reverse that perversion.

It causes the faculty of hearing to no longer follow external sounds, but instead to flow inward toward the nature of hearing itself. After a long time, the place of arising gradually becomes familiar, and the place of familiarity gradually gives way to arising;
naturally, one will not be adhered to by the sensory objects with which it was bound. Therefore, it is said: "to lose" [them].
That which enters the stream is the cessation of the roots; that which is forgotten is the forgetting of objects. As Yongjia said:
"It is not that thought does not forget objects, nor that objects do not cease while thought does not forget them. When objects are forgotten, thought ceases;
when thought ceases, objects are forgotten. When the mind's entry has become still, the two aspects of movement and stillness are clearly manifest.
The one who is born can enter this faculty; that which is entered is the object. Because the faculty that enters it flows against the current, the objects entered become quiescent.
This means that not only do the marks of movement not arise, but the marks of stillness likewise do not arise.
This is intended to separate the nature of hearing from its objects, so that they do not weave together to form delusion. This is like seeing a mountain... [not obstructed].

When this mountain sees water, it is not water; when one detaches from adhesions and lies hidden within, it is precisely at the stage of "arousing faith" (*śraddhā-utpāda*) where the characteristic of cessation is severed.

Because ignorance (*avidyā*) has severed the deluded attachment to a self (*ātma-grāha*), yet there remains the unexhausted accumulation of empty habits within the faculties (*indriya*), one must further apply effort and practice until these internal faculties are exhausted.
Thus, as this process gradually increases, that which is heard and that by which one hears are both exhausted.
Upon hearing this, the faculty of hearing immediately engages; because the prior faculties and sense objects were bound together, one was about to hear erroneously.

By turning back to hear one's own nature (*svabhāva*), one no longer engages with external objects. Although external objects have now been detached and the faculty of hearing has subsided, they have not yet attained complete purity;

therefore, next, one must exhaust the internal faculties. This corresponds to the arousal of faith to sever the ignorance of differentiated characteristics (*vilakṣaṇa-avidyā*) and thereby sever the innate self-clinging (*sahaja-ātman*).
Because of attachment, it is said that this faculty is first understood, and one first attains the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

Although the attachment to the person is empty, there still remains the wisdom that clings to emptiness; because the nature of hearing has not yet become perfect, one next empties that wisdom as well.

"Exhausting hearing so as not to dwell, the perceiver and the perceived are both empty": here, "perceiver" refers to wisdom. This means that although the hearing-faculty is emptied and the self is gone, [one must further proceed].

If one clings to the characteristic of wisdom and does not relinquish it, it becomes an obstruction to wisdom and a hindrance to the Dharma; therefore, even the awareness that perceives [this clinging] is empty.

This corresponds to the arising of faith that severs the ignorance of abiding in characteristics—that is, the two kinds of dharma-clinging, both discriminative and innate—whereby emptiness becomes perfectly luminous and constitutes liberation through the Dharma. Although the characteristic of wisdom is empty, the characteristic of emptiness...
This means that even within the previously mentioned state, one further eliminates the characteristic of emptiness.

"When the awareness of emptiness is perfectly complete and that which is emptied by emptiness ceases" means that since the wisdom of awareness has already become empty, one has reached the ground of the ultimate perfection of the nature of emptiness.

However, if the characteristic of emptiness has not yet been extinguished and emptiness still persists, then emptiness itself becomes a sickness; therefore, one must further empty that very emptiness. This is what is called "the sickness of emptiness."
"Emptiness": one should give rise to faith herein; severing the ignorance of the phase of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*) is itself emptiness—the emptiness of both [subject and object].
This is what is called the dharma of liberation: when both have become empty, there is no further arising. "When birth and death are extinguished, quiescent extinction manifests":

this means that upon first entering the stream, the objects of perception have perished and are empty, yet the sense faculties (*indriya*) still remain. These faculties are themselves the "objects" (*viṣaya*).

When emptiness is empty, there remains the wisdom that takes emptiness as its root; this wisdom is itself the object of cognition. When wisdom is empty, there remains the emptiness that takes wisdom as its root;

this emptiness is itself the object of dust, the root, wisdom, and emptiness—all of which are objects. All of these are not apart from the evolving consciousness (*karmavijñāna*) of birth and cessation.
Now, once the two attachments are eliminated and the two kinds of emptiness are also dispensed with, the evolving consciousness alone [remains].

The characteristic of differentiated movement also ceases; that which is pure by nature—neither arising nor ceasing—and which pervades the entire Dharma-realm, the true essence of the perfectly integrated three contemplations, stands forth in solitary brilliance.
This is precisely the time when Avalokiteśvara first extracts a single sense-faculty, enters samādhi, and takes the awakening of the fruit-stage as the mind of the causal stage.
Suddenly transcending both the mundane and supramundane worlds, he attained universal clarity throughout the ten directions and acquired two extraordinary excellences:
first, above, he united with the fundamental, wondrously enlightened mind of all Buddhas of the ten directions, sharing the same compassionate power as the Buddha-Tathāgatas;
second, below, he united with all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions, sharing the same sorrowful longing as all those beings.

It is said that when ignorance is suddenly severed and the true principle is suddenly realized, one transcends both the mundane and supramundane worlds in an instant, thereby attaining two kinds of sublime merit. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states:
"If one severs ignorance and realizes the Dharma-body, inconceivable karmic activities arise spontaneously. This is what is meant by "harmonizing with all Buddhas of the ten directions above."

This means that because the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transmit this wondrous mind—which is fundamentally one, perfectly interfused, and pure enlightened awareness—those who realize this mind are identical to the Tathāgatas in their compassionate power.

Regarding "harmonizing downward with the sentient beings of the ten directions," it means that what this Bodhisattva realizes is precisely what all sentient beings equally possess; thus, they realize this principle.
This refers to being able to share in the sorrows and afflictions of sentient beings, accomplishing their welfare in every way without exception. The *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra* states:
Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying, "If a bodhisattva upholds one single dharma, all the dharmas of the Buddhas will naturally be as if held in the palm of their hand.
What is this one dharma? It is called Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). The commentary explains: This is [the state of] being of the same essence (*sahaja*).
Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) also functions because this nature of great compassion pervades the entire realm of sentient beings;

thus, it can nourish all universally with a single rain, causing both orchids and wormwood to flourish together, and encompassing all in a single thought-moment so that the heterodox and the orthodox are equally saved. Question:

Since it is able to transcend both the mundane and supramundane worlds, yet also harmonizes with those above and below, for what reason is this? Answer: It is because it exclusively transcends and exclusively surpasses. Therefore—
The ability to be identical with and to harmonize with others is likewise neither exclusively noble nor ordinary; it is by means of this that one can manifest as noble or as ordinary.

It is like the moon dwelling in the void, which is then able to distribute its light and cast its reflections among the rivers, streams, and ditches, and upon the outskirts, plains, forests, and marshes.
Regarding the stages of progress, this should correspond to the first stage, the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), even though it is so called.
One portion of ignorance is severed and one portion of truth is realized;

yet, because when one is severed all is severed and when one is realized all is realized, the merits of the forty-two stages are implicitly present. Thus, it was previously said that samādhi is fully endowed with the myriad practices.
Previously, based on the illumination of causes, objects were established, whereby three kinds of continuity arose; now, by entering [the path]...

The "establishment of a locus" (*li-suo*) refers to what is ultimately attained through the process of wandering; it is the root of delusion. The "non-establishment of a locus" (*wang-suo*) is the source of awakening.

The establishment of a locus is defined in terms of the initial single thought-moment of the root of delusion, which is the most subtle. The non-establishment of a locus is defined in terms of the initial application of the practice, which is the coarsest.
This is because at the time of delusion, one proceeds from the subtle to the coarse, whereas at the time of awakening, one enters from the coarse [to the subtle].

The subtle mechanism for the transition between delusion and enlightenment does not go beyond the two characters "establishing" (li) and "perishing" (wang). However, this character "object" (so)—that which is established—is particularly difficult to eliminate.
Therefore, from the very beginning of the first fascicle, the World-Honored One took "the location of the mind and eyes" as his starting point;

thereafter, what he successively refuted was solely the single character "object," until the chapter on Pūrṇa, where he established the "object" based on "illumination" (ming) to clarify the nature of that object.

Regarding its arising, when discussing the cultivation for abandonment, it is said: "the locus of what is forgotten," "the locus of what is heard," "the locus of what is realized," and "the locus of emptiness.

To emerge from one locus is precisely to enter another locus; this single word "locus" (*sthāna*) is truly the stain that clings to the very body and is difficult to scrape away—the subtle root of the dual grasping at self and dharmas. Only upon reaching the perfection of Bodhi does one return to non-existence.

Because that which is attained and that which serves as its characteristic are both exhausted, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Sentient beings are attached everywhere; I lead them so they may emerge from these places.
"Place" (*chu*) refers precisely to that which is attained (*suo*).
World-Honored One, because I made offerings to the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara, I was granted by that Tathāgata the hearing-perfuming (*śruta-vāsanā*) which is like an illusion.

Because I have heard and cultivated the Vajra-samādhi, which shares the same power of compassion as that of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, my body has become the thirty-two transformations that enter into the lands of sentient beings.
This explains how I am identical to all Buddhas in the power of their compassionate strength; although it is attributed to me, it is truly a merit granted by them.
This also reveals that the teacher himself possesses the root of virtue. Regarding "the Vajra-samādhi of illusory hearing-perfuming and hearing-cultivation":

this nature of hearing, although it is the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), is nonetheless initiated by the internal perfuming of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) to give rise to pure seeds.
Only after severing that ignorance does one subsequently attain the adamantine, firm, and indestructible essence. By means of...
Because one has attained this essence, one is able to ascend and harmonize with the Buddha-mind, sharing in the same power of compassion;
responding to conditions as they arise, there is no land where one does not appear. "Entering all lands" refers to the "land-body" among the ten bodies.

This land-body arises because that objective world (*bhājanaloka*) is transformed into the Dharma-nature land (*dharmatā-kṣetra*); thus, it possesses inconceivable karmic functions, as described in the *Avataṃsaka*.

The pure and wondrous Dharma-body is serene and responds to all; what is now called the "thirty-two [forms]" is merely a provisional limitation established in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.

If one considers the Bodhisattva manifesting bodies within the ten dharma-realms to perfectly respond to the multitudes of beings, then there is no type of being that is not reached—how could it be limited to thirty-two responses? Nevertheless, even these thirty-two responses are capable of...
This encompasses all categories of beings.

World-Honored One, if there are bodhisattvas who enter samādhi and advance in the cultivation of untainted resolute understanding until it becomes manifest, and I appear in the form of a Buddha to preach the Dharma for them so that they may attain liberation;
or if there are those in training (śaikṣa) who possess tranquil, wondrously luminous, and most sublime [understanding]...
If there are those in training who have severed the twelve links of dependent origination and who manifest the supreme,
excellent, and wondrous nature of the severance of conditions, I appear before them in the form of a Pratyekabuddha and teach the Dharma to bring about their liberation.
If there are those in training who have attained the emptiness of the Four Noble Truths and cultivate the path, [I likewise appear before them].
Entering into the supreme nature of cessation (*nirodha-svabhāva*), I manifest in its presence in the form of a śrāvaka and teach the Dharma so that they may attain liberation;

this is the manifestation of the four noble bodies (*ārya-kāya*). As for "supreme resolve" (*adhimukti*), if we consider it from the perspective of Vijñaptimātra, it refers to the sealing [of the mind] upon a determined object.

Taking "holding" as its nature and "being unleadable" as its function, this refers here to the wisdom of realization that has already reached its ultimate limit through the cultivation of causal practices.
As for "manifesting perfection," it means that the wisdom of realization is about to be fully penetrated yet not yet fully penetrated, about to be perfected yet not yet perfected;

the Bodhisattva then manifests their body and preaches the Dharma, such that the capacity of the recipient and the teaching coincide like the simultaneous pecking of a chick and the striking of a parent bird.
Gushan says: "This refers to those with the capacities for the Separate and Perfect Teachings.

If a Bodhisattva enters the semblance *samādhi* and advances in the cultivation of the Middle Way’s outflow-free wisdom, then their partial realization of truth (*bhūta-vidarśana*) will manifest in perfection;

and if they advance further in the cultivation of the diamond-like outflow-free wisdom, then their ultimate realization of truth will manifest in perfection. Such Great Beings all manifest in the body of a Buddha to preach the sudden Dharma for them."
Question: How is it that Bodhisattvas can manifest the body of a Buddha? Answer: When the principle of the mind-nature is revealed, there is no distinction between high and low;
it is like a mirror that has already become clear—when an object is confronted with it, the image appears.

If a king happens to approach the mirror in a minister’s house, how could the image of the king not appear? If a minister happens to approach the mirror in the king’s palace, how could the image of the minister not appear?

One should know that while people have high and low status, a mirror has no distinction between noble and base; yet this does not prevent there from being excellence or inferiority among those possessing clarity. Question:

Do Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambuddha-bodhisattva) need to rely on the manifestation of a body in the First Abode (Prathamābhūmi) to preach the Dharma? Answer: If one attains understanding upon hearing the Dharma, why must one seek out others? Furthermore, if one relies on a superior physical form, it only serves to further increase internal wisdom.

Moreover, even when a celestial Māra manifests as a Buddha-image, [it is like] yeast... (Note: The final character "麴" [qǔ] appears to be an incomplete or truncated reference, likely intended to illustrate the deceptive nature of external appearances.)

If even those who highly esteem [the path] offer such reverence, how much more so for a Bodhisattva in the First Abode? Although the Perfect Enlightenment manifested through the wondrous principle is most honored, how could one dare not look up to it?
Wenling says: They emerge in an age without a Buddha; observing the transformation of things, they personally realize non-arising, and thus they are called Pratyekabuddhas (Solitary Realizers).
Because they delight in solitude and sublime tranquility, seeking natural wisdom, they are called "Tranquil and Sublimely Bright. They receive their instruction from the Buddha.

Because this teaching involves contemplating conditions to awaken to the Way, it is called "Pratyekabuddha" (Condition-Awakened). One knows that delusion regarding the supreme nature arises from the twelve links of dependent origination;

because when these conditions are severed, the supreme nature is revealed, it is called the "Supreme Nature of Condition-Severance. This supreme nature is precisely the nature of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmatā*). Juli said:

From the stage prior to the three fruits, both the ranks of the worthy (*śaikṣa*) and the ranks of the sage (*ārya*) belong to those still in training (*śaikṣa*). Through the sixteen moments of mind of the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), one severs [the afflictions].

Because one realizes the principle of the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) by means of the afflictions eliminated through the Four Noble Truths, it is said that "one attains the emptiness of the Four Truths.

Following the first fruit (*prathamaphala*), one proceeds to sever the eighty-one grades of innate afflictions across the three realms; as one realizes a portion of the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asamskṛta*) with each grade, it is said that "one enters cessation through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)."
If there are sentient beings who desire to awaken their minds clearly and not transgress against the dust of desire, seeking purity of body,
I appear before them in the form of a Brahmā King and preach the Dharma for them so that they may attain liberation.

If there are sentient beings who desire to become a celestial lord and exercise sovereignty over the various heavens, I appear before them in the form of Śakra and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve this.
If there are sentient beings who desire bodily mastery to travel throughout the ten directions,
I appear before them in the form of Maheśvara and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve it; if there are sentient beings who desire bodily mastery to fly through the void,
I appear before them in the form of Maheśvara and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve it.

If there are sentient beings who desire to govern spirits and deities and protect the land, I appear before them in the form of a Great Heavenly General and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve success.

World-Honored One, furthermore, by means of this power of the effortless and wondrous Vajrasamādhi cultivated through hearing and practicing what has been heard,

Regarding "merit": it means that when sentient beings encounter suffering, hardship, or places of fear, by merely invoking his name once, they immediately receive rescue and liberation;
they do not give rise to fear and thus obtain merit.

First, by not observing the self through observation, but rather observing the observer, I cause those suffering and distressed sentient beings of the ten directions who observe my voice to immediately attain liberation.
Second, through the revolving of knowledge and vision, I cause all sentient beings—even if they enter a great fire—to be unable to be burned by the flames.
Third, through the revolving of observation and hearing, I cause all sentient beings who are adrift upon great waters [to be saved].
Fourth, by severing and extinguishing deluded thoughts, one’s mind is free from the intent to kill, enabling all sentient beings to enter the realms of ghosts without being harmed by them.
Fifth, by perfuming the faculty of hearing until it becomes true hearing, the six sense organs are restored and harmonized with the hearing of sound;
this can cause those facing imminent harm to have their weapons shattered into pieces as they strike them, rendering the blades like water being cut.

when the permeation of hearing is refined and luminous, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, then the nature of all darkness cannot prevail, such that even though yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, ghosts, piśācas, pūtanas, and the like may be close by, their eyes cannot see. Seventh, the nature of sound is completely dissolved.

None of these can fully [describe it]. The *rākṣasa* are fearsome ghosts; the *kumbhāṇḍa* are ghosts that cause nightmares and enchantment;

Fourteenth: the ten billion suns and moons currently abiding in this trichiliocosm, and all phenomena within the world.

This causes sentient beings to invoke my name and attain fearlessness. Although the dharma-gates for self-benefit and benefiting others among these six billion bodhisattvas each differ, the fundamental root of perfect penetration that I have attained lies solely in the gateway of the ear-faculty.

Because the sound is singular, it causes one to hold its name; thus, the two blessings are equal.

This clarifies how the four inconceivables integrate the two preceding contemplations. Although the former [contemplations] clearly manifested the upward conformity and downward merging,"
All of these accord with capacities and thus still have limits; they can still be conceived by the mind and discussed through speech.

However, if one further expands this to its ultimate, perfect measure, it can no longer be grasped by conjecture or deliberation. The phrase "observing and cultivating the unsurpassed Way" refers to what is realized at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*);
therefore, Wénlǐng explains it as being the realization of Equal Enlightenment.
First, because I initially attained the most wondrous mind of hearing, and as the essence of that mind left behind all ordinary hearing,
such that seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing could no longer be partitioned, forming a single, perfectly integrated, pure, and precious awakening; therefore,
I am able to manifest many wondrous forms and preach boundless secret divine mantras, among which I may appear with one head, three heads, five heads, seven heads, or nine heads.
There are eleven heads, and so on, up to one hundred and eight heads, a thousand heads, ten thousand heads,
and eighty-four thousand śakara heads; with two arms, four arms, six arms, eight arms, ten arms, twelve arms, fourteen, sixteen,
eighteen, twenty, up to twenty-four, and so on, up to one hundred and eight arms, a thousand arms, and ten thousand arms.
With eighty-four thousand arms like mudrās, and two eyes, three eyes, four eyes, nine eyes,
and so on up to one hundred and eight eyes, a thousand eyes, ten thousand eyes, or eighty-four thousand pure jewel-eyes— whether manifesting compassion,
majesty, meditative concentration, or wisdom— they rescue and protect sentient beings, attaining great sovereignty.
This clarifies the inconceivability of one body and many bodies. It is said that among the twenty-four sages who realized perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa-abhisamaya*), each was marvelous;

yet that which I have realized—the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing—is the root of all perfect penetrations, and because it is the most marvelous among marvels, it is called "marvelously marvelous.
Regarding the phrase "the mind of hearing," the subsequent explanation states: "It is precisely this mind of hearing that knows..."
"Exquisite and exquisite" means that by pulling out the faculty of hearing from its single root, one causes all six faculties to be pulled out simultaneously;
thus, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing can no longer be partitioned, as they return to the essence of the Single True Dharma-realm.
Therefore, within a single body, many bodies are manifested, and within those many bodies, boundless mantras are taught. *Śakara* means "firm."
The *Gumudrā* (Solid Mudrā) is called the Seal of Pure Jewel Eyes, which is the Vajra’s True Eye; it serves as the head of the six applications.
The arms represent the compassion that reaches out and receives, while the eyes represent the wisdom that illuminates and understands.

Facing the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings, these manifest as eighty-four thousand hands and eyes; yet, for sentient beings, these hands and eyes are inherently present throughout their entire bodies.

Deluded and unaware, all [actions] become karmic functions; when a Bodhisattva attains this, it is like spring entering its seasonal laws or the moon moving through the sky—whatever is grasped by the hand becomes a wondrous function.
One may bestow compassion to gather the hearts of virtuous people, or manifest majesty to break the courage of demons and malevolent spirits.
Concentration (samādhi) serves to block the gate of distraction and movement, while wisdom (prajñā) serves to shatter ignorance.
Because he has clarified the caverns of his mind, he is able to respond universally to worldly afflictions and provide skillful guidance in every way that accords with the heart;
therefore, it is said that he has attained great mastery (*vaśitā*).

Second, because he has emerged from the six sense-objects through hearing, reflection, and cultivation, they cannot obstruct him—just as sound passes through a wall without hindrance; therefore, I [say this].
I am able to skillfully manifest each individual form and recite each individual mantra; through these forms and mantras, I am able to bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings.
For this reason, throughout the lands as numerous as motes of dust in the ten directions, I am called the "Bestower of Fearlessness."
This clarifies that each body and each form is inconceivable. Because the capacities of sentient beings differ, the forms manifested to suit those capacities also differ;
because the habitual tendencies of sentient beings differ, the mantras spoken to suit those capacities also differ.
Each individual body and each individual mantra bestows fearlessness upon all sentient beings, causing them to...
In all lands as numerous as motes of dust, all sentient beings shall call me the Bestower of Fearlessness.
Third, because I have cultivated the fundamental, wondrous, perfect, and penetrating root of purity, in all the worlds where I travel,
I cause sentient beings to relinquish their bodies and precious treasures to seek my compassion.

This clarifies that his transformative influence is inconceivable. Because I have attained the pure fundamental root and am entirely free from attachment to the objects of the six sense-fields, I am able to relinquish everything;

thus, in all the worlds where I travel, my spirit remains present through transformative influence even as I cast aside what is precious, seeking only that those who grieve for me may receive it. Therefore, one knows that it is only I who do not take, while others then give.

Fourth, having attained the Buddha-mind and realized the ultimate, one is able to make various offerings of precious jewels to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, extending also to all sentient beings within the six realms of the Dharma-realm: seeking a wife, one obtains a wife; seeking a son, one obtains a son;
seeking samādhi, one obtains samādhi; seeking long life, one obtains long life; and so on, even seeking great nirvāṇa, one obtains great [nirvāṇa].
Nirvāṇa. This clarifies the inconceivable nature of making offerings. "Attaining the Buddha-mind" refers to first obtaining the Tathāgatagarbha mind;
"realizing the ultimate" means fully obtaining the Tathāgatagarbha mind. Because one obtains this from beginning to end, [it is called Nirvāṇa].
Because of the *tathāgatagarbha*-mind, one is able to transport out the household treasures and extensively perform Buddha-works;
having already made offerings to the Buddhas with various Dharma-jewels, one further bestows upon sentient beings various gifts of wealth, Dharma, and fearlessness.
Since the Bodhisattva contemplates that the dharma-realm and sentient beings are entirely the essence of the Buddha, wife, children, and longevity constitute worldly bliss-samādhi.
Nirvana is the supramundane bliss.
The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration [of the faculties], and I replied that I attained mastery over the mind through the Samādhi of Universal Illumination via the gateway of the ears;
by entering the stream of the causal flow, I attained samāpatti and accomplished Bodhi—this is the foremost, World-Honored One. That Buddha-Tathāgata praised me.
Having skillfully attained this dharma-door of perfect penetration, I was granted a prediction of enlightenment within that great assembly, receiving the name Avalokiteśvara.
Because my contemplation of hearing perceives the perfect luminosity throughout the ten directions, the name "Avalokiteśvara" pervades the worlds of the ten directions.

This refers to the perfect penetration of the knots. It means that because I have entered deeply through the single gateway of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*), those six faculties of cognition must be uprooted and liberated in their totality;

thus, one attains mastery above by being equal to all Buddhas and below by harmonizing with all sentient beings, establishing teachings according to conditions without anything lacking in sovereign freedom.
As the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra* says: "To know that all things are but this single mind is called mastery of the mind."
Being able to produce various precious jewels from the palm of one’s hand and taking empty space as a treasury is called "mastery over names and things.
All actions of body, speech, and mind having wisdom as their foundation is called "mastery over wisdom.
Entering the stream through these causal signs and attaining *samādhi* refers to the "causal mind"; achieving *bodhi* refers to the "resultant awakening. Worldly... [end of fragment]
The Venerable Master further clarifies that both attaining the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) and receiving the name [of Bodhisattva] arise from this very gate.

This is because the Bodhisattva takes the ears and eyes of the ten directions as his own for the purpose of observing and hearing; thus, all observation and hearing throughout the ten directions are the Bodhisattva’s own ears and eyes. As the *Shangshu* (Book of Documents) states:
"The Heaven’s vision is through the vision of its people; the Heaven’s hearing is through the hearing of its people. This is a close parallel.

At that time, from his five limbs, the World-Honored One emitted precious light which reached far to moisten the crowns of the heads of the Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions,
as well as the Dharma-Prince Bodhisattvas. Those Tathāgatas likewise emitted precious light from their five limbs,
which came from the motes of dust in all directions to moisten the crown of the Buddha’s head and to moisten the crowns of the heads of the great Bodhisattvas in the assembly.
Furthermore, for the Arhats, the groves, ponds, and marshes all resounded with the sounds of the Dharma; their intermingling lights crisscrossed one another like a net of precious threads.
This great assembly attained what they had never experienced before, universally obtaining the Vajra Samādhi.

Immediately, the heavens rained down lotus flowers of a hundred jewels—blue, yellow, red, and white—intermingled and variegated, so that the empty space of the ten directions became the color of the seven treasures.

In this Sahā world-system, the great earth, mountains, and rivers all vanished simultaneously, and one saw only the lands as numerous as motes of dust in the ten directions merged into a single realm,
where Brahma-songs and hymns were spontaneously performed and played.

This is the Tathāgata’s perfect realization of the various holy ways of perfect penetration. That his five limbs simultaneously radiate precious light manifests that his entire body is the Great Treasury of Radiant Light (*mahā-ābhāsvara-garbha*).
That the Buddhas of the ten directions meet to confer the empowerment of the crown (*abhiṣeka*) manifests that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have collectively realized the Dharma of the Crown.
That they together empower the Bodhisattvas and Arhats signifies the perfection of what they have realized.
That all things, fundamentally devoid of superiority or inferiority, are subsumed within the single radiance of the Tathāgata;

that the sounds emanating from the forest trees and the interlacing of their lights form a web—these serve to reveal that once the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) have been dissolved, the interlacing of sound and light is not like the formation of a world through the weaving of delusive phenomena, nor is it a matter of worlds mutually impinging upon one another. That all beings universally attain the *vajrasamādhi* serves to reveal the *śūraṅgama*.
The Venerable King is precisely the adamantine jewel-like awakening, the impartial realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*).
That the lands of the ten directions merge into a single realm serves to manifest that all numerical measures are extinguished and unified into the single Buddha-land.
That the chanting of *brahman* hymns and songs is spontaneously performed serves to manifest that the Dharma-music of perfect penetration is omnipresent.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince: "Observe now these twenty-five great Bodhisattvas beyond training and Arhats, each of whom has spoken of the skillful means by which they first attained the Way. They all declare that they cultivated true and perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa-samyak-prativedha*).
In their actual practice, there is truly no distinction of superiority or inferiority, nor of priority or sequence. I now wish—"

"Please cause Ānanda to awaken to the twenty-five practices; who among them corresponds to the faculties [of beings], and after my parinirvāṇa, by what gate of skillful means can the sentient beings of this world who enter the Bodhisattva vehicle and seek the unsurpassed path achieve success with ease?"
This decree by Mañjuśrī selects the perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-āyatana*). In the practice of cultivation, there is truly no superiority or inferiority;

it is just as a single fire, depending on what it burns, receives various names such as "grass-fire" or "wood-fire," and a single water, according to its function, becomes known by many names such as "soup" or "wine"—it is not that the fire or water themselves differ. As for who should take them as their root, although this is known...
Since the realization of all the Sages is identical, who among them could match Ānanda’s capacity?

What gate of skillful means can be easily accomplished? This refers not only to the capacity of a single individual in the present, but also to how practitioners after my parinirvāṇa must enter through which gate to easily attain accomplishment.

Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, having received the Buddha’s compassionate command, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, spoke these verses in response to the Buddha:
“The nature of the ocean of awakening is limpid and perfect; its limpid perfection is the primordial wonder of awakening. Primordial luminosity shines forth, giving rise to the object;

once the object is established, the luminous nature of the subject perishes. Through delusion and falsehood, empty space arises; based upon space, worlds are established. When thought becomes limpid, they are formed.”
The perception of lands arises from the emptiness of sentient beings within the Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean.
All tainted, minute-dust worlds are born depending upon space; when the bubble ceases, space itself was originally non-existent—how much more so the various realms of the three existences?

The nature of returning to the source is non-dual, yet there are many gates of expedient means. The holy nature is all-pervasive; whether following the natural order or acting in reverse, all are expedient means for the beginner to enter.
The speed of entering samādhi differs among individuals.
This clarifies that because delusion arises from the Truth, there is a returning from delusion to the Truth;

since there are differences in speed along this path of returning from delusion to the Truth, it is necessary to select the appropriate faculty (*indriya*). It is said that the ocean of the nature of wondrous enlightenment is originally clear, tranquil, and perfect.
The perfectly clear and lucid nature of awakening is fundamentally and originally wondrous; it does not depend on artificial effort and has no spatial location.

It is because the original luminous essence of the nature suddenly gives rise to the function of illumination that it consequently falls into spatial location. Once location is falsely established, the fundamental nature of that illumination and function is lost.
This is precisely how the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) is formed based upon original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). Having thus become deluded regarding the awakened nature...

The consciousness of karma having been formed, it subsequently became deluded regarding the emptiness of nature and thus produced a stubborn void. From this, within the darkness of obscured emptiness, darkness coagulated into form;

furthermore, two kinds of worlds were established—insentient and sentient—whereby a portion of the floating vacuity was condensed through chaotic thoughts to become the insentient vessel-world, while another portion of the floating vacuity was condensed through discursive thoughts to become... [the sentient world].
There are those who claim that the sense-faculties and the physical body arise from the dual aspects of subject and object within the karmic consciousness of ignorance;
yet they fail to realize that even empty space arises within the Great Awakened Nature, no different from a single bubble emerging from the great ocean.
If this is so for space itself, how much more so for the minute, contaminated lands of the dust-motes, all of which are established upon empty space?
Their insignificance can thus be known. If one realizes that the bubble has vanished, then even emptiness is fundamentally non-existent;
