how much more so could the three realms of existence, which arise from empty space, remain alone? Therefore, know that if one attains the returning to the root of the awakened nature, there are certainly no two;
yet, if one wishes to enter this non-dual awakened nature, the skillful means are indeed manifold and do not stop at one.
The path being thus, if a sage fully realizes this nature, then all phenomena are perfectly interfused and every matter is without obstruction;
therefore, whether it be hatred or love, suffering or joy, none are not gates for entering into principle, requiring no selection.
If a person who has first resolved their mind wishes to enter samādhi, whether they possess complete faculties or incomplete faculties, day by day—
Since the characteristics of the *kalpas* differ by multiples, there is necessarily a variation in the speed [of realization]; therefore, one must select the faculties.
By "speed" is meant that among those who hear the Dharma, some attain the state of no-mind in a single thought-moment, while others do not attain no-mind until they reach the tenth stage (*bhūmi*).
The aggregate of form and perception forms a dust-like essence that cannot be penetrated; how can one fail to understand this and yet attain perfect penetration?
Sound is mixed with language; since it consists merely of names, phrases, and meanings, and one does not contain all others, how can one attain perfect penetration through it?
Fragrance is known through contact; when separated, it is fundamentally non-existent. Since its perception is not constant, how can one attain perfect penetration through it?
The nature of taste is not fundamental; it exists only when there is tasting, and its awareness is not constant or uniform—how then can one attain perfect penetration?
Touch is clarified by means of what is touched; yet since there is nothing it does not clarify, the nature of contact and separation is not fixed—how then can one attain perfect penetration?

The dharma-realm is called an internal object; relying on an object necessarily involves the subject and the object, and as such it does not universally pervade—how then can one attain perfect penetration?

This distinguishes that the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) are not the perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-āyatana*). As previously stated, their respective practices are in truth neither superior nor inferior;

however, because there are variations in slowness and speed for practitioners of this region, Mañjuśrī was thus directed to forcibly distinguish superiority and inferiority where none exists, and to forcibly differentiate distinctions where there is no differentiation. Thereupon, he weighed the twenty-four sages...

Although Jinbo and Liangyi both evaluated each dharma and found them all inadequate, they ultimately selected only the single gateway of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-āyatana*) as the most excellent—this being the fundamental beginning and end of this *pūrvayoga*.

Although Śāṭha attained awakening by contemplating that the nature of form is empty, this nature of form is merely a substance of obstruction formed by the combination of various false thoughts; since it is composed of various false thoughts...

If, upon arising, one’s discernment of the nature is unable to be clear and penetrating, how could there be a state of non-clarity and non-penetration—something dark, turbid, and distracted—that the initial mind could rely upon to realize perfect penetration?

Although Śāriputra heard the sound of the Dharma and attained awakening through it, as soon as that sound fell into the realm of verbal expression, it belonged to names and phrases; for names express intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
Phrases (*pada*) express distinctions, while sentences (*vyañjana*) are simply characters (*akṣara*); these two are what the [ancients] called "flavor" (*rasa*).

Characters are able to manifest these two, just as flavor can manifest the saltiness or blandness within food. Furthermore, since principle is perfect and words are pervasive, how could a single word possibly encompass everything?
How then, by relying on such [limited means], can one seek to realize perfect penetration?—thus said Xiangyan.
Although one may gain awakening through the fragrance-sphere, when the fragrance meets the nose there is cognition, and when it leaves the nose there is no cognition.
Since this fragrance has both meeting and leaving, this cognition likewise exists at times and does not exist at others.
Thus, the nature of sensory awareness cannot even be constant; how can one say that by means of this one seeks to realize entry into perfect penetration? O Medicine King!
Although King [Śubhavyūha] attained awakening by means of the sense-object of taste, this nature of taste is likewise not an eternally constant essence;
it exists only through the conjunction with flavors. Since one cannot cause the nature of taste to remain forever uniform, how can one seek to realize perfect penetration by means of this?
Although King Bhadrapāla attained awakening by means of the sense-object of touch, this sense-object of touch...

One must take the body as the subject that touches and objects as the objects touched; only when subject and object unite does the characteristic of contact—such as warmth, cold, roughness, or smoothness—arise.
If there were no object to be touched to unite with the subject that touches, the characteristic of contact would not manifest.
Furthermore, since this characteristic of contact is sometimes joined and sometimes separated, its nature is not fixed; how then can one seek to realize [the ultimate] based upon it?

Regarding the entry into universal penetration by Mahākāśyapa, although he attained realization through the *dharmadhātu* (mental objects), these mental objects are merely the fading shadows of the preceding five sense-objects and are thus termed "internal objects.
If this mental faculty (*manas*) exists in dependence upon these internal objects, then these internal objects must have a specific location.
Once there is a distinction between subject and object, it cannot pervade everywhere at the initial stage of practice.
How can a person, on this basis, seek to realize perfect penetration?
Although the nature of vision is lucidly clear, it illuminates what is before one but not what is behind; the four quarters are deficient by half. How can such a state attain perfect penetration?
The inhalation and exhalation of the breath pass through the present without merging; they are fragmented and do not interpenetrate. How can such a state attain perfect penetration?

The tongue is not an entrance; it has no beginning, for it arises from flavors to perceive them. When flavors vanish, perception ceases. Since there is nothing to be found, how can one attain perfect penetration?
The body and its objects of touch are likewise each lacking in perfect enlightenment. Their boundaries cannot be observed, and they do not meet in silent union.

How can one attain perfect penetration? The various faculties are confused and chaotic; though the mind may be still and clear, ultimately there is no seeing. Since thoughts and perceptions cannot be cast off, how can one attain perfect penetration?
This distinguishes the five sense organs as not being the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
Although Lūtata entered awakening by means of the nature of seeing, although this nature of seeing is indeed clear and penetrating, it can only see three directions and two corners;
it cannot see toward one direction and two corners behind. How, then, could one rely on such an imperfect faculty to seek to realize perfect penetration?
Panthaka attained realization through the faculty of the nose; yet, when the nose-faculty emerges, it grasps fragrance, and when it enters, it perceives scent.
Because its middle intersection is deficient, it becomes fragmented and interrupted, failing to interpenetrate.
How can one hope to realize perfect penetration by relying on such a fragmented thing? Pāṭaliputra attained realization through the faculty of the tongue.
However, this tongue-faculty does not manifest by entering into nothingness; it must necessarily arise in dependence upon flavors before cognition can occur.
If flavor were to vanish, then this cognition would likewise be unattainable. How, then, could one rely upon this to realize perfect penetration?
Piliṅga entered through the body-faculty; yet this body-faculty must depend upon its objects...

The characteristics of touch are identical [to those of the body], yet one realizes that touch is not the body; thus, one does not know the body, and because the body is not touch, it is not revealed.
Since there is already a subject and an object, each has its own limits and cannot achieve profound union.
How can one rely on such a limited thing to seek realization of perfect penetration? Subhūti attained awakening through the faculty of the mind, yet this...
When the faculty of cognition becomes entangled with the consciousness and chaotic thoughts have already rendered it turbid, the nature of profound clarity can ultimately not be seen.
It is just like the gods of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception who, upon entering that meditative state, cannot see even while investigating with subtle refinement;
when their retribution is exhausted, they fall back down. Thus, if even those who have practiced for a long time cannot escape conceptual thought, how much less so those at the beginning?
Does the mind wish to rely on this to realize perfect penetration?

Consciousness and seeing are a mixture of the three harmonies; when interrogated regarding their fundamental nature, they are called "non-characteristics. Since their own substance is originally without fixed determination, how can one attain perfect penetration?
The mind-hearing penetrates the ten directions and arises from the power of great causal roots; yet, because the beginner cannot enter it, how can one attain perfect penetration?
Contemplating the nose is fundamentally a provisional means intended only to cause the mind to abide; once the mind has attained abiding, how can this be considered attaining perfect penetration?

Reciting the Dharma involves playing with sounds and texts, which may awaken those who have already achieved success, yet names and phrases are not themselves untainted; how can this be considered attaining perfect penetration?

Upholding the precepts merely restrains the body, but where there is no body, there is nothing to be restrained; since it does not originally pervade all things, how can this be considered attaining perfect penetration?

"Supernatural powers are fundamentally due to past causes; how could they be related to the discrimination of dharmas? Since thoughts depend on conditions and do not exist apart from objects, how can one attain perfect penetration through them?
This passage selects the six consciousnesses as not being the path of perfect penetration.

Although Śāriputra attained awakening by means of the visual consciousness, even though this consciousness arises from the conjunction of the sense organ and its object, if one interrogates its origin, it has no fixed characteristic. Since its essence is non-existent...
"How can you rely on this meditative concentration to seek realization of perfect penetration?

Although Samantabhadra attained entry through the auditory consciousness, and though his mind was opened so as to penetrate clearly through the ten directions, this was brought about by his cultivation of the great practices of Samantabhadra;
it is not something that can be entered by those with initial resolve or limited capacities. How then can you seek to realize perfect penetration through this? Sudāna...

Rahula attained awakening by means of nose-consciousness; however, this contemplation of the nose was originally a provisional device intended to cause his scattered mind to be gathered and temporarily stabilized.
It was certainly not the non-abiding true mind. If the mind were already abiding, there would necessarily be a place where it abides.
How then could one, relying on a mind that has an abode, seek to realize perfect penetration? O wealthy one!

Rāhula entered into awakening by means of the tongue-consciousness (*jihvāvijñāna*); yet, although the one who preaches the Dharma employs language and characters through the modulation of the tongue-consciousness, it is because Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra’s past causes have matured over vast eons and he possesses the power of eloquence (*pratibhāna*) that he is able to attain awakening.
This is certainly not something achievable by the tongue-consciousness alone at a single moment; moreover, names and phrases are themselves non-associated [formations].
Since the practice fundamentally belongs to the conditioned and is not an outflow-free (*anāsrava*) dharma, how can one seek to realize perfect penetration through it?
Upāli attained awakening by means of the body-consciousness; however, this observance of precepts can only restrain the body-consciousness.
Apart from the body-consciousness, there is nothing else to be restrained. Since that which restrains this cannot restrain that, it is incapable of universal restraint.
Since all [the other senses] still leave much to be desired, upon what basis do you wish to realize perfect penetration?

Maudgalyāyana attained awakening through the mental consciousness; however, the mental consciousness is the nature of the discrimination of dharma-objects, whereas supernatural powers are the result of the force of causes from kalpas past and have no connection [to it].
Even if supernatural powers were to depend on the mental consciousness for their existence...
This mental consciousness clings to objects moment by moment and cannot be separated from them; how can one rely upon this to realize perfect penetration?

If one contemplates the nature of earth as solid and obstructive, it is not the unimpeded penetration of conditioned phenomena nor the nature of the sages; how then could one attain perfect penetration?
If one contemplates through the nature of water, then mental conceptions are not real and suchness is beyond both thought and observation; how then can one attain perfect penetration?
If one contemplates through the nature of fire, then loathing existence is not true and detachment is not the primary means for the beginning mind; how then can one attain perfect penetration?
If one contemplates through the nature of wind, then movement and stillness are not without opposition, and opposition is not supreme awakening; how then can one attain perfect penetration?

If one contemplates emptiness (*śūnyatā*), how can one attain perfect penetration? For dullness was originally not awakening; since there is no difference between non-awakening and awakening, how can one attain perfect penetration?
If one contemplates the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*), observing that consciousness is not permanent, yet maintaining a mind [of grasping] is a delusion; how can one attain perfect penetration?

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, and the nature of mindfulness is fundamentally subject to arising and ceasing; since cause and effect now produce distinct responses, how can one attain perfect penetration?
This was a rejection of the seven great methods as being non-perfectly penetrating (*an-avipula-gati*).

Although Kṣitigarbha attained entry through the "greatness" of his causal ground, this earth-element is a substance of solid obstruction that cannot penetrate freely in all directions; moreover, it requires leveling and filling, and its essential practices largely belong to conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) effort.
Only upon meeting a Buddha and attaining equanimity can one realize the nature of the sages. For a beginner now, [this method is unsuitable].
Since all things involve the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), how can one rely upon these conditioned phenomena to realize perfect penetration?
Candraprabha attained awakening through the great water, yet this contemplation of water is produced precisely by the binding of thought; it is not of a true nature.

Moreover, the essence of suchness is immovable, whereas the mind of discursive observation (*vitarka-vicāra*) is subject to arising and ceasing. How could one rely upon this [mind] to achieve distinction?
Do you seek to realize perfect penetration apart from applied and sustained thought? Ucchuṣma attained awakening through the greatness of fire;
yet that universal contemplation of the nature of fire was likewise a seeking of liberation out of aversion, not the Dharma of true primordial liberation, nor the fixed method for the initial mind.
How can you seek to realize perfect penetration by means of this? Vaidūryanirbhāsa!
Vayu entered through the greatness of wind; he perceived that the four elements, as well as body and mind, are all turned by the power of wind.
Thus there is movement and stillness—these are relative phenomena. Since there is relativity, it is not the Unsurpassed Enlightenment.
How, then, could one seek to realize perfect penetration through this? Akashagarbha entered through the greatness of space.
Furthermore, this nature of emptiness is a dull and insentient substance produced by obscurity; it lacks cognition.
Since it lacks cognition, it is not a spiritual and intelligent essence. How, then, can one seek to realize perfect penetration through it?

Maitreya entered through awakening to the greatness of consciousness (*vijñāna*); however, the nature of this consciousness arises and perishes moment by moment and is not a permanent, abiding nature.

Since these originally belong to the realm of delusion, how can one seek to realize perfect penetration through them? Mahāsthāmaprāpta attained awakening by recollecting the Buddha through the six sense faculties;
yet, all movement belongs to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Being part of the aggregate of formations, it is necessarily impermanent.
Now, if the nature of mindfulness itself belongs to the cycle of arising and ceasing, its cause will certainly be unable to realize the fruit of non-arising and non-ceasing.
"How can one seek to realize perfect penetration through this?
I now address the World-Honored One: when a Buddha appears in this Sahā world, the true essence of the teaching here is purity found in sound and hearing.
If one wishes to attain samādhi, it is truly by entering through the faculty of hearing."
From here below, the ear-faculty alone is selected as the perfect means of penetration (*āyatana*). Wēnlíng says: "The sages established their teachings differently according to circumstances;

there are Buddha-lands where the Buddha’s radiance constitutes the Buddha-work, and there are Buddha-lands where the Buddha’s Bodhi-tree constitutes the Buddha-work, and so on, including those where gardens, groves, terraces, and pavilions, or even empty space, serve as the Buddha-work."

Because [this realm] is tranquil and without verbal instruction—unlike the land of the Buddha Gandhottamakūṭa, where there are no written words or speech, but rather all devas and humans enter into the practice of discipline solely through various fragrances—the substance of the teaching in this region entirely relies on sound and hearing.

That one must necessarily enter into right concentration through hearing is because each person’s conditions and opportunities are unique. The *Zhengmai* (Orthodox Pulse) states: "In this region, [there are] two..."

The meaning of this passage is as follows: that the faculty of hearing in this region is particularly acute is entirely due to the nature of hearing pervading and penetrating immeasurable varieties of phenomena and principles.
Therefore, the Buddha, in accordance with the specific capacities of those in this region, performs buddha-work through vocal sound;
thus, he accords with the acuity of their faculty of hearing. Consequently, the union of sound and hearing constitutes the purity of this region.
Although the conventional teaching-body (*śāsana-deha*) is generally taken to be sound alone, this seems not to encompass "hearing.
One must realize that apart from the auditory faculty of the listener, sound vanishes and has no locus; how then could the teaching-body exist?
Therefore, know that while the teaching-body resides in both sound and hearing, one who wishes to enter right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) can never abandon the teaching-body.
However, one should separately choose to enter through the nature of hearing within the faculty of the ear.

This is because while vocal teachings serve merely as a preliminary lead-in, the nature of hearing is in fact the wondrous mind itself. Thus, although realization relies upon both sound and hearing, for the cultivation of samādhi, one should select only the nature of hearing;
therefore it is said that one must "enter through hearing. This, then, is the selection of the faculty.
Up until now, it was only this single phrase that definitively and clearly pointed out the ear-faculty as the fundamental root of the Perfect Penetration and the most wondrous Dharma-gate.
To leave suffering behind and attain liberation—how excellent, O Avalokiteśvara! Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, you have entered Buddha-lands as numerous as motes of dust.
Having attained the power of great mastery, you bestow fearlessness upon sentient beings with wondrous voices, the voice of Avalokiteśvara, the Brahma-voice, and the sound of the ocean tide;
you bring peace and security to all who seek salvation in the world, and by transcending the world, you have attained eternal abiding.

This praises the virtues of the one who realizes [the truth], both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others. "Free from suffering" means being free from the suffering of the two types of death;

"attaining liberation" means attaining liberation from both persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma*). To say that "liberation from bondage and mastery is attained through the nature of hearing" indicates that only Avalokiteśvara is capable of this.
When "sands of kalpas" is mentioned, it signifies that time is extremely long; when "dust motes" are mentioned...
"Land" refers to the fact that his dwelling is infinitely vast. "One who has attained the power of great mastery" praises the thirty-two manifestations that preach the Dharma according to conditions.
"Bestowing fearlessness upon sentient beings" praises the fourteen kinds of fearlessness and the salvation from suffering by responding to cries for help.

His preaching of the Dharma through the thirty-two manifestations according to their respective types, without losing his original voice, is called "Wondrous Sound. [He saves those in] the three miserable realms...
He observes the eight difficulties simultaneously and rescues all beings through the gift of fearlessness; this is called Avalokiteśvara.
His fundamental nature is pure and free from defilement; this is called Brahma-sound. He responds to all requests everywhere without missing the proper time; this is called Ocean-tide Sound.
Because he possesses these four sounds, he rescues those in the world who are in suffering and distress, so that they all attain peace and security. Furthermore—
This enables those who transcend the world to likewise attain the fruit of eternal abiding.
I now address the Tathāgata: as Avalokiteśvara has said, it is like a person dwelling in stillness when drums are struck simultaneously in all ten directions;
they hear them all at once. This is the perfect, true eye that does not look beyond obstructions; the same is true for the mouth and nose.
The body must combine with objects to know that mental thoughts are chaotic and without order; yet by listening to sounds through a wall, one can hear them both near and far.
Since the five sense organs are not uniform, this is what penetrates the true nature of sound. Whether in motion or stillness, sound exists within hearing as its presence or absence.
To claim there is no hearing when there is no sound is not true non-hearing, for it lacks inherent nature. When sound is absent, it does not cease; when sound is present, it is not born.

When one is perfectly free from both arising and ceasing, this is the eternal reality; even while in a dream, it is not subject to non-thinking, nor does it emerge from thought or observation, for body and mind cannot reach it.
This reveals the excellence of the faculty of hearing. That it hears simultaneously with all sounds striking it demonstrates its perfection (*pūrṇa*).

That it is distinct from the other five faculties demonstrates its penetration (*vyāpin*). That it remains constant throughout waking and sleeping, far removed from arising and ceasing, demonstrates its permanence (*nitya*).
Because the nature of hearing pervades all places, the objects of sound in the ten directions appear according to the time, without any sequence of before or after.
At that time, one pervasively hears all sound-objects; yet in the hearing-object there is no dharma—this is the self-evident nature, not something to be attained only upon realizing sainthood.
For this reason, Master Gaocheng said: "When the ear is active, whether in a deep valley or amidst great and small sounds, nothing is lacking.
When the bells and drums of the ten directions ring at once, the numinous light flows on, ever-present."

The continuity is what is called the "perfect reality. That the eyes do not perceive beyond obstructions means that, for example, one does not see what is outside when separated by paper or a film, nor does one see the internal organs when separated by the skin. The body knows only through contact;
the same applies to the mouth and nose. Because these three faculties all know through contact, if they are separated by even a few inches, one no longer perceives.
Although the mental faculty (*manas*) is pervasive, it is distracted and not constant like the auditory faculty;

it can hear through walls, unlike the visual faculty which cannot see through paper or skin; it hears both near and far, unlike the [other] three faculties which do not perceive beyond a certain distance;
and it is without thought and eternally still, unlike the mental faculty which is constantly thinking and agitated. This is so.
The five faculties are not equal, and the faculty of hearing is supreme; this is what is called "penetrating reality.

Furthermore, sounds have movement and stillness, and within the nature of hearing they may either exist or not exist. Yet those who are inverted take the silent absence of sound to be the non-existence of hearing itself.
However, it is not that the nature of hearing is actually non-existent, for this nature of hearing does not follow [the presence or absence of sound].
Because sound arises and sound ceases, even when one is in a dream and the solitary mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) alone is active, the nature of hearing seems to temporarily cease;
yet, if one still hears the sound of pounding and mistakenly perceives it as the beating of a drum, one knows that this nature does not cease through non-attention.
Thus, the essence and function of the nature of hearing transcend discursive thought.
Beyond this, that which is not reached by body or mind is what is called the "eternally real.
These three kinds of reality are all already fully possessed by ordinary beings; they do not depend upon realization to come into existence.
If one cultivates further based on these, it is like rowing a boat with the wind or fanning a fire with the breeze—what difficulty could there be?

Now, in this Sahā world, the science of phonetics (*śabda-vidyā*) is proclaimed and elucidated; yet sentient beings are deluded regarding their fundamental hearing, and by following after sounds, they wander through the cycle of rebirth.

Ānanda, despite your powerful memory, you cannot avoid falling into deviant thoughts; is this not because you follow that which you have sunk into, and by reversing the flow of these currents, you shall attain freedom from delusion?
This clarifies that the faculty of hearing is most suitable for beginners. It is said that the spiritual capacities of those in this region possess keen faculties of hearing;
they must rely upon verbal expression to achieve clear understanding. Therefore, in accordance with these particularly sharp faculties, all sutras and treatises have been extensively proclaimed.
Yet, that which is expounded by these sutras and treatises is none other than the revelation of the perfectly tranquil and wondrous nature—the perfectly tranquil and wondrous...
The nature [of hearing] is not separate from the faculty that hears; this nature must rely upon the discourse on sound to turn back and hear one's own original nature.

It is like using a finger to point toward the moon, yet sentient beings fail to grasp the Tathāgata’s fundamental intent and instead become further deluded regarding their own inherently existing nature of hearing.
Chasing after sounds and echoes while neglecting their own original hearing, they consequently wander along the flow of linguistic patterns.
How is this different from grasping at the finger and mistaking it for the moon? Furthermore, it is not only sentient beings who wander following sounds;

even Ānanda, though he could memorize the pure and wondrous principles of the twelve divisions of the *sūtras* of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions—numerous as the sands of the Ganges—was still unable to avoid falling into perverse thoughts and drowning in lustful attachments, thereby failing to attain liberation. Is this not so?
Is it that one follows those auditory objects and, unable to reflect upon oneself, becomes submerged and drowned?

If you know how to follow the sound back to its source, you will know how to reverse the flow and certainly attain the state free from delusion. Thus, the faculty of hearing is perfectly suited to the faculties and dispositions of those in this land;
there is no beginner for whom it cannot be employed. As the saying goes: "To cure an illness, one need not rely on a donkey."
Dhāyaya. Ānanda, listen attentively! Upholding the Buddha’s majestic power, I shall proclaim the True Samādhi of the Mother of Buddhas, the King of Vajras, the Illusory and Inconceivable.
If you hear all the secret gateways of the Buddha-microdusts [Buddhas] yet have not first eliminated the outflows (*āsrava*), [you will not attain it].
To accumulate learning and yet fall into error is a grave mistake; if one were to hold onto what has been heard, why would the Buddha not hear it himself?
This instruction is specifically entrusted to those who are ready for the teaching, and they must certainly practice according to this gateway.

When I say today that I have selected those of superior faculties, it is entirely through the Buddha’s majestic power, and not through my own independent authority or personal judgment; thus, I have made these distinctions. What has been spoken here—
This is precisely what was previously called the Vajra-King Jewel-Awakening, the Illusion-like Samādhi, and the Single Path to Nirvāṇa for the Bhagavāns of the ten directions.
What follows explains the fault of following after sounds and wandering in transmigration:

although you have already memorized and upheld a vast amount of the Buddha-dharma, because you delight only in extensive learning and do not eliminate the outflows of desire, that which you have accumulated...
The more [objects] there are, the deeper the root of craving becomes; this is of no benefit to the Way and only increases errors, which is why one cannot avoid the hardship of Māraṇa.
Therefore, the former masters said that the words of the Patriarchs are like a worn-out straw sandal: it is better to go barefoot than to wear it.
This is best used to stimulate "hearing" (śravaṇa) in the two lines [of the verse], specifically to incite "reverse hearing" (pratiloma-śravaṇa). It says: "You, take this..."
If you employ the faculty of hearing to retain the Buddha’s Dharma, why not turn this faculty of hearing back upon itself to hear its own nature?
Furthermore, the Tathāgata established his teachings for no other purpose than to lead people to realize their own original nature;

to now abandon that original nature and strive instead to pursue words and teachings—how could this be the intent behind the Tathāgata’s establishment of the Dharma? For when there is excessive learning, the mind...
Once released, it is difficult to gather back; by turning the hearing inward, the spirit becomes concentrated and entry is easy.
Therefore, he causes them to turn their hearing inward once, and they immediately attain non-delusion. These two sentences are truly the wondrous medicine for those who rely on much learning.
Formerly, Emperor Xiaozong of the Song dynasty asked an Indian monk: "What do you recite with the rosary held in Guanyin’s hand? He replied: "I recite 'Guān'."
Yinyue asked again, "I am thinking to myself: what is this so-called 'self'? [The Master] said: "Seeking others is not as good as seeking the self.
This is precisely that meaning.
Hearing does not arise spontaneously; it exists because of sound. When hearing turns back and detaches from sound, once it is able to detach, who is there to be named?
When a single faculty returns to its source, all six faculties achieve liberation. Seeing and hearing are like illusory cataracts; the three realms are like flowers in the sky.

When hearing is restored, the cataracts of the faculties are removed; as dust is extinguished, awareness becomes perfectly pure. When purity reaches its ultimate limit, light penetrates everywhere, and tranquil illumination encompasses the void.
Returning to observe the world, it is like a dream-event: Māraṅgaka is but a dream—who could possibly detain your form?
The following section most clearly reveals the benefits of "hearing-in-reverse. It states that this inverted faculty of hearing does not arise spontaneously;
rather, it is specifically because the dust of sound (*śabda-dhātu*) strikes against stillness and movement, adhering to the profound stillness (*zhan*) to trigger the act of listening.

Thus, the essence of hearing reflects the sound, eventually coiling back upon the sound to form a knot. Consequently, there arises the designation of the "ear-faculty" (*śrotra-indriya*). Once one understands that the sound has been coiled back...
One should know that the formation of a knot is released by means of sound; thus, one who desires release must turn back from hearing so as to become detached from sound.
If the objects (dust) that are to be released have already dissolved, and the faculty (root) that releases them has also ceased, how could there still be the name "ear-faculty"?
This is what is meant by: "When the objects are no longer perceived, the faculty has nothing with which to pair. If this is the case for a single faculty...

Since those who have already been liberated from the five faculties are liberated completely at that very moment, one knows that seeing and hearing are like illusory cataracts and the vessel-world is like flowers in the sky.
If seeing and hearing are once restored, the illusory cataracts are immediately removed; if the vessel-world is once dissolved, the essence of awakening is perfectly pure.
Thus, the faculties and their objects are bound together by the same bondage and liberated together by the same liberation.

When the roots are uprooted, the vessel-world naturally transcends. Yet, when the roots and sense-objects have dissolved to reach the stage of ultimate purity, this is precisely the time when the marks of clarity are pure and refined.
This Constant Samādhi Light (Cang-jig-guang) penetrates the Dharma-realm;
although empty space is vast, its silent illumination and radiant light pervade and encompass all, no less than the great ocean containing all within it.
How much more so a single bubble, which represents the vessel-world and the physical body established upon empty space?
If one can reach this state and then turn back to reflect upon the various phenomena of the world, they will see that True Suchness is like a dream;
for while in delusion, one never realized this illusion-like state and took it to be real, but upon awakening, one knows it was but a dream.
Thus, when Mātanga at that time used the power of a malevolent incantation to draw you into the chamber of lust, it was likewise within a dream.

How could a matter of a dream bind your body? It is because your seeing and hearing have not yet eliminated the cataracts of illusion that you are dazzled by these "flowers in the sky," perceiving them as real and thereby wandering through the cycle of rebirth.
Just as a skilled worldly illusionist conjures various men and women whose sense organs appear to move, yet depend on a single mechanism;

when that mechanism is withdrawn, they return to stillness and all illusions lose their substance. The six sense faculties are likewise: originally based on a single brilliant spirit, they divide into the six harmonious unities.
When they are unified in one place, they return to rest, and the six functions cease to exist. Thus, defilements dissolve in a mere thought.
When perfect, luminous, pure, and wondrous clarity is achieved, even the remaining traces of defilement are exhausted; when this clarity reaches its ultimate limit, one is a Tathāgata.

This metaphor illustrates how the liberation of a single faculty results in the uprooting of all six faculties. The illusionist represents true nature (*tathatā*), which possesses the capacity to follow conditions (*pratyaya-anuvartana*), and is thus called "skillful illusion.
The magical art represents ignorance (*avidyā*); the union of the true and the false transforms into the six sense-faculties, just as in the analogy.
The illusion of various men and women is like a single mechanism; the cord held in the hand of the illusory person is a metaphor for the single essence of clarity.
Because the cord moves from the hands of the illusionist, the mouth and eyes of the illusory person also move. Thus it is said:
"Though one sees the movement of the various faculties, it is ultimately due to the pulling of a single mechanism. If the cord does not move, then the illusory person—
Because the mouth and eyes do not move, it is said that "the mechanism ceases and one returns to stillness. All illusions thus become devoid of inherent nature.
When the six faculties merge with this single brilliant clarity, it is the fundamental brilliance of consciousness—the subtle *ālayavijñāna* (the *dāna-vijñāna*).
The six faculties serve as the dependent, while the single brilliant clarity serves as the basis; from this single brilliant clarity, one gathers in sensory objects to form knots. Each [faculty]...
Because each is distinct, they are subsequently divided into six; thus, that which resides in the eye is called "seeing," and that which resides in the ear is called "hearing," and so forth.

Therefore it is said: "Originally relying on one pure, bright spirit, it is divided into the six harmonious combinations. If a single faculty is brought to rest and restored, then all six faculties should be uprooted, resulting in perfect liberation.
As for "dust and grime": the aforementioned conceptual appearances are the dust, and the cognitive emotions are the grime. This is so.

This refers to the subtle ignorance within the *ālayavijñāna*. It is because, after the six consciousnesses have been liberated and what is heard and the hearer are exhausted, one has already realized the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
If one proceeds from this point to suddenly empty the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), then even the defilements will be eliminated in an instant;
the essence of consciousness will then transform into the perfectly interfused, pure, and enlightened jewel-awareness. However, if there remain any residual defilements...
Those who have not yet reached the end still dwell in the stage of training and have not yet completed their work;
however, if one’s clarity becomes pure and reaches the ultimate point, this is precisely the perfectly accomplished supreme fruit realized by the Tathāgata.

Thus, since this dharma-gate is so wondrous and the attainment of Buddhahood is not difficult through it, one should certainly choose this single faculty as the path for entering the gate for beginners.
O Great Assembly and Ānanda, turn back your inverted faculty of hearing and listen instead to the nature of hearing itself;
when this nature is perfected, the Unsurpassed Way is realized. Such is the true, perfect penetration. This is the single path to Nirvāṇa for all Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust.

All Tathāgatas of the past have already accomplished this path; all Bodhisattvas of the present are now each entering its perfect clarity; and those who practice and study in the future [should likewise do so].
"You should rely upon this Dharma; I have likewise realized it from within it, not only Avalokiteśvara.
Furthermore, I have extensively cited what has been realized in order to inspire a heart of admiration and to universally exhort you to practice with diligence.
The efficacy and swiftness of the results of 'turning the hearing' are such as this: you all should immediately turn back your inverted hearing."

The faculty does not follow the external but follows the internal; if you can truly turn back your hearing from the "hearing" of the Tathāgata’s secret Dharma-gate and hear the nature of hearing that is inherently present within yourself, and take this nature as the mind of the causal ground, you will be able to establish the path to supreme enlightenment.
Therefore, although there are many gates of perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*), if they are truly perfect—
This single gate alone is capable of responding to the needs of this region and curing the disease of excessive learning;
for it is the one great highway by which countless Buddhas have reached the home of Bodhi, and the primary portal for entering the ocean of Nirvana.
Thus, the Buddhas of the past entered through it, and the Bodhisattvas of the present likewise do so.
This entry [into the path] already has many precedents before us; therefore, future practitioners must certainly enter by means of this Dharma-gate.

Furthermore, not only have all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas entered through this gate, but I too have entered through this very gate—how much more so for Avalokiteśvara? Moreover, if one were to extend this principle further:
This gate is not only that through which all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas enter; the twenty-four sages likewise all enter through this gate.
Not only these twenty-four sages, but even the two masters, Confucius and Laozi, entered through this gate as well.
Thus, Zhongni (Confucius) said: "If one hears the Way in the morning, it is acceptable to die in the evening. And Mengzhang (Zhuangzi) said: "What I call 'hearing'..."

This does not mean that one merely hears of others; it means hearing for oneself. Therefore, know that the two characters "returning to hear" (*fanwen*) are truly the excellent medicine for counteracting the ailments of this land, a practice shared by all three teachings, differing only in the depth of realization attained.
That which is called "the same teaching despite differences in depth" is precisely what is meant here. Thus ends the inquiry regarding the Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance (*nianfo*).
Question: Since the three faculties are universally applicable, why is it that they are also excluded [in this context]? Answer:

Although the practice of *nien-fo* (reciting the Buddha's name) encompasses practitioners of both shallow and deep faculties, one must first allow the Name of Amitābha Buddha to flow in through the faculty of the ear;

only then can the faculty of the mind begin to maintain the thought of the Buddha without forgetfulness. Thus, even the Dharma-gate of *nien-fo* necessarily depends upon the faculty of the ear. Therefore...
The practice of Buddha-recitation is likewise distinguished [as supreme].

Truly, as the World-Honored Buddha inquired of me regarding various skillful means to save those in the final age who seek to transcend the world and achieve the mind of nirvana, Avalokiteśvara is the foremost;
all other skillful means are merely the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha.
"Abandoning worldly toil through immediate action is not a matter of long-term cultivation; the teaching is proclaimed according to the same principle of depth and shallowness.
This is a response to Your Majesty’s command. It is truly as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, inquired of me regarding various skillful means:
"Among the twenty-four sages previously mentioned, who should take up their respective capacities to save those in the final kalpa? This also addresses the previous inquiry.
"After my parinirvāṇa, among the sentient beings of this world who seek those beyond the mundane— this refers back to those who have entered the Bodhisattva vehicle—
and who have accomplished the mind of nirvāṇa— this refers back to those who have perfected the Unsurpassed Way— Avalokiteśvara shall be the foremost.
This means that among the four types of practices previously inquired about, it is solely the single gateway of Avalokiteśvara’s ear-faculty that is entirely in accord with them.
This is the foremost; as for the remaining twenty-four gates entered by the sages, they were all attained through the empowerment of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.
They occurred upon the incidental encounter with a single matter that caused the abandonment of worldly toil (*saṃsāra*);

they are not methods to be cultivated universally and permanently, nor are they teachings spoken for those of superior, middling, or inferior faculties alike. This is like the loss of sight experienced by Nandika or the encounter with thorns suffered by Pilindavatsa.
Not all people are like this; how could they enter [the path] by means of a single, uniform approach?

For instance, the great causes of Samantabhadra, the innate eloquence of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, the realization of emptiness by Subhūti, and the pure vision of Śāriputra—all these were restricted to those with profound resolve;
how could beginners enter through them? Furthermore, the lust of Śāṭha and the lack of recitation in Cūḍapanthaka were restricted only to those with shallow resolve.
How could this be the entryway for those of great resolve? Since each [method] has its own limitations, they must necessarily have their own biases;

how could they be teachings that speak equally to both the shallow and the profound? By contrast, it is revealed that the only gateway through which one may cultivate the universal and long-term, and which can be explained according to both shallow and profound capacities, is the single door of Avalokiteśvara’s "reverse-hearing.
This is intended to encourage the utmost dedication to its exclusive cultivation.
I prostrate to the Tathāgatagarbha, the untainted and inconceivable one;

may you bestow your grace upon those of the future so that they may be without doubt regarding this gateway, easily achieve its skillful means, and be fit to teach Ānanda and those sinking in the delusions of the final age.
By cultivating perfect penetration through this very faculty alone, it surpasses all others—such is the true mind.

This prostration is a request for empowerment; it means that this single gateway of the ear-organ is precisely the aforementioned three Tathāgata-garbhas, the aforementioned untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*), and the aforementioned inconceivable, illusion-like Mother of Buddhas, the True Samādhi.
May all Buddhas, through their spiritual powers, empower all future practitioners who advance in cultivation.
Entering directly with a single blade from this gate, one does not allow even a single thought of doubt to arise in the other.
If this dharma-gate is taken as the primary expedient, accomplishment is easily achieved;
thus, it is fit to teach Ānanda by means of this dharma, and it can also be used to deliver those submerged in the final kalpa. However, one uses only this single gate and no others.
Regarding the "other gates," it means that by practicing according to this one gate, one can transcend the perfect penetration of the twenty-four sages;
for with a true mind, there is only this single matter and no other method. In this sutra, Mañjuśrī is encountered four times, each instance possessing profound significance.
The first command for Mañjuśrī to take the mantra and go protect [the practitioner] was not intended for those who lack great wisdom.
Because they were unable to uphold this mantra-heart, he next asked about the two meanings of form and emptiness and their relative correctness;
for it is not possible for one who lacks great wisdom to dispel difficulties and resolve entanglements for others. Third, regarding the command to select the perfect penetration:
it is not possible for one who does not possess great wisdom and the correct eye to discern the faculties; one must be like a king of geese before one can choose the water.

Because the milk is contained within it, the reason for inquiring about the title of the *Sūtra of the Four Questions* is that the teachings of this single assembly, from beginning to end, all return to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly, with body and mind clearly illuminated, received this great instruction and contemplated the Bodhi of the Buddha.
And regarding the Great Parinirvāṇa, it is like a person who has traveled far away on business and has not yet returned, yet clearly knows the path by which they must return home.
The great assembly gathered there—the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of supernatural beings; those of the two vehicles still in training;
and all the newly resolved bodhisattvas—numbering as many as ten Ganges-sands—all attained their original mind and became free from dust and defilement.
Upon hearing these verses, the bhikṣuṇī Prakṛti-vimala-dharmanetra attained the purity of the Dharma-eye and became an arhat;
immeasurable sentient beings all resolved to attain the peerless, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

This describes the realization. In the first five fascicles, it was stated that "body and mind are bright and clear," which refers to knowing the sequence of the binding and unbinding of body and mind;

however, it was not yet known through which gateway one enters. Now, having ascertained with certainty that entry is through the gateway of the ear, there is no further doubt, and thus both body and mind are perfectly lucid.
Since *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* both refer to the ultimate fruit, [this state is so designated].
This is illustrated by the analogy of a house: the faculty of hearing is like the road.
It means that for a long time the impoverished son has fled to another land and, wishing to return home, did not know the way. Today, one path home is pointed out;
although he has not yet actually reached his home, if he proceeds directly forward, he will certainly never again encounter a forked path.

What was previously called the "path" and the "gate," and what is here called the "house," refers to the realization that the faculty of hearing is the path to the house of Bodhi and the gate for entering the house of Bodhi. This initial expedient means culminates here;
the gathering of the great assembly below attains benefit, and all obtain their original mind—this is the causal mind attained at the first stage of faith.
"Being far removed from dust and defilement" refers to the delusions that have been severed. "Attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye" refers to the thorough realization of perfect penetration.
"Taking the awakening of the fruit-stage as the mind of the causal stage" refers to the initial mind of the ten abodes.
"Arousing the bodhicitta" refers to the initial entry into the stage of faith. As the *Prajñāpāramitā* states: "The Bodhisattva of the ten wholesome paths arouses the great mind."
This is the long parting from the ocean of suffering within the wheel of the three realms.
Ānanda adjusted his robes, joined his palms in prostration before the great assembly, and with his mind and conduct perfectly luminous, a mixture of sorrow and joy arose within him.
Desiring to benefit all sentient beings of the future, he bowed his head to the Buddha and addressed the World-Honored One of Great Compassion: "I have now..."
I have awakened to and perfected the Dharma-gate; by practicing within this, one attains freedom from doubt. I have constantly heard the Tathāgata speak these words:

"The Bodhisattva’s aspiration is to first deliver others before one has delivered oneself; having perfected self-awakening, one is able to awaken others—such is the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world.
Although I myself have not yet been delivered, I vow to deliver all sentient beings of the final age, World-Honored One. This...

As sentient beings gradually distance themselves from the Buddha, and as false teachers preach the Dharma like the sands of the Ganges River, how can one cause them to gather their minds and enter samādhi?
How can one cause them to establish a site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*), remain far removed from the works of Māra, and attain a mind of bodhi that is free from retreat or discouragement?
This request establishes the ritual procedure for establishing a *maṇḍala* as a method for concentrating the mind during the final age.

"The mind and its traces are perfectly luminous" means that first one awakens to the non-arising and non-ceasing mind, which is precisely the Great *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-śūraṅgama-rāja*—this is the perfect luminosity of the mind.
Furthermore, awakening to the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) as the gateway for entering the non-arising and non-ceasing is the perfect luminosity of the traces.

"Sorrow" refers to lamenting the delusions of kalpas past; "joy" refers to rejoicing in today’s sudden awakening. Because one has suddenly awakened after long delusion, sorrow and joy are intertwined.
To desire to benefit future beings means that once one's own illness has been removed, one further takes pity on the illnesses of others.
Those who practice within this without doubt have already awakened to the Dharma of the Buddhas.
It is certain that [the teaching] enters through the faculty of hearing, and there is no doubt about this. Below, he constantly cites the words of the Buddha to encourage himself:
"One who has not yet crossed over but thinks to ferry others across is a Bodhisattva; one who has already completed their own crossing and focuses solely on ferrying living beings is a Tathāgata.
Although all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas take the ferrying of living beings as their primary task, I— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available fragment.*
What I most urgently desire is to learn to become a Bodhisattva. World-Honored One, I have now encountered the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma and already know the path of cultivation;
I enter through hearing. Yet I fear that in the final age, sentient beings will gradually distance themselves from the Buddha, and as false teachers preach the Dharma, divergent paths will multiply.
Since the false and the correct will thus become confused, it will hinder their progress in cultivation.
Since their minds have no fixed direction and they wish to gather their minds to enter *samādhi*,
how can one cause them to be established in the ground for entering the Way, so that they cannot be shaken by heterodox teachings and their bodhicitta may attain freedom from retreat?
At that time, the World-Honored One, in the midst of the great assembly, praised Ānanda, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
As you have asked, regarding the establishment of the site of enlightenment to rescue and protect sentient beings drowning in the final age—listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
Ānanda and the great assembly responded, "Yes, we shall respectfully receive your instruction. The Buddha told Ānanda: "You have often heard within my *vinaya*..."
He proclaimed the three principles of definitive practice: namely, to restrain the mind as the precept, from the precept arises concentration, and from concentration issues forth wisdom;
these are called the three trainings in the outflow-free.
The following explains the four kinds of pure instructions as the definitive standard for practice in the final age;
this is the Vinaya Piṭaka. Regarding the "Three Definitive Meanings," it means that one must definitively rely on these three types as the foundation of practice.
"Gathering the mind constitutes the precepts" means that it does not merely restrain the body, but is fundamentally about rectifying the mind.
If there is even the slightest attachment of thought, concentration arises from the precepts; as the Sūtra says, "If śīla is not pure, samādhi does not manifest.
If wisdom is elicited by concentration, as the Sūtra says, "Unimpeded and pure wisdom all arise based on dhyāna-samādhi.
Thus we know that the precepts are the vanguard for concentration and wisdom; if the root of the precepts is impure, then concentration and wisdom will not exist.
Because they arise from this, the Sixth Patriarch said: "The nature of mind being non-deficient is the self-nature precept; the nature of mind being undisturbed is self-nature concentration;
the nature of mind being unimpeded is self-nature wisdom. When these three are fully possessed without any leakage, it is called the 'outflow-free' (anāsrava) learning.
Why, then, does the subsequent text mention only the four precepts and not concentration and wisdom? [The answer is] as stated in the preceding text.

The forgetting of external objects and the exhaustion of internal faculties and so forth are all manifestations of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*); however, because the precepts (*śīla*) have not yet been mentioned, they are now specifically clarified.
Question: Previously, it was said that "flowing against the current," "returning the flow," "revolving the flow," "not following," and "not pursuing" are all methods for gathering the mind;
are these not the precepts? Answer: Flowing against the current and so forth are intended to cause one to go against present karmic activities.
The four precepts serve to hollow out one's inherent nature; for if one can first hollow out this inherent nature, then it becomes easy to contravene manifest karma.

Therefore, after clarifying concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), the precepts are presented next. These four precepts are the foundation for severing the moisture that nurtures [defilements] and the basis for entering concentration and wisdom.
They are like constructing a house where one first solidifies the foundation; without a foundation, there is none.
For it is impossible to establish a foundation upon empty space; it will certainly not succeed.
Ānanda, what is the gathering of the mind that I call "precept"? If the beings of the six realms in all worlds do not harbor lustful hearts, they will not follow the continuity of birth and death.
You practice samādhi precisely to emerge from worldly toil; yet if you harbor a lustful heart...

If one does not eliminate the dust of afflictions, one cannot escape; even if one possesses much wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before them, if they do not sever lust, they will inevitably fall into the path of demons.
There are those of the highest grade who become demon-kings, those of the middle grade who become demon-ministers, and those of the lowest grade who become demon-women.

These various demons also have their own followers, each claiming for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way. After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, there will be many such as these.

The subjects of Māra flourish in the world, widely practicing greed and lust, acting as "good friends" who cause all sentient beings to fall into the pit of craving and views and lose the path to Bodhi.
You should instruct the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi* by first severing sexual desire in the mind;
this is called the Tathāgata’s foremost, definitive, pure, and clear instruction from the Buddhas of the past.
This first explains the precept against sexual misconduct. Since all sentient beings sustain their very lives through sexual desire, they are bound within the cycle of birth and death;
because we now wish to cut off its source, the cessation of sexuality is made the primary focus.

Regarding "a mind that is not lustful," this does not mean merely refraining from physical transgressions; rather, it means that even raising a single thought of lustful intent constitutes [the violation].
Because of breaking the precepts, the Patriarch said: "When the internal mind does not go out and external objects do not enter, and the mind is like a wall or a barrier, one can enter the Way.
Thus, one does not follow the continuous succession of birth and death; for the non-arising of a lustful mind is precisely what opposes the flow of the desire for birth and death.
Here, "samādhi" refers to the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing, while "dust-labor" (the afflictions) refers to the faculty of sight.

Regarding the two delusions of thought (*samskāra-vikalpa*), if the lustful mind is not eliminated, then one will certainly be unable to sever birth-and-death through the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-saṃskāra*), nor can one escape from them.

Even if concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*) manifest before you, if you do not abandon the root of lust within meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), or if such thoughts arise, the objects of desire will appear accordingly.
Just as fire meets with fuel, how could it fail to burn? Therefore, one will inevitably fall.
The path of Māra deludes people with nothing beyond this; thus, they extensively practice lustful desire.
Those who take such persons as their "good friends" claim that performing sexual acts constitutes the work of a Buddha, and so they pass on their lust from one to another.

Those who fall into the pit of attachment and views refer to the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *saṃyojana-kleśa*). This means that those who wish to escape the pit of view and thought instead fall back into that very pit, unable to emerge.

This is like the case of Udraka Rāmaputra, who attained the state of the "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" concentration (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), yet as soon as he touched a woman's hand, lustful thoughts arose and he immediately lost his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Wénlǐng says: "In various sutras, the precept against killing is placed first, signifying that the establishment of transformation [through teaching] takes compassion as its foundation.
This sutra places the precept against sexual misconduct first, signifying that true cultivation takes the departure from desire as its foundation. Indeed...
The energy of desire is coarse and turbid, defiling the wondrous clarity; the habituation to desire leads to madness and delusion, easily causing one to lose right concentration (*samāpatti*).

Nothing is more extreme than this in terms of perpetuating birth and death and losing true constancy; therefore, it must be the primary precept and the foremost clear instruction for attaining purity.
Observe how Ānanda, when the teaching was initiated, encountered false defilement; yet at the very beginning of his resolve, he first felt aversion toward the turbidity of desire.
Regarding the three gradual stages (*san jianci*), one must first subdue [the mind] in each instance; thereafter, body and mind become perfectly luminous and attain great peace and stability.

Those at the initial stage of the Ten Faiths (*shixin*) have their craving for desire dried up, whereby their wisdom-nature becomes perfectly luminous, and they thus ascend through the Equal and Wondrous [stages].
As for ordinary people of the world, because their minds do not flow into dissipation, clarity and brightness arise within them, gradually reaching the six heavens of the desire realm.
Therefore, true cultivation that encompasses the internal must first involve the departure from desire.
For this reason, Ānanda, if you do not sever sexual desire while practicing dhyāna-concentration, it is like steaming sand and gravel in hopes of producing rice;
even after hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it would only be called "hot sand. Why is this? Because this is not the fundamental substance of rice; it is merely sand and gravel. You...
To seek the wondrous fruit of Buddhahood with a lustful body—even if one attains subtle awakening—it will all be rooted in lust.

With lust as its foundation, one revolves through the three miserable realms and can never escape. As for the path to cultivating and realizing the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa, you must ensure that the mechanism of lust is severed in both body and mind;
even the nature of this severance must be absent. Only then can one hope for the Bodhi of the Buddha. What I have spoken here is called [the method].
If it were spoken by the Buddha, it would not be as you say; rather, such speech is that of Pāpīyān.
From here below, it is definitively established that only through the cessation of sexual desire can one attain Bodhi. The passage beginning with "Like steaming" uses a metaphor to clarify this;

the section beginning with "You" applies the analogy to the case at hand. The phrase "Steaming sand to make rice" illustrates the point: even if one were to do so for kalpas—as the scripture says—this is merely called "sand. This refers to what is known as the bitter gourd (kūṣmāṇḍa).
The root is suffering. Having realized that lust is the root of birth and death, one then knows that non-lust is the foundation of bodhi.

A "trigger" (*mē*) is the cause of movement; it is like the bolt of a crossbow. The trigger of lust is precisely the mental factor of attention (*manasikāra*), which is one of the five universal mental factors (*pañca-sarvatraga*).
From that single instance of attention, the mind of lust first moves; once the mind has moved—
Because the body moves in accordance [with the mind], one must necessarily block its subtle stirrings (*ki*), whereby the roots of both physical and mental lust will be severed together.
Formerly, in the Five Indias, there was a monk named Dharmadatta who possessed eloquence and wisdom; he served the Venerable Siṃha as his teacher.

The Venerable Siṃha, knowing that he had attained realization and understanding, praised him before the assembly. When it came to transmitting the Dharma and succeeding to the lineage of the patriarchs, [the Venerable Siṃha] chose Vasubandhu.
Sudatta harbored resentment toward Dharmada and said, "Venerable Sir, you know me so well that you do not grant me the succession to the patriarchal seat;
what explanation can there be for this? After some time, one day as he was crossing a river alone, a woman was washing her feet and exposed them.
Sudatta thought to himself, "How white and fair these shanks are! He then called out to the Master.
The Venerable Son suddenly appeared by his side and said, "Every time you think of me, you do not entrust the patriarchal seat to me;
can your heart today be granted the patriarchal seat? Dhamadatta then composed his mind, prostrated at his feet, and pleaded in distress:
"Is such a subtle transgression as this so difficult to overcome? This is what is called the 'mechanism of lust. If it persists..."

To discuss this to its ultimate conclusion: although body and mind are both severed, if the nature of severance still persists, one remains within the shadow of conditions and has not yet attained radical purity;
it is still the root of birth and death. One must ensure that even the nature of severance is non-existent;
only then is it the root of Bodhi. Once its root is attained, the fruit of Bodhi may be hoped for. As I conclude below, this definitively establishes the correct principle.
The reason for establishing the formal rules for preaching the Dharma is precisely because Ānanda requested them so that, in the degenerate age, false teachings would not confuse the minds of people;
he sought for the Tathāgata to establish definitive rules so that heterodox doctrines could not cause him to waver.
When the Tathāgata spoke of these four root precepts, the single word "not" (*na*) itself signifies non-compliance, non-following, and opposition.
The meaning of "flowing" and "whirling" is that in the final age, preaching the Dharma exactly as I have taught it is the Tathāgata’s correct teaching;
if one does not speak in this way but instead claims that engaging in sexual desire does not constitute an obstacle, that is the teaching of Māra.
Ānanda, furthermore, among the sentient beings of the six realms in all worlds, if their minds do not kill, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.
When you cultivate samādhi, its purpose is fundamentally to emerge from worldly toil; if the mind of killing is not eliminated, one cannot emerge from the dust.

Even if one possesses great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before them, if they do not sever killing, they will inevitably fall into the realm of spirits. Among those of the highest grade, they become great spirits.
Those of middling power among the *bala-rākṣasas* shall become flying *yakṣas* and various ghost generals; those of inferior power shall become earth-walking *rākṣasas*.
These ghosts and spirits also have their own followers, each claiming for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma (*paścima-dharma*), many such ghosts and spirits will flourish in the world, declaring that by eating meat one attains Bodhi.
"Ti-lu, Ānanda, when I permitted the bhikṣus to eat the five kinds of pure meat, those meats were all produced by my supernatural power;
they originally had no life-force. You, O brāhmaṇa, live in a land that is mostly damp and humid, where stones, sand, and gravel abound such that grasses and vegetables do not grow.
By the application of my great compassionate supernatural power, and because of my great kindness and pity, I provisionally designated them as 'meat' so that you might obtain their flavor."
How can it be that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, those who eat the flesh of sentient beings call themselves disciples of the Śākya?

You should know that such meat-eaters, even if they attain mental clarity resembling *samādhi*, are all great *rākṣasas*. When their retribution ends, they will inevitably sink into the bitter sea of birth and death;
they are not disciples of the Buddha. Such people kill one another, devour one another, and eat one another without end.

How does such a person escape the three realms? By teaching the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi* and next to sever the taking of life—this is called the second definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored Buddhas of the past.
This clarifies the precept against killing. Those who inevitably fall into the realm of spirits— such as worldly deities of flesh and blood, powerful ghosts, or the *rākṣasas* who roam the heavens—
whom people today enshrine as emperors or celestial beings, each claiming for themselves to have attained the Unsurpassed Way,
mistake their own state for truth and fail to recognize their error, just as owls and tigers do not realize the cruelty of their nature.
He also stated that those who claim one attains the path to Bodhi by eating meat are like those who say wine and meat do not obstruct the path to Bodhi;

such things as the "five kinds of pure meat"—defined as not seen, not heard, and not suspected of being killed for oneself, plus meat from animals that died naturally or were left over by birds—are merely provisional designations for meat.
Examples include the "meat mountains" of fish and rice; these are all manifestations of great compassion through skillful means, so how could they be real?
How can it be that there are those with life who eat the flesh of sentient beings while calling themselves sons of the Śākya? A sutra says:

"Even if one obtains leftover food, one should regard it as eating the flesh of one's own child during a time of famine; how much more so for one who devours the blood and flesh of sentient beings—can such a person truly be called a son of the Śākya?
It is said that at the end of their lives, they will surely sink into the ocean of suffering within birth and death. A sutra says: "For the sake of profit, they kill..."
Sentient beings who, by means of wealth, purchase various meats— both [parties] commit evil karma and shall die to fall into the Raurava Hell.

As for the phrase "mutually killing and swallowing one another," it refers precisely to how those born together through evil karma become karmic creditors and debtors, having no way to escape their retribution.

Therefore, Ānanda, if one who does not cease killing practices meditative concentration, it is like a person who blocks their own ears and shouts at the top of their voice, yet demands that others not hear them;
such a person is said to be "hiding what is manifest while making the hidden even more exposed.
Pure bhikṣus and bodhisattvas walk along forked paths without treading upon living grass, much less plucking it with their hands—how could they lack great compassion?

If one takes the flesh and blood of sentient beings to satisfy one's hunger, yet those sentient beings do not wear the silks, floss, or brocades of the East, nor the boots, furs, or woolens of this land, nor consume its milk, curds, or clarified butter—such a bhikṣu has not truly attained liberation from the world, but merely repays old debts;
he does not roam beyond the three realms. Why is this? For by consuming their physical bodies, one remains bound to them as a condition.

If a person eats the hundred grains from within that land and their feet do not leave the ground, they must ensure that, regarding all sentient beings, neither their body nor their bodily parts—through both the physical and mental aspects—are served or consumed. I declare that such a person is one who has attained true liberation.
What I have spoken thus is called the teaching of the Buddha; what is not spoken thus is the teaching of Pāpīyān.

This establishes that only by abstaining from killing does one attain true liberation. To wish to hide what is increasingly revealed is a metaphor for wishing to emerge from birth and death while instead entering back into birth and death.
Not treading upon or uprooting [plants] extends benevolence even to grasses and trees, let alone to birds and beasts.
That one makes use of their various parts—whether sleeping on their hides or using their fur—is entirely for the sake of those beings as conditions for one's own practice.

All these are things that belong to their own bodies and serve as conditions for their formation; how much less could they take the flesh and blood of sentient beings to satisfy their hunger? As the saying goes:
"One cannot form a karmic connection with a petty person, let alone with those subject to birth and death. Regarding the phrase "feet not leaving the ground," Wēn-líng says:
"In the beginning of the kalpa, human bodies possessed flying radiance, and their feet were as if treading upon clouds; this was because they ate the earth."
Because they consume fragrant rice, their bodies are firm and heavy, and their feet do not leave the ground. "Body" refers to the physical constituents such as flesh, blood, marrow, and bones;
"parts of the body" refers to products such as milk, curd, hides, and wool. Regarding the two aspects of body and mind:
"not consuming" means that not only does the body not consume them, but the mind also does not permit even a trace of thought regarding their consumption.
Second, you must also sever the habit of covetousness.
Ānanda, furthermore, if the beings of the six realms in the world do not harbor a covetous heart, they will not follow along with the continuous succession of birth and death.

When you cultivate samādhi, its purpose is to emerge from worldly toil; if the covetous mind is not eliminated, you cannot escape from the dust of the world. Even if you possess... [the rest of the passage]... [it would be in vain].
Those with much wisdom who manifest meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), yet do not sever their thievery, will surely fall onto the paths of the heterodox.
They will be possessed by superior-grade spirits, medium-grade demons, or inferior-grade wicked persons and various malevolent ghosts.

These various evil beings also have their own followers, each claiming to have attained the Unsurpassed Way. After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma (*mofa*), such demonic and heterodox forces will flourish extensively.
In the world, there are those who harbor deceit and fraud while claiming to be "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra);

each of them asserts that they have attained the "superior human state" (uttarimanussa-dhamma) and deludes the ignorant, fearing they might lose their minds. Wherever they go, the households they visit suffer depletion and dissipation.

My teaching is for bhikṣus to wander from place to place begging for food, so as to cause them to abandon greed and achieve the path to Bodhi. These bhikṣus do not cook their own food; they rely on [the offerings of others].
With this wretched life adrift in the three realms, I have shown you but one round of coming and going; once gone, there is no returning.

How can these thieves, wearing my robes, peddle the teachings of the Tathāgata for profit and create all manner of karmic deeds, claiming them to be the Buddha-dharma, while actually reviling monks who have left home and received the full precepts as followers of the Hīnayāna path?
Because of this, they delude and mislead immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to fall into the Avīci Hell. If I—
After my parinirvāṇa, if there be a bhikṣu who resolves his mind with determination to cultivate samādhi,
and who, before an image of the Tathāgata, burns a single lamp, consumes a finger-joint, or kindles a single stick of incense upon his own body—

I declare that such a person shall at once repay all karmic debts from beginningless time; he shall bid a long farewell to the world and forever be liberated from all outflows (āsravas), even though he has not yet...

This clarifies the path to unsurpassed enlightenment: if a person has already attained a mind of certainty regarding the Dharma, even if they do not commit this minor act of abandoning the body, should they nonetheless achieve the unconditioned (*asamskrta*), they will inevitably be reborn as a human to repay their past debts, just as it was with my own "horse-barley" [incident]—the principle is exactly the same.
You should teach the people of the world that after practicing *samādhi*, one must first sever the habit of stealing; this is called the Tathāgata’s precept of the former Buddhas.
This is the World-Honored One’s third definitive and pure instruction.
This clarifies the precept against stealing. A thief does not merely steal the wealth of others;
