it includes all who assume a formal appearance to solicit the respect, offerings, and gain of others. That which is not stolen by the mind is called greed.
One attains this within a single thought; only when not even a single thought arises can birth and death be forever severed.
This conversely reveals that if the "thieving mind" is not eliminated, one will certainly be unable to escape from birth and death. As for the statement that one must fall into heterodox paths:

it means that because one’s state of mind is not upright, one feigns the appearance of the Great Radiance to deceive the ignorant; thus, one falls among the ranks of heterodox spirits, as numerous as mountains.

"Those with 'water-essence monsters' possess deviant supernatural powers; those who manifest demonic powers to bewitch people are called 'wicked people'—those possessed by various demons whose delusional words confuse the masses.

Each claims for themselves to have realized the Unsurpassed Way, yet because demons and spirits have entered their vitals, they do not recognize their own transgressions. Those who harbor deceit and fraud conceal [their true nature]."

Concealing their flaws, they falsely claim to be realized masters (*jñānin*) and use demonic speech to intimidate people, causing them to change their hearts and minds so that they revere [the deceiver] as a divine being.
Consequently, people exhaust their lives and squander their wealth to serve them; thus, wherever they go, the households waste away.
My teaching clarifies that this is a grave violation of the Buddha’s words, revealing these individuals to be demons.
Furthermore, those who follow the prescribed directions to beg for food— my disciples— are commanded to carry the alms-bowl to seek sustenance for their bodies,
solely with the intent that they may abandon craving and realize the path to enlightenment. Since I do not even permit them to cook for themselves to indulge their appetites,
I require them to eat but one meal at midday and dwell beneath a tree for a single night, so that this remainder of their lives may be like a temporary lodging for travelers.
The three realms are like a guest house; this single journey of coming and going is all there is. Once one has gone from here, one shall never return again.
How could one wish to cause them to remain attached to the human world, becoming dregs of hell?
Why do these thieves steal my robes, assume my monastic appearance, and use the Tathāgata as a broker for profit, engaging extensively in trade?
Those who sell and create the karmic causes for the three miserable realms all claim, as a single rule, that this is the Buddha-dharma.
Not only do they fail to recognize their own error, but they instead label those who practice the Right Path as followers of the Hīnayāna, while claiming what they themselves do to be the Mahāyāna.
Thus, like one blind man leading another blind man, they follow one another into the fiery pit, never to emerge again.

It has emerged! Furthermore, that which humans cherish most as their supreme treasure is none other than this body; thus, Yangzi would not pluck out even a single hair, and Confucianists dare not damage or injure it.

My teaching leads worldly people to cultivate *samādhi* by first performing the subtle cause of "giving up the body" before an image of the Tathāgata, thereby enabling them to repay the debts incurred from past lives. If one can practice this deed—
Although they may not yet be able to ascend the path to Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), such persons are certainly capable of believing in the Dharma of Great Enlightenment.
Even if they do not practice this conduct, should they attain enlightenment, they will return to the human world to repay their past karmic debts.
This was, for example, as when I once ate horse-barley for three months in the royal stables at the city of Vairaṇyā; this was due to my own [past actions].
The world reviled me, saying that a bhikṣu should eat horse fodder; thus I am now repaying this retribution.
If even for a single harsh word uttered I must still undergo such compensation, how much more so for the debts incurred in past lives—how could there be any that are not repaid?

At present, deluded sentient beings, if there is some perceived benefit, will not hesitate to enter even the pits of dragons or the dens of tigers; yet their attachment to the self is not as [strong] as this.
If one cherishes material things, then even if one were to offer a single finger, it would likely still be insufficient to repay past debts.
Therefore, Ānanda, if you do not cease your thievery and cultivate meditative concentration, it will be like a person pouring water into a leaking cup, seeking to fill it;
even if they pass through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, it will never be replenished. As for those bhikṣus who, from the remnants of their robes and bowls...

One shall not store even a fraction of the leftovers from alms; instead, one should give them to hungry sentient beings. At great assemblies, one should join the palms and pay homage to the multitude.

If someone strikes or reviles one, one should regard it as identical to praise. One must ensure that both body and mind are completely relinquished, sharing one’s own flesh, bones, and blood with all sentient beings.
One must never take the Tathāgata’s teachings of provisional meaning and twist them into one’s own interpretations to mislead beginners.
The Buddha’s seal is that one who attains true samādhi as I have described it may be said to speak the words of the Buddha; if one speaks otherwise than this, it is the speech of Pāpīyān.
This definitive determination—that one must not steal—is how one attains true samādhi. One whose speech is like a leaking cup is not a vessel for the Dharma. [End of] Chapter on Robes.
Not keeping anything beyond what is required for the alms bowl is the cessation of greed; distributing the remainder as alms to hungry sentient beings is the cessation of stinginess;
joining the palms in salutation to the assembly is the absence of pride; treating those who strike or revile one the same as those who praise is the absence of the mark of selfhood;
relinquishing both body and mind is the absence of attachment; and sharing one’s own flesh, bones, and blood with sentient beings is the relinquishment of head and eyes.
The marrow and brain are like discarded mucus and spittle; if a bhikṣu’s conduct is such as this, how could he use a covetous mind and crooked means to provide for himself?
Regarding teachings of provisional meaning, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* permits keeping one of each of a hundred items but forbids possessing more than two;
furthermore, it explains that offerings made to the body and so forth may not be diverted for one's own use.
This means that one who, being unable to practice the deeds of the Mahāyāna, instead deviously draws upon the practices of the provisional vehicles and takes them to be the fruit;

yet whose mind is pure in every thought-moment and who harbors not a single aspiration for gain or profit—such a person is permitted by the Buddha to surely attain true samādhi. Therefore, Huitang said: "Those who study today have not yet been liberated."
Where do birth and death reside? They reside in the fact that the thieving mind has not yet died.

Ānanda, although the beings of the six realms within this world may have perfected the absence of the three acts of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct in body and mind, if they engage in great falsehood, their *samādhi* will not attain purity; they will become demons of craving and views and lose [their way].

The so-called "seeds of coming" refers to those who claim what they have not attained as attained, or say they have realized what they have not realized; or those who seek worldly preeminence and supremacy, saying to others:
"I have now already attained the fruit of a *srotāpanna*, the fruit of a *sakṛdāgāmin*, the fruit of an *anāgāmin*, the path of an *arhat*, or the vehicle of a *pratyekabuddha*;
I am a Bodhisattva of the ten stages or of the stages prior to them," and thus seek worship and repentance from others.
To covet offerings is the first *icchantika* trait that extinguishes the seeds of Buddhahood. It is as if a person were to cut down a *tāla* tree with a sword;

the Buddha has declared that such a person’s roots of goodness are forever destroyed, they shall have no further insight or vision, they will sink into the ocean of the three sufferings, and they shall not achieve samādhi.
After my parinirvāṇa, I command all the bodhisattvas and the Arhats to manifest transformation bodies within that age of the final dharma to appear therein.
They manifest in various forms to deliver those wandering in saṃsāra— appearing as śramaṇas, white-robed laypeople, householders,
kings, officials, boys, girls, and even as courtesans, widows, thieves, butchers, or merchants. Engaging in their same activities,
they praise the Buddha Vehicle, causing their bodies and minds to enter samādhi, yet they never say of themselves, "I am a true bodhisattva."

A true Arhat who discloses the Buddha’s secret cause and speaks lightly of those who have not yet studied—except when, at the end of life, there remains something to be entrusted in the *skandhas*—how could such a person not delude the masses and commit a great falsehood?
You teach the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi*, and thereafter you further eliminate all great falsehoods;
this is called the Fourth Determination of the Tathāgata and the World-Honored Buddhas of the past.
This is a pure and clear instruction;

it clarifies the precept against false speech. If one’s words and actions do not correspond, it is a source of shame even for a gentleman, let alone for a disciple of the Buddha who, out of greed for offerings, points to emptiness while speaking of existence—how could such a person ever achieve samādhi?
My extinction is a profound statement to show that the Tathāgata does not speak falsely.

I have commanded all bodhisattvas and arhats to deliver sentient beings by harmonizing with them, blending with the dust of the world, and employing the "sameness of purpose" (sabhāgatā) to gather them;
by extolling the Buddha-vehicle to entice them into the Way, I do not even permit them to claim for themselves that they are true bodhisattvas or true arhats, lest they leak the secret mechanism.

For those who are beginners, one should only briefly reveal signs at the time of death to inspire in them respectful faith, as the Master Zhizhe of the Lotus Sutra said when he was about to pass away:

"I have come from immeasurable kalpas ago to accomplish the transformation of the Jetavana Land through my emanations; now I am returning south. Had I remained here, I would not have leaked [this secret]."
If he does not cease his leaking words and yet persists in them, he is clearly a person of evil intent who seeks only respect and material gain.
Therefore, Ānanda, if you do not cut off his great false speech, it will be like carving a human figure in the hope that it becomes sandalwood.

To seek fragrance [from such conduct] is impossible; it cannot be. I teach my bhikṣus that at the altar of the direct mind, even amidst all actions within the four modes of deportment, there must be no pretense whatsoever.
How could one falsely claim to have attained the Dharma of the Superior Man?

It is like a destitute person who falsely calls himself an emperor, only to bring about his own execution—how much more so for a King of Dharma to thus falsely usurp [the title]? This is because the ground was not established with directness.
If one seeks the Buddha’s Bodhi through circuitous means, it is like a person trying to bite their own navel—who can possibly achieve success?
If bhikṣus have minds as straight as bowstrings, being entirely truthful and entering samādhi, they will forever be free from demonic interference;
I certify that such people shall achieve the unsurpassed awakening of a bodhisattva. What I have spoken is called the Buddha’s teaching; anything other than this is not my teaching.
This was spoken by Pāpīyas.
From here below, it is determined that only by not speaking falsely can one attain perfect enlightenment. Those who merely seek the fragrance [of the teachings] should listen to his words;
yet if one examines his conduct, it is found to be non-existent—this is what is meant by "the nature of a sheep with the skin of a tiger. Thus says the Sūtra.
It is said that the straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment because it is free from falsehood.
Therefore, I instruct the bhikṣus that every action and every stillness must rely on a straightforward mind and straightforward speech, not permitting even a single thought of falsehood.

How can one falsely claim to have attained the dharmas of a superior person? This is no different from a commoner falsely styling himself an emperor; he only brings about his own ruin and loss of life.

Moreover, if even a minor king of a small nation will not tolerate the unauthorized usurpation of his honorable title, how much less could one wish to usurp the name and position of the Exalted and Majestic One, the supreme honor of the world-transcending?

To seek such a fruit through such causes is like a person trying to bite their own navel—it is certainly impossible. If you truly desire to achieve Bodhi, you must employ a direct mind and direct conduct.
Speech is the foundation; thus it is said that the study of the Way begins with refraining from false speech.
*The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Realization through Cultivation and Verification, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas*, Fascicle Six.
The Shurangama Sutra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathagata’s Myriad Practices Cultivated and Realized by All Bodhisattvas,
Volume Seven, Harmonizing the Tracks.
Composed by Shi Tongrun of Er-Leng-an, Ming Dynasty.
"Ānanda, regarding your question on the gathering of the mind, I shall first explain the sublime gateway for training in the entry into *samādhi*.

Those who seek the path of a Bodhisattva must first maintain these four kinds of restraint as clearly as ice and frost; [with such purity], the branches and leaves of all [unwholesome states] cannot arise.
If one is unable to maintain them, the three actions of the mind and the four of the body will inevitably have no cause for arising. Ānanda, if these four matters are not lost,"
"If the mind does not even take as its object form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or any demonic activities, how could they arise?
This is the answer to the question. "The wondrous gate" refers to the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty; the four [faculties] are the root, while the others are the branches and leaves.
The "three of the mind" refer to greed, hatred, and delusion; the "four of the mouth" refer to false speech, frivolous speech, and double-tongued speech.
"Not omitting even harsh speech" means that one keeps it constantly in mind and does not transgress even the slightest detail.
All demonic activities arise conditioned by craving for the six sense objects; since these are no longer conditioned now, such activities are naturally severed.
Thus, when the root of the precepts is pure, subsequent karma can be transcended and concentration and wisdom can be brought forth.

If there are those whose past habitual tendencies cannot be extinguished or eliminated, you should instruct such people to single-mindedly recite this unsurpassed divine mantra of mine, the Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa-Vijaya-Mahā-sātranta-praṃtara.

This is the Tathāgata’s Unseen Summit Mark (*anavalokitamūrdha-lakṣaṇa*), the unconditioned mind-Buddha, which radiates brilliance from the crown of the head and dwells upon a precious lotus flower; it is the heart-mantra spoken by him. Furthermore, regarding your own past lives...
Mātanga and I have shared causes and conditions through kalpas, and the habitual tendencies of our mutual affection are not limited to a single lifetime or a single kalpa.
When I proclaimed this, his heart of desire was forever liberated and he became an Arhat.

He was but a courtesan who had no intention to practice, yet through the secret assistance of my spiritual power, he swiftly realized the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). How much more so for you, the Śrāvakas gathered here, who seek the Supreme Vehicle!
To attain Buddhahood with certainty is like tossing dust in a favorable wind; what difficulty or danger could there be?
This is intended to enable the practitioner of mantras to eliminate past karma. Wēn-líng says: "Present karma is easy to control, as one may personally contravene it;

however, habitual tendencies from the past are difficult to eradicate and must rely upon spiritual power. Now, if a practitioner is inclined toward the correct yet remains stubbornly attached to the heterodox, [how can they succeed?]
That which is pure yet partially defiled, appearing as if driven by an invisible force from which one cannot refrain, is all summoned by past habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
These "past habitual tendencies" are the seeds of past delusions and karma. *Mahāsattva-dharaṇī*—translated as "Great White Parasol Canopy"—is the *tathāgatagarbha*, the measure of the mind;
it is called "Great" because its scope encompasses the entirety of the *dharmadhātu*.
The essence, being utterly free from delusive defilement, is called "white"; its function, covering all things, is called a "parasol. Regarding the mark of the invisible crown:

in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the spiritual benefactor of the ninth stage served as the Buddha’s wet nurse; when she first held him in her arms, she gazed intently at him but could not see the top of his head.
This demonstrates that the Dharma of the crown cannot be seen by means of seeing. One whose heart of craving is eternally liberated is like a drum smeared with poison—merely to touch it [is fatal].
It is like the *āda* medicine, which cures immediately upon ingestion; thus, those who seek the Supreme Vehicle differ from those who practice without a focused mind.
The phrase "dust raised with the wind" means that it is easy to accomplish.
If there are those in the final age who wish to sit at the site of enlightenment, they must first maintain the pure prohibitions of a bhikṣu;
they must select a foremost śramaṇa whose precepts are pure to serve as their teacher. If they do not encounter a truly pure monk, their observance of the precepts will certainly not be perfected.
Once the precepts have been perfected, they should don new, clean robes, burn incense, and dwell in seclusion.
Recite this divine mantra spoken by the Heart-Buddha one hundred and eight times;

thereafter, establish the boundary and set up the ritual site (*maṇḍala*), seeking that the Unsurpassed Tathāgatas currently dwelling in the lands of the ten directions will emit the light of great compassion and pour it upon your crown.
Ānanda, in this way, when the minds of pure bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, or lay donors (*dānapati*) in the final age are extinguished...
If one who is greedy for sensual desire maintains the pure precepts of the Buddha, makes bodhisattva vows within the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), enters and exits for bathing,
and practices the path throughout the six periods of the day and night without sleeping for twenty-one days, I shall manifest my own body before that person,
stroke their head to comfort them, and cause them to attain awakening.

This clarifies that those who wish to sit at the site of enlightenment must first select a teacher. A teacher is a person’s mold and pattern, the source from which both the heterodox and the orthodox emerge.
If the mold does not mold and the pattern does not pattern, it is rare for one to achieve success; therefore, one must select a teacher.
Once the precepts have been established, one puts on new, pure robes so that the internal and external are as one, and body and mind are unified.
"Jieya, you seek for the Tathāgata to emit light and bestow empowerment; this is to seek concentration by means of precepts. [The Master] asked:

"Ānanda saw a sign and gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, yet the World-Honored One rebuked him as being deluded. For what reason must a practitioner necessarily seek the Tathāgata’s empowerment? [The Master] replied:
"Because Ānanda saw the Tathāgata with his eyes but was unwilling to advance in cultivation, [the Buddha] caused him to turn back and contemplate. Now, [you] practice..."
Since people have thus turned their gaze inward, they desire to personally seek the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*). The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states:

"If within a thousand li there is no preceptor to bestow the precepts, one should receive them through a self-vow before the Buddha. First repent of the seven heinous offenses, then seek the dharma of the precepts;
only when one perceives auspicious signs does one know that the offenses are extinguished and the precepts are obtained. Otherwise, the precepts are not obtained. It is thus.

As for "sleeping," it refers to being so diligent and tireless— forgetting food out of zeal and forgetting sleep through one's vows— that one practices three times during the day and three times at night; thus,
the Buddhas come to one's dwelling and manifest their presence to stroke one’s head, thereby causing one to attain awakening, which means that wisdom arises from meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, having received the unsurpassed compassionate instruction of the Tathāgata, my mind has already been awakened.

I know for myself that I have cultivated and realized the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Now, as I establish a site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*) during the Dharma-ending age, how should I perform the ritual boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) in accordance with the pure regulations of the Buddha, the World-Honored One?"
This is the ritual procedure for requesting the consecration of the maṇḍala. "Compassionate instruction" refers to the four kinds of pure instructions.

"One who knows for oneself that the path of no-more-learning has been realized and accomplished" means that by progressing through this cultivation, one will certainly realize the state of no-more-learning.

"Establishing the site of practice" (the *maṇḍala*) refers back to the previous phrase regarding the establishment of the site of practice; if one wishes to establish the site of practice, how is it to be consecrated?
This realm is precisely in accord with the pure regulations of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

The Buddha told Ānanda: "If people of the final age wish to establish a site of the Way (*mārgamaṇḍala*), they should first procure a powerful white ox from the Snowy Mountains that feeds on the lush, fatty fragrant grasses of those mountains;
this ox drinks only the clear water of the Snowy Mountains, and its dung is fine."
One may take its dung and mix it with sandalwood to plaster the ground. If it is not from the Snowy Mountains, the cow’s dung is foul and unsuitable for smearing on the ground;

instead, one should dig five feet below the surface of level plains and take the yellow earth, mixing it with sandalwood, aloeswood (*agaru*), *suhaka*, frankincense (*olibanum*), saffron, *guggulu*, *sarja* resin, *candana* wood, *jintong* (*nagara*), and *gan-song* (*shikhandin*).
Together with *kakkola* incense, these ten kinds [of substances] were finely ground into powder, mixed with earth to form a paste, and used to smear the ground.
This first clarifies the ritual method for smearing the ground. The World-Honored One is the teacher of the three realms;
his movements serve as the path for the world, his words serve as the law for the world, and his conduct serves as the model for the world. Therefore, all who...
All that is done is for the sake of a single matter; what is spoken of is precisely practice, and what is practiced is precisely speech.

Therefore, when the World-Honored One, at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, desired to gather the manifested Buddhas from all directions, he necessarily transformed the pure land thrice;
this was no more than to make it luminous and pure both internally and externally, so as to inspire reverence and faith in the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas.
Because one respects this matter, it is said to be "adorned like a lotus in a pure pond.

Is it not the case that only after obtaining a superior location can one gather a community of noble ones? It is the same here: if one wishes to cultivate pure conduct, one must select pure companions;
if one wishes to accommodate pure companions, one must obtain a pure site; once a pure site is obtained, one must establish a mandala; and if one wishes to establish a mandala...
Every site must have its regulations; once these regulations are complete, they cause people to be awe-struck without severity and reverent without formality.
It is like entering a ancestral temple where one hears only the clear resonance of ritual and musical instruments; though one might wish not to be orderly or reverent, it is impossible.

Therefore, the regulations for the palaces and halls of a human king emulate the four images and five elements, while the regulations for the ritual altar of a sage-king emulate those of the human king.
Thus, because the four wisdoms and six perfections each function according to their own respective dharmas, the establishment of the ritual arena (*maṇḍala*) must necessarily follow fixed rules.
The "Path Arena" (*bodhimaṇḍa*) symbolizes the bodhicitta. The "Great Powerful White Ox of the Snowy Mountains" from the *Lotus Sūtra* symbolizes the Supreme Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Now, this [arena] symbolizes those of the highest capacity who enter directly and leapfrog over all stages, without establishing any gradations.
Furthermore, this implies that one who resolves to attain Bodhicitta must necessarily be a person of superior, transcendent capacity to be able to undertake this task.
Eating fragrant herbs signifies that this person’s entire being is imbued with the fragrance of the *pāramitās*.
Drinking the pure water of the Snowy Mountains signifies that this person does not consort with the myriad dharmas nor oppose the various sensory objects, but remains purely clear.

The state of the mind where all points are severed is one suchness. As for taking dung to smear the ground, this signifies that for such a person, not only is their refined purity the bodhicitta, but even laughter, jesting, anger, and abuse are all the wondrous bodhicitta.
Thus, those who reject [the mundane] are all fit to smear the ground. Yongjia said: "The fat and richness of the Snowy Mountains has no admixture; it yields pure ghee."
I always accept this: if it were not for the snow mountains, cow dung would be unfit for smearing upon the ground;

likewise, a mind that is neither born nor extinguished is certainly unfit to serve as a foundation. This is distinguished from what follows below to further reveal that those of superior faculties may also establish this foundation.
That is to say, if there were no individuals of the highest-of-the-high faculties, then [those mentioned here] would be considered individuals of superior faculties.

This may also be used to establish the foundation of this *maṇḍala*. Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) possess the highest of superior faculties (*mūrdha-mūrdha-indriya*), while Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) possess superior faculties.
The high ground is called the "original site" (*yuan*); the removal of the topsoil symbolizes the emptiness of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
The depth of five feet symbolizes that all five aggregates are empty. The yellow earth symbolizes those of deep faith.

Furthermore, as nothing bears things with such profound virtue as earth, one takes those of deep faith and sincere devotion as the foundation for entering the Way—what are called "superior persons who, upon hearing the Way, practice it with diligence.
Possessing this deep faith, one further blends the ten kinds of *pāramitā* incense to accomplish this site; thus, one should know that [if one desires...]
Those who take non-arising and non-extinction as the mind of the causal ground must possess the highest of superior faculties; only those of such supreme capacity will achieve accomplishment.
A square altar sixteen feet on each side is made with eight corners, and at its center is placed a lotus flower fashioned from gold, silver, copper, or wood.
Place a bowl in the center of the flowers; first fill the bowl with dew collected on the eighth day of the month. Within the water, place all available flower petals as appropriate.
Take eight round mirrors and position them in their respective directions surrounding the bowl of flowers.
This explains the ritual for binding the mandala, as well as the implements and procedures of the mandala site. A square or circle measuring sixteen feet constitutes the eight-cornered mandala;
this signifies that the two modes of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*) and sequential unfolding (*xingbu*) do not obstruct one another. The "center of the mandala" represents the central tree pillar.

Gold, silver, copper, and wood represent the stages of ground (*bhūmi*), direction, practice, and abiding. The lotus flower represents practice; it is said that [the ground] is established by means of the ground.
The tree planted at the center of this mandala represents the practice of the Dharma while dwelling, walking, sitting, or lying down.

Placing the alms bowl within the flowers signifies that the bowl is the vessel of appropriate measure, symbolizing the practice of acting according to the proper measure—staying when one should stay, walking when one should walk, facing toward when one should face toward, and remaining on the ground when one should remain on the ground. First, fill the bowl with...
The dew of the eighth month symbolizes the arising of practice from the flow of the True; that these practices accord with the True represents the primary practice (*samyak-caryā*).
Placing lotus petals within the water symbolizes the auxiliary practice (*upāya-caryā*). As for the round mirrors placed at each of the cardinal directions surrounding the flower bowl:
the round mirror symbolizes wisdom (*jñāna*), signifying that one proceeds according to the measure of reality through the practice of wisdom.

This is precisely the practice of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*). This wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena is the enumeration of the distinct phases of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.
Outside the mirror, sixteen lotus flowers and sixteen incense burners are established, with flowers interspersed as an array of adornments. The incense burners are [arranged] thus.
Burn pure aloeswood alone so that the fire is not visible;

the former represents real wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) and real practice, while this represents provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) and provisional practice. These consist of the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*) and the sixteen wisdoms.
Since Bodhisattvas also cultivate the Four Noble Truths and realize the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), this wisdom and practice regarding the emptiness of persons is itself emptiness.
The accumulation within the sense-faculties is the beginningless, empty habituation of arising. The incense burner burns pure aloeswood so that no one sees the fire;
this means burning the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body so that the fires of affliction do not manifest.

Take the milk of a white cow and place it in sixteen vessels; prepare milk pancakes, various sugar candies, oil cakes, milk porridge, *sugandhaka* (fragrant resin), honey, ginger, pure clarified butter, and pure honey.
Surrounding the lotus flower, arrange these sixteen items individually outside the flower to offer to the Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas.
At every mealtime, or if it is midnight, take half a *śoṇa* (half a pint) of honey.

Using three *liǎng* of clarified butter, set up a small fire hearth separately before the altar; take *dūrva* grass and boil it to produce scented water with which to bathe the charcoal, then ignite it until it blazes fiercely.
Cast this clarified butter and honey into the flaming hearth and burn them until the smoke has vanished, thereby making an offering to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
This explains the ritual for making offerings. First, regarding the stage of the Three Sages (Tri-bhadra), it clarifies that one makes an offering through the Dharma;
since the earth is smeared with the dregs of the cow, the essence and purest portion of the cow is used to make the offering to the Buddha.

"Milk, granulated sugar, and so forth" refers to blending the supreme flavor of *sarpis* (clarified butter) with various other flavors. Each subsequent section below clarifies the entry [into the stages].

This is the Dharma-offering of the Bodhisattva stages. The times of eating and midnight—specifically the two hours of the *mūhūrta* at sunrise and noon—are places where the divine and the numinous intersect.

Using honey and clarified butter alone symbolizes that each stage (*bhūmi*) possesses both the wisdom of uninterrupted continuity and the wisdom of liberation, whereby afflictions are severed and reality is realized.
The separate placement of a small brazier represents that which pertains to the eighth stage and above.
The realization of the awakened mind is like bathing those burning coals so that they blaze even more fiercely;
this signifies that from the first stage (*bhūmi*) through the eighth, one has burned the fuel of afflictions (*kleśa*) until it is reduced to charcoal,
which is then bathed with the fragrant water of the ten *pāramitās* to make the coals blaze intensely, representing the further increase of the fire of the Path arising from within death.

"To cast ghee and honey into the fire and burn them until the smoke is exhausted" means that one takes these two wisdoms and casts them into the awakened mind (bodhicitta), refining them with great vigor.
Not only are habitual tendencies incinerated and conditioned reflections caused to vanish, but even these two wisdoms, upon reaching this state, are likewise emptied and exhausted.
This is called the true Dharma-offering; thereafter, it is enjoyed by the Buddha. This is "birth."
"Extinction" refers to the moment when cessation has been attained and quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*) manifests before one.
One should cause banners and flowers to be hung everywhere on the four outer sides;
within the hall, images of all the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions should be installed, while images of Vairocana, Śākyamuni, and Maitreya should be displayed facing the front.
The great transformations of Akṣobhya, Amitābha, and Avalokiteśvara, along with Vajragarbha, are installed on the left and right;
Śakra, Brahmā, Ucchuṣma, and Lambodara, together with the Cāmuṇḍīs, Vighnāntaka, the Four Heavenly Kings, and Pināyaka,
are arranged at the sides of the entrance, placed to the left and right.
This clarifies the ritual for setting up the images. Wēn-líng says: "The four outer banners and flowers are the external adornments of the processional ranks.
Vairocana is the true Lord of the Tranquil Field; Śākyamuni is the true Lord of the Sahā world; Maitreya is the true Lord of the future;
Akṣobhya dwells in the East and Amitābha dwells in the West—the true Lords of Wisdom and Compassion. These are the various great transformations.
The manifested image of Avalokiteśvara is the true master who unites above and below;

Vajragarbha is the true master who constantly leads the vajra-protectors to guard those who recite mantras, subduing demons and severing obstacles; the hosts of Śakra and Brahmā on the left and right sides of the gate are the powerful external protectors.
In the Dharma-ending age, all practitioners rely upon these; if even one is lacking, [the practice] cannot be accomplished.
The accomplishment of Ucchuṣma Jvālāmukha Vajra, Kālarāja Blue-Faced Vajra, and Cundā Vajrī—these are alternative names for them.

Piṇḍola is the three-eyed one who holds a topknot; these are they. Piṇāka and Nāga are the two messengers, the Boar-Headed and the Elephant-Nosed, whose principal and retinue are fully manifested together within a single altar chamber, complete with both compassion and majesty.
It causes the mind to maintain a sense of awe, as if the deities were majestically present at one's side; how could one dare to indulge in a single thought of license?

Furthermore, take eight mirrors and suspend them facing the void, with their surfaces opposite those of the mirrors installed within the ritual altar, so that their forms and reflections interpenetrate one another in successive layers.

The eight mirrors suspended in space facing the eight mirrors within the mandala serve to ensure that the practitioner sees his own face at every location and at all times, so as not to fall into negligence;

furthermore, they are intended to make him realize the circular fusion, mutual entry, and mutual inclusion of all realms, preventing him from giving rise to thoughts of attachment or fixation. This concludes the ritual procedures for the mandala site.
During the first seven days, one should with utmost sincerity prostrate to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, the great Bodhisattvas, and those bearing the title of Arhat;

constantly reciting mantras throughout the six periods of the day and night, one should circumambulate the altar with a sincere mind and practice the Way, performing one hundred and eight recitations at each session.
During the second seven days, one should single-mindedly and exclusively maintain mindfulness, generating the Bodhisattva’s vow-mind without interruption, according to my Vinaya.
If one first makes a vow to maintain the Buddha’s *bentuo* (pāṭala) mantra single-mindedly throughout the twelve periods of the day during the third seven-day cycle,

then on the seventh day, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions will simultaneously appear at the place where mirrors reflect one another’s light; there, receiving the Buddhas’ touch upon the crown of the head,
one will be able to cultivate *samādhi* within the site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*), causing the body and mind of those practicing and studying in this degenerate age to become luminous and pure.
It is like lapis lazuli.

This clarifies that benefits are gained by reciting the mantra within the illuminated altar. During the first seven days, though one recites the mantra six times daily, it is not yet pure and consistent.

During the second seven days, although one focuses the mind and makes vows, it is still not yet pure and consistent. However, during the third seven days, if one maintains the mantra with single-minded concentration, then...
If the mind never leaves this altar and every thought never leaves this mantra, then the practice of holding the mantra will become pure and single-minded.

Yepan-che-muntā yepan-kaloradare yepan-kabani yepan-adi-mucita-kāśi-maśana-pāśini yepan-yankicita-sattva-paryāya-mama-imtu-tana-mama-ksa-tustha-cita-amatari-cita.
Uṣahara-gavahara-ruḍihara-vasahara-maṣahara-jātuhara-vibhitahara-bāṣpahari-kandahara-puṣpahara-phalahara-vyasanahara-pampacita-stambhita.
To the yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, rākṣasas, pretas, piśācas, bhūtas, kumbhāṇḍas, audumbaras, cetas, and apasmārakas.
Samarāgraha-cakṣu-ghaṭini-graha, abhyudita-graha, jāmika-graha, śakuni-graha,
mūdranandika-graha, ālamba-graha, krandupani-graha, śavara-inki.
Hike cūḍe yakka taḷe yakka caṇḍa-ṭṭakkā ṇiddhi-savara bhisama-savara bodhika bindika śrī-samitaka sani-pantika sabba-savara siri-ghide mada-vi-dāru-citta ākiṃ.
Rukṣma-kha rukṣma-kali-turukṣma-garabha-garaṇa-kaṇa-śūlaṃ danta-śūlaṃ kṛtyā-śūlaṃ mama-śūlaṃ bali-svabhāva-śūlaṃ vṛṣṭi-śūlaṃ udāra-śūlaṃ kaci-śūlaṃ vaśitī-śūlam oṃ.

Sana-kara-viṣa-yuga-agni-udaka-mara-vijñāna-tara-ākāra-mṛdu-tad-lambuka-dṛṣṭi-svika-sarva-nakula-sīghra-peta-gare-yakṣa-trāsa-mara-śi.

*Kārumita*. *Tadyathā*: Oṃ anale viśati vīra-vajra-dhare bhandabhandani vajrabhāṇi phaṭ huṃ dhuḥ vuṃ phaṭ svāhā. "Dhāraṇī" means a prayer of aspiration.
By means of this dhāraṇī, the Buddha blesses sentient beings, causing them to perfect the Way and be endowed with all virtues.
Yet they do not realize that it is like the *gonglo* (sire-wasp) which incants the *mingling* (caterpillar), saying, "Be like me! Be like me! After a long time, the caterpillar becomes its likeness.
If one speaks in terms of explicit meaning (*yì*), one relies on words to produce understanding; if one speaks in terms of implicit meaning (*mì*), one forgets words and severs understanding.

Although these two approaches differ, they are in fact mutually dependent and complementary. Thus, in the *Mahābrahmādeva-pṛcchā-sūtra*, it is asked: [The text continues with the dialogue from the *Mahābrahmādeva-pṛcchā-sūtra*.]
"Avalokiteśvara, please explain the form and characteristics of this dharani. The Bodhisattva replied: "It is the mind of great compassion;
it is the mind of equanimity; it is the unconditioned mind; it is the undefiled mind; it is the mind of the contemplation of emptiness; it is the mind of reverence;
it is the humble mind; it is the undisturbed mind; it is the mind free from views and attachments; it is the mind free from..."
One should know that the aforementioned bodhicitta—such states of mind as these—are the very characteristics of bodhicitta.
The *Zhengmai* (Orthodox Pulse) states: "Esoteric mantras are not merely Sanskrit; they are the secret language of all sages and worthies.
For while this [Chinese] land does not understand Sanskrit, it is that which is universally understood in India. As for...
"Secret mantras (vidyā-mantra) are not only unknown to ordinary people in India, but even sages of lower ranks do not comprehend the mantras of higher ranks;
therefore, they are called 'mysterious' (mi). Gu-shan said: "As a rule, the divine mantras in various sutras are not translated.
Since ancient times, masters have held many differing views, but Tiantai synthesized them into no more than the four *siddhārtha* (purposes). One says: as for 'mantra'..."

First, it is said that "dharani" refers to the name of a king of ghosts; when his name is proclaimed, the lords of his tribes revere him and dare not commit transgressions—this is the meaning within this world.

Second, it is said that "dharani" is like a secret code within an army; when the call is answered in accordance with the code, no questioning or interrogation occurs, whereas those who do not respond in accordance with it are immediately seized and punished—this is the meaning for human beings. Third, it is said that "dharani" means silent secrecy.
To prevent evil, others who lack such awareness are like lowly men who have fled to a foreign land and falsely claim, "The King’s own hand has given me his daughter as a wife.
Yet she is prone to anger and difficult to serve. A wise man from that country comes and the master tells him of this;
the man says, "When she becomes angry, you should say: 'I am without kin and have wandered to another land.'"
"Deceiving all people, coarse food is one's constant sustenance; why trouble yourself again with anger? When this verse was spoken, his silence marked the cessation of his anger;
this is the meaning of "counteracting. Fourth, regarding "mantras": these are the secret words of the Buddhas known only by the noble ones (*ārya*).
It is like a king requesting "śatapuṭa"—a single name that possesses four actual referents: namely, salt, water, a vessel, and a horse.
None among the subordinates understood it, yet only the wise minister could interpret it; the mantra is likewise thus: it is but a single dharma-word that universally possesses all powers.
When illness is cured, transgressions are eliminated, wholesome roots are produced, and one accords with the Way—this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Because it possesses these four meanings, its original sound is preserved. Among the five reasons for not translating, it is not translated because it is "secret" (*guhyaka*).
Ānanda, this secret gāthā of subtle and wondrous phrases, the *Sitatapatrā-prabhāsa*, which is the mass of light from the Buddha’s crown, gives birth to all Buddhas of the ten directions.
By means of this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
by means of this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions subdue all māras and restrain all externalists.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions mount this mantra-heart upon a precious lotus flower and respond to lands as numerous as motes of dust;
the Tathāgatas of the ten directions contain this mantra-heart within them and turn the Great Dharma Wheel in lands as numerous as motes of dust;

the Tathāgatas of the ten directions uphold this mantra-heart and are able to bestow the consecration of their heads in the ten directions; even when their own fruition is not yet complete, they likewise receive the Buddha’s consecration throughout the ten directions.

It is recorded that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, relying upon this mantra-heart, are able to rescue and deliver sentient beings from the various sufferings throughout the ten directions—namely, the sufferings of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals;
the suffering of being blind, deaf, or mute; the suffering of encountering those one hates; the suffering of being separated from those one loves; the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks;

and the intense burning of the five aggregates—including all manner of calamities, both great and small, such as the perils of bandits, the perils of armies, the perils of kings, and the perils of imprisonment. All these are simultaneously liberated.
Difficulties caused by wind, fire, water, hunger, thirst, and poverty shall dissolve at the mere thought [of this].
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, following this mantra-heart, are able to serve spiritual friends throughout the four modes of conduct in the ten directions, making offerings as they wish;

among the assemblies of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they are promoted as great Dharma-princes. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, practicing this mantra-heart, are able, in the ten...
It gathers and embraces the direct causes so that all followers of the Lesser Vehicle, upon hearing the Secret Treasury, shall not give rise to fear or terror.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions recite this mantra-heart to achieve unsurpassed enlightenment, sit beneath the Bodhi tree, and enter Great Nirvāṇa.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions transmit this mantra-heart after their parinirvāṇa to entrust them with the affairs of the Buddha-dharma, ensuring its ultimate maintenance and the purification of the precepts.

The Vinaya is entirely purified. If I were to speak this Buddha-Usnīṣa-Raśmi-Saṃcaya Pañcara mantra from dawn until dusk, with its sounds continuous and its syllables never overlapping, even after kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one could never reach the end.
Furthermore, I declare that the name of this mantra is the "Tathāgata’s Usnīṣa. You who are still in training and have not yet exhausted saṃsāra, should now resolve your minds [to seek awakening].
It is truly impossible for one who has attained arhatship but does not maintain this mantra to enter the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) with a body and mind free from all demonic activities;
this demonstrates the power of the mantra. As for what is called the "mantra-heart," it is the Great White Parasol, vast and untainted.
The Tathāgata-garbha mind, which pervades the entire Dharma-realm, is that which is formed by transforming the mind of bondage (*bandhana-citta*).
When the clarity is adhered to and vision or hearing arises, this is transforming the mantra-mind (*mantra-citta*) into the mind of bondage.

When one follows the current of reversal until quiescence manifests before one, this is transforming the mind of bondage into the mantra-mind. Thus, the mantra-mind and the mind of bondage are one and the same thing.
These two [deities] also nourish all Tathāgatas through this Dharma and give rise to all qualities of nature;
they clothe all phenomena, and thus, out of necessity, it is named the "Great White Parasol.

Because this Dharma is free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of written letters, and free from the characteristics of mental objects, it is, out of necessity, named [the Great White Parasol].
Regarding the statement that "the mantra gives birth to all Buddhas": it is because this mantra-heart (*dhāraṇī-citta*) is the true samādhi of the Mother of the Buddhas;

thus, those who attain perfect enlightenment by means of this mantra-heart do so because this mantra-heart is the cause of perfect enlightenment—only after relying upon it as the cause does one subsequently obtain the fruit.
It is also called the "esoteric cause. By upholding this mantra-heart, one subdues Māras.
"Controlling the external" means that this mantra-heart is like a vajra-sword or a Vairocana-seal;

when held, the scales of authority are in one's hand, and the power to kill or give life rests with oneself. Thus, all demons and heterodox paths are subject to one's command—this is what is meant by "grasping the Great Elephant, and the whole world follows.
To "ride upon this mantra-heart and respond to lands as numerous as motes of dust" means that "riding" refers to transporting [beings].

The meaning is as follows: because the Great White Ox Cart carries all without exception, the *Awakening of Faith* states that it is "that which all Buddhas have fundamentally ridden," and "all Bodhisattvas ride this Dharma to reach the stage of the Tathāgata.
Because they have attained this path for themselves and can further employ this path to benefit sentient beings, they are able to respond to lands as numerous as motes of dust.
"Containing this dharani-heart and turning the Great Dharma Wheel": "containing" (han) means to harbor or store. A mountain shines because it harbors jade;
a river is lovely because it contains pearls. If one lacks the root of virtue within, how could one discourse upon it without?

Therefore, one must contain this [dharani] before being able to turn the wheel. "Holding this dharani-heart and receiving the empowerment of the hand placed upon the head": "holding" (chi) means to grasp.
Because Buddha after Buddha transmits it hand-to-hand and patriarch after patriarch passes it on, there is only this one thing and no other;
therefore, by relying on this mantra-heart to rescue all from suffering—"rely" meaning to depend upon—this mantra-heart is like a wish-fulfilling jewel, capable of anything:
those in hell obtain it and find it empty, hungry ghosts obtain it and are satiated, and animals... [are satisfied].
Those born blind obtain it and are freed from blindness; the deaf obtain it and become hearing; the mute obtain it and are able to speak;
those who harbor resentment obtain it and find joy; those separated from loved ones obtain it and achieve reunion.

Because it is not obtained from without, there is no suffering of unfulfilled longing; because the aggregates dissolve and enter into clarity, there is no suffering of the blazing of the five aggregates.
Because it is neither extinguished nor born, there are no calamitous thieves and robbers; because nothing can plunder it, there is no danger from bandits;
because weapons cannot wound it, there is no danger from military conflict; because the laws of kings cannot bind it, there is no danger from sovereign authority;
because prisons cannot confine it, there is no danger from incarceration; and because wind cannot sweep it away, fire cannot burn it, and water cannot drown it, there is no danger from wind.

When one encounters the hardships of water or fire, hunger, or thirst, obtaining this [mantra] satisfies the hunger and quenches the thirst; when one is impoverished, obtaining it brings wealth and abundance.

Thus, there is nothing that does not accord with one's heart. To "follow this mantra-heart" means to comply with it without opposition, which is precisely to comply with pure awakening (*viśuddha-bodhi*).
Because one complies with pure awakening, one is able to serve spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) throughout the ten directions with the four types of offerings.

Making offerings with no lack of sincerity while practicing this mantra-heart means bestowing it upon material things and applying it to daily life, so as to cause people’s hearts to be joyful and to submit with true faith.
Thus, all those who in past kalpas had an affinity or a causal connection with this mantra shall now receive its guidance and protection; Ānanda and Dēṅgā are examples of such individuals.
Because this mantra has a karmic affinity from past lives, upon hearing it once, one does not give rise to fear; thus, the mind of attachment is forever liberated.

If those of inferior faculties and weak capacities lack the conditions for this mantra, there are none who, upon hearing it, do not experience fear—how much less could they achieve permanent liberation?
By reciting this *dhāraṇī*-heart, one attains perfect enlightenment, realizes *bodhi*, and enters *nirvāṇa*.

This refers to constantly turning this mantra without ever interrupting it. To transmit the heart of this mantra means that with this mind one transmits mind-to-mind, like lamp lighting lamp in continuous succession. It is what is meant by: "I entrust the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to you;
you should receive and uphold it so that it does not become severed. Therefore, it is said: "He entrusted the affairs of the Buddha-dharma to him."
Ultimate retention also proceeds from this, and the purification of the precepts likewise proceeds from this.

That which can never be exhausted is described in the Great Sūtra: "Even if Mount Sumeru were used as a brush and the great ocean as ink, one could not write down even a single chapter within a single gate of the Universal Eye, nor a single phrase within a single chapter, nor a single meaning within a single phrase."
This refers to the "Single-Syllable Dharma-Gate," which could not be fully recorded even with ink as vast as the ocean;

for while its verbal explanation cannot be exhausted, its written transcription likewise cannot be exhausted. It is also called the "Crown of the Tathāgata" because this mantra-heart is identical in essence to what is described in the sūtra as the "Great Buddha-Crown," though their names differ. [The passage beginning with] "You all... below exhorts one to uphold it.
Because one has not yet emerged from the *pariccheda* (segmented existence) prior to attaining the fruit, it is said that one has not yet exhausted saṃsāra.

If saṃsāra is not exhausted, one will certainly be unable to distance oneself from demonic affairs if one does not maintain this dhāraṇī. The *Jie lun* (Combined Treatise) states: "A dhāraṇī is the locus of inconceivable power;
it is not something accessible to intellectual knowledge (*jñāna*) nor can its principles be fully fathomed. It is like using tortoise shells or pottery shards for divination in the world."
Because it is devoid of principle, it possesses spiritual efficacy; because it is devoid of mind, it possesses verification.
If even such small things are thus, how much more so the great?
Ānanda, if in all worlds, according to whatever land and according to the beings born in that land, there is birch bark—
If one writes this mantra on palm leaves or plain white cotton cloth and stores it in a fragrant pouch,
or if a person whose mind is clouded and unable to recite or remember it wears it upon their body or inscribes it within their home, one should know that for as long as they live,
no poisons whatsoever shall be able to harm them.
This statement concerns the merit of writing down the mantra and wearing it. White cotton cloth (*pata*) is a precious item in India, possessing immeasurable value;
no poisons can harm one who wears this. With the mind focused on this mantra, it is like the *āgada* medicine: when any poison touches it, there is none that is not neutralized.
"Ānanda, I shall now further explain for you this mantra, which protects and saves the world, brings about great fearlessness, and accomplishes the supramundane wisdom of all beings.
This serves as a general indication of two meanings to manifest the divine efficacy of the mantra; that is, it grants salvation to the world and attains peace and security."

The intent of attaining eternal abiding in the supramundane is identical to that [of the former], being called the "perfectly interfused, pure, and precious awakening" there, and the "mantra-heart" here;
these are truly not two different dharmas.
Therefore, if after my parinirvāṇa, sentient beings in the final age are able to recite it themselves or teach others to recite it, you should know that such [persons]...
Sentient beings who maintain this recitation cannot be burned by fire nor drowned by water; they cannot be harmed by great or small poisons.
Thus, even all evil spells of devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, *piśācas*, and *mārās* cannot take hold of them.
Their minds attain right concentration (*samādhi*), and all curses, sorcery, and toxic drugs—whether of gold, silver, plants, wood, insects, or snakes—cannot affect them.
The poisonous vapors of the myriad things that enter this person’s mouth become the taste of nectar;
all malevolent stars, as well as ghosts and spirits with cruel hearts and venomous intent, cannot give rise to evil thoughts toward such a person.
Pināyaka and all the evil kings of ghosts, along with their retinues, shall all receive profound kindness and constantly provide protection.
This commentary explains how one rescues and protects the world, attaining great fearlessness.

It means that if one obtains this *dhāraṇī*-heart, then cognition and vision are withdrawn and subdued, and hearing and sight are withdrawn and subdued; even upon entering the realms of various ghosts, the ghosts cannot harm them.

"The mind attains right reception" (*samyak-samādhi*) means that because it does not receive any [defiled] sensations, it is called "right reception. Because it receives none of the various evils, all [evil] hosts... [are overcome].
No evil can move them at all. When all manner of poisons enter the mouths of those who have attained this *dhāraṇī*-heart, they become the taste of nectar (*amṛta*).

This means that by obtaining this *dhāraṇī*-heart, one can churn the long rivers into butter and curd, transform the great earth into gold, and like hot water dissolving ice, cause it to be transformed into unsurpassed awakening (*anuttara-saṃbodhi*) in accordance with one's thought; thus, even when there are various poisons, they not only... [cannot harm].
It is capable of subduing and transforming even the most virulent poisons into the supreme flavor of nectar (*amṛta*). No person afflicted by poison can give rise to malice;

for upon beholding his virtuous countenance, their intentions dissolve, and by gazing upon the breeze of his compassion, their minds are transformed. Thus, the various malevolent spirits and ghosts constantly provide protection;

not only do they refrain from causing harm, but they instead come to offer guardianship, and far from inflicting calamity, they— [...do not... (The text implies a continuation of this protective effect).
For the sake of auspiciousness, one should know that good and bad fortune, calamity and blessing, all reside within oneself. Ānanda,

you should know that this mantra is always accompanied by eighty-four thousand nayutas of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* *koṭis* of the family of Vajragarbharāja Bodhisattvas, each of whom has a retinue of various vajra-beings.

If one attends upon [this teaching] day and night, and should there be sentient beings who, even with a distracted mind or a mind not in samādhi, remember or recite this Vajra King, these Vajra Bodhisattvas—the kings of the treasury—will constantly follow them. How much more so for those who possess the resolute bodhicitta!

These Vajra Bodhisattvas, the essence of the treasury of kings, will swiftly and secretly manifest their numinous consciousness within that person; such a person shall, at that very moment, [attain realization].
The mind is able to remember eighty-four thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* eons and know them exhaustively, attaining freedom from doubt.

This explains how sentient beings attain supramundane wisdom. O Vajra Attendant, because this mantra is the adamantine jewel-like awakening (*vajra-ratna-bodhi*), like-minded sounds respond to one another and those of the same nature seek each other out; yet, with a distracted mind—
That which is maintained also constantly follows [the practitioner], for it is the dwelling place of playful laughter and the locus of the mantra-heart.
Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says: "If a person with a distracted mind enters a stupa or temple and once utters 'Namo Buddha,' they have all already attained the path of Buddhahood.
It is a place of darkness and obscurity; furthermore, that which is called the "resolute bodhicitta" is not merely...
They merely follow along, yet they are further able to bestow their supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) within the profound darkness,
swiftly causing the divine consciousness to unfold and attain awakening; furthermore, they achieve freedom from doubt, for with adamantine wisdom (*vajra-prajñā*),
they can sever the doubts of others and lead them to the ground beyond doubt.
From the first kalpa until their final birth, they will never again be born among yakṣas, rākṣasas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas,
kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, and other such beings, nor among hungry ghosts— whether with form or without form,
with perception or without perception— in any such evil states.
This clarifies that one does not fall into the evil realms because this mantra-heart is a pure and white dharma and is the most supreme goodness.
"The first kalpa" refers to the time when one first generates the bodhicitta; "the final body" refers to the time of attaining Buddhahood at the end.
During the intermediate period of cultivation, there are forever no signs of crookedness or deviation—such as those of yakṣas and the like, which are all characterized by crookedness.
Furthermore, if these sons of good family read, recite, copy, transcribe, wear, or preserve it, and make various offerings to it,
they will not be born into poverty, lowliness, or unpleasant states throughout kalpa after kalpa.
This clarifies that one will not be born into a lowly station, because this mantra-heart is a most supreme and noble dharma;

thus, those who recite, chant, copy, or transcribe it are all like a crown prince dwelling in the womb, nobly surpassing the common ministers. To read according to the original text is called "reading" (du);
to recite from memory without the original is called "chanting" (song); to transcribe a diagram or seal is called "copying" (xie); to wear it secretly upon the person is called "concealing" (zang).
Even if these sentient beings themselves do not perform meritorious deeds, all the merits of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions shall be bestowed upon this person.
By virtue of this, for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—incalculable, unspeakable, and beyond description—they shall always be born in the same place as the Buddhas;
their immeasurable merits will mutually perfume one another like a cluster of *akṣa* seeds.
By practicing this without ever allowing for distraction, one is able to cause those who have violated the precepts to purify their roots of discipline;
those who have not yet attained the precepts to attain them; those who lack diligence to attain diligence; those who lack wisdom to attain wisdom;
and those who are impure to swiftly attain purity. Even those who do not observe the fast and precepts will naturally come to observe them.

This clarifies the merits obtained in the present life. The Tathāgatas bestow all their merits upon this person because, through this *dhāraṇī*-heart, the ten thousand practices are fully perfected, and all the secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous [realms] of all Tathāgatas manifest therein.
Thus, it is said that "all Buddhas are born in one place," meaning that their vital essence (*prāṇa-bhāga*) is joined and their minds are perfectly merged with those of the Buddhas.

Because the mind is not separate from the Buddha and the Buddha is not separate from the mind, the accumulation of evil is metaphorically likened to the simultaneous cultivation of precepts, concentration, and wisdom;
for that which is cultivated by the practitioner is precisely what is realized by the Buddhas, thus forming a single, unified whole.

For one who has broken the precepts, the root of the precepts is purified—just as a single grain of elixir can transform iron into gold. This applies even to those who have not yet attained the precepts.
Those who have attained the precepts possess the faculty of morality; those who have not yet advanced but are about to advance possess the faculty of vigor;
those who lack wisdom but are about to attain it possess the faculty of wisdom; and those who are impure but seek purity possess the faculty of concentration.
This is because all obstacles are themselves ultimate enlightenment; thus, there is nothing that is not accomplished and nothing that does not accord with one's intent.
Ānanda, when these good men and women uphold this mantra, even if they have violated the prohibitive precepts prior to receiving them, all offenses of breaking the precepts—
regardless of whether they are light or heavy— are simultaneously extinguished. Even if they have consumed alcohol, eaten the five pungent roots,
or engaged in various kinds of impurities, all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, celestial immortals, spirits, and deities will no longer hold it against them.
Even if one is clothed in impure, tattered, and worn-out garments, and whether walking or standing, one is entirely equal to those who are pure;

even if one does not construct an altar, enter a *maṇḍala*, or practice the Way, yet recites and maintains this *dhāraṇī*, it is no different from the merit of entering an altar and practicing the Way.
Even if one has committed the five heinous crimes of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) or [committed offenses against] bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs...
Having recited this mantra for the four *pārājika* offenses and the eight *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses of the bhikṣuṇīs, such heavy karma as this will be completely extinguished—
just as a fierce wind scatters a heap of sand— leaving not even a hair’s breadth behind.
This clarifies the extinguishing of present karma. "Before receiving" refers to the time prior to receiving the precepts.
"Maintaining" means to hold [the mantra] and fix it within one's heart and chest so that it is never forgotten;

it means that while breaking the precepts occurs before maintaining the mantra, the destruction of sins occurs after the mantra has been maintained. Even if one should happen to drink alcohol or eat pungent foods [afterward].

Regarding "not being at fault": even if one were truly able to maintain this mantra-heart, such that one did not eliminate the auxiliary causes [of transgression], the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas would still not consider it a fault.
Nevertheless, it must be said that only those who are truly able to maintain the mantra-heart can claim that alcohol and meat do not obstruct the path to Bodhi.
As for wearing tattered and worn-out clothes versus wearing new and clean clothes, they are equal.

Entering the maṇḍala and the merit of entering the maṇḍala are equal; thus, even for those who are defiled, evil, and impure, or for those in defiled, evil, and impure places, if they are willing to single-mindedly uphold this dhāraṇī, it is no different from the merit obtained by pure persons in pure places.
Guishan said: "The four parājikas of a bhikṣu are killing, stealing," and so forth.
The four root offenses of lustful delusion are called *pārājika* in Sanskrit, which here means "abandonment.
This signifies that those who commit these four are forever abandoned by the Buddha-dharma, like a corpse cast out to sea, for the great ocean will not accept it.
For bhikṣuṇīs, there are four additional offenses of abandonment: touching, the eighth, concealing, and immediate [offenses]. Fifthly, one must not touch a man with a defiled mind.

Sixth, one must not engage in any of the eight acts with a man of lustful intent, such as holding his hand, holding his robe, entering a secluded place, standing together in a secluded place, speaking together in a secluded place, walking together, leaning their bodies against one another, or making appointments. Seventh, one must not conceal the grave offenses of others.
Eighth, one must not provide food or clothing to a monk who has been formally accused by the Saṃgha—that is, one who has already been subject to a formal act of suspension by the Saṃgha.

Regarding the method for establishing communal residence (*sāṃvāsika-dharma*), one may not follow those [transgressions] that exceed the four *pārājika* offenses; thus they are called the "eight *pārājika*.
As for "being censured by the Saṅgha," this refers to the meaning of formal accusation and exposure; there is not even a hair’s breadth of doubt that such a grave offense has been committed.
If one recites this mantra, all such [faults] will be severed.
Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who, throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas since the distant past,

have accumulated all manner of light and heavy karmic obstructions from previous lives that they have not yet had the opportunity to repent— if they can read, recite, copy, or write this mantra, wear it upon their bodies,
or place it in their dwellings, houses, gardens, or pavilions— then such accumulated karma will vanish like clouds dissolving in hot water; before long, it shall all be extinguished.

They attain the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This extinguishes past karma; that is to say, just as a single lamp can dispel the darkness of a thousand-year-old room, before long they all attain the realization of the patience of non-arising.
This concludes the preceding section on the accomplishment of sentient beings’ supramundane wisdom.

Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are women who have not yet given birth to sons or daughters and wish to conceive, if they can recollect this mantra with a sincere heart, or wear this *Sitatapatra* (White Umbrella) on their person, they will give birth to sons or daughters endowed with merit and wisdom.
Those who seek long life shall immediately obtain long life; those who seek the swift fulfillment of karmic rewards shall obtain them.
In this way, they will swiftly attain the perfection of their bodies, lives, physical forms, and strength;

likewise, after their lives end, they will be reborn in the lands of the ten directions according to their vows, certainly never being born in remote regions or among the lowly, much less in mixed forms.
This clarifies that all sought-after wishes are fulfilled. Among the thousand kinds of treasures of the ocean, one first seeks the wish-fulfilling gem;
because this mantra is its heart, it is a wish-fulfilling jewel. One may take from it without limit and use it without exhaustion;

therefore, during life, one attains mastery according to one’s will, and at the time of death, one likewise attains rebirth in accordance with one’s vows. As for not being born into lowly circumstances, it is by means of this mantra.
The mind is peerless, and the Dharma is the most precious thing; therefore, it goes alone and comes alone, being honored everywhere.

Ānanda, if there are lands, prefectures, counties, or villages suffering from famine, pestilence, or the calamities of weapons, bandits, strife, and all other such misfortunes, one should write this divine mantra and place it at the four gates of the city, as well as in all...
At a caitya or atop a stūpa, one should cause all sentient beings within the kingdom to welcome this mantra with reverence, prostrate, pay homage,
and make offerings with single-minded devotion; furthermore, one should have the people each wear it upon their person or place it in their respective dwellings,
so that all calamities and misfortunes shall be entirely extinguished.

This reveals that the national borders are peaceful and secure. Because this mantra-heart is a treasure for stabilizing the state, it cannot be equaled by the Beryl of Huánzhì or the "Illuminating the Chariot" pearl. Famine, pestilence, and warfare are the three calamities.
Wēnlíng says: *Cetiya* (支提) means a place worthy of offerings; it is a general term for a pure land (*viśuddha-kṣetra*). *Dhvaja* (脫闍) means a banner.
Those who make offerings with single-minded devotion must focus their hearts and pay respectful homage before they can obtain spiritual efficacy;
thus, all calamities and misfortunes are extinguished, just as boiling water poured onto ice or snow cast into a red-hot furnace.
Ānanda, wherever there are sentient beings in any land who possess this dhāraṇī, the devas and nāgas will rejoice, wind and rain will follow their proper seasons,
the five grains will be abundant, and the myriad people will live in peace and happiness.
This reveals that the people are harmonious and the years are bountiful.

Because this mantra is the essence of the four seasons and the sovereign of the myriad phenomena, when the hearts of humans rejoice, the hearts of devas and nāgas likewise rejoice; thus rain and sunshine follow their proper seasons. Zhuangzi said:
"When the spirit is concentrated, it causes the people to be free from pestilence and ensures that the years and the grains are ripe."
Furthermore, it can subdue all malevolent stars and their various transformations according to the directions, so that calamities and obstacles do not arise;
people shall suffer no untimely deaths, and they shall not be bound by shackles, fetters, or manacles. Day and night they shall sleep in peace, never having evil dreams.
Ānanda, in this Sahā world there are eighty-four thousand calamitous and malevolent stars, among which twenty-eight great malevolent stars are the most prominent.

Furthermore, at its head are eight great malevolent stars that act as its masters; when they manifest in various forms in the world, they can produce all manner of calamities and anomalies for sentient beings.
Where this dhāraṇī exists, they are all completely extinguished within an area of twelve yojanas, which becomes a consecrated boundary (sīmā) where no evil omens or disasters can ever enter.

This reveals the transformation of the ominous into the auspicious. Since transformations such as portents, calamities, and obstacles are all produced by the deluded karma of one’s own *sabhāga* (homogeneous) class, this mantra-heart causes them all to dissolve.
That one constantly has no evil dreams is truly because there are no inauspicious objects during the day; therefore, what appears in dreams are all the realms of Bodhi. As for malevolent stars...
The eighty-four thousand [teachings] all arise because they are evoked by the eighty-four thousand afflictions of sentient beings;
thus it is said that human actions are performed below while the Way of Heaven responds above, and the hexagram lines move within while good fortune and misfortune respond without.
The twenty-eight [lunar mansions] consist of seven in each of the four directions, which are the twenty-eight constellations. The eight great evils...

The "stars" refer to the five elements as well as Rāhu, Ketu, and Śanaiścara. It means that the twenty-eight lunar mansions and the eight great malefic stars can both bring about auspiciousness and misfortune.
As the scripture says: "Blessed is he who follows the right path; calamitous is he who follows the perverse.
This is like how ginseng and poria cocos can kill a person, yet arsenic and lethal poisons can also save a person; here, we are citing the cases of their adverse effects.

Therefore, they are collectively called "malevolent stars. That [the malevolent stars] can never enter is because where this mantra-heart resides, heaven and earth harmonize in their virtue, the sun and moon harmonize in their brilliance, the four seasons harmonize in their order, and ghosts and spirits harmonize in their auspiciousness and misfortune;
thus, there is no fissure through which calamities or portents may enter.
Therefore, the Tathāgata proclaims this mantra for the sake of protecting all beginners and practitioners in future ages as they enter samādhi,
so that their bodies and minds may be at ease and attain great peace and security, and so that no demons, spirits, or malevolent deities,
nor any karmic debts from beginningless time, grudges, or past calamities, shall come to afflict or harm you and those among the assembly.
If all those in training (*śaikṣa*) and all practitioners of future ages, relying upon my maṇḍala and maintaining the precepts according to the Dharma,
receive these precepts from a preceptor who encounters pure monks and do not give rise to doubt or regret regarding this dhāraṇī-heart,
yet these good sons fail to attain mental penetration within this body born of their parents, then the Tathāgatas of the ten directions would be speaking falsehoods.
This is the exhortation that one should uphold. "The body born of parents" refers to manifesting the present body to attain realization.

"Penetration of the mind" means clarifying the mind and seeing its nature. Wuxing said: Regarding "penetration of the mind," based on what was previously explained, it does not go beyond three meanings.
First, as for attaining the fruit: there were those of keen faculties who, after sitting upright for a hundred days, did not rise from their seats.
Second, those who have attained the stage of *srotāpanna* develop understanding and relinquish attachment to body and mind;

though the holy fruit is not yet fully realized, they know with certainty that their attainment of Buddhahood will not be in error. Third, regarding past lives, such persons are able to recall eighty-four thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* eons at will, comprehending them exhaustively and without doubt.
Having spoken these words, immeasurable hundreds and thousands of *vajrapāṇis* in the assembly simultaneously joined their palms before the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and addressed him, saying:
"As the Buddha has taught, we shall with sincere hearts protect those who thus cultivate bodhicitta.
At that time, Brahmā-rāja, Śakra-devendra, and the four Great Heavenly Kings also simultaneously prostrated before the Buddha.

He addressed the Buddha, saying: "Truly, if there are such virtuous persons who practice this training, I shall protect them with all my heart and utmost sincerity, ensuring that everything they do throughout their lives fulfills their wishes.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable yakṣa generals, rākṣasa kings, bhūtanāga kings, kumbhāṇḍa kings, piśāca kings, vināyaka spirits, and various great ghost kings."
