The various ghost generals also joined their palms before the Buddha and prostrated themselves; I too vow to protect and sustain these persons, causing their bodhicitta to be swiftly brought to full perfection.

Furthermore, immeasurable sun and moon devas, masters of wind, masters of rain, masters of clouds, masters of thunder, along with the Lord of Lightning and others—the officials who cycle through the years and the retinues of all the stars—were also present within this assembly.
Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "I, too, shall protect these practitioners of the Way, establishing them in the *dōjō* so that they may attain fearlessness.

Furthermore, there are immeasurable mountain deities and ocean deities, all the spirits of the earth, water, land, and air, the essences of all things, as well as the Wind Deity Kings and the gods of the Formless Realm, who simultaneously prostrate themselves before the Tathāgata."
And he addressed the Buddha, saying: "I, too, shall protect these practitioners so that they may attain Bodhi, forever free from demonic interference.
This clarifies that the various deities protect the mantra. At that time, the host of Vajrapāṇis descended;

furthermore, immeasurable celestial hosts descended; furthermore, immeasurable yakṣas descended; furthermore, immeasurable hosts of the eight classes of beings descended; furthermore, immeasurable hosts of sun and moon deities descended.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable mountain deities and terrestrial spirits who, because this mantra is the heart-seal of Vairocana, provide protection through a hundred spirits at every location;
it is like a military commander’s tally: once the tally arrives, orders are executed and naturally observed.

At that time, eighty-four thousand nayutas of koṭis of Vajragarbha-rāja Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, rose from their seats within the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, as for us who have long accomplished the karmic merits of our practice and attained bodhi, we do not yet take up nirvana; we constantly follow this mantra to provide protection.”
World-Honored One, for those practitioners of samādhi who cultivate correct practice in the final age— those who thus train the mind seeking right concentration—
whether they are in a place of practice, walking in meditation, or even when their minds are distracted as they wander through villages,
we and our followers shall always follow and protect such persons, even if Māra or Maheśvara seek an opportunity against them.
Ultimately, it is impossible for minor spirits and ghosts to approach these virtuous people even ten *yojanas* away,
except for those who have resolved their minds to joyfully practice meditation. World-Honored One, if such evil Māras or their retinues should come to harass these virtuous people,
I shall shatter their heads with my precious mace until they are like fine dust, so that the work of these people may always proceed unimpeded.
So be it. This is the protective mantra of the Bodhisattva. The Śūraṅgama King is also named the Vajra Samādhi.
Bodhisattvas on the stages all sever delusions by means of the mind of vajra-wisdom; for fundamental ignorance is most extremely subtle and firm.
Since it is truly impossible to shatter [delusions] without a vajra-like mind, and because the Vajragarbha King constantly bestows secret protection,
one should know that even if there are those in the degenerate age who cultivate practice and possess the wisdom of a vajra that cuts through delusions,

they cannot achieve success without the secret assistance and protection of the Vajragarbha King. As for those who constantly attend and guard them whether their minds are concentrated or distracted, although they are...
A Bodhisattva, out of profound compassion for those who uphold mantras, should likewise give rise to respect for them and not look upon them with disdain.
If one seeks a means [to assist them] and ultimately finds none, then even though they may be nearby, one must not look upon them with the eyes;
however, those who have resolved their minds to joyfully practice dhyāna may remain close to the seat of the Tathāgata and attain it.
One may also gaze upon [the deity] from nearby. As for "crushing the head with a jeweled vajra," this refers to a Great Expedient Bodhisattva who regards killing as compassion.

Regarding the practice herein, there is both the direct and the auxiliary. If one possesses sharp faculties, it is sufficient to engage in direct cultivation through the single gateway of the ear-faculty.
If one's capacity is somewhat inferior, one must enter the maṇḍala and maintain the mantras.

The section on the factors conducive to practice (*sambhāra-mārga*) and the factors for the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanā-mārga*) is hereby concluded. Below, the realization of the path (*darśana-mārga*) is revealed.
One must understand the sequence of the stages (*avasthā*) where practice and realization proceed in tandem;

for if one does not recognize these stages, one’s practice will remain merely a hollow simulation of the sages’ ranks, mistaking it for the Buddha’s realm without knowing its shallow or deep gradations. Therefore, one must inquire clearly regarding the preceding [stages].
The perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing is like gaining entry through the gate; this is like ascending to the hall and entering the inner chamber to exhaust its profound mysteries.
This is the direct answer to the request concerning how the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain the realization of Bodhi.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha: “We are dull-witted and fond of mere erudition;

regarding our minds of outflows, we had not yet sought liberation. Having received the Buddha’s compassionate instruction, we have attained correct cultivation, and our bodies and minds are filled with joy, gaining great benefit.
World-Honored One, such is the cultivation and realization of the Buddha’s samādhi, though we have not yet reached nirvāṇa.”
"What is meant by the stage of 'Dry Wisdom' (śuṣka-vipaśyanā)? From what point do the forty-four minds arise? Through what gradual sequence does one attain the vision of practice?
By proceeding toward what destination is one said to have entered the stages (bhūmi)? And what is meant by the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi)?

Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; the great assembly, with single-minded devotion, waited for the Buddha’s compassionate voice, gazing up at him with fixed and vacant eyes.
This request concerns the stages of cultivation and realization. [The Master] said, "The word 'good' (*hao*) is a disease. He continued, "My faculties and nature are inferior;

I have sought only extensive learning and did not seek liberation from outflows. Now that you have revealed the two gates of the ear-faculty and the preparatory application (*prayoga*), I have gained certainty regarding the entrance to practice and am thus relieved in body and mind. What is the gradual sequence for attaining this cultivation?"
The current presentation of the three gradual stages is merely a designation for practice;
thus, one knows that these two phrases are misplaced and should appear below the section on "not yet having reached nirvana. It previously stated: "Bodhi and nirvana are still far off," and further:
"Contemplating Buddha-bodhi and Great Nirvana is like a person who has gone away on a distant journey for some business and has not yet returned."
Returning to clearly understand the path by which one’s family is reached:
although Ānanda has now learned the way back home starting from his heels, he does not yet know how many stages of the journey lie ahead until he arrives at home;
therefore, he asks how many stages there are from beginning to end. This is like a traveler asking for directions on a long journey. If it were a distant [journey]...
If a traveler does not know the distance of the route, they will become weary midway and halt at the "transformed city" (the *pariṇāmika-nirvāṇa*), taking it for the true destination;
therefore, one must know the path and its distance so as not to be stalled halfway, but to proceed directly to the Tathāgata’s Great Parinirvāṇa.
Here, "Nirvāṇa" refers to the ultimate fruit (*phala-koṭi*), while "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*) refers to the very beginning.
The minds of faith, dwelling, practice, and direction, along with the four stages of preparatory application, are termed the forty-four minds;
these three gradual sequences constitute the objective of cultivation, while from the first stage up to Equal Enlightenment is termed "correct entry."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda, saying: "Excellent, excellent!

You have been able to universally provide for the great assembly and all sentient beings of the future age who cultivate *samādhi* and seek the Mahāyāna—leading them from the stage of ordinary beings to the ultimate Great Nirvāṇa—and to reveal in advance the unsurpassed path of correct cultivation. Listen attentively now; I shall speak for you."
Ānanda and the great assembly joined their palms, hollowed their hearts, and silently received the instruction.
This "allowing to speak" is a distant [proclamation]. Previously it was said that they were "distantly in accord" with the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity;

here it is said that he "suspendedly reveals" the Tathāgata’s true path of cultivation, spanning from the three gradual stages up to the stage of Sublime Enlightenment. In between, one passes through...
"Passing through fifty-five stages before reaching the home of the *dharmatā* of Bodhi—is this not far?
I say that although you have not yet entered it, I now reveal and show it to you in advance; thus, from beginning to end, you shall go straight toward the precious abode without any detours.
"To hollow out" (*kū*) means to carve away; it refers to emptying one's mind in order to receive the teaching.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda, you should know that the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and free from all names and marks; originally there were no worlds or sentient beings.

Because of delusion there is birth, and because of birth there is extinction. Birth and extinction are called delusion; the cessation of delusion is called truth. This is what is meant by 'True Suchness'."
Ānanda, the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed Bodhi and Great Nirvāṇa are both designated as the "twofold transformation of the basis.
If you now wish to cultivate true samādhi and proceed directly to the Tathāgata’s Great Nirvāṇa, you must first recognize these two causes of inversion regarding sentient beings and the world;
when inversion no longer arises, this is the Tathāgata’s true samādhi.
This first clarifies that the *tathatā* (suchness), which serves as the basis, is free from all marks.

"Wondrous nature" refers directly to the essence of *tathatā*, which is called "perfect" (*yuan*) because it universally encompasses and is fully endowed with all virtues, and "luminous" (*ming*) because it uniquely illuminates the collective darkness.
It is "free from all names and marks" because within the realm of *tathatā*, the provisional designations of "sentient beings" and "Buddhas" are utterly transcended and leveled.

Within the state of equality, there are no forms of self or other; thus, not only has the world and its sentient beings never existed from the very beginning, but furthermore, neither does bodhi nor nirvāṇa exist. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"When observing all lands and all things within the ten directions with the Buddha-eye, one does not even perceive non-existence, let alone the existence of dharmas."

The dharma of ultimate emptiness can destroy delusions; yet even the attainment of Buddhahood by a Bodhisattva cannot be apprehended as a real entity, let alone the deluded, existent dharmas of ordinary beings and devas. The three phrases following "due to delusion" indicate that the names "sentient beings" and "worlds" exist only because of defiled conditions. This is truly because the wondrous nature is free from names and transcends forms, fundamentally devoid of all delusions. By means of... (text continues) ...it is thus. Because it is thus, there is no arising of delusion. Because there is no arising of delusion, there is no cessation of delusion. Because there is no arising and no cessation, there is no coming and no going. Because there is no coming and no going, there is no birth and no death. Because there is no birth and no death, there is no bondage and no liberation. Because there is no bondage and no liberation, there is no Nirvana and no Samsara. Because there is no Nirvana and no Samsara, there is no Buddha and no sentient beings. Because there is no Buddha and no sentient beings, there is no Bodhi and no afflictions. Because there is no Bodhi and no afflictions, there is no path and no fruition. Because there is no path and no fruition, there is no practice and no realization. Because there is no practice and no realization, there is no dharma and no non-dharma. Because there is no dharma and no non-dharma, there is no duality and no non-duality. Because there is no duality and no non-duality, there is no distinction and no non-distinction. Because there is no distinction and no non-distinction, there is no difference and no non-difference. Because there is no difference and no non-difference, there is no discrimination and no non-discrimination. Because there is no discrimination and no non-discrimination, there is no thought and no non-thought. Because there is no thought and no non-thought, there is no mind and no non-mind. Because there is no mind and no non-mind, there is no object and no subject. Because there is no object and no subject, there is no grasping and no rejecting. Because there is no grasping and no rejecting, there is no attachment and no detachment. Because there is no attachment and no detachment, there is no increase and no decrease. Because there is no increase and no decrease, there is no gain and no loss. Because there is no gain and no loss, there is no light and no darkness. Because there is no light and no darkness, there is no purity and no impurity. Because there is no purity and no impurity, there is no truth and no falsehood. Because there is no truth and no falsehood, there is no right and no wrong. Because there is no right and no wrong, there is no good and no evil. Because there is no good and no evil, there is no merit and no demerit. Because there is no merit and no demerit, there is no cause and no effect. Because there is no cause and no effect, there is no beginning and no end. Because there is no beginning and no end, there is no middle. Because there is no middle, there is no boundary. Because there is no boundary, there is no limit. Because there is no limit, there is no direction. Because there is no direction, there is no location. Because there is no location, there is no space. Because there is no space, there is no time. Because there is no time, there is no succession. Because there is no succession, there is no simultaneity. Because there is no simultaneity, there is no sequence. Because there is no sequence, there is no order. Because there is no order, there is no chaos. Because there is no chaos, there is no confusion. Because there is no confusion, there is no obstruction. Because there is no obstruction, there is no hindrance. Because there is no hindrance, there is no gate. Because there is no gate, there is no entry. Because there is no entry, there is no exit. Because there is no exit, there is no dwelling. Because there is no dwelling, there is no movement. Because there is no movement, there is no stillness. Because there is no stillness, there is no activity. Because there is no activity, there is no quiescence. Because there is no quiescence, there is no manifestation. Because there is no manifestation, there is no concealment. Because there is no concealment, there is no appearance. Because there is no appearance, there is no disappearance. Because there is no disappearance, there is no birth. Because there is no birth, there is no extinction. Because there is no extinction, there is no permanence. Because there is no permanence, there is no change. Because there is no change, there is no transformation. Because there is no transformation, there is no creation. Because there is no creation, there is no destruction. Because there is no destruction, there is no formation. Because there is no formation, there is no disintegration. Because there is no disintegration, there is no aggregation. Because there is no aggregation, there is no dispersion. Because there is no dispersion, there is no collection. Because there is no collection, there is no accumulation. Because there is no accumulation, there is no depletion. Because there is no depletion, there is no fullness. Because there is no fullness, there is no emptiness. Because there is no emptiness, there is no existence. Because there is no existence, there is no non-existence. Because there is no non-existence, there is no being. Because there is no being, there is no non-being. Because there is no non-being, there is no self. Because there is no self, there is no other. Because there is no other, there is no duality. Because there is no duality, there is no non-duality. Because there is no non-duality, there is no distinction. Because there is no distinction, there is no identity. Because there is no identity, there is no difference. Because there is no difference, there is no unity. Because there is no unity, there is no multiplicity. Because there is no multiplicity, there is no one. Because there is no one, there is no many. Because there is no many, there is no part. Because there is no part, there is no whole. Because there is no whole, there is no substance. Because there is no substance, there is no attribute. Because there is no attribute, there is no characteristic. Because there is no characteristic, there is no mark. Because there is no mark, there is no sign. Because there is no sign, there is no name. Because there is no name, there is no form. Because there is no form, there is no phenomenon. Because there is no phenomenon, there is no dharma. Because there is no dharma, there is no non-dharma. Because there is no non-dharma, there is no object. Because there is no object, there is no subject. Because there is no subject, there is no knower. Because there is no knower, there is no known. Because there is no known, there is no knowledge. Because there is no knowledge, there is no wisdom. Because there is no wisdom, there is no ignorance. Because there is no ignorance, there is no enlightenment. Because there is no enlightenment, there is no delusion. Because there is no delusion, there is no awakening. Because there is no awakening, there is no realization. Because there is no realization, there is no attainment. Because there is no attainment, there is no non-attainment. Because there is no non-attainment, there is no gain. Because there is no gain, there is no loss. Because there is no loss, there is no increase. Because there is no increase, there is no decrease. Because there is no decrease, there is no birth. Because there is no birth, there is no death. Because there is no death, there is no life. Because there is no life, there is no extinction. Because there is no extinction, there is no Nirvana. Because there is no Nirvana, there is no Samsara. Because there is no Samsara, there is no Buddha. Because there is no Buddha, there is no sentient being. Because there is no sentient being, there is no Bodhi. Because there is no Bodhi, there is no affliction. Because there is no affliction, there is no path. Because there is no path, there is no fruition. Because there is no fruition, there is no practice. Because there is no practice, there is no realization. Because there is no realization, there is no dharma. Because there is no dharma, there is no non-dharma. Because there is no non-dharma, there is no duality. Because there is no duality, there is no non-duality. Because there is no non-duality, there is no distinction. Because there is no distinction, there is no non-distinction. Because there is no non-distinction, there is no difference. Because there is no difference, there is no non-difference. Because there is no non-difference, there is no discrimination. Because there is no discrimination, there is no non-discrimination. Because there is no non-discrimination, there is no thought. Because there is no thought, there is no non-thought. Because there is no non-thought, there is no mind. Because there is no mind, there is no non-mind. Because there is no non-mind, there
The first thought of non-awakening (ajñāna) is a false movement, which gives rise to the characteristic of birth;
because of this characteristic of birth, there further arise the characteristics of abiding, change, and extinction. Precisely because there is birth and extinction, it is termed "false.
Consequently, there are two kinds of inversion: namely, that non-awakening exists by virtue of fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi). [This concludes] the fifth section on extinguishing delusion.
It is through the purity of causal conditions that the names "bodhi" and "nirvāṇa" exist. This means that by transforming the world’s basis of inversion, one attains bodhi;
by transforming the sentient beings’ basis of inversion, one attains nirvāṇa. It is said that because of non-awakening (abodha), there is initial awakening (ādi-bodhi).
Therefore, the *Zongjing* says: "The precious awakened true mind is perfectly complete in each and every being; originally, it cannot be named as 'this' or 'that.'"

The Buddha is likewise not named a sentient being; it is simply because this mind is subtle, wondrous, and sovereign, not abiding in its own nature, that it follows the conditions of delusion or awakening to manifest the affairs of the holy or the ordinary.
It is like gold which, following the conditions of a craftsman, is transformed into a finger-ring when fashioned;
yet when the finger-ring follows the condition of the furnace fire and is destroyed, it immediately returns to being gold. Thus, formation and destruction revolve in succession.
However, just as gold remains without distinction, the *tathāgatagarbha* mind is likewise:
when following defiled conditions, it is deluded and becomes the *ālayavijñāna*; when following pure conditions, it is awakened and becomes the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Since they are ultimately nothing but this single mind and there is never any difference between them, it is said: "If consciousness has no beginning, then the *dharmatā* itself is ignorance."
If one knows that today, ignorance itself is the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), and that this dharma-nature universally produces all phenomena within ignorance—this is termed "defilement";
and that ignorance universally responds to various conditions within the dharma-nature—this is termed "purity":
this is precisely the "Gate of the Perfect Accomplishment of the Mind’s Reversion" among the Ten Mysterious Gates. If it is reversed, it is termed...
When Nirvana is viewed in its forward progression, it is termed birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); this is because both birth-and-death and Nirvana do not transcend the Tathāgatagarbha-mind.
Ānanda, below [this point], the two fruits of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) are directly shown; these should be sought within the two types of causes of inversion.
Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "The liberation of all Buddhas should be sought within the mental activities of sentient beings."
Seeking that which is the non-arising of these two kinds of inversion is precisely the Tathāgata’s true samādhi; this is what was previously stated:

"The mad mind ceases of its own accord; this cessation is itself bodhi. Thus we know that both the paths of the ordinary person and the sage are established based on birth-and-death versus delusion-and-awakening, yet within the gate of True Suchness (tathatā), such things do not exist at all.

Ānanda, what is meant by the "inversion" of sentient beings? Ānanda, because the nature of the mind is luminous and the nature of the mind is perfectly full, from this luminosity the nature is activated;
from this activation of the nature, false seeing arises. From that which is ultimately non-existent, there is established that which is ultimately existent.
This existence and its objects have no cause for their cause, nor any abode for their abode; they are utterly without root. Based upon this lack of abiding, the world is established.
"And all sentient beings.
This is a general indication that the ignorance-infused *tathatā* (suchness) constitutes its defiled function as the cause for two kinds of inversion.

The characters "sentient beings" (*zhòngshēng*) should be a scribal error for the characters "two kinds" (*èrzhǒng*). "The nature of luminous mind" refers to the essence of original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*).

Yuan (also) states that "pervading both the false and the true" refers to the fact that when one clarifies the manifestation of the nature (*xing*), "clarifying" specifically points to ignorance (*avidyā*).

"Manifesting the nature" means the nature manifested by ignorance, which is precisely the *karmic-consciousness* (*karma-vijñāna*). "False seeing" refers to the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*), while "ultimately existing" refers to the aspect of form (*nimitta-bhāga*).
This explains that from the substance of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-pratibhāsa*), a single thought-moment of deluded movement gives rise to ignorance; because of this ignorance...
When clarity transforms, it becomes the causal consciousness of karma (*karmavijñāna*); because of this karmic consciousness, there arises the objective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*);

and because of the objective aspect, there arise the sense organs, the body, and the external world. This is what is meant by "within that which is devoid of identity or difference, a blazing diversity is formed.
Furthermore, it is explained below that these three subtleties all suddenly arise from within non-existence; therefore, it says: "This ignorance that has the capacity to create... and so forth.
All sentient beings and worlds are fundamentally without cause, for the causes from which they arise likewise have no abiding place.
They are like flowers in the sky or dreams during sleep; when interrogated, they have no root, and when sought, they have no foundation.
It is precisely from this non-abiding ignorance that the world and its multitudes are thus established.
Because two kinds of inversions arise, we know that the world of sentient beings exists in its entirety through the perfuming and transformation of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Since ignorance and [the afflictions of] views and thought arise in mutual interaction, there are the inversions of sentient beings;
since ignorance and the faculties and objects interact, there are the inversions of the world.
Delusion regarding one's original perfect luminosity gives rise to false imagination; this false nature has no substance and has nothing upon which it relies.

When one seeks to return to the truth, that which is sought as "truth" is already not true. The nature of True Suchness is not something to be attained through seeking; yet, by mistakenly seeking to restore it, one instead creates the appearance of non-existence.

It is neither arising, nor abiding, nor mind, nor phenomena, yet through their mutual interaction they give rise to one another. The power of this arising manifests and perfumes the mind to form karma; through the resonance of shared karma, beings are brought together.
Because there is the characteristic of the extinction of one karmic condition and the arising of another, sentient beings thus undergo perversion.
This specifically clarifies that the perversion of sentient beings arises from views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).

It is said that these sentient beings are called "perverted" because, deluded regarding the essence of perfect luminosity, they momentarily forget its movement and thereby transform this perfect luminosity.
This substance constitutes false delusion; this nature of false delusion originally arises from the initial phase of ignorance (*avidyā*).
It has no real substance, nor does it have a real locus of dependence.
Now, if one wishes to return this ignorance back to its original truth, even this single thought of desiring truth still belongs to delusive ideation and is not yet the true *tathatā*.
One's nature must desire to exhaust [delusion] before it will cease. If one does not seek restoration with a heart that truly desires it, then one merely accumulates delusion upon delusion;
by what means could one see the original face? One sees only the dust and toil filling the eyes, forming entirely illusory appearances.
What is called "non-appearance" refers internally to the two kinds of ignorance: birth and abiding.
The perfuming and arousal of the two dharmas of external mind and objects cause them to arise mutually;
because this leads to the successive arising of the two delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and mental afflictions (*kleśa*), it is said: "neither arising nor abiding, neither mind nor dharma.

Through this successive production, the power of the arising of these two delusions of views and mental afflictions excels, perfuming and forming the characteristic of karma (*karma-lakṣaṇa*). Once the characteristic of karma is formed, there is the suffering bound by karma.
Because characteristics shift and flow without ceasing, the cycle of rebirth turns without end; it is for this reason that sentient beings who possess such characteristics are called "inverted.

Thus, the *Huayan ji* states: "If one fears having a mind of attachment even while practicing wholesome dharmas with aversion to the world, how much more so when one indulges the passions to commit evil?
It further states: "Even when entering into principle to contemplate the Buddha, one still fears giving rise to thoughts that will lead to the further creation of evil karma."
In particular, this directly contradicts the ultimate teaching when Dongshan said, "To learn the matters on the Buddha's side is still a mistaken application of the mind.

This implies that if one seeks the True while it is already not the True, and seeks the nature of True Suchness while it is not the True, one will instead fully produce the characteristic of non-existence.
Ānanda, what is meant by the "inversion of the world"? It is that which exists as having something to possess, where segments falsely arise;
it is established through this realm, yet is not caused by a cause, and does not abide in an abode. It flows and migrates without staying still, and thus the world is formed.
The three periods of time and the four directions intermingle and interact, transforming sentient beings into the twelve categories. Therefore, the world arises from movement.

There is sound because of sound; there is form because of form; there is fragrance because of fragrance; there is touch because of touch; there is taste because of taste; and there is the cognition of dharmas because of dharmas.
These six delusive false thoughts constitute the nature of karma. Thus, the twelve divisions revolve by means of this cycle.
Therefore, throughout the world, sound, fragrance, flavor, and touch undergo twelve transformations, returning as a single rotation; driven by this revolution, one falls into perversion.
By way of characteristics, there are worlds of egg-birth, womb-birth, moisture-birth, and transformation-birth; those with form and those without form;
those with perception and those without perception; those that are neither with nor without form; and those that are neither with nor without perception.
This is a separate explanation of how the world’s inversion arises from the faculties and their objects. The world is originally pure; how could there be inversion?
It is entirely due to the inverted delusions of sentient beings that they weave together false appearances, forming the twelve categories of beings.
Therefore, the world itself becomes inverted. Thus, the basis for the world’s inversion lies in sentient beings; hence, it is "Great."
The Sūtra states: "Sentient beings lack the vessel for the Dharma, and the world becomes defiled.

This "existence" (yu) refers precisely to the sentient beings produced by prior ignorance; because they possess the segmented physical bodies of the roots, the boundaries of sentient beings are established.
It is from this that the name of this realm (dhātu) is derived. Fundamentally, there is no cause, yet it is the cause from which those [beings] are born.

Furthermore, there is no fixed place where they abide; rather, because they shift and flow from moment to moment, they come to constitute the three periods of time—the name "this world" (the present) being established thereby.

Because these worlds—three and four, four and three—revolve to form twelve, and because they harmonize and interpenetrate one another, the twelve classes of beings likewise arise through calculation and transformation, as was previously discussed regarding the path of cultivation.
It is clear that when world-phenomena interpenetrate, they form meritorious virtues; it is also clear that when world-phenomena interpenetrate, they form delusions.
Therefore, at the lower level, based on a single moment of deluded movement, the internal faculties and external objects are neither before nor after, but are fully present simultaneously.
Thus it is said: "Because of movement, there is sound," and so forth. Just as in the world, when the myriad things move, they necessarily [interact].
Where there is sound, there must be a place for sound; where there is a place for sound, there must be form; where there is form, there must be air; where there is air, it can necessarily be smelled;
where there is touch, one thereby knows its taste; and where there is taste, one immediately knows what object it is.

Since the objects (*viṣaya*) are thus, the sense organs (*indriya*) are likewise so. Indeed, the three—karma, transformation, and manifestation—arise collectively from a single thought of non-awakening.
Arising from false movement, these twelve, though categorized into distinct classes, are likewise produced by a single thought-moment of false movement.
Thus, the eye grasps forms, the ear grasps sounds, the nose grasps odors, the tongue grasps tastes, the body grasps tangibles, and the mind grasps mental objects;
as the six faculties and six sense-objects interweave, they form a wheel of transmigration. Therefore, for each faculty and its corresponding object...
When one karma is currently created, the other faculties and other objects likewise remain in latent potentiality, together constituting a single karma.
Therefore, by citing one faculty, all six faculties are fully present; by citing one object, all six objects are simultaneously revealed.
Since the creation of karma by the six faculties is identical, the same applies to the six objects. Thus, the faculties and their objects exhaustively undergo these twelve transformations.
Regarding the term "one cycle of rotation" (*xuánfù*): this refers to the faculties and objects undergoing twelve transformations to complete one full cycle of rotation and recurrence.

Because these underlying causal faculties and objects possess twelve [transformations], the resultant sentient beings who ride upon them likewise possess twelve classes. These twelve inversions are, in their entirety, deluded views.
Arising from both the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*):
the two types of birth from a womb or an egg, along with those possessing form and perception, are characterized by delusion regarding the objective aspect;

they mostly dwell in moist or transformational births, and are neither formless nor without perception. Furthermore, the inversion of sentient beings is the distinct karma of individual sentient beings.
Because one perceives what is solitary, the world undergoes inversion; because it is the common karmic mark of sentient beings, it is shared.

If one shatters the grasping at a self, realizes the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), severs birth-and-death with fixed limits (*prābandhika-saṃsāra*), and realizes *nirvāṇa* with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*) to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, then the inversions of sentient beings will finally cease.
If one shatters the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), realizes the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), and severs birth-and-death through transformation (*pariṇāmi-saṃsāra*).
When one undergoes birth and death yet realizes nirvana without remainder and attains great bodhi, the world’s inversions first become empty;
therefore it is said that "inversions do not arise. This is the Tathāgata’s true samādhi.

Ānanda, because the world is characterized by the false cycle of rebirth and the inversion of movement, the combination of vital breaths produces eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts of flying and sinking;
thus there exist the egg-born kalala stages, circulating through lands as fish, birds, turtles, and snakes,
their various kinds filling the realm.
This clarifies the cause and effect of birth from an egg (*aṇḍaja*). That which is born from a shell is called an "egg. From "due to causes" below, the creative cause is clarified;
from "thus" below, the created effect is revealed; the same applies to all subsequent passages. "Falsehood" refers to conceptualization (*saṃjñā*);
since an egg is produced solely through conceptualization, it is said that "movement and inversion" refer to suddenly becoming deluded regarding the true essence of immovability.
Yet, when false movement arises therein, one bows and looks up at heaven and earth and again caresses the four seas; being arrogant and unrestrained, one cannot be bound.

Is this not a perversion? That which is formed by the harmonious blending of the vital energies is called "perversion," for all such perversions are produced by the movement of the wind of ignorance (*avidyā*).
As for "confused thoughts of flying and sinking," this refers to how these deluded thoughts suddenly arise and suddenly perish, suddenly ascending and suddenly [descending].
Because there is no fixed certainty below [the human realm], the *kalala*—translated here as "coagulated mucus"—is the first stage within the womb.
When each of the twelve classes of beings speaks of eighty-four thousand [forms], it is entirely because they are the transformations induced by eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*).
Fish, birds, turtles, and snakes are all fruits induced by the chaotic thoughts of flying or sinking; thus, the fish...
When a bird transforms into a snake or a tortoise transforms into a turtle, they suddenly forget their coiled and curved forms and acquire a lumbering substance;

when [a creature] suddenly forgets its swimming manner and acquires a body for flying and singing, all these are brought about by the intermingling of vital energy (*qi*) and spiritual transformation.
As for cranes calling to one another and egrets gazing at one another, these are likewise the fruits of the intermingling of vital energy.
Furthermore,
due to the inversion of desire within the world’s defiled cycle of rebirth, eighty-four thousand horizontal and vertical disordered thoughts are combined and nourished into being;
thus there exist the states of gestation, the *arbuda*, and the flow of births among lands, humans, animals, dragons, and immortals.
These types fill the world;
this clarifies the cause and effect of womb-birth (*jarāyu-ja*). That which emerges from being contained and stored is called "womb-born.

As for what is termed "defiled," it is because one suddenly falls into the dust of emotions due to delusion regarding this intrinsically pure and luminous essence, thereby muddying the true nature; thus, one desires to fall into error.
To be "upside-down" (viparyāsa) is like receiving a physical form that does not perish until its exhaustion;
it is to abandon one's original wife and fail to be intimate with her, while instead falsely seeking a mate for union—this is not inversion?

That which is formed through harmonious combination is nourished by the same growth of craving, such that greed cannot be stopped. That thoughts are disordered, whether horizontal or vertical, is the presence of lust.
Regarding the distinction between the correct and the deviant: sexual misconduct with one's own spouse is considered correct, while seeking it further outward is deviant.

Because the emotions involved possess these biases of correctness and deviation, the resulting fruits are likewise characterized by either verticality or horizontality. "E-po-t'an" (遏蒲曇) is translated here as "blister," which refers to the second stage within the womb.
Humans and immortals are fundamentally vertical, whereas dragons and beasts are fundamentally horizontal; such is their respective fruit. However...
Because there are internal and external perceptions, as well as worldly and spiritual emotions, one who is able to transform these emotional perceptions is in true samādhi.
Due to the world's attachment to the cycle of saṃsāra and its inverted tendencies, the combination of warmth forms eighty-four thousand [afflictions].

Because such inverted and chaotic thoughts exist, there is the moist characteristic (*sneha-lakṣaṇa*), whereby the *bīśa* (the corpse-like embryo) transmigrates through various lands, filled with crawling and wriggling creatures.
This clarifies the cause and effect of moisture-born birth (*saṃsvedaja*). That which is born by means of borrowed moisture is called "moisture-born"; "clinging" refers precisely to coagulation.

Because moisture arises from the convergence of conditions, those who pursue inverted perceptions do so because they fail to realize that the true mind is non-abiding—like a mani jewel that manifests colors according to its surroundings yet possesses no fixed form of its own. To rush toward objects like a gale and cling to circumstances as they shift—is this not an inversion?
That which is formed through the combination of warmth is due to human sentiment’s total inclination toward bustling and clamorous places of pursuit and service.

What is called "wealth and honor" is the convergence of others; "reversal and disorderly thoughts" refers to turning one's hand to create clouds and covering it to bring rain, like the gate of Lord Zhai which could once trap sparrows, or the guests who filled the halls again when Mengchang returned to Qi.
This obscures the corpse; what is here called "soft flesh" is the third stage within the womb, containing crawling insects.

Their movements are like those of vinegar-mites or midges; because throughout their lives they failed to align themselves with the Way and righteousness, and were deficient in every matter, lacking the spirit of a true man, they receive this retribution of being dull and devoid of consciousness.

Due to the causes of the world’s shifting cycles and the provisional nature of inverted perceptions, the conjunction of contact gives rise to eighty-four thousand types of new and old disordered thoughts;
because of this, there exist transformed beings, *kalala* embryos, and those that flow, transmigrate, or fly through the lands,
their various species filling the realm.
This clarifies the cause and effect of transformation-birth (*upapāduka*). That which is "suddenly existing where there was nothing" is called transformation;

that which involves shifting and revolving is called the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*), such as being suddenly reverent and suddenly indolent, or suddenly joyful and suddenly angry—like the saying "three in the morning and four in the evening.

These are termed "false inversions" because one does not know the true host who remains unchanging while following conditions, and instead turns one's back on this by following conditions while remaining unchanging.
To turn one's back on what is right while having sweet words but a bitter heart—is this not a perversion?

That which is formed through the conjunction of contact refers to this provisional person, who changes their conduct at every point of contact and loses their original mind. Thus, new and old thoughts become disordered: one grows weary of the old and delights in the new;
one prefers crimson over plain white, and when wealthy, easily changes wives, and when noble, easily changes friends. How could such a person know that clothing is never truly wearied?
The new person does not tire of the old; this is what Jien meant by "hard flesh," which refers to the fourth stage within the womb.

As for those that undergo transformation and fly, such as a sparrow changing into a clam—this is the transition from flying to sinking—or a dung beetle transforming into a cicada—this is the transition from crawling to flying.
It is precisely because they have no integrity throughout their lives and undergo change at every turn that they experience [such consequences].
This is the fruit.
Because the causal world is characterized by obstruction, saṃsāra, hindrances, and inversion, these combine and coalesce to form eighty-four thousand deluded thoughts of radiant clarity;
thus, there arise the physical forms of the *kalala* (embryonic stage) that circulate through various lands, manifesting as auspicious or inauspicious spiritual potencies.
Their kind fills [the world].
This clarifies that the cause and effect of form is the realm of form (rūpadhātu). Regarding those who are obstructed by impediments and transmigrate:

their subtle radiance (*tejas*) arises from clarity, and clarity arises from attachment; thus, subtle radiance has something to which it clings. As for those who are inverted: it is because they do not know this.
The self-nature inherently possesses the light of great wisdom that pervades the entire dharma-realm; it is fundamentally without obstruction.

Yet, you instead serve water and fire, the sun and moon, seeking the cause of illumination. By establishing your basis through such illumination, you ultimately create obstructions and fail to attain perfect penetration—is this not a delusion?
Those who achieve results through combination and attachment cast aside their own inexhaustible radiance.
On the contrary, they take that which is "bright and numinous" (*zhāozhāo línglíng*) to be the ultimate principle;
this is what the various heavens of the Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*) all rely upon, for all those devas possess a radiance that accompanies their bodies.

Thus, the "refined brilliance of distracted thought" is what the ancients called "playing with the essence-soul. The "refined brilliance of portents" refers to things such as the sun, moon, and stars.
That which is auspicious is called rest, and that which is inauspicious is called retribution; even the light of a torch or the luster of an oyster shell are caused by this.
Because the world-system dissolves due to delusion and inversion within saṃsāra, darkness combines with these to form eighty-four thousand obscure and chaotic thoughts.
Thus, there exist the formless *kalala* (embryonic) states that circulate through various lands, dispersing, dissolving, and sinking into emptiness.
Their kind fills [the realm].
This clarifies that the cause and effect of the formless are the formless realm itself.

As for "dissolving the cycle of rebirth," it is because they do not know that within the body with signs there is a body without signs, and that upon the mountain of ignorance there is no path to birth; therefore, they extinguish the body.
To return to non-interruption of wisdom is to immerse oneself in the void. Those who are deluded and inverted—do they not mistake the tainted heavens for the unconditioned?
To achieve union with darkness means to cling to this state of profound stupor, silence, and deep obscurity as the ultimate realm;
all the devas of the four formless heavens sit therein, which is what is called "obscuration and gloom."

Regarding those whose empty, obscured, and chaotic thoughts neither exist nor do not exist, and who seem to exhaust yet do not exhaust: they proclaim the nature of exhaustion within the inexhaustible;
thus, their emptiness disperses, dissolves, and sinks. This means that they intend to grind away and submerge this body and mind, causing them to disperse and enter into emptiness.
These two aforementioned types are transformations of the emotional mind.
Due to the causes of the world’s illusory cycles of rebirth and inverted perceptions, the conjunction of memories forms eighty-four thousand latent knots of chaotic thoughts;
because of this, there exist the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages of gestation that circulate through various lands,
filled with all manner of gods, ghosts, and spirits.
This clarifies the existence of the cause and effect of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). "Wandering in a phantom-like cycle" means that things are indistinct, superficially similar, and not truly real.
"The inversion of shadows" arises because they do not know their own nature and do not perceive the fundamental source;

thus, they cling to shadows while neglecting true suchness (*tathatā*). When it is said that "the Way, as a substance, is hazy and indistinct," and so forth, these are all instances of perceiving its shadow.

Yet, to not truly see one's original face—is this not a delusion? As for "forming through the union of recollection," it refers to such practices as gathering the mind morning and evening to suspend it in a single place, or guarding the center and following the督 (dū) channel.

As for "concealing and binding chaotic thoughts," it refers to the state of being "subtle and continuous, as if something exists, yet its use is not strenuous. Because its use becomes more prolonged, the thoughts become increasingly bound and do not [dissolve].
As for "dispersal," spirits, ghosts, and numinous beings—such as those described in the *Pañcaskandhaka-prakaraṇa*, celestial māras, monsters, and phantoms—all arise because of erroneous practice;

they obtain the shadow but not the reality. Thus, even if one possesses the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), because one has not yet attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), there is a monk who asked an ancient worthy:
"When two [reflections] appear side by side, what then? The Worthy replied: [The text here implies a response regarding the non-duality of appearances].
It is said that one is a shadow, for it gives rise to a semblance-wisdom rather than true wisdom.
Due to the causes of worldly ignorance, dullness, saṃsāra, delusion, and perversion, these combine with stubbornness to form eighty-four thousand parched and chaotic thoughts;
thus there exist the lands of the non-perceptive kalala, where the spirit is transformed.
Earth, wood, metal, and stone—these types fill the world.

This clarifies the cause and effect of the non-conceptual (asaṃjñika). Those who are dull and revolve in saṃsāra are "dull" because they are obstructed by dharmas, and "stupid" because they possess the afflictive hindrances (kleśāvaraṇa).
As for those who are deluded and inverted, it is said that they do not know that self-nature is originally perfect and alive.
The eye can see and the ear can hear; like the color of a jewel in the midday sun, it has no fixed form.
It is like a gourd upon the water—impossible to press down or forcibly subdue—like grass crushed by stones or fish trapped between ice.
The ancient masters called this "a dead man whose soul has not yet dispersed. Is this not a state of perversion? It is that which is formed through the union of insentient matter.
This refers to the destruction of the physical body and the suppression of intelligence to enter a state of dullness and obstinacy.
Those whose chaotic thoughts have withered away are like cold ashes or dry wood, lacking the warmth of life;

thus, those who become like earth, wood, metal, or stone—such as the case of the *huabiao* pillar producing a spirit or Huangtou being transformed into stone—are practicing a semblance of dhyāna, not true dhyāna. Thus it is said.

The former two types are transformations of perception (*saṃjñā*) themselves; because those in the realms of form (*rūpa-dhātu*), the formless (*ārūpya-dhātu*), and neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) all practice yet fail to attain the truth, they are divided into four categories.

Due to the world of causes, which is characterized by mutual dependence, cyclic existence, falsehood, and inversion, these factors combine to form eighty-four thousand defiled thoughts based on causal conditions.
Because of such disordered perceptions, there exist non-material forms that take on material characteristics as *kalala* (embryonic stages), circulating through various lands;
such as the *siphonophora* (sea-squirts) and other species that use shrimp as their eyes, filling the world in great numbers.
This clarifies that it is not a matter of material causes and effects.
Those who revolve in dependence have something to rely upon, like a shadow depending on a form or a reflection depending on a scene;

such false inversions arise from not knowing one's own nature—that which does not oppose the various sensory objects nor takes the myriad dharmas as companions, but stands preeminent before all things—yet instead relying on others.
To believe that one's own power is not a perversion—when things are formed through the combination of defilements—is like the influence of dyeing or the reliance on fame and reputation;
to depend on disordered thoughts is like a fox feigning the majesty of a tiger or a traveler executing the orders of his master.
This is not the case for those who form the *kalala* (embryonic stage) from material characteristics, for they originally lack power and must wait for it to be established by others.
Therefore, the fruits thus elicited are fundamentally not possessed of form, yet they depend upon external objects to manifest as form.
This is like the *siphonophora* (water-mother) which takes water-foam for its body and uses shrimp for its eyes;

it extends even to all the ghosts and spirits that rely upon grass and wood, as well as the eighty-four thousand families of worms within the body—all of these are results of this same cause. Hence it is said: "It depends upon King Wen."
Those who thus arise are not heroic sages.
Because they are drawn along by the characteristics of the world and their natures are inverted, they combine with mantras to form eighty-four thousand deluded thoughts of summoning;
it is for this reason that there exist those who are neither form nor formless, such as the *kalala* and *arbuda*, as they transmigrate through various lands.
Curses and malevolent incantations arise, their various types filling the world.
This clarifies that it is not the case that there is no causality within the formless realm. "Mutually inducing and revolving" refers to drawing people in through perverse speech and perverse karma.
"Perversion of nature" arises because they do not know that their own nature possesses [virtues] as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Innate virtues cannot induce its arising; rather, it is led astray by the habitual conditioning of false speech and false actions, which transform its nature—is this not perversion?
That which is accomplished through the conjunction of mantras refers to the conversion of a person through the power of incantations and curses.
That which summons disordered thoughts is like the practice today of writing talismans and performing ritual gestures (*mudrā*) to invoke deities.
Summoning classes of ghosts is like calling out to a host; if one calls and summons in this manner, one can thereby induce merits that accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Now, instead of inducing these for oneself, one induces them for others; instead of calling and summoning for oneself, one calls and summons ghosts and spirits.
Therefore, this constitutes a state of confused conceptualization (*vikalpa*). As for "having no form or appearance" and "no *kalala* of form," it is because...
Curses exist because they have a cause; they are not non-existent. Without the curse, they do not exist; therefore, they are non-existent.

Those who are oppressed by curses and incantations—such as the spirits of the *zhāngliǔ* tree and others—are a distinct class of heterodox deities and heterodox ghosts in the world who listen to and are employed by humans.
As for orthodox deities, they cannot be moved unless one possesses utmost sincerity and supreme virtue; how could they ever respond to the frivolous?
How could it be summoned by humans? This is because spirits and deities were summoned during the causal stage; therefore, they are summoned by humans at the resultant stage.
The two types mentioned above constitute the transformation of combination.

Because the world arises from the union of causes with delusive saṃsāra and inverted views, these disparate elements combine to form eighty-four thousand types of reciprocal and chaotic conceptualizations.
Thus, there exist the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages of formation through the conceptualization of non-existence as existence.
In the case of creatures such as the *pulu* (maggots), different substances mutually transform one another, and their kind fills the lands.

This clarifies that it is not the case that there are causal conditions for conceptualization. Those who falsely conjoin with the cycle of saṃsāra actually remain detached from it yet forcibly unite with it;
this is called "false conjunction. As for those who are deluded and inverted, it is because they do not know that the True Lord is their most intimate possession, yet instead turn their backs on Him.
Thus, they take that which is not their own kin to be kin, and that which is not their own child to be a child.

To treat what is not one's own property as if it were one's own property for the sake of a child—is this not a perversion? That which is formed through the combination of different elements is not of the same kind;
therefore, it is called "different. Regarding "reciprocal and confused conceptualization," this means taking what belongs to another and mutually regarding it as one's own.
Regarding "the perception of non-existence forming the perception of the kalala," this refers to the property of others.

Originally there was no mind or self, hence it is said that there is no perception; yet I forcibly conceive of one, and thus the perception of a self is formed—hence it is called "the formation of perception.
It is like the caterpillar (pulu): originally it is a mulberry worm, yet without having the perception of being a bee, it eventually forms the perception of being a bee.

Due to the cycle of enmity and killing in the world, and because of inverted perceptions, these factors combine to produce eighty-four thousand types of beings who harbor the notion that they are eating their own parents.
Thus, there exist non-ideational and ideationless *kalala* (embryonic stages) that circulate through various lands,
such as the earth-owl which fashions its young from clods of earth, and the mirror-cracking bird which embraces the fruit of a poisonous tree to raise its offspring.
When their offspring matured, both parents were devoured by them, and their kind filled the world.

This clarifies that it is not the case that there is no cause and effect regarding the state of non-perception. As for those who revolve in the cycle of enmity and harm, they were originally united yet have become estranged;
thus, enmity and harm arise. Those who fall into the inversion of killing likewise do so because they fail to realize that all sentient beings are of one single essence.
All these were parents, relatives, and kinsmen in previous lives; due to their delusion and ignorance, they devoured one another and became mutual enemies—is this not a perverse inversion?

This union of monsters to form the notion of eating one's own parents means that while parents love their children with boundless affection, seeking to repay such infinite kindness, [the children] now, in turn, forget that supreme grace.
"To love someone and yet harm them by eating them—this is truly unbearable. I wish to hear about this most extraordinary matter in the world.
It is not that they lack the perception of form; rather, the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages are like the earth-owl (*tuchāpa*), which takes a clod of earth as its offspring.
Since the clod of earth originally lacks the thought of being a parent, it is called 'without perception. Yet, through the incubation of the owl's egg, it ultimately becomes an owl."

Because they regard food as being like their parents, it is said that they are not without thought (*asaṃjñin*). Regarding the "earth-owl" (*tǔxiāo*) and the "broken mirror" (*pòjìng*, *kapiñjala*), according to the *Shiji* (Records of the Grand Historian), in the "Basic Annals of Emperor Xiaowu," it states: "In the sacrifice to the Yellow Emperor, one uses a *xiāo* and a *pòjìng*.

Meng Kang explains: "*Xiāo* is the name of a bird that eats its mother; *pòjìng* is the name of a beast that eats its father. The Yellow Emperor wished to exterminate these species, so he used [their flesh] for the sacrifice. It says "one hundred... [to indicate the number of offerings].
In the sacrifices to spirits, all [of these] are used. The "broken mirror" (pòjìng) is like a *chú* (a wild beast) with tiger-like eyes;
that it is now called a "bird" (*niǎo*) is likely an error by the translator, or perhaps the character "bird" should have been "equal" (*děng*), which was later arbitrarily altered.

If one consults Dàojiān Fǎshī’s “Proclamation Against Māra” (*Xiémó wén*), which states, "The *xiāo* and *zhì* arise in competition," then "mirror" (*jìng*) should indeed be "zhì. These two types above are [the first].
This is the transformation of separation.
These are called the twelve types of sentient beings;
they are designated as numerical categories.

Ānanda, it is thus: within each and every category of sentient beings, there are likewise each possessed of twelve inversions, just as...

By pressing upon the eyes, the chaotic flowers arise, giving birth to perversion; thus, the wondrous, perfect, truly pure, and luminous mind is endowed with such empty and delusive discursive thoughts.
This phrase connects what precedes with what follows. As for the statement that "each possesses [them]," it means that within each instance of perversion, one individually possesses ten.

The two are inversions; one is manifest while the other remains latent. Although each is said to be fully endowed with twelve types of chaotic thoughts, when one investigates their source, they are all inversions of the wondrously perfect true mind. They possess no substantial reality whatsoever;
rather, they arise from the ignorance that perfumes the True Suchness (tathatā), forming defiled functions that constitute the twelve classes of sentient beings.
The section on causes is concluded. Hereafter, it is explained how True Suchness (tathatā) permeates ignorance to produce pure functions, which serve as the cause for the fifty-five stages of Bodhi.
You are now practicing and realizing the Buddha’s samādhi; based upon this original cause of deluded thought, three gradual stages are established.

Only then can it be eliminated, just as when one removes poisonous honey from a clean vessel, washes that vessel with various decoctions and mixed ashes and perfumes, and subsequently stores clarified butter (*ghṛta*) within it. What are called the three gradual stages?
First, practicing to eliminate its auxiliary causes; second, authentic cultivation to excise its primary nature; third, advancing to oppose its manifest karma.
This clarifies that purity is established by reversing defilement. The "original cause" refers to the cause of inversion.

Regarding the establishment of the three gradual stages based on this original cause of deluded thought, it is taught that one must reverse defilement to achieve purity by taking action precisely where the defilement arises—what is called "arising in this very place and ceasing in that very place.
Therefore, the former masters said: "Shadows arise from forms; echoes follow..."

When sound comes, one toils with the body to manipulate its shadow, yet fails to realize that the body is the very source of the shadow; when sound is raised, one strives to silence the echo, yet does not know that the sound is the origin of the echo.
To eliminate afflictions while seeking nirvana is like discarding the body to search for the shadow;

to distance oneself from sentient beings while seeking the fruit of Buddhahood is like remaining silent while searching for an echo. Thus we know that delusion and awakening are one path, and that the wise and the ignorant are not two.
This is to say that when one cultivates and realizes the Buddha’s samādhi, one must enter through the fundamental cause of the originally disordered thoughts.
The metaphor of the floating vessel represents the essence of the true mind inherently present within the faculties, which is fundamentally pure from the beginning;

"removing the poison and honey" represents eliminating the auxiliary causes and hollowing out the false nature; and "washing the vessel with ash-water" represents contravening and exhausting current karmic activities.
The subsequent "storing of nectar" is a metaphor for attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) and being securely established in the stage of a sage.

As for the passage beginning with "How," it sets forth the names of the gradual stages; it means that if one wishes to cultivate the perfect penetration of the ear-organ, one must first establish these three kinds of gradual stages before one can attain realization and entry.
The "auxiliary cause" refers to the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), while the "true nature" refers to the root of birth and death.

Fundamentally, causes and conditions manifest karma; these are the root-condition, the object-condition, and the field-condition. If one removes these three types of conditions, then the Dharma of ambrosial quiescence will be revealed. It is asked: "What level does this fall under? The original answer states: "The Noble Truths do not belong to any level whatsoever.
Thus, one knows that dharmas have no gradual progression; gradual progression arises from the person.

The Tathāgata observes capacities and adapts his teaching, forcibly establishing a gradual sequence within that which has no gradual sequence, and forcibly establishing steps where there are no steps—this is for those of the highest faculties.
To know that which is illusory is itself to leave it; to leave the illusory is itself awakening—how could there be any gradual stages? What are the auxiliary causes?
Ānanda, these twelve classes of beings in this world cannot sustain themselves by their own power;
they abide by means of the four kinds of nutriment, namely: edible food, contact-food, volition-food, and consciousness-food. Therefore, the Buddha said that all sentient beings...
"Ānanda, all beings dwell in dependence upon food; they live because they eat what is sweet, and they die because they eat poison.
Therefore, those who seek samādhi must sever the five kinds of pungent vegetables of the world. These five pungent vegetables, when eaten cooked, arouse lust;
when eaten raw, they increase anger. Thus, in this world, those who eat pungent things, even if they can proclaim the twelve [dhātus],"
The celestial immortals (*deva-rṣi*) of the ten directions loathe their foul stench and all depart from them;

various hungry ghosts (*preta*), taking advantage of the time they eat, lick their lips and mouths, constantly dwelling with them so that their merit and virtue daily diminish, resulting in long-term lack of benefit.

For those who consume pungent roots while practicing *samādhi*, the Bodhisattvas, celestial immortals, and benevolent deities of the ten directions will not come to protect them, nor will those of great power.
The Mara King, seizing an opportunity, manifests in the form of a Buddha and comes to preach the Dharma to them; he reviles the prohibitions and precepts while praising lust, anger, and ignorance.
At the end of their lives, they become members of the Mara King’s retinue. Once their demonic blessings are exhausted, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
Ānanda, those who cultivate Bodhi must forever sever the five pungent roots; this is called the first stage of progressive advancement in cultivation.
This is a separate explanation regarding the removal of auxiliary causes. That which is most essential for the daily use of sentient beings is food and drink;
if there were no food and drink, life could not be sustained. Therefore, one dwells in reliance upon the four kinds of nutriment. Master Tanzi said:
"Oxen can be made to carry burdens, horses can be made to draw carriages, hawks can be made to strike, and dogs can be made to guard. Thus we know.

The twelve classes of sentient beings all subsist by means of food, and since food is that upon which the life-faculty depends, one must carefully distinguish between what is wholesome and what is poisonous.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Food benefits the sense faculties, the primary elements, and the mind and mental factors;

because it can produce joy and pleasure and maintain their continuity, there are four kinds. Regarding the first, *kavaḍīkāra-āhāra* (edible food), the original text says: "It is called *piṇḍa* (lump)."
The Tang monk Yijing translated *āhāra* as "segmental food" (*duànshí*), meaning food consisting of distinct portions or segments.

It is called "food" because, at the time when the three factors of odor, flavor, and tangibility in the desire realm are being properly digested and transformed, they possess the quality of providing nourishment and benefit.

As for "contact-nutriment" (*sparśāhāra*), it refers to the conjunction of the three—sense organ, object, and consciousness—which is capable of inducing the arising of contact associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), thereby confronting and engaging with the preceding [object].
The object that can produce joy and bliss, benefiting the sense faculties as well as the mind and mental factors, is what is called "food.

This refers to volition (*cetanā*) associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which operates in conjunction with desire (*chanda*) toward a desirable object; its predominant aspiration toward such an object possesses the quality of providing benefit.

As for "consciousness-food" (*vijñānāhāra*), it refers to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which abides by means of the aforementioned three types of food, supported by the conditions provided by those three types of food.

The eighth essence, the "auxiliary power," is called "nutriment" (*āhāra*) because it possesses a superior capacity to sustain the sense faculties and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and because it has the function of providing nourishment and benefit as a cause for the growth of all phenomena.
Generally speaking, these four types of nutriment may be complete or incomplete; while humans possess all of them, ghosts and spirits are satiated by the mere touch of food.

The gods of the *dhyāna* heavens subsist on the food of contact (*spraṣṭavya-āhāra*), and the gods of the *vijñāna* heavens subsist on the food of consciousness (*vijñāna-āhāra*). Since these have neither form nor color, they exist solely by virtue of consciousness and mental ideation.

As for the "five pungent vegetables" (*pañca-garaka*), they are leek, garlic, chives, scallion, and *hiṅgu*. The root of *hiṅgu* resembles a radish; it is pungent and foul-smelling when it emerges from the earth.
Because this plant does not exist in this region [of China], it is not translated. These five pungent vegetables are capable of inciting lust and increasing anger.
It must be severed. Thus, those below surpass the celestial immortals; the hungry ghosts loathe its foul stench and lick its lips, yet the Bodhisattvas do not come to provide protection.
The Māra gains the opportunity, whereby evils increase and merit wanes.
The dross remains near while the pure void recedes afar. If one does not sever and eliminate it, then day by day and month by month, one will gradually become [corrupted].
This is why the retinue of Māra must first eliminate those who have newly entered the Way.

How so? Ānanda, such sentient beings entering *samādhi* must first strictly maintain pure precepts, forever sever the mind of lust, abstain from wine and meat, eat food purified by fire, and never consume raw, living breath. Ānanda!
If a practitioner of the path does not sever lust and the taking of life, it is impossible for them to transcend the three realms.

One should contemplate sensual desire as being like a venomous snake or encountering a hostile thief. First, one should uphold the four parājikas and eight *śrāmaṇera*-śikṣāpadas of the śrāvaka, holding the body motionless;
subsequently, one practices the pure discipline of a bodhisattva, holding the mind so that it does not arise. Thus, the prohibitions and precepts are perfected.
Thus, in this world, there will forever be no karma of mutual birth or mutual killing; acts of theft and robbery will not occur, nor will there be mutual burdens of debt.
Furthermore, in this world, one shall not have to repay past debts. Such a person of purity, practicing *samādhi*, need not rely on the divine eye;
naturally, they will perceive the worlds of the ten directions with their own physical bodies, beholding the Buddhas, hearing the Dharma, and personally receiving the holy instructions.
Attaining great supernormal powers to roam through the worlds of the ten directions, with a pure past life and freedom from all hardships—this is called the second stage of progressive cultivation.

This specifically explains the "rectification of nature" (*zhengxing*); it is termed "correct" (*zheng*) in contrast to its "auxiliaries. For if [the tendencies of] lust and killing are firmly established...
That which exists as a thing does not depend on instruction to be able to arise together with the body and exist together with its nature;

it is the true nature of birth and death, and therefore it must be excised. Those who do not consume living energy—meaning those who lack sentience—still cannot bear to harm that which possesses life;
how much less so for those who possess sentience and have a life-force? This is also to prevent small evils from becoming great and to stop gradual developments before they become manifest.
The ultimate point is this: Gao Chai did not trim the square corners of his hair, and Liu Mochu did not clear the weeds from his courtyard; both were expressions of this same intent.
One should regard lustful desire as a venomous snake or a vengeful enemy, for it is invariably through this that the Dharma-body is harmed and the life of wisdom is damaged.
Since these two cannot coexist, if I do not harm it, it will certainly not harm me. If one views it in this way...
A venomous snake cannot be looked upon with intimacy, for it is like a hostile thief that one dares not approach;

thus the Sūtra says, "That which causes people to be deluded and obscured is love and desire," and it further says, "Only by departing from this gate does one emerge as a *arhat* from the net of dust.
Therefore, the venomous snake is used as a metaphor to teach and command observation. The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* states that Mañjuśrī said to the devas:

If you, my son, are single-minded and diligent, whenever a mind of greed arises within you, you should immediately recognize it and employ skillful means to dispel it, returning it to a state of tranquility.
How should you dispel it? You should reflect thus: "This is empty; this is impure.
Where does this desire that has arisen seek its origin? Where does it cease? From where does it come, and to what place does it go? Within it, there is nothing."

"Who is defiled? Who is attached? Who is the defiler? What is the phenomenon of defilement? When one contemplates in this way, one does not see the defiler, one does not see the defiled, and one does not see the act of defiling. Because these are not seen, there is no grasping;
because there is no grasping, there is no abandoning; because there is no abandoning, there is no receiving. Since there is neither abandoning nor receiving, then—
This is called the desire-free, tranquil Nirvana. To refrain from arising [evil] through the body is to not transgress the seven limbs of conduct;
to refrain from arising [evil] through the mind is for not a single thought to arise. By severing lust, one does not give rise to mutual rebirth;

by severing killing, one does not kill one another; by severing theft, one does not repay past debts. When the three karmas are thus eliminated, one is called a pure person who cultivates the Three [Trainings].

"Mudrā" (samādhi) refers to the cultivation of concentration based upon precepts. Regarding "observing the worlds of the ten directions with the fleshly eye," this is the sign of the exhaustion of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*);
as the subsequent text states: "The ten directions open wide, and there is no longer any darkness.

According to the stages, this corresponds to the first stage of faith (*prathama-śraddhā*), equivalent to the initial fruit of the Small Vehicle (*srotāpanna*). This is the time when a Bodhisattva first severs the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya-kleśa*). Beholding...

The four lines following the Buddha’s words describe the signs of the exhaustion of the *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). The subsequent text states: "Going and staying are free and easy, with no further obstructions," and again:
"Attaining the body of mental birth (*manomaya-kāya*), one proceeds wherever one goes without hindrance.

According to the stages, this corresponds to the second stage of faith (*śraddhā*) and the second fruit (*phala*), where past lives are pure and one encounters no hardships; these are the signs of the exhaustion of the *skandha* of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). The subsequent text [describes] this.
It is said that regarding the awakened, luminous mind, it is like removing dust and grime; throughout the beginning and end of a cycle of birth and death, there is perfect illumination.
What is now called "purity of past lives" refers to removing dust and grime so as to clearly perceive birth and death.

Furthermore, it is said that one attains freedom from hardship and peril because one has thoroughly penetrated past lives; if one were to set aside one's own power of aspiration, one would never again mistakenly enter the evil realms.

Therefore, one departs from the perilous difficulties of birth and death and the evil destinies. According to the stages, this corresponds to the fourth and fifth levels of faith, which are equivalent to the three small fruits [of the śrāvaka path].
