How so? Ānanda, in one who thus purely upholds the prohibitive precepts, the mind is free from greed and lust for external things.

The six sense objects do not cause further wandering because, by ceasing to wander, one returns to the source. When the objects no longer serve as conditions, the faculties have nothing with which to pair;
thus, the flow is reversed and the six functions cease. The lands of the ten directions become brilliantly pure, like a bright moon suspended within lapis lazuli.
Body and mind are blissful, wondrous, perfect, and equanimous, attaining great peace and stability in every respect.
The secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous [qualities] of the Tathāgata all manifest therein; this person immediately attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

From this point, they gradually cultivate according to their initial practices and establish themselves in the stages of the noble ones (*ārya-bhūmi*); this is called the third stage of progressive cultivation.

This is a specific explanation regarding the contradiction with present karma. Thus, a person who purely maintains the prohibitive precepts refers back to the aforementioned five faiths and three fruits;

by maintaining the precepts as the cause, they give rise to concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Because the nine grades of afflictions of thought (*karma-kleśa*) within the desire realm have already been exhausted, the mind is free from lustful craving.
Because there is no lustful craving internally, one does not flow excessively toward the external six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*).

The reason it is said that there is no such thing as "dissipation" where it is utterly non-existent is that within the sense-faculties (*indriya*), beginningless habitual tendencies have not yet been fully purified;
the objects (*viṣaya*) they correspond to still exist and manifest, and current karma has not yet been contravened.

For this reason, the following section clarifies that when the objects are forgotten and exhausted, the faculties finally contravene current karma. That is to say, once one no longer flows out toward external objects, one does not follow after those preceding sensory objects.
When the arising of knowledge and vision returns once more to the primordial *tathatā*, then externally there is nothing that enters and internally there is nothing that issues forth;
the sense organs and their objects do not meet, nor do they pair with one another. Only then can one turn back from the flow of desire and perfect the single brilliant clarity.
At this point, when the six sense organs encounter their objects, they no longer give rise to discrimination, for it is like a mirror reflecting images. Therefore it is said:

When the flow is reversed and the six functions cease to operate, this is precisely the sign that the aggregate of formative forces (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has been exhausted; it corresponds to what is said below:

"The six sense organs are empty and still, no longer wandering or escaping. According to the stages, this is equal to the seventh stage of faith and corresponds to the fourth fruit of the Small Vehicle.

Following the section on the ten directions, the subsequent manifestation of forgetting objects and exhausting the faculties represents the sign that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) has been exhausted; according to the stages, it corresponds to [the eighth stage].

The latter three stages of faith are simultaneous; because the faculties do not contact sensory objects, the world is pure, and thus one perceives the ten directions of the lands as transparent inside and out, like lapis lazuli with a bright moon suspended within. As the subsequent text states:
"When the aggregate of consciousness is exhausted, the worlds of the ten directions, along with body and mind, contain within them a precious moon, like vaidūrya."

As stated in the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* (*Yuánjué jīng*), when a single world is purified, and even up to many worlds being purified, because the sense objects do not intersect with the sense faculties, there is no binding;

thus, body and mind are blissful, and because the dimensions of body and mind are equal and unmoving, it is called "wondrously perfect and impartial," attaining great peace and stability. As stated in the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra*: [and so forth].
One should know that the four great elements are immovable; the nature of awakening is equally immovable, and because it is immovable, it is secure and peaceful.
Regarding "the secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous of all Tathāgatas": "secret" means it is esoteric, profound, firm, and remote, such that no one can reach it;
"perfect" means it is complete, mutually pervasive, and inclusively encompassing in infinite layers; "pure" means it is clear...
"Pure and luminous" means that because its essence is so refined and pure, not even a speck of dust can arise;
"wondrous" means that it is divinely subtle, such that all transformations and manifestations do not constitute any obstruction. These are the four virtues of the fruition.

"All are manifested therein" means that these virtues of fruition are all manifested within the mind of this person. This refers to what the Great Sūtra calls "the inexhaustible ocean of all dharma-gates."
When one universally assembles within the single Dharma site of the *bodhimaṇḍa*, this person immediately attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

This "person" refers to the aforementioned individual who purely maintains the prohibitive precepts; when their spiritual efficacy reaches this point, they no longer perceive the arising of even the slightest dharma, nor do they perceive the cessation of even the slightest dharma.
Only then do they attain the realization of the fruit-ground of non-arising and non-ceasing as the cause.
Because it is the mind of the ground, it is called "attaining the endurance of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), which refers to wisdom arising from meditative concentration.
All the *anutpattika-dharmakṣānti* realized by the various great patriarchs throughout the successive dynasties of this land are subsumed within this stage;

this corresponds to the Bodhisattva’s severing of the afflictions of thought (*klesha*) and the *rajas* (dust-like) afflictions. Regarding the phrase "gradually cultivating from here," this generally indicates what follows.

The assembly also said that by taking this non-arising and non-ceasing as the mind of the causal ground (*yin-di-xin*), one subsequently achieves the complete realization of the fruit-ground (*guo-di*).
This is because one first awakens to the Dharma-realm of Vairocana and subsequently cultivates the practice-gate of Samantabhadra. Therefore, the subsequent text states:
"Abiding establishes virtue; virtue establishes practice; practice establishes aspiration; and aspiration establishes the ground for severing delusions and realizing the truth."
All take this stage as their foundation. This answers the previous question regarding the gradual sequence by which one attains the goal of cultivation.
Ānanda, when these good men’s craving for existence has withered away, and the faculties and objects no longer meet, the remaining physical residue no longer continues to arise.
Their grasping mind becomes empty and luminous, consisting purely of wisdom; the nature of this wisdom is bright and perfect, polishing the ten directions and making the dry world moist.
This wisdom is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavipaśyanā-bhūmi*); the habit-energy of desire is first dried up, yet it has not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s stream of Dharma.

This refers to the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) contained within the preceding three gradual stages, which are here subsumed to manifest this initial Dry Wisdom.
As Mount Gan (Gushan) said: "The so-called unification of the ten faiths constitutes Dry Wisdom. [This concludes] the four [stages] of desire-love.
The first seven phrases indicate that the seeker of faith has already severed the afflictions of thought (*saṃyojana*) within the three realms and exhausted them;

thus, the conditions for rebirth in the three realms are utterly severed, and there is no longer any portion of existence through which one would receive a future birth. This is the state where concentration arises from precepts, which is the characteristic of having already exhausted the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).

The two phrases concerning "clinging to the mind" precisely manifest the exhaustion of the afflictions of thought and the dawning of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*). This corresponds to the Tiantai school’s [stage of] "Dwelling in the Truth."
The two phrases "exhausting the afflictions of thought and realizing all-knowledge" summarize the latter three stages of faith;

they correctly manifest that the nature of wisdom is perfectly luminous, its illuminating function pervading the entire realm. This reiterates the description from the preceding text regarding the state where the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) has been exhausted, which corresponds precisely to the Tiantai school’s stage of severing the "afflictions of dust" (*rajas-āvaraṇa*), suddenly opening the Dharma-eye, perceiving the principle of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and accomplishing the seeds of the Path.

This wisdom arises from concentration; thus, it is said that "concentration gives rise to wisdom. However, for a person of perfect capacity (*yuanren*), the original aspiration was not to sever the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava* and *bhāva-āsrava*) or the afflictions of the sands of the Ganges (*rajas*).
Their intent lay in entering and abiding [in the stages] to sever ignorance (*avidyā*) and perceive the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).

It is like smelting iron: coarse impurities are removed first, though this is not the primary objective, which is to produce a vessel. Before the vessel is complete, these impurities naturally fall away first; although they are seen to depart first, [they are not the intended goal].
That person does not have a single thought of joy; why is this? Because they have not yet accomplished what they intended. It is the same for the practitioner of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*):
although it was not their original intention, the obstructions are naturally severed first. Below, the text explains the reason for naming this stage "Dry Wisdom" (*ganhui*).
This is because among the three—present manifestations, seeds, and habit-energies—the habit-energy is the most subtle; now, as for the statement...

"The initial drying up of the habituation to desire" refers to the very subtle habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of craving for desire first becoming parched. These most subtle habitual tendencies are the nature of that which is to be severed (*prahātavya*).

Although the nature of what is to be severed has already vanished because the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vitarka-kleśa*) have been exhausted, the fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) remains entirely intact;
it has not yet come into contact with the water of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-stream. Therefore, it is said that "its wisdom is dry."

If one enters the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) and, by breaking through the divisions of ignorance, partially realizes the True Reality (*tattva*), then one connects with the Dharma-stream of the Tathāgata.

Question: Since it has already been stated that both "conduct" (*caryā*) and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) are exhausted, why does it further state that "the habit-energies of desire are only beginning to dry up" and that one has not yet connected with the Dharma-stream of the Tathāgata?

Answer: There are two explanations for this. First, regarding a person of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan-jiao*), there are the two types of delusions: the pervasive (*pian*) and the specific (*bie*). [The former refers to the delusions of the three realms, while the latter refers to the delusions of the two vehicles.]...

Simultaneously exhausting [the hindrances] all at once, one is able to transcend directly into the final mind of the Vajra stage; because the Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-jñāna*) does not pass through successive stages, the subsequent text says:
"If the aggregate of consciousness is exhausted, then your six present sense-faculties will function interchangeably.

From within this mutual functioning, you can enter the Bodhisattva’s Vajra Dry Wisdom. The perfectly luminous, refined essence of the mind gives rise to transformations therein, like pure lapis lazuli."
Like a precious moon contained within lapis lazuli, one thus transcends the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten dedications, the vajra-like stage, and the stage of equal enlightenment;
with perfect clarity, one enters the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornment, fulfilling Bodhi and returning to non-attainment.
As Avalokiteśvara’s state of cessation manifests before him, he suddenly transcends both the mundane and supramundane worlds.

This refers to attaining two kinds of excellence. If a person of the Perfect Teaching (yuanren) aims to sever the distinct delusions (biehuo), yet the pervasive delusions (tonghuo) are severed first, they will enter the initial Stage of Dry Wisdom (ganhui-di) and progress through the successive stages. Question:

Since the ten levels of faith (shixin) were already included within the aforementioned gradual sequence, and the Stage of Dry Wisdom was further consolidated into a single position, why are they opened up again in the following text?

The "Ten Faiths" (daśa-śraddhā) respond to the preceding [discussion]: the Ten Faiths mentioned previously merely serve as a general summary that binds together the beginning and end of the auxiliary and primary stages of perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-vyūha*) to serve as the skillful means for the initial mind of the subsequent stages.
However, the Ten Faiths that constitute the actual realization of the three voids (*trividha-śūnyatā*) through the process of perfect penetration actually reside after this [initial] stage;
they possess a distinct set of Ten Faiths whose names borrow from conventional usage but whose meaning is entirely different, as they are opened up at the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*).

Because it has emerged, this very mind flows inwardly into the center, becoming perfectly subtle and fully blossomed; from this true, wondrous, and perfect state, there again arises true, wondrous, and perfect faith.
This abiding in all things, where all delusive thoughts are extinguished without remainder and the Middle Way is purely true, is called the "Abode of Faith."
This clarifies that the abiding of the mind of faith is precisely the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*). This "mind" refers back to the preceding mind of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*).

Regarding "flowing into the center of the center": although the beginner in the cultivation of perfect penetration directly contemplates the nature of hearing without clinging to emptiness or existence, this is likewise the Middle Way of the absolute, numinous mind;
yet, while coarse defilements have first fallen away and both person and phenomena have been simultaneously eliminated, [the subtle defilements remain].

To be exempt from spontaneously tending toward the emptiness of perfect luminosity is not yet the pure Middle Way; only upon reaching this stage do all things become empty, such that the prior Middle Way no longer arises, and thus it becomes increasingly pure. Therefore, it is called "flowing into the Middle of the Middle," signifying that having reached the Middle and then the Middle again, one enters deeply in accordance with the flow of the Dharma. The mutual functioning of the six sense faculties is called "perfection" (*yuan*). As for "sentiment" (*qing*): The six faculties mutually function, and the five aggregates are completely fused. The three realms are like an illusion, and the four elements are like a dream. The ten thousand phenomena are originally non-existent, and the myriad dharmas are fundamentally empty. The mind-ground is vast and boundless, and the nature of reality is perfectly bright. The ocean of consciousness is tranquil and still, and the mirror of wisdom is clear and pure. The moon of the Tathāgata shines everywhere, and the sun of the Buddha illuminates all. The Dharma-body is eternally abiding, and the Nirmanakaya appears according to conditions. The Sambhogakaya is adorned with marks and signs, and the Dharma-realm is pervasive and unobstructed. The three bodies are one and the same, and the four wisdoms are non-dual. The eight consciousnesses are transformed, and the five eyes are fully opened. The six supernatural powers are spontaneously attained, and the three liberations are naturally realized. The great compassion is impartial, and the great vow is inexhaustible. The wheel of the Dharma turns without ceasing, and the banner of victory is raised high.

The great assembly gathers like clouds, and the sublime teachings rain down like dew. Sentient beings are guided according to their capacities, and the path is revealed to those who seek it. The light of the Dharma dispels the darkness, and the fragrance of virtue pervades the world. All afflictions are extinguished, and all obstacles are removed. The ocean of suffering is dried up, and the mountain of ignorance is leveled. The city of Nirvana is entered, and the palace of liberation is reached. This is the ultimate fruit of the Bodhisattva path, the supreme state of the Tathagata. May all beings attain this realization, and together reach the shore of enlightenment.

Regarding "the vessel transcends both to become wondrously blossomed": this refers to being like a flower that has just begun to open. The following two phrases clarify that by means of this opening of the mind, one's progress increases further.
"From the truly wondrous and perfect" means that this is not like the previous stages where it was merely similar to the wondrous and similar to the perfect;
rather, it is the truly wondrous and the truly perfect. The repetition of "truly wondrous" is intended to cause that which is truly wondrous to advance even further.

Regarding "wondrous true perfection," one further advances toward the perfect; this should be understood as the faculties and objects mutually pervading one another, with the body and the land becoming increasingly vast and layered, like a flower in full bloom.
"Wondrous faith" refers to personally seeing that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated, which is a faith beyond mere analogy or inference.
"Permanently abiding" means being firm and immovable, unlike the lightness of the preceding stages.
If the delusive thoughts like a goose’s down are extinguished, then the notions of self, phenomena, and non-phenomena will surely be swept away simultaneously;
this is also the cessation of the views of the holy and the ordinary, and the forgetting of the sentiments regarding cause and effect.

The final two lines summarize the preceding meaning to establish the mind of faith; for this pure and true Middle Way is not like the previous stages, which were still accompanied by a tendency toward emptiness.
Furthermore, because one personally perceives this principle and deeply endures it with joyful aspiration, it is called "faith" (*śraddhā*); this is the mark of its accomplishment.
"Abiding" means dwelling permanently in non-retrogression. All that follows is based on this.

Moreover, since this stage incorporates what was accomplished during the preceding stage of "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*), and since dry wisdom itself combines the ten stages of faith contained within the three gradual approaches, one knows that this stage represents the ultimate consummation.
Having completed the preceding ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), one arrives at fulfillment; this is why the "Abiding in Faith" (*śraddhā-vihāra*) is uniquely highlighted.
If it were merely the initial stage of the common ten faiths, how could it possibly correspond to such meanings as "perfect, wondrous, eternally abiding," and "the absence of all delusive thoughts"?
Gusuan (Gushan) said: "The ten faiths below, although identical in name to the ten faiths in other sutras, [differ in their meaning]..."
Since each name below is concluded with the term "abiding" (zhù), we know that these refer to the initial abidings (*prathamābhūmi*).
How much more so when it is said that the Middle Way is "pure and true"—how could this be a stage of semblance?

Thus, we know that from beginning to end, this sutra employs nothing but the wondrous contemplation of the Middle Way to contemplate the eternally abiding, wondrous principle. If it were not thus, how else could this sutra be revealed?

From "Pure and Perfect" (*chúnyuán*) onwards, up to the Ten Dedications (*shíhuíxiàng*), one should arouse the mind of practice and understanding (*jièxíng fāxīn*) as described in the *Awakening of Faith*.
With true faith and clear understanding, one realizes that the three—aggregates (*yīn*), bases (*chù*), and elements (*jiè*)—are entirely interpenetrating and cannot act as obstructions.
Thus it continues until all habitual tendencies (*xíqì*) from the countless kalpas of past and future, involving the casting off and receiving of bodies, manifest before one.
These good sons are all able to recollect everything without any loss; this is called the dwelling of the mind of mindfulness (*smṛti-citta-vihāra*).

The dwelling of the mind of mindfulness is precisely the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*). The first two phrases trace back to the preceding stage to give rise to the "perfect penetration" (*yuan-tong*):
because every faculty and every object pervades the Dharma-realm, it is termed "all-encompassing perfect penetration. By virtue of this all-encompassing perfect penetration...

Therefore, because the *skandhas* cannot conceal it, the *āyatanas* cannot confine it, and the *dhātus* cannot obstruct it, one is consequently able to recollect the past for countless *kalpas*, as well as the bodies one has cast off and will receive in the future for countless *kalpas*.

Even the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and habitual perfumings (*vāsanā*) conditioned by the power of karma all manifest before one; such a person is able to remember them all with perfect clarity, without any omission.
The loss of these [two faculties] pertains to the two supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*) and the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

Regarding "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*), according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, three types are not distinguished: those of names and words (*nāma-pada*), self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*), and the links of existence (*bhava-aṅga*).

What is here called the "feeling of equanimity" (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is mostly the link of existence, which is the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*). However, the term "all" (*sarva*) necessarily includes the other two as well. If it occurs within the state of self-clinging, then...
This refers to the subtle habitual shadows left behind by seeds during the stage of attachment to dharmas—such as the pride of Piṅgala or the anger of Śāriputra.

Furthermore, the distinction between these two stages is that the former is the stage of deep faith in the inherently existing Buddha-nature, while this stage is the stage of recollecting and cultivating the nature of the seeds.
This is the reason for the difference between these two positions.

The wondrous, perfect, and pure reality gives rise to transformation through its essential purity; this permeates the habitual tendencies of beginningless time into a single, unified luminous clarity.
To advance toward true purity solely by means of this luminous clarity is called the "mind of diligence.
This mind of diligence is precisely the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*). The first four phrases trace back to the preceding two stages to establish the single character "purity" (*śuddha*).
"Also, 'refining the essence' refers to the power of the wondrous, perfect, and pure contemplation gradually becoming refined and bright over time.

'Emitting transformation' means that the wisdom of contemplation is so powerful it can initiate the functional capacity to melt away delusions. This is because transformation arises from refinement, and refinement is further enhanced by transformation.
The next two lines follow upon the mind of mindfulness; the upper line directly follows [the previous], while the lower line clarifies its [nature]."
Because the preceding habitual tendencies are melted away without remainder and all become wisdom, it is said that "one penetrates the single refined brilliance.

This is because in the previous stage, there were still fundamental and adventitious tendencies that had not yet merged into one; reaching this point, they are entirely melted into the single essence of the body of wisdom.
The next two phrases build upon the character "refined" (*jing*) from before by adding the character "advance" (*jin*), thereby establishing the two qualities of refinement and diligence.
"Principle" (*yi*) refers to clarity and brilliance, which is the essence of *bodhi* and also the essence of the wisdom of *tathatā*.

"True purity" (*zhenjing*) refers to the essence of *nirvāṇa* and also the essence of the principle of *tathatā*. Now, by advancing from clarity and brilliance toward true purity, one is purely employing the wisdom of *tathatā* to accord with the principle of *tathatā*.
Yongjia said: "If one can but untie the soiled garment within one's breast, who else could [attain it]?"
To boast of one's diligence toward others is what this refers to.
When the essence of mind manifests before one, being purely characterized by wisdom, it is called the "abiding of the wisdom-mind.

This abiding of the wisdom-mind is precisely the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). At the higher stage, the habitual tendencies of delusion are transformed into wisdom; this clarifies the nature of delusion.
When [the defilements] are exhausted, the wisdom-mind manifests, and the essence of Bodhi is no longer subject to false admixture. Question:

Why is "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*) not called a "dwelling," while this stage is called a "dwelling"? Answer: It is because it was previously stated that the mind of grasping is empty and luminous, yet there is still grasping present;
whereas here it is said that the essence of the mind manifests before one, such that that grasping is completely integrated and transformed. It was previously described as "pure" alone...
This wisdom still retains a trace of "is-ness" here; when it is said to be "purely wisdom," it means that in daily life, everywhere one acts is wisdom, and even the notion of "is-ness" is forgotten.
Because of this function—meaning that one recognizes the treasure and is able to employ it—this wisdom is called "abiding.
To recognize the treasure and be able to employ it is why this wisdom is named "abiding."
The sustained clarity of wisdom, which is all-pervasive, tranquil, profound, and eternally concentrated, is called the "abiding of the settled mind.
This abiding of the settled mind is itself the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). In the preceding stage, because the mind was seen to be brilliantly penetrating, wisdom was purely clear;
however, if this clarity of wisdom were not sustained by the power of concentration, deluded thoughts would arise, causing it to become partial and localized rather than all-pervasive.
When right mindfulness is lost and interrupted, it is not constant; this so-called "illumination without stillness" is like a lamp in the wind.
Therefore, it is called "universal stillness" (*biàn jì*) and also "constant concentration" (*cháng níng*), both of which are characteristics of the Great Samādhi.
This is what is meant by "the unmoving single mind entering all dhyānas. These five are all called "roots" because they are like the roots of a fruit-bearing tree.
The light of Samantaprabha illuminates the luminous nature, entering deeply with only progress and no retreat; this is called the "Non-retrogressive Mind.

The Non-retrogressive Mind is itself the power of progress (*vīrya-bala*). From this point downward, it belongs to the five powers (*pañca-balāni*), just as when the roots of a fruit tree have been established for a long time, they possess an irresistible force.
Thus, "the light of Samantaprabha illuminates" means that wisdom arises from meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Furthermore, those who have deeply penetrated the nature of clarity speak of not dwelling in clarity; it is like polishing a mirror, where the more one polishes, the clearer it becomes, and as this clarity continues without end, it is called "deep penetration.
Because of this deep penetration, there is only progress and no retreat, which is why it is named "Non-retrogression."

The mind advances with serenity, maintaining its state without loss; the interconnection of the vital energy (*prāṇa*) of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions is called the "mind that protects the Dharma.
This mind that protects the Dharma is precisely the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Regarding "the mind advancing with serenity":

although one previously did not regress and remained diligent and uninterrupted, there was still the involvement of effortful cultivation; here, although one is vigorous, no sign of exertion is perceived.
Therefore it is said: "Tranquilly maintain the mind; reaching tranquility, one moves with ease and expansiveness, forever preserving the state of non-abiding.
But what is that which is maintained? And what is that which is not lost? It is the life-vein of the Dharma-body of all Buddhas.
By maintaining this life-vein of the Dharma-body without loss, one naturally attains union with all [Buddhas].
Because the Buddha’s breath and one's own are mutually pervasive and perfectly integrated, it is called "protecting the Dharma" (*dharmapāla*).
With awakened clarity, one maintains and preserves this state, using wondrous power to turn the Buddha’s compassionate light back toward the Buddha and abide therein;

it is like two mirrors facing each other, their radiance intermingling so that their wondrous reflections enter into one another in infinite layers—this is called the "mind of dedication" (*pariṇāmanā-citta*).

The mind of dedication is the power of wisdom. The first phrase refers to the wondrous power of the awakened essence sustained by the preceding power of concentration; this is indeed the power of wisdom.

Although previously one’s affinity with the Tathāgata was first established through contact with the Buddha’s compassionate light and was sustained by his grace, there still remained a distinction between self and other.
Now, however, one further employs one's own wondrous power to redirect the Buddha’s compassionate light back toward himself.
Abiding in the Buddha of one's own mind, there is truly no duality; like eye meeting eye, mind illuminates mind.
The mind does not depart from the Buddha, nor does the Buddha depart from the mind. Like two mirrors reflecting one another, their radiance is transmitted without end;
therefore, it is called dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

When the light of the mind subtly turns back, one attains the Buddha’s constant, supreme, wondrously pure, and unconditioned abiding; having attained this without loss, it is called the "abiding of the mind in precepts.

This abiding of the mind in precepts is precisely the power of faith. The first phrase follows upon the preceding "subtle turning of the light of the mind," as one has already attained one's own nature.
The body of the Tathāgata of Unmoving Original Nature abides in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) without the slightest leakage into the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
To allow even a single drop to infiltrate the conditioned is called breaking the precepts; thus, as the mind becomes increasingly subtle and dense, the precepts become increasingly strict.
This is what is meant by the "Buddha-nature precept-jewel" being forever without loss, and is therefore called the "precept-mind."

Abiding in the mastery of ethical discipline (*śīla-vaśitā*), one is able to travel throughout the ten directions; wherever one goes, it accords with one's vows—this is called the "abiding of the mind of aspiration" (*praṇidhāna-citta-vihāra*).
The abiding of the mind of aspiration is precisely the power of mindfulness (*smṛti-bala*). The first phrase follows upon the preceding [section]:

having already established the essence of the immovable mind through abiding in ethical discipline, this now gradually brings forth the function of mastery. Thus, there is no request that is not fulfilled and no destination that is not accessible; therefore, [the text says...]

If one who has departed according to their wishes can proceed with such carefulness and circumspection even among the "Man" and "Mo" barbarians, how much more so for one who dwells in the mastery of the precepts without any forced effort—what place could they not reach? The Ten Faiths are concluded.

Ānanda, these good sons, through true skillful means, give rise to these ten minds; as their mental essence radiates brilliance and these ten functions interpenetrate one another, they perfect a single mind—this is called the Abiding of the Arising of the Mind.
This clarifies the first stage of the resolve for enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*), which corresponds to the "resolve through faith" (*śraddhā-cittotpāda*) in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
Regarding "true skillful means": it refers to the re-emergence of the true and wondrous from within the true, wondrous, and perfect [nature].

That is to say, although the ten mental states and their wondrous functions are inherently complete within the mind of True Suchness (*tathatā*), they can never be brought forth without skillful means; therefore, one now relies upon True Suchness.
Thus, one gives rise to these ten kinds of wondrous minds, in which not even a hair’s breadth of defilement can find entry;
they are purely wisdom, and the mind is thus refined. Once the mind is refined, its radiance becomes ever more manifest, and the five faculties and five powers are all fully perfected.
Thus, the one mind is the ten minds, and the ten minds are the one mind; they interpenetrate in layers upon layers, fundamentally possessing no dual nature.
Because the mind is entirely perfected and fulfilled, it is called the "Abiding in the Production of the Thought" (Cittotpāda-vihāra).

Thus, one should know that apart from these ten preceding minds, there is no separate essence for this abiding. As for the term "production of the thought," it means that from the single mind, the ten minds are initiated;
through these ten minds, the beginning of the mind is established, and the myriad practices are fully realized. The subsequent sections do not go beyond an expansion of these ten minds.
Because it leads to the ultimate ear, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "At the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one immediately attains perfect awakening.

Tiantai’s commentary explains: "First generating the mind" refers to the name of the First Stage (*prathama-bhūmi*). "Immediately attaining perfect awakening" refers to the realization of the Eightfold Manifestation of Buddhahood (*aṣṭākāra-abhisambodhi*).

This is the fruit of partial realization (*pradeśa-prativedha*). If one were to claim that [the Bodhisattva] has already attained the stage of Sublime Awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), then all the subsequent stages from the Second Stage onward would be rendered superfluous.
The "initial aspiration for enlightenment" mentioned previously refers precisely to this. It is like the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which takes up prior karma to form its own aggregate-body.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* further states: "The initial aspiration and the ultimate [enlightenment] are not two;
of these two minds, the former is more difficult. Tiantai’s commentary explains: "This clarifies the principle that subtle consciousness is non-dual. Thus, the Dragon Girl immediately...

Since all śrāvakas who have attained perfect enlightenment and received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of future Buddhahood possess the characteristics of attaining Buddhahood at this very stage, the *Zongjing* states: "This bodhicitta possesses great power;
it is like the sinew of a lion for a bowstring, like a lion’s roar, like a vajra-hammer, and like Nārāyaṇa’s arrow; it is fully endowed with all treasures and is able to..."
It eliminates poverty and suffering like a wish-fulfilling jewel; even if one is slightly indolent or slightly lapses in dignified conduct, it still surpasses the merits of the three vehicles.
To state the essential point: this mind itself possesses all the virtues of a bodhisattva and can accomplish the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of the three periods of time.
For this reason, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* extensively praises the inexhaustible merits of this mind. (6)
Upon hearing the passage in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* concerning "generating the mind without abiding anywhere," the Patriarch suddenly attained awakening and said:
"How unexpected that the self-nature is originally pure! How unexpected that the self-nature is originally perfect and luminous!
How unexpected that the self-nature is originally complete! Only then can it be called the true and correct generation of the bodhicitta. If one follows the Flower Garland [Sūtra]...

This Bodhisattva adorns their resolve by taking ten kinds of dharmas as its object: namely, the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible; the knowledge of the retribution of good and evil karma;
the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of sentient beings; the knowledge of the differences in various inclinations;

the knowledge of the differences in various elements; the knowledge of the paths leading to all destinations; the knowledge of the meditative concentrations, liberations, and samādhis; and unimpeded knowledge of past lives.
The wisdom of the divine eye is unimpeded; the wisdom that all outflows throughout the three periods of time are universally exhausted. Why is this?

It is because one desires to cause the bodhisattva’s mind to expand further within the Buddha-dharma, so that whatever Dharma they hear is immediately understood by themselves rather than being awakened to through another.
From this stage up to the tenth bhūmi, the bodhisattva should sever (extinguish the characteristics of dwelling in difference), namely, ignorance which is called "exhaustion."
Hearing that the perceiving subject does not abide and that the perceived object is empty,

one illuminates within the mind as if pure lapis lazuli reveals refined gold within; because one treads upon this wondrous primordial mind to accomplish the stages, it is called the Dwelling of Cultivating the Ground (*bhūmi-kāra-bhūmi*).

This clarifies the second stage, the Dwelling of the Ground of Purification (*śuddhābhūmi-vihāra*). The first phrase follows upon the preceding metaphors: the lapis lazuli for wisdom and the refined gold for principle.
That which was previously called the "wondrous mind" is the mind of the first dwelling (*prathamabhūmi*) accomplished through the ten functions;
this serves as the foundational ground, finally becoming fit for treading. From this point on, at every step one’s feet tread upon solid ground, at all times and in all circumstances.

Because one borrows sentient beings as the locus to train and purify the ground of the mind, whereby all wholesome dharmas naturally arise and great compassion increases, it is called the Ground of Purification (*bhūmi-viśodhana*).
This is like the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which, driven by the power of karma, forms its own objective sphere and serves as its basis of support.
As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "This bodhisattva gives rise to ten kinds of minds toward all sentient beings."

That is to say: a mind of benefit, a mind of great compassion, a mind of peace and happiness, a mind of steadfast abiding, a mind of pity, a mind of gathering, a mind of protection, a mind of a teacher, and a mind of a guide.
Why is this? Because they desire to cause sentient beings to increase their great compassion toward all Bodhisattvas;
by possessing these ten minds, the mind-ground is naturally governed without being intentionally cultivated.
When the mind-ground and its cognitive functions both attain clarity, and one traverses the ten directions without obstruction, this is called the Stage of Cultivation (Pratipatti-vihāra).
This clarifies the third stage, the Stage of Cultivation. The first phrase refers back to what preceded it:

having taken the ten minds and traversed them to form the ground, one then proceeds through the spheres of seeing forms and hearing sounds, amidst the daily activities of movement and stillness; thus, each and every day—

To see and hear with true, singular clarity, without confusion or error, and to traverse the ten directions in this manner—moving spontaneously and freely without obstruction—is what is called "passing through a grove of hundred-petaled flowers without a single leaf clinging to one's body.
Is it not fitting to call this dwelling in cultivation? It is like seeing distant objects in the intermediate state as if they were right before one's eyes.
What was previously mentioned regarding moving swiftly without being obstructed by mountain crags or walls is as follows. A Great Sūtra states:

"This Bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena through ten modes of practice, namely: all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, non-self, uncreated, flavorless, not as they are named, locationless, free from conceptual discrimination, and lacking solidity. When one contemplates phenomena in this way, what obstruction can there be?"
Possessing these qualities,

his conduct becomes identical to that of a Buddha; receiving the Buddha’s spiritual influence like an intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) seeking its parents, he attains a profound and mysterious communion and enters the lineage of the Tathāgata—
this is called the Stage of Noble Birth (*janmaja-vihāra*).
This is the fourth stage, the Dwelling Born of Noble Lineage. The first phrase refers back to the Great Sūtra, which states:
"This Bodhisattva is born from the holy teaching and accomplishes ten dharmas, namely: never regressing; generating profound pure faith toward all Buddhas;
skillfully examining phenomena; and thoroughly understanding sentient beings, lands, worlds, karmic actions, retributions, birth, and death."

Nirvāṇa can also fully comprehend all Buddha-dharmas of the three periods of time, cultivate and accumulate all Buddha-dharmas of the three periods of time, bring to perfection all Buddha-dharmas of the three periods of time, and understand the equality of all Buddhas. Why is this?
It is because one desires to advance further so that the mind attains equality within the three periods of time. When one's practice is thus, then...
To be borne upon the shoulders of the Tathāgata is to be covered by the Tathāgata’s robe;
to receive the Buddha’s *dhātu* (elemental essence) such that what was previously obstructed becomes permeable and what was excluded becomes included—this is to uphold the Buddha’s physical legacy.

At the initial entrustment to the holy womb, it is just as when a prince dwells in the womb, his noble status surpassing all ministers; therefore, this is called "Birth from Nobility. What was previously termed the "interconnection of *dhātu*" refers to this.
This is like two things becoming one; here it is said that receiving the Buddha’s portion of energy and entering the Tathāgata-lineage is nearly the same as becoming one.
This is like the intermediate state (antarābhava) merging with the parents and their karma in a single place.

Having already roamed within the womb of the Way and personally received the lineage of the Awakened One, just as one who has been fully formed in the womb possesses all human features without deficiency, this is called the "Abode of Fulfillment through Skillful Means.
This is the fifth abode of skillful means. The first phrase, "personally receiving the lineage of the Awakened One," refers to gathering in the Buddha.

The two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate reality coalesce to form the "sacred embryo. This is like the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) seizing the two drops of red and white [semen and blood] to form the embryo;
once the fetal form has developed and the human features are complete, it is said that the six sense organs (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are perfected.
Just as one who is fully endowed with all skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) to deliver sentient beings bears a resemblance to the Buddha without any deficiency, so too is this stage.
The intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) possesses the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) fully developed and resembles its parents. As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"All the roots of goodness cultivated by this Bodhisattva are for the purpose of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings, benefiting all sentient beings, bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, having compassion for all sentient beings, and liberating all sentient beings. It causes all...

Because sentient beings are freed from calamities, born beyond birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), have given rise to pure faith, are all thoroughly tamed, and realize *nirvāṇa*, it is called "endowed with skillful means" (*upāya*).
Their physical appearance is like that of a Buddha, and their mental characteristics are likewise identical; thus, it is named the "Abiding in the Right Mind" (*samyakcittavihāra*).

This explains the sixth stage, the Abiding in Right Mindfulness (*samyaktva-cittatā-vihāra*). The first phrase, "the characteristics of the mind are likewise as before," means that the mind is also identical to that of a Buddha.
As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "When this Bodhisattva hears ten kinds of teachings, his mind remains fixed and unmoving.

That is to say, hearing praise of the Buddha or disparagement of the Buddha, his mind remains fixed and unmoving; hearing praise of the Dharma or disparagement of the Dharma, his mind remains fixed and unmoving... [and so forth].

The Bodhisattva remains steadfast and unwavering in mind when disparaging the bodhicitta; remains steadfast and unwavering in mind when praising the conduct of a bodhisattva or disparaging the conduct of a bodhisattva;
remains steadfast and unwavering in mind when speaking of sentient beings as being finite or infinite, easy to deliver or difficult to deliver;
and remains steadfast and unwavering in mind when speaking of the Dharma as being finite or infinite, subject to formation or destruction, existent or non-existent. Only...
The first is called the Dwelling of the Rectified Mind because it is unmoved by anything; were there even a hair’s breadth of mental movement, its rectitude would be lost.
Thus, a verse from the *Ratnakūṭa* praising the Buddha says: "Unmoved by praise or blame, like Mount Sumeru, one regards the good and the bad with equal compassion."
The integration of body and mind, increasing day by day, is called the Stage of Non-retrogression (*avinivartanīya-vihāra*).
This clarifies the seventh stage, Non-retrogression. The first phrase refers back to what preceded, meaning that the internal and external are of one suchness (*yathābhūta*).
"Increasing day by day" means that through nurturing and incubation, there is gradual growth. As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says: "This bodhi..."

Whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, whether there is the Dharma or no Dharma, whether there is a Bodhisattva or no Bodhisattva, whether there is the practice of a Bodhisattva or no practice of a Bodhisattva—

whether the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of practice leads to deliverance or not, and whether the mind is non-retrogressive— [the Bodhisattva] hears that there were Buddhas in the past or no Buddhas in the past,
that there will be Buddhas in the future or no Buddhas in the future, and that there are Buddhas in the present or no Buddhas in the present. His mind [remains steadfast].

Non-retrogression means that upon hearing that the Buddha’s wisdom is both finite and infinite, and that the three periods of time are of a single characteristic and yet not of a single characteristic, the mind does not regress;
because it is immovable, it is called non-retrogression.
The simultaneous perfection of the spiritual characteristics of the ten bodies is named the Stage of Youthful Truth (Kumārabhūmi).
This clarifies the eighth stage, the Stage of Youthful Truth (*kumārabhūmi*). Regarding the ten bodies (*daśakāya*), they are:

the body of enlightenment (*bodhikāya*), the body of vows (*praṇidhānakāya*), the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), the body of power (*balakāya*), the body of adornment (*vyūhakāya*), the body of majesty (*anubhāvakāya*), the mind-born body (*manomayakāya*), the body of merit (*puṇyakāya*), the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*).
Whereas previously one was merely increasing [these qualities], here one possesses them fully; however, while the Tathāgata’s wisdom, virtues, and marks are present, they are still subtle and minute.
Because his power is not yet fully perfected, he is called "Childlike Truth" (*kumārabhūta*). A great sutra states: "This bodhisattva abides in ten kinds of activities, namely:

bodily action, verbal action, and mental action, which are without fault; taking birth at will; knowing the various desires, various understandings, various elements, and various karmas of sentient beings;
knowing the formation and destruction of worlds; and mastery over the supernormal power of spiritual travel (*ṛddhi*) in all that he undertakes."
Furthermore, being unimpeded, they know all Buddha-fields, as well as the service and offerings made to countless Buddhas within all those fields;
because they are fully endowed with ten kinds of karma, the auspicious marks of the ten bodies are also simultaneously perfected.
The formation [of the body] is called the "Abode of the Dharma Prince," as one is born from the womb and becomes a true son of the Buddha.
This clarifies the ninth stage, the Abode of the Dharma Prince. "Formation" refers to following upon the preceding stages where [the qualities] were not yet fully manifest;

reaching this stage, they blaze forth with brilliance and intensity. Therefore, it is said that one is "born from the womb," capable of inheriting the family business of the Tathāgata and possessing [all its attributes].
The portion of the Tathāgata’s precious treasury refers to being born from the Buddha’s own mouth, born through transformation by the Dharma, and being the eldest son of the Buddha.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "This bodhisattva practices the ten kinds of observations of the Dharma King, namely:
the skillful methods and regulations of the Dharma King, the palace, the entry [into the path], the observation, the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*), the sustaining power, and fearlessness."
Because he dwells in repose and even receives the praise of the Dharma King, it is called the Stage of the Dharma Prince (*dharmarājaputrabhūmi*).
This signifies his attainment of full maturity, just as a great king of a nation delegates all state affairs to the crown prince;
when that son of a Kṣatriya king has grown up and is invested with the ceremonial sprinkling (*abhiṣeka*), it is called the Stage of Consecration (*abhiṣekabhūmi*).
This clarifies the tenth stage, the Stage of Empowerment (*abhiṣeka-vihāra*). The first phrase follows upon the preceding stage to complete the virtues of a person.孤山 (Gushan) says:
"That which signifies becoming a full person is the capacity to perform the Buddha’s work. The distinction in wording between *taizi* (crown prince) and *shizǐ* (heir apparent) is merely textual;
the *Spring and Autumn Annals* states, "The Crown Prince was met at Shouzhi," and the *Book of Rites* states, "The Heir Apparent of King Wen"—both refer to the Son of Heaven.
Regarding the "son of a son," the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* describes the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) as follows:

When the crown prince born to a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*), whose mother is the principal queen and who possesses a complete physical form, sits upon a magnificent golden throne supported by a white elephant, a great net-canopy is spread, various musical instruments are played, and the waters of the four great oceans are taken and placed within a golden vessel. The King then holds this vessel.
When the crown of the Crown Prince is sprinkled with water, he is immediately said to have received the rank of king; the reception of office by a Bodhisattva is likewise so.
Because the waters of the wisdom of all Buddhas are poured upon his crown, he is called one who has received the office of Great Wisdom.

That tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), is known as the stage of the Consecrated Bodhisattva (*abhiṣikta-bodhisattva*); now, this tenth dwelling also partially attains that [status]. However, it is [only] complete...

Since the division of the teachings, it has been truly understood that all possess practical application; however, when discussing the power of wisdom, there are indeed degrees of superiority and inferiority.

Thus, from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, one manifests the signs of the ten realms within a hundred Buddha-worlds to benefit and assist sentient beings, with each successive stage entering deeper and becoming doubly superior.
What is elucidated in the sutras does so according to a specific perspective; yet, if one considers a single stage as possessing the merits of all stages, [the truth becomes manifest].
Thus, these ten meanings are all-pervasive throughout the ten stages (*bhūmi*); as it is with the ten stages, so it is with all other positions.
As the Great Sūtra says: "This Bodhisattva accomplishes ten kinds of knowledge, namely: shaking countless worlds; illuminating, sustaining, and visiting countless worlds;
purifying countless worlds; revealing [the Dharma] to countless sentient beings; observing countless sentient beings; knowing..."
They cause countless sentient beings to develop their faculties, lead countless sentient beings to enter [the path], and bring countless sentient beings to discipline;

furthermore, they exhort them to study the ten kinds of knowledge, namely: knowledge of the three periods of time, knowledge of the Buddha-dharma, unimpeded knowledge of the dharma-realm, boundless knowledge of the dharma-realm, knowledge that fills all worlds, knowledge of all sentient beings, and knowledge of...
The wisdom that knows all phenomena is the wisdom of the infinite Buddhas. Why is this? It is because one desires to cause all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*) to increase;
therefore, it is now called "consecration" (*abhiṣeka*), for it is a consecration with the water of wisdom.
All wealth and treasures belong to the son; what was previously brought forth or deposited is known by the son. Thus, whatever a son of the Buddha ought to obtain—
Having already attained the virtues of a mature person and being fit for great responsibility, he is assigned administrative duties to transform and guide the ten directions;
this serves as a trial of the fundamental principles of practicing the Way. The Ten Abodes are concluded.

The above ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) constitute the foundation for accumulating merit, while the ten abodes (*vihāra*) represent the gradual progression of that accumulation. Upon reaching this stage, the Way is perfected and virtue is complete.
Because those who do not save sentient beings are merely individuals seeking their own liberation, they practice the Six Perfections extensively to perform the great work of Buddhahood;

this is followed by the Ten Practices, which are described as "flowing forth from the source. The *Yi Jing* says, "The superior man takes the perfection of virtue as his conduct," and further states, "The great carriage carries its load;
though it is piled high within, it does not collapse. This speaks of how one's virtue is vast, and thus one's conduct is likewise vast.
Ānanda, once these good men have become sons of the Buddha, they are endowed with the immeasurable, wondrous virtues of the Tathāgatas; because they accord with the ten directions,
this is called the "Practice of Joy."
This is the practice of the first perfection, the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). As the Great Sūtra states:
"The practice of a Bodhisattva is inconceivable and equal to the Dharma-realm and empty space;

because the Bodhisattva trains in the example of the Buddhas of the three periods of time and practices accordingly, this Bodhisattva is a great donor who bestows all possessions whatsoever, with a mind of equanimity and without regret."
Without stinginess and without expectation of fruit, fame, or gain, but solely for the sake of protecting,
gathering in, and benefiting all sentient beings, when a bodhisattva practices this path, they cause all sentient beings to rejoice and delight;
and by the power of their vows, wherever there are lands of poverty and destitution, they take birth there as noble, wealthy, and affluent persons.
With inexhaustible jewels, he extensively practiced the giving of material wealth; even when those who sought his own flesh appeared, he immediately gave them his flesh and body to make them rejoice.
Thus, immeasurable sentient beings who begged for his flesh were redoubled in their joy. He further thought:
"These sentient beings are my field of merit and my virtuous friends; they have neither sought nor requested [anything from me]."
And having come to teach me to enter into the Buddha-dharma, I shall not oppose the minds of all sentient beings. Furthermore, I form this thought:

"May all roots of goodness that I have performed, am currently performing, or shall perform in the future cause me to receive a vast body among all sentient beings in all worlds; may the flesh of this body suffice [for them]."
May I not relinquish my life until all sentient beings suffering from hunger have been satisfied, even if there remains but a single small creature who has not yet attained full satiation;
may the flesh of my body that is thus cut away never be exhausted.
By this root of goodness, may I realize Bodhi, and may all sentient beings who eat my flesh also attain Bodhi and extensively perform the work of a Buddha. Thus it is.
He benefits sentient beings while being free from the notion of a self, the notion of sentient beings, not perceiving the gift, and not perceiving the recipient;

because he has previously perfected sublime virtues that permeate his being, he dwells as a son of the Buddha, with a serene countenance and a back suffused with joy, such that great delight pervades his entire body.
Now, by extensively practicing generosity once again, those nearby admire his virtue.
Because they cherish this grace, they accord with it throughout the ten directions; thus, the name "Joyful" (Pramuditā) is appropriately formed.
From here until the four stages of application, one should give rise to the resolve of the mind through the practice of faith and understanding.
Being well able to benefit all sentient beings is called "the practice of benefiting others.
This is the second perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). It receives this name because it benefits sentient beings through the virtue of ethical discipline;
for if one lacks the root of internal virtue, how could one benefit others? Thus, seeing the countenance of such virtue causes the minds of others to be transformed.

Within there must necessarily be a fundamental basis. The Great Sūtra says: "When this Bodhisattva upholds the pure precepts, he is unattached to form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or mental objects, and he likewise proclaims this to sentient beings.
When a Bodhisattva maintains the pure precepts, even if within a single day there should be immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of great evil Māras..."

Each one was accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of celestial maidens, all skilled in the practice of the five desires, beautiful and lovely enough to bewitch the human heart, and carrying various precious playthings with the intent to come and disturb the Bodhisattva’s resolve for the Way.
The Bodhisattva thought to himself: "These five desires are..."
These dharmas that obstruct the path even hinder unsurpassed bodhi; therefore, he does not give rise to a single thought of desire, and his mind is pure as that of a Buddha.
Except for employing skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings, he never abandons the mind of omniscience.
A bodhisattva does not afflict a single sentient being on account of desire; rather, he would sooner sacrifice his own body and life than ever do so.
Since the Bodhisattva first beheld the Buddha, he has never once conceived a single thought of desire, let alone engaged in such acts.

At that time, the Bodhisattva should reflect: "Throughout the long night of saṃsāra, all sentient beings have contemplated the five desires, rushed toward the five desires, and been greedily attached to the five desires; their minds are firmly resolved upon them."
"Addicted, immersed, and following along with the flow, they cannot attain self-mastery. I shall cause these Māras and these celestial maidens to abide in the unsurpassed precepts;

having caused them to abide in the pure precepts, their minds shall never retreat from the mind of omniscience, even to the point that they themselves attain liberation while enabling others to attain liberation, and they themselves experience happiness while causing others to experience happiness," and so forth.
This refers to benefiting sentient beings in such a manner.
To awaken oneself and awaken others without encountering opposition is called the practice of non-anger and non-hostility.
This third practice is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). As the Great Sūtra says: "This bodhisattva constantly practices the dharma of patience and remains humble."
Reverent and not harming oneself or others, neither grasping for oneself nor causing others to grasp, he reflects only thus:

"I shall preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings so that they may leave all evil behind and sever greed, hatred, delusion, pride, concealment, stinginess, envy, flattery, and deceit, causing them to dwell constantly in patience and gentleness. When a Bodhisattva has accomplished the dharma of patience, even if a hundred...
Trillions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of sentient beings came to where he was;

each and every one of these beings manifested hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of mouths, and from each mouth issued hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of words—
namely, unpleasant words, words contrary to the wholesome Dharma, and so forth, up to...
They are capable of hearing words that disparage and insult the Bodhisattva with such speech; furthermore,
each of these sentient beings possesses hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of hands,
and each hand holds hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of weapons to oppress and harm the Bodhisattva, continuing in this manner for asankhyeyas of eons.

Throughout kalpas there has never been a rest; yet when the Bodhisattva undergoes such extreme and agonizing suffering that his body hairs stand on end and his life is about to be severed, he reflects thus:

"If my mind were to be disturbed by this pain, I would fail to discipline myself and fail to protect myself, even falling into self-attachment. How then could I cause the minds of others to attain purity?"
At another time, he again thought: "Since beginningless kalpas, I have dwelt in birth and death, undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction.
Reflecting thus, he redoubled his diligent efforts to purify his mind and attain joy;
he skillfully disciplined himself and was able to abide securely within the Buddha-dharma, and he also caused sentient beings to likewise attain this Dharma.
One is able to dwell securely within the Buddha-dharma and awaken through self-realization; furthermore, one causes sentient beings to also attain this Dharma and awaken others.
One is able to joyfully endure all forms of verbal abuse and physical assault without opposition or resistance.
Therefore, the *Vajracchedikā* says: "If a bodhisattva possesses the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span..."
When one's limbs are being severed, one should give rise to resentment; therefore, know that only when there is no anger toward such humiliation is it called true patience (*kṣānti*).

That which gives birth to all categories [of beings], extending to the end of the future, equal throughout the three periods of time, and penetrating the ten directions, is called inexhaustible practice (*akṣaya-caryā*).

This is the fourth perfection, the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*). The Great Sūtra states: "The bodhisattva cultivates various forms of vigor, namely the foremost vigor up to the universally pervasive vigor.
Because his nature is free from the three poisons and pride, he never practices vigor for the sake of harming even a single sentient being;
rather, he practices it solely to sever all afflictions and delusions at their root and to eliminate them."
They practice diligence while abiding in all habitual tendencies solely for the purpose of knowing the realms of all sentient beings,
their deaths and rebirths from this life to the next, the afflictions, mental inclinations, objects of experience, and the superior or inferior faculties and mental activities of all sentient beings;
they practice diligence solely for the purpose of knowing the entire dharma-realm and knowing all Buddha-dharmas.
Because they fundamentally know the equality of all Buddha-dharmas, know the equality of the three periods of time,
attain the light of wisdom regarding all Buddha-dharmas, realize the wisdom of all Buddha-dharma-knowledge,
and even attain the wisdom that analyzes and expounds the meanings of the phrases of all Buddha-dharmas, the bodhisattva practices diligence; thus does the bodhisattva practice diligence.

Furthermore, suppose there were someone who said: "Are you able to cause every single sentient being among all the sentient beings in countless worlds to undergo all manner of sufferings in the Avīci Hell for countless eons,
so that those sentient beings may encounter the appearance of countless Buddhas in the world, and by seeing those Buddhas, fully experience all manner of happiness?"
"Is it possible that one may enter into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and attain *bodhi*?
Upon hearing these words, a bodhisattva does not give rise to even a single thought of regret or resentment; rather, they increase their joy and leap for gladness even further.
Those of such a kind as these shall continue until the end of the future, exhausting all [afflictions]."

The *Nasi Zhongsheng Zhonglei Jing* (Sūtra on the Various Species of Beings with Nose-Sense) states that throughout incalculable kalpas, one causes all beings to enter nirvana without remainder and attain bodhi.
"Equality of the three periods" refers to practicing diligence because of knowing the nature of equality across the three periods of time.
"Pervasive penetration of the ten directions" refers to practicing diligence because of knowing the entire dharma-realm. Indeed...
The mind of birth from the various categories is the foremost; the mind that extends to the end of the future is the eternal mind;
the equality of the three periods of time is the non-erroneous mind; and the penetration throughout the ten directions is the vast mind. Because these four are all inexhaustible, they are so named.
The harmonious integration of all various Dharma-gates without error is called the practice of being free from delusion and confusion.
This is the fifth stage of the perfection of dhyāna. As the Mahāyāna Sūtra says: "This Bodhisattva achieves right mindfulness;
his mind is without distraction and free from delusion. By means of this right mindfulness, he skillfully understands all worldly speech."
They maintain the verbal expressions of all supramundane dharmas—namely, they maintain the verbal expressions for form-dharmas and non-form-dharmas;

they maintain the verbal expressions for establishing the intrinsic nature of form, and so on, up to maintaining the verbal expressions for establishing the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Their minds are free from delusion and confusion as they die here and are born there within the world, entering and emerging from the womb.
Having resolved upon the mind of enlightenment, they serve spiritual friends, diligently cultivate the Buddha-dharma, recognize the works of Māra, and remain free from all demonic activities.
Throughout unspeakable eons, they practice the bodhisattva path with a mind free from delusion or confusion.
This bodhisattva accomplishes such immeasurable right mindfulness, having followed all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends throughout immeasurable eons.
Regarding the sublime Dharma he has heard, throughout immeasurable eons he does not forget or lose it; his mind constantly recollects it without interruption.

Furthermore, various sounds cannot delude or disturb this bodhisattva—namely, loud and high-pitched voices, voices that cause extreme terror, or even voices that could destroy the six sense faculties—even if such sounds were to fill the entirety of the *ābhāsvara* heaven.
Throughout *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, they have never for even a single thought-moment had a distracted mind;
rather, they have skillfully entered all doors of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), know that all samādhis share a single essential nature, and understand that all phenomena are without limit.
All these various dharma-gates, which herein are unified as one, are sustained by the power of a single moment of concentrated mind.
When all dharmas are attained without error, one hears immeasurable Dharma-sūtras and does not forget or lose them throughout immeasurable kalpas.
This is because a concentrated mind that cannot sustain the various dharma-gates is a "deluded concentration" (moha-samādhi);
such a mind remains subject to error regarding the dharma-gates and is still a distracted mind. Now, with a single moment of concentrated mind, one sustains the manifold [dharmas].
The Dharma possesses various sounds, yet it cannot be deluded or confused; because each and every aspect is perfectly clear and not deficient by even a hair’s breadth, there is no error.
Thus, one knows that it is free from both ignorance and confusion.
Thus, within the midst of sameness, a multitude of differences manifest; each distinct characteristic is individually seen as having the same name, "skillful manifestation.
This sixth practice is the wisdom of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*dharmatā-dharma*). The Great Sūtra states:

"This Bodhisattva’s three karmas are pure, dwelling in non-apprehension. Whatever is manifested is without intrinsic nature and without dependence, abiding like the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), transcending [all limitations]."
All worldly realms have no basis; they enter into the dharma that is free from conceptual differentiation, unbound, and unattached;
they enter into the most supreme wisdom, the reality-dharma; they enter into the supramundane dharma that cannot be understood by any worldly beings.
This is the manifestation of the signs of birth through the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of this Bodhisattva. This Bodhisattva forms this thought: "All..."
Sentient beings have non-nature as their nature; all dharmas have the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as their nature;
all lands have signlessness (*animitta*) as their characteristic. All three periods of time are merely verbal designations.

It is even said that the Buddha-dharma is not different from worldly dharmas, and worldly dharmas are not different from the Buddha-dharma. There is no confusion between the Buddha-dharma and worldly dharmas.
Through the non-discriminative realization that the essence of the *dharmadhātu* is equal, one further increases the great bodhicitta and acts as a locus of reliance for all sentient beings.
In this context, "the same" refers to supramundane equal dharmas, while "the different" refers to mundane differentiated dharmas. To manifest difference within sameness is equality.
To manifest the differentiated within the Dharma means that within difference, sameness is manifested; this refers to the manifestation of the dharma of equality within the dharma of differentiation.
Because the ultimate and conventional truths are thus mutually integrated, it is called "Well-Manifested" (Sudṛśa).
In this way, even unto the point where the empty space of the ten directions is filled with atoms, such that within each and every atom the worlds of the ten directions appear—
where the appearance of the atoms and the appearance of the worlds do not obstruct or hinder one another— is called the Practice of Non-attachment.

This seventh practice is the wisdom of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*dharmadharmāpratighajñāna*). Together with the following three practices, these all constitute the fulfillment of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

It is not merely that the identical and the different mutually merge; rather, when this principle is expanded and applied, the large and small contain one another, and the one and the many are without obstruction.
As it is said: "Within every single atom of all the worlds in the Flower Treasury (*Gandavyūha*), the entire Dharma-realm is manifested."
Furthermore, they do not obstruct one another: when the elements (dhātu) enter the sense-fields (āyatana), the elements do not become small;
thus the small does not obstruct the great. When the sense-fields contain the elements, the elements do not become large; thus the great does not obstruct the small. The Third Patriarch said:

"The ultimate large is identical to the small, such that no boundaries or manifestations are seen; the ultimate small is identical to the great, such that all states and limits are forgotten. This is possible only through non-attachment.
If there were even a hair’s breadth of attachment, how could the great and the small be mutually integrated? The Mahāyāna Sūtra says:
"This Bodhisattva, with a mind free from attachment, is able in every thought-moment to enter incalculable worlds; yet within those worlds, his mind has no attachment.
In every thought-moment he beholds innumerable Buddhas; yet in the presence of those Buddhas, his mind has no [attachment]."
Furthermore, they manifest the entire Dharma-realm upon the tip of a single hair;
within the space of a single hair-tip, they teach and discipline all sentient beings throughout unspeakably unspeakable numbers of eons.
As it is with one hair-tip, so it is with every hair-tip, until such time that they do not give rise to attachment to a self for even the duration of a finger-snap.
This is precisely the notion of "self" and "what belongs to self.
These various manifestations are all the first *pāramitā*, named the Practice of Reverence.
This eighth practice is the ultimate wisdom that reaches the other shore. As the former masters said: "Luminous at the head of the hundred grasses; luminous..."
The meaning of the Patriarch’s teaching is that all present phenomena are the foremost *pāramitā*;
among the six perfections, it is only *prajñā* that is most honored, hence it is called the "practice of honoring.

The *Avataṃsaka* calls it the "difficult-to-attain practice," for through the practice of wisdom, all practices reach the other shore; thus, this bodhisattva accomplishes roots of goodness that are difficult to attain.
In every thought-moment, they are able to undergo incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) births and deaths without abandoning their great bodhisattva vows.
Although these bodhisattvas realize that sentient beings do not exist, they do not abandon the realm of all sentient beings.
These bodhisattvas dwell neither in saṃsāra nor in nirvāṇa; while not dwelling in the middle stream of saṃsāra, they are able to ferry those on this shore across.
Having been born on the other shore, in a place of peace, security, fearlessness, and freedom from sorrow and affliction, one does not have any attachment to the category of sentient beings.
Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva enters deeply into the realm of sentient beings as if it were the Dharma-realm;

the realm of sentient beings and the Dharma-realm are equal and non-dual. Within this non-dual dharma, there is neither increase nor decrease; therefore, it is said that they manifest in various ways.
The preceding [eight] are all the first *pāramitā*.
Such perfect interfusion that can establish the norms for the Buddhas of the ten directions is called "excellent Dharma-practice.
This ninth practice is the wisdom of preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings. Since its merit of such above-described perfect, unimpeded interfusion is identical [to the others],...

In their practice of the Tathāgata’s conduct, they are equal to all Buddhas; thus, every single word and deed accords with the norms of the Buddhas of the ten directions, and for this reason it is called the Great Sūtra of Wholesome Dharmas. As the sūtra says:

"This bodhisattva acts as a pool of coolness for all the world—including devas, humans, māras, brahmās, and brahmins—upholding the True Dharma and ensuring that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed."
It is this: having attained the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence, one accords with the faculties, natures, and inclinations of all sentient beings;
using a broad and long tongue, one manifests immeasurable sounds within a single voice, preaching the Dharma at the appropriate time so that all are made to rejoice.
Each and every one is pure, untainted, the single true, unconditioned nature that is inherently so; therefore, it is called "True Practice.

This tenth practice does not contradict the wisdom of the true mark (*dharmatā*), because the entire nature is cultivation and thus constitutes a rule, and because the entirety of cultivation is the nature and is thus fundamentally unconditioned.
Now, having fully possessed these sublime virtues, one gives rise to sublime conduct.
Although there are ten thousand transformations, they all ultimately belong to the One True Reality. As the Great Sūtra says:
"This Bodhisattva accomplishes the foremost speech of truthful reality; as he speaks, so he acts, and as he acts, so he speaks.
