This Bodhisattva studies the true speech of the Buddhas of the three periods of time and attains the non-dual speech of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, because he follows and learns from the Tathāgata until his wisdom is perfected."
All that has been taught and all that has been practiced are entirely true. The above concludes the ten practices (daśabhūmi). Below, the ten dedications (daśapariṇāmanā) are clarified.
This is because, although the ten stages (daśavihāra) all exclusively employ the Middle Way, the texts therein never explicitly mention matters of benefiting sentient beings;
thus, these stages consist mostly of practices tending toward emptiness. It is only within the stage of the ten practices that such matters are first made clear.
To speak of "delivering sentient beings" refers to the most supreme form of compassion within the provisional emergence from the mundane;

these ten dedications clearly demonstrate the simultaneous operation of compassion and wisdom, the mutual integration of the ultimate and the conventional, and the fulfillment of the Middle Way in every stage and every vow.
This method of dedication does not exceed three points: dedication to sentient beings, dedication to Bodhi, and dedication to the Reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi). This is based on the *Huayan* [Sūtra].
The dedication of merit in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is precisely the excellent practice of making vows. This is because if there is practice without vows, the practice will surely be aimless;
if there are vows without practice, the vows are merely empty formalities. Therefore, when practice and vows are mutually supported, one enters the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa.
Ānanda, when these good men have fulfilled their supernormal powers and completed the work of attaining Buddhahood— being pure, pristine, and true, far removed from all lingering afflictions—
they shall deliver sentient beings and eliminate the very notion of "delivering" them. Turning their minds away from the unconditioned toward the path of Nirvāṇa,
this is called the Dedication to Protecting and Delivering All Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings.
This first stage of the dedication free from marks and the subsequent stages are all dedications for the sake of sentient beings.

The preceding four lines build upon the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*)—which are pure and untainted (*anāsrava*), thus being purely one true reality (*eka-tathatā*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and being quintessentially real and far removed from all lingering afflictions—thereby encompassing the ten practices. Since the ten practices are fully prepared, whatever actions are performed are [all dedicated].
Because there is no obstruction, at the very time one is saving sentient beings, one does not perceive any sentient beings who can be saved;
this is to be engaged in conditioned activity all day long while remaining truly unconditioned. To direct the unconditioned mind toward the path of Nirvana is called dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
If, while saving sentient beings, one maintains the mark of "saving," one is attached to the notions of self and person; this merely adds shackles and fetters and is not the dharma of dedication.
As the Great Master of Mount Nanyue said: "If the Buddhas of the three periods of time swallow all in a single mouth, where else could there be sentient beings to be saved?
This is true dedication. The Mahāyāna Sūtra says: "When this Bodhisattva practices the six perfections, he makes this vow:
'May these roots of goodness universally benefit all sentient beings, causing them all to become pure.'"

As for that which ultimately and forever leaves behind the immeasurable sufferings of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals—if one possesses roots of goodness but does not wish to benefit all sentient beings, it is not called dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

Only when one takes all sentient beings as the object of focus for every single root of goodness is it called dedication; it is the establishing of sentient beings within the dharma of non-attachment.
When a bodhisattva of essential nature performs dedication in this way, they deliver and liberate sentient beings without ever ceasing, yet they do not dwell upon the marks of phenomena;
that is to say, they rescue and protect all sentient beings while remaining free from the mark of "sentient beings."

To destroy that which is destructible, to distance oneself from all forms of distancing, and to name this the "Non-Destructible Dedication"—this is the second Non-Destructible Dedication. "Destroying that which is destructible" refers to the aforementioned extinguishing of the characteristics of the perfections (*pāramitā*).
"All forms of distancing" refers to the aforementioned distancing from sentient beings. "Distancing oneself from all distancing" refers to distancing from [the concept of] sentient beings.
"Characteristics are also far removed," and "the name 'unbreakable' refers to the unbreakable activity of delivering sentient beings.

According to the discussion of the higher stages, although one delivers sentient beings at this stage, one does not cling to the characteristic of delivering them; therefore, it is called "far removed.
At this stage, although one does not cling to the characteristic of sentient beings, this does not hinder the delivery of sentient beings; therefore, it is called "unbreakable wisdom."
The union of compassion is the middle way between the two benefits of self and others. As the Great Sūtra states:
"This bodhisattva attains indestructible faith toward all sentient beings, regards them with eyes of loving-kindness, and dedicates their roots of virtue for the universal benefit of all beings;
this constitutes having sentient beings who may be delivered."
"Original enlightenment is serene and its awakening is equal to the awakening of the Buddhas; this is called the dedication that is equal to all Buddhas.
This third stage is the dedication equal to the Buddhas, wherein wisdom is identical to the Buddha-wisdom. The four stages below this are all dedications toward the Buddha-way.
"Original enlightenment is serene" means that one's own original Buddha manifests; "its awakening is equal to the Buddhas" means...
"Awakening" means that one's mind-essence is perfectly interfused and identical with that of all Tathāgatas.
"Dedicating in accordance with all Buddhas" means that I and the Tathāgata’s precious, awakened true mind are non-dual and perfect. As the Great Sūtra says:
"This Bodhisattva follows and trains in the path of dedication practiced by all Buddhas; thus training, they dedicate."
While traveling, when seeing all forms up to tactile objects and mental phenomena—whether beautiful or ugly—he gives rise to neither attachment nor aversion;
his mind attains mastery and is free from all faults. Vast, pure, joyful, and blissful, he is detached from all sorrow and affliction;
his mind is supple and his faculties are cooled. When the Bodhisattva has attained this peace and happiness, he further resolves:
One turns the mind toward all Buddhas and forms this thought and vow: "May the bliss of all Buddhas, through the roots of goodness I have now planted, increase even more and become ever more sublime.
Because all Buddhas turn [roots of goodness] in this way, and I likewise turn them in this way, it is called the "Equal Turning-over to All Buddhas."
The dedication of the stage of refined truth and luminous manifestation, which is named "Reaching All Places" (*sarvatragāminī*), is the fourth dedication.
Its objective realm is identical to the Buddha-realm. "Refined truth" refers to the essence of original enlightenment;
"luminous manifestation" refers to the unfolding of the wondrous stage of practice. "The stage is like the Buddha-stage" indicates that one is manifesting one's own ground of causality.
The boundless realms contained within the mind are entirely identical to the immeasurable lands manifested at the stage of fruition of all Buddhas.
Regarding "reaching all places," this conveys the sense of exhausting the entire realm of the Buddhas. As the Great Sūtra says:
"When this Bodhisattva cultivates roots of goodness, he forms this thought: 'May the power of the merit of these roots of goodness reach all places.'"
Just as the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) reaches everywhere— reaching all things, reaching all worlds,
reaching all sentient beings, and reaching all lands— may these roots of goodness likewise reach all Tathāgatas,
so that they may be filled with offerings just like the various celestial articles of worship.
Filling immeasurable and boundless worlds, and even entering all worlds through the three karmas to perform Buddha-work, and so forth;
because worlds and Tathāgatas mutually interpenetrate without obstruction, this is called the dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit.
This fifth inexhaustible dedication concerns the mutual fusion of bodies and lands:
if the world enters the Tathāgata, then within a single pore there are immeasurable jewel-adorned buddha-lands, subtle and wondrous;
if the Tathāgata enters the world, then within a single atom there are immeasurable Tathāgatas turning the great wheel of Dharma, attaining unimpededness.
It is said that when the Tathāgata traverses the world, he is not obstructed by it and immediately enters the world;
when the Tathāgata traverses the world, he is not obstructed by the world and immediately enters the Tathāgata.

This is called the "Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit" (*akṣaya-guṇa-kośa*), because both the Buddha-body and the Buddha-realm each possess immeasurable adornments, fully manifesting inexhaustible merit. Furthermore—
The Sūtra says: "This Bodhisattva takes the conduct of Samantabhadra as the foundation;

it is adorned with the exquisite jewels produced from the Tathāgata’s wisdom—filling the entire Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, boundless, limitless, and inexhaustible—namely, all incense, flowers, garments, and even music, such as these, immeasurable and infinite."
Adorned with countless ornaments, they adorn all throughout the entire dharma-realm and the realm of empty space;

these are the various karmas arising in the ten directions, known by the Buddhas and proclaimed by the Buddhas, in all worlds, even down to those abiding in this dedication, which attain ten kinds of inexhaustible treasuries: namely, attaining the inexhaustible treasury of seeing the Buddhas, and seeing the Dharma...

The "Inexhaustible Treasury" refers to this very fact: because these are the merits manifested by the adornments of the Flower Treasury World (*kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*), which take the great practices and vows of Samantabhadra as their root, it is described in such a way.
Within the stage that is identical to the Buddha-stage, each gives rise to the causes of purity; relying on these causes, they are brought forth to attain the path to *nirvāṇa*.
This is called the dedication of roots of goodness that accords with equality;
it is the sixth dedication of equality. That is to say, within this inexhaustible treasury where body and land are mutually fused, each gives rise to inexhaustible causes of purity;
furthermore, by relying upon these pure causes, one realizes the fruit of purity.
This means that the essence of the lamp of wisdom illuminates every single thing, and the practice-gate of Samantabhadra is present in every instance;
because it is like gold fashioned into vessels where every vessel is entirely gold, it is called the "Root of Merit of Equality. The Mahāyāna Sūtra says:

"This Bodhisattva may become a sovereign ruler presiding over a great kingdom, his majestic virtue widely pervading and his fame shaking the world; holding a single parasol, he provides universal shade for the myriad beings."

He employs the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) to gather all sentient beings as a Wheel-Turning King, providing for them all around—whether by bestowing external wealth or by giving his own body—and dedicates these merits to sentient beings. This constitutes the various causes for generating purity within each stage;
by relying on these causes, they are brought forth, leading to the path of *nirvāṇa*.
Once the true roots are established, all sentient beings of the ten directions are my own fundamental nature; as this nature is perfectly accomplished, it does not lose the name "sentient beings.
Thus, one practices the dedication of merit by observing all sentient beings with equal contemplation in accordance with this truth.
This is the seventh [type of] dedication through equal contemplation. The Mahāyāna Sūtra states:

"When this bodhisattva cultivates various roots of goodness with the power of a pure vow and the mind of bodhicitta, they form this thought: 'These roots of goodness are all accumulated by means of the mind of bodhicitta;
they are all for the sake of having compassion for all sentient beings and for the sake of seeking all [virtues].'"
When the One of All-Knowledge (sarvajñajñāna) forms this thought, his roots of goodness increase and he never regresses.

The Bodhisattva dedicates the roots of goodness he has accumulated in every moment of thought in this way: that is to say, he vows that all sentient beings may have abundant wealth and treasures, lacking nothing;
and he vows that all sentient beings may achieve a great treasury of merit, equal to [the Buddha’s].
At the time of this dedication, sentient beings do not conflict with all lands; lands do not conflict with all sentient beings; lands and sentient beings do not conflict with karma;
karma does not conflict with lands and sentient beings; intention does not conflict with mind; mind does not conflict with intention;
intention and mind do not conflict with objects; objects do not conflict with intention and mind; and the equality of the world does not conflict with the equality of the Buddhas.
The equality of the Buddhas does not contradict the equality of the world; the bodhisattva practice does not contradict omniscience (*sarvajñatā*);

omniscience does not contradict bodhisattva practice. When the bodhisattva dedicates in this manner, they attain the equality of karma, the equality of retribution, the equality of sentient beings, and the equality of all Buddhas of the three times. Within each of the preceding stages and grounds, they give rise to purity.
As for the cause of purification, it consists in transforming provisional roots of goodness into true roots.

Once these true roots are established, the sentient beings of the ten directions become a single, perfectly interfused, pure, and enlightened jewel-awareness. Therefore, one perceives all sentient beings as beings of one's own original nature;
by accordantly contemplating each and every one with equal vision, they are all fully perfected and accomplished, such that none are ever lost.

The vow of a single sentient being that all sentient beings may achieve the treasury of great merit is precisely why the Bodhisattva Never Disparaging, upon encountering anyone, would prostrate and say: "I do not dare to disparage you;
you shall all become Buddhas."

That is, all dharmas are free from all marks; this dedication of the mark of *tathatā* (suchness), which is the non-attachment to both "being" and "leaving," is the eighth dedication of the mark of *tathatā*.
From here on, the three subsequent stages are all dedications toward the Great *Tathatā*.
The Sūtra says: This Bodhisattva, with clear and lucid right mindfulness, remains far removed from delusion;

with single-minded dedication to practice, his profound resolve is unshakable, and he accomplishes indestructible karma. He proceeds toward all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) without ever regressing, giving rise to supreme roots of goodness and cultivating pure, white dharmas.
Through wisdom and skillful means, he dedicates [these merits]—in this way, through all such various gates and modes.
Regarding various objects, various characteristics, various divisions, various practices, and so forth— the Bodhisattva at that time surveys all roots of goodness with the eye of wisdom;
seeing them as immeasurable and boundless, he realizes they are all established by a mind directed toward the vehicle of the Ten Powers,
and he dedicates them all to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) as one and non-dual, even to the point of non-attachment to the world.

In the interim, one does not grasp at sentient beings; their mind is pure and without dependence, equal to suchness which pervades all places without limit. The dedication of roots of goodness is likewise so.
Herein, "all dharmas" refers to those very mundane and supramundane dharmas that have been cultivated, namely, various objects.
Regarding the equality of characteristics, phenomena, and practice, "being free from all characteristics" means not clinging to the world and not grasping at sentient beings;

the mind is pure and has no point of reliance. Although previously there was seeking above and transforming below, one had not yet emerged from the interval between identity and separation of characteristics.
Now, by simultaneously forgetting both identity and separation, one finally accords with the characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Indeed, truly attaining that which is as-it-is (tathatā), unimpeded throughout the ten directions, is called the dedication of liberation without bondage.

This is the ninth dedication of liberation. Previously, "separation" referred to being doubly separated; this is called the characteristic of true thusness (tathatā-lakṣaṇa). If one were to become attached...

If the characteristic of *tathatā* (suchness) were itself a binding characteristic of *tathatā*, then one would simultaneously forget that characteristic of suchness; this is called "truly attaining suchness.
If one truly attains suchness, then everything in every place is suchness—what further obstruction could there be? As the Great Sūtra says:
"By means of a mind of non-attachment, non-binding, and liberation, one accomplishes the physical, vocal, and mental actions of Samantabhadra with vigor."

From the power of mastery over progress up to the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna* that encompasses the entire *dharmadhātu*, one attains one hundred and fifty-six kinds of profound and subtle wisdom. Thus, where could one go that would not be within one's own mastery?
This is called "unfettered liberation," which is precisely entry into the inconceivable liberation of the *dharmadhātu*. The preceding stages were the principle (*li*).
The non-obstruction within this stage is precisely the twofold non-obstruction of principle and phenomena, and phenomena and phenomena;
because its inherent virtues are perfectly fulfilled and the measure of the dharma-realm has ceased, it is called the "Dedication of Infinite Dharma-Realm."

This is the tenth immeasurable dedication. Because one attains the entire substance of the nature-virtues through non-attachment and attains the great function of the nature-virtues through non-obstruction, it is said that "the nature-virtues are perfectly accomplished.

As for the "extinction of the measure of the dharma-realm," it is because the substance is all-pervasive and the function is all-encompassing; thus, a single hair and a single speck of dust are each equal to the dharma-realm.
Although there was previously no limit in this way, it still remained within the measure of the *dharmadhātu* and had not yet reached the point of dissolving that measure.
Now, as every sense organ and every object pervades the *dharmadhātu*, the sentiment of limitation is forgotten and one does not fall into various numerical categories;
therefore, it is called the "Infinite *Dharmadhātu*. As the Great Sutra says: "This Bodhisattva uses a stainless silk..."
Binding it upon their crowns, they abide in the station of Dharma-teachers, extensively practicing the gift of Dharma and acting as leaders for all sentient beings.
They dedicate these roots of goodness from the gift of Dharma, making this aspiration:
"May we attain, cultivate, accomplish, increase, and expand all unimpeded realms and so forth. With such thoughts, they resolve: "I shall, throughout all worlds, act as..."

The diligent cultivation by all sentient beings that results in attaining immeasurable bodies of sovereign mastery throughout the entire Dharma-realm, as well as immeasurable roots of goodness for benefiting sentient beings throughout the entire Dharma-realm—all these are of the measure of the extinction of the Dharma-realm.
The above concludes the ten dedications. Below, the four stages of application (*prayoga*) are clarified; according to the distinct teaching (*pṛthagdharma*), they are named as the first three.
Regarding the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*): "equipment" (*sambhāra*) refers to requisites, and "provisions" (*āhāra*) refers to food.

This means that since what has been accumulated is vast, the destination must necessarily be far away; just as one traveling a thousand *li* must gather provisions for three months, one employs the ten abodes (*vihāra*) to perfect internal virtue, the ten practices (*caryā*) to perfect the virtue of benefiting others, and the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) to perfect the mutual integration of self and others.

When these virtues are fully perfected, one may enter the realm of the sages; yet, because there still remains a subtle obstruction here, the stage of *prayoga* (preparatory application) is established once more.
Were it not for the World-Honored One’s profound and penetrating clarity regarding the most esoteric mysteries, who could discern this? Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:
"To manifestly posit a slight object as being the nature of consciousness-only—because there is something apprehended—it is not the ultimate truth."

The statement that "abiding in consciousness-only involves few things" refers to the subtle obstruction (*sūkṣma-āvaraṇa*). Here, although the specific names are borrowed from another [teaching] and the general names are the same, their actual meaning differs.
This is because the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*) is equal to the first abiding (*vihāra*) of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-śāsana*);
thus, in the Perfect Teaching, one severs one grade of ignorance at the first abiding, and subsequently proceeds from the second abiding through to the tenth abiding.
Each severance of one grade of ignorance corresponds to the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*) of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyākhyāna*);

next, from the first practice (*ādikarmika*), the severance of one grade of ignorance corresponds to Equal Enlightenment (*samābodhi*); then, entering the second practice corresponds to Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
From the third practice onward, those of the Separate Teaching do not even know its names, let alone subdue or sever [ignorance], because the Separate Teaching merely breaks [delusions].
This is because they have already transcended the eleven grades of ignorance; how much more so for those who possess the four kinds of wondrously perfect preparatory practice (*prayoga*)!

However, in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, each of the four stages of preparatory practice has its own meditative concentration that can be aroused, the contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) that is aroused thereby, and the dharmas that are the objects of such contemplation.
Examining this sutra carefully, none of these meanings are present; it relies solely on the two characters "Mind" and "Buddha."
Because they are established as only four stages through debate,
they are not the same. This good man Ānanda has fully perfected the forty-one pure minds and subsequently accomplished the four kinds of wondrously perfect preparatory practices (*prayoga*).
This clarifies that the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) serve as the superior progress for entering the stages (*bhūmi*). Wénlǐng states:
"The forty-one minds consist of one stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-jñāna*), ten stages of Faith (*śraddhā*), and ten each for Dwelling (*vihāra*), Practice (*caryā*), and Direction (*abhimukha*).

Both the Small Vehicle and the Shared Teaching possess these four preparatory stages, yet they are neither wondrous nor perfect. Therefore, this [present teaching] specifically designates them as "wondrous and perfect," such that they cannot be categorized by the ordinary preparatory practices.
The preceding text states: "Desiring the True" is already not the True; the nature of True Suchness involves three gradual stages.

This first arising of the thought of desiring the True is from the truly wondrous and perfect, wherein one again gives rise to the truly wondrous. This second arising of the thought of desiring the True continues through the four stages of application (*prayoga*).
Upon reaching the first stage (*bhūmi*), this is the third arising of the thought of desiring the True, wherein the coarse thoughts of desiring the True [are eliminated].

The desire for truth is severed up to the eighth stage; even the subtle thoughts of that desire are severed at the stage of wondrous enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), where the most subtle thoughts of desire are forever cut off.
To take the Buddha’s awakening as one’s own mind—whether it has emerged or not—is like drilling wood for fire while using water as the fuel; it will never ignite.
This is called the Stage of Warmth (*uṣmagata*).
This clarifies the Stage of Warmth. What was previously stated—that "enlightenment is equal to the Buddha's enlightenment"—refers merely to the arousal of aspiration and seeking;
there is still a sense of "awakening" remaining, and one has not yet been able to transcend the Buddha. Now, however, this mind seeks to transcend the Buddha’s vision and put it into practice.
Because one’s own mind has already ignited yet the Buddha-vision has not been forgotten, and because one desires to transcend but is not yet able to transcend immediately, it is said:
"If it has emerged but not yet emerged. This is illustrated by the metaphor of drilling for fire: when one wishes to ignite the wood but it has not yet caught, there is only the sign of warmth.
Therefore, it is called the Stage of Warmth (*uṣmagata*). Thus, Longya said: "Studying the Way is like drilling for fire; when you encounter smoke, do not stop. Wait until—"
When Venus appears, one returns home for the first time.
Furthermore, taking one's own mind as the Buddha’s path traversed—whether relying or not relying upon it—is like ascending a high mountain and entering empty space;
when there is even a slight obstruction below, this is called the "Crown Ground" (Mūrdha-bhūmi).

This clarifies the stage of the Summit (*mūrdhan*). Previously, it was said that "the stages are like the Buddha-stage," which refers to making vows and aspirations while one has not yet transcended one's own views to become a Buddha;
this is what one traverses. Only upon reaching this stage does one begin to take one's own mind as the path traversed by the Buddhas.
However, because one's own views have not yet been forgotten, if one relies [on them], it cannot be called a true reliance. It is analogous to a person climbing a high mountain.
Although the body has entered into empty space, the heels still touch the ground with a slight obstruction;
as one is not yet able to grasp the sun and moon to travel through the eight directions, it is called the Ground of the Summit (*mūrdhan*).

When the mind and the Buddha are identical and one skillfully attains the Middle Way—like a person enduring an insult, being neither resentful nor exultant—it is called the Ground of Patience (*kṣānti*).

This clarifies the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*). From its beginning, one flows into the midst of the middle, reaching the point where one takes the Buddha’s awakening as one's own mind, and again uses one's own mind to become what the Buddha traverses.
Yet, to speak of "using" or "becoming" still retains the duality of two aspects; this is not yet skillfully attained.
Upon reaching this stage, the entire mind is the Buddha and the entire Buddha is the mind, such that [the distinction between them] can no longer be maintained.
Because they are divided, they are called "two," yet it is also said that they well attain the Middle Way. However, this is called "well-attaining" rather than "truly attaining.
For instance, when enduring someone, one harbors no resentment in the heart nor expresses it through speech;
this is called "skillful endurance," but because it is not true endurance, it is named the "Stage of Endurance" (Kṣānti-bhūmi).

When quantity is extinguished within the Middle Way that transcends both delusion and awakening, such that neither of the two has a name, this is called the "World-First Ground" (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

This clarifies the World-First. As previously stated, although one has skillfully attained the Middle Way where mind and Buddha are not divided, the numerical distinctions have not yet been forgotten;
only upon reaching this stage do mind and Buddha merge as one, and numerical distinctions finally dissolve—this is what is meant by "non-mind."
Because it is not the Buddha, Nanquan said: "Do not recognize the mind; do not recognize the Buddha. Even if you were to recognize them, they are still objects.
The ancients called this the "ignorance of the known" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Thus, Mazu Daoshi said: "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing.

When one reaches this point, both delusion and awakening are beyond the reach of the Middle Way, as there is nothing for them to be designated. To be deluded regarding the Middle Way is to be deluded regarding one's own self.
One who, by means of the awakening mind, realizes the Middle Way possesses the resultant wisdom of the Tathāgata. That which is "non-dual" refers to the absence of two extremes:
not seeing one's own mind below, and not seeing the Buddha-wisdom above. If there is delusion on one side and awakening on the other, such people may still be pointed out by others;
they cannot be called "transcendent. Only when delusion and awakening are both exhausted and the Middle Way itself vanishes can one truly transcend the worldlings.
That which is above this is called the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (laukikāgradharma), meaning that there is only heaven above and no mountain equal to it.

If one advances further to ascend the stage of the Path (mārga), it is then termed "Transcending the World" (lokottara); surpassing even wondrous enlightenment, it is further named the "Supreme Transcendent World.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "Because these four kinds of preparatory practice (prayoga) are all accompanied by mental signs (sanimitta), they have not yet been able to realize the truth."
Because those two aspects of emptiness and existence have not yet been eliminated, their contemplative mind still retains these aspects and perceives something attained;
therefore, they do not truly abide in the principle of true *vijñapti-mātratā*. Only after those aspects have ceased can one truly abide therein.

Here, the terms "by means of," "accomplished by," and "well-attained" all refer to that which still retains aspects. As for the state where there is nothing to be aimed at, one is close to it, yet has not yet ascended to the supramundane.

Because this is the ground [of the mundane], it is called the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*); from there until the fulfillment of Bodhi and the realization of non-attainment, it is the "Supreme Transcendent.
The *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse) says: "In the first stage, the Buddha is the mind; in the second stage, the mind is the Buddha; in the third stage, it is both mind and Buddha;
in the fourth stage, it is neither mind nor Buddha. Therefore, these four stages do not depart from the mind and the Buddha."
The stages are clearly defined. In the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), the dual characteristics of existence and emptiness have not yet been eliminated;

thus, the dual characteristics of mind and Buddha have not yet been exhausted. This, too, borrows a specific name for the Perfect [Teaching]. The section on the Four Preparatory Stages (*prayoga*) is concluded. Next, the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*) are clarified.

For it is because one does not abide [in these stages] that one cannot accomplish virtue; because one does not accumulate virtue, one cannot benefit oneself; and because one does not benefit oneself, one cannot [benefit others].

For the sake of benefiting others, once all virtues have been accomplished, spiritual powers attained, and great vows fulfilled, one further establishes four kinds of wondrous and perfect preparatory practices (*prayoga*) to refine the mental capacity.
One must ensure that both the subjective mind and the objective Buddha are forgotten, such that not even a hair’s breadth remains established;
only when the Middle Way itself no longer exists does one ascend to the stages (*bhūmi*). As for "stages," it means the accumulation of the aforementioned dharmas.
As for the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, it states that all Buddha-dharmas arise based upon this [ground], as the ground takes "solidity" (*sāra*) as its substance and "arising" (*utpāda*) as its cause.

According to the preceding text, if one takes the awakening of the fruition-ground (*phala-bhūmi*) as the mind of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*), then from the stage of Initial Resolve (*cittotpāda-vihāra*) up to Equal Enlightenment (*samaya-jñāna*) all belong to the causal ground; only ultimate wondrous enlightenment constitutes the fruition-ground.

Question: Since, according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one is already partially severing ignorance and partially realizing True Reality (*tattva*), why is it that upon reaching this point, one must again employ the four kinds of preparatory practices (*prayoga*) before entering the [final] stage? Answer:

If one speaks in terms of sudden enlightenment (*tongwu*), then the cause encompasses the ocean of the fruit, and the fruit reaches back to the source of the cause; at the very moment of the initial aspiration for enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*), one has already attained perfect awakening (*abhisambodhi*).
If we speak in terms of cultivation and realization, since the Ten Grounds (daśabhūmi) are called "true cultivation," it follows that the stages prior to them are all "semblance cultivation.
Since the Buddha-stage is "true realization," it follows that the Ten Grounds are also "semblance realization.

Thus, although the ultimate principle is identical from the first thought-moment onward, the sequence of shallow and deep stages proceeds without confusion; in this way, both the perfectly integrated (yuanrong) and the sequential (xingbu) aspects are present.
There is no mutual obstruction.

Ānanda, this son of good family has attained excellent penetration into Great Bodhi; his awakening and penetration reach the ultimate limit of the Tathāgata’s Buddha-realm, and this is called the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi).
This clarifies the first stage (*bhūmi*). By means of the four preceding types of wondrous and perfect preparatory practices (*prayoga*), both mind and Buddha vanish;

when the Middle Way is no longer established as a fixed entity, one attains transcendence from the world and enters the true realm of the Buddha. Great joy pervades the entire body, hence it is named the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, this Bodhisattva abandons the obstacle of the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*) and first attains the nature of a noble one (*āryatva*). This constitutes realization.
The *sarvatraga-tathatā* (all-pervading suchness) is so called because this suchness, as revealed by the two kinds of emptiness, is present in every single dharma;

thus it is said that "Awakening penetrates [all], reaching the full extent of the Buddha's realm. Consequently, the treatise establishes this stage as the "stage of penetration" (*prativedha-avasthā*).
As the Great Sūtra states: "If there are sentient beings who have deeply planted roots of goodness, well-cultivated all practices, and well..."
Accumulating the aids to the path, making excellent offerings to all Buddhas, skillfully gathering pure and white dharmas, being well-guided by spiritual friends, and purifying the profound mind;
establishing a vast resolve and generating great understanding; bringing forth compassion before one;
for the sake of seeking Buddha-wisdom, for the sake of attaining the ten powers, for the sake of attaining the great fearlessnesses, and for the sake of attaining the equality of all Buddhas.
For the sake of the Dharma, for the sake of purifying great compassion, for the sake of attaining the knowledge that leaves nothing remaining throughout the ten directions,
for the sake of purifying all Buddha-fields without obstruction, for the sake of knowing all three periods of time in a single thought-moment,

and for the sake of turning the Great Wheel of Dharma with fearlessness— the Bodhisattva, with such a mind, immediately transcends the stage of ordinary beings and enters [the stage of the noble ones].
Born into the lineage of the Tathāgatas as one in the stage of a bodhisattva, one cannot be described as having any flaw in their spiritual ancestry;

having departed from worldly realms and entered the supramundane path, they attain the dharma of enlightenment, abide in the station of enlightenment, and enter into the equality of the three periods of time.
Within the lineage of the Tathāgatas, they are certain to attain unsurpassed enlightenment. When a bodhisattva abides in such dharmas, it is called "abiding."
In the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), because it corresponds to immovability, the bodhisattva dwelling in this Stage of Joy rejoices by recollecting all Buddhas,
rejoices by recollecting the Buddha-dharmas, and so on, up to "rejoices because of entering into the equality of all bodhisattvas. Among these,
the two characters "awakening" (*jue*) and "pervasion" (*tong*) refer to personally reaching and directly realizing [the truth].

This is not to be known by mere comparison; although it was said that one is "mind itself is Buddha" during the preceding stage of Patience (*kṣānti*), one was still at the threshold of realization rather than having fully realized it, and thus it was called "skillfully attaining the Middle Way.

Although it was said that during the stage of Supreme Worldly Dharmas (*laukikāgra-dharma*) there is no objective referent for either delusion or awakening within the Middle Way, traces of influence still remained and it was not yet termed "transcending the world. Upon reaching this stage, however, one truly realizes that which is neither mind nor Buddha.
Only through this principle can one transcend the mundane world and enter the true realm of the Buddha; therefore, it is said that one "skillfully attains Bodhi.
From this point until the attainment of Subtle Enlightenment (*miao-jue*), this constitutes the "evidence of the arousal of faith" (*qi-xin-zhi-zheng*) within the *Awakening of Faith*.
The stage where distinct natures enter into the same nature, and that same nature is also extinguished, is called the Stainless Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*).

This clarifies the second ground. Because in the preceding stage one abandons the nine realms of distinct natures and enters the equality of Buddha-nature, it is said that "distinct natures enter into the same.
However, although one has for the first time realized this equal Buddha-nature, one is not yet able to forget it.
Furthermore, the Buddha-realm as it appears before one's mind is also a mere speck of defilement within the pure awakened mind;

therefore, by eliminating even this "sameness-nature" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), one finally attains stainless purity. This is because "difference-nature" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) is a defilement on the side of turbidity, while "sameness-nature" is a defilement on the side of purity;
thus, both must be abandoned. According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the entry of difference-nature into sameness-nature constitutes liberation.

Having overcome the obstacle of being an ordinary worldling (*pṛthagjana*), one first attains the *tathatā* of universal application; because great joy arises from this preceding stage, any transgressions of the three types of action are termed "wrong conduct.
Now, by severing this obstacle, one realizes the most pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) and becomes far removed from even subtle infractions and afflictions;
therefore, it is called "Stainless" (*vimalā*). If one follows the *Avataṃsaka*, its intrinsic nature is already free from these ten [obstacles].
The stage where the stains of unwholesome karma and broken precepts are removed is called the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
The stage where extreme purity and luminosity arise is called the Radiant Stage (*prabhākari-bhūmi*).
This refers to the third stage; because one has already abandoned the aforementioned stains of phenomena and is thus termed "extremely pure," it is called the "Pure Awakening."
The radiance manifests spontaneously, which is what is meant by "the ultimate purity of the pervasive penetration of light.

If one follows the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it is because by destroying the hindrance of dullness and obtuseness, one achieves superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the great dharma-dhāraṇī, thereby being able to emit the light of boundless, wondrous wisdom.
Thus, the Great Sūtra states: "In this stage, the Bodhisattva practices the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments merely as a matter of conforming to the Dharma."
Because one practices without any defilement or attachment and realizes the six great supernormal powers (ṣaḍ-abhijñā), it is called the Radiant [Stage];
this is precisely the internal luminosity that radiates light.
When clarity is supreme and awakening is full, it is named the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi).
This clarifies the fourth stage (*bhūmi*). Previously it was said that "clarity arises like a fire just beginning to burn";
here it is said that "clarity reaches its peak like a great mass of fire. As the former masters have said: "The diamond-flame wisdom (*vajrajvālā-prajñā*) is like a great mass of fire;

whatever it touches, it burns away, and all objective images (*ālambana-ākāra*) are completely incinerated. This is what is meant. "The awakening is fulfilled" refers to this very peak of clarity, which is the Tathāgata.
It is not called "wisdom" (*prajñā*) but rather "blazing wisdom" (*jñānārci*), for it is the ultimate state of wisdom.
According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, this Bodhisattva destroys the obstacle of the active manifestation of subtle afflictions and dwells in the most excellent factors conducive to enlightenment;

because the flames of wisdom burn the fuel of the afflictions, it is called "blazing wisdom. As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "This Bodhisattva cultivates ten gateways of the light of Dharma, namely, contemplation..."
He examines the realm of sentient beings, the dharma-realm, the world-realm, the realm of space, the realm of consciousness, the realm of desire, the realm of form, the realm of formlessness,
the realm of vast mind and resolute belief, and the realm of great mind and resolute belief. Having attained entry into the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*) and abiding therein,
he observes the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), whereby he burns the fuel of afflictions and thereby attains greatness.
The fire blazes intensely.
That which cannot be reached by any similarities or differences is called the "Difficult to Conquer" stage (*sudurjayā bhūmi*).
This clarifies the fifth stage. The wisdom prior to the stages is called "different," while the wisdom of the stages is called "same"; now, [this wisdom] is utterly pure.
When awakening is fulfilled, both identity and difference are incinerated; therefore, neither identity nor difference can reach it.
If there were some difference that could be reached, then ordinary sentiment could surpass it; if there were some identity that could be reached, then the understanding of the sages could surpass it.

Now, all differences and identities, as well as ordinary sentiment and the understanding of the sages, have already been incinerated. Since even "reaching" cannot be achieved, who then could possibly do so?
Excellent! Your analogy of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is apt. On this stage, one eliminates the obstacle of the parinirvāṇa of the lower vehicles;

for those who weary of saṃsāra and seek nirvāṇa possess both weariness and seeking, which are precisely the sentiments of ordinary beings wherein even the understanding of the sages has not been forgotten—hence it is called an "obstacle.
Since this obstacle consists of the non-discriminative wisdom of the fifth stage, it is eliminated upon reaching that stage. Thus, the Mahāyāna Sūtra says regarding this stage: [text follows].

The Bodhisattva enters this stage by means of ten kinds of pure minds, namely: the pure mind of the equality of the Buddha-dharma of the three periods of time, up to the pure mind of the equality in teaching and transforming all sentient beings.
Having entered this stage, they know these four noble truths as they truly are, and they know all conditioned phenomena as they truly are.
The Dharma is illusory, deceptive, and delusive toward the foolish; therefore, toward all sentient beings, he increases his great compassion and gives rise to the radiance of great loving-kindness.
Never abandoning any sentient being, he constantly seeks the wisdom of a Buddha.
For the sake of benefiting and covering all sentient beings, there is no worldly art or craft that this Bodhisattva does not master, including writing, calculation, and cartography.
From the handling of seals and insignia down to playful laughter and conversation, he excels in all such matters;

this is truly because the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of the two wisdoms—the ultimate and the conventional—are mutually contradictory, yet here they are joined and made to correspond. Therefore, it is called "Difficult to Conquer" (*durjayā*).
Because it transcends both identity and difference, neither identity nor difference can reach it.
The unconditioned *tathatā*, being pure and luminously manifest by nature, is called the "Manifest Stage" (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*).

This clarifies the sixth stage: because all prior mundane sentiments and supramundane understandings have been completely eradicated, the unconditioned true essence is naturally and spontaneously revealed;
hence it is called "Manifest. According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, at this stage, one abandons coarse characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Because it brings to manifestation the supreme non-conceptual *prajñā* induced by the wisdom of dependent origination regarding the abiding of active hindrances, those hindrances obstruct the path of non-defilement and purity in the sixth stage;
thus, upon entering the sixth stage, one is able to sever them forever, for both the presence of defilement and the presence of purity are termed "coarse characteristics.
If one follows the *Avataṃsaka*, the Bodhisattva at this stage [cultivates] the ten equalities.
The Dharma serves as the remedy, namely: because all phenomena are signless, they are equal, without essence, without arising, and without cessation;
they are primordially pure, free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), without grasping or abandoning, and quiescent, even to the point of being the non-duality of existence and non-existence.
Thus, they are equal. When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they enter the samādhi of emptiness, which is the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).

The single meaning of emptiness, the foremost emptiness, the great emptiness, the combined emptiness, and so forth, up to hundreds of thousands of gateways to the signless and wishless samādhis, all manifest before one;

this is called the Ground of Manifestation (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*). This is because when a person of perfect capacity resolves their mind, they immediately and suddenly awaken to the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*Tathatā*) and forget the realm of the Buddha;
yet, as the five abidings have not been shattered and the defilements of the mind have not been eliminated, regarding that—

Since even *tathatā* (suchness) still belongs to the realm of inferential knowledge (*anumāna*), how could it be directly realized [here]? Now, through what resembles cultivation, one passes through true cultivation;
as the practices of the conditioned reach their ultimate limit, the power of the unconditioned is about to be attained.

Therefore, in this stage, *tathatā* finally becomes manifest for the first time and is directly realized. However, the great function of *tathatā* should occur in the eighth and ninth stages, and specifically in the eighth...
On this ground, true effortlessness is attained; here, for the first time, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is reached and True Suchness (tathatā) is fully revealed.
Reaching the limit of True Suchness is called the Ground of Far-Going (*dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*).
This clarifies the seventh ground. Since True Suchness has already been made manifest on the higher grounds, this [ground] exhausts its boundaries.
Ordinarily, one gazes at it and does not see its boundaries; one seeks its depths and does not exhaust its measure.

Now, however, it is revealed throughout the entire realm and throughout all space, not merely in the present moment. According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, this is the severing of the obstacle of the active manifestation of subtle signs (*sūkṣma-nimitta-pravṛtti-āvaraṇa*);
because of the preceding contemplation of emptiness, these subtle signs cease to manifest, and one enters the seventh stage.
At this stage, one is able to permanently sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of that level and practice the immeasurable and effortless (*anābhoga*) as an antidote;
thus, the *Avataṃsaka* states: "The Bodhisattva on this stage cultivates ten kinds of skillful means and wisdom to give rise to the sublime path, namely:
although they skillfully cultivate the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they do not abandon sentient beings due to their compassion."

Although they have attained equality with all Buddhas, they delight in making offerings to the Buddhas; although they enter the gate of wisdom that contemplates emptiness, they diligently cultivate merit and virtue;
although they have completely transcended the three realms, they adorn the three realms—only then do they enter the seventh stage.
Having entered it, they enter the realm of immeasurable sentient beings and the pure web of the world-systems of the karma of immeasurable sentient beings.
Regarding the various distinct phenomena of the buddha-fields, the bodhisattvas on this stage fully accomplish each of the ten pāramitās in every thought-moment;
likewise, they bring all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) to perfection in every thought-moment.

Because they cultivate the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta-dhyāna*) on this stage and enter meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in every thought-moment, they attain exhaustion [of all afflictions].
This is the limit of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
The single mind of True Suchness is called the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*).
This clarifies that the eighth ground is reached because the "Far-Reaching" (*dūraṃgamā*) has already exhausted its limit; thus, one fully attains its essence.
Regarding the term "immovable," it refers to perceiving the essence of immovability through far-reaching travel.

Because, in this stage, every speck of dust and every hair on the Bodhisattva’s faculties, body, and environment is the very essence of the immovable *tathatā*, one moves away from the karma of present appearances;
having attained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (receptivity to the non-arising of phenomena), one now attains direct realization—what is called "penetrating the Dharma."
Because he has reached the source and bottom [of reality], he is named Acala (the Immovable One).

According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, at this stage, the Bodhisattva eliminates the obstacle of applied effort (*prāyogika-āvaraṇa*) within the signless (*animitta*), such that the signless contemplation no longer arises merely through effort.

In the preceding five stages, contemplation with signs (*sanimitta*) was frequent while contemplation without signs (*animitta*) was rare; however, upon reaching the sixth stage, contemplation with signs becomes rare while contemplation without signs becomes frequent.
In the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), although the contemplation of the purely signless (*animitta*) is constantly continuous, it still involves applied effort (*prayoga*).

Because there is applied effort within the signless state, one is not yet able to manifest signs and lands spontaneously. Such an obstacle of applied effort obstructs the effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*) of the eighth stage;
upon entering the eighth stage, one is then able to sever it forever and attain the two masteries (*vaśitā*). Therefore...
The Sūtra says: "This Bodhisattva enters into all phenomena as being fundamentally unborn, unarisen, signless, and having non-existence as their nature;
they are entirely equal throughout the beginning, middle, and end, and are the sphere entered by non-discriminative suchness-wisdom (*tathatā-jñāna*).
Free from all conceptualizations of mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*), they are without grasping or attachment, entering [them] like empty space."
The nature of all phenomena being like space is called the attainment of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When a Bodhisattva accomplishes this patience, they enter the eighth stage, the Immovable (*acala-bhūmi*). Being free from all clamor and contention, quiescence manifests before them;

they abandon all deliberate effort and attain the path of non-effort (*anābhoga-mārga*). Their activities of body, speech, and mind, as well as their mental exertions, all come to rest, and they abide in the state of fruition.
When practicing, even the Buddha-mind, the Bodhicitta, and the Nirvana-mind do not manifest, let alone the arising of worldly thoughts;
because of this Bodhisattva’s power of original vows, after being exhorted by all Buddhas, he then manifests the ten bodies and attains great self-mastery.
Within this, the single mind of True Suchness is also the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

The stage where the function of True Suchness (Tathatā) is manifested is named the Stage of Excellent Wisdom (Sādhumatī-bhūmi). This clarifies the ninth stage. While in the preceding stages one has already attained the entire substance of True Suchness, this stage is the manifestation of the great function of True Suchness;
this is precisely the arising of function from the true substance. In the preceding stages, every single atom and every single hair...
Being identical with true suchness and pervading the entire dharma-realm, each and every thing mutually encompasses and enters one another; thus, it is both all-pervasive and all-encompassing.

Therefore, from the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vitarka*) up to this point, it is designated as "Good Wisdom" (*sādhumati*), because for the first time one realizes the unimpeded wisdom of the dharma-realm.
According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, this constitutes the abandonment of the obstacle of lack of desire to act for the benefit of others (*parārthānabhimukhatva-āvaraṇa*).
Delighting in cultivating one's own benefit for others obstructs the ninth stage; upon entering the ninth stage, one is able to permanently sever [this obstruction]. The Great Sūtra states:
"The Bodhisattva of this stage knows, as they truly are, the activities of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas;

they know, as they truly are, the various characteristics of the minds of sentient beings; furthermore, they know the characteristics of the faculties—whether dull, middling, or superior. Furthermore, they know...

They further know the various characteristics of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the various characteristics of the arising of rebirth, the various characteristics of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), and the characteristics of those who are rightly fixed, wrongly fixed, or indeterminate.

By means of the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), these Bodhisattvas expound immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* phrases and meanings without end; acting as great Dharma masters, they extensively deliver all classes of beings.
Because it accords with the timing and is harmonious with the principle, it is called "Excellent Wisdom. [Question:

What is the difference between this and the mutual manifestation of the realms of the seven practices, or the mutual interpenetration of the five directions regarding the reliance and the supported? [Answer: It is because the seven practices are merely these practices and the five directions are merely these vows;
they have not yet been personally realized as the self-substance. Since [the latter] arises from the substance as function, they are not the same.
Ānanda, from this point onward, these bodhisattvas cultivate their practice until its completion and their merit reaches perfection;
this stage is also termed the "Stage of Cultivation" (*bhāvanā-avasthā*).

This [term] generally concludes the preceding stages; as for the word "these" (*zhè*), it refers distantly to the higher stages and proximately to the four preparatory practices (*catasraḥ prayogabhūmayaḥ*).
The phrase "up to the ninth stage" also refers to all the stages prior to the ninth; for,
having personally realized the wondrous True Suchness from the first stage onward, one proceeds through these successive stages of cultivation and severance until reaching this point,
whereby the entire substance and great function of True Suchness fully manifest before one, and the cultivation of supramundane merit reaches its fulfillment.
Because all preparations have been completed, this stage is called "Perfection" (*niṣpanna*).

Furthermore, this stage is specifically designated as "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) to clearly indicate that within death, one revives, extensively practices all deeds, extensively delivers sentient beings, and extensively accomplishes the work of a Buddha.
Moreover, this stage is regarded as the beginning of cultivation, while that which is realized by *samyak-saṃbodhi* is [the culmination].
This concludes [the section on] the end.
The "Cloud of Dharma" (*dharmameghā*) stage is so named because the subtle cloud of the compassionate shade covers the ocean of *nirvāṇa*.
This clarifies the tenth stage. Compassion is like the shade, and sublime wisdom is like the cloud; these are the causes of the Bodhisattva.
Virtue is the ocean of *nirvāṇa*, which is the fruit-virtue of the Tathāgata.

When a Bodhisattva reaches this stage, their compassion and wisdom are like the five aggregates (*skandha*) or like clouds; thus they are adjacent to the fruit of Buddhahood and cover the ocean of *nirvāṇa*.

According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, this Bodhisattva eliminates the obstacle of not yet attaining mastery over all phenomena; that obstacle [prevents] the Great Dharma-Wisdom Clouds of the tenth stage.
Because the activities contained within and arising from [these obscurations] are forever severed upon entering the tenth stage, the Great Sūtra states:
"This Bodhisattva emits from beneath both feet and from the crown of his head light rays as numerous as the atoms in ten million asaṃkhyeya trichiliocosms,
universally illuminating all worlds in the ten directions where the Buddhas reside."
Circling the assembly at the Tathāgata’s place of enlightenment ten times to the right, they remained suspended in mid-air,
forming a lattice of light and initiating various kinds of offerings to worship the Buddha. When these great luminous beings had finished performing such acts of worship,
they again circled all the assemblies at the places of enlightenment of the Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Having circled ten times, they entered from beneath the feet of all the Tathāgatas.

At that time, all the Bodhisattvas who had received their consecration in the ten directions emerged great rays of light from the mark of virtue on their chests adorned with vajras, named "Able to Destroy the Myriad Enemies of Māra.
With a retinue of one million asaṃkhyeya rays of light, they shone universally throughout the ten directions and arrived.

Upon entering this mark of the Bodhisattva’s virtue of the adamantine-ornamented chest, at that time all Buddhas emit from between their eyebrows a pure light called "Augmenting All-Knowledge and Spiritual Powers," which universally illuminates all worlds in the ten directions;
it enters through the crown of the great Bodhisattva’s head. At that moment, this Bodhisattva attains [the state] previously...

The hundred thousand samādhis not yet attained are now called "already attained," marking the stage of receiving consecration, entering the realm of the Buddha, being fully endowed with the ten powers, and falling within the number of Buddhas.
While the Tathāgata flows against the current, this Bodhisattva proceeds along it until the boundaries of enlightenment intersect; this is termed Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).

Regarding these eleven stages, the phrase "the Tathāgata flows against the current" means that the Tathāgata has already previously realized and entered the ocean of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and thus has no further progress or attainment to seek; yet, he does not abandon sentient beings and instead steers the compassionate vessel against the current.

This is because the Bodhisattvas at these stages have not yet completed their progress and attainment, and are still moving toward the ocean of the fruit by following the current. This is the realization.

Regarding those who enter the boundary of convergence, the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbuddha*) and the Buddha of Wondrous Enlightenment (*prakarṣa-saṃbuddha*) are exactly equal in their respective portions; it is only that they differ in terms of following or reversing [the flow].

The *Yingluo jing* (Sutra of the Necklaces) states: "Equal Enlightenment is illumination within stillness; Wondrous Enlightenment is stillness within illumination"—this is precisely the meaning. Wenzheng says:
"The Bodhisattvas of the Ten Grounds are identical to the Tathāgata in benefiting sentient beings, but they differ in the direction of their inclination—whether following or reversing."

The Tathāgata’s "differentiation" and the Tathāgata’s "reversal-flow" are identical to the ten thousand things. When a Bodhisattva flows with the current directly toward wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and has already reached the limit of awakening, it is therefore called "entering the intersection.

Because one has not yet heard from the Buddha, it is called "Equal Enlightenment" (*Samyaksambodhi*). This is the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) preceding the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Thus, the initial stage of "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*) is said to be when the habit-energy of desire is first dried up, yet one has not yet attained [the state of] the Tathāgata.
"Coming to connect with the Dharma-stream of the Tathāgata" means that this so-called "entering the intersection of awakening" precisely connects with the Tathāgata’s Dharma-stream.

One says "not yet connected" and one says "entering the intersection"; thus we know that the subsequent dry-wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) is no different from the initial dry-wisdom, but they are distinguished into two stages based on whether there is an intersection or not.
This corresponds to the severance of the ignorance of the arising-phase (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*) as taught in the *Awakening of Faith*.
At that time, what is called the "perfectly complete awakening to emptiness" is the extinction of both the emptiness and that which is emptied.
Ānanda, from the stage of Dry Wisdom up to Equal Enlightenment, this is the beginning of awakening; it is the initial stage of Dry Wisdom within the Diamond Mind.

This passage clarifies the manifestation of wisdom (*prajñā*). It states that from the initial stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), it is only upon reaching Equal Enlightenment that one first attains the Vajra-mind within the stage of Dry Wisdom. Question: For what reason does one only obtain [this] from the initial stage of Dry Wisdom up to Equal Enlightenment?
Answer: Because the essence of Dry Wisdom is without duality from beginning to end; yet, it is necessary to reach [Equal Enlightenment].

From this point onward, the term "initial attainment" is used; the *prajñā* of dry wisdom at the beginning is likened to the moon on its first day, while the subsequent *prajñā* of dry wisdom is like the full moon at night.
In reality, there is no difference between the moon on its first day and the moon at night;
it is simply that the moon on its first day still possesses much yin energy, whereas the moon at night has exhausted its yin energy and shines with light.
It is bright, blazing, and perfectly full; yet one cannot say that the newly risen moon is different from the moon on the night of the full moon.

This mind of dry wisdom is also like this: having already used diamond-like wisdom to sever the ignorance of dualistic characteristics, it has attained a portion of manifest radiance, like the newly risen moon. Now...
Upon reaching Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one likewise employs the final vajra-mind to sever the ignorance of the "mark of arising" (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*);

only then does one attain the perfection of radiance, like the full moon at night. If we employ the hexagrams of the *I Ching* as a metaphor: initial Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) is like the hexagram Fu (*Fù*), where the single Yang line first returns;
the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) are like Lin (*Lín*); the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*) are like Tai (*Tài*); and the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) are like...
The ten stages of the *Dàzhuàng* hexagram correspond to the *Guài* hexagram, up to the *Qiánhù* (dry wisdom) of Equal Enlightenment, which corresponds to the *Qián* hexagram.

At this point, the yin has been exhausted and the substance of yang is complete. Therefore, it was previously stated that one takes the "unborn and undying" as the mind of the causal ground (*yīndì xīn*), and subsequently realizes the perfect fruition of the ground of enlightenment (*guòdì xiūzhèng*). To say "perfect fruition" (*yuánchéng*) means that it is fully perfected.

Since the accomplishment [of Buddhahood] is termed "wonderful enlightenment" (myōgaku) as the perfect realization (enjō), it is known that from the first stage (shojū) onward, all are partial realizations.

The *Tongyi* states: "Regarding the beginning and end of the two stages of 'dry wisdom' (kan'e), interpretations since antiquity have not been uniform, making it difficult for students to rely upon them;
this is merely because they have not observed the source of the Buddha-dharma. This is because the nine realms of sentient beings are designated by the name of the three kinds of flow (sanhiryū).
The afflictions of the five abodes give rise to two kinds of birth-and-death. The five abodes are:
the abode of desire-attachment, the abode of form-attachment, the abode of formless-attachment, the abode of all views, and the abode of ignorance. Regarding the three floods (*ogha*):
they are the flood of desire, the flood of existence, and the flood of ignorance. The first four afflictions constitute the categories of the flood of desire and the flood of existence.
Segmented birth-and-death (*bhava*) is already severed at the first stage of faith;
that which is called "birth-and-death through transformation" (*nirmāṇa-bhava*), caused by the influence of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*), is severed only upon reaching the fruit of Buddhahood.

In this sutra, because the focus regarding the defiled conditions of birth-and-death lies primarily on the character "flowing" (*liu*), it is said that within the six sense faculties they "flow and disperse toward objects"; conversely, when observing the practice of returning to the unreal, it is said they "return the flow and revolve."
The first entry into the stream (*srotāpanna*) specifically takes the three types of flowing characteristics as the basis for both the true and the false.
Now, because the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama is collectively named the Vajra-like Illusory Samādhi, the preceding text states:
"These various stages are all observed with the vajra, gradually entering deeper. Thus, we know that from the very beginning of the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*), it is so.

By employing the adamantine contemplation (*vajra-vipaśyanā*), one’s initial resolve at the stage of generating the bodhicitta aims to directly sever the ignorance of the arising-characteristic (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*);

why wait for the final moment of mind at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samābodhi*)? To prove this by means of this [teaching], the first stage, the Dry Wisdom Ground (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*), employs the adamantine mind to spontaneously and first sever the two outflows of desire, thereby exhausting the birth-and-death of the segmented realm; thus it is said that "the craving of desire is dried up."

When the sense faculties and their objects no longer encounter one another and the remaining physical substrate no longer continues to arise—just as when turbid water is clarified and the sand and silt settle of their own accord so that clear water appears—this is called the "first subduing of adventitious afflictions.

As for the flow of ignorance, from the moment one enters the stage of faith, one has already resolved to sever it; however, because ignorance is profound and thick, one must pass through fifty-four stages before it is directly eliminated.

Upon reaching Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), the mental marks of ignorance (*avidyā*) are just dried up; because this ignorance is severed within the contemplative mind, it is said that this is the beginning of awakening.
One then attains the Vajra-mind, the initial stage of Dry Wisdom (*prathamā śuṣka-vijñāna-bhūmi*). The five abodes are fully exhausted and the two deaths are forever extinguished.

When the flow of ignorance reaches this point of being just dried up, one enters Sublime Enlightenment (*sūkṣma-saṃbodhi*) and emerges from the death-and-rebirth of transformation (*nirmāṇa-vaiparītya-jāti-maraṇa*).
What is called "removing the mud to reveal pure water" refers to the permanent severance of fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*).

This scriptural passage serves as proof that while these stages have a beginning and an end, there is no sequence in terms of prior and posterior; rather, they are ordered according to the depth of one's practice and realization.
In this manner, through successive layers of single and double stages totaling twelve, one exhausts the wondrous enlightenment and accomplishes the Unsurpassed Way.
This clarifies the ultimate fruit of the Tathāgata: the first two phrases conclude the stage of causes, while the latter two phrases clarify the stage of realized fruition.
"Single" refers to a single name or a single position; "double" refers to a single name with multiple positions. As for the "twelve," it means:

The stages of dry faith, abiding, practice, and orientation, as well as the levels of warmth, summits, patience, and the worldly grounds, are "excellent. The first eleven serve as causes, while the final one serves as the fruit.

If one reaches this "dry wisdom" (śuṣka-prajñā) and proceeds through to Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), one has merely attained it; only upon reaching Supreme Enlightenment (anuttara-saṃbodhi) does one fully attain it.

Thus, as long as there is still something to be attained, one has not yet reached the ultimate. When attainment is exhausted, one returns to non-attainment. This corresponds to the Tiantai teaching of the exhaustion of cessation (*jiedun wu*).

This clearly demonstrates the realization of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). Now, as for this wisdom being called "sublime," how could it surpass the initial stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*)?
It is simply that the initial mind of dry wisdom is polished and refined until it reaches the ultimate state of luminous clarity, thereby manifesting its sublimity.

As for what is called the "unsurpassed path," it means that although the initial mind of the Perfect and Sudden [teaching] is identical to that of the Tathāgata, [it is so designated to distinguish its potential].

The single path of awakening, when considered merely in terms of its stages, becomes increasingly superior as one proceeds from the earlier to the later, such that even up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), it is still said to have something "above" it.
Only upon reaching this [stage] is there nothing further above; hence it is called "Unsurpassed.

The preceding "Supreme Worldly Stage" (*laukikāgra-dharma*) is unsurpassed within the mundane world, whereas this is unsurpassed in the supramundane. This is due to the twelve classes of beings mentioned previously.

The twelve transformations are exhausted to become a single cycle of return; therefore, the cultivation of causes and the realization of fruits also possess the twelve [stages] in both their simple and complex forms. Question: In the "Chapter on Avalokiteśvara’s Perfect Penetration," the causal mind was revealed through birth, abiding, change, and extinction (*jāti-sthiti-anyathātva-nirodha*). Why is it that here, the awakened fruit is revealed through birth, abiding, change, and extinction? Answer: The former was spoken in terms of the path of cultivation, and thus referred to the cause. The latter is spoken in terms of the ultimate fruition, and thus refers to the fruit. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of a single thought-moment, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the entire duration of a kalpa. Moreover, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the five aggregates, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the six sense bases. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three realms of existence, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three bodies of the Buddha. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the two vehicles, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the One Vehicle. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three teachings, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the one principle. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three obstacles, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three virtues. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three poisons, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three natures. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three karmas, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three liberations. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three afflictions, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three wisdoms. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three realms of rebirth, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three bodies of the Buddha. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three types of sentient beings, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three types of Buddhas. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three types of dharmas, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three types of nirvana. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three types of practice, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three types of realization. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three types of delusion, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three types of awakening. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three types of bondage, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three types of liberation. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three types of suffering, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three types of bliss. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three types of emptiness, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three types of reality. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three types of non-self, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three types of self. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three types of impermanence, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three types of permanence. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three types of arising, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three types of cessation. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three types of conditioned phenomena, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three types of unconditioned phenomena. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three types of worldly dharmas, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three types of supramundane dharmas. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three types of outflows, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three types of outflowlessness. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three types of grasping, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three types of non-grasping. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three types of attachment, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three types of non-attachment. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three types of craving, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three types of non-craving. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three types of views, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three types of right view.
