Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three types of ignorance, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three types of true knowledge. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three types of deluded thoughts, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three types of enlightened thoughts. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three types of false speech, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three types of true speech. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three types of wrong action, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three types of right action. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three types of wrong livelihood, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three types of right livelihood. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three types of wrong effort, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three types of right effort. Furthermore, the former was explained by way of the four phases of the three types of wrong mindfulness, whereas the latter is explained by way of the four phases of the three types of right mindfulness. The mind is the beginning; since this is spoken in terms of realizing the fruit, it takes the awakening to the fruit as the end. This precisely reveals that the fruit is identical to the cause, for the fruit is not separate from the cause, and the cause is not separate from the fruit.
That which is the cause of the fruit is not distinct from the fruit itself, and that which is the fruit of the cause is not distinct from the cause itself.
All these various stages are realized through the gradual and profound entry into *śamatha*— observing all things as like illusions by means of the ten kinds of deep metaphors—
and through the purification of *vipaśyanā* according to the Tathāgatas.
This generally clarifies the practice of the various stages. "Various grounds" refers to the aforementioned ground of causes and the ground of fruition.
As for "Vajra," it refers to the adamantine precious awakening, the sharp instrument for severing delusions.
Regarding the "ten kinds of profound metaphors": one contemplates all karma as being like an illusion, all phenomena as being like a flame, and all bodies... [as being like a reflection].
The exquisite forms are like the moon in water; the exquisite sounds are like echoes; the buddha-fields are like cities of the gandharvas;
the buddha-activities are like dreams; the buddha-bodies are like shadows; the reward bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*) are like images; and the dharma-bodies (*dharmakāya*) are like emanations.

Because all things are empty and cannot be grasped or discarded, this statement does not merely contemplate that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are all empty, but contemplates that even the unconditioned is empty.
Because they are likewise like dreams and illusions, they are called "profound metaphors. One observes by means of these ten kinds of profound metaphors and severs delusions with vajra-wisdom.
Alternatively, Master Guan says: "Cultivate the myriad practices as empty flowers; sit in meditation within a water-moon dharma-hall;
subdue the celestial Māras within a mirror; and realize the fruit of Buddhahood within a dream. This is śamatha."
That which is the self-nature fundamentally settled is, through this observation, termed "subtle and secret contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).

This *vipaśyanā* is precisely the illusory-like *samāpatti*. To say that this adamantine precious awakening is nothing other than a distinct entity refers to the "subtle and secret contemplation" in the second fascicle and the "*samāpatti*" in the third fascicle. Thus it is used.
By means of this observation, one is able to arise from nature into cultivation, attain realization through cultivation, and gradually enter deeper;
it is here that the conclusion is reached, returning to the attainment of the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* of Bodhi.
Ānanda, it is precisely by means of these three progressive advancements that one is well able to accomplish the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi.
One who contemplates in this manner is said to have right contemplation; any other contemplation is said to be wrong contemplation.
This emphasizes the initial mind, desiring that people "study below and reach above. Wuxing says: "The three stages of advancement are precisely the three gradual sequences (*tri-śan-tsai*).

Because it was previously stated, 'this is called the gradual sequence of advancing cultivation,' and further stated, 'from this gradual sequence, according to what is practiced, one establishes the noble ranks'—the fifty-five ranks begin from the Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vitarka*)."

Wisdom up to the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are all paths for entering the house of Bodhi; Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and Sublime Enlightenment (*vibuddha*) constitute the house of Bodhi itself.
This is intended to cause those of inferior aspiration to abandon the heterodox and return to the orthodox. Wuxing said:

"One must know that, outside of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), all that is cultivated by the three vehicles belongs to heterodox contemplation (*xieguan*); the single character 'heterodox' (*xie*) is used in contrast to the 'superior' (*sheng*)."

Distinguishing the inferior as "false" refers not to the "falsehood" of one who has left the Way, but rather to the "falsehood" of one who is not yet on the Path. The section on the "Certification of the Way" is now complete;

from the first fascicle up to this point, the single topic concerning the "Primordial Pure Essence of Beginningless Bodhi and Nirvana" has been finalized. Below follows the section on the "Concluding the Sutra."
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What should this sutra be named? How should I and all sentient beings uphold it? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"This sutra is named 'The Great Buddha-Crown, the Supreme Jewel Seal of Sitatapatra.'"

The Pure Ocean-Eye of the Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions; also named the Rescue and Protection of Kinsmen, which delivers Ānanda and the bhikṣuṇī of this assembly by nature, enabling them to attain the Bodhicitta and enter the ocean of universal knowledge; also named the Definitive Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata;
also named the Great Vaipulya King of the Wondrous Lotus, the Dhāraṇī that is the Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions.
This mantra is also called the "Mantra of Consecration" (*abhiṣeka-pada*). It is the foremost of the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas, the *Śūraṅgama*. You should uphold it.
This sutra, in its initial approach, first breaks down the mind to reveal the seeing; it refutes both causes and conditions as well as spontaneity;

it dismantles the three aggregates, the seven elements, and the six consciousnesses, leading people to awaken to this nature of non-arising and non-extinction. Next, it examines the causal mind within oneself and traces back to the root of karma, pointing directly to the faculty of hearing.
The first chapter serves as a skillful means for practice, enabling people to cultivate this nature that is neither born nor extinguished;
next, it extensively elucidates the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi, enabling people to realize this nature that is neither born nor extinguished.
Thus, the Tathāgata intends for those who seek awakening to awaken to this, those who practice to practice this, and those who realize to realize this; yet they simply do not know it.
That which is neither born nor extinguished—what is it called that causes people to receive it upon their heads, uphold it, and never lose it?
Therefore, the World-Honored One bestowed upon it the name "Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa. Because it is without form that can be perceived, it is the supreme Uṣṇīṣa-dharma realized by all Buddhas;
thus it is called the "Great White Parasol," which covers and protects all sentient beings, nourishing them like [the earth].
Because one comes to the Realm of the Wondrous Jewel King, it is called the "Unsurpassed Jewel Seal";
because it is sealed by the three categories, seven greats, and one dharma, it is held as such to command and subdue humans, devas, māras, and non-Buddhists;

because it is the pure ocean-eye that perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm without omitting a single thing, this name is established based on wisdom and principle. It is also named "Rescue and Protection."

"Proximate cause" refers to Ānanda’s own cause, which is that of Māgadha; through the secret divine mantra of fearless radiance, one is able to escape all calamities and cause that proximate causal mind to realize the ocean of fruition. Thus, this name is established based on its functional application.
It is also called "The Definitive Meaning of the Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Cultivation, and Realization," for it is that which all Buddhas have cultivated and realized.
Because both the true cause and the true fruit are perfectly complete, this title is established based on the person and the dharma.

It is also called the *Mahāvaipulya-saddharmapuṇḍarīka-rāja* (The Great Vaipulya, Wondrous Lotus King), because its essence, attributes, and function are primordially pure in their threefold clarity, pervading the entire dharma-realm;
and because cause and effect interpenetrate so thoroughly that nothing is not sovereign. Thus, these two titles—*Avataṃsaka* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*—are in fact one and the same.
The *Dhāraṇī-mantra of the Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions* is so named because it gives birth to all Buddhas and upholds (*dhāraṇī*) all dharmas;
this name is established according to both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings.

It is also called the "Mantras of Consecration" (*abhiṣeka-pada*), for this sutra flows forth from the *Abhiṣeka-varga*. As for the "Śūraṅgama," the foremost of the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas:

Because by cultivating this samādhi, one fulfills the ten thousand practices within a single mind to the ultimate degree of firmness, it is thus named in accordance with its teaching, practice, and establishment.

One should know that this sutra encompasses all aspects—manifest and secret, principle and wisdom, teaching and practice, person and dharma, and function—because it possesses such various kinds of merit; therefore, it has various titles.
"You must carefully guard and uphold this; do not let it be lost.

Having spoken these words, Ānanda and the great assembly immediately received the Tathāgata’s revelation of the meaning of the secret seal, the *Paṭala*, and upon hearing the definitive titles of this sutra, they suddenly awakened to the stages of holy progress in the cultivation of *dhyāna*.
Through the supreme and wondrous principle, the mind becomes empty and concentrated, severing the six grades of subtle afflictions cultivated within the three realms;
this describes the attainment of the canopy by those suited to the teaching. "Secret Seal" (*guhyamudrā*) refers to the secret heart-seal, while *paṭṭala* is the Great White Canopy;
this describes the reiteration of the preceding mantra for the sake of the audience. Furthermore, it mentions the name of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

"Eye" refers to the names of the aforementioned five stages. "The sublime principle of the progressive advancement through the noble stages of sudden enlightenment in *dhyāna*" refers to the aforementioned sudden realization of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);

from this point, one establishes the noble stages, advancing gradually step by step until reaching the ultimate state of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). "The mind and its deliberations become void and concentrated" means that one has reached this point.
Thus, the stages of the primary and auxiliary practices of cultivation and realization, as well as the meanings of the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings, are all clearly understood without any doubt;
consequently, with the mind empty and contemplation concentrated, the six grades of outflows of desire are severed, and the second fruit is realized.
Wénlǐng says: "Regarding the delusions to be severed through the cultivation of the Path, the Lesser Vehicle divides the Three Realms into nine stages."
On each stage (*bhūmi*), there are nine grades of abandonment; by abandoning the first six grades of the desire realm, one realizes the second fruit (*phala*);

by abandoning the final three grades, one realizes the third fruit; and by abandoning the nine grades of each of the two higher realms, one realizes the fourth fruit. Ānanda heard the entire sūtra in its completeness yet only realized the second fruit;
this demonstrates that the inferiority of mere extensive learning (*bahuśruta*) does not equal the progress made through the cultivation of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
The section on the Sūtra of the Conquering of Bonds is concluded. Below this, the second major section clarifies the fundamental root of beginningless birth and death.

Although from the first fascicle up to this point both the True and the Delusory have been explained in alternation, the primary intent has been to elucidate that the originally pure essence of bodhi and nirvana—the nature of non-arising and non-extinction—is the fundamental cause for cultivation, by means of which one attains realization.
Regarding the "fruit that is neither born nor extinguished," the following section extensively clarifies how birth and extinction serve as the cause to evoke a fruit of birth and extinction.
This is because the first fascicle states: "All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have followed various inverted karmic fruits that arise spontaneously like clusters of akṣa berries.

World-Honored One, if this wondrously luminous, truly pure, and sublime mind is fundamentally pervasive and perfect, then even down to the earth, grasses, trees, crawling insects, and all sentient beings—their original source, True Suchness—is itself the Tathāgata’s accomplishment.
"The true body of the Buddha and the reality of the Buddha's essence— how can there further be the paths of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals,

This question concerns the causes for the arising of the seven destinies. "Compassionate voice" refers to teaching without weariness or stinginess;
"skillfully revealing" means demonstrating with ingenuity. "Subtle, latent afflictions" refers to those abandoned during the previous fifty-five stages.

thus, all insentient and sentient beings are, in their entirety, identical to the Tathāgata’s single, perfectly integrated, and pure nature."
How is it that within the Jewel-Awareness there further arise various distinct and diverse forms, each with its own differences?

Furthermore, from what do these diverse forms emerge? Are these various hells fixed in specific locations, or do they arise spontaneously for each individual?

Karma is individually and privately experienced; we pray that you will bestow great compassion and enlighten us, the ignorant, so that all sentient beings who uphold the precepts may hear this definitive meaning, receive it with joy and reverence, and remain pure and untainted by transgressions.
This is a detailed inquiry concerning hell. In the Sanskrit language it is called *niraya*, which here is translated as "hell" (*dīyù*).
It is also named "lack of autonomy," because those who commit offenses are bound and restrained by the jailers and *asuras* (āpáng), and thus lack self-mastery.

The Bhikṣu Bāoliánxiāng violated the precept against sexual misconduct and slander, thereby incurring retribution in the present life; Rúlǐ, on the other hand, violated [the precept against] killing and likewise incurred retribution in the present life.
Regarding the precept against killing, Shanxing (Sunakṣatra) violated the precept against false speech and fell [into hell]. Wénlǐng says:

"King Virūḍhaka, the crown prince, deposed his father and established himself as ruler; harboring old grudges, he slaughtered the Śākya clan and took twelve thousand Śākya maidens, mutilating their ears and noses and severing their hands and feet, then pushing them into pits and ditches. The Buddha prophesied that in seven days he would [fall into hell]."

"Entering hell" refers to King Ajātaśatru, who sailed across the sea to escape; [the fire] was naturally extinguished in the water. "Speaking of old grudges" (*sukheda*) refers to long-standing resentment.

(When the Buddha was in the world, King Prasenajit, having newly ascended the throne, sent an envoy to seek a marriage alliance with a family of the Śākya clan in Kapilavastu. At that time, Mahānāma’s maidservant gave birth to a daughter of upright and beautiful countenance, whom she sent to King Prasenajit.

Later, she bore a son named Virūḍhaka. When he reached the age of eight, he went with the son of a Brahmin, Bhadrika, to the house of Mahānāma. At that time, a new lecture hall had been built in Kapilavastu, and they wished to invite the Tathāgata.)
At that time, when Prince Vairāṭa arrived at the lecture hall, he ascended the lion throne. Upon seeing him, the Śākyas reviled him, saying, "How dare this offspring of a slave sit upon this seat?

Vairāṭa spoke to the brahmin Bhadraka, saying, "These Śākyas have brought me such humiliation; if I succeed to the throne, you must inform me. Later, when Vairāṭa had succeeded to the throne, Bhadraka informed him of these previous events. Vairāṭa then assembled his troops and went to wage war against the Śākyas.

The Buddha said to the bhikṣus, "In the past, when this city of Rājagṛha was a fishing village and the world suffered from famine, there was a pond in that village containing many fish. At that time, many people from the city went to the pond to catch and eat the fish. Within the pond were two..."

There were two kinds of fish: the first was called *piṣṭa* (the Flour Fish), and the second was called *bahujihva* (the Many-Tongued Fish). Each harbored a grudge for revenge. At that time, a young child standing on the bank saw the fish leaping and, out of joy, struck the head of a fish with a stick.

Those people of Rājagṛha are now the Śākyas; the *piṣṭa* fish is King Virūḍhaka; the *bahujihva* fish is the Brahmin Kokālika; and the young child is none other than myself. For this reason and these conditions, King Virūḍhaka killed the Śākyas because he harbored an old resentment.
As for Sunakṣatra, he was the Buddha’s cousin. He falsely preached that all phenomena are empty and denied the existence of cause and effect. Because of the power of his karma, he fell into hell.

Even when the physical body is forced down into it, such is this hell; does it have a fixed location that exists inherently from the beginning, or do those who commit such karma each individually receive their retribution according to their own deeds?
The Buddha told Ānanda, "How excellent is this question! It shall cause all sentient beings not to enter into false views. Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
Ānanda, all sentient beings are in truth fundamentally pure from the beginning. Because of that deluded perception, deluded habits arise;
because of this, the division between the internal and external occurs."

This generally clarifies that the two divisions of internal and external constitute the causes for the seven destinies (*gati*). Because this accords with the Buddha’s original intention, it is called "how joyous!
Since violating precepts and breaking prohibitions are all based on false views and are not the true cause, [the Buddha] uses questioning to ensure that sentient beings do not enter into false views.
As for the statement that the essence of the seven destinies is truly fundamentally pure and clean, it means that the substance of the seven destinies is indeed...
This is fundamentally true, pure, and free from all delusive defilements; yet, due to being deluded regarding this truly pure mind, one subsequently gives rise to delusive views.

Because of these delusive views, delusive habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) further arise. What is called "delusive views" refers to the active manifestation of afflictions (*kleśa*), while "delusive habitual tendencies" refers to the karmic latencies (*karma-vāsanā*).
With these afflictions and karma as causes, one consequently divides into two parts: the internal and the external. Regarding the internal part:
This refers to emotion (*qing*). Because emotion stirs within and gives rise to thoughts from the physical shell, it is called "external division. This refers to perception (*xiang*).

Because perception conditions the external and gives rise to thoughts from superior objects, the previous section took emotion and perception as the root of the twelve classes of beings, while this section takes emotion and perception as the source of the seven destinies (*saptagati*). Although emotion and perception do not... [text truncated]
Although there are differences in their relative superiority or inferiority, in sum they all belong to a single delusion.
Ānanda, the internal division refers to the internal causes within the realm of sentient beings: from various attachments and defilements, deluded sentiments are aroused;
as these sentiments accumulate without ceasing, they can produce the water of craving. Therefore, when a sentient being’s mind recalls delicacies, water flows from the mouth; when the mind recalls...

Whether out of pity or resentment, the eyes of former people fill with tears; when greedily seeking wealth and treasures, the heart gives rise to a flow of saliva, making the entire body glossy and moist;

when the mind becomes attached and engages in sexual intercourse, the fluids of both male and female organs naturally flow. Ānanda, although these various forms of craving differ, their underlying tendency toward flowing and binding is the same:
they are moistening and do not ascend, but naturally fall downward. This is called the "internal portion" (ādhyātmika-bhāga).
This is the internal analysis within the detailed explanation. Because emotional attachment (*sneha*) is something inherent within the realm of sentient beings, it is called "internal.
Initially, one gives rise to clinging toward an object; this is "attachment" (*rāga*). To be infatuated and unable to let go is "deluded emotion" (*moha*).
As this emotion accumulates without ceasing, it becomes "water," flowing everywhere without exception. Therefore, below, its nature as desire (*kāma*) is verified.
When one remembers choice delicacies, water flows; when one thinks of a former person, tears fill [the eyes]; when one covets wealth and treasures, the body becomes moist;
and when one indulges in sexual misconduct, fluids flow—all these are caused by the defilement of craving. Ānanda, the following clarifies that the "water of craving" inevitably falls:
although the objects of affection differ from one another, they all cause [the mind] to become firmly bound.
If one does not understand this, then the mind of attachment is no different [from water], for since emotional affection belongs to the nature of water, it flows downward and solidifies;
thus, because it falls and does not rise, it becomes the cause for the three miserable realms.

Ānanda, the external division refers to the external factors of sentient beings. Through various forms of longing and yearning, they bring forth empty conceptions (*śūnyasaṃjñā*) which accumulate without ceasing;
this can produce a superior vital energy (*viśiṣṭavāyu*). For this reason, when sentient beings maintain the prohibitive precepts (*śīla*), their entire bodies become light and pure.

When they maintain mantras and mudrās, their gaze becomes majestic and resolute. When they desire to be born in the heavens, they dream of flying aloft. When they fix their minds on the Buddha-lands, they perceive sacred realms.

When the manifestations of the dark realm appear and one regards the spiritual friend as more precious than one’s own body and life, Ānanda, although these various thoughts differ, their lightness and elevation are the same;
they soar and move without sinking, naturally transcending—this is called the "external division."

This is a separate explanation of the external realm (*bāhyabhāga*). Because the superior vital energy (*śreṣṭhavāyu*) does not belong to the internal constituent parts of sentient beings, it is called "external.
"Thirsting with longing" means to yearn for the sublime realm of the sages, just as one who is thirsty looks up toward water.

"Illuminating empty conceptions" refers precisely to the conception of the True Persons beyond the heavens. "Superior vital energy" is the *haoran* (vast and pervasive) qi. At the very beginning, one hears it...

When one aspires toward a sublime realm, it becomes a thirsting longing; when this longing reaches its peak, the spirit gallops forth without ceasing. This constitutes a "sublime breath" (*śubha-vāyu*);
as it accumulates through such contemplation, it increases further until there is nowhere it cannot reach. Therefore, one may verify that this contemplation functions as a sublime breath:
when one observes the prohibitive precepts, the entire body becomes light and pure; when one maintains mantras and mudrās, [the body] turns...

To gaze with heroic resolve toward rebirth in heaven and dream of soaring upward, to contemplate the Buddha-lands until sacred realms manifest in the depths of one's being, and to serve spiritual teachers while disregarding one’s own life—all these are summoned by superior vital energy (*śukra*).
Ānanda, the following clarifies that such superior energy must inevitably ascend; though the objects of one's contemplation may each differ, they all cause one to become light.
If one is buoyant and does not sink, then the vital energy (*prāṇa*) will not differ [from its natural state]; because this vital energy belongs to the element of fire, it is light and ascends.
Thus, by transcending without falling, it becomes the cause for the higher realms.
Ānanda, throughout all worlds, the cycle of birth and death continues: birth proceeds from habitual conformity, and death proceeds from transformative flux.

At the moment of the end of life, before warmth and sensation have been relinquished, the good and evil of a single lifetime appear simultaneously and instantaneously. Death is contrary to the flow of birth, yet these two habits intersect.
The above clarifies that emotional thoughts constitute the seven destinies; the following clarifies the fruits summoned by those emotional thoughts.

"Birth follows habitual practice, while death follows the flow of transformation" means that at the time of birth, the two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—created are all performed in accordance with one's intentions, without any contradiction.
When death approaches and the body has not yet relinquished its warmth and tactile sensation, then [the karma] from throughout one's life...
Those who follow their habitual tendencies all transform into corresponding manifestations that appear before them;

thus, when a wholesome mind arises, a jeweled palace appears, and when an evil thought stirs, a city of fire manifests. Therefore, in a single lifetime, both good and evil appear simultaneously and instantaneously—this is what is meant by "the wandering soul undergoes transformation.
Regarding the phrase "the two habits of life and death intersect," it refers to those who commit evil while alive.
If one who follows the path of evil dies, they will surely encounter adversity; if one who has lived virtuously dies, they will surely encounter favorability.

Just as those who have committed evil find pleasure in the delights of female beauty during their lives, indulging their passions and following their whims, at the moment of death—even if golden chariots and jade maidens appear before them—all such things will repel their desires.
Conversely, for those who have lived virtuously, the pleasures of female beauty were met with aversion during their lives.
Furthermore, because one steadfastly maintains the precepts and prohibitions, at the time of death, golden banners and jade maidens come to welcome them;

as these all accord with their inclinations, the two habitual tendencies of good and evil intersect as opposing and conforming forces. These two phrases should follow the section on "Warmth and Touch" to clearly manifest consciousness.
As the *Xiǎnshí jīng* (Sūtra on Manifesting Consciousness) states: "The Great Medicine addressed the Buddha, saying: 'World-Honored One, when sentient beings cast off their bodies...'"
"How does one take birth among the devas, and even how does one take birth in the hells? The Buddha said:

"When sentient beings are at the point of death, those whose karma of merit serves as their support cast off their original vision and obtain a sublime vision. They see the six heavens of the desire realm;

they see their own bodies moving and shaking; they see celestial palaces and so forth. This continues until, whether asleep or awake, they pass away in peace and tranquility as they are about to relinquish their life."
At the time of his passing, the celestial father and mother sat together upon a single seat; from the hand of the celestial mother, a flower spontaneously emerged.
Seeing the flower, the celestial mother looked toward the celestial father and said with joy, "The time for celebrating our son's departure is not far off.
As the celestial mother then began to play with the flower with both hands, his life came to an end, and his formless consciousness was cast away.

Abandoning the faculties while maintaining the function of the faculties; relinquishing the objects while maintaining the activity of the objects; abandoning the realms while maintaining the function of the realms;

and undergoing the transformation of karmic fruition like one mounting a horse, discarding one mount to mount another, or like the sun drawing forth its light, or fire arising from wood—consciousness, supported by wholesome karma, swiftly takes rebirth within the lotus, where the celestial father and mother sit together.
Beholding them like nectar, a wind blows through the flowers in the seventh month; precious earrings adorn their bodies with a dazzling radiance.
The celestial youths, pure and bright, appear in the hands of the Mother of Heaven. If sentient beings have accumulated roots of unwholesomeness, at the moment of death they will think:
"Now this body of mine shall abandon my parents, kinsmen, and loved ones; what great sorrow and suffering!"
He sees the various hells and perceives his own body as one destined to enter them; he sees his feet above and his head inverted, looking downward.
Furthermore, he sees a place where the ground is entirely composed of blood. Having seen this blood, a mind of attachment arises;
conditioned by this mind of attachment, there is the power of the causal force of the foul, putrid, and stinking waters of hell, and consciousness is deposited therein. This is the analogy.
Just as foul-smelling excrement gives rise to maggots, one knows that the mind creates heaven and the mind creates hell.

If one’s thoughts are purely of the pure, one will surely fly upward and be born in the heavens. If within the flying mind there is a combination of merit, wisdom, and pure vows, the mind will naturally open and one will see the Buddhas of the ten directions and all the Pure Lands;
according to one's vows, one will be reborn therein. This occurs when the emotional afflictions are slight and the pure thoughts are predominant.
Leaping lightly, they are not far from becoming flying immortals, powerful ghost-kings, flying yakṣas, or earth-walking rākṣasas who roam through the four heavens, unhindered wherever they go.
Among them, there may be those with virtuous vows and virtuous minds who protect and uphold my Dharma;

or those who protect the prohibitive precepts according to those who maintain the precepts; or those who protect divine mantras according to those who maintain the mantras; or those who protect meditative concentration.
Those who preserve and sustain the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti) are those who dwell intimately beneath the seat of the Tathāgata.
This clarifies that for those whose conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) is predominant and whose afflictions are few, they die in a state of opposition [to the world] but are reborn in accordance with it.

Those born in heaven through pure conceptualization merely establish their residence in heaven rather than roaming through it; all the heavens within the triple world are induced by the mind of conceptualization.

Among them, those who practice the six perfections while contemplating the Buddha-lands may also attain rebirth according to their contemplation, such as those who, by contemplating the Western Land, are born there.
As for those who ascend lightly without traveling far: vertically they do not exceed the four heavens, and horizontally they do not go beyond the Cakravāḍa mountains.
With one state of mind and nine thoughts, one becomes a flying immortal; with two states of mind and eight thoughts—
Those with three emotions and seven thoughts become powerful ghost-kings; those with four emotions and nine thoughts become flying yakṣas;
and those who wander as earth-roaming rākṣasas do so for a temporary period rather than dwelling there long-term.

"Among them" refers to the aforementioned four classes, who bring peace and security. Those who sit beneath the Tathāgata’s seat have transformed their evil minds to become protectors of the Teaching.
The spirits are of the same category as the eight classes of beings.

When their emotions and perceptions are balanced, they neither fly upward nor fall downward, being born among human beings; if their perceptions are clear, they are intelligent, and if their emotions are obscure, they are dull.

"Balanced" refers to the five emotions and five perceptions. "Neither flying upward nor falling downward" means that above they do not remain in heaven, and below they do not [fall into the realms of suffering].

Abiding on earth, one participates in the space between heaven and earth; yet, from the highest wisdom to the lowest folly, the emotional and conceptual dispositions (*saṃjñā*) are equal, for both clarity and dullness are inherently possessed.
If one’s conceptual clarity advances further, the clear-sighted become even clearer and thus achieve the highest wisdom.
If one’s emotional obscurity advances daily, the dull-witted become even duller and thus achieve the lowest folly. If it were otherwise for those of lofty intelligence...
If one applies the mind in a state of darkness during daily life, this mind will also become increasingly dark; thus, what was sharp is transformed into dullness.
Conversely, if one who is dim-witted and dull applies the mind in a state of high clarity, this mind will also become increasingly clear;
thus, what was dull is transformed into sharpness. Therefore, Guan Yin said: "Ascending the *hun* is noble; descending the *po* is base. One should value the *hun*.
Lightness and clarity constitute the *hun* soul, while heaviness and opacity constitute the *po* soul. That which is neither light nor dark is that which possesses both souls in equal measure;
thus we know that what humans possess is half-light and half-dark. If those who are dark-prone practice clarity, they transform darkness into light;
if those who are light-prone practice darkness, they transform light into darkness. This is the source by which the sharp and dull, the wise and the foolish, are distinguished.
When emotions predominate and thoughts are few, one flows into the realm of horizontal birth; the heavy become the fur-bearing beasts, the light become the feathered tribes.

When seven emotions and three thoughts prevail, one sinks beneath the water wheel and is born at the boundary of fire, receiving breath from fierce flames and becoming a hungry ghost whose body is constantly burned.
Water can only harm oneself, with neither food nor drink for hundreds of thousands of kalpas. When nine emotions and one thought remain, one descends through the fire wheel.
When the body enters the two intersecting realms of wind and fire, the earth becomes light, giving rise to two types of hells: the Intermittent and the Uninterrupted.

Those consisting purely of sentient emotion immediately sink into the Avīci Hell. If, while sinking, the mind harbors slander of the Mahāyāna, destruction of the Buddha’s prohibitions and precepts, deceptive and false preaching of the Dharma, hollow greed for offerings of faith, or unwarranted acceptance of reverence, and commits the five heinous crimes or the ten grave offenses, they shall be reborn in the ten directions.
In the Avīci Hell, although one invites rebirth there by personally creating evil karma within a particular class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*), that realm also contains the fundamental lands.
This clarifies that those with much feeling (*vedanā*) and little perception (*saṃjñā*) are born in accordance with their nature and die against it;

those with six feelings and four perceptions are born as horizontal creatures (*tiryag-yoni*); those with heavy feeling and slightly lighter perception become the hairy flocks; and those with light feeling and slightly heavier perception [become...]

For birds, there are seven afflictions (*kleśa*) and three perceptions (*saṃjñā*); for hungry ghosts (*preta*), as Wēn-líng says, the *Abhidharmakośa* states that at the very bottom of the great earth are the three wheels of gold, water, and wind, with the eight cold and eight hot hells situated above these three wheels.
This present text, however, speaks of sinking beneath the wheels of water, fire, and wind, which suggests that the hells are below the three wheels; this is a point of doubt.
What is referred to here is not the three wheels beneath the earth, but rather the three wheels of hell. The phrase "the water wheel at the limit of fire" refers to the eighth cold hell.
Regarding "receiving the fierce fire," this means receiving fiery vapors to form one's body, whereby one is constantly burned by fire;
even if one obtains water to drink, it transforms into fire. Thus it is said: "Water can harm oneself—this is the true limit."
It is said: "With eight feelings and two perceptions, one is born in the *sāntara* hells; with nine feelings and one perception, one is born in the *avīci* hell.
*Sāntara* refers to the eighteen hells, while *avīci* refers to the eight *anantarya* (uninterrupted) hells. The phrase "the lower cavity of the wheel of fire" refers to the eight hot hells.
Regarding the phrase "the body enters the ground where wind and fire intersect": "intersection" (*jiaoguo*) means "mutual overcoming" (*jiaosheng*). It is in the midst of fire.
The wheel is also close to the wind-wheel; this is a place where wind and fire are intensely confluent, and one can know the suffering of being situated therein.
Those of pure emotion fall into Avīci, which is the Great Uninterrupted Hell (*Mahā-avīci*). Wēnlíng says:

"It is called 'five uninterrupted' because the five factors—the suffering of retribution, the instruments of punishment, the body's dimensions, the duration of the kalpa, and the lifespan—are all without interval."
Among these, those whose emotional karma is heaviest fall [into hell] and remain until the kalpa is destroyed before they emerge.
If they also slander the Mahāyāna and so forth, then even when this kalpa is destroyed, they enter the Avīci hell of the ten directions with no prospect of emergence;
for those who slander the Dharma cause infinite beings to give rise to false views. As for those who destroy the Buddha’s prohibitions and precepts, it is as in the case of Ratnapadmagandhā.

Those such as bhikṣuṇīs who deceive others by preaching false doctrines, those like Shanxing (Sunakṣatra) who preach the emptiness of dharmas recklessly, those who greedily crave the faithful offerings of others despite having no merit—this is called "vainness";
those who receive the respect and veneration of others despite lacking virtue—this is called "imposture.
Even those who commit the five heinous crimes and the ten grave offenses are all of the lineage of the Avīci hell throughout the ten directions. Is this not so?
How formidable! Following the preceding question, the answer concludes by addressing whether these various hells have fixed locations or are individually experienced.
It states that although one invites suffering through one's own actions and experiences it privately, this occurs within a common collective destiny (*nikāya-sabhāga*).

Furthermore, there are original grounds and original locations, which are fixed places; this specifically refers to the fact that while individuals act separately, they experience the results together. Thus, we know of the seven destinies.

All things take emotional conceptualization as their basis; if one does not cling to emotion, the three miserable realms are empty, and if one does not cling to conceptualization, the heavens are empty.
When both emotion and conceptualization are empty, although one remains in the human world, it is truly a pure land.
If the seven destinies have an original ground, the pure land likewise has an original ground; thus, Lingbian said: "This mind can destroy all things."

Because it can accomplish all things, all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma. The mind creates the heavens, the mind creates humans, and the mind creates ghosts, spirits, animals, and hell-beings; everything is produced by the mind. Whether good or evil, both arise from the mind:

one may attain realization through birth, and one may also attain it without birth. If one understands that there are no phenomena outside the mind, then not a single dharma will ever confront the mind.

All things are liberation; thus it is said that the Abhaya (Fearless) rests upon the constant locus of the ultimate sage’s own mind, wherein the Dharmakāya of all Buddhas is not separate from the single thought-moment of the lowest ordinary person.
Ānanda, all these are the results of the karma produced by those sentient beings themselves; they created the ten causes of habitual practice and undergo the sixfold retributive responses.

This summary is stated briefly to give rise to a detailed explanation. Previously, it was clarified that emotional thoughts serve as the cause for the seven realms of existence. Regarding the seven realms...

To clarify that the fruits of emotional and conceptual thought result from the ten habitual practices—which serve as the causes for the three miserable realms—and that the three miserable realms are the fruits of those ten habitual practices, it is said that these are "induced by one's own karma.
This means they are neither created by Heaven nor established by Earth, nor bestowed by other people; rather, they are self-created and self-experienced.
Therefore, it is said: "One should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm: all is created solely by the mind."
What are the ten causes? Ānanda, first is the habit of lustful practice. Through the act of sexual intercourse, there arises a mutual friction that grinds and rubs without ceasing.
Because of this, a great and fierce fire blazes forth from within, just as when people rub their hands together, the sensation of warmth appears before them.
Because these two habits ignite one another, there arise such things as iron beds and copper pillars. Therefore, throughout the ten directions...
All Tathāgatas characterize sexual misconduct with the same term: the "fire of desire. Bodhisattvas view desire as they would avoid a pit of fire.
This section provides a detailed explanation of the causes and effects of the habit of lust. First, the passage beginning with "As for the first" presents the causes practiced in daily life;

next, the passage beginning with "It is like a person" sets forth a metaphor to verify the reality of these causes; and third, the passage beginning with "The second habit" clarifies what occurs after death.

"Feeling this, the retribution descends; all subsequent instances follow this pattern. 'The connector' is the beginning of the structural formation; 'the initiator' is the movement at the moment of occasion; 'the receiver' is the staining of the mind;
'the assembler' and 'the polisher' are the greedy pursuit of pleasure; and 'the toucher' is the indulgence in joy. King Shu said:

"When the habit of lust is polished and ground without ceasing, one naturally exhausts their own essence, causing the fire element to blaze intensely. Even during their lifetime, they suffer from parching thirst."
It is only natural that one who suffers from internal fevers and similar ailments should encounter a great fire at the moment of death; this is due to two types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*):
the habit of karma (*karmavāsanā*) and the habit of seeds (*bījāvāsanā*). The habit of karma arises from mutual friction, while the habit of seeds results from incessant grinding.
Because these two habits blaze together, one consequently experiences this bitter retribution. Thus, we know that the brocade quilt and horn pillows of the past are [the cause of] the present...
That which was once the basis for embracing one another upon iron beds has now become the medium for the copper pillars;

cause and effect correspond with each other without the slightest discrepancy. If one’s thoughts of the Way were identical to one’s worldly passions, then the lustful mind would have been transformed into the fire of wisdom, as in the case of Ucchuṣma—how then could there have been iron beds and copper pillars? Thus it was said by the Tathāgata.
That which is called "fire" is so named because if one is not stained by it, that is well; but once stained, it inevitably leads to a scorched head and blistered brow.
That a Bodhisattva avoids it as if it were a pit means that if one does not fall into it, that is well; but once fallen, one loses body and life. Alas, fire!
This is what the Tathāgata has rebuked and what the Bodhisattva avoids. May I, in every world and throughout all births, never [be stained by it].
First, they throw themselves into pits of fire.
Second, the habits of greed interact through mutual plotting, arising from a reciprocal attraction that grasps and seizes without ceasing;
because of this, there is accumulated cold and solid ice within which one freezes, just as when a person draws in air with the mouth, a sensation of cold arises—these are the two habits.
Because they mutually oppress one another, there arise such states as *ṭha-ṭha*, *pa-pa*, *ra-ra*, and the blue, red, and white lotus hells, as well as the Cold Ice Hell; for this reason,
all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate excessive seeking with the same name as the "water of greed," and Bodhisattvas view greed as they would avoid a sea of miasma.

This is a detailed explanation of the causes and effects of the habit-energy of greed (*rāga*). "Greed" refers to the nature of grasping at existence and the requisites of existence, characterized by defiled attachment.

"Calculation" refers to mental reckoning, such as counting on wooden tally-sticks, piercing plum pits, combing hair strand by strand, or counting grains of rice while cooking; these are examples of such reckoning.
Greed and grasping belong to the element of water; when this grasping is not ceased, it coagulates water to form ice, and thus one perceives solidity.
The realm of freezing ice is invaded by mutual transgression; because these two habits overcome one another, one receives the retribution of *Ṭaṭataṭa* and *Lalala*.
*Ṭaṭa-ṭa-ṭa-bha-bha-ra-ra* are all sounds of enduring the cold, while the blue, red, and white lotuses are all colors of frost.
If one exerts effort to move forward and open one's own treasure-trove, one may take from it without limit.
Since it is inexhaustible, what need is there for further deliberation? To speak of "greedy waters" is like the "Greedy Spring" (Tanquán) of the present day;
drinking from it causes people to become greedy. Thus, those who seek much—the more they obtain, the more they feel insufficient—and will surely drown before they cease.
To speak of the "miasmic seas" is like the pestilential vapors of the south, which kill one upon contact.
These words speak of the extreme danger that must be avoided. When greed for profit is such as this, other forms of greed are likewise so.
Third is the habit of pride, which involves mutual disparagement arising from reciprocal reliance; it flows on without ceasing. Thus, there is leaping and rushing, where accumulated waves form water.
It is like the human mouth and tongue, which by tasting one another’s flavors cause water to be produced; these two habits [give rise to this].
Because they strike one another, there arise such things as rivers of blood, rivers of ash, seas of hot sand and poison, and the swallowing of molten copper poured upon them; for this reason,
all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate pride as "drinking the water of delusion," and Bodhisattvas view pride as they would avoid a great drowning.

This is a detailed explanation of the causes and effects of the habituation to pride (*māna*). Pride has the nature of exalting oneself above others based on one's own self, and its function is to give rise to suffering.
This means that when one possesses pride regarding virtues or those who possess virtue, the mind fails to be humble;

because of this, one revolves endlessly in birth and death, undergoing all manner of sufferings such as being insulted, deceived, and oppressed. "To rely" (*shi-yi*) means to depend upon. One who is haughty and arrogant must necessarily [possess these qualities].

That upon which one relies—whether it be wealth, power, fame, status, literary learning, wisdom, valor, talent, or even a single skill or craft—is necessarily relied upon as one's own excellence before one treats others with contempt and looks down on all things; hence it is said that this "arises from mutual reliance.
Little do they realize that this Dharma is equal and without high or low, yet when pride arises, they act accordingly.
When the feet are raised, the mind also becomes turbulent; thus, like a subsequent wave surging over a preceding wave, it rushes forward without ceasing.
Therefore, one experiences states of leaping, galloping, and rushing—what is called "waves and billows on level ground.

It is like when a person uses their tongue to press against the upper palate, causing saliva to flow profusely; matters such as the flowing of rivers of blood are all likewise induced by such conditions.
Regarding the retribution for delusion, there is water in the Western lands which, when drunk, causes one to become deluded, much like the "Thirsty Spring" (Tan-quan) of this region.
The *He lun* states: "A flood that submerges the heavens originates from a single drop; a towering pavilion arises from the tip of a hair.
That which begins as something extremely minute ends in something that cannot be resisted. Therefore, the Sage was most diligent regarding those things he practiced.

Caution is required, for habitual tendencies are difficult to eradicate; even one as close to the World-Honored One as Ānanda had the habit of lust, constantly gazing at women during dharma assemblies, while Pilindavatsa had the habit of pride, calling the goddess of the Ganges a "little slave.
These were all sages who had attained the fruit of the path, yet they still had to subdue their lust and pride.
If this is so even for residual habits, how much more so for sentient beings? Therefore, one must be careful regarding what is practiced.

Fourth, the habit of anger involves mutual conflict; it arises from opposition, and when that opposition coalesces without ceasing, the heat of the mind ignites like fire, forging the vital energy (*prāṇa*) into metal.
It is because of this that there exist the mountain of knives, iron spikes, the sword-tree, the wheel of swords, axes, halberds, spears, and saws, just as in the human realm.

The murderous breath of resentment flies about as the two habits strike one another; thus there arise various matters such as imprisonment, mutilation, decapitation, hacking, mincing, piercing, and beating.
For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions characterize anger as "the sharp sword," and Bodhisattvas view anger as they would avoid execution.

This is a detailed explanation of the causes and effects of the habituation of anger (*dveṣa*). As for the habituation of anger, its nature is to increase resentment toward suffering and the instruments of suffering, and its function is to serve as the basis for unwholesome conduct.
This means that anger necessarily causes heat and affliction to the body and mind, giving rise to various unwholesome karmas due to its inherently non-virtuous character.
"Mutual conflict" refers to the clashing and jostling between oneself and others; as the proverb says: "A single word that does not harmonize brings forth a fit of rage."
This refers to mutual conflict and rebellion; because one opposes another, the vital energy (*prāṇa*) is stirred and the fire of anger (*krodha-agni*) arises.
Because this fire of anger smelts the gold of the vital energy, one first perceives the realms of mountains of knives and trees of swords.

Little do they realize that being able to accord with sentient beings is itself to accord with the nature of enlightenment (*bodhi-svabhāva*). If the fire of anger were removed, the gold of the vital energy would not be smelted.
Thus, there would be no place for their blades to be applied. "Dismembering" refers to removing their genitals; "cutting" refers to cutting off their noses;
"severing and hacking" refers to decapitating them or amputating their arms; "crushing and piercing" refers to crushing their bones and piercing their flesh;
and "sharp swords and blades" means that touching them results in immediate death, while violating them results in injury.
Fifth, the habit of deceitful association arises from mutual seduction and incitement, leading to instability;

thus there are ropes, wooden stocks, strangulation, and cross-examination, just as when water drenches a field, grass and trees grow. Because these two habits extend one another, there are cuffs, shackles, pillories, fetters, whips, staves, clubs, and maces.
Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions identify such craftiness and falsehood with the same name.
When a slanderous and malicious person sees a bodhisattva, they view them with trepidation as if facing a jackal or a wolf.
This is a detailed clarification of the causes and effects of the habit of flattery (*śāṭhya*). "Deceit" (*māyā*) refers to the minor derivative affliction of flattery;

because its purpose is to delude others, it takes the nature of assuming artificial postures and crookedness, thereby luring, deceiving, and cheating. "Coaxing" (*kuhana*) means to toy with others using flattering words.

"Enticement" refers to those who employ guile and stratagem, setting up clever devices to lure others into their intricate snares—like ropes binding wood, fetters constricting and shackling so that there is no escape.
Thus, it evokes the imagery of being bound by ropes and wood, or constrained by fetters and stocks (the *jiā* is a neck-shackle);
as the *I Ching* says, "The neck-shackle reaches to his ears. Such are the methods used by the guileful to entice people through artifice.

One must surely have soaked them for a long time until their hearts are pleased and they submit, and only then lead them into the shell, just as water soaking a field causes grasses and trees to grow.
If one were to use a straightforward mind and straightforward speech in daily life, one could advance directly toward the ocean of the Tathāgata’s fruition.
"To draw out" means to prolong; "slanderous and treacherous persons" refers to those who use slander.
Because they slander others, they are likened to thieves, jackals, and wolves; for these creatures can predict where an event will emerge and are certain to catch their prey.
Because they use guile and deception to entice others, succeeding in every attempt, people fear them.
Sixth, the habit-energy of deception: through mutual cheating, they give rise to one another’s delusion; their falsehoods do not cease, and with a wandering mind they create wickedness.
Because of this, there are impurities such as dust, soil, excrement, and urine—filthy and unclean, like dust driven by the wind where each person can see nothing.
As these two habits combine, there arise various states such as drowning, being tossed about, flying and falling, and drifting in the currents. Therefore, throughout the ten directions, all...
The Tathāgata designates deception as being identical to "killing by robbery" (*kāla-haraṇa*). When a Bodhisattva encounters such deception, they view it as treading upon a venomous snake.

This passage provides a detailed explanation of the causes, conditions, and results of the habit of deception. Deception (*śāṭhya*) has the nature of guile and fraud for the sake of gaining profit and sustenance, and its function is wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
Misrepresentation (*mṛṣāvāda*) consists of claiming that what exists does not exist, or pointing to emptiness as being existent. To "deceive" (*vañcayati*) means to lead others astray.

This refers to deceiving those who do not know or see by mocking them. When one’s mind flies toward the creation of evil, a net is spread in all four directions without the slightest sound or color; thus, various evils are committed without others perceiving them.
Because their intent lies in deceiving others, they are caused to be obscured and covered by impure dust and soil, so that even they themselves cannot see [the consequences]. Therefore...
Because one deceives others through false speech, one experiences drowning; because one mocks others through false speech, one experiences being tossed about;
and because one leads others astray from heaven or into the abyss through false speech, one experiences either flying up or falling down.

How could one know that non-deception, non-falsity, and not self-deceiving are all the direct causes for attaining Buddhahood? As for what is called "killing by the sword," it refers to encountering this [retribution].
Because they inevitably cause injury to life, those who encounter snakes and vipers must necessarily sever their wrists.

Seventh, because the habit of resentment and mutual dislike arise from harboring hatred, there are flying stones, thrown rocks, and [punishments] such as being confined in boxes, placed in carriage enclosures, stored in jars, or crushed in sacks—just as a person of hidden malice harbors and nurtures evil within; because these two habits converge, there are [these consequences].
Because of such acts as hurling, seizing, striking, shooting, tossing, and grasping, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate an enemy as a "hostile and harmful ghost" (vihaṇi-ghoṣa);
thus, when a Bodhisattva encounters an enemy, they view them as if drinking poisoned wine.
This is a detailed explanation of the causes and effects of the habituation of resentment (*vaira*). "Resentment" (*vaira*) is synonymous with hatred (*dveṣa*).
Its nature is to harbor malice without relinquishing it, preceded by anger (*krodha*), and its function is to cause feverish distress. It is characterized by enmity and concealment;

because one conceals the heart of hatred, it brings about events such as flying stones and the hurling of projectiles. "Chamber" (*saṃpuṭa*) refers to a chest or bed; "carriage-crate" (*śakaṭa-puṭa*) refers to... [text fragment].
The "prison wagon" refers to cases such as "inviting a lord to enter a jar.
As for "sack-pounding," it means to place a person in a sack and beat them to death, as in the *Shiji* account of the First Emperor of Qin "sack-pounding" his two younger brothers.
"Devouring one another" refers to those who harbor resentment and desire only to bite and eat their flesh; they do not realize that they should regard their enemies as kin.
Not dwelling on past wrongs, but cherishing kindness rather than harboring resentment, is the true cause for transcending the world.
To violate and harm others, to oppose the principles of antiquity, and to injure people in secret—these are the most evil among ghosts.
As for *zhèn* wine, it is made from the most venomous *zhèn* bird; its wing feathers are used to stir the wine, and whoever drinks it dies instantly.

Eighth, because the habit-energies of views interact with clarity—just as the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and various karmas born of false awakening give rise to opposition and produce contradictions—there are kings, messengers, officials, and clerks who rely on documents for testimony and enforcement.
Thus, like travelers meeting one another on their way back and forth, these two habit-energies intersect; therefore, there are interrogations, deceptions, examinations, and investigations.
Investigating, scrutinizing, and illuminating good and evil, this youth holds documents and records and eloquently adjudicates all matters;

therefore, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate this evil view with the same name: "The Pit of Views. When Bodhisattvas encounter various false and biased attachments, they regard them as if facing a precipice of poison.
This is a detailed explanation of the causes and effects of the habit-energy of views (*dṛṣṭi-vāsanā*).

"View" has the nature of defiled wisdom that erroneously investigates the principles of the various truths, and its function is to bring about suffering. There are five distinct types of characteristics for these views:

first, *satkāya-dṛṣṭi*, here translated as the view of a self-body (*ātma-grāha*), which refers to the attachment to a self within the body through various conceptualizations; second, the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), which [regards] all things... [as either eternal or annihilated].

The attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), the attachment to self (*ātmagrāha*), the three false views including the view of permanence (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*), the four types of wrong understanding and erroneous interpretations that deny cause and effect,

the four types of adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) which regard what is not a fruit as a fruit— such as taking the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) to be *nirvāṇa*— and the five types of adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) which regard what is not a cause as a cause—
such as observing the vows of cattle or dogs as a cause for rebirth in heaven: because these accord with the perverse and oppose the correct, they are said to "originate from."
They resist and reject one another, asserting that "this is right" and "that is wrong," or "that is right" and "this is wrong"; thus it is said they give rise to mutual opposition.

Because they refuse to follow others toward what is correct, they provoke the king’s envoys to bear witness and rely upon written records to adjudicate their right and wrong—just as travelers coming and going who meet on a narrow path have no place to escape.
"Furthermore, 'using expedient means and guile' refers to employing skillful transformations and deceptive arts to entice them into speaking;

'investigation' refers to thorough examination and interrogation to discern right from wrong; and 'illumination' refers to having them look into a karmic mirror so that they may see clearly without concealment.
How could one know that being free from the four propositions and transcending the hundred negations is the Tathāgata’s..."
"Right view indeed! That which is called the 'pit of views' means that once one has fallen into this view, one can never emerge from it.
As for the 'poisonous ravine,' among all poisons, the poison of views is the deepest; because it can cause one to fall into the Dharma-body, it is likened to a ravine."

Ninth, the habit-energy of injustice intermingles and gives rise to false accusations and slanders. Because of this, there are mountains and stones joined together to crush, grind, plow, and rub [the offender], just as slanderous thieves oppress and wrongfully accuse the virtuous.
Because these two habits repel one another, there are various matters such as pressing down, hammering, squeezing, straining, and measuring.
For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate the act of malicious accusation and slander by the same name.
When the Bodhisattva Chanhu saw his own injustice, it was like being struck by a bolt of lightning.
This is a detailed clarification of the causes and effects of the habit of injustice. One who is unjust is one whose nature is fundamentally innocent yet to whom guilt is attributed;
whose principle is fundamentally not crooked yet is forcibly called crooked. Thus, through their haughty aura, they suppress others by means of coercion.
To harm the virtuous and afflict the minds of others without compassion is what is subsumed under "harming.
"Slander" refers to falsely accusing someone with matters that did not originally exist. "The Conjoined Mountains" means two mountains closing together so that there is no escape;
because one uses their influence and power to unjustly oppress the virtuous, they experience the realm of the conjoined mountains and rocks. "The Pressing" refers to...
"Pushing and pressing" (*tui-pai-ya-na*) means that when the mind does not submit, one forcibly suppresses and restrains it.

"Beating and pressing" (*chui-an*) means that when the will is not compliant, one forcibly presses down and strikes it. "Cramping and squeezing" (*cu-lu*) means clenching the hands and feet, pressing them down, and draining the blood.
"Balance" (*heng*) refers to the scale-beam; "measurement" (*duo*) refers to the garment-measure; these mean weighing their lightness.

How could one know the weight of their severity based on the length of the punishment? Even when the guilt is proven and the facts are established, one still desires to show compassion and grant clemency;
how much more so when there is no crime and the person is being unjustly coerced! Slander can injure a person, hence it is called a "tiger's roar";
thunder can strike a person, hence it is called a "thunderbolt."

Tenth, the habit-energy of litigation arises from concealment and mutual clamor; because of this, there is the mirror of discernment that shines with illumination like the sun, wherein one cannot hide one's shadow.
Because these two habits present themselves together, there are evil associates, the karmic mirror, and the fire-pearl, which reveal past karma and verify all matters.
Therefore, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate the act of concealment by the same name.
The Bodhisattva Yinzei (Secret Enemy) contemplates concealment (*mrakṣa*) as being like carrying a high mountain upon one’s head while treading upon a vast ocean.
This is a detailed clarification of the causes and effects of the habit of contention (*vivāda*). Contention is the habit of concealment;

because concealment gives rise to contention, that which conceals—having the nature of hiding one's own actions for fear of losing gain and sustenance—has the function of causing regret and distress. "Chatter" (*prapañca*) refers to dispute.
"Competitiveness arising from concealment" means that because one exposes hidden secrets, litigation is formed.
This is because throughout one's life, instead of concealing evil and praising good, one has instead sought out flaws and attacked the faults of others while hiding one's own;
thus, when the realm of the mirror of discernment shines its light upon them, all hidden secrets are fully revealed before the karmic mirror and the fire-pearl.
There is no place for exposure to remain covered; that which is called "attacking the faults of others" will likewise be attacked by others.
"Secret malice" (*yinzei*) refers to hidden injury; though people may not know one is a thief, one is indeed a thief.

"Bearing mountains and treading upon the sea" means that as what is borne becomes heavier, the drowning becomes deeper. The above are the ten habitual tendencies: greed, anger, pride, and [wrong] views—these four.
The fundamental afflictions are as follows: lust is subsumed under a portion of greed; resentment is subsumed under a portion of hatred;

deceit is subsumed under a portion of greed, being identical to the flattery among the minor secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*); guile is likewise subsumed under a portion of greed; crookedness is also subsumed under a portion of hatred;

and litigation is subsumed under a portion of both greed and delusion, being identical to the concealment among the minor secondary afflictions. Although these ten manifest both as causes and as effects, [they are categorized here according to their predominant nature].

Because what is emphasized here is the cause, it is called the "Ten Causes. Because the Buddhas of the ten directions clearly perceive their roots through these ten kinds of causes, and because the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions are reverent and pure without transgression, it is appropriate that only Buddhas and Bodhisattvas could say there are no seven destinies.
To claim otherwise—that they do not exist—is to speak falsely of the emptiness of dharmas. Nowadays, there are those with overweening pride who practice meditation [and hold such views].
To speak with such arrogance as to look upon the Tathāgata as a child and the Bodhisattvas as slaves—how can one’s words be considered anything but unreliable?
How truly fearsome this is!
What are these six retributions? Ānanda, for all sentient beings, the evil retributions summoned by the karma created through the six consciousnesses arise from the six [sense organs].
The Roots Emerge.

Hereafter follows a detailed explanation of the sixfold mutual retribution. Among the twelve classes of beings mentioned previously, it was stated that within a single cause all causes are fully present;
here it is stated that within a single fruit all fruits are fully present. The preceding section clarified how a single faculty returns to its source. The six...
"Roots and liberation": this clarifies that while karma is created by a single root-faculty (*indriya*), the retribution is received by the six faculties.
Regarding the creation of karma by the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*): both the projecting and completing karmas are summoned by the six consciousnesses.

As for the emergence of evil retribution from the six faculties, it is because the six faculties belong to the eighth *karma-vijñāna*. To speak in broad terms, the creator of karma is the six consciousnesses; yet...

Regarding those who receive retribution, if one investigates the fundamental consciousness of karma (*karmavijñāna*), it is ultimately the case that the *karmavijñāna* itself creates and the *karmavijñāna* itself receives.
This is because the six consciousnesses are induced by the *karmavijñāna*. Thus, while the preceding passage in the "Examination of Karma" asks, "Who acts? Who receives?
it concludes by stating, "One creates for oneself and receives for oneself."
How is it that the retribution for evil arises from the six sense faculties? First, as for the retribution of seeing that invites evil fruits:

when this faculty of seeing interacts with karma, at the moment of death one first sees fierce fires filling the ten directions. The deceased’s consciousness flies and falls, riding on the smoke to enter the Avīci Hell.
This manifests two aspects: first, the aspect of clear vision, by which one can see all manner of evil things everywhere.
They give rise to immeasurable fear in two ways: first, seeing darkness and being unable to see anything; second, giving rise to immeasurable terror from such visions.
They see fire burning that can turn into boiling cauldrons of molten copper to burn their breath; it can turn into black smoke and purple flames to burn their sense of taste;

it can turn into glowing iron balls and molten iron gruel to burn their touch; and it can turn into hot ashes, furnaces, and charcoal to burn their hearts, producing sparks that scatter and fly about.
It stirs up the realm of empty space.

This refers to the mutual retribution of the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*). Regarding "the retribution of seeing invites evil fruits," this means that when the visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*) acts in conjunction with the mental consciousness (*manas*), it creates karma that invites the visual faculty to undergo evil fruits. The following section on "this seeing" concerns what occurs at the time of death.
Because the realm of what is seen and the seeing-consciousness belong to the element of fire, they evoke a fierce fire that pervades the ten directions;

one descends into hell riding upon purple smoke, which is the opposite of "riding a flying dragon to govern the heavens. The *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* states that those of extreme goodness or extreme evil have no intermediate state (*antarābhava*), and thus enter directly [into their destination].
The frequent mention of "entering directly" throughout the six realms of rebirth refers specifically to the gravity of these cases.

The following section elucidates the realm seen upon entering hell. Because during the causal stage one was unable to reflect inwardly and instead allowed the senses to flow outward, rushing toward forms, there is no difference between the vision of light and the vision of darkness experienced here in hell and that experienced in the human world.

This is because, while in the human world, one committed various evil deeds with eyes wide open and heart bared, possessing a mind entirely devoid of fear; therefore, one now remains here within this state.
Seeing evil objects everywhere, one gives rise to immeasurable fear.
As for what are called "evil objects," they include things such as iron snakes, copper dogs, sword-trees, knife-mountains, and the ox-headed *āpāṅgas*.

Because one practiced various evil deeds while secretly deceiving others in the human realm and remained unconcerned, one now finds nothing at all in this place; yet, one gives rise to immeasurable terror, being struck with dread.
Born from the objective realm yet fearing it will be hidden within the mind—it is thus that the following section provides a detailed explanation of the causes of mutual retribution.

Regarding what is heard by the ears during this causal state: whether it be the sounds of drums and music, stringed songs, coquettish voices, or elegant speech, now, being burned by fire, one hears only the sounds of boiling cauldrons, furnaces, and burning charcoal within the ears.
As for what was smelled by the nose during the causal state—such as dragon incense, musk pods, and so forth—[the same applies].
The fragrance of flowers and the scent of wine are now being burned by fire; what was once smelled by the nose has all become black smoke and purple flames.
That which was tasted by the tongue during the causal stage—fine delicacies and exquisite flavors that delighted the palate—is now being burned by fire;
what was once tasted by the tongue has all turned into charred balls and molten iron dregs. That which was touched by the body during the causal stage... [the text here is incomplete].
The Lady Yueyan was once soft, supple, and smooth; now that her body is being consumed by fire, whatever it touches is transformed into hot ashes and glowing coals.

That which she previously cherished in her heart—traversing heaven and earth and roaming through the nine provinces—is now, as her heart is scorched by the flames, entirely turned into sparks that scatter throughout the void. This is due to...
Unable to turn back and see the source of the flow, one instead chases after the retribution of form; this is what is meant by "following along with life and going against death.
Second, hearing-retribution invites evil fruits: when these karmic acts of hearing intersect, at the time of death one first sees waves and tides, drowning in them as heaven and earth vanish.
The deceased’s consciousness descends and flows into the Avīci Hell, manifesting two appearances.

First, when the ears are open, they hear various clamors that cause the spirit to become confused and disordered; when the ears are closed, they hear nothing in silence, and the dark soul sinks into oblivion.
Thus, the waves of hearing pour forth: when hearing pours forth, it can act as reproof and interrogation;
when seeing pours forth, it can act as thunder and roar, and as the breath of evil poison; when breathing pours forth, it can act as rain and mist, sprinkling upon all venomous insects.
When these [karmic forces] pervade the body, if they infuse the sense of taste, they can produce pus and blood, as well as various kinds of filth;
if they infuse the sense of touch, they can produce animals, ghosts, excrement, and urine; if they infuse the mind, they can produce lightning and hail that shatter the heart and soul.
This is a detailed explanation of the retribution experienced through the faculty of hearing.

Since the act of hearing belongs to the element of water, at the time of death one first sees waves and surges, being submerged and drowning as the heavens pour down floods; "riding the current" refers to the consciousness riding that flow as it enters hell.
This is different from the case where, even when the great waters submerge the heavens, one does not drown. As for "opening the hearing," the ears possess...
Regarding what is heard: listening to various kinds of clamor means that within the ears one hears only cacophonous sounds, like surging waves, all of which are disagreeable;
these cause the spirit to become dazed and disordered, leaving it without a master.
"Closed listening" means hearing nothing at all, causing the dark soul to sink into oblivion without awareness. If one holds others accountable for this based on its causes:
Because one’s own clarity is obscured by resentment, when receiving retribution, one likewise hears matters of being accused of crimes and interrogated regarding one's intent.

During the causal stage, one rouses intense energy, groaning and shouting, closing the eyes and staring with wide-open pupils; thus, in the experience of hearing, water pours forth, and in the experience of seeing, fire transforms into the roar of thunder and the breath of foul venom.
Because of spitting mist during the causal stage to delude others, and casting sand to shoot at shadows, these results manifest accordingly.
When listening to the sound of water pouring as one breathes, it transforms into rain and mist, and poisonous insects pervade the body, turning into a source of harm.

Those flavors once craved during the causal state—sturgeon, shark, choice cuts of meat, and the eight kinds of sacrificial offerings—now, upon hearing the sound of water pouring, all their tastes are perceived as the stench of putrefaction, pus, blood, and various impurities.
