As for those things that touched the body during the causal state:
The breath of beautiful youths and young maidens was once fragrant and pure, but now it is poured out as the urine of beastly ghosts.

Having used their influence to strike unexpectedly and harm others, leaving people unable to respond, they are now struck by the waters of *ting* (hearing/obedience), which transform into thunder and hail that shatter their hearts and crush their souls; this is due to [their failure to...].
This is the retribution for turning one's hearing inward toward self-nature instead of letting it flow outward and rush toward sounds.

Third, the retribution of smelling invites evil fruits; when this karma of smelling intersects with other conditions, at the time of death, one first sees poisonous vapors filling the near and far surroundings.
The deceased’s consciousness emerges from the earth and enters the Avīci Hell, manifesting two distinct appearances.

First, when the sense of hearing is open and is permeated by various noxious vapors, the mind becomes extremely disturbed; second, when the sense of hearing is blocked and the vapors obstruct it, one faints upon the ground.
Thus, when these vapors strike the breath, they can become a solid substance or a shoe; when they strike the sight, they can become fire or a torch;
when they strike the hearing, they can cause drowning, submersion, melting, or boiling; and when they strike the sense of taste, they can likewise [cause harm].

Whether as hunger or as delusion, upon being struck, they can cause bursting and rotting; there are great mountains of flesh with hundreds of thousands of eyes, from which immeasurable things suck and devour.
When thoughts are struck, these can turn into ash, miasma, or flying sand and gravel, shattering the body.
This is a detailed explanation of the retributive responses associated with the olfactory faculty. Nasal respiration belongs to the realm of *qi* (vital energy);
it possesses both inhalation and exhalation. When inhaling, it enters from above; when exhaling, it exits from below.

Therefore, at the time of death, one perceives the consciousness (*vijñāna*) surging up from the earth and then falling back down from above. As for "universal hearing," it refers to the nose being affected by whatever it smells.
The stench and filth of these odors permeate the nose faculty to such an extreme that they cause the mind to become agitated and disturbed.
"To block what one hears" means that the nose perceives nothing at all; thus, as the breath is stifled and cannot pass through, one faints upon the ground, losing all consciousness and perception.
Because in the causal state one relied on this empty breath to strike others, it now penetrates everywhere throughout its path; now, it strikes directly at the very root itself.
It is obstructed by its own substance and cannot move. "Substance" refers to physical obstruction; this foot, which serves as the support for walking, is itself unable to move.
Because in the causal state it relied on the sight of fire to harm others, now that it has ceased its assault upon the sight of fire, the fire blazes all the more fiercely.
Thus, it becomes a torch that burns itself, with no place to flee or hide. This is because in the causal state it relied on the acuity of hearing.
It is beneficial and reaches everywhere; now, when the breath strikes the ears, if it is blocked, one becomes submerged and drowned, hearing nothing and giving rise to fear;
if it is open, it becomes a vast ocean or a boiling sea, producing the sound of waves and tides and giving rise to dread.
Within this, flavors are taken as satiation or as something to refresh the palate; now, when the breath strikes these flavors, they all become [objects of terror].
"Rotten and decayed" refers to the transformation of the marvelous and divine into foul putrefaction. Gu Shan says that the *Tongshu Wen* states: "The rotting of fish is called *nai*;

the rotting of soup is called *shuang*. Because they rely on their internal vital energy, they use sharp knives and swords to strike at the flesh of sentient beings, tearing it into four parts and eight pieces to be made into minced meat (*hai*) or dried meat (*fu*), thereby fattening their own bodies. Now, when their breath strikes that touch, it becomes... [text truncated]
It bursts open and rots into a great mountain of flesh, upon which immeasurable sentient beings feed and devour it—so-called "eating half a catty and returning eight taels.
This is because, in the past, one relied on one's own temper, deceiving the mind and obscuring the self, secretly harming others so that they remained unaware;
now, as the breath strikes the thoughts, it becomes ash, miasma, sand, and gravel, shattering the body.

This means that what issues forth from you will return to you; all these are instances of failing to turn back and rest in the source, instead following the flow and rushing toward the retribution of fragrances.
Fourth, the retribution of flavors invites evil fruits; when the karma of flavors intersects, at the time of death one first sees an iron net.
Fierce flames blaze intensely, enveloping the world; the consciousness of the deceased descends through them, suspended head-downward in a net, entering the Avīci Hell.
Two manifestations appear: first, the inhaled breath solidifies into freezing ice that numbs and chills the flesh and bones;
second, the exhaled breath flies forth as fierce fire that sears and rots the marrow. Thus one experiences these flavors; by experiencing them repeatedly, one becomes capable [of perceiving them].
When experienced through the sense of smell, it becomes capable of burning gold and stone; when experienced through the sense of hearing, it becomes capable of sharp weapons;

when experienced through the sense of touch, it becomes capable of great iron cages that cover the entire land; when experienced through the sense of contact, it becomes capable of bows, arrows, crossbows, and projectiles;
and when experienced through the faculty of thought, it becomes capable of raining down flying red-hot iron from the sky.
This clarifies the retribution for the faculty of the tongue. The faculty of the tongue belongs to the trigram Dui, which represents metal.

Because in past lives one used various nets for this faculty of the tongue to ensnare birds and beasts to satisfy one's palate, at the time of death one first sees iron nets covering the entire world;
as the consciousness descends from above, one is thus enticed and suspended upside down within the nets.
Their heads enter directly into the Avīci Hell. The breath drawn in from without belongs to the element of water, thus it solidifies into cold ice;
the breath exhaled from within belongs to the element of fire, thus it flies forth as fierce flames.

Because they cultivated this flavor during their causal lives, they devour living beings, causing them to endure agony and suffer pain; thus, even as they experience these tastes, they must likewise endure and accept such suffering.
One undergoes suffering for the sake of this flavor, being roasted over fires by means of cannons;
thus, one encounters fire as molten metal and stone, which cannot be eaten. For the sake of this flavor, one carves and slices with knives;
thus, one encounters sharp weapons and blades that instead turn against and harm oneself. For the sake of this flavor, one captures birds and beasts in cages; thus, one encounters the flavor.
When the *kan-lek* (tasting-iron) subsides, it becomes a great iron cage that covers the entire land;
for the sake of this taste, one uses bows and crossbows to strike birds and beasts. Because of this taste, the *kan-lek* manifests as contact with bows and crossbows to shoot oneself.
For the sake of this taste, one imagines flying birds descending from the sky; thus, when the *kan-lek* manifests as thought, hot iron descends from the sky.
This lower state results from being unable to withdraw the sense of taste and instead following its flow, resulting in a frantic rush toward flavors;

this is the retribution for such conduct. Fifth, the retribution of touch invites evil fruits: when the karma of touch intermingles, at the moment of death one first sees great mountains approaching from all four sides, leaving no way out;
the deceased’s consciousness then perceives a great iron city filled with fire-serpents and fire-dogs.

Tigers, wolves, lions, ox-headed hell-wardens, and horse-headed rākṣasas, holding spears and lances in their hands, drive them through the city gates toward the Avīci Hell, manifesting two kinds of contact:
first, contact by compression, where mountains press against the body until the flesh and bones are crushed and the blood flows;

second, contact by separation, where blades and swords strike the body and mind, hacking and tearing the liver and heart. Thus, through such contact by compression and successive contact, [the suffering] is able to occur.
When encountered through the eyes, it can burn and scorch; when encountered through hearing, it can strike, clash, pierce, and shoot;
when encountered through the breath, it can confine, enfold, interrogate, and bind;
when encountered through the tongue, it can plow, clamp, sever, and cut; when encountered through thought, it can cause one to fall or fly away.
"Being fried or roasted" clarifies the retributive interaction of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*). That which the body-faculty encounters is the cause of contact (*spraṣṭavya*);

because within this cause there is the pleasurable contact of male and female physical forms, at the time of death one encounters the painful contact of a great mountain coming to press upon one—this is what is seen.

These are all the iron cities, fire snakes, and so forth; since both contact through union and separation are tactile sensations pertaining to the body and its household [of faculties], the sensation of contact through union causes mountains to press against one's body, while the sensation of contact through separation causes the liver and heart to be hacked and torn apart. This body is the body of the five sense-faculties;
because during the causal stage one ran along the paths for the sake of this body and wandered among gardens and pavilions, it is therefore called the "body-faculty" (*kāyendriya*).
As one passes through and touches [the surroundings], they can serve as paths, as pavilions, as halls, and as courts. The "paths" are the roads leading to hell;

the "pavilions" are the two watchtowers at the gate of the King of Hell; and the "halls" and "courts" are all places for punishing criminals, as well as the locations where the faculty of touch (kāya-indriya) resides.
Because this body touches forms, everything currently seen by the eyes is burning and hot, unbearable to behold.
Because this body touches sounds, every sound heard is a touch of collision, piercing, and shooting—
like thrusting a blade into flesh or shooting an arrow into the body. Because this body touches breath,
every breath is a touch of confinement, binding, and obstruction— whereby "confinement" (*kuòdài*) refers to being like a tied-up bag (*kuònáng*).
To bind its mouth so that it cannot breathe out; "binding and tying" means to fetter the body so that it cannot move.
Because this body seeks flavors, every tasting becomes the touch of being plowed, shackled, and severed—touches that are unfit for the mouth.
Because this body clings to objects through conditions, every thought becomes the suffering of falling, flying, boiling, and roasting.
When one contemplates agreeable contacts, they may sometimes rise and sometimes fall, or lead to feverish distress;
this is the retribution for failing to cultivate oneself through self-reflection and instead allowing the mind to flow outward in pursuit of sensory contacts.

Sixth, when one contemplates the retribution that invites evil fruits, and this karma of volition intersects with other conditions, then at the time of death, one first sees an evil wind blowing away and destroying the land.
The deceased’s spirit-consciousness is blown up into the air, whirling and falling; driven by the wind, it falls into the Avīci Hell.
Two manifestations of this are revealed: first, if one is not awakened, delusion reaches its extreme, and one rushes about wildly and incessantly; second, if one is not deluded.
When one becomes aware of it, suffering is immeasurably incinerating and its pain is so deep as to be difficult to endure.
Such perverse thoughts, when bound together, can become a vessel or that which is contained within it; when they form views, they can become a mirror or a witness;
when they bind hearing, they can become a great congealing of stones, ice, frost, earth, or mist; and when they bind the breath, they can become a great fire-cart, a fire-boat, or a fire-cage.
When bound by the sensation of taste, it can produce great wailing, regret, and weeping;
when bound by the sensation of touch, it can manifest as large or small, undergo ten thousand births and ten thousand deaths within a single day, and exist in either a prone or supine position.

This clarifies the retributive response of the mental faculty (*manas*). Since the mind is the primary source from which the winds of ignorance emerge, at the time of death one first perceives evil winds blowing away the land. Then, the consciousness is blown by the winds of ignorance into empty space;
subsequently, it falls from that space and, riding upon the wind, enters the Avīci Hell. This is different from those who travel by controlling the wind.
Furthermore, "not awakening" means that because delusion is extreme and one does not know the path, one runs about in wild confusion without ceasing.
If one were not deluded, one would realize that immeasurable torments and pains are difficult to endure. For the mind has no fixed location and its origin is unknown;
yet, once a single instance of perverse thought is formed, it acquires a direction and a location, whereby evil is concealed within the midst of the wholesome.
Because one clings to what is perceived as good, perverse thoughts become fetters and views that serve as proofs; thus, the evil mind is made manifest without concealment.

The fetter of the fire of the mind causes those who would flow like water to be bound by great rocks, those who are hot to be transformed into frost and ice, and those who are bright to be turned into dust and mist.
The fetter of the fire of the mind causes the cessation [of breath] to become fire-chariots, fire-boats, and fire-cages—these being the chariots.

The ship’s railing is a vessel for carrying things, a transformation of qi; because qi can carry things, when the fire of the mind burns the root of the tongue, one is able to cry out, lament, and weep.
When the pain becomes unbearable, one calls out to Heaven and strikes the earth, yet it is of no avail.
When the fire of the mind forms attachments, it results in the great and small cycles of birth and death and the process of reclining and rising; this is indeed the influence of the heterodox.
Because that which is touched by thought is unstable and subject to reversal, the resulting contact (*sparśa*) is likewise indeterminate.
This arises from the retribution of failing to reflect upon one's own faults and instead rushing headlong toward the flow of phenomena. Question:

Why is it that when a single faculty performs an action, all five faculties universally experience the result? Answer: When the six faculties create karma, they are mutually cognizant within their nature; therefore, the retribution is also thus.

Because their mutual functions are contrary within the aggregate of characteristics, and because the various faculties are distinct, one can believe that the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is not deceptive.
These six reciprocal retributions are all transformations produced by the熏变 (*vāsanā*) of inconceivable karmic power; this karmic power is profoundly deep and especially unfathomable.
Only the Buddha-eye clearly perceives its outlines; it truly cannot be known by a mind of conceptual thought.
Furthermore, if one discusses this in terms of cause and effect, not even the slightest discrepancy occurs; thus, the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) states:

"Since the ten causes have been created, how could the six retributions fail to arise? All of these arise from a single thought of unwholesome discernment, giving rise to inverted perceptions that take external objects as causes and produce them as provisional manifestations.
These are driven by the mind of continuous succession according to emotional attachments, rather than being observed with the correct vision of wisdom.

Consequently, one falls into the karmic paths of ordinary beings; though for a single lifetime one may follow one's whims, one fails to consider that for ten thousand kalpas one’s body shall sink into oblivion.

Therefore, all Tathāgatas together proclaim this as something to be scrutinized with such gravity that it should be engraved upon one's bones; the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions are all struck with fear, and it is truly a matter that should cause one’s heart to tremble.
Ānanda, these ten causes and six effects of the hells are all created by the deluded ignorance of sentient beings.
This concludes the discussion on the prior false karma: it is all produced by following one's karma while being deluded regarding the true mind; it is not substantially real.
If one were to realize one’s own mind, there would not be even an inch of soil upon the great earth, let alone a hell.

If sentient beings collectively commit evil karma and enter the Avīci Hell to undergo immeasurable suffering for immeasurable kalpas, it is because they have committed offenses with each of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
Furthermore, if one commits such acts through both the organs and their respective objects, that person enters the Eight Uninterrupted Hells (*aṣṭāv-avīci-naraka*).

If one commits the three acts of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct through the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, that person enters the eighteen hells; however, this does not apply if the three karmas are not combined.
If, in the interim, one commits one instance of killing and one instance of stealing, such a person enters thirty-six hells;
if they commit each of the single offenses of the [ten] roots individually, they enter one hundred and eight hells.
Thus, sentient beings act and create separately, entering the common realm within the world; these arise from deluded imagination and do not exist inherently from the beginning.

This clarifies the relative gravity of causes and effects. "Joint commission" refers to these six faculties being fully endowed with the ten causes at all times, such that there is no moment when they do not act in concert;
this is the most grave [karma], leading one to enter the Great Avīci Hell and undergo suffering for an extremely long duration, lasting for immeasurable kalpas.
"Individual commission by each of the six faculties" likewise involves the full endowment of the six faculties.
The ten causes are complete, yet because they occur at different times—prior and subsequent—they are said to be "separate.

As for their effects, whether involving both objects and faculties, or involving one faculty and one object separately, or two faculties and two objects separately, and so on up to three or four, these offenses are slightly lighter than the preceding ones that lead to the eight Avīci hells. This applies to those [offenses] of body, speech, and mind.
The three roots [of unwholesome action] produce only the three [crimes] of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; they do not involve the others, being somewhat lighter than the preceding [set].
Regarding entry into the eighteen hells, the *Niraya Sūtra* states that there are eight fire hells and ten cold hells, which may constitute eighteen sub-hells (*kalābu-niraya*).

"Not involving all three karmas" means possessing two, such as killing and stealing, while lacking one, such as sexual misconduct. Alternatively, it may mean [possessing two] with the exception of sexual misconduct.
The abbreviated outline contains nine phrases: first, offenses committed by body and speech—namely, killing, stealing, killing and sexual misconduct, sexual misconduct and stealing;

or second, offenses committed by body and mind—namely, killing, stealing, killing and sexual misconduct, sexual misconduct and stealing; or third, offenses committed by speech and mind—namely, killing, stealing, killing and sexual misconduct, sexual misconduct and stealing.

Furthermore, these are slightly lighter than the preceding [offenses], leading one into thirty-six hells. As for "seeing," the commentator of Wuxing interpreted it as the "seer" being able to see the "seen."

When one perceives a single object through a single sense organ and commits a single transgression among killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct—whether it be physical killing, physical stealing, or physical sexual misconduct;

or verbal killing, verbal stealing, or verbal sexual misconduct; or mental killing, mental stealing, or mental sexual misconduct—this is again slightly lighter than the preceding cases, yet one enters one hundred and eight hells.
Regarding this, "lower fetters" refers to those who act separately and undergo the results separately. This means:
Each person creates their own [karma], yet upon entering the same level of the realm, their karma is identical; therefore, they experience the same hells of that level.
Because of the previous question—asking whether these hells exist inherently from the beginning or arise from the deluded habitual tendencies of sentient beings—the concluding answer states:
"They are born of deluded imagination; they do not exist inherently from the beginning. Alas, the earth!
The suffering of hell is ten trillion times greater than that of human prisons;
yet people remain complacent and unaware of this fear, willingly creating karma and falling into it themselves—how extreme is their folly! Some might say:
"Is it not also pitiable to speak of the retribution of the three periods as mere empty talk, and to falsely describe the cycle of the six realms? Master Zhuang said:
If one does evil in the light of day, people will catch and punish them;
if one does evil in the profound darkness, ghosts will catch and punish them. How truly fearsome this is!

Furthermore, Ānanda, these sentient beings—who violated the codes of discipline, broke the bodhisattva precepts, and destroyed the Buddha’s nirvāṇa—along with other miscellaneous karmic offenses, undergo burning for kalpas.
Only when their retribution is exhausted do they receive the forms of various hungry ghosts (*preta*).

If, in their original cause, they committed an offense out of greed for material things, then upon the exhaustion of their retribution, they take form by encountering objects; such are called "monster ghosts" (*kūṭapreta*). If they committed an offense out of greed for sensual beauty...
When this person’s retribution for their sins is exhausted, they encounter the wind and take form, becoming what is called a *pó-guǐ* (drought-demon); their sin was greed and delusion.
When this person’s retribution for their sins is exhausted, they encounter a beast and take form, becoming what is called a *mèi-guǐ* (possessing-demon); their sin was greed and resentment.

When this person’s retribution for their sins is exhausted, they encounter an insect and take form, becoming what is called a *gǔdú-guǐ* (poisonous charm-demon); their sin was greed and obsessive recollection. When this person’s retribution for their sins is exhausted, they encounter decay and take form, becoming what is called a *lì-guǐ* (pestilence-demon).
Those who commit the sin of greed and arrogance, when their retribution is exhausted, encounter *qi* (vital energy) to form a body; they are called hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Those who commit the sin of greedy deception, when their retribution is exhausted, encounter the dark and obscure to form a body; they are called incubus ghosts (*yamadeva*).

Those who commit the sin of greed for brilliance, when their retribution is exhausted, encounter spiritual essence to form a body; they are called *wangliang* ghosts. Those who commit the sin of greed for achievement, when their retribution is exhausted, encounter light to form a body.
Those known as "ghosts who employ others" and "greedy factions" fall into sin; when these people's karma is exhausted, they encounter human forms and are called "transmitting ghosts.
Ānanda, all such beings fall because of their pure emotional attachments; the fires of karma burn them dry, and upon emerging, they become ghosts.
All of these are summoned by the karma of their own deluded thoughts. If one awakens to Bodhi, then the wondrous, perfect, and luminous state is fundamentally non-existent [of such things].

All of this refers to entering the realm of hungry ghosts after completing one's punishment in the aforementioned hells; it is not a case of slandering [the Dharma], but rather of violating and breaking [the precepts].
Having already slandered the precepts and further broken them, those who violate the Bodhisattva precepts do so by breaking them alone, without slandering or defaming the Buddha.
To slander *nirvāṇa* is to simultaneously slander the Buddha and the Dharma. All other miscellaneous karmas are the ten causes.
The precepts are the instrument for sentient beings to emerge from suffering; the Buddha is the teacher who extracts sentient beings from suffering;
and the Dharma is the ground where sentient beings exhaust suffering. To slander these three is called severing the lineage of the Buddha; therefore, its transgression is particularly grave.
Entering hell, they are scorched by the fires of karma for kalpas; only when their karmic retribution in hell is exhausted do they subsequently assume the form of a ghost and become a ghost.
If this is so, then those suffering in hell do not yet possess a ghostly body—what kind of body receives this retribution?
The answer is: these are the bodies of sentient beings' *karmic consciousness*, manifested in accordance with that consciousness; one simply awaits this [exhaustion].
Only when the body of karmic consciousness is exhausted does one receive a ghostly body and enter the realm of ghosts (*preta*). "Preta" in Sanskrit means "ghost";
"pitrda" in Sanskrit means "hungry ghost," so called because for many kalpas they have not heard the names of water or grain.
They are also called "ghosts" because they are driven and employed; they are constantly made to serve by the various devas in all places, always running about.
Therefore, it is further said that those who have "longing" are called *preta* (ghosts), because these hungry ghosts constantly seek food and drink from others to sustain their lives.
If one examines this in detail below, it clarifies that within the realm of ghosts, attachment gives rise to emotion, and emotion begins with greed.
Thus, among the ten causes of habitual practice, greed is mentioned first; for one who loves virtue regards gold and jade as mere tiles.
If one who seeks much regards gravel as mere excrement and soil as if it were gold, because they hold themselves lightly while cherishing material things,
greedily accumulating rare and extraordinary objects with stingy attachment and refusing to let them go, their residual habits will attach themselves to these strange objects to form a shape—
just as when precious metals, jade, or magical fungi attach themselves to form essences or monsters. Therefore, it is said that "strange ghosts delight in virtue."
The human mind is like a massive boulder, utterly immovable;

yet for those who indulge in lustful desires, their passions flow and circulate, causing residual habits to attach to the wind and take form as *pó* ghosts. These spirits drift east or west, unsettled by the wind.
Because these *pó* ghosts result from excessive yang, those with fraudulent habits employ only sweet words to bewitch and delude others.

As for the former, those whose residual habits (*vāsanā*) encounter animals and take form as *mèi* ghosts—such as fox-spirits or monkey-spirits who manifest beautiful forms to seduce people—are examples of this.

As for the habituation of resentment, because it arises from harboring hatred, its residual habits attach to venomous insects to take form as *gǔdú* ghosts, which use poison to harm people; for instance, there are malevolent arts in the south that cause such things.
When a person contracts the *gǔ* disease, it is presided over by this ghost. Their habituated anger manifests as resentment arising from perceived opposition;
they recall past evils that pierce the heart and enter the bones, waiting for the victim's strength to decline in order to exact retribution.

Furthermore, these residual habits take form when encountering a period of weakness, manifesting as pestilential ghosts—such as those who now spread epidemics or malaria. Their habituated arrogance manifests through mutual...

Because they relied on internal, unsubstantial virtues to harbor empty pride and arrogance toward others, their residual habits cause them to take on the form of a hungry ghost (*preta*) when their breath condenses.
Since hungry ghosts lack food and drink to fill their bellies and possess nothing but a weary, lingering breath, the habit of deception arises from mutual entrapment;
they cloud the good conscience and deceive or oppress others, remaining in this state for the rest of their lives.
Because they reside in a state of darkness, their residual habits encounter the obscure and take form as *yāma-pretas* (suffocating ghosts);
these still oppress people within the dark. This is because those who are awake cannot be oppressed by them, whereas those who are in a state of delusion can still be oppressed.

When habitual tendencies arise from the intersection of clarity, they are certainly not right view; they are merely a perverse kind of illumination, and thus their residual habits attach themselves [to beings].
When the essence becomes a *wangliang* and the ghost arises from that perception of unreality, it is dark and elusive;
thus it becomes a spectral entity, appearing as if existent yet non-existent. These habitual tendencies arise from false accusations and bring about human evil;
yet within their own minds, they clearly know these are groundless, and merely force others to admit them—thus, the remaining habits cling to what is manifest.
They take form as "servant-ghosts" (*yōki*) because they were clearly aware of being employed by those [spirits], and thus serve as messengers for celestial deities.

The habit of litigation arises from noisy disputes and the forming of factions to provide mutual testimony against one another; consequently, its residual habit attaches to humans and takes form as a "transmitting ghost" (*senshōki*).
This is what the Master [Zhuangzi] meant when he spoke of spirits "attaching themselves to shamans and diviners to transmit good and bad fortune. This is truly because...

In their causal state, they form factions to expose the private secrets of others; because they transmit these matters, they become ghosts who also attach themselves to people to report those secrets.

Ānanda, the following concludes the section on delusion: according to the preceding text, it is only in Avīci that there is "pure emotion," where nine parts emotion and one part thought lead to birth in the Uninterrupted Hell, while eight parts emotion and two parts thought lead to other births.

Regarding the mention of "pure emotion" (*qing*) here when there are actually intervals [of other factors]: this is a case of citing the heavy to include the light. As for "the fire of karma burning it dry":
since emotion belongs to the element of water, if this water of emotion is now burned dry by the fire of karma, then the cause of the hell realm is exhausted and its fruit is ended;
thus, one is born into the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). All such things are summoned by deluded karma; within the wondrously perfect mind, these matters do not originally exist.
What is meant is this: if one has realized it, karmic obstacles are fundamentally empty; if one has not yet realized it, one must repay past debts.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when the karma of ghosts is exhausted, both emotion and thought become empty;

only then, within the world, will they encounter those to whom they originally owed a debt, facing them as enemies, and taking birth as an animal to repay their past debts, or as a ghost of material monsters.

When their retributions for material things are exhausted, they are born into the world as many as owls and the like; when the spirits of wind-demons and drought-demons have their winds dissipated and their retributions exhausted, they are born into the world as many as portents of calamity and various other species;
when the spirits of animal-possessing demons have their animals die and their retributions exhausted, they are born into the world as many as foxes and the like;
when the spirits of insect-pestilence demons have their pestilence extinguished and their retributions exhausted, they are born into the world.

For the most part, those who were of the poisonous class become ghosts of decay and pestilence; when their retribution for decay is exhausted, they are born into the world. For the most part, those who were of the parasitic class become ghosts that consume vital breath;
when their breath is dissipated and their retribution is exhausted, they are born into the world. For the most part, those who were of the predatory class become ghosts of lingering obscurity;

when their obscurity is dissolved and their retribution is exhausted, they are born into the world. For the most part, those who were of the servile class become ghosts of blended essence; when their blending is dissolved and their retribution is exhausted...

Those born in the world who were mostly *yinglei* (responsive) and *mingling* (luminous) ghosts, their retribution exhausted, are mostly reborn as *xiuzheng* (auspicious omens) among all classes of beings as ghosts that depend upon humans.
Those whose human life has ended and whose retribution is exhausted are mostly reborn in the world as *xunlei* (conformative) ghosts, Ānanda;
these are all dried up by the fire of karma to repay their past debts, serving as [attendants] to others.
These various beings of the animal realm are likewise all summoned by their own false and delusive karma. If one awakens to Bodhi, then these false conditions are fundamentally non-existent.
As you have said regarding the Jewel Lotus Fragrance [Incense], King Vaidūrya, and the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra—such evil karma is originally manifested from within;
it does not descend from heaven, nor does it emerge from the earth, nor does it come from anywhere else.

That which humans receive as retribution for their own delusions returns to be experienced by themselves; within the mind of bodhi, these are all merely the solidification of floating and empty false conceptions.
This follows from the previous point that when the karma of ghosts is exhausted, one is born into the realm of animals. For those whose emotional thoughts are entirely empty, there is only emptiness.
In the Avīci Hell, there are nine feelings and one thought; in the Uninterrupted (Avīci) realms, eight feelings and two thoughts; in the Interrupted realms, seven feelings and three thoughts;

and in the realm of hungry ghosts, six feelings and four thoughts. These are all scorched dry by the fires of karma, yet they remain with six feelings and four thoughts to serve as moisture for rebirth.
Thus, they are born among the fur-bearing and winged species to repay their karmic debts incurred from previous lives.
In Sanskrit, *tiryañc* means "animal" (*chùshēng*). "Animal" (*chù*) refers to being raised or nurtured;

it signifies that these beings are born crosswise, their natures are dull and ignorant, and they cannot sustain themselves independently, relying instead on others for nourishment. Regarding the various animals and monsters detailed below:
because of past habits of greed, they became ghosts of animal-monsters; thus, when the objects they possessed dissolve, the life-force of the ghost likewise perishes.
Following their remaining habitual tendencies, they are mostly reborn in this world as owls. Owls are unfilial birds;
they eat their own parents at birth, and when they nest by attaching clods of earth, the fledglings likewise eat their parents.
This is a matter of great wonder; therefore, it was said previously that through greed, eighty-four thousand thoughts of eating one's parents arise from the combination of these strange occurrences.

Through the habituation of form (*rūpa*), one becomes a *fēngbó* ghost that brings calamity; thus, when the karmic retribution of the ghost is exhausted, it is born again according to its residual habits as an omen of misfortune (*jiǔzhēng*).
An omen of misfortune is a preliminary sign of impending disaster, such as the *shāngyáng* bird dancing in the water or the *jiāngtún* porpoise bowing to the wind.
Through the habituation of greed and delusion, one becomes a *mèi* ghost; when the karmic retribution of the ghost is exhausted...
Furthermore, they manifest as foxes to create seductive charms to delude people; due to the habituation of resentment, they become poisonous ghosts.

When their karmic retribution as ghosts is exhausted, they are reborn among poisonous species, where they exert themselves by biting and stinging to harm others. This is because *māra* spirits often rely upon foxes;

thus, they ultimately become "fox-pestilence" (*hugū*) and, being gathered among poisons, they finally become poisonous creatures—all driven by residual habits. This is due to the habituation of anger.

They become *li* demons; when their *li* karma is exhausted, they become worms. Originally relying on humans, they acted as pestilential fevers; now relying on the intestines, they consume food and drink.
Although this is a residual habit, it is also because they were once extremely violent that they have now been transformed into something extremely gentle.

Due to the habit of arrogance, they become hungry ghosts (*preta*); when their ghostly karma is exhausted, they are born among those who eat [the dead]. This is because of their "empty stomachs and haughty hearts."
Those whom people grind their teeth against all desire to sleep upon their skins and eat their flesh; thus they ultimately become a class of food.

Because humility is the ultimate virtue, those who habitually practiced deception become the "mian" (subtle) and "you" (dark) *yan* ghosts; when the karma of these ghosts is exhausted, they return to become a class of draft animals (*fu*).
This is because, while acting as ghosts, they constantly deceive and bewitch people from the shadows; therefore, they become oxen and horses.
Donkeys and mules, when encountered by clarity, become spirits who serve as mounts for humans; when their karmic retribution as ghosts is exhausted, they return to their corresponding species.
This is like the swallow and the wild goose, which arrive in response to the seasons—it is clearly seen as a remnant of their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

When those with the habit of being wronged encounter clarity, they become spirits who perform labor and service; when their karmic retribution as ghosts is exhausted, they return to be auspicious omens.
For auspicious qilin and rare phoenixes to manifest as omens of good fortune is also due to the residual habit of craving brilliance.
Those with the habit of litigation crave factions and rely on others; though they become ghosts, once their karmic retribution as ghosts is exhausted, they return to the class of domestic animals.
Because they previously followed and obeyed humans, even though they are now among different species, they can still be tamed and kept, such as the classes of chickens, dogs, cats, and monkeys.

"Furthermore, Ānanda," [the text] concludes here by summarizing the three miserable realms (*durgati*). "Inherently self-manifested" means that these evil karmas of the three miserable realms are all manifested by oneself;
they were not created by Heaven nor established by Earth, nor were they bestowed by others.

Since they are fundamentally self-inflicted and self-experienced, one knows that in reality there is not a single dharma that comes from without; they are all formed by the coagulation of deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*).
It is just like water becoming water again.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when these animals repay their former debts, if the debtor exceeds what was owed,
these beings shall once more become human and demand back the surplus, just as one who possesses both power and merit might do.
Thus, among human beings, they do not relinquish their human bodies to repay that power; if they lack merit, they instead become animals to compensate for the remaining balance.
Ānanda, you should know that whether by using money and goods or by employing their labor, once the repayment is complete, it ceases.
However, if in the interim one kills their life or eats their flesh, this continues even through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust.
They devour one another and slaughter one another like a turning wheel, alternating between high and low status without rest;
this state cannot cease except through *śamatha* or the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
This refers to those who, having exhausted their karma as animals, subsequently assume human form. As for ghosts becoming animals, it is due to their six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
The four perceptions serve as the moisture for rebirth, repaying karmic debts from previous lives; once these debts are settled, both parties shall have no further connection.

If the repayment exceeds what is due, these sentient beings will again use the balance of their emotional perceptions as the moisture for rebirth, being born once more among humans, yet they will be called upon to pay for the surplus—“to call in” (zhēng) meaning to collect the remainder, just as one collects taxes on a surplus. This is what is meant.

Furthermore, they seek to collect the remainder of the debts they owe. If those who owe the surplus have superior power from their wholesome karma, or possess both merit and virtue such that they dwell in wealth and nobility, they shall repay the remaining debt among human beings through such means as being robbed or plundered.
However, if their wholesome karma is not superior and they do not possess merit and virtue, there is no [place for them to repay].
To repay the debt, he is further reborn as an animal to settle the remaining balance. Ānanda, this passage further clarifies that while debts are easy to repay, a life-debt is difficult to repay.

This means that if such a person were to repay the remaining value by carrying heavy loads for others over long distances to sell their goods for money to settle the debt, or by farming fields and tilling the soil to labor for them until the debt is fully paid; once it is paid, [he is released].

If one halts the executioner after having already used his money and obtained his labor, yet then kills him and eats his flesh, then life after life beings will devour one another like a waterwheel in a well, alternating between high and low with no end in sight.
Unless one attains the Way for oneself or the Buddhas appear in the world, this cycle of enmity can never be resolved. I pray that...
"O virtuous ones, you should treat them with a heart of loving-kindness and provide them with protection;

you must not exert excessive force upon them, nor should you greedily satisfy your own appetites at the cost of their lives, so as not to betray the earnest and compassionate exhortations of the Tathāgata."
You should now know that those of the owl class, once their retribution is exhausted and they regain their physical form, will be reborn among humans as members of the dull-witted class;
those of the omen-of-fault class, once their retribution is exhausted and they regain their physical form, will be reborn among humans as members of the eccentric class;

those of the fox class, once their retribution is exhausted and they regain their physical form, will be reborn among humans as members of the mediocre class; and those of the venomous class, once their retribution is exhausted, will likewise regain their physical form.
Those who, having been born among humans, were combined with the class of the stubborn— those of the *ō* (roundworm) category— once their retribution is fulfilled, they take form again among humans,

combined with the class of the subtle— those of the *shoku* (feeding) category; those who, having been born among humans, were combined with the class of the supple— those of the *fuku* (clothing) category—
once their retribution is fulfilled, they take form again among humans, combined with the class of the laborious— those of the *ō* (response) category.
Having fully repaid their debts and returned to form within the human realm, they join the class of the refined; those who are like the auspicious omens.

Having fully repaid their debts and returned to form within the human realm, they merge with the class of the enlightened; those who follow the proper order. Having fully repaid their debts and returned to form within the human realm, they join the class of the accomplished.
Ānanda, all such as these, having fully repaid their karmic debts from former lives and returned to form in the human realm, are entirely without [further suffering].
From the beginning, their karmic calculations have been based on inverted views, leading to mutual birth and mutual killing;
not having encountered the Tathāgata nor heard the True Dharma, they naturally revolve within the midst of worldly afflictions—such as these are called those who are to be pitied.
This clarifies that when the karma of an animal is exhausted, one resumes human form. In Sanskrit, this is called *manuṣya*, which here means "human.
It signifies "one who can bring afflictions to rest," as among the six realms of existence, humans are able to cease their defilements; thus, "human" carries the meaning of "cessation.

Furthermore, "human" (*manu*) means "endurance," because in the world, whether confronted by adversity or favor, one is able to remain composed and patient. [Regarding the phrase] "craving for things constitutes a monster": it refers to...
The "xiao-xiao" (the hooting owl) is further characterized as being obstinate; its mind cannot fathom the principles of virtue and righteousness.
To be obstinate is, in general, to be ignorant of benevolence and righteousness, lacking a sense of shame, and devoid of human ethics—someone who cannot be transformed into goodness.
As for those whose speech is a conflation [of human and non-human], they carry the residual habits of beasts while mingling and intermingling with the midst of humanity; these are the *pó* ghosts.

As for the emergence of these signs of calamity among those who are once again deluded by ignorance, it originates from being rooted in greed and lust, drowning in attachment, and failing to see that every action constitutes a transgression;
thus they manifest as omens of calamity. Although they possess human forms, they remain foolish, dull, and obtuse, unable to achieve clarity or precision in any matter.
As the Sūtra says: "It is love and desire that render people ignorant and obscured. These are like possessing spirits and ghosts.
The *hú-hú* again becomes the "commoner" (*yōngzhě*). Formerly a fox-seductress, though possessing a human form, she merely distorts her feelings and adorns her appearance;
wagging her tail to beg for pity, she flatters the world to seek acceptance and cannot stand on her own feet with distinction.

This is what is called "relying on others to achieve one's ends"—a mere, mediocre commoner. The *gǔguǐ* (poisonous ghost) acts as poison; that poison, in turn, becomes the "obstinate one" (*hěnzhě*), which is precisely this.
Those with bee-like eyes and jackal-like voices—obstinate, arrogant, and willing to exert their venom to sting others without realizing their own faults—are *lì-guǐ* (pestilence ghosts).
Those who act as *huí* (roundworms) and further become *wēi* (insignificant) are *huí* that attach themselves to objects through decaying qi;
now these *wēi* refer to those of lowly status whom people, even when they personally associate with them, do not deign to acknowledge. [The next category] is *è-guǐ* (hunger ghosts).
Those who were once eaters become further softened by becoming "soft" (róu) because they treated others with arrogance;
thus, though they possess human form, they have lost the spirit of a man and become a class of mere eaters—men of such feeble and indolent character that they cannot exert themselves.

Those who were once "possessed by ghosts" (yàn guǐ) become "servants" (fú), and servants further become "laborers" (láo) because in their previous lives they bore heavy burdens over long distances and were constantly in a state of servile toil.
Now, Xu is likewise driven and enslaved by others, serving as a running ox or horse, toiling without rest; this is what is called "exerting one's labor" in service to man.

As for the manifestation of *wangliang* spirits and their subsequent production of texts, it is because in past lives they possessed intelligence and insight but failed to attain the truth, and thus fell to become *wangliang*. Their current production of literary works is merely [the result of that].

These minor sentient beings possess a limited capacity for understanding texts and meanings; when interacting with others, they do not lose the proper order of things, and their conduct is merely worthy of observation.
Their writings are not of the caliber that spans the heavens and weaves the earth.

That they are employed as auspicious omens is because, due to past habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), they have relied upon clarity to take form and are thus born into a class of luminous beings. This, too, is a manifestation in response to the world.
It is merely the light of a single crack, not the great illumination that shines upon heaven and reflects upon earth. That which is transmitted is gradual, and that which is attained is thorough;

this is because they have long followed the inclinations of the human heart and now possess a practiced familiarity with worldly affairs and a comprehensive understanding of human nature—it is not that they are able to penetrate all things. Based on these ten kinds [of knowledge], one may know this.
In the human realm, thirteen percent possess clear understanding through their thoughts, while seventy percent conform to the depths of emotional entanglement;

thus, those who are ignorant, dull, and stubborn are many, while those who are enlightened, refined, and exceptionally gifted are few. Those who aspire upward are scarce, whereas those who flow downward are abundant.
Nevertheless, because this realm is a place where the five destinies dwell together, when one examines their mental application, it is found that they belong to the human destiny.
Beings capable of assuming various forms exist across all five destinies, not limited to the single class of animals alone.
For instance, when the Indian monk Jīvaka entered Luoyang during the reign of Emperor Hui of the Jin dynasty, the bhikṣus prostrated before him.
Jīvaka pointed to Zhī Fānyuán and said, "This bodhisattva has come from among sheep," and he further pointed to Zhú Fǎxīng and said, "This bodhisattva has come from among the devas. Furthermore...
When the monk Tan-yi was born, there were pheasant feathers on his ribs; thus he was named Yi.

Because he had heard the *Lotus Sūtra* in a previous life, he attained liberation and was reborn with the body of a pheasant. Thus, among the various classes of human beings, there are not merely one type:

those who are wealthy and noble yet compassionate and kind appear as if they have come from the heavens, while those who are intelligent yet detached and carefree appear as if they have come from among the immortals.
Those who are fierce, hateful, and headstrong seem to have come from among the asuras; those who are poor, lowly, and constantly cold and hungry seem to have come from among the pretas;
those who are stubborn, deluded, and devoid of knowledge seem to have come from among the animals;

and those who are perpetually imprisoned, with disheveled hair and soiled faces, seem to have come from among the denizens of hell. Indeed, their species differ, and their degrees of excellence and inferiority vary accordingly.
If they were different, one would know that their path of origin must not be from a single place;

now, however, we specifically address those who have taken form within the single realm of animals to demonstrate how difficult it is to regain a human body, and how even more difficult it is to regain a human body once the *kāṣāya* has been lost.
Thus, Lord Pei’s preface to the *Awakening of Faith* says: "Ghosts and spirits suffer the bitterness of sinking into the dark, while birds and beasts harbor the distress of wandering in confusion."
At this point of sorrow, while the asuras are in the midst of rage and the devas are in the midst of pleasure, one can only rectify the mind and incline toward bodhi through the human path alone;
if one is a human and does not do so, I can do nothing for them. Having read this, would one not be struck with trepidation and admonish oneself?
Ānanda concludes the section below by expressing pity to admonish humanity, saying "Furthermore... (fu).
"Form" refers to those who, while previously in the human realm, committed the karma of the three miserable destinies and received the retribution of those three destinies;
once that retribution was exhausted, they again assumed human form. All of this is because, from beginningless time, ignorance obstructed their minds and afflictions obstructed their intentions;

they did not cherish the lives of other beings, but instead indulged their passions in killing and devouring as their livelihood. Thus, throughout kalpa after kalpa and birth after birth, they must repay their debts.
When past debts have been fully repaid, one returns to human form;

yet even while receiving a human body, if one does not encounter the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world and fail to hear the Tathāgata’s True Dharma to transform their killing into compassion, then this human life will before long lead them back into the three miserable realms as ghosts or animals. Such is the nature of obtaining a human body.
It is extremely difficult to lose the human body, yet it is exceedingly easy for the Tathāgata to regard this class of people as truly pitiable.
Ānanda, there are further followers who do not rely on perfect enlightenment to cultivate *samādhi*, but instead cultivate deluded thoughts and maintain mental fixations.
There are ten kinds of immortals who dwell in the mountains and forests in places inaccessible to humans, Ānanda.
Those beings who steadfastly consume medicinal elixirs without ceasing, until the path of medicine is perfected, are called earth-walking immortals (*bhūcarā ṛṣayaḥ*).

Those who steadfastly cultivate herbs and plants without ceasing, until the path of medicine is perfected, are called flying immortals (*khecarā ṛṣayaḥ*). Those who steadfastly refine metals and stones without ceasing... [the path of medicine is perfected].
The perfection of the transformative path is called the Wandering Immortal (*cāraṇa-ṛṣi*), who remains firm in movement and stillness without ceasing;

the perfection of vital essence is called the Space-Walking Immortal (*ākāśa-gāmin-ṛṣi*), who remains firm in the flow of fluids without ceasing; the perfection of moistening virtue is called the Heaven-Walking Immortal (*divya-gāmin-ṛṣi*), who remains firm in the luster of the essence without ceasing;
the perfection of absorbing the refined is called the All-Passing Immortal (*sarvatra-gāmin-ṛṣi*), who remains firm in incantations and prohibitions.
Through unceasing skillful means, the perfection of practice leads to the Immortal of Firm Mindfulness;

through unceasing recollection, the perfection of contemplation leads to the Immortal of Illuminating Practice; through unceasing sexual union, the perfection of resonance leads to the Immortal of Essential Practice;
and through unceasing transformation, the perfection of awakening leads to the Immortal of Transcendent Practice.
Ānanda, these individuals all refine their minds among human beings, yet they do not cultivate true awakening;

instead, they separately attain a mode of existence, living for ten million years in deep mountains or on great ocean islands, far removed from the realm of men. This, too, is the circulation of deluded thoughts within saṃsāra;

failing to cultivate samādhi, when their retribution is exhausted, they return once more to be scattered among the various realms of existence. (The first five lines of characters are to be read with level tones; the subsequent five lines of characters...)
(Read with the departing tone).
This refers to progressing from the human path to enter the path of the immortals (*ṛṣi*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Immortal (*xian*) means to transfer;
to grow old without dying and transfer into the mountains. Although there is a specific realm for the immortals, it is not established separately because it is subsumed within the human path.

Next, those in the celestial realms do not maintain the precepts and lack concentration and wisdom; thus, the karmic actions leading to the three lower realms all take the ten habitual tendencies as their cause.
Even when first attaining a human body, one still carries the remnants of these ten habitual tendencies, whereas this realm of the immortals has no connection to them at all.
Nevertheless, this realm is likewise characterized by a distaste for impermanence and a longing for permanence.
Yet, because they do not attain the Way, their mistaken understanding of cultivation is to be pitied;
had Lü Dongbin met Huanglong and cast aside his drifting zither, would that not have been fortunate? To "follow others" means to advance and cultivate along the path of humanity.
Those who do not rely on the correct awakening to practice *samādhi* do not rely on the Tathāgata’s true teaching regarding non-arising and non-ceasing.
Taking the fundamentally pure essence as the basis of practice is distinct from practicing based on deluded thoughts.

Those who practice based on deluded thoughts cling to the five aggregates of this body, believing there is a nature that can be cultivated, a life-force that can be sustained, or that it can be made to live long and dwell eternally in the world.
They do not know that this body is originally formed by the congealing of deluded thoughts; even if they remain in the world for eighty thousand kalpas, they will ultimately fall into emptiness.
"Regarding 'the dead' and 'preserving thoughts to solidify the form': although there are ten different types [of cultivation], preserving thoughts to solidify the form is the general key.
To say 'preserve thoughts' means it employs various deluded imaginings and cannot be compared to the dissolution of all mental states.
To say 'solidify the form' means it is a false identification with the physical body and cannot be compared to ultimate, indestructible solidity."
"Places where forest-dwellers cannot reach" refers to deep mountain regions inaccessible to human tracks, such as the *dongtian* (cave-heavens) and *fudi* (blessed lands) of this region.
Ānanda, following this, the various immortals (*ṛṣi*) are formally enumerated; there are ten types. The first three involve external cultivation, while the latter three involve internal cultivation.
"Those who are firm in taking medicinal elixirs" means that they solidify their physical forms by ingesting such elixirs. It is like this.
Nowadays, people merely consume autumn stones (*qiúshí*), red lead (*hóngqiān*), and the like; these can only arrest the decline of age but cannot grant the power of levitation.
Thus it is said they are "earth-walkers" (*dìxíng*). This is the case with figures such as Asita of the Western Regions and Peng Zu and Jie Zi of this land.

Little do they realize that a single satiation of the nectar of immortality (*gānlùjiāng*), the food of dhyāna-joy (*chányuèshí*), the rice of the golden ox (*niúnjīnfàn*), or the cakes of Yúnmén can cause one to forget a hundred hungers.

Furthermore, there are those who are firm and robust through consuming plants and trees; that is, by eating such things as *huangjing*, *cangzhu*, pine, cypress, *fuling*, and *changpu*, they solidify their forms.
Because their bodies become light through long-term ingestion, they are able to fly upward;
thus they are called "flying beings," like the figures of Master Mao and the Lady Mao. Yet they do not realize that even the *agada* medicine would affect them upon contact.

Then the faculties and fetters will all be extinguished, and one will proceed everywhere without obstruction; by taking this, all myriad sufferings are eliminated and one’s lifespan becomes immeasurable.
That which is called "solidifying metal and stone" refers to alchemical medicines of refined metals and stones;

by taking them, the body is made firm, such as the five metals, eight minerals, nurturing cinnabar, and joining mercury—categories such as the nine-fold great return (*jiǔzhuǎn dàhuán*). "Transforming the Way" means turning [the hair] white.
Transforming stone into gold and changing the ordinary body into the skeletal remains of an immortal, one is thus able to travel through the world without obstruction,
like Lü Dongbin or He Xiangu. Yet they did not realize that by opening their own precious treasury,
they could realize this indestructible body, sport in spiritual powers, and purify Buddha-lands everywhere.
How could one wait for the path of transformation to be perfected before wandering forth? Thus, the *Heart Cinnabar Secret Instructions* of Dongshan say:
"I have a medicine called Heart Cinnabar, which has been refined within the furnace of afflictions for years and ages. Know that its color within the womb does not change;
its radiant brilliance pervades the great trichiliocosm. Opening the Dharma-eye, one beholds the tip of a single hair, where the ordinary and the holy can be transformed in a single kṣaṇa."

One must know how to distinguish the true from the false and bring it to fulfillment through practice; at all times, one should refine and examine it to see that there is neither cessation nor arising.
Even the myriad phenomena are all driven [into service]; regardless of whether they are like clay or mud, if they are brought into this furnace, there is nothing that is not this.
This is precisely the true elixir of the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity. That which is firm and stable in movement and stillness is called "the One."
Whether moving or at rest, one maintains the vital breath (*qi*) to solidify the physical form.
This is what Zhuangzi meant by "maintaining pure *qi*" and what Laozi meant by "subtle and continuous, as if it existed, yet its use never exhausts.

When the vital breath is perfected through the essence (*jing*), the essence transforms into *qi*, *qi* transforms into spirit (*shen*), and spirit transforms into the void (*xu*). Thus, one is able to encompass the sun and moon, ride upon the flying dragon, and roam [in the Dao].
That which lies beyond the four seas is called "Empty Practice" (*ākāśa-caryā*), similar to the manner described here in this land regarding Liezi riding the wind.
It should be known that not relying on breath, not relying on form or color, and not relying on earth, water, fire, or wind—this is true Empty Practice.
"Solidifying the vital fluids" refers to retaining the saliva and swallowing the essence to solidify the physical form; thus the virtue of moisture becomes perfect.

"Success" refers to overturning the yin and yang so that water ascends and fire descends; once the essence is complete and firm, the form becomes radiant and smooth, the skin like snow and the countenance like that of a child.
Not eating the five grains and not engaging in worldly desires, one resembles Heaven;
thus it is called "Heavenly Practice. This is like the class of divine beings on Mount Gushan, yet they remain unaware of their own true nature.
The nature of water is true emptiness, pervading the entire Dharma-realm and penetrating the ten directions;
its fluids, saliva, and froth all flow through as a single channel with the ocean of fragrant waters, not requiring the consolidation of essence before they are formed.

As for "consolidating the essence and color," this refers to consuming the radiance of the sun and moon and inhaling the quintessence of clouds and mists in order to solidify the physical form. Inhale...
Regarding those who have perfected the essence through refinement: once they have absorbed the pure essence for a long time, dust and dross are daily removed while clarity and emptiness daily arrive.
Thus, they are able to penetrate metal and stone, tread upon water and fire, with not the slightest hindrance—much like the class of immortals possessing the five supernatural powers.
Yet they do not realize that their own radiance illuminates heaven and earth, penetrating everywhere through the gates of the six sense faculties, requiring no further absorption.
Only after attaining purity does one achieve penetration. Those who are firm in incantations (dhāraṇī) use the power of these spells to solidify their physical forms;
it is said that by reciting them for a long time with a concentrated mind and remaining motionless, one may likewise attain the Way. This spell was widely transmitted in the Western Regions;
if one recites it within a well for three years, one can spontaneously fly out from the well oneself, and is therefore called "The Practice of the Way" (Dàoxíng).
To know that the *Siddhārthapātra* (悉怛多般怛囉) is the heart-mantra for transforming the ordinary into the sagely, yet to take this as the Way rather than the True Path, is not correct.
As for "firmly contemplating": it is like visualizing the crown of the head while binding the mind to the ocean of vital energy (*citta-samudra*) to solidify the physical form;
it is like the texts of the immortals (*ṛṣi*), which first bind the mind at the navel wheel (*nābhi-cakra*), then penetrate the coccyx (*mūlādhāra*), and ascend through the spine.
Thus one reaches Nirvana by piercing the crown; this is what is called "passing through the twin barriers of the spine to penetrate the gate of the summit.
Yet even this is achieved through recollection, and it is also termed "turning the light back to reflect. Therefore it is said, "illumination is practice.

How could one know that when neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil, the fundamental body of original purity, clarity, and stillness perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm? This is the firm intersection.
"Encountering" (*gòu*) refers to taking the *kǎn* (water) trigram to fill the *lí* (fire) trigram in order to consolidate the physical form.

"The resonance is perfectly accomplished" means that by matching the male of *kǎn* with the female of *lí* as husband and wife, within the space of a finger-snap their mutual resonance can produce the elixir;
once the elixir is perfected, one ascends to the Nine Heavens. This is because the human body possesses a single point of true essence (*zhēn-jīng*).
The primal essence (*pradhāna*) of the Supreme One of the Pre-Natal (*prākṛta*) is the "essence within" mentioned by Laozi and the "essence not to be shaken" mentioned by Guangcheng.
Once this essence is attained, one achieves the Way immediately; hence it is called the practice of essence.
Yet few realize that the fundamental substance of consciousness-essence is originally pure and luminous; once it receives form, its actions become identical [to those of the physical body].

To never have been separated from the source yet to abandon it without a second thought, seeking instead the primal essence (*taiyi-yuanjing*) elsewhere to engage in union—what is this if not deluded imagination?
As for "firmly stabilizing transformations," it means observing transformations in order to stabilize one's physical form.

This involves contemplating that all in the world is entirely like an illusion, thereby awakening to and penetrating the principles of transformation, so as to preserve the form within the world. If...
Figures such as Liu Gen and Zuo Ci could even move mountains, overturn rivers, and alter the four seasons;
these were the ultimate feats of the Way of the Immortals. Formerly, Lao Chengzi studied illusion under Master Yin Wen, who told him:
"The vital breath of living beings and the forms of physical shapes are all illusions. They are what the creative transformation begins with—the yin and yang."

That which marks the end of all things is called birth and death; that which exhausts the constants and penetrates the changes, shifting according to forms, is called illusion and transformation (*māyā*).
Once one knows that illusion and transformation are no different from birth and death, only then can one learn the art of illusion.
"I and you are both illusions—what need is there to learn it? Having returned home, Lao Chengzi applied the words of Yin Wen and contemplated them deeply for three months.
Thus, he was able to exercise mastery over life and death: he could cause thunder to roll in winter and water to arise in summer;
those who fly could run, and those who run could fly. Yet throughout his entire life, he never attached himself to these arts, and so they were not transmitted to the world.

Although this constitutes the practice of ultimate transcendence through understanding illusory transformations, one does not know from whence these illusory transformations originate; it is by transcending all relativity that one achieves the practice of ultimate transcendence.

Furthermore, Ānanda, regarding those who conclude that there is a principle for obtaining life apart from delusion— meaning they fail to realize that their own adamantine jewel-like awakening is true,
eternal, and unchanging throughout past and present, yet instead seek within the confines of the physical frame a principle for prolonging life for a thousand million years—
they do not know that such longevity merely serves to surpass brevity; it is like the morning glory compared to [the lotus].
The pine and cypress trees compared to the cicada and the *huigū*, though differing in their longevity, are they truly immortal?
Thus, the Yellow Dragon was dismissed as a corpse-guarding ghost, and Xuan Sha called him a "dead man whose soul has not yet dispersed.

Such beings are also included within the reckoning of saṃsāra; it is because they do not know that nature is fundamentally without life, and that life is not falsely established, that they cling to this [notion].

This is for the sake of the Way of long life and far-reaching vision. If, within this state, one encounters a holy teacher and turns the carriage around to change course, one may enter the wondrous *samādhi*.

If, however, one stubbornly clings to it and refuses to let go, once the retribution of the immortals is exhausted, one will still undergo a transformation of head and face and fall among the various classes of beings.
Furthermore, the lifespan of the gods in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception is eighty thousand [great kalpas].
After kalpas, when one’s retribution finally ends, one may again receive the body of a flying weasel;

how much more so for those who seek to become immortals, whose lifespans last but ten million years—scarcely even a single day and night in the heavens of the four formless realms. Is it not a tragedy that the common people compare themselves to such [immortals]?
Therefore, students of the Way should worry that they hear the Way too late, rather than worrying that their years and lifespan will not be long. —Zhong.
The Bhikṣuṇī said: "To hear the Way in the morning and to die in the evening—how profound these words are!
Recently I have observed that those who envy long life are all a kind of deluded people of wealth and status who seek to dwell in the human realm to enjoy sensual pleasures for a long time.
If longevity could truly be sought and sensual pleasures could truly be enjoyed forever, then Qin Shihuang and Han Wudi would surely not have died so soon, despite their wealth and power."
That the deluded mind is habituated in such a way is truly enough to provoke a laugh.

Ānanda, when people of the world do not seek the permanent and are unable to renounce their attachment to wives and concubines, yet their minds do not wander in lustful misconduct but instead become clarified and polished so that inner luminosity arises—after their lives end, they will be situated near the sun and moon. Thus it is.
One class is named the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*).
This clarifies that it is the first heaven of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). "Heaven" (*deva*) has the meaning of sovereignty; it also has the meaning of radiating light;

furthermore, "heaven" (*deva*) means "summit," signifying that they stand at the head of all beings. There are three types of heavens, namely: those of the Desire Realm, the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), and [the Formless Realm].

The Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu). As for the heavens of the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu), from the waist and summit of Mount Sumeru up to the celestial abodes in space, they all possess food and drink, sexual desire, and sleep;
because they are fully endowed with these three desires, they are called "Desire Heavens" (kāmadeva).

The marriage and taking of wives and concubines among their men and women are also like those of the human world; however, all these devas have neither flesh nor bones, and they lack both excrement and urine.
His impure body emits radiance, distinguishing no difference between day and night; he has attained the five supernormal powers as a natural reward, and his form is without obstruction.
Thus one knows that among the realms of the celestial destiny, he is the most honored within the boundaries.

As for those spoken of as "people of the world," they likewise enter the heavenly path by practicing from the human realm. Those who do not seek the permanent abide neither in the conditioned nor in the unarisen.
Taking the cessation of the mind as the fundamental cause for cultivation, one takes the ten wholesome actions as the fundamental cause for cultivation.

Seeking worldly happiness and inexhaustible five desires as the fruit—such a person, although they uphold the precept against sexual misconduct, considers sexual intercourse with their own wife or concubines to be "right" sexual conduct, while sexual intercourse with the wives or concubines of others to be "wrong" sexual conduct. This person merely lacks wrong sexual conduct; furthermore—

There is right sexual conduct. To say that "the mind does not flow or stray" means that not only does the body refrain from committing illicit sexual acts, but the mind likewise lacks even a single thought of transgression.

"Clarifying and polishing until radiance arises" means that because desire-thoughts do not occasionally cause the mind to become disordered and agitated, the water of craving is clarified and polished, and the ground of the mind becomes pure. At the time of death, one abandons the physical body and receives [a new form].

The reward land where the celestial bodies reside is situated at the midpoint of Mount Sumeru, adjacent to the palaces of the sun and moon, and is named the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*).

Because the four sides of the mountain’s waist are occupied by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, and Vaiśravaṇa, each presiding over one side and guarding one continent, those who possess only a mind for sexual misconduct that does not flow into dissipation can purify and polish their nature until clarity arises. Thus...
Know that within the purity of observing the precepts while contrary to worldly karma, the mind does not wander;
the lands of the ten directions appear therein as brilliantly pure, and all things—secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous—are manifested within them, which can be understood by analogy.

That those in the human realm flow downward into the three miserable realms and hells is primarily due to the habit of lust; that those in the human realm ascend... [is primarily due to the habit of non-lust].
For the various devas of the upper realms, subduing the habit of lust is paramount; for those in the human realm who ascend to become sages and worthies, severing the habit of lust is paramount.
The harm wrought by the habit of lust is no less than that of a vengeful enemy or a venomous serpent. Beware! Beware! of it!
Those whose sensual desire for their own wives is slight and who do not find full satisfaction even when dwelling in the Pure Abodes,
and who after death transcend the brilliance of the sun and moon to dwell at the summit of the human realm— this class of beings is called the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

This explains the second heaven of the desire realm. It is said that such a person not only refrains from sexual misconduct, but even with his own wife, he does not indulge excessively or dissipate himself.
Even when thoughts arise during moments of pure solitude, they do not fully savor their objects.
Because he has surpassed the previous type of person by a factor of ten, after death he ascends on high.
Twice as high as that is the summit of Mount Sumeru, named the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (the Heaven of the Thirty-three).
"Trāyastriṃśa" translates here as "Thirty-three," referring to the realm governed by Śakra. The two heavens above this are called "earth-dwelling" because they have not yet departed from the earth.
Nevertheless, the sexual union of beings in these two heavens is no different from that of humans; however, as soon as the vital energy is released, the outflow of desire ceases.
If there are those among human beings who, despite having impurities flow forth,
encounter desire and engage in it only briefly, yet thereafter depart without further thought or recollection; and while in the human world they are active for little and tranquil for much—
after the end of their lives, these people shall dwell serenely and clearly in the midst of empty space, where the light of the sun and moon cannot reach above them.
Those who possess such self-radiance are called the Suyāma Heaven;
this is the third heaven of the Desire Realm. It is said that these individuals do not give rise to lustful thoughts even when encountering objects of desire;
should they encounter such objects, they engage in intercourse only once and feel no further longing or attachment, remaining as if already dwelling in tranquility.

Because they obtain the full flavor [of their meditative attainment], their minds are moved by desire less and remain tranquil more; thus, they are twice as superior as those before. Consequently, after death, they dwell resplendently in the realm of space. Question:
