Since there is no earth element in the realm of space-dwellers (*ākāśavāsin*), upon what do their palaces rest?

Answer: The seven-jeweled *vaiḍūrya* is no different from the great earth. However, when they wish to descend, it becomes vacuous and unobstructed, just as in the following example: [the palace of the *paranirmitavaśavartin* gods].
Humans, the great earth, sages, gods, and ghosts are all able to move freely up and down through the vast void without obstruction.
One should know that all phenomena are illusory, brought about by the power of karma; thus, both the empty and the real manifest together, yet those who are deluded have truly not yet realized this.
This heaven is twice as high as Mount Sumeru, and therefore the light of the sun and moon cannot shine upon it from above; it possesses its own light.

The radiance of their bodies illuminates one another. As for the *Ābhāsvara* (translated here as "Time-Portion"), the Master [Xuanzang] states that day and night are defined by the opening and closing of the lotuses; this is indeed correct. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* says:
"These devas may gather in groups of a hundred or a thousand upon a single lotus filament; they sit together without it being cramped or narrow, due to their own virtuous karma."
Due to the power of their karma, the inhabitants of this heaven engage in sexual union solely through embracing; they do not engage in physical intercourse.
They remain tranquil at all times, and even when objects of touch arise, they are unable to transgress against them.

After death, they ascend to a subtle and refined realm, never descending to the levels of humans or devas of the lower realms. Thus, even when the kalpa is destroyed by the three calamities, such a class of beings remains untouched.
It is named Tuṣita Heaven.

This clarifies that it is the fourth heaven of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Regarding the phrase "tranquil at all times," this means that between movement and stillness, there is entirely no thought of lust;
having already surpassed the state of "movement being more and stillness less," it is twice as superior. It is simply a state of having attained the ultimate satisfaction of the mind.
Since sensory objects inevitably bring about corresponding contacts that press upon one from without, it is impossible to remain without a mind;
because one cannot avoid compliance with them, after death one is born in the Heaven of Contentment (*Tuṣita*), for one is able to give rise to contentment regarding the five desires.
As for the phrase "ascending to the refined and subtle," this refers to Maitreya’s Inner Court (*abhyantarikā*); this heaven possesses both an inner court and an outer court.
In total there are fifty tiers, each containing five hundred billion celestial palaces; within these, there are forty-nine inner palaces and one outer palace.
The Great Maṇi Hall where Maitreya Bodhisattva resides is situated in its center.
This is the retribution-land of those free from outflows (*anāsrava*), which constitutes the distinct retribution heavens—similar to how the five *anāgāmins* reside within the fourth dhyāna.

Furthermore, because this inner court is the dwelling place where Bodhisattvas in their final birth before Buddhahood reside, the outer court cannot even glimpse its inner sanctum, let alone the various heavens of the lower realms;
hence it is said that it is subtle and refined, and does not connect with the lower realms.
Even when the kalpa is destroyed and the third dhyāna is ravaged, this inner court is not reached by the three calamities, nor has it ever been destroyed.
Because this is manifested through the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the sages, the *Śūramgama-samādhi Sūtra* states: "The lord of gods here is named Maitreya.
Those who have fully cultivated the three grades and nine categories of practice, generating great vows in every thought-moment, shall attain birth in that place;
by the power of their outflow-free (*anāsrava*) merit, the three calamities cannot reach them—this is what is meant by "the three calamities cannot reach [them] here."

This passage provides a general description of both the outer and inner courtyards. Specifically, the outer courtyard is a place produced for those who, from among the ninth grade [of practitioners], were not fully diligent.

After seven days have passed there, Maitreya Bodhisattva emits light and rains down flowers to lead them into the inner courtyard’s Small Maṇi Hall, where he subsequently preaches the Dharma to cause them to give rise to the power of thorough penetration. Thus it is.
Subsequently, they are led to enter the Inner Court. Outside of these two courts, there is another realm called the Karma-vipāka Heaven;
this is formed by the results of tainted (*sāsrava*) karma and is thus the General Reward Heaven (*saṃvartanīya-sāmānya-phala-deva*). Those who practice the ten wholesome actions are reborn there.
Because it is a result of tainted karma, it can be destroyed by the three calamities. Although it is the same heaven as the others, because it is the general...
If the outer court of retribution is already like the separation between the divine and the mundane, how much more so the inner court?
This text perhaps first mentions the outer heavens and subsequently includes the inner court; this is merely the translator’s excessive abbreviation.
Otherwise, how could this heaven—by means of meager desires and inferior merit—so suddenly protect such a superior retribution that transcends the third dhyāna?

I have no desire for the mind, yet I comply with your actions; when you lie across me, the flavor is like chewing wax. After the end of life, one will be born in the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati).
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations.

This is the fifth heaven of the desire realm. While those in the preceding [heavens] still possess objects of touch and possess minds that respond to them, for this person, objects of touch are presented before him, yet he lacks any mind that responds to them; there is no flavor at all, like chewing wax.
Because this is twice as superior as the former, at the time of death, one is born transcending the Realm of Emanated Beings (*nirmāṇarati*). "Transcending emanation" means that one is able to...
Because they transcend the lower heavens and can further transform objects of pleasure at will, they are called the "Devas Who Delight in Transformations" (*Nirmāṇarati*).
Since these devas take laughter as their sexual desire, they delight in what they themselves have transformed. As for the phrase "laid across," it means arranged horizontally before one.
It is as stated in Sima Xiangru’s *Fu on the Love of Beauty*: "Floral beauty presents itself; the jade body lies across."
The ancient poem by Chen You says, "A single glance brings forth a hundred thousand [possibilities]," which is precisely this meaning.
Those who lack worldly minds yet engage in worldly affairs, remaining clearly transcendent amidst their interactions with such activities, and who, after the end of life,

are universally able to transcend and transform both realms of the transformed and the untransformed— this class of beings is called the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).

This clarifies that this refers to the sixth heaven of the desire realm. Regarding the phrase "having no worldly mind," it means that the mind of this person who observes the precepts aspires to the higher realms; they lack even a single thought of worldly passion.

Although they temporarily act as husband and wife in accordance with worldly custom, at the time of union, not only is there a complete absence of flavor, but they are also clearly transcendent, without the slightest attachment.

Because their defilement is twice as great as that of the former [Heaven of Delighting in Creations], after the end of life they transcend the realms of both the "created" (*nirmāṇa*) and the "uncreated" (*anirmāṇa*);
"created" refers to the fifth heaven, while "uncreated" refers to the four lower heavens.

They are named the Paranirmita-vaśavartins because they do not trouble themselves to create objects of sensual pleasure, but instead enjoy them with mastery through what is created by others. These gods merely gaze at one another.
For the sake of sensual desire, they are increasingly superior to the lower heavens.
Ānanda, although the forms of these six heavens involve movement, their mental traces still intermingle; from this point downward, it is called the Realm of Desire (kāmadhātu).
This is a summary. "Movement" here refers specifically to the agitation of the desire-mind;
when worldly people are moved by desire, they are like rushing currents, runaway fires, intoxicated elephants, or mad monkeys—leaping and galloping beyond all control.

Now, being able to gradually restrain this until reaching stillness, it is called "exiting movement. Yet this has not yet reached true non-mind, for though body and mind do not interact, there remains a subtle trace.
Therefore, it is collectively termed the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). From this point downward, all the way down to the Avīci Hell, is subsumed within the Desire Realm;
this is called the Ground of the Five Destinations’ Intermingled Dwelling.

the Ultimate Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Volume Eight.

Explanatory Notes by Shi Tongrun of Erleang’an.
Ānanda, among all those in the world who cultivate the mind, there may be those who do not rely on *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) and lack wisdom;

yet they are able to restrain their bodies and refrain from sexual desire. Whether walking or sitting, their thoughts are entirely absent, no defilement of attachment arises, and nothing remains [in the mind].
Those in the desire realm who think of themselves as companions of Brahmā are called the *Brahmapāriṣadya* (Heaven of the Retinue of Brahmā).
This clarifies the eighteen heavens of the four dhyānas within the form realm. Wēn-líng says: "The previous section clarified the six heavens;

although they have emerged from the disturbances of the mundane world, they have not yet severed desire, and thus they are collectively termed the 'Desire Realm. From here downward, the eighteen [heavens] are clarified."
Although the heavens are free from the defilement of desire, they still possess material form; therefore, they are collectively termed the "Form Realm" (*rūpadhātu*).

Furthermore, they are collectively termed the "Brahma World" because they have already abandoned the defilement of desire. They are also collectively designated as the "Four Dhyānas" because they have already abandoned distraction and agitation.

While the gods of the Desire Realm are born there through the influence of the ten wholesome actions, these heavens are born through both the ten wholesome actions and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Nevertheless, they maintain the six objects of contemplation associated with impure dhyāna.

Regarding the six practices of the ear: one feels weary of the desire realm as being suffering, coarse, and an obstruction, while rejoicing in the form realm as being pure, sublime, and free from attachment.
This is the path by which ordinary persons suppress afflictions and transcend the desire realm. Question:

According to the teachings of Tiantai, the karma of the six heavens of the desire realm all takes the ten wholesome actions as their basis; if these are combined with a mind that protects the Dharma, they constitute the four [wholesome paths of action].

If the karma of the Heavenly King is combined with benevolence and compassion, it is the karma for the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; if it is combined with non-affliction toward sentient beings and skillful mastery, it is the karma for the Yāma Heaven;
if it is combined with the cultivation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it is the karma for the Tuṣita Heaven;

if it is the concentration of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*), it is the karma for the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; and if it is the "not-yet-arrived" concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*), it is the karma for the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. This is so.
Question: On the day before yesterday, there were also instances of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), yet why is it that this realm alone is designated as "meditation"? Answer:
As stated in the previous conclusion, although the body has emerged from movement, the traces of the mind still intersect with the external.

From this point upward, there is an absolute absence of women; both body and mind are detached, and there is no further intersection. Furthermore, hunger and sleep are absent, and the three desires are all forgotten; one feels only a slight sensation of hunger.
When weary, one enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), and upon emerging from it, one is satiated and becomes clear and vigorous;
this is simply taking the joy of meditation as food and as rest. Ānanda, [the following] first clarifies the first heaven of the first dhyāna.

It says that regarding all those in the world who cultivate the mind—referring to the devas and humans of the three realms—although they have not truly attained the genuine method for cultivating the mind, they nevertheless...
Each person claims to have already attained the cultivation of the mind; thus, it is said that this is the mundane cultivation of the mind, not the supramundane cultivation of the mind.
"Not relying on dhyāna" means lacking the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. "Lacking wisdom" means lacking the Vajra-like Wisdom.
"The body does not engage in sexual misconduct" means taking impure meditative concentration as the cause.

When the mind restrains those sexual habits so that at all times both thought and perception are entirely absent, then because both body and mind are pure and there is no further dwelling in the lower realms, one will be reborn in the Brahma-world at the time of death through the power of mindfulness as a member of the Brahma-folk.

Thus, it is known that although the physical form may still be active, if the traces of the mind remain entangled with objects, one cannot be called a "Brahma"; this applies until the point where both thought and perception are entirely absent.

This is merely being a companion to the Brahmā Heaven; as for what is called "Brahmā," compared to the defilement and turbidity of the Desire Realm, this state is indeed pure and unstained, yet it does not possess the full characteristics of the pure and white Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*).
When the habitual tendencies of desire have been eliminated and the mind free from desire manifests, such a person delights in and accords with all forms of discipline;
being able to practice the virtues of Brahma at the proper time, this class of beings is called the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahma (Brahmapurohita).
This is the second heaven of the first dhyāna. The first two phrases conclude the preceding section; here, the primary heaven is correctly elucidated.
This means that since the habitual tendencies of desire have been eliminated, the concentrated mind is clearly manifest.

Because this heaven loves and accords with the concentration-associated precepts (*samādhi-saṃvara*) without exception, at the time of death one does not forget past habits and acts in accordance with mindfulness; thus it is called "Brahma-Virtue" (*brahma-guṇa*).
Those who assist and correct the Lord of Brahmā are named the Heaven of Brahmā’s Ministers (*Brahmapurohita*).
Their bodies and minds are wondrously perfected, their deportment is flawless, and they are endowed with pure precepts and clear insight;
such persons are able to lead the assembly of Brahmās at the appropriate time and become Great Brahmās (*Mahābrahmā*). This class of beings is called the Heaven of Great Brahmā.
This is the third heaven of the First Dhyāna. The first two phrases conclude the preceding section on purity; the following portion correctly elucidates this heaven.

Because it manifests from the concentrated mind of the preceding stage, its body and mind are perfectly subtle and wondrous. Furthermore, because it possesses the virtues of Brahmā, its majestic deportment is never deficient.
This heaven gives rise to wisdom from within meditative concentration and precepts; however, its nature of wisdom is not yet perfectly luminous or brilliant throughout.

The comparison of their spatial dimensions arises from the superiority of their wisdom; because they are capable of serving as the Brahmā Lord over the heavens below, at the time of death, they should be mindful of being reborn there.
According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, [the Great Brahmā] dwells alone, possessing majestic power and radiance, produced by the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of "without vitarka but with vicāra.
The two lower heavens possess both vitarka and vicāra. Furthermore, at the end of the kalpa...
Later, when the kalpa was forming, the non-Buddhists who had previously arrived could not discern its origin; they consequently clung to it as being eternal.
Furthermore, because they gave rise to the thought that they saw a heaven-born being, they clung to this being as the sole cause capable of producing the world.
Ānanda, these three superior streams cannot be oppressed by any suffering or affliction;
although they are not yet the true, correct Samādhi, because the various outflows do not disturb their pure minds, they are called the First Dhyāna.

This section indicates that the names of these three heavens constitute the First Dhyāna. Regarding the term "superior stream" (*viśeṣa-srotas*): it does not mean being a "stream-enterer" (*srotāpanna*) who has attained the first fruit;
rather, it is called "superior" because they have turned their backs on the flow of desire belonging to the lower realms.

These heavens, by means of vitarka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), and the contemplations of impurity, loving-kindness, and compassion, counteract the obstacles of sensual desire, ill-will, and harmfulness belonging to the Desire Realm; thus, they are able to abandon the five desires.
Having eliminated the ten non-virtues and exhausted the five hindrances, one is no longer oppressed by the suffering and afflictions of the desire realm;
this is called the Stage of Joy and Bliss Born of Seclusion. Because one has abandoned the evils of desire, joy arises; because the body and mind are pliant and tranquil, bliss arises.
Although this is not yet the true, primary Samādhi—distinguishing it from the Great Śūraṅgama Samādhi—it nevertheless involves that [stage of] precept-keeping.
With a pure mind, the outflows having been subdued, and being unmoved by the habitual tendencies of desire, one becomes free from all sensual desires, evil, and unwholesome states;
possessing directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and experiencing the joy and happiness born of seclusion, one attains the first *dhyāna*.

Because there is not a single moment of entry interrupted by discursive thoughts, it is called the First Dhyāna. Although this deity is free from the fire of desire, they are internally disturbed by directed thought and sustained thought.
When the mind is directed toward an object, it is called *vitarka* (applied thought); when the subtle mind performs detailed discernment, it is called *vicāra* (sustained thought).

This means that by relying on the stage of "not-yet-reached" (*anāgamya*), one gives rise to the pure material phenomena of the first dhyāna in the form realm; these touch the body-faculty and mind of the desire realm, causing a great awakening.
At that time, there arises a tactile sensation within the body. Because this contact with form possesses unprecedented merit and benefit, it is so named.

Having realized the merits of the first dhyāna through the awakening factors (*bodhyaṅga*), one uses the subtle mind to discern the various excellent qualities of the material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) within this meditative concentration. These objects are clearly manifest and free from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

Because such merits do not exist in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they are called the factor of investigation (*vicaya-anga*), which refers to applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*). In the first two heavens, both applied and sustained thought are present.
Upon reaching the third heaven, there is no *vitarka* (applied thought) but there is *vicāra* (sustained thought);
because of the internal presence of *vitarka* and *vicāra*, fire arises externally, and thus the first dhyāna is destroyed by fire.

According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, if these three heavens are divided vertically, they should consist of three tiers separated by double distances; the celestial subjects, ministers, and kings each occupy one level.

How could these layers constitute a single unified realm? Furthermore, while it may be permitted for subjects and citizens to be numerous, how could there be multiple Heavenly Kings occupying the heavens while residing alone on a single layer?

If both are kings, by what means could one command the other? It is likely that they are ranked as three distinct levels based on a comparison of their relative virtues—whether they serve as subjects, as assistants, or as sovereigns.
Thus, they are categorized as three rather than one; it is not that all inhabitants of the heavens are merely subjects and citizens.
There is no king over whom all the heavens are subject, nor are there ministers or subjects. According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, the Brahmā Heaven has no separate location;
rather, within the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahmā (*Brahmapurohita*), there is a lofty tower where he resides. It further states that his majestic power and radiance cause him to dwell alone.
This suggests that while the Brahmā King is uniquely honored, the Brahmā beings and the Ministers of Brahmā reside together in the same heaven.
To serve and attend [to the Buddha] is the function of these three heavens; thus, they all reside together in the First Dhyāna on a single level.

The *Ratnakaraṇḍa-avadāna Sūtra* (Renwang jing) states that even among the eighteen Brahmā heavens there must be distinctions between sovereigns and subjects. Furthermore, it says that within the Fourth Dhyāna there is the Great Tranquil King (*Mahāśāntirāja*).
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* (Yingluo jing) states that each dhyāna has its own Brahmā King. The root sūtra also speaks of the four levels of heavens within the Fourth Dhyāna.

Your Majesty, consider now that since the Great Brahmā is the king of the first dhyāna, yet the three sūtras all state that there is a king in the fourth dhyāna, we know that Ābhāsvara, Śubhakṛtsna, and Bṛhatphala likewise have kings.
As for the others, they all follow the principle of having only one minister and one subject.
In some places it is said that among the devas of the form realm, only these [four] heavens possess rulers, ministers, and common subjects; above these, there are none.
It may be that because Brahmā-rāja rules over the Sahā world, he alone is designated as "Honored One.

Therefore, Master Zhipan arbitrarily divided the four dhyānas into four stages: the first, second, and third dhyānas each have three heavens and constitute one stage, while the fourth dhyāna has nine heavens and constitutes one stage; this should be taken as the standard.
Ānanda, next there is the Brahmā Heaven, which governs the Brahmās and perfects the Brahma-conduct; with a tranquil mind unmoving, its profound stillness gives rise to light.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Limited Light (Parīttābhā).
This is the first heaven of the Second Dhyāna. The first three phrases describe ascending by stepping upon the Brahma-heavens, merely adding the quality of perfection.

"The mind becomes clear and unmoving, and from profound stillness, light arises": previously there were vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), which were coarse movements that gave rise to the three consciousnesses;
now, with internal purity and single-mindedness, vitarka and vicāra are absent, and one only takes internal objects as conditions, which differs from the First Dhyāna.
Because the three consciousnesses have ceased, the water of the mind becomes clear and undisturbed, giving rise to a radiant luster;
yet this radiance is still inferior and has not reached its ultimate measure, which is why it is called "Limited Radiance" (Parīttābhā).

It is like the celestial light that emerges when the Great Void is settled, yet it cannot be compared to the all-pervading, profound stillness, for even the slightest trace of the dual attachments to self and phenomena remains unbroken.
Light illuminates light in mutual radiance, shining forth without end; it reflects throughout the worlds of the ten directions, pervasively transforming them into lapis lazuli.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (*Apramāṇābha*).
This is the second heaven of the Second Dhyāna. Because they emit even more light than the previous Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābha*), their lights illuminate one another.
Its brilliance shines boundlessly, reflecting throughout the worlds of the ten directions so that they take on the color of lapis lazuli;

although this has reached the ultimate limit of its magnitude, it has not yet produced sound, and is therefore called "Immeasurable Light. Nevertheless, it is not comparable to pure lapis lazuli containing a precious moon within.
Inhaling and sustaining the circular radiance (*maṇḍala-prabhā*), they accomplish the essence of the teaching and manifest pure applications of transformation that are inexhaustible;

such a class is called the Heaven of Radiant Sound (*Ābhāsvara-deva*). This is the third heaven of the Second Dhyāna. Regarding "inhaling the circular radiance to accomplish the essence of the teaching": because this heaven is already free from [gross] form...

Because they lack discursive thought and investigation, they have no speech; rather, they manifest pure transformations through light to express verbal meanings and reveal teachings according to the capacities of beings, their application being inexhaustible; therefore, they are called "Light-Sound" (Ābhāsvara).
Ānanda, these three superior streams cannot be assailed by any anxieties or preoccupations;
although they are not yet the true, correct Samādhi, because coarse outflows have already been subdued within the pure mind, this is called the Second Dhyāna.
This section indicates that these three heavens constitute the Second Dhyāna. These three heavens are collectively termed the "Ground of Joy and Bliss Born of Samādhi.

Because the mind of *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) has ceased, it is called "born of samādhi. Furthermore, because it is like a clear mirror upon still water, the body and mind experience a sense of well-being and pleasure;
thus, it is also called the "Dhyāna Accompanied by Joy. This is because when samādhi arises, joy emerges simultaneously with it, yet this state exists as the cessation of both samādhi and joy.

Because one is not afflicted by the worldly anxiety of craving, one cannot be overwhelmed by distress. "The coarse outflows have already been subdued" means that through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the first five consciousnesses have been subdued;

because the first five are subdued by the second dhyāna, there is no *vitarka* (applied thought) or *vicāra* (sustained thought). However, because the sixth consciousness has not yet been subdued, there is still joy and bliss.
Since the internal waters of joy cause agitation, this externally manifests as a water disaster, and thus the world is destroyed by water.
In the first three heavens of the second dhyāna, the gods excel through their ethical discipline; in these [next] three heavens, they excel through their meditative concentration.

Ānanda, when the celestial beings of this class have perfected their radiant halos, mastered their voices, and revealed their subtle qualities, and when they have developed refined conduct and attained the bliss of tranquil extinction—this kind of being is called the Heaven of Limited Purity (Parīttaśubha).
This is the first heaven of the third dhyāna. The two phrases regarding the "perfect light" (*pari-maṇḍala*) build upon the preceding heaven to advance upward.
It is said that although the preceding heaven possesses perfect light as its teaching-substance (*śāsana-tattva*), when one "unfolds the light," the wondrous principle reveals itself spontaneously.

However, because there is still a mind of joy (*prīti-citta*) that discriminates and causes agitation, it can obstruct the bliss of meditative concentration (*samādhi-sukha*). This heaven is more tranquil; therefore, by relying on the principle, it brings about the perfection of refinement.

Practicing so as to penetrate the bliss of quiescence through the bliss of meditative concentration, one first manifests the purity of emptiness; therefore, it is called "Slight Purity" (*parītta-śubha*).

Herein, the three mental factors of equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and clear comprehension (*samprajanya*) are employed to suppress the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) of the six consciousnesses;

this separation from the factor of joy (*prīti-viveka*) constitutes refined practice. As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "By repeatedly cultivating equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, one causes the mind to leap upward."

The joyful sensation (*sukha-vedanā*) that arises concomitantly with the leaping [of the mind] is then extinguished; being free from joy and tranquil, a sensation of bliss (*sukha-vedanā*) contrary to joy arises.
At that time, because the physical body and the mental body experience the bliss of sensation and the bliss of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), it is said that "one experiences bliss with the body.
This bliss of cessation results from the suppression of the sixth consciousness, and thus resembles that of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
This cessation is not like the manifestation of cessation that occurs when arising and ceasing have already been extinguished;
rather, it is the manifestation of pure emptiness that induces boundless physical and mental pliancy, thereby accomplishing the bliss of cessation.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (Apramāṇaśubha).

This is the second heaven of the third dhyāna. Because one subdues the six consciousnesses and thus resembles the realization of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), it is said that "pure emptiness manifests before one.

This refers to ascending further based on what preceded it. "To induce the boundless" means that by expanding and fulfilling this state, the mind of joy becomes increasingly tranquil and pure emptiness becomes increasingly vast;
consequently, both physical and mental sensations attain pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). Up to this point...
This is the cessation of pleasure, which has already become pure emptiness and is called "Immeasurable Purity.
When the world, body, and mind are all perfectly pure, and the accomplishment of pure virtues manifests as a supreme support for the presence of quiescent bliss,
such a class is named the Śubhakṛtsna (Universal Purity) Heaven.

This is the third heaven of the Third Dhyāna. It is said that in the preceding heavens, the bliss of the "pervading mind-ground" (ceti-bhūmi) remains confined to body and mind and is not yet called "universal.
Now, throughout the sense-faculties, the physical body, and the vessel-world (bhājana-loka), there is no place touched by anything that is not sublime bliss.
The sublime bliss within this heaven has reached its ultimate limit and can be further increased; thus, they take this to be the land of pure and supreme bliss, and therein they come to an end.
Because it is the ground upon which the body relies and entrusts itself, it is called "entrusted" (*to*) and "returned to" (*gui*).
Because one attains pure bliss in every place through that [state], it is called "Universal Purity" (*Prasrabdhi*). The *Xianyang lun* (Treatise on Manifesting the Teachings) states:

"That which is moistened by the bliss apart from joy—moistening everywhere, bringing pleasure everywhere, and pervading everywhere—is what is meant by the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the third dhyāna; this occurs within this very body."
In all places, there is not even the slightest area that is not pervaded by the bliss of joy (*prīti-sukha*);

this is called the fundamental third dhyāna. As for the term "preparatory stage" (*sāmantaka*), it refers to the dhyāna being incomplete; as for the term "fundamental," it refers to the dhyāna being complete.
Ānanda, these three superior streams possess great conformity; body and mind are at peace and they attain immeasurable bliss.
Although they have not yet truly attained authentic samādhi, because their hearts are filled with joy within a state of tranquility, this is called the third dhyāna.
This section indicates that the three heavens are called the "Three Dhyānas. Regarding the phrase "possessing great conformity":
it means that this wondrous bliss conforms to the mind and accords with the intention in every respect; thus, it is called "great. Regarding the phrase "the body and mind are at peace and secure":

it means that in the preceding two dhyānas, because the mind possesses the sensation of joy (*prīti*), there is much distraction and movement, and one cannot personally experience physical bliss. Now, since that sensation of joy has ceased...
Because one personally experiences immeasurable, wondrous bliss throughout both body and mind, one attains tranquility;

the phrase "complete joy" indicates that both body and mind receive this bliss. This is because the lower stages lack such bliss, and while the higher stages possess equanimity (*upekṣā*), they lack bliss.
Therefore, the disciples of the Buddhas declare that the third dhyāna possesses both.
Because one is able to relinquish [pleasure], possesses mindfulness and clear comprehension, and yet experiences bliss, the third dhyāna alone is supreme among all states of bliss.
The *Dharmaskandha* designates this as "the dhyāna accompanied by bliss," for the merit of this meditative absorption arises together with a bliss that pervades the entire body.

Because the consciousness-faculty (*manovijñāna*) has already been subdued in this heaven, there is no longer the feeling of joy (*prīti*), and since it is disturbed by the presence of inhalation and exhalation, external wind-disasters (*vāyu-vyādhi*) arise.
Furthermore, the wind disaster destroys the third dhyāna.

Ānanda, moreover, when gods and humans are no longer oppressed by the causes of physical and mental suffering, and that pleasure has been exhausted—since such pleasure is not permanent and will surely perish after a long time—they simultaneously and instantaneously abandon both the mind of pleasure and the mind of suffering; coarse characteristics are extinguished, and the nature of pure merit arises. Thus it is.
One class is named the Puṇyaprasava Heaven;

this is the first heaven of the fourth dhyāna. Furthermore, the preceding section concludes by describing the virtues of the bliss of the third dhyāna, while the following section reveals the faults of suffering in the lower realms.
Below, the "Puṇyaprasava" is properly indicated; for in the first dhyāna, one is free from painful sensations yet still possesses sorrow.
In the second dhyāna, one is free from sorrow and experiences the feeling of joy; in the third dhyāna, one is free from joy and experiences the feeling of bliss.
This deity understands that even this feeling of bliss is not permanent, for bliss, once it has endured for long, must inevitably perish; and when it perishes, it becomes suffering.

Therefore, one simultaneously and suddenly relinquishes both the mind of suffering and the mind of bliss. Once bliss has faded and ceased, there is the concentration of immovability accompanied by equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Because it has been aroused, the inner mind is serene, neither suffering nor joyful; this is called the stage of purity of equanimity and mindfulness (*upekṣā-smṛti-pariśuddhi-bhūmi*).

The *Yogācārabhūmi* states that all calamities of the lower stages have already been severed—namely, applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), suffering (*duḥkha*), joy (*sukha*), mental ease (*saumanasya*), and physical ease (*praśrabdhi*), as well as inhalation and exhalation (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*).
Therefore, within this state, equanimity and mindfulness are pure and bright. Consequently, the mind of this dhyāna abides without movement.

Because of the simultaneous relinquishing of suffering and pleasure, the characteristic of *dausthulya* (coarseness/heaviness) is extinguished; this *dausthulya* refers precisely to the seeds of discrimination within the six consciousnesses.
Because one no longer experiences sublime pleasure, pure merit arises, which is called the "Ground of Merit-Birth" (*puṇyaprasava-bhūmi*).
It is also referred to as the "Dhyāna Conjoined with Equanimity."

Those who possess a perfected mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*), whose resolute understanding (*adhimukti*) is pure, who attain marvelous conformity within unobstructed merit, and who endure until the end of the future—this class of beings is called the Heaven of Merit-Love (*Puṇyaprasava*).
This is the second heaven of the Fourth Dhyāna. While the mind of equanimity first arose previously, it had not yet reached perfection; here, it has attained such a state.

Because not even a single hair’s breadth of a thought of attachment is abandoned, it is called the "perfectly integrated mind of relinquishment. Within this mind of relinquishment, one further gives rise to resolute conviction;
because one definitively accepts, confirms, and maintains this state without being swayed by other conditions, it is called "pure resolute conviction.
Due to the perfect integration of the mind of relinquishment, pure merit likewise encounters no obstruction. Now, [the practitioner] abides in purity.
Merit is unobstructed; because there is nothing one seeks that is not fulfilled as desired, one attains great sovereignty that extends to the end of the future.
To say it "extends to the end of the future" means that through the two paths of merit and love, the reception of retribution is inexhaustible;
it does not mean that one truly attains permanence. As for "merit and love," this refers exclusively to the merit of the various devas.

The Heaven is the most beloved because it is not reached by the three calamities; alternatively, this heaven has accumulated merit such that there is a distinct longing for it, namely the hope for the two higher paths.
Ānanda, from within this heaven there are two diverging paths: if one possesses the merit of the previous mind of immeasurable pure light, [one follows the first].
Those who dwell having cultivated and realized perfect luminosity in this manner are called the gods of the Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala) Heaven.
This is the third heaven of the fourth dhyāna. Regarding these gods of the "Beloved Merit" (Puṇyaprasava), there are two diverging paths:

one is the direct path leading to the Vast Fruit Heaven, and the other is the circuitous path leading to the Unconscious (Āsaṃjñika) state; the former mind refers to those who have perfected the Beloved Merit.
"Melting away the mind" refers to immeasurable purity; "pure light" is the meditative light produced by the dhyāna associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Regarding "abiding in the realization and cultivation of perfected merit": because the ethical discipline (*śīla*) of the first dhyāna is superior, and both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) of the second and third dhyānas are superior, this pure virtue is perfectly luminous.
Upon reaching the fourth dhyāna, it is entirely a reward of merit; thus, this pure merit is perfected.

Because they are luminous, they proceed from the Heaven of Love and Merit (*Puṇyaprasava*) through the immeasurable light to cultivate the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), thereby increasing their merit and realizing the vast fruit;

thus they are named the Heaven of Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*). Among the various heavens of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), the meritorious retribution experienced reaches its ultimate limit here, for these three heavens alone constitute the objective sphere of the retribution of the fourth dhyāna.
Therefore, the fourth [heaven], the Heaven of Non-conception (*Asaṃjñisattva*), is included within the Heaven of Love and Merit.
The five classes of Non-returning Devas (Anāgāmin) are distinct abodes for noble ones who have attained the third fruit; therefore, it is asked:
since the fourth dhyāna is free from the disturbances of the three calamities, why is it not eternal? The answer is: because it is destroyed by momentary impermanence (kṣaṇika-anityatā).

If one, through a mind of equanimity, feels simultaneous aversion toward both suffering and pleasure, and diligently investigates the continuity of the state of equanimity until it becomes uninterrupted and the path of equanimity is fully realized, such that body and mind both cease and the mental faculties become ashen and still for five hundred kalpas—because this person takes birth-and-death as their cause, they cannot give rise to the nature of non-birth-and-death;
thus, for the first half-kalpa there is cessation, and for the latter half-kalpa there is birth. Such is one class of beings.

It is called the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*). This is a distinct branch of the fourth dhyāna. While the former [the Heaven of Merit-Love] also refers to the cultivation of merit and love, the Bṛhatphala [Heaven] cultivates merit and wisdom while becoming weary of suffering and pleasure;
this heaven (the Heaven of No-Thought), however, becomes weary of suffering and pleasure and refines the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*). These are the two heavens.

This is why there is a branching point. The first two phrases follow up on the previous "thorough investigation" (*pravicaya*); the latter three phrases reveal the place where this stage of *dhyāna* exerts its effort.
"Thoroughly investigating the mind of equanimity" means using the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to deeply search and minutely examine that mind of equanimity.
"Continuous and uninterrupted" means that one's practice is without interval or cessation. "Completely exhausting the path of equanimity" means having the resolve to reach its ultimate consummation.

Exhausting this mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*), one perfects the meditative absorption of equanimity through the three stages of body and mind, thereby attaining the retributive fruit (*vipāka*) of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi*).
It is said that by using the absorption of equanimity to eliminate the mind of equanimity, the mental deliberations become ashen and congealed, temporarily ceasing to function;
like a fish trapped in ice or grass pressed under a stone, one is unaware of the subtle flow of arising and ceasing, and falsely claims it to be *nirvāṇa*.
This "nirvāṇa" is not true nirvāṇa. The phrase "passing through five hundred kalpas" refers to great kalpas (*mahākalpa*);
it means that from birth until the end of life, a total of five hundred great kalpas have elapsed.

This person has severed their erroneous practice and failed to attain the true fruit because they take that which is subject to arising and ceasing as their cause, and thus cannot produce a fruit that is free from arising and ceasing. Part One.

Regarding those who attain cessation after half a kalpa: it is said that those born into this heaven practice meditative concentration for half a kalpa before first attaining the perception of cessation;

those born later in the second half of the kalpa will have their perceptions and mind arise again after four hundred and ninety-nine and a half kalpas, once the retribution of this heaven is exhausted.

Question: What is the difference between this "attainment of non-perception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the "attainment of cessation" (*nirodha-samāpatti*)? Answer: As for the attainment of cessation...

Since the sixth consciousness has been extinguished, along with the defiled portion of the seventh consciousness, those in the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) merely extinguish the conceptual views of the six consciousnesses;

yet even these various false views have not yet been exhausted, let alone others. Question: Since both the body and the elements are empty, how does this differ from the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*)?
Answer: They are not the same because [the body] exists once one emerges from meditative absorption. These three realms collectively possess...

Of the thirty-two heavens, two are exclusively the realm of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and five are exclusively the realm of the noble (*ārya*). All others are where ordinary beings and noble ones dwell together.

Regarding those that are exclusively the realm of ordinary beings: this refers to Mahābrahmā, who does not understand the causes of karma and claims, "I alone am able to create all the heavens, earths, people, and things.
Relying on this arrogance, he treats all noble sages with contempt; therefore, [the noble ones] do not dwell there.

They do not dwell in this Heaven of No-Thought; rather, they are merely ordinary beings who, having practiced the meditative attainment of non-conception as externalists, receive for five hundred kalpas the retribution of being without mind. These externalists, failing to realize the truth, falsely take this state to be nirvana.
Once their retribution is exhausted, they inevitably give rise to false views and slander the Arhats; thus, they undergo further existence and fall back into hell.
Even these sages do not abide therein. Fifth, as for the "sage positions," they refer to the five lower *anāgāmins*.
Ānanda, these four superior streams cannot be moved by any worldly states of suffering or pleasure;
although they are not the truly unconditioned stage of immovability (*aniñjya-bhūmi*), because their mental efforts and attainments are fully matured, they are called the "four dhyānas."
This section indicates that the names of the three heavens constitute the fourth dhyāna. Because both suffering and pleasure have perished, the mental formations are unmoving;
this eighth stage of the noble ones, which realizes true unconditionedness (*asaṃskṛta*), is named the "Immovable Ground" (*Acalā-bhūmi*).

However, because the sixth [consciousness] is extinguished and the seventh is exhausted, this immovability involves something to be attained and is therefore not true unconditionedness, as it merely serves to suppress the six consciousnesses.
Thus, the boundaries between the noble ones and ordinary beings are clearly demarcated and do not overlap. Above this, in the dhyāna heavens:
in the first dhyāna, the two consciousnesses of nose and tongue are suppressed because there is no solid food; in the second dhyāna, the first five consciousnesses are suppressed;

in the third dhyāna, the manifest activity of the mental consciousness’s discrimination is suppressed, whereby one attains sublime bliss; and in the fourth dhyāna, the seeds of the mental consciousness’s discrimination are suppressed, whereby one attains equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The mind merely subdues the sixth consciousness’s afflictions of discursive view; thus,
Mencius’s "immovability at forty" and Zhuangzi’s "immovability regarding life and death," when compared to the immovability of the Dhyāna heavens, are as different as heaven and abyss—
how much more so when one seeks to pilfer and imitate the essence of the Tathāgata’s true samādhi of immovability!
Ānanda, herein there are furthermore five types of non-returners (anāgāmin) whose nine grades of habitual tendencies (vāsanā) in the lower realm are extinguished simultaneously,

wherein suffering and pleasure both cease, and because they no longer have a dwelling place below, they establish their residence within the homogeneous class (nikāya-sabhāga) of the mind of equanimity (upekṣā-citta).

This clarifies that the five types of non-returner heavens (*anāgāmin*) are the specific retributions of this celestial realm. As for the term "non-returner," it refers to the third fruit of the path;
because one has completely severed the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara-kleśa*), one will no longer undergo rebirth in the desire realm.
Regarding "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*), these are the seeds of the afflictions of thought—namely, greed, hatred, delusion, and pride—which arise spontaneously and subtly.

Because these delusions are difficult to eliminate, they are divided into eighty-one grades for their severance. Specifically, the three realms are divided into nine stages (*bhūmi*), each stage being further divided into nine grades.
Now, by severing the nine grades of one stage—the Desire Realm—suffering perishes and the Desire Realm no longer has a place to dwell.
Furthermore, by severing the nine grades of each of the [upper] three stages, bliss perishes and the Form Realm [is likewise abandoned].
In the third dhyāna there is no place to dwell, as only the fourth dhyāna constitutes its homogeneous sphere; therefore, one dwells here alone.
Ānanda, when both suffering and pleasure have perished and the conflicting minds no longer interact, such a class of beings is called the Heaven Free from Affliction (Avṛha).
This is called the first of the five non-returner heavens (*anāgāmin*). When suffering and pleasure have not yet ceased, the two minds of delight and aversion battle within the breast;
therefore, there is agitation and vexation. Now that both have ceased, the mind no longer engages in conflict and gradually enters a state of detachment;
thus, there is no vexation or agitation. This heaven resembles the stage of the bliss born of seclusion from the nine successive stages of concentration.
Contemplating the afflictions of the realm of form:
when the "trigger" (ji) moves alone and the "bolt" (kuo) is withdrawn so that there is no ground for further engagement, such a class of beings is called the Heaven Free from Heat (Atapa).

This is the second heaven of the Non-returners (Anāgāmin). "Trigger" refers to the arousal [of mental activity], and "bolt" refers to its withdrawal and containment; this describes the state of the mind.
Whether arising or ceasing, there is no attachment to suffering or pleasure; because one always acts in solitude, it is called "the trigger-mechanism acting alone.
Previously, although the fighting mind did not engage [with others], there was still a ground for engagement. Now, even that ground of engagement has been thoroughly refined away.
Thus, the mind is like a crystal pitcher—cool, clear, and transparent; what heat could there be? Heat is a subtle form of agitation. This is the state of Heaven.
Those who have severed the nine grades of afflictions of the stage that gives rise to joy and bliss,

and whose vision of the worlds of the ten directions is wondrous, perfect, and clear, such that no further dust or images appear and all defilements have subsided— this class of beings is called the Sudarśana Heaven (Heaven of Good Vision).

This is the third stage of the Non-returner (Anāgāmin). Since the feverish distress has been eliminated and the inner mind is limpid and translucent, one develops the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Consequently, the scope of vision pervades the realms of the ten directions; because the objects perceived are wondrous at every point of contact, it is called "Wondrous Vision" (*Sudarśana*).

Perfectly clear and tranquil, the "dusty images" are the objective realm and the "sinking dregs" are the afflictions (*kleśa*). This precisely reveals that both mind and object have been forgotten, and thus—
To see all as good is the mark of this heaven, which resembles the stage of wondrous bliss where joy has been severed and abandoned;
it is the nine grades of afflictions of thought that have been refined away until their manifestation is unimpeded. This class of beings is named the Heaven of Good Manifestation (Sudṛśa).
This is the fourth heaven of the Non-returners (*anāgāmin*). "Modeling" refers to the earth; "casting" refers to gold.
Because their divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is already purified, they perceive everything at once upon a single glance; thus, they possess mastery over melting and refining.

Just as objects are cast by a smith or a potter according to their will and are accomplished without further obstruction, this realm is therefore called Sudarśana (Good Appearance). It is so named because that which is seen and manifested arises from the mind's engagement.

It is not yet entirely perfected because, although the mind does not struggle, all that is seen and manifested is thoroughly excellent; thus it is called "Excellent Vision" (*sudarśana*) and "Excellent Manifestation" (*sudarśanīya*).
This resembles the ninth grade of the delusions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) on the stage of pure mindfulness and equanimity (*smṛti-upekṣā-pariśuddhi-bhūmi*), which has been severed and abandoned.

Having ultimately exhausted the subtlest particles (*paramāṇu*) and thoroughly investigated the nature of form (*rūpa-dharmatā*) until entering the boundless limit—this class of beings is called the Heaven of Ultimate Form (*Akaniṣṭha*).

This is the fifth heaven of the Non-returners (*anāgāmin*). "Ultimate" (*akaniṣṭha*) means to have thoroughly investigated and exhausted; "particles" (*aṇu*) refers to the minute. It is said that they have exhausted form...
As for the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), it is not merely that one exhausts the limits of form down to the ultimate atom;
one can further exhaust the nature of form’s nature. From where does it arise? Thus one knows that the nature of form is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true form;
they are pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. Therefore it is said: "Entering the boundless. Only by investigating in this manner will one finally understand.

The ultimate limit of form is called Akaniṣṭha (the Ultimate Form). This heaven resembles the severance of the thirty-six grades of afflictions associated with thought within the four stages of the four formless realms.
It is called the ultimate limit of form because it is the final exhaustion of form, as all four formless realms are ultimately free from form.
Ānanda, as for those gods of the Non-returners and the various Heavenly Kings of the four stages of the fourth dhyāna, they can only hear of them with admiration but cannot know or see them.
It is just as in this world, where vast wildernesses, deep mountains, and sites of the sacred path are all maintained by Arhats;
therefore, they cannot be seen by the coarse people of the world.
This passage indicates that the five heavens are exclusively the abodes of noble ones (*ārya*).

To be born in those heavens, one must essentially be a practitioner progressing toward the stage of *anāgāmin* (non-returner) who has attained the four dhyānas, developed untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), and produced the karma of perfumed dhyāna (*vāsita-dhyāna-karma*)—either by producing even a single grade up to nine grades of such karma—only then can one be born there.
Because ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) lack this karma of perfumed dhyāna, they cannot be born in those various heavens.

The following passage clarifies that not only do gods and humans fail to see these four heavens, but even the Four Great Heavenly Kings merely revere their names without knowing their minds or seeing their forms;
this is because the four heavenly kings cultivate mundane, impure meditative concentrations (*sāsrava-vaipākika-dhyāna*),

whereas the five heavens cultivate supramundane, pure meditative concentrations (*anāsrava-ārya-samādhi*), and thus the mundane and the supramundane do not reach one another— just as it is with the Four Great Heavenly Kings.
If even blind men and the deaf are thus, how much more so the devas and humans? Formerly, Yunju Deng built a hermitage at Sanfeng and did not go to the hall for ten days.
Dongshan asked him, "What have you been doing lately that you do not go to the hall? He replied, "Every day there are devas and humans bringing offerings.
Dongshan said, "I took you for a man of substance, yet you still hold such a view! That evening, Deng came to see him.

Late in the evening, when Yangshan arrived at the mountain, [Zhaozhou] called out to him, saying, "When you are neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil, what is this? Yangshen returned to his hut and sat in silent meditation.
The devas and humans searched for him for three days; when they could not find him, they ceased [their search].

The four kings' failure to see him and the five heavens likewise not seeing Master Yangshen are just like the case of the devas and humans not seeing him. Now, using the human realm as an analogy, we clarify the Sage.
As for sites for the practice of the Way, such as Tiantai, Emei, and Wutai:

Ānanda, these eighteen heavens are solitary and without mutual intercourse; because they have not yet exhausted the burden of physical form, they are termed the Realm of Form (rūpadhātu). From this point downward, they are likewise called the Realm of Form.
"These fetters belong to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). Gu Shan said: "They act alone without association because they lack sensual desire;

yet because those who have not yet exhausted the burdens of the physical body still possess material substance, everything from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) down to the Brahma Assembly (*brahmakāyika*) is subsumed within the realm of form.
Confucius said: "I have never seen one who loves virtue as much as they love beauty. If it were by way of desire...
If one divides the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) into two, then among those in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are many whose minds are inclined toward desire;
yet those who delight in form (*rūpa*) are utterly non-existent—it should be said that I have never seen anyone who delights in virtue as much as they delight in desire.
Furthermore, Ānanda, from within this limit of form at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there are again two divergent paths.

If one illuminates wisdom through the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*) and the light of wisdom becomes perfectly penetrating, one then transcends the realm of dust to become an Arhat and enter the Bodhisattva vehicle;
such a class of beings is called "Great Arhats who have turned their minds."
This indicates that the Noble One stands alone. Because he ultimately dwells at the summit of the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*), it is called the "Peak of Existence" (*bhavāgra*);

because he borders upon the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it is called the "Limit of Form. Due to the three fruits and the faculties being either sharp or dull, the state of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*) is further divided into two paths.
Those with sharp faculties investigate the nature of form until they penetrate and perceive true emptiness, giving rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) and the light of wisdom.
Those who achieve universal penetration by transcending horizontally into the formless realm and enter the Bodhisattva vehicle are called Great Arhats; if they are of duller faculties,

they likewise exhaust the aggregate of form through the mind of relinquishment, giving rise to the formless realm, gradually severing and realizing [the stages] as they ascend out of the three realms.

If, through a mind of equanimity, one achieves the abandonment of aversion and perceives the body as an obstruction, such that by dissolving this obstruction one enters into emptiness—this class of beings is called the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
This is the first heaven of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); it refers to those who enter meditative absorption by contemplating emptiness and extinguishing the three kinds of form.
The practitioner of the concentration of the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi) becomes weary of form (*rūpa*) as if it were a prison and desires to escape from it;

thus, they cultivate the wisdom of insight (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) to break through form and enter into space—this is called the "sphere of infinite space. The first two phrases refer back to the previous heaven [the Heaven of Infinite Space], where one perceives the body below as an obstruction;
"perceiving the body as an obstruction" means perceiving that having a body constitutes a physical impediment and a lack of mastery. This concludes the explanation.
Regarding those who enter emptiness through obstruction: they cultivate the contemplation of emptiness, thereby extinguishing the body and returning to non-existence. The *Mahāyāna Sūtra* states:

"That is to say, transcending all perceptions of form, extinguishing perceptions of resistance, and not attending to various perceptions, one enters the boundless space and abides in the sphere of infinite space.
The commentary explains: "Transcending all perceptions of form" means transcending visible, resistant forms. To extinguish...
Regarding "the perception of resistance": because the perceptions associated with the consciousnesses of the ear, nose, tongue, and body have ceased, this cessation makes resistant form invisible.

Regarding "not attending to various perceptions": because one does not attend to the perceptions associated with mental consciousness—and since mental consciousness discriminates all phenomena, it is called "various"—this cessation makes the non-resistant invisible.

Regarding the entry of the mental consciousness into infinite space: this means that when the three types of perception of form are extinguished, one immediately enters the principle of emptiness, which is vast and boundless.
Because one grows weary of form and relies upon space, it is called the "Sphere of Infinite Space.

The four heavens below this all fail to realize that the nature of form is true emptiness; they merely labor to dissolve obstructive matter. How could they know that abandoning existence is the way to reach non-existence?

Changshui says that there are two ways of abandoning the mind: first, if one uses the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) to sever delusions and enter emptiness, this is the *sukha-vihārin* Anāgāmin;

second, if one uses the tainted path (*sāsrava-mārga*) in the Heaven of Vast Fruit (*bṛhatphala*) to suppress delusions and enter emptiness, this is the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) or the non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*).
When all obstructions have dissolved, there is neither obstruction nor cessation; therein remains only the ālayavijñāna, together with half of the manas, which is subtle and elusive.
This class of beings is called the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana).

This is the second heaven of the Formless Realm. It is called the "Concentration of the Sphere of Consciousness" (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*) for one who, having abandoned the sphere of space, enters meditative absorption by taking consciousness as the object.

A practitioner who becomes weary of the sphere of infinite space and finds that excessive focus on it leads to distraction and disrupts the concentration abandons space and turns the mind to take consciousness as the object.
When the mind is in correspondence with the dharma of consciousness, it is called the Concentration of the Sphere of Consciousness (Wenling).

It is said: "Once all obstructions have been dissolved, there is 'non-existence' (wu), yet this does not rely on form (rūpa). When even the 'non-existence' of non-obstruction is extinguished, one does not rely on space (ākāśa).
Only the *ālayavijñāna* and the *manas* remain; this is to loathe emptiness and rely upon consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The *ālaya* is the eighth consciousness, and the *manas* is the seventh consciousness. Why is it that only half a portion of the *manas* remains?"

The subtle [attainment] functions by transforming the manas; its efficacy lies in the sixth [consciousness], because once the sixth has already subdued one portion of the manas, it also subdues one portion of the innate (*sahaja*) active manas. Thus, the Mahāyāna Sūtra says:
"Transcending all spheres of infinite space, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness. This is the explanation.
It is said: Because the mind takes internal consciousness as its object and forms infinite modes of activity, it is so named.
First, one transcends the sphere of infinite space; this is the departure from hindrances. What is it that is hindered? It is external mindfulness, which is coarse. How is it counteracted?
By seeing the faults of coarse conceptualization in that external mindfulness, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness. This is the benefit of the practice. Question:

Question: How is it known that the *manas*, the *ālaya*, Arhats, and ordinary outsiders have not yet realized [the truth], while the *anāgāmin* has? Answer: This is because the Buddha’s eye perceives them directly and bestows these names accordingly;
it is not granted that they themselves possess such knowledge. In their own view, they indeed consider themselves to have transcended form and transcended emptiness, which is the true nature;

yet they remain deluded, being essentially no different from those in the state of non-conceptualization. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says of sentient beings: [they are like those who... (The text implies they are like those who mistake a dream for reality).
Abiding in various stages, only the Tathāgata knows them as they truly are.
When both emptiness and form have vanished and the conscious mind is utterly extinguished, the ten directions are silent and there is nowhere to go;
such a state is called the Sphere of Nothingness.

This is the third heaven of the formless realm. If one abandons the mind of the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*) and enters meditative absorption by relying on the dharma of nothingness (*akiṃcanya*), it is called the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*).

The practitioner, becoming weary of consciousness—the consciousness of the three periods of time—because its objects are boundless and manifold and thus lead to distraction, abandons the object of consciousness and turns the mind to rely on the dharma of nothingness; this is called "nothingness."

Regarding the statement that "in some places, the first phrase of the fixed [state] refers to the preceding mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and that which is called 'total cessation' refers to the manas of the former half-period":

this means that by relying on profound meditative power (*samādhi-bala*), its active manifestation (*pravṛtti*) is suppressed so that it does not function. This is, for example, like the suppression of the six active manifestations in the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*);
it does not mean that both the seeds and the manifestations are severed as they are in the case of an Arhat. "Utterly non-existent" refers to cessation.
The realm realized within the meditative concentration of consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) is precisely that which involves wearying of consciousness and returning to non-existence.

That which is called the "profound and obscure place" or the "region of dimness and silence" is what non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) cling to as the "Primal Truth" (*avidyā*), and what Laozi and Zhuangzi call the "Mysteriously Formed" (*hun-cheng*);
it all resides herein. As the Great Sutra says: "Arising from the station of infinite consciousness, one enters the station of nothingness."
Regarding the "Sphere of Nothingness" (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), the commentary states that it is the absence of both internal and external [objects].

"Transcending the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness" clarifies the departure from hindrances. Why must one transcend? Because objective phenomena and mental recollections are coarse. How is this countered?
By perceiving the faults of coarse recollection and the discrimination of phenomena. Entering the Sphere of Nothingness clarifies the benefits of cultivation. Previously, through equanimity...
Because external conditions are internalized, they become coarse thoughts; since there is nothing grasped, the grasper also does not exist.
Thus, when both internal and external are absent, this is called "benefit," which is termed "non-existence."
The nature of consciousness is immovable; by investigating through cessation until reaching the inexhaustible, one proclaims the nature of exhaustion within that which is inexhaustible.
It is as if existing yet not existing, as if exhausted yet not exhausted. This class of beings is called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.

This is the fourth heaven of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). It is called the "attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samāpatti*) because one enters meditative absorption by abandoning the two extremes of perception.
Practitioners become weary of the perception of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), regarding it as delusion, while regarding the sphere of perception (*saṃjñāyatana*) as a boil or a sore.
There is another concentration called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception," which involves abandoning even the sphere of nothingness.

The state of meditative concentration in which one dwells upon the object of mindfulness as a phenomenon that is neither with perception nor without perception is called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
Previously, the seventh manas was taken as the consciousness-mind; here, the eighth is taken as the nature of consciousness. For those who exhaustively investigate through cessation:
since the previous heaven already suppressed the manas by means of the power of concentration, this heaven further applies effort to investigate and penetrate it.
If one desires to extinguish the nature of consciousness, one fails to realize that without the diamond-like wisdom (*vajra-jñāna*), it cannot be extinguished.
This lies in a state where it cannot be exhausted; yet one claims it has been extinguished. In reality, it is as if it exists but does not exist, and as if it is exhausted but not exhausted.
If one considers it to exist but not yet exhausted, then the nature of consciousness remains unmoving; if one considers it not to exist...
Yet, even within that [attainment], there remains something to be extinguished and thoroughly investigated; therefore, the Great Sūtra says:
"Transcending the sphere of nothingness, one dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. The commentary explains:

"Transcending the sphere of nothingness" refers to that which is to be abandoned as an obstacle. How is it countered? Because one perceives the faults of its coarse aspects, namely, the absence of that "nothingness."
Question: Since the antidote has already been stilled and is non-existent, why is it called "coarse"? It is because there still remains the perception of non-existence (*akiṃcanyasaṃjñā*).
As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "First, one enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and transcends all perceptions of existence;
now, one further transcends the perception of non-existence. Some say: since it is called "neither-perception" (*naivasaṃjñā*), it is also called "neither-non-perception" (*naivāsaṃjñā*).

This is not like the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi*) or the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), where all conceptualizations (*saṃjñā*) have been entirely extinguished, and only a subtle conceptualization remains, functioning by taking the object of non-conception as its sphere.

Therefore, the reason one does not transcend the three realms (*tridhātu*) therein is that, because it takes the object of non-conception as its sphere—which is itself a subtle conceptualization—non-Buddhists fail to understand it and mistake it for *nirvāṇa*; they are thus unable [to attain liberation].

How could that which lacks an object be divorced from mind and mental objects? Moreover, if one reckons this as "self" and further gives rise to attachment for its flavor, one must recognize this affliction and seek further advancement.
Seeking a superior object of focus, one ultimately finds nothing to be obtained. Because nothing is obtained, it ceases and does not revolve;

thus, one attains the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodha-samāpatti*). If one has not yet attained this absorption, one should cultivate aversion toward perception and first contemplate perception.
If one does not practice [the path], one enters the state of non-conceptual absorption (asaṃjñi-samāpatti). This is another major critical juncture between the noble ones and ordinary beings.

Among those who exhaustively pursue emptiness but do not fully realize the principle of emptiness—such as those who have reached the end of the path through the noble way in the Heaven of Non-Retreat (anāgāmin)—this class is called the "dull-witted Arhats who do not turn their minds.
If, however, they exhaustively pursue emptiness from the perspective of the various non-Buddhist heavens of non-conceptualization and do not return [to the human realm], [they remain there].
Deluded, leaking, and lacking learning, they enter the cycle of transmigration.

This passage generally clarifies the ground from which the noble and the ordinary emerge or fall. The phrase "these [beings]" collectively refers to the humans of the four heavens mentioned previously:
the first heaven exhausts form and returns to emptiness; the next heaven exhausts emptiness and returns to consciousness; the third heaven exhausts consciousness...
The mind returns to non-existence, and the four elements exhaust their cognitive nature until it reaches its end.

When one has thus exhausted emptiness in this way, how could they possibly comprehend the principle that the essence of form is true emptiness—the core teaching of the Perfect and Sudden? Furthermore, they fail to understand the principles of the two kinds of emptiness: the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena.
Thus, they falsely desire to give rise to a mind to dissolve, negate, extinguish, or exhaust [phenomena]. How could they know that in the end, they will never succeed?

It means to dissolve into emptiness and reach total extinction. Therefore, those who enter this heaven from the Five Non-Returner Heavens by exhausting emptiness still possess a fundamentally correct root;
they await the completion of eighty thousand kalpas to sever all afflictions of thought and exit the triple world.

Such individuals are called Arhats of dull faculties, for they are contrasted with those from the Peak of Existence (*Bhavāgra*) who have turned their minds [toward liberation], and thus they are termed "dull. If...
Is the fundamental origin of those who enter this heaven from the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñika*) and exhaust emptiness such?

Because they deludedly mistake this contaminated (*sāsrava*) heaven for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), once their retribution for eighty thousand kalpas is exhausted, they have no place of refuge and thus fall into ruin.
One asks: The sutras state that those in the state of non-conceptualization slander the Buddha at the time of death and fall into hell; how then can they enter [this heaven]?
While it may be that there are occasionally those who possess non-perception, how could it be that all the gods of the Heaven of Non-perception (asaṃjñisattva) are like this?

The World-Honored One cited one case merely to admonish the multitude. For instance, during the time when the Buddha was in the world, there was a bhikṣu who attained the fourth dhyāna and gave rise to overweening pride (adhimāna), claiming he had attained arhatship and no longer sought further progress. As his life was about to end, he perceived within the fourth dhyāna...
When the signs of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arise, one immediately gives rise to false views, thinking, "There is no nirvana; the Buddha has deceived me.

Because such evil and perverse views arise, one loses the intermediate state of the fourth *dhyāna* and perceives the signs of the intermediate state of the Avīci Hell. Upon the end of that life, one falls directly into the Avīci Hell.
These cases are like those of practitioners who sit in meditation and maintain the precepts, yet because of a single moment of deluded realization, they sink into the sea of suffering.
Now, if practitioners of meditation consider a small attainment to be sufficient and allow their minds to run wild with deluded thoughts, what will their retribution be?
Since the Sages have clear instructions on this, how could one not be struck with trepidation and reflect upon oneself?
Ānanda, those various devas among the heavens are all ordinary beings for whom the fruits of their karma have been requited;

once that retribution is exhausted, they will enter the cycle of rebirth. Those celestial kings, however, are bodhisattvas who, while traversing samādhi, gradually advance along the path of practice dedicated toward the ranks of the sages.
This generally concludes the distinct categories of the devas and humans of the three realms, as well as the ordinary and the noble. "Devas and humans" refers to the subjects of heaven;

they are comprised within the category of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Regarding "the retribution of karma, answers, and so forth," this means that because one cultivated the ten wholesome paths and the eight meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) during the causal stage, one receives retribution in the form of the six heavens of desire and the four *dhyānas*; thus, when the retribution is exhausted, one enters the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*). The Heavenly King is none other than a Bodhisattva.
Regarding "Bodhisattvas and others," as explained in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: the first bhūmi is that of the King of Jambudvīpa; the second bhūmi is that of the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin);
the third bhūmi is that of the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; the fourth bhūmi is that of the King of the Yāma Heaven; and so on, up to the tenth bhūmi, which is that of the King of Maheśvara.
These are all positions in which Bodhisattvas entrust themselves for progressive cultivation, yet they do not fall into saṃsāra.
Furthermore, this section should appear below the discussion on the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Ānanda, in these four heavens of emptiness (*ākāśānantyāyatana*, etc.), the body and mind are extinguished, and the nature of stability manifests; from this point until the end, there is no form resulting from karmic fruit, and thus it is called the Formless Realm.
