This fetter belongs to the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*). In the first two heavens of that realm, both physical form and space are absent; thus, there is the extinction of the body.

In the latter two heavens, the manifest activity of consciousness is suppressed; thus, there is the extinction of the mind. Because both body and mind have ceased, the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) manifests before one.

As for the absence of "form as karmic fruit" (*vipākaja-rūpa*), it does not refer to the sense-faculties or the physical environment produced by the retribution of karma, as found in the desire and form realms.

Because these realms possess superior meditative concentration, they enjoy mastery over the transformation of both the environment and its inhabitants; this refers to what is known as "matter produced by concentration" (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*).
From the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception down to the Sphere of Infinite Space, these are collectively termed the Formless Realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*).

All these arise from failing to understand the wondrously enlightened, luminous mind; through the accumulation of delusions, the three realms of existence falsely manifest, and within them, sentient beings (*pudgala*) sink and drown according to the seven destinies, each following their own kind.
This is a summary of the three realms. This term encompasses all six heavens of the desire realm up to the Heaven of Neither Thought nor Non-Thought;

for all beings therein fail to realize the wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind inherently present within them. Through accumulating delusion upon delusion, they falsely give rise to the three realms.
Consequently, when the karmic retributions of gods and humans are exhausted, they cannot avoid sinking again into the seven destinies during the interim, finding no rest.
*Pudgala* (補持伽羅) is translated here as "one who repeatedly takes birth" (*saṃsārin*), referring specifically to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Because it is able to repeatedly undergo birth and take up various realms of existence (*gati*), the World-Honored One once asked the bhikṣus, using soil on a fingernail as an analogy:

"Is the soil on my fingernail more, or is the soil upon the earth more? The bhikṣus replied, "The soil upon the earth is far more; it cannot be compared [to the soil on the nail]. The Buddha said: [This is so].
To say that those who pass away from the heavens are reborn among humans is like the soil on a fingernail falling to the ground, whereas those who fall into hell are like the soil upon the earth.

Why is this? Because they originally resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, or because they accumulated various merits within meditative concentration, they are able to be reborn among humans and hear the Buddha-dharma; thus we know that their pure karma has reached full maturity.

Beholding the celestial palaces with one’s own eyes, yet seeing hell manifest before the mind as evil karma is about to be completed—just as a person of merit takes pebbles and turns them into gold, while a person of poor karma transforms gold into pebbles. Pebbles are not gold, yet gold appears;
gold is not pebbles, yet pebbles arise. That gold arises is merely the mind arising; that pebbles appear likewise manifests from the mind. Transformation lies within me.
How could gold among gravel arise? Those who harbor doubts may now understand this principle.
Furthermore, Ānanda, within the three realms there are four types of asuras:

those who, belonging to the realm of hungry ghosts, enter the air by means of supernatural power through the protection of the Dharma; these asuras are born from eggs and are categorized within the destiny of hungry ghosts.

If among the devas they descend through a loss of merit and are cast down so that their dwelling is adjacent to the sun and moon—these asuras are born from a womb and are categorized within the human realm.

There are asura kings who uphold the world, whose power is profound and fearless, and who can contend for authority with Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings; these asuras arise through transformation.
Ānanda, there is a distinct class of inferior asuras included within the celestial realm who dwell in the depths of the great ocean and sink into the mouths of underwater caverns;
they roam through the void by day and return to their watery abodes at night. These asuras, due to their moisture-based existence, are categorized within the realm of animals.
This clarifies the four types of asuras. In Sanskrit, *asura* is translated here as "non-deva" (fei-tian), meaning that although they possess celestial fortune, they lack celestial conduct;
hence they are also called "the ill-formed," because while the husbands are ugly, the wives are beautiful.

They are also called "those without wine," because their anger prevents the harmonious atmosphere necessary for brewing, so that wine cannot be produced. Thus, they are said to belong to the realm of ghosts (*preta*).

This indicates that his prior cause was the generation of the aspiration for enlightenment while in the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). Such as guarding the precepts, guarding meditative concentration, guarding the sutras, and guarding mantras—all these are termed "guarding the Dharma" (*dharmarakṣā*).
This means that by relying on the power of guarding the Dharma while in the realm of hungry ghosts, he was born into this destination;
those who are able to ride upon supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to dwell within the empty realm are, in terms of their present fruit, egg-born (*aṇḍaja*), because they emerge from an egg.

Because they arise from perception, they are categorized according to their cause; or perhaps they are yakṣas who personally resided beneath the Tathāgata’s seat and were subsequently reborn there, and thus should be subsumed under the realm of hungry ghosts (preta). As for the phrase "among the devas," this refers to their prior causes.

"Declining virtue" means that while in the deva realms, their merit was diminished and they were demoted as punishment. "Dwelling adjacent to the sun and moon" means that they do not depart from them.

Humans are indeed born from the womb and are included within the human realm (*manuṣya-gati*). Those who "sustain the world" are said to be able to command spirits and deities, bringing about both calamity and fortune;
those whose power is "penetrating and fearless" are so called because their strength pervades both the human and celestial realms, such that their minds are free from dread.
The Sūtra describes their transformation body as being sixteen thousand eight hundred *yojanas* in height.
When he shook Mount Sumeru with his hand, the various devas were struck with terror; Śakra and the Four Heavenly Kings were constantly engaged in battle with him.
Now, it is said that even the Brahmā King contends [with him]; perhaps this means that if Śakra is not victorious, those from the Brahmā realm downward all lend their assistance.
If they still cannot prevail by force, he hides himself within the hollow of a lotus fiber—knowing that he can contract or expand at will—is proof of this.

The power of those born by transformation is equal to that of the devas; as they are included within the realm of the gods (*deva-gati*) and are the most preeminent among the four types [of *asuras*], they are called "kings.
Specifically, this refers to Rāhu, the King of the Asuras. Regarding the phrase "born from the water-mouth at the heart of the ocean":
the Sūtra calls him Vemacitra, the King of the Asuras—this is translated as "Resounding Height"—and he is also known as the "Cave-Dweller."
Emerging from the depths of the great ocean, he utters a great sound, proclaiming: "I am Vemacitra, dwelling in a sea-cave.
Because he causes waves to rise from the ocean waters and emits this sound, one might suspect him to be a *nāga*.

However, because he dwells at the bottom of the water and is of inferior nature, he is categorized among the animals (*tiryagyoni*). The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states that the food and clothing of the asuras are produced spontaneously.
Their crowns, sashes, and garments are made entirely of the seven treasures and are as fresh and pure as those consumed by the gods.
Food and drink appear according to their thoughts, all possessing a hundred flavors; yet whenever they eat, the very last mouthful transforms into green mud.
Therefore, the Sūtra says that they are not equal to humans.

Ānanda, in this way—the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, seers and immortals, devas, and asuras—when you minutely examine these seven realms, they are all states of delusion, the characteristics of conditioned existence.
One undergoes birth through false conceptualization and follows karma through false conceptualization.

Within the wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind that is fundamentally unconditioned, these are all like flowers in the sky, originally having no place of attachment; they are but a single void delusion, and nothing more.

Prologue: This concludes the summary of delusion. It states that upon meticulous investigation, the causes of the seven realms of existence are entirely the two kinds of delusive thoughts—arousing and moistening—which serve as the causes for afflictions and karma;
thus, one undergoes birth in accordance with these delusive thoughts, and it is because of these delusive thoughts that [birth occurs].

As for receiving retribution: if one, within the perfectly luminous and effortless fundamental mind, illuminates these delusions and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), they are seen to be exactly like flowers in the sky, having no place of attachment or falling;
they are merely a uniform unreality, devoid of any root or causal sequence from which they arise. Therefore, the *Zongjing* asks: "This is the gate of the equality of emptiness."

If the wondrous principle of the One Mind is such that good and evil have no boundary and both ordinary beings and sages are equally perfect, why is it that there are differences in what is received as nourishment and inequality in suffering and joy?
Answer: Ten thousand matters are created by oneself; the single principle of the Mind alone is without deficiency.
Good and evil arise solely from one's own thoughts; how could retribution be obtained from another? Thus, Xi Shi loved the Yangtze River while the ugly Mu-mu detested it.
The mirror is, in truth, ignorance; thus one knows that this mind is the abode of both ordinary beings and sages, and the source of both objects and the perceiving faculty.

It is only because ordinary beings cling to it as the *ālayavijñāna* that it becomes the cause of the suffering of birth and death. When the sage realizes it as the *ālaya-citta*, they receive the fruit of the eternal bliss of *nirvāṇa*.
If one speaks of it as the *ālayavijñāna*, it has a name but no substance, for it is merely a conceptual construct based on emotional attachment.

Because clinging to it as existing is not ultimate, its name is abandoned at the moment of realization. If one speaks of the "storehouse mind" (*ālaya-citta*), however, it possesses both name and substance;
because it is innately present and is not a product of deluded attachment, its name will not be severed until the end of the future.
Yet, if one is oblivious in every thought-moment to the nature of the Tathāgata’s *dharmadhātu*, one will, step by step, create the karmic fruits of a sentient being.

Due to these causes, evil karma increases daily and the conditions for suffering are inexhaustible; one gives rise to a mind of decay and affliction toward places of peace and security, and within liberation, one produces the fruit of bondage.
One receives a body with a flaming mouth and a needle-like throat, burned by the fires of hunger for kalpas;
one takes on a body of fur-covered beasts with horns, where every touch is entangled in nets and snares; or one falls into the... [unfortunate realms].

Some dwell in the intermediate hells, enduring intense suffering while remaining for long periods within the wheels of fire; others are born in the palaces of the asuras, where they constantly rain down swords and blades in their struggles;
some temporarily reside in the human realm, where in a mere instant they are tormented by the eight sufferings;
and some occasionally inhabit the celestial palaces, where in a flash the five signs of decay appear—all because they fail to realize the Tathāgatagarbha mind and have thus lost it.

The wondrous nature of Consciousness-Only has turned its back on the True Compassionate Father; it takes labor as a hired hand in foreign lands, abandoning the Great Wisdom King to seek refuge in other kingdoms.
For this reason, the Buddhas were startled and entered the burning house, and the Patriarchs came from the West specifically to point toward the True Home.

Yet they did not go there, and they showed the Right View while not allowing it to be seen; all of this is because the seeds have been perfumed in the *ālayavijñāna* since beginningless time, resulting in stubborn and firm attachments.
Its sentiment is profound, like ten thousand layers of icy cliffs; its roots seem deep, like a thousand-fold dark chamber.

Now, in broad illumination of the profound and abstruse, it directly reveals the One Mind. It may be said that the celestial nature has been realized at this very moment, with no other kind remaining;
the father-and-son relationship is settled today, as there is but one family style. All who possess knowledge should naturally investigate this deeply.
Ānanda, these sentient beings do not recognize their original mind and undergo this cycle of rebirth for immeasurable kalpas without attaining true purity;

all this is due to their compliance with killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. If they turn away from these three, there arise those who are called ghosts and spirits, and those who are called devas.
As existence and non-existence contend with one another, the nature of saṃsāra arises. If they attain...
One who has wondrously given rise to samādhi is wondrously and eternally quiescent; both existence and non-existence are absent, and even non-duality is extinguished.
Since there is not even the [conceptual] non-killing, non-stealing, and non-lustfulness, how could one further follow after the acts of killing, stealing, and lust?

This means that while one is deluded, these states falsely appear to exist, but after awakening, they are fundamentally non-existent. The "original mind" refers precisely to the wondrous, perfect, bright, and unconditioned original mind.
It is said that all sentient beings in these seven realms of existence undergo this cycle of rebirth because they fail to recognize their original mind;
though they pass through many kalpas, they do not attain true purity, but instead constantly dwell in delusive defilement due to following along with [delusion].

Because of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, the three unwholesome [paths] are formed; conversely, by refraining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, the three wholesome [paths] are formed.
When the three unwholesome paths exist, one falls downward into the three miserable realms; when the three unwholesome paths do not exist, one ascends upward to the celestial realms.
Because the presence and absence of these wholesome and unwholesome states mutually oppose and displace one another, ascent and descent likewise revolve without end. Thus it is said.
Both good and evil belong to saṃsāra; one must necessarily give rise to this wondrous samādhi-mind that is neither good nor evil, for then it is wondrous, eternal, and quiescent.

If one enters this samādhi, the two paths of good and evil and the two fruits of ascent and descent will be extinguished at once, and one will realize the emptiness of persons and transcend the three realms. Therefore it is said:
The two extremes of existence and non-existence are both absent; not only do the two natures of good and evil vanish at that moment, but even the nature of non-duality cannot be apprehended.
Therefore it is said, "Non-duality is also extinguished. This not only transcends birth and death, but further transcends the *nirvāṇa* of the Lesser Vehicle.
Since even non-duality does not exist, how could one follow after duality? Thus it is called "As It Is" (*tathatā*).
Since one has not yet seen the state of non-killing, non-stealing, and non-lust, how could one further follow after the acts of killing, stealing, and lust?

Ānanda, if the three karmas are not severed, each has its own private cause; because of these individual privacies, there is a collective affinity among these privacies—it is not that they do not exist.
The locus of concentration arises from one's own delusions; this arising of delusion is without cause and cannot be traced to its origin.

You must exhort yourself in practice: if you wish to attain Bodhi, you must eliminate the three delusions. If you do not exhaust these three delusions, even if you should acquire supernatural powers, they will all be mundane, conditioned functions.
If habitual tendencies are not eliminated, you will fall into the path of Māra. Though you wish to eliminate delusion, you will instead increase your falsehoods. Thus it is, O Tathāgata.
To say that one who is worthy of compassion has falsely created for themselves the fault of non-enlightenment—this is called the correct teaching;
if anyone else were to say this, it would be the teaching of Māra.
This concludes the response to the question and exhorts one toward authentic cultivation. The previous question asked:
"Is there a fixed location, or does it arise spontaneously, such that each person creates their own karma and each receives their own retribution? In response, it was restated:

"Because these three kinds of good and evil karma are not severed, each person privately creates their own causes; because each privately creates them, they exist within the collective of private karmas."

Within the realm of commonality (*sabhāgatā*), it is not that there is no fixed location; however, while it is said that one receives retribution privately for the karma one has created, such a fixed location does indeed exist.
Yet, from where does this fixed location originate? It is fundamentally what is summoned and evoked by one's own delusion.
Since that which is produced is illusory and truly lacks a cause, its point of origin cannot be investigated. Exert yourself with diligence!

Furthermore, the three delusions are the very root of the three evil and three good karmas. Since the three karmas arise rooted in these delusions, one must directly point to their source and cause them to be severed.
If one does not sever the root of the delusions, even if one attains the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), they are all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and not the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).

This is because one has merely suppressed the active manifestations while the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) have not been eliminated; thus, the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) cannot be attained.
One will inevitably fall into the path of Māra; though one wishes to eliminate delusion, it is like using fire to extinguish fire, which only increases the problem.

This is what the Tathāgata deeply pities and takes great compassion for. Because Ānanda initially asked, "What is the true nature of the Buddha-body, and why are there still the various realms of existence?
the Buddha replied: "These are created by your own delusions; it is not the fault of the Buddha-body."

"Ti" is the very essence of the Buddha; therefore, he further warns: "If, in the final age, one exhorts others to abandon these three kinds [of phenomena], such a person is speaking as the Buddha speaks.
If, in the final age, one praises these three kinds as being unimpeded, such a person is speaking as Māra speaks.
Thus, it is only by severing the three delusions that one can enter the true Threefold Truth.
The *samādhi* section above concludes the detailed explanation of the seven destinies; below follows the detailed discernment of the realms of Māra.

At that moment, as the Tathāgata was about to conclude his session upon the lion throne, he took up a seven-jeweled desk from the Purple Gold Mountain, returned to lean against it, and addressed the great assembly and Ānanda, saying: "You who are still in training—the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas—"
Today you have turned your mind toward great bodhi and unsurpassed, wondrous enlightenment; I have now explained the methods for true practice, yet you still do not recognize them.
When the subtle demonic activities and demonic realms of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* manifest before you, you will fail to recognize them.
Your mind will be cleansed of what is not correct, and you will fall into false views—whether it be the *skandha-māra* or the *deva-māra*.

Some are possessed by ghosts and spirits, or encounter *chimei* (goblins), their minds clouded such that they mistake the thief for their own son; furthermore, some achieve a small measure of progress and consider it sufficient.
Like the bhikṣu in the fourth dhyāna who, being ignorant, falsely claimed to have realized the state of an *arhat*, his celestial retribution ended and signs of decay appeared before him;
he slandered the *arhats* and, undergoing further existence, fell into the Avīci Hell. You should listen attentively.

I shall now, for your sake, provide a detailed analysis. Ānanda, arise! Together with those in this assembly who are fellow students, receive it with joy, prostrate yourselves, and listen humbly to my compassionate instruction.
First, I shall clarify why the World-Honored One spoke of his own accord without being questioned; it is because the World-Honored One directly and straightforwardly reveals true practice.
However, Ānanda and the others had not yet personally experienced the journey and were unaware of the hardships and obstacles along the way.
The World-Honored One, being one who had already passed through them, had experienced every peril and difficulty firsthand;

therefore, as he was about to conclude his sitting, he turned back and remained to point out each detail of what they would encounter on the road, so that they might recognize it themselves and prepare for unforeseen circumstances. This is like [the case of] Nanda.
When a son travels far away, his compassionate mother, at the moment of his departure, entrusts him with words to act well along the way;
the Tathāgata’s inexhaustible compassion is likewise. You should understand that these are my earnest instructions regarding Māra.
True practice of the Dharma refers specifically to the single gate of "listening inwardly. Although I have pointed out *śamatha* for you, [the remainder follows].
Within *mātr̥kā*, you have not yet clarified the subtle path of wondrous cultivation; the demonic activities that arise along this path are extremely refined.
Unaware and unperceiving, they suddenly manifest before you, all of them capable of harmonizing with the human mind.

If you do not recognize whether they are deviant or correct, and if there is even a hair’s breadth of deviant thought within your breast that has not been washed away, then [these demons will surely take hold].
Thus, by seizing upon this single hair’s breadth of an opening, they are able to draw you into false views.

What is called the "demon of the aggregates" (skandha-māra) refers to that which first manifests from within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), arising spontaneously rather than coming from without.

The heavenly demons, ghosts, spirits, *chi* and *mei* monsters, all manifest from within the aggregates of sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*). When these demons appear, one must at that very moment...
If you can develop the discerning eye that distinguishes dragons from snakes, you will not be deluded by them;

but if your Dharma-eye is not clear, you will be turned by them, eventually mistaking a thief for your own son and plundering your family treasure until it is exhausted. Both the demons of mind and vision lack external objects;
what is manifested by the *saṃskāra-skandha* and *vijñāna-skandha* is entirely one's own mind. Having attained a small measure of insight, one falls into false views.
This is the fault of being satisfied with what one has attained. To take one example from among those who claim to have "no further hearing":
they cultivate only the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñā*) as their ultimate goal; they take no pleasure in hearing the Dharma and do not know how to practice correctly.

Believing themselves to have realized the Unsurpassed Way, when their retribution is about to end, their conceptual mind arises again and signs of decay appear. They fail to realize that they were never originally enlightened.
The noble ones, having slandered the noble ones and subsequently encountered future existence, fell into hell because they slandered the Dharma;
such is its poison—how can one not stand in awe of it? If you all turn your minds toward Great Bodhi, how could you fail to understand its benefits and harms?
Therefore, I have analyzed this for you in detail; it is not a matter of casual treatment. As for the subsequent passage:
Those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) have already destroyed four of the five aggregates (*skandha*), leaving only the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) undestroyed.

The Buddha told Ānanda and the great assembly: "You should all know that in this world of outflows (*sāsrava*), the twelve classes of beings share the same fundamentally awakened and wondrously luminous essence of mind;

this perfect awareness and the core substance of the mind are no different and no distinct from those of the Buddhas of the ten directions. It is solely due to your own deluded thoughts [that you are thus]."

Delusion regarding principle is the fault; from ignorance and craving, birth arises, and as birth repeatedly occurs, universal delusion ensues. Thus, while the nature of emptiness remains, the transformation of delusion does not cease, and the world-systems come into being.
Consequently, these lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, are not free from outflows; they are all established through the stubborn, deluded false thoughts of sentient beings.
You should know that empty space is born within your own mind, like a fragment of cloud appearing within the vast clarity of the great sky.
How much more so for all worlds that exist within space? If even one person among you awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the worlds of the ten directions will all be dissolved;
how then could the lands existing within space not tremble and shatter?

This statement regarding the cause for the movement of Māra means that the fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*) is perfectly luminous, and there is no duality between the living being and the Buddha.

It is precisely because a single thought of deluded imagination (*vikalpa*) stirs that one becomes confused regarding this essence of the enlightened mind-body, thereby giving rise to faults and transgressions.

Thereupon, the two kinds of ignorance—those that initiate karma and those that nourish rebirth—suddenly arise. Once they have arisen, the essence of enlightenment becomes universally obscured. Thus it is said:

The formation of emptiness refers to what is called "obscured darkness as emptiness. Once one is deluded regarding this, the transformation of delusion continues without ceasing, and thus the world arises;
this is what is meant by "establishing the world based on emptiness. Thus, all the tainted lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, are established upon false imagination.
How could they know that emptiness arises from the Great Awakening, like a speck of cloud in the sky?
The Great Clarity is already subtle and minute; how much more so the worlds established upon it—its extreme subtlety can be known even further.

Moreover, if all people in the world were to ceaselessly give rise to delusions, following sounds and pursuing forms without anyone awakening to the Truth, then the establishment of the world would remain as it is.
However, if even a single person were to awaken to the Truth and return to the Source, then...
If even empty space were ground to powder and the great earth were submerged, how much more so would all the lands that depend upon empty space not be shattered?
Question: From antiquity to the present, there have been no few who have realized the Truth; for what reason, then, do the worlds remain exactly as they were before? Answer:
The world is fundamentally the manifestation of the collective karma of sentient beings. When one person realizes the Truth, it is only that one person’s [karmic burden] that is transformed.
If the world were to perish, and if all the people of the world were to give rise to true awakening, then the entire world would completely perish.
This is because the world arises from delusive thoughts (*vikalpa*); its establishment depends upon these thoughts, and it can only perish once they are exhausted.
Therefore, those whose delusive thoughts are exhausted perceive the world as perishing, while for those whose delusive thoughts are not yet exhausted, the world still persists.
Nevertheless, this is how it is established.
When you practitioners cultivate dhyāna and adorn samādhi, the minds of the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the great Arhats with outflows will be in perfect accord;
at that point, all will be profoundly still and serene, such that even all Māras, ghosts, spirits, and ordinary devas [will be unable to disturb you].
They saw their palaces collapse and crack for no apparent reason, and the great earth tremble and split apart; all creatures of land, water, and air were struck with terror.

Ordinary people, shrouded in darkness, did not perceive these calamities. They had all attained the five supernatural powers, yet they alone lacked the extinction of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) and remained attached to this world of dust and toil.
"How could we allow you to tear this place apart? they cried, and thus the ghosts, spirits, and various heavenly Māras [obstructed him].
"Manes and spirits will all come to harass you during your time in samādhi.
This means that when one moves the demons and causes disorder, one must provide for them with solemnity and defense.

It means that when you practitioners cultivate dhyāna and are precisely at the moment of giving rise to the truth, your essence and flavor accord with those of the sages and worthies; your minds penetrate and merge so completely that they become one.

"Abiding in that place, profoundly still, pure, unmoving, and not mutually disturbing one another. "Māra" refers to the celestial Māras; "ghosts and spirits" refers to all classes of *piśācas* and *bhūtas*;
"ordinary beings in the heavens" refers to those in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*); "those dwelling in water" refers to the spirits of rivers and the spirits of the ocean;
"those dwelling on land" refers to the ghosts and spirits of mountains, forests, lands, streams, and peaks; and "those who fly" [refers to the spirits of birds and other aerial beings].
Those who dwell in the air—such as the Great Powerful Ghost Kings and the flying yakṣas—speak thus:
when a practitioner is precisely at the moment of manifesting the Truth, the great earth trembles with alarm and palaces collapse;

yet among the Māra kings dwelling in water, on land, or in the air, there are none who are not struck with terror, except for the ordinary beings of the lower realms who have not yet [attained realization].
Having attained the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), they were so dazed that they did not perceive the false report of the earthquake; thus, they felt no alarm.

Those Māras, gods, and spirits had all attained the five supernatural powers, yet they had not eliminated their residual habitual outflows (*vāsanā*). Since they were still attached to worldly toil (*saṃsāra*), they were determined not to allow the palace to collapse.
Each relied upon his own abilities, desiring only to destroy meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*); therefore, they all came to cause disturbance.
It is a state of confusion.

Yet, although those various demons may be filled with great rage, within your sublime awakening amidst these defilements, they are like wind blowing against light or a blade cutting through water—they do not touch one another at all.
You are like boiling water, and they are like solid ice; as the warmth gradually approaches, [the ice will surely melt].
They will not last long before they perish; you merely rely on their supernatural power, becoming their guest and thereby allowing them to achieve your ruin and disorder.
This is because the master of the five aggregates within your mind has become deluded, allowing the guests to gain the upper hand.

If you abide in *dhyāna* and awaken without confusion, then those demonic affairs will be powerless against you. When the aggregates dissolve and you enter into clarity, then all those evil spirits will receive only their own dark, obscured energy.
Luminosity can destroy darkness; yet if it were to vanish near its own source, how could it dare remain to disturb meditative concentration?

If you do not attain clear awakening and are deluded by the *skandhas*, then you, Ānanda, will surely become a child of Māra and accomplish the work of a Māra-demon, no different from the lowly Maṭaṅga.
He merely used incantations to break your Buddha-discipline, destroying but a single precept among the eighty thousand practices.

Because the mind is not yet pure, you have not yet sunk into ruin; yet this shall cause your entire body of precious awakening to fall apart, like a high minister’s family suddenly encountering confiscation of their property—tumbling into decay beyond all hope of rescue.
This clarifies that through awakening there is no fault, whereas through delusion one undergoes affliction.
Because that [anger] is a thing within the realm of worldly toil (*kleśa*), while you are one among those of wondrous enlightenment (*samyagbodhi*), even great rage cannot inflict harm upon you.

It is just as when the "wind-sword" blows upon light or cuts through water; it can ultimately never cause the light or the water to move or suffer damage. Not only can it not inflict [harm], [but it is also powerless].
Even though they seek to harm you, you are instead able to transform them; this is like the proximity of boiling water to solid ice—the warm vapor presses upon it, and the ice naturally melts.
Although they rely on their five supernormal powers, they remain outsiders.
It is easier to observe and manage those who come from without; the accomplishment of their ruin does not depend on the guest, but entirely upon the host. If...
If you do not clearly recognize the thief in your own mind as being your son, then the guest will take advantage of the opening to enter, causing chaos and tyranny.

If you, as the host, remain in *dhyāna*, alert and lucid, refusing to accept superficiality, then even though the power of that māra be strong, it will have no way to disturb you. That you cannot be done anything by him is due to you yourself.
Once the yin-qi has been eliminated, one attains the Great Treasury of Radiance;
those who were previously subject to dark qi and dwelling in a realm of stupor and obscurity will find that their dark qi naturally vanishes upon approaching this light—
just as an owl cannot be seen when entering the daylight, or a rākṣasa facing the sun, how could they dare remain long to cause disturbance?

"Is this your meditative concentration? If you allow the five aggregates to dominate your mind such that you lack clear awakening and perceive illusory phenomena, you may give rise to fear or attachment; deluded by these aggregates, you will instead fall into their category.
This would be like transforming a household into a state—this ruin of yourself and your family is also due to you, just as in the case of Mātaṅgī."
That person is weak and inferior; even if they could cast a spell upon you, it would only break a single precept, and the harm would still be minor.

Moreover, since your mind remains pure and has not yet reached the point of drowning, such Māra kings are no comparison for your weakness, and your entire body of precious enlightenment is no comparison for a single precept.
The harm [of violating the precepts] is exceedingly great, comparable to that of a prime minister’s family.

If one suddenly encounters the confiscation of property by the Heavenly King (the Emperor), not only will one lose their office and be dismissed from duty, but one’s very life will not escape execution;
thus, as one falls into ruin day by day through such successive misfortunes, even if one possessed divine power, how could it possibly save them?
Ānanda, you should know that when you sit at the site of enlightenment and eliminate all thoughts, once those thoughts are exhausted, then all states free from thought will be luminously refined;
movement and stillness will not shift it, and recollection and forgetfulness will be as one. You should abide in this state and enter samādhi.
It is like a person with clear vision situated in great darkness: the essential nature is wondrously pure, yet the mind has not yet emitted light. This is what is called:

If the realm of the aggregate of form is as clear as a bright eye, such that the ten directions are opened wide and there is no longer any darkness or obscurity, this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of form.
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of the kalpa. If one examines its origin, one finds that solidified false imagination is its root.

This describes the characteristics of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) from its beginning to its end. Because the appearances of objects differ according to whether they have not yet been destroyed or have already been destroyed, one first clarifies their beginning and end.
There are two types of sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*): the "site of phenomena," such as the eight-cornered altar and so forth;
and the "site of principle," which is the turning back of hearing to focus intently so that the mind does not flow outwardly, thereby dissolving all discursive thoughts.
"Equal" (or "the same") refers to having focused one's attention on the practice of "hearing back" for a long time until all discursive thoughts naturally depart;
this is what the *Awakening of Mahābodhi* (Yuánjué) calls "not giving rise to deluded thoughts at any time. This state of being free from thought is like empty space;
at all times it is alert and unclouded, clearly and constantly aware. Therefore, it is called "the brilliant clarity of freedom from thought," which is then [united with] movement and stillness.
This is the state where there is no interference from the consciousness of recollection or forgetfulness; it is the moment when [mind and object] are perfectly integrated as one.
One should abide in this place of luminous clarity free from thought, and then one may enter the Samādhi of the Perfect Illumination of the Ear-organ.
However, because one is still shrouded by the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and the mind has not yet emitted light, all that is seen before one's eyes is only darkness.
The characteristic of darkness is precisely the nature of *tathatā* (suchness) as it is delimited by the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), like a house;
therefore, it is called the "enclosure of the aggregate of form. This is the state when the aggregate of form has not yet been shattered.

If the light of the mind is allowed to radiate forth so that all obstructions are permeated, then even with the physical eye, the ten directions will be seen with transparent clarity, and the preceding darkness will be transformed into light.
The light penetrates inward through the five viscera and outward through the mountains and rivers;

both the heavens and the human realm are as clear as the palm of one's hand—this is precisely the sign that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) has been shattered, occurring when the lands of the ten directions are brilliantly pure.
This is because this aggregate of form originally arises from the obscuring darkness of emptiness and is formed by that very darkness; thus, once this form exists, [the light shines forth].
Thus, the kalpa-turbidity is formed; since this turbidity has no substance apart from that aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), when the aggregate of form is exhausted, the kalpa-turbidity transcends.
Only upon reaching this point does one come to know that the aggregate of form originally coagulated from solidified false discrimination (*vikalpa*).
Because of this false discrimination, one stubbornly clings to the external four great elements as "mine," and furthermore, one stubbornly clings to the internal four great elements.
It is for my sake that this body of the dark aggregate of form has been formed.
Ānanda, you should investigate with precision within this state the wondrous clarity; before the four elements have even interwoven, in a brief moment, the body can pass through obstructions.
This is called the refined spirit flowing out toward external objects; it is merely a temporary attainment of such power through functional application, and is not [the ultimate reality].

When one realizes the holy state without giving rise to a mind of holiness, it is called a "wholesome realm"; if one instead gives rise to a mind of superior attachment, one will immediately succumb to various delusions.
The following ten types clarify the signs of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) when it is on the verge of being destroyed but not yet destroyed. First, it clarifies external penetration;

this is because the hidden mind (*cittatathatā*) universally encompasses the four lands, remaining inseparable from its current location and unobstructed even at the tip of a hair. It is solely due to...
Enveloped by the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), how could one fail to see? It is not only that one cannot see the [realms] above;

even those currently manifesting clearly within the same single land are unable to do so. Now, as the practitioner enters meditative absorption, having abandoned the light of this limited region and entered entirely into boundless darkness—at the moment before the aggregate of form opens, while still in this state of brilliant clarity free from thought—it is precisely at this point that [the obstacle] should manifest.
By exerting effort to investigate and exhaustively study this wondrously luminous nature, through such inquiry, the four great elements become void and harmonious, like clouds or shadows;
thus, the worlds do not intersect one another. Consequently, in a brief moment, this body passes through walls and barriers without the slightest obstruction.
This occurs because, within meditative concentration, one has applied effort and practice to the ultimate degree of intense pressure.
This causes the light of the mind to leak outward, allowing for a temporary experience of the objective realm as empty and fused;

yet this is gained and lost in succession, unlike the attainment of the fruits of sainthood, which once achieved is forever retained. Even if a practitioner encounters such a state appearing before them—level, even, and plain—they should not give it a single thought.
Whether moving or resting, they should remain as usual, without giving rise to joy, continuing as before to simply maintain their watchfulness.
The *huatou* (critical phrase) is sufficient to verify where one’s practice has gained strength; it is truly a wholesome state.

However, if the practitioner lacks discernment and lacks internal cultivation, and should they encounter this state even briefly and falsely claim to have realized sainthood (*samyaksambodhi*), then demons will find an opening and enter through that隙 (gap).
Thereafter, this will gradually become a great harm. Therefore, the former masters said: "As soon as..."
To have anything upon which one places weight is not to be a śramaṇa. It is also said: "Simply exhaust all ordinary sentiments; there is no separate 'sage's understanding'.
Ānanda further used this mind to investigate the wondrous clarity until it penetrated through his body. Suddenly, this person picked out a *rāji* worm or a *kṛmi* from within his body;
yet his physical form remained intact, without injury or damage. This is called the overflowing of refined clarity.

These physical forms are merely the temporary attainment of refined practice; they do not constitute holy realization. If one does not conceive of them as being holy, they are called "wholesome states";
if one interprets them as holy realization, one will immediately succumb to various delusions.
This clarifies internal penetration (*neiche*). As for internal penetration: the light of the mind suddenly penetrates through the body;
looking inward at the five viscera, one directly sees the *rāhu* and *kṛmi* worms, and can pick them out with the hand without the body being harmed or destroyed.
This is the overflowing of refined light, whereby the physical form temporarily attains such a state, yet it cannot be made permanent. What is called the "joy of the path" is ultimately not the end.
This is what it means to have arrived home.

Furthermore, when one uses this mind to investigate the interior and exterior with meticulous refinement, at that time the *po*, *hun*, *yi*, *zhi*, and *shen*—with the exception of the body which they grasp and maintain—all enter into one another and act as both guests and hosts.
Suddenly, one may hear the sound of the Dharma being preached in the midst of empty space, or hear it from the ten directions.
The same applies to the exposition of the secret meaning: this is called the "intermingling of essence and spirit," which accomplishes wholesome seeds and temporarily produces such states.

This is not the realization of a sage; if one does not conceive the thought of being a sage, it is called a "wholesome state. If one interprets it as the realization of a sage, one will immediately succumb to various delusions.
This clarifies that both the internal and external have been thoroughly penetrated. The medical scriptures state: "The *āśraya* (soul) is stored in the liver;

the *pudgala* (spirit) is stored in the lungs; the *manas* (mind) is stored in the spleen; the *cetanā* (will) is stored in the gallbladder; the *vīrya* (essence) is stored in the kidneys; and the *vijñāna* (consciousness) is stored in the heart.

To say that, apart from this body which is grasped and sustained (*upātta*), all else is "involved and enters" means that, setting aside this eighth [consciousness] which sustains the body, everything else remains unaltered and pervasive.
The remaining spirits and souls all lose their original positions and interpenetrate one another, acting as both guests and hosts;
that is, one acts as the host while the other five act as guests. "Hearing the Dharma preached in the air" means hearing it preached in one location;
"the ten directions preaching together" means hearing it preached throughout the ten directions. "Interchanging separation and union" refers to...
The Master Yue said: "It may be that the essence (jing) leaves its original position and merges with the spirit (hun), or that the spirit leaves its original position and merges with the essence;
'leaving' means losing one's original position, while 'merging' means moving to another position.

This occurs because, having first heard of the mutual functioning of the six sense faculties, one has cultivated wholesome seeds; thus, they occasionally manifest within meditative concentration. It is not like..."

The Sage enters perfect penetration; once attained, it is attained forever. Master Huan said: "What one has heard through past cultivation can naturally be brought forth, yet there is something truly heard.

Now, when one focuses the mind with deliberate effort to the utmost in discussion, even extraordinary texts and elegant compositions may never have been consciously considered, yet they often emerge brilliantly in dreams and visions. This is the power of the spirit."
The occasional manifestations of the one who inspires the divine may be understood through analogy.
Furthermore, when this mind is clear, revealed, and luminously penetrating, its internal radiance shines forth, making the ten directions everywhere the color of Jāmbūnada gold;
all species are transformed into Tathāgatas. At that time, one suddenly beholds Vairocana seated upon a terrace of celestial light.
Surrounded by a thousand Buddhas, one simultaneously appears together with ten billion lands and lotus flowers;
this is called the heart-soul’s spiritual awakening and the illumination of the mind’s light, which shines clearly upon all worlds. To experience this for a brief moment is not a holy realization.
If you do not conceive of it as a holy attainment, it is called a "wholesome state"; if you take it to be a holy realization, you will immediately fall under the influence of various demons.
This clarifies the manifestation of the Buddha-realm. Because the function of "hearing back" (pratyāśravaṇa) is supreme, the substance of the mind becomes increasingly luminous;

thus, the water-like clarity is revealed with brilliant transparency. As the wisdom of initial enlightenment (ādi-bodhi) permeates and penetrates, the mind of original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi) is manifested.
Consequently, all perceived forms are the forms of the Buddha, and all shapes are the shapes of the Buddha. In Sanskrit, this is called Vairocana.
It is said that the light shines universally upon ten billion lands and lotus flowers; that is to say, one flower contains ten billion lands, and in each land there is one Śākyamuni.

This is also because in past lives his ear-organ had heard the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and other scriptures, and the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) thus infused into his mind have now been illuminated by the light of the heart through current study, shining upon all things.
This is merely a rare manifestation within the world; it is not a definitive or permanent realization.

Furthermore, as one uses this mind to investigate the wondrous clarity with unceasing observation, suppressing, subduing, restraining, and transcending [delusions], there may suddenly come a time when the empty space of the ten directions becomes the color of the seven treasures or a hundred treasures, simultaneously filling them all.
When blue, yellow, red, and white appear purely and distinctly without mutual obstruction, this is called a temporary attainment resulting from excessive application of effort;

it is not a realization of sagehood. If one does not conceive the thought of being a sage, it is a virtuous state; but if one interprets it as a realization of sagehood, one will immediately be possessed by various demons.
This clarifies that emptiness is perfected as the color of jewels. Originally, through obscurity and dullness, emptiness was formed; through the binding of darkness, form was produced.

Now, by reversing the hearing and applying effort with intense, continuous, and uninterrupted mindfulness—further suppressing past thoughts, further subduing present thoughts, and further restraining future thoughts—in this manner, [form is transformed].

If one exerts effort with excessive urgency and intensity, one may suddenly see empty space take on the color of the seven treasures, or the color of a hundred treasures, or colors such as blue, yellow, red, and white.
This occurs because the subtle luminosity, being pushed to its limit, radiates forth and manifests;
thus, seeing such various extraordinary phenomena is not the realization of true reality.

Furthermore, if one uses this mind to investigate until it becomes transparent and its refined radiance is undisturbed, one may suddenly see various objects in a dark room at midnight as clearly as in broad daylight, yet the objects in the dark room do not vanish.
This is called the "subtlety and density of the mind" (citta-sūkṣma-gāmbhīrya), wherein the vision is clarified so that what is seen penetrates the profound darkness;
such a temporary attainment is not a holy realization, nor should one conceive of it as such.
If one regards these as "auspicious signs" and forms a holy understanding of them, one will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.
This clarifies that one sees objects in the darkness; that "the essential light is not disturbed" means the mental light is concentrated and stable, such that light and darkness do not shift.
As for "seeing various kinds of objects," these are not things that originally existed within the room, but are [perceived] in the midst of the darkness.
They appear as ghosts, spirits, and enchantments, or as objects of strange and monstrous form;
yet all the objects within this dark room remain exactly as they were before. This is because ghosts, spirits, and enchantments constantly mingle with human dwellings, yet do not see one another;
now, because the application of the mind is subtle and refined, and the clarity is likewise dense, those things normally unseen are now perceived.

All this is a matter of clear vision; it is also the result of the power of study reaching a state of translucent purity, a temporary manifestation rather than the true attainment of the constant radiance that remains as one throughout past and present.
Furthermore, when this mind enters perfectly into the void and fusion, the four limbs suddenly become like grass and wood—whether burned by fire or cut by a blade.
One has no sensation whatsoever; furthermore, the firelight cannot burn or scorch, so that even if one’s flesh were cut, it would be like shaving wood.

This is called the "simultaneous exclusion of sensory objects," wherein the nature of the four great elements enters exclusively into purity for a time. While this is a favorable state, it is not a realization of sainthood.

If one does not conceive of it as a state of sainthood, it is called a "favorable condition"; if one interprets it as a realization of sainthood, one will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.

This clarifies that the body is identical to grass and trees. "Rounding into the void and merging" means that through the diligent practice of "turning the hearing inward," pure awareness remains while the body is cast aside;
thus, the four limbs are like grass and trees—burned yet not feeling it, rubbed yet not knowing it.
Because there is no feeling and no knowing, fire cannot burn them and blades cannot wound them. This is called "listing what is not [subject to] below."

The reason one does not suffer injury is as Master Huan described: when the five sensory objects are simultaneously dissolved and the four elements are cast aside, pure awareness remains while the body is left behind;
thus, there is no contact with harm. This, however, is merely a temporary manifestation and is not the true attainment of the nature where form is empty and emptiness is form.

Furthermore, as this mind achieves the perfection of pure purification, suddenly the great earth, the mountains, and rivers of the ten directions all become lands endowed with the seven treasures, filled with pervasive radiance.
One also sees Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges filling the void of space within magnificent palaces;
looking down, one perceives the hells, and looking up, one beholds the celestial palaces, attaining unimpeded vision.

This is called the deepening of joyful and loathing contemplation through focused visualization; as the visualization persists for a long time, it transforms into something non-substantial. This is not a holy realization, yet if one does not conceive of it as such, it is termed a "wholesome state.
If, however, one interprets it as a holy realization, one will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.

This clarifies that "beholding the realm" refers to beholding the Buddha. "The merit of the pure mind reaches its ultimate limit" means that the power of mental purity has here reached its highest point.
"Suddenly seeing the Buddha-land" refers to the *sahā* (co-resident) pure land.

"Furthermore seeing the various Buddhas" refers to seeing the Tathāgatas currently residing in those pure lands. "Furthermore seeing the hells and celestial palaces" refers to the impure *sahā* world.
Because the power of his pure mind has reached its ultimate limit, he perceives clearly everything from the highest to the lowest, whether pure or defiled.
This arises because, through hearing the teachings concerning the two lands of purity and defilement, he gave rise to thoughts of delighting in purity and loathing defilement;

these were cultivated until they became a concentrated visualization that, after a long time, was transformed into this vision. It is merely a temporary manifestation and not the true attainment of the Land of Quiescent Light (Sukhāvatī).

Furthermore, when you investigate with this mind into the profound and distant, suddenly in the middle of the night you may see from afar the marketplaces, streets, and alleys, or your kinsmen and relatives, or hear their voices.
This is called the "oppressed mind," which, being driven to its extreme limit, flies out; thus, one sees things separated by great distances.

It is not a sign of saintly realization. If you do not conceive the thought that it is a state of sainthood, it is called a favorable state; however, if you interpret it as a realization of sainthood, you will immediately be possessed by various demons.

This clarifies seeing and hearing from afar. "Investigating the profound and distant" means that by applying the mind to investigate until reaching the ultimate depth and furthest reach, the light of the mind is forced to the limit and flies forth; thus, one is able to see and hear through all obstructed places.
This is also merely a temporary manifestation and not the actual realization of the ocean of infinite lands being no more separated than a hair's breadth.
This is a sign of the end.
Furthermore, if with this mind you investigate to the utmost limit and perceive the physical form of a true teacher shifting and changing,

so that in a brief moment it undergoes various transformations without cause, this is called a perverted mind harboring demons, or being possessed by a celestial Māra who has entered one's heart and belly.

To preach the Dharma without cause and penetrate the subtle meaning does not constitute a sign of saintly realization; if one does not give rise to the mind of a saint, demonic activities will subside.
If one interprets this as a sign of sainthood, one will immediately succumb to various delusions.
This clarifies the vision of knowledge and wisdom. Those who have reached the ultimate limit of their research mean that the power of their investigation has attained its finality.
At the stage of ultimate refinement, one truly merges with the essence of the Buddhas' minds;
thus, when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is about to be broken, the demonic mind is struck with alarm, and demonic disturbances likewise manifest at this critical juncture.

When one perceives various transformations of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), it is because the practitioner sees that the perceived friend is originally none other than the practitioner themselves.
It may happen that one who previously harbored a deviant mind and internalized deviant seeds suddenly reveals them upon reaching this stage. This is not true realization of the holy state;
rather, it is a case where a māra has entered the practitioner's body and seized their mental faculty, causing the practitioner to preach the Dharma without cause.
Furthermore, they may appear to penetrate subtle meanings, gradually giving rise to a deranged wisdom that is not the actual realization of holiness. Such is the practitioner.
Having reached this point, although one is no longer constrained by the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), one is nevertheless bound by the snares of Māra;
therefore, those who apply their minds must not fail to be vigilant.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of manifest states in dhyāna are all appearances resulting from the interaction between the mind and the aggregate of form.

Regarding this matter, sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves. When encountering these manifestations before them, they are so bewildered that they fail to recognize them for what they are, claiming instead, "I have attained the state of a Sage.

Having committed such a great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell. You all should, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, proclaim and reveal this meaning, ensuring that no celestial Māras find an opportunity to exploit you, and by maintaining and protecting it, bring it to fulfillment.
This is the "Superior Path.

This is an exhortation to provide protection; it means that these ten objects manifested within *dhyāna* are all the result of the practitioner’s own meditative contemplation and solid deluded thoughts attacking and fighting one another, resulting in either victory or defeat as these ten [objects] appear.

When a single wholesome object appears, it is because the power of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) overcomes deluded thought; when it briefly appears and then vanishes again, it is because deluded thought overcomes the power of contemplation.
Because these two emerge and enter one another alternately without being able to merge, this is why Māra seizes such an opportunity to intrude.
Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded, failing to measure their own level of realization against that of the Buddha.
What kind of effort is this? How is it that upon encountering such a state, its manifestation is immediately taken as proof of sainthood?
This is the great falsehood of claiming to have attained what one has not attained and to have realized what one has not realized;
it leads to falling into the Avīci Hell—what is called "first attaining heaven and later entering the earth. You should transmit this meaning to future practitioners of dhyāna and contemplation.

This is to cause them to understand clearly so that the celestial Māras may find no opportunity to act. Regarding the terms "sustaining" (*bao*), "maintaining" (*chi*), "sheltering" (*fu*), and "protecting" (*hu*):
"sustaining" means to guarantee; "maintaining" means to support; "sheltering" means to screen; and "protecting" means to guard.

This means that one should employ spiritual power to provide secret assistance so that they do not fall into delusion. The characteristics of the Māra of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) are now complete.

Ānanda, when that good man, while practicing the samādhi of śamatha, has exhausted the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), he perceives the minds of all Buddhas appearing like reflections in a clear mirror. Although he seems to have attained something, he is as yet unable to employ it;

he is like a person suffering from a nightmare whose hands and feet are perfectly intact and whose sight and hearing are unconfused, yet whose mind is touched by an external malevolent spirit so that he cannot move. This is...

This is called the domain of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). If the affliction of being stifled by a nightmare ceases, the mind detaches from the body and turns back to observe its own face;

it can come and go with freedom, no longer subject to lingering obstructions. This is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation. Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).
When one contemplates its origin, one finds that empty, luminous false imagination is its root.

This clarifies the signs of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) being unbroken and already broken. The six phrases from "cultivating the three" (*xiu san*) onwards follow upon the previous exhaustion of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*);
seeing the minds of all Buddhas appearing like reflections in a mirror is precisely the sign that *śamatha* has been perfected.
Thus, the *Awakening of Mahāyāna* (*Yuanjue jing*) says: "Tranquil *śamatha* is like a mirror reflecting various images. This refers to the initial stage.

This is the stage of faith (*śraddhā*). If one has attained something but is not yet able to employ it, this means that although one has personally witnessed the original source and already attained its essence, one has not yet been able to give rise to sovereign function in accordance with that essence, because the *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has not yet been shattered.
The two phrases regarding hands and feet metaphorize having a mind of attainment; the two phrases regarding touching metaphorize not yet attaining its function. This is so.
Thus, the two phrases "having substance but being unable to function" refer precisely to the confinement and obstruction of the *vedanā-skandha* (the aggregate of sensation).

This covers the mind, which is fundamentally not confined within the body; yet due to beginningless deluded attachments, that which is inherently unconfined becomes confined, giving rise to the confinement of the living state and the confinement of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) after death.
How could there ever be a freedom apart from the body? All of this is the result of being bound by the *vedanā-skandha*.

If this aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is fundamentally shattered once, one is immediately able to manifest its function and attain the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*), proceeding everywhere without obstruction.

As the former masters did—regarding birth and death as departing or staying, and viewing this body as a merchant’s temporary lodging—all such states are signs that the aggregate of sensation has been exhausted.

Because this aggregate of sensation is the root of the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), when sensation is exhausted, one is detached from the body, and the view of self-identity [is eliminated].

Liberation allows one to transcend the turbidity of views; only upon reaching this stage can one personally realize that the fundamental mind does not reside within the body, but is merely the false reception of the *vedanā-skandha* (feeling aggregate), which manifests through emptiness. Because it is empty, there is receiving;
because it is luminous, one is able to receive without error. This "receiving" consists precisely of suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, and equanimity.
Ānanda, that good man, while within this state, will attain a great radiance and his mind will become luminous.

However, if he suppresses [the mind] excessively within, he will suddenly give rise to inexhaustible compassion at that point. Thus, even upon seeing a mosquito or a gadfly, he regards it as an infant;
a heart of pity arises and he unconsciously sheds tears. This is called "the function of effort suppressing and overcoming" (功用抑摧); when one awakens to this, it is [the stage of] Awakening.
"Absence of fault" does not constitute proof of saintliness; it is merely the realization that one is no longer deluded, which will naturally dissipate over time.

If you take this to be a mark of saintliness, then the demon of pity will enter your heart and viscera. You will see people and weep uncontrollably, losing your correct meditative absorption and inevitably falling into ruin.
This clarifies the signs of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) being about to break and yet not yet broken. First, one suppresses the arising of pity within;

herein, while the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has been broken and the aggregate of sensation has not yet been broken, one attains a great radiance. This means that the ten directions open up through and through, with no further gloom or darkness.
As for "the mind’s illumination becoming manifest," it refers to seeing that all sentient beings equally possess [this nature].

The Buddha’s light has been needlessly subjected to the cycle of rebirth. To suppress [one's emotions] excessively is to reproach and blame oneself for not having awakened early enough to deliver sentient beings.
Because infinite compassion arises within meditative concentration, one perceives even mosquitoes and gadflies as if they were one's own children;

tears flow involuntarily. This too is due to compassion arising from the realization of the same essence (samatā), yet it occurs simply because [the emotional force] was suppressed and crushed too much.
Yet for such a state to arise from within right concentration (samādhi) is inappropriate.
If the practitioner immediately realizes it is not so and turns back to their original inquiry, failing to claim a holy realization, it will naturally vanish after a long time.

If one claims to have attained the same-body great compassion (sahaja-mahākaruṇā) of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, then the demon of compassion (karuṇā-māra) will take advantage of the interval to enter; seeing others, one feels compassion, and compassioning them, one is possessed by it.
Failing to persist, he consequently lost his meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and fell downward; it was as if a high minister’s family suddenly encountered the confiscation of their property.

Furthermore, within that concentration, Ānanda, those good sons perceived the dissolution of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and the clarity of the superior signs of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
When one experiences an overwhelming sense of gratitude in the present moment, a boundless vigor may suddenly arise within that state;

the mind becomes fierce and sharp, and one’s resolve becomes equal to that of all Buddhas, thinking that the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* can be transcended in a single thought-moment. This is called "the transgression of overreaching through effortful application.

If this is realized as it truly is, there is no fault, and it will naturally dissipate after a long time without becoming a point of delusion. However, if one takes this to be a realization of sainthood (*ārya-siddhi*), then [error follows].
When a mad demon enters his heart and marrow, he sees others and boasts of an incomparable arrogance;
his mind reaches such a state that he perceives neither Buddha above nor other people below, and having lost right concentration, he shall surely fall into ruin.

This clarifies that one regards oneself as a Buddha. Regarding the manifestation of superior signs: it means that when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is exhausted, one perceives the minds of all Buddhas.
"Excessive emotion" refers to the fact that until now one had only heard that the mind itself is the Buddha and had never personally seen it;
having now finally attained the vision of one's original Buddha-nature, one feels intense agitation and exerts great courage, thinking to oneself: [I have realized it].

To claim that one can attain Buddhahood in this very life without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*—though one may not know the principle—that sudden awakening is sufficient while practice must still be gradual—is due to arrogance, negligence, overstepping one's station, and self-aggrandizement; thus such words are spoken. If one reflects inwardly and recognizes this as wrong, returning to the path, there will be no fault.
But if one remains deluded and does not repent, then mad demons will enter the mind, giving rise to great *māna* (conceit).
From "There are no Buddhas below" to "there are no sentient beings," [the patriarch] declared, "Above the heavens and below the heavens, I alone am honored.

This loss of *samādhi* and descent into doubt are as certain as the words of Nanyue, who said, "I do not seek liberation from the various sages," and Qingyuan, who said, "Even the Noble Truths are not for me.
Is this not a transgression of overstepping one's bounds? Answer: This arises from exalting oneself too highly.
It was only because the Sage hesitated out of fear and reluctance to advance that he used these words to spur him on;
how could he have known that Mount Gui Shan distinguished between the stages of faith and human nature, or that Changsha spoke of cause, effect, and nirvana? Alas!
A sage who has shattered the skandha of form claims that three *kalpas* can be transcended in a single thought—this is still called reckless, overstepping, and the madness of a demon.

Those who enter the mind and now claim to have attained the "one stroke above," mimicking others by reviling the Buddhas and scolding the Patriarchs, do not know how many *skandhas* they have shattered or what stage they have reached;
yet they dare to speak with great boastfulness, indulging in arrogance and self-importance while remaining complacent and unaware of their fearlessness.
Since the Sages have provided clear instructions on this matter, one should reflect upon and admonish oneself.
Furthermore, within that samādhi, those good sons may perceive that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has dissolved while the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes clear;
yet, with no new realization before them and having lost their former ground, their power of wisdom declines and they fall into a state of desolation.

Seeing nothing at all, a great parching thirst suddenly arises in their hearts, and at all times they remain submerged in recollective thought without dispersal, taking this to be the mark of diligent vigor.
This is called cultivating the mind without wisdom; one loses the realization oneself, yet there is no fault in that. It is not a sign of saintly attainment.

If one mistakes this for such an attainment, the demon of recollection will enter one's heart and viscera, seizing the mind morning and evening and suspending it in a single place. One will lose right concentration and shall surely fall into ruin.
This state of being submerged in recollection due to a lack of wisdom means that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has not yet been shattered, as there is no new realization.

That one falls back from the former abode means that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has already been shattered. At that time, one should use the power of wisdom to illuminate and shatter the aggregate of sensation, realizing its fundamental emptiness;
thus one may enter [the state of liberation]. If the power of wisdom declines, one will fall between the two pillars, having nothing on which to rely. To enter [this state]...
When the center collapses, both front and back become lost in confusion, and one sees nothing at all. Because it lacks the irrigation of the water of wisdom, a sudden parching thirst arises.
Since one is detached from both front and back and has no ground for advancing or retreating, one must at every moment deeply contemplate and maintain mindfulness, not daring to act restlessly;
furthermore, one takes this non-dissipation of mindfulness as diligent *vīrya*.
To examine the characteristics [of the mind] and yet desire to destroy the aggregate of sensation—is this not an error? This is called "losing oneself through a lack of wisdom.

If one recognizes this and reforms swiftly, one will immediately be free from fault. If one takes the non-dissipation of deep recollection to be a sign of saintly realization, then the demon of recollection (*smṛti-māra*) will take advantage of the interval to enter.
If one concentrates the mind by hanging it upon a single point day and night, one will lose right concentration (*samādhi*) and follow after [the demon].

[The practitioner] asks the former masters: "If placing the mind in one spot allows nothing to remain unresolved, why is it that in this [practice], concentrating the mind in one spot instead leads to the loss of right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*)? The answer is: This serves as a medicinal counteragent for those whose minds are excessively distracted;
it is not like making the suspension of the mind in one spot the primary form of diligence.
Furthermore, within that samādhi, those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear and bright.

Their power of wisdom surpasses the state of meditative concentration, yet they lose its sharp intensity. Holding various superior natures within their minds, they themselves begin to doubt whether they are Vairocana;

having attained but a little, they consider it sufficient. This is called losing constant discernment through the application of the mind, becoming mired in intellectual views; yet if they awaken to this, there is no fault.
This is not a true realization of the holy; if you mistake it for such a realization, then the demon of inferiority and easy contentment will enter your heart and marrow.
Seeing others, you will claim, "I have attained the supreme, ultimate truth," thereby losing your correct meditative absorption and falling into ruin.
This wisdom causes one to become excessively deranged; the fault of losing its sharp intensity lies in the excessive sharpness of that wisdom.

Those who harbor the supreme nature within their hearts—meaning they believe that Buddha-nature is inherently complete and does not require cultivation—doubt themselves, thinking, "I am already Śākyamuni," and thus no longer seek further progress, considering a small attainment to be sufficient. This is called "using" [wisdom].
If the mind loses its way, one must constantly and carefully examine whether one's own practice is comparable to that of the Buddha;
otherwise, one merely sinks into one's own views, believing them to be the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, thereby clinging to one's nature while abandoning cultivation.
If one quickly regrets this and recognizes it as wrong, there will be no fault; however, if one relies solely on *samādhi* (śamatha), [the fault remains].

If one abandons cultivation and fails to progress, the māras of the same class will take advantage of the interval to enter, causing one to utter great deliriums and inevitably leading to a fall into ruin.
When asked of the former masters, "The mind is originally Buddha; why is it said that it does not require cultivation to be realized?

they replied, "This is merely a medicinal counteragent for those who cling to the idea of realizing [Buddhahood] through cultivation and thereby neglect their own spiritual nature. Nevertheless, there are also...

How could such expressions as "causing one to undergo a great death once more," "advancing further from the tip of the staff," and "reaching the ultimate limit of the present moment" ever abandon the practice of cultivation and realization?
Furthermore, within that samādhi,
those good sons see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear and bright, yet they have not yet attained a new realization.
Therefore, having lost his mind, he surveys the two limits [of past and future] and spontaneously encounters peril;

within his heart, an inexhaustible anxiety suddenly arises, as if sitting upon an iron bed or drinking a lethal poison. His heart has no desire to live, and he constantly seeks someone to end his life so that he may quickly attain liberation.
