This is called "losing the skillful means" in one's practice; if one awakens to this, there is no fault, yet it does not constitute a realization of the holy.
If one forms a noble understanding [of these states], then a portion of the demon of constant sorrow and anxiety will enter their heart and inner organs;

grasping a sword or blade, they will cut their own flesh, rejoicing in the relinquishing of their life-span. Or, being constantly sorrowful and anxious, they will flee into mountain forests, unable to bear the sight of people, and having lost right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), they shall fall into ruin.
This awakening gives rise to anxiety regarding perilous situations; "surveying both extremes" refers to falling into a state of ruin in the middle.

"Spontaneously giving rise to hardship and danger," and so forth, is like standing on a precipice in fear of falling, which thus gives rise to anxiety. This anxiety originally arises from the practice of being cautious and fearful;
however, when it becomes excessive and one lacks the skillful means to liberate oneself, it eventually reaches such a state.
If one can understand this, the Great Way is found to be exceedingly level; simply letting go is sufficient to dispel sorrow.
If one clings to a mind of anxiety without resolving it, then demons will take advantage of the interval to enter.

Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, when those sons of good family perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear and pure, their minds become settled and secure.
Thereafter, suddenly and spontaneously, an infinite joy arises within their hearts, such that they cannot restrain their own exultation.

This is called "light ease" (*praśrabdhi*). If one lacks wisdom and restrains oneself [from further progress], there is no fault; however, it is not a realization of the holy ones (*ārya*). If one takes this to be a holy attainment, [it is an error].
Then there is a certain class of Mara, fond of pleasure and delight, who enters their hearts and bellies;

seeing people, he laughs by the side of the road, singing and dancing to himself, claiming that he has already attained unimpeded liberation, yet he has lost right concentration and is destined for a fall.
This is because when one practices with concentration, the mind attains tranquility and suddenly gives rise to great joy;
yet, being unaware that this is merely the pleasure of the path and that one has not yet reached the destination, it is called "self-restraint born of a lack of wisdom.

If one observes with the eye of wisdom, one realizes that what has been attained is but a shallow realization—how could it warrant such deep rejoicing? Thus, the wind of joy naturally subsides. Furthermore...
Returning to the source brings no blame; yet if one rejoices without ceasing, the māras will take advantage of the interval to enter.
One will then claim that the mountain of knives and the mass of fire are all simply sites of practice, and that wine shops and brothels are nothing other than liberation.

Thus, one should know that within the pure mind not even a hair’s breadth of anything should be established; if a single thought of anxiety arises, the māra of anxiety will take advantage of the interval to enter.
If a thought of joy arises in a single instant, the Mara of Joy seizes the opportunity to enter;
that is to say, when there is attachment to something, one loses what is correct, and when there is fondness for something, one loses what is correct.
Furthermore, within that samādhi, those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear and bright;

they consider themselves sufficient and suddenly experience groundless, great conceit (*māna*). Thus it continues until conceit, excessive conceit (*atimāna*), and super-conceit (*mānātimāna*), or overweening conceit (*adhimāna*), or inferiority conceit (*ūnamāna*) all arise simultaneously, such that even in their minds they hold the Tathāgatas of the ten directions in contempt.
How much more so for those of lower rank, such as the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; this is called "superior vision," yet it lacks wisdom to save oneself.

If one awakens to this truth, there is no fault; it is not a mark of saintly realization. If, however, one takes this to be a sign of sainthood, then a portion of the demon of great *māna* (pride) will enter their heart and viscera.
They will cease to pay homage to stupas and temples and destroy scriptures and images, saying to the donors: "These are merely gold and copper, or perhaps clay and wood."
The sutras are made of tree leaves or folded flowers, yet the physical body is true and eternal; to fail to respect it oneself while instead venerating earth and wood is truly a perversion.

Those who have deep faith in this [truth] will, by destroying and burying [the sutras], cause sentient beings to fall into the Avīci Hell through their delusions and errors, and they shall sink into ruin, losing their correct meditative absorption.

This refers to the conceit of regarding one's views as superior (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa-māna*). To say "one considers oneself sufficient" means that when one perceives the cessation of form (*rūpa*) and the manifestation of sensation (*vedanā*), one immediately gives rise to contentment;
because of this self-exaltation and arrogance, the mind of conceit arises, and one looks down upon the noble ones (*āryas*).
What is called "self-conceit" (*asmimāna*) is simply relying on oneself to overstep others and treat things with disdain. Although this self-conceit constitutes one of the seven types of conceit...
The first [type] is also the general category of all forms of conceit (*māna*). To consider oneself superior to those who are inferior, or equal to those who are equal, is simple conceit (*māna*).

To consider oneself superior to those who are superior, or superior to those who are equal, is excessive conceit (*atimāna*). To consider oneself superior to those who are truly superior is conceit beyond conceit (*mānātimāna*).

To claim attainment of what has not been attained, or to consider oneself superior to those who are actually inferior, is the conceit of overestimation (*adhimāna*). [To claim attainment] when one possesses nothing at all is the conceit of self-delusion (*asmimāna*).

"Virtue" refers to the conceit of thinking oneself possesses virtue; it is the opposite of "false pride. When one encounters those who are superior or more excellent, one willingly accepts an inferior position, failing to show respect or seek [instruction].
This arises from the conceit of inferiority. All such instances originate from the view that regards oneself as superior;
because there is no wisdom to remedy this flaw, they arise abruptly. If one were to see that all phenomena are equal and without high or low...
Below this level, one does not yet perceive even a single sentient being toward whom one might feel pride, let alone the various sages;
yet if one persists in delusion without reform, the great māra of self-conceit (*mahāmāna*) will seize the opportunity to enter. In recent times, this māra is everywhere:

they destroy Buddha images, regarding them as mere gold, copper, wood, or clay; they treat the Buddhist scriptures as if they were merely palm leaves or silk brocade; and they fixate upon the physical body.

To claim to be a truly eternal living Buddha while guarding vulgar speech as the "Scripture of No Words," to indulge in self-indulgence and boastful claims without shame—deceiving oneself and others, obscuring both heaven and earth—is one who, when measured against the scriptures, ought to fall into the Avīci Hell; how can such a person not stand in awe? One might ask: what of Linji’s failure to pay respects at the ancestral pagoda, or Danxia’s burning of the wooden Buddha, or Deshan’s [beating of the monk]? [The response: These were instances of the "unimpeded liberation" (*asaṅga-vimokṣa*) of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. They were like the Great Physician who administers bitter medicine to cure a chronic illness. It was not that they lacked reverence for the Buddhas and Patriarchs; rather, it was because their compassion was so vast that they acted thus to save sentient beings. If you do not understand this principle, you will surely fall into the error of the "Hundred-foot Pole" (the stubbornness of clinging to views). How could you possibly avoid falling into the pit of the "Three Subtle Obstructions"? You must be careful! You must be careful! Do not let your own mind deceive you. If you wish to attain the Way, you must first sever the root of your own deluded mind. Only then will you be able to see the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Otherwise, you will merely be adding fuel to the fire of birth and death. How tragic! How tragic! If you do not believe me, go and consult the *Lankavatara Sutra* and the *Diamond Sutra*. If you still do not believe, then go and consult the *Avatamsaka Sutra*, the *Lotus Sutra*, the *Nirvana Sutra*, and the *Mahaprajnaparamita Sutra*. If you still do not believe, then go and consult the *Vimalakirti Sutra*, the *Surangama Sutra*, the *Shurangama Samadhi Sutra*, and the *Sutra of the Ten Stages*. If you still do not believe, then go and consult the *Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*, the *Sutra of Cause and Effect*, the *Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish with Causes and Conditions*, and the *Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish with Explanations*. If you still do not believe, then go and consult the *Vinaya*, the *Abhidharma*, the *Samyukta Agama*, and the *Ekottara Agama*. If you still do not believe, then go and consult the *Mahasamnipata Sutra*, the *Ratnakuta Sutra*, the *Mahamegha Sutra*, and the *Maharatnakuta Sutra*. If you still do not believe, then go and consult the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Former Vows*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Prophecy*, and the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Prediction*. If you still do not believe, then go and consult the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Final Nirvana*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Entry into Nirvana*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Parinirvana*, and the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Great Parinirvana*. If you still do not believe, then go and consult the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Birth*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Descent from Heaven*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s First Turning of the Wheel*, and the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Teaching of the Dharma*. If you still do not believe, then go and consult the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Transformation*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Miracles*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Supernatural Powers*, and the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Divine Manifestations*. If you still do not believe, then go and consult the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Response to Questions*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Explanation of Doubts*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Clarification of Meaning*, and the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Resolution of Confusion*. If you still do not believe, then go and consult the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Admonition*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Warning*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Caution*, and the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Urgency*. If you still do not believe, then go and consult the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Compassion*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Mercy*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Benevolence*, and the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Kindness*. If you still do not believe, then go and consult the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Protection*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Sheltering*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Guarding*, and the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Safeguarding*. If you still do not believe, then go and consult the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Deliverance*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Salvation*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Liberation*, and the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Release*. If you still do not believe, then go and consult the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Enlightenment*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Awakening*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Realization*, and the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Attainment*. If you still do not believe, then go and consult the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Truth*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Reality*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Suchness*, and the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Tathata*. If you still do not believe, then go and consult the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Permanence*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Eternity*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Constancy*, and the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Unchanging Nature*. If you still do not believe, then go and consult the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Purity*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Clarity*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Tranquility*, and the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Stillness*. If you still do not believe, then go and consult the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Emptiness*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Non-existence*, the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Non-self*, and the *Sutra of the Buddha’s Signlessness*. To say that expounding the entire Great Canon is like wiping away snot and spittle with a cloth, or that Yanhou’s description of the Patriarchs’ words as "tattered straw sandals" constitutes great arrogance—is this not so?

The answer is: these were spoken in such a harsh and rigorous manner to rouse those who cling to external seeking without realizing their own mind, or who cling to verbal teachings and refuse to advance in practice. This is a single piece of truth.
Maitreya, who would say that he harbors a mind of arrogance? If even the Patriarch truly possessed a mind of arrogance, he would not have avoided the hells;
how much less could others do so?

Furthermore, within that state of meditative concentration, those good sons perceive the dissolution of the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), and their experience becomes sharp and clear within the essence of spirit.

When Yuanwu’s refined understanding attains great accord, his mind suddenly gives rise to immeasurable lightness and ease (*praśrabdhi*). He then claims to have become a sage and attained great self-mastery;
this is called obtaining various states of lightness and purity through wisdom. If he realizes this is not a sign of saintly realization, there is no fault.
However, if he takes it to be saintly realization, then a degree of the "delusion of lightness and purity" will enter his heart and viscera, leading him to believe he has reached fulfillment.

Furthermore, do not seek further advancement; for if you do so excessively, you will become like a bhikṣu who lacks learning, misleading future generations, falling into the Avīci Hell, and losing right concentration, thereby sinking into ruin.

This light ease is sufficient in itself. Because the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) has already been shattered, one attains clarity and vigor; because the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is about to be exhausted, [one attains this state].
Being able to perfectly realize the subtle principle and obtain a mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*), one attains great compliance such that all directions accord with one's will;
suddenly, a sense of lightness and ease arises, leading one to claim for oneself that one has ascended to the state of a sage and attained great liberation.

One ceases to seek further progress because of this arising wisdom and temporary attainment of lightness and purity, yet remains unaware that even if there were wondrous realization, it must still be spat out. If...
If one settles into a state of complacency within a shallow and superficial cave, refusing to exert oneself forward with diligence even when mired in the mud and water of worldly attachments,
then Māra will seize the opportunity to enter; ultimately, one will become a monk of no renown, giving rise to doubt and slander, and falling into a great ruin.
Furthermore, within that samādhi, those good sons see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear.
Within this state of luminous awakening, they attain a nature of empty clarity. Suddenly, they turn toward eternal extinction, repudiating cause and effect, and enter exclusively into emptiness;
as this empty mind manifests before them, they develop a long-standing understanding of annihilationism. This is not a fault, nor is it a realization of the holy ones.

If one interprets this as a realization of the holy, then the "Empty Mara" will enter their heart and viscera; they will then slander those who uphold the precepts, calling them followers of the Small Vehicle.

Claiming to have realized emptiness, such a person asks what there is to be maintained or transgressed. Consequently, they constantly drink wine and eat meat, and engage extensively in sexual misconduct before faithful donors.
Because of the power of the demon, these people do not give rise to doubt or censure, and the ghost’s influence enters them deeply over time.

Or, by consuming excrement, urine, wine, food, and the like—where both are equally empty—one violates the Buddha’s disciplinary code (*vinaya*), erroneously incurs the guilt of a human offense, and loses right reception (*samyag-samādāna*), thereby falling into ruin. This refers to one who, while attached to emptiness, destroys the precepts;
such a person is said to have attained the nature of "empty clarity" (*vivaśa-vidyā*) because they have already broken through the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) and perceive emptiness.

The essence of clarity is fundamentally devoid of even a single thing; yet, suddenly giving rise to nihilism and repudiating cause and effect, one enters into the emptiness of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
How could such a person know that while two aggregates (*skandha*) are empty, three aggregates remain unemptied?

If one realizes that this emptiness is a wrongly grasped emptiness (*durgṛhīta-śūnyatā*) rather than ultimate emptiness, then there is no fault; but if one stubbornly clings to it without changing, it remains a fixed emptiness.

The Māra took advantage of an opportunity to enter, claiming that drinking alcohol, eating meat, and all such acts are entirely empty; he asserted that committing theft and engaging in sexual misconduct were none other than the Way.

He viewed those who upheld the precepts as followers of the Hīnayāna or as being attached to dogmatic views, while regarding those who broke the precepts as Mahāyāna practitioners who had attained thorough realization.
His self-delusion and deluding of others were beyond counting; how could he have known that these were all the very embodiments of Māra?

As for those who claim that the words spoken from the mouths of demons—such as Master Zhigong, Kumārajīva, the Three Chariots, Xianzi, the Wine Immortal, Pūguai, and others—are likewise [false], how should one answer?

These were all great Bodhisattvas manifesting in response-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) who utilized these forms to perform Buddha-work and untie the bonds of sentient beings; how could this possibly be called a denial of cause and effect?

Furthermore, within that state of concentration, when those sons of good family perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear and bright, they may relish its empty luminosity so deeply that it penetrates to the very marrow of their bones.
Suddenly, an infinite longing arises in their hearts; when this longing reaches its peak, they become deranged, falling into lustful desire.

This is called a state of concentration where the mind enters smoothly and complacently; lacking the wisdom to maintain self-control, they mistakenly fall into various desires. If they awaken to this, there is no fault.
This is not a realization of sagehood; if one takes it to be such a realization, then the demon of desire will enter their heart and entrails.
Such a person will invariably claim that desire is the path to Bodhi and will convert laypeople to practice desire equally with them.

Those who engage in sexual misconduct will be called "sons of the Dharma," for by the power of spirits and ghosts, they will gather the foolish and ordinary people in the final age, their numbers reaching as many as a hundred, and so on.
Whether there be one hundred, two hundred, or five or six hundred, up to many millions, the māras will develop a sense of weary detachment;
their bodies and majestic power will vanish, they will fall into royal peril, lead sentient beings astray into the Avīci Hell, lose their right concentration, and inevitably descend into ruin.

This refers to being attached to the flavor of sexual intercourse. Regarding the phrase "tasting its emptiness and clarity," it is because one does not relinquish the attachment to that emptiness and clarity that a mind of craving arises.
This is because within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), there naturally exists the state of wondrous touch and pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) which accords with the human mind;
if one becomes indulgent in tasting this, it transforms into lustful desire. This is called the state of concentration being peaceful and compliant, thereby entering the mind.

Because one lacks the guidance of wisdom, one mistakenly enters into various desires. If one awakens to the realization that no feelings are received, this is called "right reception" (*samyak-samādhi*);

one will then no longer be attached and shall return to faultlessness. If, however, one remains deluded and does not relinquish them, the demon of desire (*kāma-māra*) will seize the opportunity to enter, transforming into demonic retinues;
thus one will fall into ruin through endless wandering, beyond all hope of rescue.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of visionary states appearing during *dhyāna* all arise because the mind is applied in a conflicted manner within the *vedanā-skandha*; thus these phenomena manifest.

Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded, failing to reflect upon themselves; encountering such conditions, they are confused and fail to recognize them for what they are, claiming instead that they have attained the state of a sage.
Because they have committed this great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell. You, too, should take the words of the Tathāgata as my own.
After my parinirvāṇa, transmit and reveal this throughout the age of the final dharma, causing all sentient beings to awaken to this meaning;
do not allow celestial Māras to find any opportunity, but maintain and protect them so that they may achieve the unsurpassed path.
This is an exhortation to provide protection. Those who are deluded do not recognize this for themselves, claiming instead that they have attained the state of a sage (*ārya*).
Because they do not understand what causes and conditions give rise to feelings of compassion and joy, they mistakenly believe they have attained the state of a sage.

Ānanda, when that good man cultivates samādhi and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is exhausted, although his outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet ended, his mind is already detached from its physical form like a bird escaping from a cage.

He has already been able to achieve this, ascending from this ordinary body through the sixty sacred stages of a Bodhisattva to attain the mind-born body (*manomaya-kāya*), moving everywhere without obstruction.
It is, for example, as if there were a person who, while in a deep sleep, utters words in a dream. This person—
Although there is no further object of cognition, his speech has already formed its own rhythms and sequences, causing those who do not sleep to all awaken to his words;

this is called the realm of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of mental formations). If one exhausts all stirring thoughts and eliminates all floating imaginings, so that the mind of awakened clarity is like a dust-free surface, and one can perfectly illuminate the beginning and end of the cycle of birth and death within a single category, this is called the exhaustion of the *saṃskāra-skandha*. Such a person is...
Thus one is able to transcend the turbidity of afflictions and contemplate their origin, realizing that pervasive delusive conceptualization (*vibhava-vikalpa*) constitutes their root.

This clarifies the characteristics of when the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is not yet exhausted and when it is exhausted: when the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) is exhausted, the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*) are exhausted and the discriminative grasping at a self (*parikalpita-ātma-grāha*) is also exhausted;
however, because the afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) have not yet been eliminated, the innate grasping at a self (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*) still remains.
It is said: although the outflows have not yet been exhausted, one reaches the stage of the seven levels of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) where subsequent existence is no longer received;
it is only at this point that the habitual outflows (*vāsanā-āsrava*) are finally exhausted. Since this [stage] falls within the second or third level of faith, they are not yet fully exhausted.

Nevertheless, although one has not attained the exhaustion of outflows, nor the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*) and eighteen transformations of the four fruits, the aggregates (*skandha*) have already been exhausted. Because one does not cling to the characteristics of the body, the mind is able to detach from them.

"His form is like a bird escaping from its cage, moving toward wherever it wishes. Regarding the "sixty stages of the sages," Mount Gu said they begin with the three gradual stages and culminate in the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Question: For what reason can an ordinary body traverse these stages? Answer:

This refers to those of the most sharp faculties in the Perfect and Sudden Teaching; they do not grasp at realization as being real, and thus they traverse the various stages while remaining in their ordinary bodies.
This reveals that perfect interfusion does not obstruct sequential progression, as seen in the cases of Sudhana and the Dragon Girl;
it is not like the Separate Teaching (biejiao), where one must take actual realization as real and thus pass through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* before attaining the fruit. Question:

Since those who have exhausted their karmic retribution can pass through the stages of the sages, why does the text below state that they fall into the Avīci Hell? Answer: In the Separate Teaching, one passes through the stages over the course of kalpas.

It is definitively established that realization is attained in a single stage, wherein there is no falling back; this is the Perfect and Sudden teaching that does not pass through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, but enters directly in one leap.
In the interim, no further realizations are sought, and taking the first *bhūmi* (stage) as the very first summit is what is called "non-retrogression.

Thus, the statement "from this point, he is still an ordinary person" clearly shows that he does not yet grasp the fruits of the sages; rather, he subsequently traverses the stages of the sages from above. This is merely...

One merely passes through them; how could one attain realization in each and every one? Therefore, as long as the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness-aggregate) has not been shattered and one has not yet entered perfect penetration (*samyag-vyutthāna*), it is not impossible to fall back.
Regarding the "mind-born body" (*manomaya-kāya*), the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"It is called 'mind-born' because it is as swift and unimpeded as the movement of the mind. Furthermore, there are three types: first, the mind-born body born of the bliss of *samādhi*.

Because the waves of consciousness arising from the body do not manifest and one dwells securely within the ocean of the mind, one attains the bliss of samādhi and right reception (*samyaksamāpatti*);
this corresponds to the stage of entering emptiness from the first faith through the seventh faith. Second, the "mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*) that realizes the self-nature of phenomena:
because one has thoroughly penetrated the self-nature of all dharmas, one is able to universally enter the buddha-fields; this corresponds to the eighth faith.

This refers to the stage of emerging from the provisional position. "Three" refers to the birth-body produced by non-conceptualizing attention (*amanasikāra*) that arises simultaneously with one's species;
because it awakens to all Buddha-dharmas, it corresponds to the middle stage of cultivation within the nine or ten stages of faith.

Although one has exhausted [the karmic retribution] and attained the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*), the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has not yet been shattered. It is just like when the faults of Māra have ceased but one has not yet awakened from deep sleep.
To speak in a dream is for the dreamer themselves to be unaware of what words they are uttering;
yet the speech produced forms a rhythmic cadence with a logical sequence that is not disordered, such that those who hear them awake can all understand the meaning.

This is analogous to one whose aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) has not been shattered, who, though unable to fully illuminate the cycle of birth and death for themselves, [can still manifest it].
Thus, throughout the aforementioned sixty stages of the sages, there is a sequential order that is not disordered;
all Buddhas know that one will surely attain the direct realization of this state—the characteristic of the *ābhāsa-skandha* (the aggregate of appearances) not yet being shattered.

When the clarity of awareness is like a mirror and floating thoughts are like dust, once the dust is cleared, the essence of the mirror naturally becomes bright; when thoughts are eliminated, the clarity of awareness naturally becomes pure. Thus, the three realms become one.
One is able to know that for all types of death and rebirth within the realm of segmented birth and death (*prātibhāsika-vaipākika-maraṇa-jāti*), birth comes from nowhere and death goes nowhere;
therefore, it is said that "the beginning and end of the cycle of birth and death are perfectly illumined. This is the sign that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted.

Because this aggregate of perception is truly the root of afflictions (*kleśa*), once the aggregate of perception is exhausted, one transcends the turbidity of afflictions. Thus, perception is [the obstacle].
"Integration" refers to such things as when one thinks of a sour plum and saliva flows from the mouth.

Ānanda, when that good man’s aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) has become empty and subtle, and he is not beset by perverse thoughts, his perfect concentration becomes luminous and he enters samādhi.

At that time, his mind comes to cherish this perfect clarity; he sharpens his refined contemplation and greedily seeks skillful means. It is then that the celestial Māra watches for an opportunity to seize him.

He then sends his emanated essence to enter another person's mouth to preach the Dharma; that person is unaware they are possessed by a demon and claims for themselves that they have attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
He comes to the place of those seeking skillful means, sons of good family, and spreads out a seat to preach the Dharma.
For a brief moment, his form may appear as a bhikṣu so that the person may see him, or he may become Śakra, or a woman, or a [lay] devotee (*upāsaka*).
When a bhikṣuṇī sleeps in a dark room and her body emits light, this person is deluded by folly and takes her to be a bodhisattva;
they believe her teachings and allow their minds to be shaken, thereby violating the Buddha’s disciplinary code while secretly practicing lust.

Such people delight in speaking of calamities, auspicious signs, and strange portents, or they claim that the Tathāgata has appeared in a certain place, or speak of the kalpa-ending fire, or describe the terrors of war.
If they cause a person’s family wealth to dissipate without cause, this is called a *guàiguǐ* (strange ghost).

When it grows old, it becomes a *mó* (demon) and harasses that person until it becomes weary and satisfied, then leaves the person's body. Both the disciple and the teacher will fall into royal peril.
You should perceive this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

This refers to the skillful mastery over craving. Since the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are the root of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), the first ten types [of sensations] all speak of the dissolution of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
Since the delusions of thought (*saṃjñā-kleśa*) are the root of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), the subsequent ten types all arise from craving and attachment.
Regarding the "empty and wondrous" nature of the aggregate of sensation: it means being able to detach from the body and, in reverse contemplation, attain mastery over its functions.
"One who does not encounter perverse thoughts" means they are not moved or disturbed by the ten objects.

"Perfect concentration (yuan-ding) brings forth illumination" means that because the afflictions of views have already been eliminated through the destruction of the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha), one no longer gives rise to discrimination regarding the various sensory objects;

thus, it is called "perfect concentration. "The mind loves perfect clarity" means that because the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is not yet exhausted, within the mind of awakened clarity there still remains...
There are those who, possessing defilements and not yet having attained perfect clarity, now cherish that perfect clarity;

such persons give rise to a mind of attachment and delight, desiring to exhaust all delusive thoughts so that the awakened mind may be perfectly clear and luminous, with nothing unknown. Through skillful means, they achieve everything without exception;
wishing to deliver sentient beings, they practice through teaching and transformation, thus rousing their indignation and sharpening their reflections as they greedily seek the good.
It is precisely this single craving that constitutes the root of the movement of Māra.

In Sanskrit, *māra* means "the slayer," for it can destroy meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and kill the life-force of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*). The harm caused by Māra to concentration is like that of a petty person harming a gentleman;
he must wait for a vulnerability before entering. As the saying goes: "Even those of lofty brilliance find their doors gazed upon by ghosts."
Therefore, when a gentleman deals with petty people, he is not malicious but maintains a dignified gravity to prevent them;
if there were even one person in the world who had truly attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), demonic hordes would swarm at his left and right to watch for an opening.
Yet, if his mind were like a wall, without the slightest leakage, then even if the eyes of demons were numerous, they could not peer within.
If there is even a single hair’s breadth of leakage, then [the demons] will enter through that fissure.

Now, if this practitioner has even a single thought of craving for skillful means, the celestial Māra will seize upon the gap of that one thought and immediately dispatch his essence to possess a person and preach the Dharma to delude them.
As for what is called "dispatching his essence," these essences are as described in the following text: river-essences, earth-essences, and all manner of spirit-demons.
The "essence" that flies refers to its flight being like that of a fluttering insect; it is a metaphor for dispatching it with urgency.

As for "attaching to a person," it means attaching to someone who has long been subject to perverse delusions. Because the essence of a person who has reached the end of their [karmic] retribution cannot enter the heart or viscera of another, the demons instead dispatch a spirit to attach to a bystander, using it to fan and delude them so that they will destroy their own settled mind. This is...
This is precisely the Māra’s skillful artifice. Such a person is one possessed by Māra;

being unaware, they do not realize that Māra has taken possession of their body. Thus, while reciting the sūtras and the Dharma, they claim for themselves that they have attained realization of *nirvāṇa*.
Thereupon, before those who seek such cleverness, they manifest transformations and preach the Dharma according to what those people desire.
They employ various skillful means to delude their minds; once these seekers of skill have been deluded, they become Bodhisattvas who are willing to incline their hearts and accept instruction.
Thereupon, their former concentrated minds are now shaken, and their former ethical discipline is now destroyed, such that each and every one falls into the midst of demonic arts and cannot escape.

This is brought about by the skillful artifice of a single thought of greed. Had there been no mind seeking such artifice, then the entire earth would be the realm of celestial Māras, yet they could not disturb or move one;
how much less so a minor demon-ghost? The three phrases regarding "shaking and swaying" are the designs of Māra.
If the practitioner’s eye of wisdom is clear and penetrating and the root of their precepts is firm, even if they open their mouth—
One will then see that their courage is such that they take these three words and use them as a mirror to reflect the Māra; how could he possibly delude or disturb them?
Thus, in the first four root precepts, it is concluded in each case: "If one does not speak thus, it is the speech of the Māra King.

As for those who are fond of speaking of calamities and auspicious omens, this refers to the strange and deceptive utterances made by those possessed by Māra; in short, all of it is [the work of Māra].
These are merely words that delude the human mind. The appearance of a Buddha in the world is an auspicious omen; the fires at the end of an eon and the calamities of war are all disasters.
This name refers specifically to the designation of a harmful and strange ghost:

it is the habit of greed that takes form upon encountering objects, becoming an agent of Māra only upon reaching old age. This is precisely a spirit dispatched by the celestial Māras to bewilder people. Therefore—

"Pointing out their names" means causing others to identify them. "The thought of weariness arises and they leave the person's body" means that after a long time, the demons become weary and depart from the bodies of those they have possessed. "Disciples" refers to those who seek out clever people;
"teachers" refers to those who preach the Dharma. "Those who were previously awakened" refers to all those who, having violated the precepts, entice others into sexual misconduct.
He then knows this is Mara and will certainly not follow after his heels; therefore, he does not fall. Had he failed to recognize it, he would have followed him and surely fallen.

Ānanda, furthermore, when a good man’s aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, and he is not beset by deviant thoughts, his perfect concentration manifests the clarity of samādhi.
In his heart, he takes pleasure in wandering and flight; his refined thoughts are greedy for experience.

At that time, a celestial Māra seizes the opportunity and sends its essence to possess a person, who then speaks of the sutras and the Dharma. This person is unaware they are possessed by a Māra, yet claims to have personally attained unexcelled Bodhi.
He comes to the place where the seeker of wandering dwells, spreads out a seat, and preaches the Dharma, his own form—
Without changing their state of listening to the Dharma, those listeners suddenly see themselves sitting upon precious lotus flowers, their entire bodies transformed into a mass of purple-gold light;
each person in the assembly experiences this, attaining what they have never known before. These people are deluded by folly and take themselves for Bodhisattvas;
their minds are licentious and they violate the Buddha's Vinaya, secretly practicing greed and desire while fondly speaking of the Buddhas with their mouths.
"In such-and-such a place, a certain person of this world shall be an emanation of a certain Buddha come here;

that person is none other than a certain Bodhisattva who has come to transform those among humanity. Because people see this, their hearts give rise to yearning and thirst, while false views secretly arise and the seeds of wisdom are extinguished.
This is called the *pūtana* ghost, which becomes a demon in its old age to harass and disturb these people. Once it becomes weary and satisfied, it departs from them.
If both disciple and master fall into royal calamity, you must first perceive this; do not enter the cycle of rebirth through delusion and ignorance, lest you fall into the Avīci Hell.
This is the experience of greedy seeking. As for wandering in love and craving experiences, it is like traveling between South India and the Five Terraces of the North.
The land of the transformed person is in the ravines of Kunlun; one may travel everywhere throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions without exception.
How could one know that the boundless ocean of lands is not separated from the tip of a single hair? When the fruit ripens and the cause is perfected, it manifests naturally;
there is no need for greedy seeking. It is precisely because of this single thought of greedy seeking that the celestial Māras immediately dispatch their spirits.
They follow people forward to delude and confuse them; they do not transform their own forms, but rather transform the forms of others.
As for those who manifest birth as Buddhas, it is because of the other's greedy seeking and their journeying through Buddha-lands that they manifest a Buddha-field to cater to their preferences.
"This person" refers to the practitioner. Their minds are licentious and dissolute; they transform a concentrated mind into one that is unrestrained and profligate.
That which issues from the mouth of Māra all points to this present Buddha-field; because those people are fond of licentiousness, he uses this to entice them.
"Those people" refers to the practitioners as well. Having seen the various Buddhas and heard their teachings, they incline their hearts with thirsty longing and abandon themselves to follow others.
The "possessing ghosts" (mèiguǐ) are precisely the habituation to lust; when encountering the wind, they are formed.
These ghostly beings in physical form are now the emissaries of Māra.

Furthermore, when a good man’s aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, and he is not beset by deviant thoughts, his perfect concentration manifests as the samādhi of illumination;

at that time, if his heart craves a continuous, lingering state and he clarifies his refined contemplation in a greedy pursuit of spiritual resonance, the celestial Māra will watch for such an opportunity to seize him.

A flying spirit takes possession of a person who speaks of the Dharma and its methods; yet that person is truly unaware of it, and the demon-possessed one also claims to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
He comes to the place where the seeker of harmony—the son of good family—is located, spreads out a seat, and preaches the Dharma.
His form and those listening to the Dharma undergo no outward change, yet he causes those listeners to experience spontaneous awakening of mind even before they have heard the Dharma.

From moment to moment their states shift and change; some attain the power of recollecting past lives, some possess the knowledge of others' minds, some see the hells, or know all manner of good and evil affairs among humans.
Some speak verses aloud, while others recite sutras themselves; each finds such joy as they have never known before.
These people are deluded fools who falsely claim to be bodhisattvas; with hearts of lingering attachment, they violate the Buddha’s precepts and secretly indulge in lustful desires.

They take pleasure in speaking of how Buddhas are superior or inferior, claiming that "this Buddha is earlier" or "that Buddha is later," and within these ranks there are likewise true Buddhas and false Buddhas, male Buddhas and female Buddhas;
the same applies to Bodhisattvas. Because people see such things, their original minds become corrupted and they easily fall into heterodox enlightenment.
These are called *mèiguǐ* (possessing ghosts), who, having grown old, become *māra* demons to harass and disturb these people until they become weary and satisfied.

When that person’s body perishes, both disciple and teacher shall fall together into the king’s calamity; you must be the first to realize this so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth, for through delusion and ignorance you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

This refers to the greedy pursuit of "harmonious accord" (*qihe*). When love is so pervasive and intimate that one greedily pursues harmonious accord, it is "pervasive and dense" (*mianmi*); "intimate" (*wên*) refers to the seamless union.
"Harmony" means that by means of this mind, one conforms upward to the Buddhas and harmonizes downward with sentient beings.

Little do they realize that if one's practice reaches the stage where quiescence manifests before them, then naturally one will be identical above and harmonious below; there is no need for greedy seeking.
It is because the practitioner has a mind that craves such harmony that demons also manifest matters of silent resonance, causing every thought-moment to shift.
"Change" refers to those whose minds are opened, whose thoughts differ from moment to moment as described below:
some gain knowledge of past lives, whereby they suddenly come to know what they were previously unaware of;
some gain knowledge of others' minds, whereby they now also know what others are constantly thinking; and so on, up to reciting verses and chanting sutras.
All of this is to delude the mind by manifesting secret esoteric matters.
As for those who harbor deep affection in their hearts, it means that when a practitioner is deluded, they also secretly cherish [the demon] and desire to fulfill what that mind seeks.
Furthermore, the mouth of the māra uses demonic speech to agitate the practitioner; having already seen before them someone possessing secret esoteric powers, and having also heard...

From the mouth of Māra, demonic and heterodox words issued forth; consequently, the mind that had previously been established in right concentration was washed away without remainder, and he turned instead toward false knowledge and false understanding.
As for the "malignant ghost" (mèiguǐ), it is a deceptive entity that assumes form by encountering animals;
because the practitioner was fond of seeking spiritual resonance, this ghost manifested the five supernatural powers (pañcābhijñā) to bewitch him.

Furthermore, when the son of good family’s aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has become empty and subtle, and he is no longer beset by deviant thoughts, his perfect concentration illuminates the *samādhi*.

At this time, if he becomes fond of the fundamental root and exhaustively examines the transformations of things to the very end of their nature, refining his mind with such clarity that he greedily seeks analytical discernment—then a celestial Māra will watch for an opportunity and dispatch a refined spirit to possess a person, who then speaks of sutras and teachings. This person, however, had not previously...
He perceived that this was the work of Māra’s possession, yet he declared, "I have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa.

He went to the place where the seeker Yuan Shananzu was, spread out a seat, and preached the Dharma. His body possessed majestic spiritual power, which subdued the seeker and caused those beneath his seat to submit naturally in their hearts even before hearing the Dharma.
These people took the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa* and the *dharmakāya* of Bodhi to be [the ultimate reality]."
The fact that my physical body is currently present, with fathers and sons succeeding one another in mutual generation, is itself the eternally abiding Dharma-body without interruption;
this very presence is pointed out as the Buddha-land, distinct from no other Pure Abode or golden-hued form.
Those who believe and accept this forget their former minds, surrendering their bodies and lives in refuge to what they have never experienced before; such are the delusions of the ignorant.
The Bodhisattva investigates their mind and finds it violates the Buddha’s discipline, secretly practicing lust.
They delight in saying that the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are all pure lands, and that the male and female organs are the true locus of bodhi and nirvana.
Those who lack wisdom believe these defiled words; this is called the evil spirits of *gudu* and *yan-sheng*, who have become demons in old age to cause confusion and disturbance.
When this person’s mind becomes weary and satisfied, they depart from that human body; both the disciple and the teacher fall into royal calamity.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; through delusion and ignorance, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
This refers to the earnest pursuit of analytical discernment. Regarding "the root of craving," it means seeking the fundamental source of all things.

It involves exhaustively examining the beginning and end of the nature of transformation among phenomena—such as why a crow is black and why a crane is white—and refining one’s mind with such clarity that the transformations of all things are thoroughly penetrated to their very core, leaving no room for doubt or obstruction. This is to make them precise.
Because one’s spirit and clarity are suddenly expanded, one greedily seeks analytical discernment; yet all of this pertains to the Tathāgata’s ultimate realization of his nature.
For a beginner to falsely hope for such a state is like seeking midnight by looking at the hour of the Rabbit (the second watch). This single thought is the very beginning of inviting demons;
thus, demons take advantage of the interval to cause delusion. When the body possesses majestic spiritual power that crushes and subdues those who seek it, [this is the mark].
They subjugate the minds of people through the power of sorcery; these individuals are those who employ magical arts to successively convert and delude the hearts of others.

Because those practitioners greedily seek the source of transformation, they point to that which is presently subject to annihilation as being eternally abiding, and take what is fundamentally defiled and impure to be pure, thereby catering to the desires of their followers.
Once people have accepted his words, they proceed to discard their capacity for discernment all at once;
they then believe that the succession of fathers and sons appearing before their eyes, reproducing one after another, constitutes the fundamental nature of the transformation of things.
From that day forth, they investigate demonic thoughts and demonic speech as ultimate truth, thereby entering his faction and becoming his followers forever. Such is that demon.

Since those who are refined have already caused the faction of Māra to spread defiled words to fan delusion within themselves, and they further produce defiled words to authenticate Māra’s deception of others, their stratagem is truly ingenious; how could there be anyone who is not deluded?

A *gūi* (demon) is one who, having harbored resentment, undergoes transformation into an insect-like form through habitual practice; because of that greedy pursuit of analytical discernment, the *gūi* manifests its form.
This is merely to delude and bewitch them.

Furthermore, when a good man’s aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, and he is no longer beset by deviant thoughts, his perfect concentration gives rise to illumination within the samādhi.

At that time, his heart craves a response from afar; he circulates his mind, refining his research with a greedy pursuit of mysterious resonance. It is then that the celestial Māra watches for his opportunity.
A flying spirit may possess a person who then speaks of the Dharma and the teachings; yet the person is fundamentally unaware that they are possessed by a demon.

The demon also claims to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. Coming to the place of a virtuous man who seeks a response, it spreads out a seat and preaches the Dharma, causing the audience to momentarily behold its form as if for hundreds of thousands of years.
Their hearts become stained with attachment, and they are unable to let go, becoming the spirit’s slaves.
They provide the four kinds of offerings without feeling weary, each causing those in their retinues to realize that these are their former teachers and original spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
They engender a distinct dharma-love that adheres like glue or lacquer; such people have never before experienced this.

These deluded and confused individuals take them to be bodhisattvas and draw near to them, yet they violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code and secretly practice lust. In their mouths, they delight in speaking thus:
"In a previous life, during such-and-such a birth, I first delivered such-and-such a person; at that time they were my wife, concubine, or brother.
Now they have come to deliver me, accompanying me back to such-and-such a world to make offerings to such-and-such a Buddha. Or it may say:
"There is another Great Radiant Heaven where a Buddha dwells; it is the place of rest for all Tathāgatas. No one there knows [of this]."

To believe that this is deceptive and to lose one's original mind is called becoming a fierce ghost; growing old, one becomes a demon who harasses and disturbs this person until they become weary and complacent, at which point the spirit leaves the person's body.
Both the disciple and the teacher will then fall into the calamities of the King of Hell. You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth;
if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
This refers to greedily seeking a response. To "suspend one's love for a response while seeking a hidden resonance" means desiring to seek the response of the Buddhas through a concentrated mind.
Furthermore, the way of resonance is like water clearing so that the moon appears, or mountains echoing when valleys resound;
how can it be sought with the intentional mind? As soon as this mind arises, demons and malevolent spirits will take advantage of the opening to respond.
When one suddenly beholds his body as if he were hundreds or thousands of years old, it is because Māra manifests the appearance of an old man.
By seeing his advanced age, those in the assembly recognize him as their teacher from former lives and spiritual kin from previous births;
consequently, they give rise to a distinct "Dharma-love" that binds them as firmly as glue or lacquer and cannot be untied. All of this is a deceptive manifestation of a hidden influence.

Because of these matters, practitioners become deluded by them; day after day they draw near to such things, unaware and unperceiving, and thus they turn the disciples of the Buddha into the retinue of Māra.
Since those Māras feign mysterious responses and further feign speaking words of such responses from their own mouths, how could people not believe them?
These fierce ghosts are those who, having encountered decline, were dominated by the habit-energy of anger.
This refers to those who have attained formative mastery.
Furthermore, when a good son’s aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, and he is not beset by deviant thoughts, his perfect concentration (*samādhi*) becomes luminous.

At this time, within the state of *samādhi*, his mind loves to penetrate deeply; he exerts himself with self-discipline, delights in dwelling in the stillness of the aggregates, and greedily seeks tranquility. At that moment, the celestial Māra—
Waiting for an opportunity, he sends forth his refined essence to attach itself to a person’s mouth, whereby that person speaks of the sutras and dharmas.
Originally, the person was unaware of it, yet when possessed by the māra, they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.

Coming to the place of a virtuous man who seeks the aggregates (*skandha*), he spreads out a seat and preaches the Dharma, causing those listening to each recognize their own past karma. Or, at that location, he may say to one person: "You have not yet died."
Having manifested as an animal, he commanded one person to step on his tail from behind; the man was instantly unable to rise.

Thereupon, the entire assembly bowed their hearts in humble admiration. When someone conceived a malicious thought, he knew the very inception of it. Beyond the Buddhist monastic discipline, he further intensified his ascetic practices with extreme austerity.
He slandered bhikṣus, reviled their followers, and exposed their private affairs, showing no regard for the censure or reproach of others.
They take pleasure in speaking of future calamities and blessings, and when they reach those points, not even a hair’s breadth is missed.

This powerful ghost has grown old and become a demon, harassing and confusing this person until he grows weary and complacent; then the spirit leaves the person's body. Both the disciple and the teacher often fall into royal punishment.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

This refers to craving for past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*). The phrase "the mind cherishes the four lines" should be exchanged with the phrase "the mind cherishes the three lines" from the following chapter so that the preceding and succeeding sections correspond.

One who craves knowledge and views and is greedy for past lives is a practitioner who desires to fully know the realms of the three periods of time and desires to fully see the minds of others; thus, they cherish past lives without realizing [their true nature].

When knowledge and vision are established, demonic influences enter. That you have already become an animal even before death is due to your attachment to the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), whereby you falsely manifest this power.

That someone arouses a thought and you already know its inception is due to your attachment to the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*), whereby you manifest this power.
Beyond the Buddha’s discipline (*vinaya*), you further impose upon yourself severe asceticism.
These are instances of feigning diligence to delude the minds of others, such as plucking out one's hair, fumigating the nose, lying upon a pestle, or sleeping upon thorns.
The two phrases concerning "slander" refer to accusing upright people of being depraved.

The two phrases concerning "exposure" involve exposing the private secrets of others in an attempt to compel their faith and submission. The four phrases beginning with "in the mouth" feign the appearance of celestial [powers].
The divine eye and divine ear are among these; these five higher powers (abhijñā) are falsely manifested by powerful *piśāca* spirits who roam in the realm of emptiness.

Furthermore, O son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes void and subtle, and one is not beset by deviant thoughts, the perfect concentration gives rise to illumination within the state of *samādhi*.
One whose mind cherishes knowledge and views, who diligently and painfully researches and seeks after past lives, at that time becomes vulnerable to the celestial Māras.
These Māras seize the opportunity to send their essence to possess a person, who then speaks of the Dharma and scriptures. That person is entirely unaware they have been possessed by a Māra;

they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. They come to the dwelling of a seeker of knowledge, such as a good man, where they arrange seats and preach the Dharma. This person does so without any basis...
In the place where the Dharma is being preached, he obtains a great precious jewel.

That Māra may at times transform himself into an animal, with its mouth holding that jewel along with various rare treasures, books, scrolls, and other extraordinary objects; he first presents these to the person [preaching], and then attaches them to his body.
Or he may entice the listeners to bury them underground, where there is a bright moon-jewel that illuminates that spot for all those who listen.

Having obtained unprecedented medicinal herbs in great quantities, they do not eat fine delicacies; sometimes for days at a time they consume only a single sesame seed or a single grain of barley, yet their bodies remain plump and robust because they are sustained by the power of Māra.
They slander bhikṣus and revile the assembly, showing no regard for the censure of others.
In their mouths they delight in speaking of hidden treasures in other regions and the secret abodes of sages throughout the ten directions, leading those who follow them there.
One often encounters individuals who appear strange and extraordinary; these are spirits of mountains, forests, lands, city-protectors, rivers, peaks, and ghosts who have grown old and become demons.
Some may preach licentiousness and violate the Buddha’s precepts, secretly indulging in the five desires with those who serve them;

others may be diligent practitioners who subsist solely on grasses and trees, yet their conduct is erratic, and they seek to disturb and confuse such people until they grow weary of them and give rise to thoughts of resentment.
When that person departs from their body, both the disciple and the teacher shall fall into royal calamity. You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth;
if you remain deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

This refers to the craving for tranquility and stillness. Tranquility and stillness are the ultimate state of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*); others do not know them, but only a Buddha does.
One can know that others cannot enter this state, for only a Buddha can enter it;

yet one must not fail to realize that if one's practice has not reached its full measure, there will be no perfection. Even when entering deep stillness and tranquility, one must not harbor attachment.

Should a single thought of attachment arise, demons will seize upon that attachment to manifest illusory phenomena of the five aggregates to delude the practitioner. Such a person is like one who unexpectedly obtains a great precious jewel.
The practitioner obtains the pearl from the place where the Dharma is preached; or the demon first holds the pearl in its mouth and offers it to people to attach to their bodies;

or it first hides the pearl underground to lure people; or it consumes medicinal herbs, hemp, or wheat to appear plump and robust—all these are deceptive displays of hidden tranquility, matters beyond human knowledge, intended to pander to their preferences. Once the māra has manifested these hidden deeds...
They deceive people by further recounting matters of the five aggregates (skandhas) to delude the masses;
these are all spirits dwelling on land who, over time, become demon-messengers. There are others even lower than these, who form demonic factions in groups and bands to disturb and confuse travelers.
Furthermore, when a son of good family’s aggregate of feeling is empty and subtle, and he has not encountered deviant thoughts, his perfect concentration illuminates the Samādhi.

At that time, if he takes pleasure in various supernatural transformations and studies the source of these transformations, greedily seeking spiritual powers, then a celestial Māra will watch for such an opportunity and send a refined spirit to possess a person, who will speak the teachings of the sūtras. That person, being truly unaware, does not realize they have been possessed by a Māra.
It is also said that having personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*, he went to where those sons of good family seeking supernatural powers were, spread out a seat, and preached the Dharma.
Some among those people held torches in their hands; they gathered the flames and distributed them over the heads of the fourfold assembly who were listening.
On the crowns of all these listeners, the flames rose several feet high, yet they possessed no heat and never burned.
Sometimes he walked upon water as if treading on level ground; sometimes he sat motionless in mid-air; sometimes he entered into a jar or stayed within a sack;
crossing windows and penetrating walls, he encountered no obstacles. Yet, regarding weapons, he could not exercise mastery.
He claimed to be a Buddha, wore white robes, and accepted prostrations from bhikṣus; he slandered dhyāna and the Vinaya, and reviled his own followers.

They expose the private affairs of others without avoiding censure or suspicion; they constantly speak of supernatural powers and mastery, or cause others to see Buddha-lands by the side of their path.
Their demonic power deludes people and lacks any truth. They praise sexual misconduct and do not condemn coarse behavior, taking various vulgarities to be the transmission of the Dharma.
These are called the mountain spirits, sea spirits, and wind spirits of great power within heaven and earth.

The essences of rivers and the essences of soil, the accumulated spirits of all plants and trees over many kalpas, or dragon-spirits, or immortals who have reached the end of their lifespan and returned to life as demons,
or those whose allotted time as immortals has expired and they ought to die according to the reckoning of years yet whose forms do not decay—

these, when possessed by other monsters, become demons in old age and disturb these people. Once they have grown weary and satisfied, they depart from the person's body, leaving the disciple and the master [behind].
If both fall into royal calamity, you must be the first to perceive it; do not enter the cycle of rebirth through delusion and ignorance, lest you fall into the Avīci Hell.

This refers to the greedy pursuit of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). As for spiritual penetrations and powers, one naturally attains the mutual functioning of the six sense organs once they are fully perfected;
how can one greedily pursue them as a singular attachment? To seek them greedily invites demonic affairs. Therefore, the ancients valued only this: [the realization that]...
Yanshan pointed at the arhat, saying, "The arhat’s supernatural powers are indeed not lacking, but as for the Buddha-dharma, it must be someone like me who can attain it.
This man was a fraud who manifested the eighteen transformations below to delude people;
he feared only weapons, which shows that his mouth was filled with demonic charms used to confuse others by speaking of supernatural powers.
That people praise lust while not condemning coarse conduct is sufficient evidence that these are demonic teachings;
they are all manifestations of various spirits dwelling in water or on land who falsely display supernatural powers.
Furthermore, when a good man’s *skandha* of sensation is empty and subtle, and he is not beset by deviant thoughts, his perfect concentration becomes luminous within the state of *samādhi*.
With hearts fond of entering cessation and investigating the nature of transformation, they greedily seek profound emptiness.

At that time, celestial Māras, waiting for their opportunity, cause their refined spirits to possess people who then preach the Dharma and sutras. These individuals remain entirely unaware they are possessed by demons;
they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. They come to the dwelling of those good men who seek emptiness, spread their seats, and preach the Dharma within the great assembly.
Their forms suddenly vanished into emptiness so that the assembly could see nothing; then, from the void, they emerged abruptly, appearing and disappearing with sovereign ease.
Sometimes they manifested their bodies as transparent as lapis lazuli; sometimes they extended their hands and feet, emitting the fragrance of sandalwood;

or they excreted waste like thick rock honey. They slandered the precepts and disparaged those who have left the household life, constantly speaking of causelessness and the non-existence of karmic fruit.

Once dead, they are extinguished forever, never again taking rebirth among either the ordinary or the holy. Although they have attained a state of empty stillness, they secretly indulge in lustful desires;
those who receive their desires likewise attain a "mind of emptiness" and deny the law of cause and effect.

These are known as the sun and moon eclipsed, vital energies, gold and jade, cinnabar grasses, qilin, phoenixes, tortoises, and cranes—beings that do not die for thousands of myriad years and become spirits born within this land.
When they grow old, they become demons who harass and disturb this person; once their desires are satisfied, they leave the person's body, and both the disciple and the teacher fall into royal peril.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

This refers to the deep craving for profound emptiness (*śūnyatā*). When deluded thoughts are exhausted, true emptiness manifests; when birth and death are eliminated, quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*) appears.
Profound emptiness and quiescent extinction are not objects to be craved; if one gives rise to a craving mind, there will immediately be demonic interference.
In the passage following "among the great assembly," because they crave emptiness, [the Buddha] manifests emptiness to satisfy their desires. This constitutes slander.
The second type slanders the Dharma and treats the Sangha with contempt because they take emptiness as their cause;
they speak of "lower emptiness" (undermining emptiness) in their mouths to negate cause and effect. Though they may attain a state of empty stillness, they secretly practice greed and desire;

this means they can empty that which is empty but cannot empty that which is not empty, for while their mouths discourse on emptiness, their minds remain attached to existence. Thus, they receive and indulge in such desires.

"One who has attained the realization of emptiness is possessed by the power of Māra and transforms along with it. This is called "lowering" (xià), intended to cause people to recognize the name and guard against it strictly.
Regarding "eclipse" (bóshí), Wei Zhao says: "The movement of a vapor that presses upon [the moon] is 'thinning' (bó); its impairment and destruction is 'eclipsing' (shí)."

Furthermore, when a son of good family’s aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has become empty and subtle, and he is no longer beset by deviant thoughts, his perfect concentration gives rise to illumination within *samādhi*.

At this time, if his heart cherishes long life and he undergoes arduous refinement of the subtle, greedily seeking eternal years and abandoning the birth of segmented existence to suddenly hope for the permanent abiding of the subtle marks of the transformational body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), then a celestial Māra will watch for such an opportunity.
He will dispatch a refined spirit to possess a person, who will then orally expound upon sutras and dharmas.
That person ultimately does not realize they have been possessed by a māra; they also claim to have attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
They go to the place where that seeker of birth—a son of good family—resides, arrange seats, and preach the Dharma.

They speak favorably of traveling to and from other directions without obstruction, returning in a mere instant even after traversing ten thousand *li*, or claiming to retrieve items from those distant places as if they were right there in a single location within one’s own home.
Within the space of a few paces, he caused them to go from the east to the western wall; though they walked with great haste for many years, they could not reach it.
Because of this, their minds were filled with faith, and they doubted that the Buddha had appeared before them. They constantly said: "All sentient beings of the ten directions are my children;
I give birth to all Buddhas; I bring forth the worlds; I am the primordial Buddha who appears spontaneously in the world, not attained through cultivation."

This is called "Abiding in the World with Sovereignty. The celestial Māra may cause his retinue—such as Cāmuṇḍa, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the Piśāca youths who have not yet resolved for enlightenment—to take advantage of one’s empty clarity to consume their vital essence.
Alternatively, practitioners may personally behold [these spirits] without relying on a teacher; they are called Vajradhara and grant them long life, manifesting in the form of beautiful women.
When greed prevails for no more than a year or two, their livers and brains will wither away and they will speak only to themselves, appearing like malevolent spirits;
though the people before them do not yet discern this, many fall into royal calamity, dying of parched exhaustion even before facing formal execution.

This affliction and confusion lead those people to their ultimate demise. You must perceive this first so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you remain deluded and ignorant, you shall fall into the Avīci Hell.
This greed seeks eternal years. What is sought here is the fruit of Arhatship; it is attained naturally once the hindrances to practice have been destroyed.

Now, because you are restlessly seeking rapid attainment, you encounter the disturbances of Māra. Only when the delusions of the three realms within the cycle of birth and death (*pariccheda-jarāmaraṇa*) are exhausted can one begin to leave them behind.
Those of the Two Vehicles who have reached the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and Bodhisattvas who have ascended the stages all attain the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Now...
Because those who have not yet abandoned defilement suddenly desire to transform the coarse into the subtle and the short into the long within their own *pariccheda* (segmented) bodies,
it is said that they "discard the segmented birth" and "suddenly aspire to the transformational. That one can arrive ten thousand *li* away in an instant,
while another fails to reach the same place after months of rapid travel, demonstrates how the present moment can be extended or compressed at will to satisfy their desires.
To suspect that the one appearing before the Buddha was someone else is to mistake You Meng for Shu Ao. The subsequent mention of longevity in the text is intended to arrest the listeners' attention.
As for the *Svayambhū* Heaven (the Heaven of Self-Existent Lords), it refers to the Māra King of the Desire Realm, who is subsumed within the sixth heaven.

When it says he causes his retinue to act, this specifically reveals that the Māra King himself does not manifest his own body, but rather that a flying spirit possesses a person. This serves to refute [such claims].
*Vemacitra* was formerly called "the jealous woman" and also "the slave deity," which refers to a ghost employed as a servant. *Piśāca* means "one who devours vital essence";
both belong to the four classes of celestial beings (*deva*). If they have already resolved their minds [toward the Dharma], they protect people;

if they have not yet resolved their minds, they devour people. This is because the practitioner’s power of meditative concentration is empty and luminous, and thus [the spirits] consume their vital essence.

This is because they cause harm; sometimes it does not rely on the words of a teacher, for the body of a māra does not necessarily manifest by possessing a person to preach the Dharma, but may instead appear directly before the practitioner’s own eyes.
When one hears a voice calling out "Vajra" while a beautiful woman appears, this is a clever stratagem of a māra used to harm people.
As for the case where the voice speaks independently, the *Suwen* states that "delirious speech" is caused by [an imbalance of] qi.
This beautiful woman speaks alone; listen closely to her words, for they may be those of a *yācā* or a *mārī*.
If a traveler does not discern their intent and acts upon her seductive speech, many who become lewd and debauched fall into royal peril.
Even before the execution is carried out, their spirits wither first, and they die. This is because they are tormented by the power of Māra.
Even to the point of losing their bodies and forfeiting their lives—
Ānanda, you should know that these ten kinds of māras, during the time of the final age, will go forth from home to practice the Way within my Dharma;
they may either possess a person or manifest their own forms, all claiming to have already attained the realization of Right and Universal Enlightenment, and praising sexual desire.

Those who violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code—former evil Mara-masters and their demonic disciples—who transmit their lust from one to another, thus allowing these perverse spirits to bewitch the core of their hearts and viscera;
for nine lifetimes at most, or even exceeding a hundred ages, they cause those of true cultivation to become entirely the retinue of Mara.
After their lives end, they will surely become subjects of Mara, lose right universal knowledge, and fall into the Avici Hell. You need not yet [fear this].

First, I shall attain quiescent extinction; even if I achieve the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), I will remain by the power of my vow within that age of the final Dharma, giving rise to great compassion to rescue and deliver those sentient beings who possess a correct mind and deep faith, ensuring they do not fall under the influence of demons and that they attain right knowledge and vision.
Now that I have delivered you and you have emerged from birth and death, if you follow the Buddha’s words, this shall be called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.

This entrustment is intended for those present to leave behind their vows to deliver sentient beings. Of the ten preceding types of māras, only the tenth manifests its own form; the others all attach themselves to human beings.
Formerly, while the Buddha dwelt in the world, various māras attempted to destroy the Dharma, but due to the Buddha’s spiritual power, they were unable to do so.
The māras then made a vow: "After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, we shall leave the home-life in accordance with the teachings and destroy the Buddha-Dharma. The Buddha then...
Shedding tears, he said, "There is nothing I can do for you. It is like a worm within the body of a lion that eats the lion's own flesh.
He continued, "Know that in the final age, those bhikṣus who destroy the Dharma are all companions of Māra. You must now descend and offer correct exhortation to those whose faculties are ready.
Then Ānanda stepped forward and made this vow: "May I now attain the fruit and become a Treasure King, returning to deliver beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
