The assembly here again earnestly entreated him to remain and ensure that the teachings would circulate throughout the human realm. As it was previously stated:

"To offer this profound mind to all lands is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness. Furthermore, he was instructed that to follow the Buddha’s words, transmit the Dharma, and deliver sentient beings is itself the repayment of his debt of gratitude.
Thus, we know that Ānanda entered the Vāyu-pravega Samādhi (the Samādhi of the Swift Wind).
The entry into nirvana of the four schools was also based on the Buddha’s words, as they remained in this world by their vows to provide secret salvation.

Ānanda, these ten kinds of present states within *dhyāna* all arise because the mind is applied in a state of mutual interaction during the *saṃjñā-skandha* (aggregate of perception); thus these things appear.
Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded, failing to reflect upon themselves; encountering such conditions, they are confused and fail to recognize them for what they are, saying:
To falsely claim to have attained the state of a sage is a great lie that leads to falling into the Avīci Hell.

You must take these words of the Tathāgata and transmit them to the age of the Final Dharma after my parinirvāṇa, so as to cause all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to this meaning. Do not allow celestial Māras to find any opportunity;
protect and sustain them so that they may achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
This is an exhortation to provide protection. The reason the Venerable One compiled the various sūtras was to fulfill the Buddha’s entrustment.
Is it not precisely through the Venerable One’s compassionate heart for the world and the power of his sorrowful salvation that the teachings now circulate?
The section on the demonic signs of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is hereby concluded.
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas,
Volume Nine. The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas.
*Hezhai*, Scroll Ten.
Explained by the Venerable Tongrun of Er-Leng-an.
Ānanda, when that good man practicing *samādhi* has exhausted the *saṃjñā-skandha* (the aggregate of perception), his ordinary dreams and thoughts—
Extinguishing both waking and sleeping, there is constant, singular, awakened clarity; empty and still, like a cloudless sky, it is free from the coarse and heavy shadows of external objects.
One observes the worlds, the great earth, mountains, and rivers as if in a mirror: they come with nothing to adhere to and pass away leaving no trace.
Empty yet responsive to illumination, all habitual tendencies are utterly cleared away, leaving only the single, pure, and true essence. From this, the very root of birth and death [is severed].

One perceives all twelve classes of beings throughout the ten directions, exhausting every category; though one has not yet penetrated the individual origins of their destinies, one sees the common foundation of their births.
It is like a shimmering mirage, flickering and turbulent, the ultimate pivot-hole for the floating roots and objects of sensation.
This is called the realm of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). If this flickering, shimmering, fundamental nature enters into...

When the turbidity of the original movement subsides and transforms into clarity, like waves ceasing to be and becoming still water, it is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of sentient beings; by observing its origin, one finds that its root lies in subtle and hidden deluded thoughts.

This clarifies the signs of the saṃskāra-skandha being unbroken and already broken. First, it clarifies that when ideation (*saṃjñā*) is exhausted and formations (*saṃskāra*) manifest, whether in the daytime or in dreams at night, the independent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is the primary agent. Therefore, when ideation is exhausted, waking and sleeping are one and the same;
its nature is wondrously luminous, empty, still, and unmoving—just like a clear, bright, vast sky where every trace of fine cloud has vanished, leaving nothing behind.

Since all phenomena have already become empty as objects of consciousness (*dharmadhātu*) and coarse, heavy characteristics have been extinguished, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) becomes the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).
It contemplates all worlds—the great earth, mountains, and rivers—as being exactly like images reflected in a mirror, with nothing to be discarded or retained.
Receiving through emptiness and responding through illumination, it is entirely free from the lingering traces of former habitual tendencies of self-clinging (*ātma-grāha-vāsanā*). Only...
This is the state where the essence of the eight consciousnesses, pure and true, remains solitary and transcendent; it is the mark of the exhaustion of these perceptions.

The root-source of arising and ceasing is precisely the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). Because it involves constant flux and volitional construction, it serves as the source of arising and ceasing.

Since its coarse and heavy aspects were previously manifest, its subtle and hidden nature was not seen; now that the coarse and heavy have ceased, that which was subtle and hidden finally becomes apparent.

Revealing that one thus knows the root source of birth and death within the triple world is not related to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), but rather that the seeds contained within the eighth consciousness serve as its basis;

therefore it is called the subtle *nāda*-consciousness. Because the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have formed a violent torrent, by perceiving this fundamental root, one is able to see exhaustively that the twelve classes of beings all arise from this very source of arising and ceasing.
Regarding the phrase "although they have not yet understood the origins of their respective life-forces," this refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), which is the union of consciousness,
vitality, and warmth. Although they have not yet known the specific causes and conditions by which each of the twelve classes of beings receives its life-force,
the foundation for the common birth of these twelve classes has already begun to appear, like the light of a shimmering mirage.
Because it flickers and is unstable, it is said to be "like a wild horse" (*marīci*). The phrase "glistening and turbid" refers to this movement.
As for "wild horse," it refers to the drifting vapors of the fields; on a clear spring day, they can be seen hovering over the ground, appearing like water with a light like a flame.
Thirsty deer mistake them for water, yet they are not actually water; they are a mirage (*mṛgatṛṣṇā*). The term "turbid" refers to the movement of this [consciousness].

The *āyatanas* (skandhas) are obscure, tranquil, and disturbed; their movement is not like that of the mental consciousness, which is like a great torrent. Regarding the "pivot" (*śu*) and "socket" (*xué*) of the ultimate axis of the floating sense-bases and objects:
the door-lintel is called the "pivot," and the door-sill is called the "socket"; these are the essential points for turning and moving.

To say that the arising and ceasing of the sense-bases and objects both take the *saṃskāraskandha* as their pivot and socket refers to the state in which the *saṃskāraskandha* has not yet been exhausted.

It is because the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of mental formations) is like a great torrent, while the *saṃjñā-skandha* (the aggregate of perception) is like a fine stream, and the *vijñāna-skandha* (the aggregate of consciousness) is like a waveless flow.
When the preceding *saṃjñā-skandha* has ceased—like the subsiding of the great torrent—and this *saṃskāra-skandha* manifests, it is like a fine stream arising.
If one were to take the nature of these subtle currents of original habituation and cause them to re-enter the fundamentally clear essence that is free of waves, then the original habituation...
It becomes clear, as if returning to its original state; once it is clarified, these fine currents all become pure, limpid water.
This is what is called "pure water appearing before one," which signifies the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*).

This is also the sign that the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) has been exhausted, and it is the moment when the seventh consciousness is transformed into the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*). For such is the turbidity of sentient beings.
Since this arises from the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), when the aggregate of formations is exhausted, one transcends the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).
At this point, one knows that the shifting and changing nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and their non-arising [nature] are both governed by the aggregate of formations. Master Huan said:

"Birth and death ceaselessly continue, and karmic destiny constantly shifts; this is called the turbidity of sentient beings. Therefore, when the aggregate of formations is exhausted, one transcends it by means of the aggregate of formations."
This subtle shifting, occurring without one’s awareness, is called "hidden delusive thought.
Ānanda, you should know that when these virtuous men attain right knowledge within *śamatha*, their minds become concentrated, luminous, and upright;

at that point, the ten classes of celestial Māras cannot find an opportunity to interfere, and they are able to investigate with refinement the root of all living beings within the very nature of those beings.

As for the manifestation of the source of birth, one contemplates that profound, pure, and perfectly agitated source of movement; if, within this perfectly circular source, one gives rise to conceptual calculations, such a person falls into the two theories of causelessness.
The following clarifies the ten signs that occur when the skandha of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is about to be destroyed but has not yet been destroyed. One who attains correct knowledge...

When one says that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has already been shattered and one no longer encounters perverse deliberations, one then attains correct knowledge; the subsequent shattering of the latter two aggregates is called "pervasive suchness" (*yathābhūta*).
Within *śamatha*, this is the manifestation of perfect concentration (*samādhi*). Being "congealed" means immovability; being "luminous" means freedom from delusion;
being "correct" means freedom from partiality. When the mind is employed in this manner, the celestial Māras cannot find an opportunity to exploit it. This is because...
When the two aggregates of sensation and perception have not yet been shattered, the power of contemplation is still shallow;

even the celestial Māra can then observe one’s mental activity and wait for an opening to destroy one’s right concentration. Now that these two aggregates have already been shattered, there remains only the single, refined, and true reality;
thus, external Māras have nothing to observe regarding its depth or shallowness, so how could they possibly cause disturbance? Therefore, the ten types [of Māras] mentioned below are all internal.
Only when Māra ceases his malevolent interference can one thoroughly investigate and exhaustively penetrate the fundamental nature of the various classes of living beings.

This means that once the *saṃjñā-skandha* (the aggregate of perception) is exhausted and the celestial Māras no longer cause disturbance, one is able to apply diligent effort and practice to thoroughly investigate and exhaustively penetrate the root of the twelve classes of beings;
thus, the root-source of these twelve classes of beings is finally revealed. It is the profound, pure, and perfect source of movement and agitation.
That which is hidden and difficult to perceive is called "mysterious agitation" (*you-rǎo*); that which stirs the subtle ripples with slight movement is called "clear agitation" (*qīng-rǎo*);

and that which shares the same basis as these twelve is called "perfect agitation" (*yuán-rǎo*). To speak of them collectively, they are termed the "Element of Movement" (*dòng-yuán*). Nevertheless, although one observes this Element of Movement, it does not actually purify the seeds of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*);
thus, one suddenly gives rise to erroneous views and falls into the view of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*).

First, this person perceives that there is fundamentally no cause. Why is this? Because this person, having attained the full development of the life-faculty (*jīva-indriya*), relies upon the eight hundred merits of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) to see all sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas, their karmic currents winding and circling as they die here and are born there.
They see only the cycle of rebirth of these sentient beings within those eighty thousand kalpas; beyond them, everything is dark and nothing can be observed. Thus it is.
Holding such a view, they conclude that these sentient beings of the world throughout the ten directions have existed spontaneously without cause for eighty thousand kalpas;
by such reckoning, they lose their correct universal knowledge, fall into the ranks of external paths, and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This person calculates that the mere fact of constant flux and non-abiding constitutes impermanence, thereby giving rise to the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).

When this person points to one whose perceptions and formations (*saṃskāra*) have already ceased, they say, "There was originally no cause," meaning there was no cause for the prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*).

That the mechanism of birth is completely shattered means that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) has been fully exposed. Because the aggregate of formations is entirely shattered and the six faculties of cognition no longer function, one rides upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

The merit of the middle faculty of the eye penetrates to see all classes of sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas of the past, as they drift with the waves of karma, dying here and being born there in an uninterrupted succession. Beyond those eighty thousand kalpas, however, it is dark and nothing is seen;
they falsely calculate this state of darkness where nothing is observed to be the "Dark Principle" (mṛtyu-tattva), or "Spontaneity," or "Chaos," not realizing that it is simply their own—
Because their capacity for perception is limited, they give rise to false conceptualizations, believing that all sentient beings have existed without cause since eighty thousand kalpas ago.
Through such deliberation, they become deluded by this *amūrta-tattva* (the obscure principle), mistaking it for the nature of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Remaining seated and guarding this state, they do not advance further; this is what is meant by "continuing as before to mistake a thief for one's own son."
It is said that they fall, they perish, and they are deluded; those who speak of "external paths" (tīrthikas) are those of heterodox views.
This is because they do not perceive the fundamental root and thus give rise to erroneous calculations.
Second, these people see only the branches and deny the cause. Why is this? Because although these people have perceived the root of birth, they [fail to understand it].
When humans are born as humans, they awaken as humans; when birds are born as birds, they remain birds. Crows have always been black, and cranes have always been white.
Human beings are originally upright, while animals are originally horizontal. White is not produced by washing, and black is not created by dyeing.

From eighty thousand kalpas ago, nothing has changed or shifted; even now, at the end of this present form, it is likewise so. Since I have never seen Bodhi from the very beginning, how could there be any further attainment?
Regarding the matter of Bodhi, you should know that today all phenomena are fundamentally without cause;

by such conceptualization, one loses right and universal knowledge and falls into the ranks of externalists, deluded about the nature of Bodhi. This is called the first type of externalist who establishes the doctrine of causelessness.
"Endless causelessness" refers to the absence of cause at the future limit (*aparānta*). The following passage infers the future limit by means of the past limit (*pūrvānta*):
"I have never seen Bodhi from the very beginning in the past limit; how then could there be any further matter of attaining Bodhi in the future limit?
This arises because one has not yet perceived the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) and is thus unable to discern the individual threads of each life, seeing only the whole.
It is likely that most sentient beings, having long held this view without change, simply perceive it thus upon meeting one another.

If those who have attained the four fruits of arhatship were to exercise the power of manifesting consciousness (*vijñāna-kṣaya-jñāna*), they would be able to discern the individual life-continuities of each; they would never, however, cling to the notion of spontaneous existence (*svabhāva*).

Master Yue stated that the character "root" (*ben*) in the phrase "the root of no-cause" (*wuben-yin-zhi ben*) should actually be the character "branch" (*mo*); [it refers to] the one who possesses correct and universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbuddha*).

To maintain that there is no cause is not correct knowledge. Because one fails to discern the past and future limits—stopping at eighty thousand kalpas—and because one does not realize that good and evil manifest according to karma, one falsely calculates that before eighty thousand kalpas all existed spontaneously and after eighty thousand kalpas all will exist spontaneously as nothingness.
This constitutes the doctrine of annihilationism and is subsumed within wrong views.

Ānanda, when these good sons within samādhi concentrate their luminous and upright minds so that Māra finds no opportunity, they investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source.
If, within this perfect and eternal state, they give rise to conceptual calculations, such persons fall into the four theories of universal permanence.
The first is when these persons investigate the nature of both mind and objects and find that neither has a cause; having practiced this, they conclude that all things are permanent.

First, they are able to know all births and deaths among sentient beings throughout the ten directions within twenty thousand kalpas; these cycles revolve without ever being lost, yet they reckon them to be permanent.
Second, these people exhaustively investigate the source of the four great elements and the permanence of their four natures;

through cultivation, they are able to know all births and deaths among sentient beings throughout the ten directions within forty thousand kalpas, seeing that their essence is eternally constant and never... [lost].
Third, these people exhaustively investigate the six sense faculties;

because the manas-clinging consciousness perceives that within the mind, intellect, and consciousness there is an original source and locus whose nature is eternally constant, they cultivate the ability to know that all sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas circulate without losing their fundamental, ever-abiding nature, and thus they reckon this imperishable nature to be permanent. Fourth—

Once this person has exhausted the source of perception, the principle of their nature is such that there is no longer any flowing, ceasing, moving, or revolving; the conceptual mind of birth and death has now been eternally extinguished.
Within this principle, it naturally becomes non-arising and non-ceasing. Because of the mind they employ, they calculate this state to be permanent.

Due to this calculation of permanence, they lose correct and universal knowledge and fall into the ranks of external paths, deluding themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi. This is called the second [delusion].
The non-Buddhists establish a doctrine of pervasive permanence;
they conceive of that which flows and shifts without ceasing as being universally eternal, thereby giving rise to the view of permanence. Changshui says:

"Because the birth-and-death of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) continues in succession without being lost, it is called 'permanent. This is because they reckon these four types [of permanence] to pervade all phenomena."

Therefore, it is called "Perfect" (*yuan*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Based upon the superior, middling, and inferior levels of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one gives rise to the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*) and produces four types of eternalist theories.

The first [type] calculates that the mind and its objects are eternal; this is the notion of a self (*ātman-saṃjñā*). It destroys [the view of] conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and manifests as a vehicle.
Relying on this mind, one investigates from where the two natures of the mind and its objects arise. However, one perceives that they exist through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."
Because of these limitations, when one reaches the limit beyond twenty thousand kalpas, one is unable to see further;

thus, one calculates that all sentient beings exist within those twenty thousand kalpas without cause. Yet, one does not calculate that there is no cause beyond the kalpas as being annihilation, but only calculates that the continuity within the kalpas is pervasive and eternal.
As for the second type of mental state, which differs from the former calculation, it calculates the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) below.
Third, there are also practitioners whose minds open through this practice and who investigate that the fundamental nature of the four great elements is originally and eternally abiding.

By cultivating according to this, because the measure of their mental capacity is limited, they perceive that although sentient beings undergo birth and death within forty thousand kalpas, the essence and nature of the four great elements remain constant; however, this too is merely what is perceived within a specific span of kalpas. Third.

The lower calculation refers to the eight consciousnesses: "constant root" (*changgen*) is a corruption of the character for "root" (*gen*); the six consciousnesses are those of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
*manas* is the seventh consciousness; and "grasping and receiving" (*zhishou*) is the eighth consciousness.

This arises because the practitioner, by means of the awakened mind, exhaustively investigates the fundamental source of the mind, thought, and consciousness, thereby realizing that their original nature is eternally constant and majestic.
The Master said: "The fundamental source and locus refers to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).

By practicing in reliance upon this, one is able to observe that throughout eighty thousand kalpas, all sentient beings die here and are born there, yet their fundamental nature remains eternally abiding.

This is because both the sixth and eighth consciousnesses take the seventh consciousness as the root-source of their arising and ceasing; therefore, they falsely reckon this root-source of arising and ceasing to be eternal."

To dwell upon the nature [of mind] as one perceives a fine stream and call it "stilled water" is still not to have glimpsed the true, constant flow of the eight consciousnesses, let alone the wondrous nature of Bodhi.
What is called the "root of birth and death throughout immeasurable kalpas" is what the deluded person calls the "original person.
Fourth, the lower calculation of the exhaustion of thought is the fundamental perception of the *skandha* of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). It arises...

The *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is the principle of activity. Practitioners delusively claim that the flow and cessation of transmigration all belong to the mind of perception (*saṃjñā-citta*);
now that these have been eternally extinguished, they assume that the principle of neither-arising-nor-ceasing naturally belongs to formations.

Without needing to investigate or observe further, they recklessly conceive of it as permanent, not realizing that the *skandha* of formations is precisely the root source of arising and ceasing. These four [types of practitioners] all reckon [the state] in terms of arising and ceasing.
The view of permanence is subsumed within the extreme views of eternalism.

Furthermore, O sons of good family who are firm and concentrated in samādhi, if your minds are upright and demons find no opportunity, yet you fail to exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and instead contemplate that profound, pure, and eternally quiescent source as being subject to agitation;
if you give rise to speculative calculations regarding self and others, such a person falls into [the error of permanence].
Regarding the first of the four inverted views, the doctrine that one part is impermanent and one part is permanent:

this person contemplates the wondrously luminous mind as pervading the worlds of the ten directions, regarding it as a profound and tranquil ultimate *ātman*. From this, they calculate that this self pervades the ten directions, remaining firm, luminous, and unmoving;
they hold that all sentient beings are born and die within their own heart, and thus [they conclude] that the nature of their own mind...

To call that which is subject to arising and ceasing "permanent" is truly the nature of impermanence. Second, such a person does not contemplate their own mind, but instead surveys the lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
seeing places where kalpas are destroyed, they designate this as the nature of ultimate impermanence, while seeing places where kalpas are not destroyed, they designate this as ultimate permanence.
Third, such a person separately contemplates their own mind as being subtle, refined, and profound.
It is like fine dust circulating throughout the ten directions; its nature does not shift or change, yet it causes this body to arise and perish in each moment.
This indestructible nature is called the "nature of the self" (*ātman*) and is eternal. All births and deaths flow forth from this self, which is termed the "nature of impermanence.

Fourth, when this person knows that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted and sees the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) flowing on, they reckon this constant flow of the formations to be the nature of permanence.
The extinction of form, sensation, perception, and so forth is termed "impermanence.

Because they calculate that one part is impermanent while another part is permanent, they fall into the ranks of the non-Buddhists and delude themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi; this is called the third type of non-Buddhist doctrine:
the theory of partial permanence.
This refers to the dualistic calculation of permanence and impermanence; "self" refers to one's own body, while "others" refers to sentient beings and the land.

Indeed, within the nature of equality, there is fundamentally no self or other, yet one falsely calculates self and other. In the definitive meaning of the Middle Way, there is originally no biased attachment, yet one falsely clings to the two extremes.
This is what the National Preceptor meant when he said that in the Southern tradition of Buddhism, the Dharma is half-born and half-extinguished.
Furthermore, the first [category] refers to those who, while abiding in the states of self and others, calculate [the self] as permanent or impermanent;

the first two phrases cite their meditative practice (*vipaśyanā*), while "serenely" and what follows clarify their falling into the calculation of a *puruṣa* (spiritual self). This is the final of the twenty-five *tattvas* (principles of darkness).
That "the self pervades the ten directions" means that the measure of the self is equal to empty space. This is because they calculate that there exists a true self.
Because that which pervades the ten directions is without birth or cessation, it is eternal; because sentient beings arise within my mind and undergo birth after death, they are impermanent.
Second, to reckon the three calamities and the places beyond their reach as being eternal or impermanent:
this arises from not observing one's own mind, but only observing the physical realm, wherein everything from the third dhyāna downward is subject to the three calamities.
One calculates that [the realms] above the fourth dhyāna, which are beyond the reach of the three calamities, are permanent; this constitutes the third [type of calculation].
Furthermore, one calculates one's own body and mind as being both permanent and impermanent; because the body is coarse while the mind is subtle, one contemplates them separately.
Although the mind transmigrates through the ten directions, its nature does not undergo change, and thus it is regarded as permanent, capable of governing this body.

Because birth and death are impermanent, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that their essence is permanent and subtle, as fine as a single atom (*paramāṇu*), and because it secretly functions within the body to perform its activities.
Fourth, one observes the four aggregates (*skandha*) below and makes a dualistic calculation:

having already calculated that the first three aggregates have ceased and are thus impermanent, one names the present flux of the fourth aggregate, the mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), "permanent. This concludes the section below.
Establishing external treatises— this is also subsumed within the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Furthermore,

among those sons of good family in samādhi who have stabilized their upright minds so that Māra finds no opportunity, when they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound,
pure, yet eternally agitated source, if they engage in conceptual calculations regarding its various states, such a person falls into [error].
Regarding the four theories on finitude: first, there are those whose minds reckon that the source of birth flows and functions without ceasing;
they consider the past and future to be finite, while considering the continuous mind to be infinite.

Second, there are those who observe eighty thousand kalpas and perceive that before these eighty thousand kalpas, sentient beings were silent, with nothing heard or seen; this state of no hearing or seeing is termed "infinite."
There are sentient beings who dwell in what is called "having limits" (sānta). Third, these people reckon that their self possesses the nature of boundlessness through universal knowledge;

yet all those beings currently exist within the scope of my knowledge, while I have never known the nature of their own knowing—thus they are said not to have attained a mind of boundlessness, but rather possess only the nature of limits.
Fourth, these people exhaustively investigate the emptiness of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha), based on what they perceive.
With the mental path, one calculates that within the single body of every sentient being, all are characterized by half-arising and half-ceasing;
one clarifies that within all worlds, everything is half-finite and half-infinite.

By calculating in this way regarding the finite and the infinite, one falls into the ranks of the externalists and becomes deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi. This is called the fourth type of externalist.
Establishing the thesis of having limits:

this involves a dual reckoning of both having limits and being limitless. There are four stages [of analysis], namely: views regarding the three periods of time (*traiyadhvika*), what is seen and heard, the self and others, and arising and ceasing.
First, below, one reckons having limits and being limitless by means of the three periods of time, wherein the source of birth flows forth in its functional operation.

"Non-ceasing" refers to observing that the aggregates of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) flow and shift in the present without interruption, and consequently reckoning the past as already gone and the future as yet to come as having limits, while reckoning the place where the present continuity remains uninterrupted as being limitless.
This is to falsely establish boundaries within that which has no boundaries; it is like carving lines upon empty space. How could this be?
To know that the Way of Bodhi has no past, future, or present—this is the first. Second, regarding the calculation of "having limits" or "being limitless" based on what is seen and heard:
the places within eighty thousand kalpas where there is seeing and hearing are considered "having limits," as they are restricted by the number eighty thousand;
the places where there is neither hearing nor seeing are considered "limitless," as they are infinite and boundless.
It cannot be known; these three [views] are inferior reckonings that judge both self and others as being finite or infinite.

Because they reckon their own *ātman* (self) to perceive forms when forms come and hear sounds when sounds come, knowing them all without exception, they claim for themselves alone the nature of infinity, while regarding all other sentient beings as merely manifestations of their own nature.
Furthermore, I merely see the person and do not see the nature of that person; thus, I reckon that the person does not possess boundless nature and name it "bounded nature.
How could you know that it is your own failure to perceive this, rather than the nature of that person being bounded?
Fourth, regarding the calculation of permanence and impermanence based on arising and ceasing: this person exhausts this *xing-yin* (aggregate of formations).
To claim that there is first existence and subsequently emptiness, or first birth and subsequently extinction,

and based on one's own limited perceptions to falsely calculate that within the body of a sentient being half belongs to birth and half belongs to extinction— thereby judging birth to be the finite limit and extinction to be the infinite limit—
is subsumed under false views. This deludes the nature of bodhi, for the nature of bodhi has no such divisions or stages.
Because it is boundless. Furthermore,
among those sons of good family within samādhi who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, if Māra finds no opportunity and they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings,

observing that profound, pure, and eternally quiescent source of constant agitation, yet within their cognition and views give rise to conceptual calculations, such persons will fall into [the following state].
The four kinds of perverted views, the immortality of evasive equivocation, and the pervasive false discourses are as follows:

First, this person contemplates the source of transformation; seeing the place where things shift and flow, they call it "change. Seeing the place where things continue in succession, they call it "permanence. Seeing the place where what is perceived arises, they call it "birth.
Not seeing the place where perception itself ceases, they call it "extinction. This refers to the nature of the cause of continuity, the place where the essence is never severed.

That which is called "increase" refers to the state within the midst of the continuous succession [of phenomena] when they are free from [extremes]. That which is called "decrease" refers to their respective places of arising.
That which is called "existence" refers to their mutual presence; that which is called "non-existence" refers to their mutual absence.

Contemplating this entirely through principle, yet perceiving it differently according to one's mental application, when seekers of the Dharma come to ask about its meaning, I answer: "I now hold that there is both arising and ceasing, and both existence and non-existence."
Furthermore, at all times they increase and decrease [the discourse], confusing their speech so that the person before them loses the chapters and sentences;

second, this person observes the mind intently and finds it nowhere, and because there is nothing to be attained through such observation, when someone comes to question them, they answer with only a single word, saying merely "non-existence," and apart from this non-existence, they have nothing further to say; third, this person...

Observe their minds closely: each has its own particular state, and because they have attained realization, when someone comes to question them, they respond with only a single word, saying simply "It is so.
Aside from this, they have nothing further to say. Fourth, there are those who perceive both existence and non-existence;
because their objective realm is fragmented, their minds are likewise distracted. When someone comes to question them, they answer by saying, "It is both existent and non-existent."
Furthermore, within this state of "neither being nor non-being," there is no room for any deceptive equivocation that can withstand rigorous inquiry;
because of such conceptualization, one falls into the external paths through deceptive sophistry and empty nothingness, thereby deluding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the fifth type of externalist, characterized by the fourfold perversions, the "immortal equivocation," and the pervasive conceptualization of empty discourse.

These constitute four kinds of evasive equivocation (*vāg-vibhramśa*). The former views—namely, the extremes of permanence and impermanence, or finitude and infinity—have not yet reached such confusion;
however, this [view] which asserts both permanence and impermanence, as well as both finitude and infinity, is a total equivocation and the most extreme form of perversion (*viparyāsa*).
As for "knowledge and vision" (*jñāna-darśana*), it refers to that which is known and seen within that meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

The *Abhidharmavibhāṣā-śāstra* states that non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) maintain that the heavens are eternal and designate this as "immortality. They believe that by answering questions without confusion, one will be reborn in those heavens;

thus, fearing that providing an answer while actually lacking knowledge would constitute evasive equivocation (*vāg-vibhramśa*), they respond to inquiries by saying, "This is a secret and should not be disclosed," or they provide indefinite answers. The Buddha’s teachings rebuke this, saying: [The Buddha said: "If one does not know, one should say, 'I do not know. If one knows, one should say, 'I know. To claim 'I do not know' when one knows, or to claim 'I know' when one does not know—this is called false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*). Furthermore, if one claims 'I do not know' regarding what one actually knows, or 'I know' regarding what one does not know, this is called deceptive speech (*saṃpramoṣa-vāda*). If one says, 'This is a secret and should not be told,' or provides an indefinite answer, this is called evasive equivocation (*vāg-vibhramśa*). One who practices such speech will surely fall into the hells. Thus, the Buddha strictly forbids evasive equivocation and insists on speaking with clarity and truthfulness. This is because such deceptive speech obstructs the path to liberation and leads to rebirth in the miserable realms. Therefore, practitioners should cultivate a mind of straightforwardness and refrain from all forms of equivocation.

This first type of "true equivocation" clarifies that the eight [states] are also equivocations; by taking the single life-and-death *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) and calculating it as eight kinds—namely, the four pairs within the four propositions—one posits the state of having limits (*antavat*) during its upward migration and flux, and the state of being limitless (*anantavat*) during its intermediate continuity.
This does not accord with the principle of non-alteration according to conditions, even regarding the eighty thousand [dharmas].
The places seen within a kalpa are called "arising," while those not seen beyond eighty thousand kalpas are called "extinction.

This is the principle that the fruit arises and the cause perishes, wherein the continuity remains uninterrupted; this constitutes "increase. The places separated from that interval constitute "decrease";

this is the principle that is neither increasing nor decreasing. The place of arising is "existence," and the place of extinction is "non-existence"; thus, both existence and non-existence are simultaneously discarded.

The purport of this is that those who contemplate through the principle as a whole are observing the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Those who apply their minds to see distinctions generate eight separate meanings.

Because they lack a settled view of their own, whenever they encounter someone and are questioned, they answer with a confused mixture of the "two pillars" doctrine, thereby preventing the interlocutor from grasping the meaning within the phrases and sentences; thus, as soon as they hear it, [they lose it].

The first [point] explains that this person lacks both; the second clarifies that they are merely devoid of deceptive confusion (*kuhaka*), for when this person contemplates the mind from the standpoint of non-existence, there is an entryway from that very standpoint of non-existence;
thus, when questioned by others, they respond that "everything is non-existent. The third clarifies that they are merely characterized by deceptive confusion;
for when this person contemplates the mind from the standpoint of existence, they find an entryway from that very standpoint of existence.

On the road, he encountered people who questioned him and he answered; this was the case everywhere. Previously, he had presented eight propositions simultaneously, which could be termed "evasive" (vāg-vibhāṣita);
now, however, he calculates existence and non-existence individually and answers with a single word—why is this also called "evasive"?
Answer: To cling to objects while failing to accord with principle is "evasion" (kuhaka); to lack a central point of correctness within is "confusion" (vyākula). Now, observe the [fifth] chapter...
First, regarding the fourth [type of] speech, both possibilities are permitted; it mostly confuses the mind and ultimately does not accord with principle, while also involving pretension.
Third and fourth, these types of speech involve only a one-sided, pretentious intent; they mostly confuse the mind and ultimately do not serve as a correct standard.

Since they both lead to confusion, they are collectively termed "pretentious and confusing" (kuṭila-vyākarana). Fourth, below, it clarifies the pretentious confusion regarding existence and non-existence, wherein both existence and non-existence are [confused].
The observer means that having already seen their mutual existence, they also see their mutual non-existence.
Because the object is bifurcated, the mind is likewise disturbed; this means that since the perceived object is not fixed, the perceiving mind is also not fixed.
Thus, when a questioner asks, one immediately replies: "That which is 'also existent' is precisely 'also non-existent,' because existence is itself non-existence."

To be not exclusively focused on non-existence (*wu*) is also not to be incorrect; yet there is something by which non-existence is not [the ultimate]. To be not exclusively focused on existence (*you*) is likewise so.
This is truly because within the confusion of views and the profound obscurity of the indistinct, there is no fixed standard;

thus, it all ultimately results in nothing but distortion and disorder. This is also subsumed under false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). If one is a person who has attained the truth, they speak of both existence and non-existence.
The Way has no total existence, yet there is a living path for emerging from it. Furthermore, within samādhi,
those sons of good family who have stabilized their correct minds so that Māras cannot find an opening, yet who exhaustively investigate the origin of all living beings and observe that profound,
pure source which is constantly subject to agitation— those who harbor speculative calculations regarding this inexhaustible flow fall into [the following state].
Regarding the notion that there is a sign after death, one may give rise to inverted thoughts or cling to the body, saying, "Form is the self";

or seeing the self as encompassing and pervading the lands, saying, "The self possesses form"; or seeing the preceding objects of perception revolve according to the self, saying, "Form belongs to the self";
or again, seeing the self as persisting within the continuity of formations, saying, "The self is within form. All such conceptualizations are termed the view that there is a sign after death.

Thus, in this cyclical process, there are sixteen aspects. From this, one may reckon that ultimate affliction and ultimate enlightenment—these two natures—proceed side by side without ever touching one another.
Because of such speculative reckoning, one falls into the heterodox paths by asserting existence after death;
thus, one deludes oneself regarding the nature of bodhi. This is called the sixth heterodox path, which establishes the aspect of existence after death within the five aggregates.
The Discourse on the Perversion of Mind.
This calculation consists of sixteen types of perception regarding the future limit (*aparānta*). The "inexhaustible flow" is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*);

because one perceives characteristics within this aggregate of formations, it—along with the previously extinguished aggregate of perception (*vijñānaskandha*)—all becomes characterized by marks. Furthermore, form (*rūpa*) possesses four characteristics.

Regarding these four views: first, "form is the self," which means that form itself is the self; second, "the self possesses form," which means the self is large and form is small, with form existing within the self;
third, "form belongs to the self," which means the self exists apart from form; fourth, "the self is in form," which means form is large and the self is small, with the self existing within form.
Since this is the case for the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), it is likewise so for the other three aggregates.
This is because, by inferring from the existence of birth in the present life that there is likewise death in the future, one speaks of "the signs of existence after death.
This constitutes four of the sixty-two views. From here below, further speculative reckonings are established:
it is said that "afflictions" encompass all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*), while "bodhi" encompasses all pure phenomena (*vyavadāna-dharma*). Having understood these four...
If the *ālayavijñāna* (the storehouse consciousness) were permanent, one would know that the two natures of affliction and bodhi proceed side by side without ever touching one another;

thus, the ordinary person would remain definitively ordinary and the sage would remain definitively a sage, and there would absolutely be no such thing as transforming the ordinary into the sage or transforming afflictions into bodhi.
Those who confuse the nature of bodhi are deluded regarding the principle of the unchanging following conditions.
Because they recognize death as being permanent, they are said to be deluded; this is also subsumed within the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

Furthermore, among those sons of good family who are firm and concentrated in their correct minds during samādhi, such that Māras find no opportunity, they exhaustively investigate the origin of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, and eternally quiescent source of agitation.
Among those who first eliminate form, sensation, and perception, there are those who engage in conceptual calculation.
This person falls into the inverted view of the "signless" (animitta) resolve after death;

they perceive the cessation of form (*rūpa*) as having no basis for its shape, observe the cessation of perception (*saṃjñā*) as having nothing to which the mind is bound, and know the cessation of sensation (*vedanā*) as being without further connection. The nature of the aggregates (*skandha*) dissolves and scatters;

even if there remains a principle of physical existence, it lacks sensation and perception, being identical to grass and trees. Even this physical substance, when manifest before one, cannot be apprehended.
After death, how can there still be various signs? Examining this through comparison, one finds that after death, signs are absent; thus, in this cycle, there are eight states of signlessness.
From this, some may reckon that the causes and effects of *nirvāṇa* are all empty, existing merely as names, and ultimately resulting in total annihilation.
Because they speculate that there is nothing after death, they fall into the ways of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), deluding their own nature of Bodhi.
This is called the seventh heterodox doctrine: the inverted view of mindlessness after death established within the five aggregates (*skandhas*).

This calculation concerns the eight signs of non-existence regarding the future limit (*aparānta*). Because one perceives that the first three aggregates have already ceased and are signless, one consequently calculates that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is entirely signless as well.
Since form (*rūpa*) exists because of shape (*saṃsthāna*), when form ceases, shape is non-existent.

Because the mind is bound by causes, conditions, and perceptions, when perception ceases, the mind has nothing to which it is bound. Since there is sensation (*vedanā*), it maintains and connects form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*);

therefore, when sensation is absent, there is no further attachment. Once the three aggregates (*skandha*) have dissolved, even the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra*) will ultimately return to cessation.
This is the deduction through negation. Now, observing this body in the present, it does not yet possess the characteristics of the aggregates.
If one can attain death, how could there be any marks of the *skandhas*? This further uses the body to verify death, decisively knowing that there are no marks of the *skandhas*.
From this point downward, the calculation shifts to the view that the causes and effects of *nirvāṇa* are entirely non-existent, all returning to annihilationism.

Those who are deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi do so because they fail to establish even a single speck of dust within the nature of Bodhi, yet fail to discard even a single dharma; it is truly [thus].
"Emptiness is wondrous existence, and wondrous existence is true emptiness; it is not annihilationism. Therefore, this too is subsumed within the view of extremes.

Furthermore, among those sons of good family in samādhi who have stabilized their upright minds so that Māras cannot find an opening, they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and observe that source which is profoundly pure yet constantly subject to agitation.
While abiding in the state of activity, they simultaneously suppress sensation and perception, dualistically calculating both existence and non-existence."

Those who refute the intrinsic nature and characteristics [of phenomena] fall into the inverted doctrine that after death there is "neither-existence-nor-non-existence. Within form, sensation, perception, and mental formations, they perceive both existence and non-existence;

as conditioned activities flow on, they internally contemplate them as neither existent nor non-existent. Thus they cycle through these states until the aggregates, elements, and sense bases are exhausted.
Encountering any single condition, they claim that after death there is either a mark of existence or a mark of non-existence, and they further calculate the nature of all conditioned formations.

Because their natures have undergone transformation and distortion, their minds give rise to a realization that both existence and non-existence are neither true, and they lose track of the distinction between the void and the real.

From this, they engage in speculative calculation that after death there is "neither [existence nor non-existence]," and because their future state is shrouded in darkness and beyond description, they fall into the path of externalists, deluding themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the eighth externalist doctrine: the inverted view of mind within the five aggregates that asserts "after death, there is neither [existence nor non-existence]."

This calculation is that both existence and non-existence are negated. To calculate both existence and non-existence means to calculate existence based on the place where [the self] persists and non-existence based on the place where it ceases.

Their intrinsic natures mutually subvert one another: existence is subverted by the present existence of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations), which refutes the prior non-existence of the [first] three aggregates;
and the prior non-existence of the [first] three aggregates subverts the present existence of the *saṃskāra-skandha*. After death, both...
"Non-" refers to the refutation of "non-existence," which establishes that it is not non-existent; the refutation of "existence" establishes that it is not existent.
Therefore, it is said to be neither existent nor non-existent. Regarding the observation of existence and non-existence within form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), and perception (*saṃjñā*):

this means that although one observes the activity of formations (*saṃskāra*) within the cessation of form, sensation, and perception, these are likewise like the cessation of form, sensation, and perception—namely, they are non-existent. Within the flux of formations, one internally contemplates their absence.

"Not non-existent" means that while within the agitation of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), although the previous three [aggregates] have already ceased and are no longer present, they nonetheless exist as part of the ongoing continuity and are thus not non-existent.
Thus, by investigating the four aggregates in this manner, the pervasive conceptualization results in eight "neither-is-nor-is-not" characteristics;
therefore, whichever single aggregate one mentions, it all becomes a case of "double negation. Furthermore, when conceptualizing the various formations, they are certainly not taken in isolation.

Pointing to a single practice while simultaneously pointing to the myriad dharmas, it is said that these myriad dharmas, in their flux and transformation, are all subject to "double negation" (ubhayābhāva);
therefore, it is called the "arising of universal awakening. Regarding the phrase "neither void nor real": because it is not non-existent, it cannot be called void;
because it is not existent, it cannot be called real. Based on this reckoning, one concludes that after death, both [existence and non-existence] are negated.
This means using the case of the living as an analogy for what follows after death. Regarding the phrase "the future limit is obscure and cannot be spoken of":
the "future limit" refers to the period of the future following death; it is "obscure," meaning it is profound and dark.

This implies that the matters of the future limit are so remote and indistinct that one cannot say that existence exists, nor can one say that non-existence does not exist; both are beyond description. Thus, it cannot be spoken of.
If one has not attained true and penetrating insight, but merely speculates based on vague impressions to compose such a treatise, it is problematic.
However, for one who has truly realized the vision of the Truth (satyadarśana), it does not matter whether they speak of existence or non-existence; both constitute a sublime discourse.

For those who are deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi, to say that the nature of Bodhi is neither existent nor non-existent—since its nature transcends the paths of speech and thought—is itself subsumed under the category of false views.

Furthermore, among those good sons within *samādhi* who have stabilized their minds in right concentration such that Māras find no opportunity, they investigate the root of all living beings and observe that source of profound clarity which is yet constantly subject to agitation.
If, regarding this, they subsequently engage in speculative calculations concerning non-arising, these people fall into the seven theories of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*).
They may speculate on the extinction of birth and death, or the extinction of desire, or the extinction of suffering, or the extinction of ultimate bliss.
Or, by utterly relinquishing and extinguishing such cycles until the seven limits are exhausted, one manifests their total destruction;
yet once destroyed, they no longer reckon that there is a gradual extinction or falling away after death.
This is the delusion regarding the nature of bodhi among the ninth class of outsiders, who establish within the five aggregates a perverse doctrine of annihilation after death.

This is the calculation that there is cessation and extinction at seven locations; that what follows and follows is non-existent, meaning the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations) perishes moment by moment.

Or one calculates birth and extinction as follows: this calculation holds that the nature of the aggregates (*skandhas*) is like water from a sourceless spring—some flow for a short distance before being exhausted, while others flow for a long distance before being exhausted.
Therefore, although the seven locations of birth differ in their proximity or distance, in the end they are all cut off and exhausted. Seven.
The "limits" refer to the four continents, the six heavens of the desire realm, and the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas, as well as the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*).

The extinction of the body refers to humans and devas of the desire realm; the exhaustion of desire refers to the first dhyāna; the exhaustion of suffering refers to the second dhyāna; supreme bliss refers to the third dhyāna;
and supreme equanimity refers to the fourth dhyāna and the formless realms. As for "extinguishing before one's eyes," the three aggregates have already [ceased].
The cessation of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is likewise. In all seven locations, there is manifest severance and extinction; after death, one will certainly not be reborn again.

If the later followers of the Confucian school here merely calculate that extinction occurs within the human realm, they still do not permit that the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) obstruct the nature of Bodhi.
This is because the nature of Bodhi is eternally abiding and uninterrupted throughout the past and the present.
This is also subsumed within the view of extremes. Furthermore,
O sons of good family who are firm and concentrated in right mind within samādhi, if Māra finds no opportunity because you have exhausted the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound,
pure, and eternal source of agitation, yet subsequently engage in speculative calculations regarding future births, such a person falls into [the view of extremes].
Regarding the five theories on nirvāṇa: some take the desire realm as the true basis for transformation (*parāvṛtti*), because one perceives its perfect clarity and gives rise to a longing for it;
some take the first dhyāna, because its nature is free from sorrow; some take the second dhyāna, because the mind is free from suffering;

some take the third dhyāna, because of its extreme accordance with bliss; and some take the fourth dhyāna, because both suffering and pleasure have perished and it is not subject to the nature of saṃsāric birth and death.
Deluded regarding the tainted heavens, they take them to be unconditioned; finding security in these five locations, they regard them as the supreme, pure refuge.

Thus they cycle through these five locations until reaching their ultimate end, whereby they calculate that there is nirvana within these five present states. Falling into the ranks of external paths, they confuse the nature of bodhi.
This is called the tenth external path: the inverted doctrine of the five aggregates which posits five forms of nirvana in the present.
This calculation refers to the attainment of nirvana within the five realms of existence. Alternatively, the term "or" indicates an uncertainty;

those who take the desire realm to be nirvana are like the practitioners of the Immortal school who reckon that the Jade Emperor presides over the thirty-three heavens as the supreme realm of the Mysterious Metropolis (Xuandu Shangqing), a place of neither birth nor death.
They do not realize that this is none other than Śakra, the Lord of the Six Heavens of Desire. From this heaven, clarity arises.
Ying [the master] gave rise to clarity that surpassed the sun and moon, and thus reckoned this state to be the manifestation of *nirvāṇa*.
However, according to the preceding text, the first dhyāna is free from the sensation of suffering (*duḥkha-vedanā*) such that no suffering can oppress it;

the second dhyāna is free from the sensation of grief (*daurmanasya-vedanā*) such that no grief can reach it. Therefore, the claim that "the first dhyāna is without grief" and "the second dhyāna is without suffering" is an error.
Furthermore, in the third dhyāna, one attains the bliss of ultimate peace because of having attained the joy of cessation (*śānti-sukha*);

in the fourth dhyāna, both suffering and pleasure are simultaneously extinguished, such that one cannot be moved by any worldly conditions of suffering or pleasure, is not destroyed by the three calamities, and is free from arising and ceasing.

These states are all delusions regarding the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) conditioned realm, wherein they mistake the conditioned for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and take birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) for nirvāṇa. This arises from perceiving the lower realms.

Because they find no peace there, they instead reckon these five places to be secure; because they perceive the defilement and turbidity of the lower realms, they reckon these five places to be superior and pure.
As for the term "ultimate," they reckon that all five of these places constitute the final fruit.
Regarding "nirvāṇa in the present," it means that these five places are nirvāṇa in the present, as one experiences happiness in the present life.
Because they do not await a future life, these are also subsumed under wrong views; they delude the nature of Bodhi because Bodhi and Nirvana still lie far in the distance.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of deluded understandings regarding *dhyāna* all manifest because the mind is applied in a state of mutual conflict within the *saṃskāra-skandha*.
These sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they fail to reflect upon themselves when encountering these manifestations before them.
Mistaking delusion for enlightenment, they claim to have attained the state of a sage. Having committed such a great falsehood, they shall fall into the Avīci Hell.

You must take these words of the Tathāgata and, after my parinirvāṇa, transmit them during the Age of Dharma-Decline, so that all sentient beings may universally awaken to this meaning and not allow the demons of their own minds to arise.
Deeply protecting and shielding [beings] from the concealment of false views, he instructs their bodies and minds to awaken to the true meaning;

ensuring they do not encounter bypaths on the Unsurpassed Way, he prevents them from seeking little and being satisfied with it, so that they may become Great Enlightened Kings who point clearly toward purity.
This is an exhortation to provide protection; thus, those who manifest such awakening have their minds give rise to false awakening.
They recognize it as awakening but do not realize it is delusion, thereby giving rise to deep calamity within themselves. This means that external demons do not disturb them;

rather, it is the demons of one's own mind that create calamity—what is called "creating calamity for oneself. Therefore, know that when the mind is correct, the affairs are correct; when the mind is deviant, the affairs are deviant.
If one has not yet realized the single mind, then every path encountered will be false; even correct practice becomes deviant conduct, and the Buddha-dharma transforms into the gate of Māra.
If one understands the single mind, then there is no action that is not beneficial: even asceticism becomes sublime practice, and a heterodox school is itself the orthodox teaching.
For example, regarding the single method of the non-Buddhist who "roasts the body until it is cooked five times"—if one understands this, then...
Jvalanāntaka is the gateway to the flame of non-conceptual wisdom; if one is obscured by it, the Nirgranthas will produce the great false view of a "blazing" interpretation.
Therefore, since phenomena have no path of right or wrong, the Way lies in its adaptability.
One who does not encounter forked branches on the Unsurpassed Path speaks of these ten kinds as being like the branches of a tree rather than its root, or like the byways of a road.
To diverge from the path is to deviate from the correct; do not allow the mind to seek only a little and consider it sufficient—this is "seeking through prayer.
Do not let the mind's desires limit itself with the vision of the "dormant mouse" or the "jiao-liao bird.

For upon encountering a forked branch, one falls into external paths (mārga-antara), and upon finding a little and considering it sufficient, one falls into the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha). Therefore, I exhort you to act for the sake of all sentient beings.
This serves as a signpost for attaining Buddhahood, directing one to proceed straight ahead without encountering detours along the way.

Ānanda, when that good man practices *samādhi* and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is exhausted, the subtle, clear, and restless commonality of all worldly natures and the generative forces of life suddenly shatter;
the fine and hidden cords [of existence] and the *pudgala* who repays karma [are likewise dissolved].

The profound pulse of resonance was suspended in the Nirvana-heaven; the Great Enlightenment was about to dawn like the crowing of a rooster. Looking toward the east, there was already a refined radiance.
The six sense-faculties were empty and still, no longer wandering or escaping; internally and externally, they were limpid and bright, entering that which has nothing to enter.

He profoundly penetrated the ten directions and the twelve classes of beings, observing the fundamental source of their receiving life and the origin of their grasping at existence. All classes [of beings] were thus perceived.
When one has not yet been summoned into the ten directions but has already attained their shared essence and color, such that they do not sink away but manifest as profound secrets—
this is called the domain of the *vijñāna-skandha*. If, within this state of collective summoning, one has already attained the shared essence and proceeds to dissolve the six gates,

achieving the integration of opening and closing so that seeing, hearing, and the other faculties function interchangeably in pure clarity, then the ten directions, the worlds, and one’s own body and mind become like the *vaiḍūrya* gem.

When the lapis lazuli of the inner and outer is transparently clear, it is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of life;
observing its origin, one finds it to be a phantom-like voidness, with inverted false thoughts as its root.

This clarifies the characteristics of the consciousness aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) when it has not yet been exhausted and when it has been exhausted. "The nature of all worlds" refers to the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
"The generative potential of the common lot" refers to the basis for shared birth. "Basis" indicates the root of birth; "potential" indicates the beginning of movement.
The "subtle and deep cords" also refer to the formations aggregate (*saṃskāra-skandha*), which is called "subtle and deep" because it is hidden, obscure, and profound.

Because it constitutes the essential pivot of birth and death, it is called the "mainstay and knot. Through the aforementioned practice of maintaining a firm and concentrated right mind without ceasing, one reaches this point where the mainstay and knot of birth and death suddenly burst asunder.
*Pudgala*—translated here as "the one who repeatedly undergoes rebirth"—refers to the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*).
Once the mainstay and knot are established, one receives birth within the various realms of the three worlds to repay one's karma.

In these deep pulses, where this is stimulated and that responds, all are suspended far apart and utterly severed; this is the sign that the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) has already been exhausted.
Because birth and death have been cut off, the nature-heaven of *nirvāṇa* is about to break forth with great clarity, like the crowing of a rooster at dawn.
Indeed, the nature-heaven of *nirvāṇa* is shrouded by the five aggregates, remaining as dark as a long night. Each time...

The first aggregate (skandha) appears like the first crow of a rooster; the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) appears like the rooster’s initial crow, the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) like its second crow, and so on until the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) appears like the rooster’s final crow.

Looking back toward the nature-heaven of Nirvāṇa, there is already a subtle glimmer of its essential color, yet it cannot yet be seen with transparency because of the presence of this layer of the aggregate of consciousness.
This is because the boundaries of the physical realm have not yet been shattered. However, once the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is exhausted, there is no further flux;

the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) then attain a state of empty stillness and no longer wander or stray. Thereupon, the internal faculties and external objects transform into a single flavor of profound clarity and luminosity.
Thus, internally one does not perceive the existence of a faculty that enters, and externally one does not perceive the existence of an object that is entered.
"Dust is but consciousness" means that because one is free from the characteristics of the two graspings (subject and object), one attains true abiding in consciousness-only.

"The source of receiving life" refers to the aforementioned individual threads of life, pointing specifically to the eighth consciousness. This is because once the faculties and their objects have dissolved, the karmic consciousness first reveals itself;
now that one has contemplated and seen the source of receiving life, one is further able to maintain and uphold the fundamental basis of rebirth.

Therefore, among the twelve classes of beings, one can no longer be drawn back into rebirth. Upon reaching this stage, the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) is severed, and the universal true suchness (*sarvatraga-tathatā*) is realized;
thus it is said that "one has already attained identity throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
This is merely the initial sign of entering the [first] stage (*bhūmi*), the first realization of true suchness, and the first vision of the Buddha’s realm—like seeing the eastern [quarter].
Now that there is already a refined clarity, this is certainly not the same as the previous state of dullness where one gazed at the Buddha-realm but saw nothing.
However, what is seen of the Buddha-realm is like seeing objects at dawn; it is not like the great brightness of the sky where everything is transparently clear.
This is the sign that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) has not yet been exhausted. If, regarding the various classes of beings, one is still unable to summon them...

Furthermore, one attains identity with those in the ten directions. If one employs the power of Vajra-wisdom to grind away the six sense-gates, such that what is divided is reunited and what is obstructed is opened, all shall be accomplished. Then the six faculties will communicate like neighboring houses, capable of mutual function;
the world, the body, and the mind will be transparent inside and out, becoming as one, like pure Vaiḍūrya crystal.

This perfectly interfused, pure, and precious awakening is not a case of manifesting some hidden mystery; it is the sign that the *vijñāna-skandha* (the aggregate of consciousness) has been exhausted.
The *Zangjing yinyi* (Pronunciation and Meaning of the Canon) states: "Vaiḍūrya" is the name of a jewel; this jewel is blue in color and its substance is extremely hard.
No sword made of any other jewel can destroy it, nor can it be melted or cast by smoke or flames. Only...
Those spirits and deities who possess supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) can fashion it into weapons;
it is also said that they use the egg of the *garuḍa* as a metaphor because it is clear, translucent, and brilliant like a diamond (*vajra*), being indestructible.

Thus, one knows that those who have exhausted their karma and committed no transgressions abide in the stage of the seventh faith (*saptama-śraddhā-bhūmi*), while those whose consciousness is exhausted are equal to the Lesser Arhats (*śrāvaka-arhat*) at the tenth stage.

At the initial stage of the "Abiding in the Mind of Perfected Faith," one first attains entry into perfect penetration; thus, we know that whenever it is said that an Arhat attains perfect penetration, it refers to the first abode (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*).
This is because the perfection of this abode is equal to the separate stages (*pṛthag-bhūmi*), for these are Mahāyāna Arhats.
Indeed, the turbidity of the life-span originates from the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness-aggregate); once the *vijñāna-skandha* is exhausted, the continuity of the physical form [is severed].
Because the mind that was not yet severed has also been completely exhausted, one attains transcendence of the turbidity of life-span (*āyuṣkaṣāya*).
Only here does one see the source of receiving life: it is presided over by the phantom-like, empty non-existence of deluded thought.
To speak of "phantom-like" and "empty non-existence" means that this emptiness is hazy and unreal; it is but a shadow of arising and ceasing within true consciousness, and is not true emptiness.

Ānanda, you should know that this good man has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned formations and returned to the source within consciousness; he has already extinguished arising and ceasing, yet his subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction is not yet perfected.
Consequently, he can cause the obstructions between his own sense organs to merge or open, and likewise [affect] those of the ten directions.

If one perceives that all categories of beings possess a universal consciousness capable of penetrating and entering the perfect source, and establishes this as a true, eternal cause for that to which they take refuge, thereby giving rise to a resolute conviction, such a person falls into the attachment to causes and their underlying causes.
They become a companion to the followers of the Pāśupata school who take refuge in the obscure principle (Pradhāna).
Having lost sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi, they have forfeited true knowledge and vision; this is called the first instance of establishing a mind that clings to what is attained.

They become those who have attained a fruit that is merely a place of refuge, yet which is remote from perfect penetration; they turn their backs on the city of Nirvana and give rise to the seeds of external paths.
The following clarifies the signs of the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) being about to end and not yet ended; there are ten such types. First:

"Because of the cause of causes, one clings to the exhaustion of all formations into emptiness" means that one clearly perceives the emptiness of the formation-aggregate (*saṃskāra-skandha*). "Returning to the source within consciousness" refers to...
The modes of activity dissolve and return to the ocean of consciousness, just as waves subside and transform into clear water.

At this time, birth-and-death has already ceased and the state of quiescent extinction is about to manifest; yet, because the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) has not been shattered, it still remains a covering, such that one has not yet attained perfection regarding the subtle and wondrous principle of quiescent extinction.
Nevertheless, it causes the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) that were previously separated to become unified.
This is the initial convergence; it is also the same as the universal awakening of all categories of beings throughout the ten directions.
That which is not summoned by these various categories has already attained their commonality—this is the manifestation of consciousness when practice is exhausted.

"Awakened awareness is universally interfused, able to enter the perfect source" means that this awakened awareness above communicates with all Buddhas and below is seamlessly merged with all sentient beings. Thus...
The origin of receiving life and the origin of awakening both stem from this. Now that the four aggregates (*skandhas*) have been completely cleared away, the entire body dwells within it;
therefore, it is said that one "is able to enter the perfect origin. This is precisely the realm of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

If, at this point, one gives rise to attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) within this state, one falls into the ranks of the externalists. "That to which one returns" refers to the perfect origin. This means:
One immediately takes this "Perfect Origin" as the place of ultimate rest, and thus establishes it as the cause of true permanence, regarding it as fixed and unchangeable.
Not knowing that this Perfect Origin is in reality not the cause of true permanence, one falsely clings to it as such;
therefore, one falls into the attachment to the cause and the caused. If one holds such a view, then one is no different from the Yellow-Headed Heretic.

The *pradhāna* (primordial matter) clung to by the [Sāṃkhya] path is of the same category as the *tattva* (ultimate principle). Regarding this *tattva*, the *Śataśāstra* states: "From *pradhāna* arises *buddhi* (intellect);
from *buddhi* arises *ahaṃkāra* (ego-consciousness); from *ahaṃkāra* arise the five *tanmātras* (subtle elements); from the five *tanmātras* arise the five great elements (*mahābhūtas*);
