and from the five great elements arise the eleven organs. The *puruṣa* (spiritual self) is the sovereign; it is eternally conscious and remains unimpaired within the sphere of phenomena."
Regarding the "unimpaired grasping of all dharmas," that which is clung to here as the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) is considered the primary truth.
From this *pradhāna*, twenty-three intermediate factors arise; the *puruṣa* (spiritual self) is that which experiences these twenty-three factors.
"Deluded regarding bodhi" means not knowing the correct fruit; "losing knowledge and vision" means not knowing the correct cause. This is so.
Regarding the statement that "the external seeds are established as names, and the mind of attainment is established as the fruit of ultimate refuge":
this is because one fails to realize that perfect Bodhi returns to non-attainment, yet falsely calculates that there is something to be attained and a place of refuge.

Previously, the faculties were obstructed while the Perfect Penetration was opened; now, that which was "perfect" has become pervasive and that which was "penetrating" has become obstructed, thus contradicting and distancing oneself from the goal.
"Previously, regarding Nirvana, you were about to attain great and clear awakening; now, you turn your back on the city of Nirvana and do not see it.
Previously, your awakened mind was about to emerge, and you would have become a child of the Buddha; now, you have instead become of the lineage of external paths."
Ānanda, furthermore, if a good man, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to the point of emptiness, has already extinguished birth and death,
yet his subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction is not yet perfected; if he regards the object of his refuge as his own self,

and develops the superior conviction that all sentient beings within the twelve categories throughout the entirety of space arise from a single stream within his own body— this person then falls into the error of "the subject and the non-subject."
The ability to grasp at Maheśvara, manifesting boundless bodies to become his companions, thereby deluding the Bodhi of the Buddha and losing right knowledge and vision—
this is called the second: establishing the "capable" as the mind, accomplishing the fruit of capable activity, being far removed from perfect penetration, turning one's back on the city of Nirvana,
and giving rise to the seeds of the great prideful heavens where the self is omnipresent and all-pervading.
This is the attachment to the capacity and incapacity of the self. Previously, one recognized the aggregates (*skandhas*) as the locus of reliance;
now, one takes that very locus of prior reliance and grasps it as the essence of consciousness, asserting that all sentient beings flow forth from the essence of this self.

Consequently, one clings to the notion that the self can produce them while they cannot produce it; thus, it is called the attachment to capacity and incapacity. This arises from [the activity of] conceptualization.
This interpretation is precisely of the same category as that of Maheśvara.
For Maheśvara can manifest the bodies of infinite sentient beings, thereby asserting that all sentient beings are his own emanations;

he can perceive the ocean and see the bubbles arise from it, yet remains unaware that his own body has not yet emerged from those bubbles. Thus, he is able to act as the mind and perform the functions of the fruit.

This means: "I am the agent" and "I am the cause who accomplishes affairs"—since the cause and its fruit are always myself, this is the Great Arrogance Heaven (*mahāmāna*), which specifically refers to Maheśvara.
Because he clings to the notion that "I can produce all things," he treats all others with contempt. As for the "seed of pervasiveness and perfection":
it means that because I am pervasive and because I am perfect, the twelve classes of beings are all emanations flowing forth from me.

Furthermore, a good man who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and extinguished birth and death, yet whose subtle and wondrous state of cessation is not yet perfected, may have a point of return upon which he relies.
If he suspects that his own body and mind flow forth from that [point], and that the empty space of the ten directions all arises from it,
he will take that ground of universal origination— the source from which all flows— as the cause of true permanence, lacking the understanding that it is subject to neither birth nor death.
Within the midst of arising and ceasing, they prematurely calculate that there is permanence; thus, they are deluded regarding non-arising and confused about arising and ceasing.

Those who dwell in this deep-seated delusion yet form a resolute conviction in it will fall into the dualistic attachment to permanence and impermanence, taking the Lord of All (Īśvara) as their companion.

They lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit true knowledge and vision; this is called the third [delusion]: establishing a cause based on the mind, thereby forming a false calculation of its results.
This violates and distances one from perfect penetration and turns one's back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of inverted perfection.

This is the attachment to the eternal where there is no eternity; it means that when the aggregate of consciousness manifests at the end of the aggregate of formations, one takes this aggregate of consciousness to be the place to which one returns and the foundation upon which one relies.
Consequently, one suspects that the body, mind, and the world all flow forth from within that [consciousness].

To emerge from this state is precisely the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing. To take this state of profound stillness and immovability as being "non-arising and non-ceasing" not only fails to perceive the true nature of non-arising and non-ceasing, but also leads to delusion regarding the phenomena of present arising and ceasing.

Because one mistakes the impermanent for the permanent, it is said that such a view is "permanence is not permanence. To hold fast to this interpretation is exactly equivalent to calculating the existence of Īśvara.
Those who regard the cause of the myriad things as being of a single category, how could they know that the *Īśvara* is also not the eternal Heaven?
Because the non-Buddhists do not understand this, they consequently cling to it as the fundamental source for the creation of heaven and earth. Wēnlíng says:

"Because one relies on the source of consciousness (*vijñāna-mūla*) and falsely calculates it to be eternally abiding, it is called 'establishing the cause' (*hetu-vyavasthāpana*); because one relies on the mind and completes false calculations, it is called 'establishing the effect' (*phala-vyavasthāpana*). This refers to the former calculation.
I am the complete producer of beings, and those beings are the complete producers of me; therefore, it is called the inversion of "complete production. Question:

The teaching that "all phenomena are but consciousness" (*vijñapti-mātra*) is the correct teaching of the Tathāgata. Why, then, do all these [propositions] fall into the category of external seeds? Answer:

In our own school’s teaching, all phenomena are but consciousness, arising through conditions like illusions or dreams; they do not truly arise. Therefore, we do not establish [the categories of] knowledge or views.

To give rise to attachment to dharmas—now termed establishing the mind that is attained, establishing the mind that is the causal support, and establishing the mind that is the agent—is to establish knowledge through views;
thus, one falls altogether into the ranks of external paths.

Furthermore, O son of good family, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena into emptiness, you have already extinguished arising and ceasing, yet regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, you have not yet perfected it.

If, because one’s knowledge of all that is to be known is universal and complete, one establishes a conviction based on that knowledge— thinking that the grasses and trees of the ten directions are all called sentient beings and are no different from humans,
and that when these "humanized" grasses and trees die, they return to being the grasses and trees of the ten directions without distinction—
one who thus gives rise to such a superior conviction is first falling into the attachment of knowing what is unknowable, the Pāṭha and Śākya attachments to the awakening of all things.
Forming such a partnership, they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit their true knowledge and vision;

this is called the fourth calculation, wherein the mind that seeks perfection falls into the fruit of false delusion, straying far from perfect penetration, turning its back on the city of Nirvana, and giving rise to the seeds of inverted knowledge.
This reckoning is the knowledge of non-knowledge. That which is known is precisely the object of observation within the *vijñāna-skandha*.

To say that this consciousness is "pervasive and perfect" means that the nature of this consciousness is omnipresent, reaching everywhere. Because one relies on this pervasive perfection of consciousness to establish a view, one gives rise to a false understanding, falsely claiming that insentient things such as grass and trees are no different from humans, failing to distinguish between the sentient and the insentient.
It is said: "If one claims that this person has no discernment, then they fall into the category of those who hold that both sentient and insentient things possess consciousness;
this would make them of the same class as the two types of heterodox teachers, the Bhāṭṭas and the Sāṃkhyas.

Wēnlíng says: "This is a deluded calculation that takes perfect knowledge to be the causal mind; thus, the result will ultimately be empty and erroneous. To take non-knowledge as knowledge is inverted knowledge. Question:

Question: What is the difference between National Teacher Guanding’s teaching that sentient and insentient beings are one body, and National Teacher Zhong’s discourse on insentient beings attaining Buddhahood?
Answer: The internal teachings (Buddhism) state that through delusion regarding True Suchness (*tathatā*), the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*) is formed;

from this karmic consciousness, the objective and subjective aspects (*nimitta-dṛṣṭi*) arise, whereby sentient and insentient beings are established as distinct entities. Once these have been so established...
After awakening, one transforms the *karmic consciousness* (*ālaya-vijñāna*) into True Suchness (*tathatā*);

therefore, sentient and insentient beings are identically interfused within the pure, wondrous, and precious awareness, universally constituting a single Buddha-land. This is called the Dharma-nature body and the Dharma-nature land;
the entire body is the land, and the entire land is the body. How could there then be grasses and trees that are not people, or people who are not grasses and trees?

These various distinctions refer to what is taught within our own tradition—that insentient things preach the Dharma. This refers to the time after consciousness has been shattered and everything has merged into the One Mind;
yet, because the karmic consciousness still persists and the aspects of subject and object (xiàngjiàn) still remain, they have not yet been fused into a single entity.
To claim otherwise would be a false conceptualization. Question: In the preceding text, it was stated that grasses, trees, metals, and stones can all manifest as demons. How is this so?

[Question: "Are those who manifest as malevolent spirits not sentient beings? [Answer: These are spirits that rely upon grass and cling to wood; they possess consciousness, but it is not the case that the grass and wood themselves originally possessed consciousness. [Question:
"If an old maple tree transforms into a feathered immortal (*yuren*) and withered wheat transforms into a butterfly, this is a transition from the insentient to the sentient.

But what of a virtuous woman transforming into a stone of chastity, or a mountain earthworm transforming [into something else]?"* *Note: The final sentence is incomplete in the source text. The provided fragment ends with "山蚯化" (mountain earthworm transforms).*
If you ask why these sentient beings transform into insentient things, what is the meaning of this? The answer is that they transform due to a sudden stirring of emotion;
it is not that the old maple tree or the withered wheat were originally sentient, nor is it that the virtuous woman or the earthworm were originally insentient.
This is because those who have not yet shattered the veil of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) falsely claim that heaven and earth share a single root.

"All things as one body" refers to those such as Bhaṭṭa and Śāṇin. Long ago, when the Elder Huitang was engaged in a discourse on the Way with Xia Yigong, they reached the point of realizing that the myriad dharmas are oneself, and that sentient and insentient beings are of one essence.
At that time, a dog was lying beneath the incense table; [Huitang] struck the dog with a ruler and then struck the incense table, saying:
The dog has sentience and thus departs; the incense table lacks sentience and remains stationary. How can sentience and insentience suddenly become one body?
Last summer I could not answer this; Master Tang said, "As soon as you enter into contemplation, it becomes a superfluous dharma.
When have you ever realized that the myriad dharmas are yourself?"

Furthermore, good son, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and extinguished birth and death, yet not having perfected the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa*):

if, within the mutual functioning of the perfectly interfused sense organs, one has already attained adaptability and accordingly seeks the radiance of fire from the perfect transformations of all things,
the purity of water, the circulation of wind, or the accomplishment of the sensory objects (*viṣaya*), each pursuing their own respective veneration;
Because these ministers activate their original causes and establish a view of permanence, such people fall into the attachment to birth and non-birth.
Together with the Kāśyapas and the Brahmins, they diligently exert themselves physically to serve fire and revere water, seeking to escape birth and death;

thus they become companions in error, deluded regarding Buddha-enlightenment and having lost their true knowledge and vision. This is called the fifth: the attachment to the worship of external objects.

The deluded mind follows after external objects to establish false seeking; because it seeks falsely, it hopes for a false fruit. Thus it becomes remote from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of perverted transformations.

This is the attachment to birth and non-birth within the consciousness aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*). When the consciousness aggregate is exhausted, the six gates are dissolved and worn away, and the various sense faculties become mutually functional.
Although they have not yet attained mutual interpenetration, they have already attained conformity with the eighteen divine transformations;
thus, they are able to perceive the fundamental transformative characteristics of the four great elements and falsely claim that all transformations arise from these four elements.
Consequently, they turn their backs on the fire-light of their own inherent nature while seeking fire-light elsewhere, and turn their backs on the water of their own inherent nature.
Seeking purity while seeking pure water is to turn one's back on one's own nature; the circulation of wind while loving the circulation of wind is to turn one's back on one's own nature.
Since the earth-element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) does not fail to arise, one falsely calculates the earth-element to be the "producer.
Thus, regarding the phenomena of water, fire, wind, and earth, one seeks to transcend birth and death, taking these four great elements as [the means].

The source of the creator having established these four great elements as the true sovereigns over things, one falsely calculates that they can give birth to the myriad phenomena, yet in reality they cannot give birth to them; therefore it is said: "Birth is non-birth.
Kāśyapa, those who hold such a view are of the same class as the fire-worshipping heretics; their minds are deluded.
To pursue external objects is like saying one has turned one's back on awakening and joined with the dust of sensory defilement. To seek what should not be sought is called "vain seeking";
to hope for what should not be hoped for is called "vain hoping. The four great elements are that which is produced and transformed, yet they are not themselves the producers or transformers.
To cling to these—which are incapable of producing or transforming—as being capable of producing and transforming is called "perverted transformation."

In principle, the mind is the source of transformation and consciousness is the seed of transformation; yet now, being deluded, the mind follows external objects, abandoning the root to pursue the branches—what is this but perversion?
One who wishes to transcend birth and death instead enters further into birth and death.

Furthermore, if a good man, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and extinguished birth and death, has not yet perfected the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*),
and if he reckons the voidness within the perfect luminosity as non-extinction while regarding the permanent extinction of all transformations as his refuge,
thereby giving rise to a superior resolve— this person falls into the attachment of "taking refuge in that which is no refuge" among the Śūnyatās in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*).
Forming such a companion, they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and delusively forfeit their true knowledge and vision; this is called the sixth fruit:

the "perfectly void mind of non-existence," which results in a state of empty extinction, far removed from perfect penetration and turning one's back on the city of Nirvana, thereby producing the seeds of annihilationism.
This reckoning is the attachment to that which has no refuge. "Perfect luminosity" (*yuanming*) is precisely the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Upon perceiving this perfect luminosity, one then reckons the indistinct, void, and non-substantial essence within that luminosity to be the nature of ultimate emptiness;

consequently, one desires to extinguish the body and obliterate cognition, seeking eternal extinction in emptiness as a place of rest. One fails to realize that this eternally extinguished emptiness is likewise a phantom-like illusion.

It is not a true refuge. The Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) is mentioned briefly as "not non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) to encompass all four formless attainments (*ārūpya-dhātu*), as they belong to the same category.
Those who "perfectly realize the voidness of mind" take the formless, imageless void as their cause;
those who "achieve the fruit of empty extinction" take the cessation and extinction of emptiness as their fruit.

Furthermore, good son, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and extinguished birth and death, if one’s subtle and wondrous state of extinction has not yet reached perfection,

and if one forms a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) that by fixing the body in permanence one may become identical with that subtle and perfect essence, remaining forever without decay or passing away,
such a person falls into the attachment of craving for what is not truly craved; they become companions to those Āśīrvādakas who seek long life.
To be deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and to lose one's true knowledge and vision is called the seventh:

clinging to the source of life, establishing a firm cause of false delusion, pursuing the fruit of long-lasting toil, straying far from perfect penetration, turning one's back on the city of Nirvana, and giving rise to the seeds of protracted delusion.
This calculation—that craving is not an attachment to craving—is the realization that even the perfect and eternal is a cause for consciousness.

To contemplate the perfect and eternal while desiring to solidify the body so it remains permanently, equating this with the perfection of the essence (*jing*), is likewise like this; it represents the intent of the dual cultivation of nature and life (*xing-ming shuangxiu*) and the simultaneous refinement of form and spirit (*xing-shen ju miao*).
"Craving is not an attachment to craving" means that this is merely the deluded generation of craving and clinging to preserve the physical form within the mundane world.
One does not realize that this body is fundamentally ungraspable and cannot be considered permanent, for this body is like a plantain tree, a flash of lightning, or a drop of dew.
Asita—here translated as "Incomparable"—was an ancient seer. Those who cling to the source of life take the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) to be the essence of longevity;
those who establish a false cause for stability believe the body is not permanently abiding and will inevitably perish.
Because they are born, to seek longevity is a profound delusion. For those who pursue long toil as their fruit, life exhausts them while death provides rest;

thus, to desire long life is itself a protracted labor. To extend the seeds of birth through delusion is to fail to realize that the *dharmakāya* is a substance that persists through all eternity, neither decaying nor perishing, yet one still hopes to prolong the duration of one's lifespan.
Because it persists for a long time, it is called "delusion.

Furthermore, O son of good family, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and extinguished birth and death, yet not having perfected the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*), he perceives that life-force is interpenetrating;
fearing that his remaining defilements might be entirely consumed, he sits within a lotus palace at this very juncture.

They extensively acquire the seven treasures and increase their many precious concubines, indulging their desires at will; yet those who give rise to such superior resolve fall into the attachment to "the real" within the unreal.
They become companions to the Takṣaka-garuda, becoming deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and losing all true knowledge and vision.
This is called the eighth: giving rise to the cause of perverse thought to establish the fruit of blazing dust, far removed from perfect penetration and turning one's back on the city of Nirvana.
This gives rise to the seeds of celestial and demonic states;

this is the attachment to what is truly non-existent as being truly existent. Regarding the observation that life-force is mutually pervasive: one takes the uninterrupted continuity of consciousness, vitality, and warmth to be "life.
Now, observing the origins of each individual life-force, one sees that all are primarily governed by the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
The aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) interpenetrates all life. If the aggregate of consciousness were exhausted, then the aggregates of self and other would likewise be exhausted;
who then would realize the True Constant, and who would deliver sentient beings? Therefore, one intentionally retains worldly toil to consolidate the life-root.
Fearing further depletion, one transforms oneself into maidens adorned with the seven treasures, indulging in the utmost luxury and desire as the practice of a Great Bodhisattva.
Not knowing the reality of things, he has long indulged his mind in perverse thoughts;
this is not like a Bodhisattva who truly perceives the source of life and employs attachment to the Dharma to deliver sentient beings.

Because he falsely reckons this to be the true practice of a Bodhisattva without realizing it is not true, it is said that "true" and "not-true" constitute an attachment. *Ṭakkirāja* is the deity Īśvara, the Lord of the Summit of Desire.
Those who are able to transform the objects of desire for their own amusement initiate the cause of perverse thoughts, thereby establishing the fruit of blazing afflictions.
At first, they intended to take the complete purification of thoughts through conditions as the cause, but now they instead take the indulgence of perverse thoughts as the cause.

At first, they intended to take the non-arising of even the slightest dust of defilement as the fruit, but now they instead take the flourishing of worldly toil and affliction as the fruit. Thus it was in the past...

When Udraka Rāmaputra, by means of mundane wisdom (*laukika-jñāna*), suppressed the afflictions of the lower stages, attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), and possessed the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), the King honored and welcomed him into the palace. There, the women of the palace prostrated at his feet;
when Udraka touched the hands of a woman, he immediately gave rise to craving and attachment, whereby he lost his supernormal powers. Thus it is said: "As soon as a single thought of desire arose."
He immediately lost his five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). How could one harbor such perverse thoughts and be so inflamed by worldly dust without falling into ruin?

Furthermore, O son of good family, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and already extinguished birth and death, you have not yet perfected the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*).

Within the clarity of life, you discriminate between the refined and the coarse, and resolve upon the true and the false; though cause and effect correspond to one another, you seek only to invoke a response.

To turn one's back on the path of purity—namely, by viewing suffering, abandoning its origin, realizing cessation, and cultivating the path—and then, having come to rest in cessation, no longer advance but instead give rise to a fixed conviction, such a person falls into the category of those of fixed nature among the Śrāvakas.

They become companions to the ignorant monks who possess overweening pride; they are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their knowledge and vision. This is called the ninth stage of perfect refinement.

With a mind that has achieved the fruit of tranquility, yet remains far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvāṇa, one gives rise to the seeds of entanglement within emptiness.
This refers to those Śrāvakas of fixed nature; "life-intelligence" (*ming-ming*) is another term for "life-light," which is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

Since this consciousness contains both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) seeds, it is within this [aggregate] that the seeds of suffering and its origin are differentiated and determined.
That which is with outflows (*sāsrava*), coarse, and false is the seed of the path to cessation;

that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*), refined, and true is the cultivation of the path as the cause, termed "inspiration" (*gati*), and its realization through reduction as the fruit, termed "response" (*prati*).

All of these involve actual cultivation and actual realization, seeking only the swift emergence from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) toward *nirvāṇa*. Yet they fail to realize that within the pure path, there is fundamentally no birth-and-death.
Furthermore, because they seek only nirvana, Yongjia said: "Knowing suffering, they constantly harbor a sense of weary detachment; severing the accumulation [of karma], they always fear its arising;

longing for cessation, they personally realize the unconditioned (*asamskrta*); and in cultivating the path, they discuss only their own deliverance. Thus, once they dwell in quiescent extinction, they immediately come to rest;
they do not give rise to a fond interest in the playful supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) of the bodhisattvas or in purifying buddha-fields.

Therefore, those who remain attached to the "transformed city" (the provisional nirvana) and do not hasten toward the "jeweled city" (the ultimate goal) are called "determined-nature śrāvakas," which refers to dull-witted arhats who do not turn their minds [toward the Mahayana].
"Unlearned monks" refers to śrāvakas of the "Dharma of the Ignorant" (fo-fa), who claim to have attained what they have not attained and claim to have realized what they have not realized.
"Perfectly refined responsive mind" means to fulfill the cause of seeking a responsive state through single-minded diligence, thereby accomplishing it.
Feeling alone that the ultimate truth of quiescence is realized here, this "Nirvana with Remainder" merely coincides with the level of the seventh faith;

being still shrouded by the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), one has not yet attained the ground of universal penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*). How, then, could one reach the ground of the fruit of "Nirvana without Remainder"?
This is because one is bound by emptiness, considering small knowledge and small views to be sufficient, thereby losing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and being unable to advance.
This is because one faces the ground of the Great Vehicle’s quiescent extinction; it is what is meant by the difficulty of turning back once outside the "Night-Bright" curtain.
Furthermore, good son, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena into emptiness, you have already extinguished birth and death;

yet, while your essence of quiescent extinction has not yet reached full perfection, if you apply yourself to investigating the profound subtlety within the perfectly fused, pure, and luminous awareness, you will establish yourselves in *nirvāṇa* and fail to advance further.
Those who give rise to such superior resolve will fall into the category of those fixed in the nature of pratyekabuddhas and solitary awakeners;

if they do not turn their minds back [toward the Mahayana], they will become their companions, becoming deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and losing their knowledge and vision. This is called the tenth fruit of the perfect enlightenment-mind:
the attainment of a tranquil and luminous state that is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to a seed of "untransformed" perfect clarity.
This clarifies the pratyekabuddha of fixed nature: dissolving the six sense bases into one constitutes perfect interfusion; breaking through existence to return to emptiness constitutes purity;
and fully perceiving the source of life constitutes awakening intelligence. Those who investigate the profound and subtle do so in two ways:

the *dujue* (solitary realizer) contemplates the transformation of phenomena to give rise to profound and subtle awakening, while the *yuanjue* (conditioned realizer) contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination to give rise to profound and subtle awakening.
Upon awakening, they immediately establish a state of profound subtlety as the ground for nirvana and rest, clinging to it without relinquishing it;

they remain stagnant on the path of perfect luminosity and fail to hasten toward the precious destination—this is what is meant by "the moon is full and the water is clear, yet the practitioner grieves.
A *pratyekabuddha* of fixed nature surpasses the *śrāvaka* by one step, for he is able to penetrate and sever the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
It is because of the *qi* (vital energy). As for "the Perfect Enlightenment (*yuanjue*) merging with the mind":

although both the Solitary Realizers (*pratyekabuddha*) and the Conditioned Realizers (*śrāvaka*) all merge with the luminous enlightenment, they do not possess the perfectly interfused, pure, and precious enlightenment; rather, they are minds that merge with a refined awareness.

Therefore, they achieve the fruit of primordial clarity, tranquility, and luminosity. Those who do not transform into the perfect seed are like Bodhisattvas, in whom there remains a sense of subject-object duality.
Because constant awakening does not abide, it is called "non-transformation. Formerly, a monk asked Caoshan, "When the bright moon is suspended in the sky, what then?

Caoshan said, "It is still a person standing at the foot of the steps. The monk said, "I pray that the Master will receive me onto the steps. Caoshan replied, "We shall meet after the sun and moon have fallen.
[The text asks: "Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are all world-transcending sages; for what reason are they also listed [among the ranks]?"
Māra answered this sutra by taking perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) as its central principle; even the slightest trace of attachment constitutes a violation of perfect penetration.
Therefore, regarding the point where they cling to dharmas, they are in reality no different from the various Māras.

However, we select only those who refuse to turn their minds back [to the Dharma]; had they been willing to turn their minds, they would have been called Great Arhats and would not have fallen into this state.
It is so. Ānanda, among these ten kinds of *dhyāna*, those who become deranged midway are caused by delusion;

they give rise to a sense of fulfillment within what is not yet fulfilled, and thus reach this stage because their mental application within the *vijñāna-skandha* is conflicted. Such sentient beings are stubbornly ignorant.

Failing to examine themselves when encountering these manifestations before them, each rests content with their own cherished habitual delusions, regarding this as the ultimate ground of refuge and peace.
Claiming to have attained unsurpassed Bodhi, they commit a great falsehood;

moved by such karma, they become externalists and demonic spirits, and at the end of their lives, they fall into the Avīci Hell. As for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, they fail to achieve further progress.

"You all should maintain this resolve and uphold the Way of the Tathāgata; after my parinirvāṇa, transmit this Dharma-gate to the final age so that all sentient beings may universally awaken to and understand its meaning.
Do not allow them to encounter demons or create their own calamities for themselves.

Protect, sustain, and compassionately rescue them, causing evil conditions to subside, so that their bodies and minds may enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, achieving it from the very beginning without encountering divergent paths."

This is an exhortation to provide protection. In the midst of this, one may become deranged; in the first eight stages, there is often a lack of contentment, while in the latter two stages, it is mostly due to this.
According to the words of those who are deluded, these ten types all arise based on the false attachments of ignorance.
That which is loved and previously practiced is the perfuming habit-energy accumulated since beginningless time when falling into the realm of craving and attachment. Now...
Because they each manifest [visions] within their own meditative concentration, they draw their own conclusions midway and fail to progress, falsely claiming to have reached the ultimate goal;
all such cases fall into the category of great falsehood. The first seven are non-Buddhists (tīrthika), while the eighth is a demonic spirit (māra).
Since both these demons and non-Buddhists are moved by deviant minds and produce deviant karmic merit, neither has severed their afflictions (kleśa); therefore, when their karma is exhausted—

One will certainly fall [into lower realms] regarding the latter two types; however, once one has been able to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*) and attained realization, there is neither further progress nor falling away.
Regarding the "view of Māra," Master Jue distinguishes it as follows:

the first seven are purely views, while the eighth is both view and craving (*dṛṣṭi-rāga*), because it generates a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) that retains worldly toil (*saṃsāra*). As for the view and craving within the realm of the Two Vehicles:

Although [the afflictions] are exhausted, if attachment to the Dharma still persists, it remains entirely within the delusion of discriminative views; this is what is meant by "pacifying" false conditions, which refers specifically to the thorns of such views.

Once these thorns of views are removed, one naturally realizes and enters the ground of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana-bhūmi*), wherein there are no longer any intermediate, circuitous characteristics.
Therefore, the first fascicle states: "All [this] arises from not knowing the eternally abiding true mind."
When all deluded thoughts reach this point, one knows that these very thoughts are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
If even a single hair’s breadth of impurity remains within these five aggregates of deluded thought, one cannot enter the Buddha's knowledge and vision.

Only by shattering the five aggregates can one attain the true *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena). It is like General Guan Yu, who could only see the truth after having passed through the five passes and slain the generals.

The Master’s intention is as follows: these fifty kinds of views mentioned above are all delusions regarding the fundamental principle and losses of the essential purport; they turn their backs on profound stillness and deviate from the truth.
They are like pressing one's eyes to see flowers where there are none, or mistaking a reflection for one's own head; they are like striking ice to seek fire, or climbing a tree to catch fish;

they are like fearing shadows and fleeing into emptiness, or feeling the air to grasp lightning. Such suffering is not the seed of sweetness; how could sand ever be the cause of rice? None of them can [lead to enlightenment].
The Dharma-nature is harmoniously integrated and unified in its single purport; yet those who exhaust themselves in deluded expedients all enter the entanglements of views.
Failing to reach the orthodox teaching, they all cast themselves into the net of views.
Therefore, know that as long as there is something valued or relied upon, one establishes knowledge and establishes understanding—this is not even a hair’s breadth from the view of self.
Since remaining within [any state] without losing it leads entirely to becoming a heterodox teacher, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "When seeing exists, one is an ordinary person;
when seeing is lost, one is a Buddha. The Master said: "There is no need to seek the Truth; one need only cease delusion.

Therefore, even those who have awakened to the fundamental principle may not yet possess "no-seeing" and "no-understanding"; how much less can they follow words and cling to their own intentions, thereby giving rise to "having-seeing" and "having-understanding"?

Indeed! Such Dharma-gates as these were, in the past, during kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the means by which Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust mounted this mind to open it and attain the Unsurpassed Way.

This section clarifies that all Buddhas have attained realization together. The phrase "such Dharma-gates" refers to the methods for discerning the nature of phenomena within the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate).
Among the Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there has never been one who did not achieve unsurpassed Bodhi by means of destroying and eliminating the conscious mind.
As the preceding text states: "The subtle *ālayavijñāna* (the *dāna-vijñāna*) forms a violent torrent through its habitual tendencies; it is truly not [the ultimate reality]."

I truly fear that people will be deluded by me and fail to receive this teaching; for if one is deluded by it, one becomes deranged midway through the path, whereas if one awakens to it, consciousness is transformed into wisdom.
Thus it is said: "All Tathāgatas of the past have already accomplished this gateway."

If the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted, then your present sense faculties will function interchangeably; from this mutual functioning, you can enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine stage of dry wisdom (*vajra-śuṣka-jñāna*).
With a perfectly clear and refined essence of mind, transformation arises within it like a precious moon contained within pure lapis lazuli.
In this manner, you shall transcend the stages of the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten transferences, and the four preparatory minds of the Bodhisattvas.
Practicing the ten stages of the Vajra-bhūmi and attaining the perfect clarity of equal enlightenment, one enters the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wondrous adornments;
having perfected Bodhi, one returns to the state of non-attainment.
This clarifies that the Bodhisattva, upon entering and abiding [in the stages], takes this non-arising and non-ceasing as the foundation for practice, and only thereafter achieves perfection.

Because this is the stage of cultivation and realization of the fruit, it is said that if the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) is exhausted, then a single faculty can perform the functions of all faculties.

This is precisely the position of the first *bhūmi* (ground) of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). Since within the first *bhūmi* one can directly enter the final mind of *Samyaksaṃbodhi* (Equal Enlightenment) without further detours, it is said:
"From within the mutual functioning [of the faculties], one is able to enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine *śuṣka-prajñā* (dry wisdom)."

To investigate the reason for this, it all stems from the mind of the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*), where the essence refines its radiance and the ten functions interpenetrate to perfect the one mind—this is what is meant by "the present Bodhisattvas each entering perfect clarity.
From this heart of perfect clarity, pure transformations are emitted, just as a precious moon is contained within lapis lazuli; in this manner, they transcend the four [realms].
From the fourteenth mind up to the final mind of Equal Enlightenment, the manifestation of transformation reaches its ultimate perfection;

thus, one transitions from the Vajra Path of No-Interval into the Path of Liberation. Therefore, it is said that one enters the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wondrously adorned realm—what is called "transcending through a single gate onto the path of wondrous adornment. Perfecting Bodhi, one returns to the state of non-attainment.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "If there were even one dharma that could be attained, then Dīpaṃkara Buddha would not have bestowed a prediction of enlightenment upon me.
Therefore, attaining non-attainment and realizing non-realization is precisely what constitutes seeing one's nature and becoming a Buddha; it is not obtained from without.

This is what the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* means when it says that at the very moment of first generating the bodhicitta, one immediately achieves perfect awakening. Because this Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) is supreme, [it is so].
Those of superior faculties transcend [the stages] all at once in a single lifetime, like the Dragon Girl or Sudhana, both of whom leaped ahead from the first stage (*ādikṣānti*).

As stated in the preceding text, "later [stages] are for ordinary beings," whereas those of superior capacity traverse the sixty holy positions of the Bodhisattvas; indeed, in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*), there are only two positions:
first, one who severs the pervasive delusions prior to the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxingwei*) and leaps directly into the first stage; second, one who proceeds through the stages.

Furthermore, one does not realize the two types of abandonment [of afflictions and obstacles to knowledge] in between; rather, after the subsequent delusions are severed, one proceeds directly from entering the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) through to Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) in a single leap.

In the interim, there is no further realization, unlike the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna*), where one must necessarily pass through many kalpas, gradually severing and gradually realizing the stages until the three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are completed, at which point the cause is perfected and the fruit is fulfilled, and one realizes Bodhi. This is the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna*).
In the sudden dharma-gate, those of the highest capacity realize that this very moment is it, with nothing further lacking;
those of the two vehicles who realize this turn their minds and advance to attain Great Nirvana.

This *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* are therefore called "wondrous awakening" (*miaojue*), for they cannot be attained through ordinary contemplative practices; thus, it is first termed "wondrous *śamatha*."

The former concludes by saying, "The ocean of wondrous enlightenment and wondrous adornment," while the latter begins with, "Awakening to the wondrously luminous mind, the fundamentally perfect and eternally abiding ground of the heart," and concludes with, "Perfecting Bodhi, returning to non-attainment. The General Commentary states:
"To immediately enter the adamantine stage of dry wisdom from within the mutual functioning [of the faculties] means that the aggregate of consciousness has been shattered."

Thus, without passing through the various stages, one transcends directly and immediately attains the perfect realization of Buddhahood; this is for those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom, such as Avalokiteśvara, whose faculty of the ear achieved perfect penetration.
Once birth-and-death has ceased and tranquil extinction manifests before them, they suddenly transcend both the mundane and supramundane worlds.

Therefore, now that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is shattered, the six sense-faculties function interchangeably; from within this mutual functioning, [the practitioner proceeds].
One immediately enters the Bodhisattva’s adamantine stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*);

this simply destroys the ignorance of the mark of arising, whereby one attains the fruit of Buddhahood without necessarily passing through all the stages. Thus, one should know that the sequence of the five aggregates does not necessarily require experiencing each one individually;
rather, they are presented one by one as a general guide for the contemplation of the mind.
This is a subtle demonic affair and demonic realm that appeared before the past Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, while they were practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
If you can recognize it, the defilements of the mind will be washed away, you will not fall into false views,
the *skandha-māras* will be extinguished, the *deva-māras* will be crushed, and powerful spirits and ghosts will lose heart and flee, as will the *chi-mei* and *wang-liang* demons.
"Without further rebirth until reaching Bodhi, free from all lack and inferiority, they advance toward Great Nirvana with minds that are neither deluded nor distressed.
These words show that the Buddhas of the past transmitted the mind-dharma to practitioners; it is said that these are all demonic activities.
The ancient Buddhas, while within *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, employed the wisdom of initial awakening (*ādikṣānti-jñāna*) to observe demonic activities with vivid clarity.
Although it is the demons who harm meditative concentration, those who bring about these demons are actually the masters of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
If the master’s mind is pure and you can recognize them for what they are, then even when demonic events manifest before you, you will not give rise to attachment nor fall into false views.
Then the demons of the *skandhas*, celestial spirits, ghosts, and *piśācas* will all lose their souls and flee, never to be reborn again.

If one sets out with resolve, one will not fall into perversion midway nor become insane; rather, one will proceed directly to the perfection of Bodhi, fully endowed with the adornment of myriad virtues.
Should one be an inferior *śrāvaka* who lingers at the illusory city, one would not [attain this].
Those who hasten toward the place of treasure will advance by means of this until they reach the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, never again becoming confused or bewildered.
If there are sentient beings in the final age who are dull-witted and ignorant, who do not yet recognize *dhyāna* nor know how to preach the Dharma, yet delight in practicing *samādhi*:
If you fear falling into heterodoxy, concentrate your mind and earnestly exhort others to uphold this Buddha-uṣṇīṣa-dhāraṇī mantra.
If you are unable to recite it, write it down and place it either in a meditation hall or carry it upon your person; then no demons whatsoever will be able to move you.
You should reverently honor this as the ultimate instruction left by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions for their final guidance.

This is a further demonstration of the efficacy of esoteric cultivation. If one possesses sharp faculties, from the stage of "Abiding in the Initial Resolve" (Cittotpāda-vihāra), they may leap directly upward without further demonic obstacles or hindrances.

However, for those of dull faculties who neither recognize *dhyāna* nor understand the preaching of the Dharma, yet whose minds still delight in practicing the Great Samādhi of Direct Audition, you fear that they might fall into false views.
By what means can one protect them so that they may focus their minds single-mindedly on upholding this dhāraṇī-heart?

Thus, all māras will naturally be unable to disturb them. This is because both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings are the most supreme and preeminent Dharma-gate of the Great Uṣṇīṣa, an inconceivable realm;
therefore, he concludes with the practice of upholding the dhāraṇī as his final instruction.
If one refers to this specific sutra, this demonic activity occurs at its very end, and is thus called "final.
If one refers to the teachings of a single great period, this sutra was preached after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and is likewise called "final.
The second major section is hereby concluded.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat; having heard the Buddha’s instruction and admonition, he received it with the highest reverence and mindfulness, retaining it without loss.

In the midst of the great assembly, he addressed the Buddha once more: "Regarding what the Buddha has said—that within the characteristics of the five aggregates there are five kinds of delusion which serve as the original basis for the mind—we, in our ordinary state, have not yet received the Tathāgata’s subtle and detailed exposition. Furthermore, do these five aggregates..."
The sequential exhaustion [of these afflictions] constitutes their dissolution. Thus, for what realm do these five layers serve?

We only pray that the Tathāgata will manifest great compassion and proclaim this for the sake of this assembly, clarifying their minds and eyes, so as to serve as a guiding eye for all sentient beings of the future age.
Furthermore, we ask why these five aggregates are called "deluded thoughts" (*vikalpa*).
World-Honored One, you have generally only taught that these five aggregates arise by relying on causes and depending on conditions;

you have never yet said that these five kinds all fundamentally arise from deluded thoughts, such as saying that form is called the "solidified deluded thought" and sensation is called the "empty-luminous deluded thought," and so forth.
Although I have just now heard this subtle instruction, I do not yet understand why these five aggregates (*skandhas*) are all explained as being nothing but false imagination (*vikalpa*).
If these five aggregates are collectively termed "false imagination," should they be eradicated all at once, or should they be removed gradually and step by step? As for their severance...
"In what place can one reach the ultimate limit of this? We further pray that, out of great compassion and without weariness, you will once again proclaim it for us.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "The essential, true, wondrously bright, fundamental enlightenment is perfectly pure;

it does not harbor birth-and-death nor any defilements, even down to empty space—all of these arise because of deluded thoughts. This is fundamentally the wondrously bright, true essence of fundamental enlightenment."
To falsely give rise to the various vessel-worlds is like the case of Yanratu, who, being deluded, mistook his own head for its reflection;

this delusion has no fundamental cause, yet within such false conceptualization, one establishes the nature of causes and conditions. Those who are deluded regarding causes and conditions call it "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*).

That nature of space is itself like a real illusion produced by causes and conditions; both causes and conditions and spontaneity are merely the calculations of the deluded minds of sentient beings. Ānanda, you must recognize this as delusion.
The causes and conditions for giving rise to false discourse—if these false causes and conditions were originally non-existent, then from the very beginning there would be nothing at all;

how much more so when one fails to realize that they are merely a natural presumption? Therefore, the Tathāgata has clarified with you that the fundamental cause of the five aggregates is likewise nothing but false conceptualization.
This collectively demonstrates that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) all take deluded thought as their root.

It states that the essence of this refined, true, wondrously luminous, and fundamentally awakened awareness is inherently complete and inherently pure; it is not stained by even a hair’s breadth, and not a single thing remains within it.
Thus, from the body and its faculties (*indriya*), the physical world (*bhājana-loka*), and even up to empty space, none of these are things existing within the pure mind.
The root-body is birth and death; the vessel-world is dust and defilement. This root-body and vessel-world, along with empty space, all arise because of deluded thoughts.
That which is called "obscuration" becomes emptiness; within this obscure and dark emptiness, the gathering of darkness becomes form (*rūpa*);
form mixed with deluded thoughts, and the characteristics of these thoughts, become the body. This is originally the wondrously luminous true essence of fundamental awakening.
Originally perfect and pure, all things arise from deluded thoughts; the various vessel-worlds are fundamentally not real, yet they are falsely perceived as real.
This is no different from Yaññadatta losing his head and mistaking the reflection in a mirror for the real thing.
Since they arise from delusion, they have no cause. You all commonly know only the five aggregates.

Arising from causes and conditions, they do not exist through delusive conceptualization; yet one fails to know that the nature of these causes and conditions all arises based on ignorance, karma, and craving.
Because one is deluded by this ignorance, karma, and craving, one further reckons them as existing spontaneously within the wondrously luminous mind of fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).
Furthermore, this empty space [arises] from a single thought-moment within the pure and clear awakening.

That which arises from obscured ignorance is not even substantially real; how much less so those things arising from causes and conditions or spontaneously, which are all produced by the deluded conceptualization and discrimination of sentient beings—how could they possibly be real?

Nevertheless, because I have previously seen that sentient beings falsely cling to the five aggregates as being real dharmas, I have forcefully taught that the five aggregates arise from the deluded mind.

Arising from causes and conditions, now that you know the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) have fundamentally no location, it is said that their delusive nature is such that causes and conditions themselves fundamentally do not exist.
Therefore, when I say that the various phenomena of the five aggregates arise from causes and conditions, this is not a definitive statement;
thus I say: "Phenomena produced by causes and conditions—I declare them to be empty, yet they are also called provisional."

This name also signifies the meaning of the Middle Way. Since all phenomena produced by causes and conditions do not even substantially exist and are merely provisional designations, how much more so those who, failing to understand causes and conditions, speculate that all phenomena arise from spontaneity—how could these not be delusions?
Therefore, today the Tathāgata has revealed to you that the original cause of the five aggregates is likewise [the same].
I wish for you to understand through false conceptualization that all phenomena take delusion as their root.
Your body was originally produced by the conceptual thoughts of your parents; had your mind not been conceptual, it could not have entered into this state of thought to transmit life.
As I previously stated, when one thinks of the taste of vinegar, saliva is produced in the mouth; when one thinks of climbing a high place, a tingling sensation arises in the soles of the feet.
Since there is no sour substance on the precipice and none has yet arrived, your body must not be devoid of delusion;
otherwise, how could your saliva flow out merely by speaking of sourness? Therefore, you should know that this present physical form of yours is called the first false discrimination of solidity.
This aggregate of form and name (*nāmarūpa-skandha*) is a solidified delusion. Do you not yet know that the aggregate of form is a solidified delusion?
It is because your physical body first arose from the delusions of your parents; it was through their craving and attachment that the red and white elements came to be.
Even though the thought of father and mother existed, it was because of the craving-fluid of your intermediate state (*antarābhava*) that [the body was formed].
If one does not give rise to the thought [of a mother], one can never flow as the seed of craving to enter the parents' conception and form a fetus to continue one's life;
thus, we know that the entire body is composed entirely of deluded thoughts. Fearing that this may not be understood, it is further clarified through analogy:
"It is just like imagining the taste of vinegar and saliva flowing out, or imagining a precipice and one's feet becoming numb and hanging over it."
The cliff has never possessed sour things, nor have they ever come here.

If your body were not of the same nature as deluded thought, how could the water in your mouth flow forth because of someone speaking of sour plums? This is why the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is called "solidified deluded thought.
To speak of it as "solid" means that the three—the father, the mother, and oneself—congeal together in one place.
Because it is formed through such binding,
this very state of mind you have described— imagining yourself at a great height— which causes your physical form to truly experience a sensation of aching and constriction,

and which, arising from that cause, can move the substance of your body: this present state of yours, driven back and forth by the two manifest conditions of the favorable and the harmful, is called "empty brightness" (vimala).
The second false conception:
this clarifies that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is a false conception of empty luminosity.

It takes what was previously manifested as the sensation of aching and tingling in the soles of the feet and illuminates it—what is called "a single drop of ink forming two dragons. This refers to the precipice [of realization].

This has caused your soles to truly experience a stinging sensation; is this not because your mind has already first received the words regarding the steepness of the precipice, thereby moving your physical body and causing your form to truly feel the stinging sensation?
Furthermore, in your present state, two types of sensations—beneficial and harmful—arise from the two objects of favorable and unfavorable conditions, driving one another.
They run back and forth without ceasing; this is why the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is called "empty and luminous delusion.
There are three types of sensation: painful sensation, pleasant sensation, and neutral sensation. Loss and gain are simply subsumed within the two sensations of suffering and pleasure.
Because it is empty, sensation receives [objects] like the great void receiving things; because it is luminous, sensation receives [images] like a clear mirror receiving reflections.
It is because of your thoughts that they drive your physical body; yet the body is not of the same category as thought. For what reason does your body follow the dictates of thought?
Various mental images arise and take form in accordance with thought. When awake, it is the conceptual mind; when asleep, it becomes various dreams.
Thus, the movement of your thoughts and the agitation of your deluded emotions are called the third false imagination, known as "interfusion."
This clarifies that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is a deluded thought of mutual integration. "Thoughts and considerations" refer to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);
it means that within a single body, the mental consciousness serves as the sovereign, such that the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, as well as the hands and feet, all obey its commands.
If your body were not of the same nature as the mental consciousness, for what reason would it be made to serve at will? Therefore, in all cases—
The various forms of perception at present must necessarily arise because the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) moves first, after which the sense faculties (indriya) then apprehend them;
thus we know that this body is in accord with thought and is never separated from it for even a moment. It is just like a dancer or a performer who follows the beat of another:
when the beat is slow, the steps are slow; when the beat is rapid, the steps are rapid. The five sense faculties are likewise so.

It merely follows the transformations of the mental ground (*manobhūmi*). When the mental ground arises, the physical wheel of the body moves; when the mental ground ceases, the faculties and their objects become tranquil.
Thus, when awakening connects with form, it is called "perception" (*saṃjñā*); when slumbering intersects with the spirit, it is called "dream.

You should know that your body is entirely composed of such perceptions, stirred by the movement of deluded emotions. This is why this aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is named "pervasive integration."

As for the statement that "delusive thoughts are also said to be interfused," this means that when this conceptualizing mind resides within the five sense organs, whether one is awake or asleep, it acts as the sovereign master;
therefore, it attains perfect interfusion and pervasive penetration.
The principle of transformation does not abide; it shifts and moves in secret. The fingernails grow and the hair grows; the vital energy wanes and the face becomes wrinkled.

Day and night they replace one another, yet there is never any awakening to this. Ānanda, if this were not you, how could the body undergo such change? If it were truly you, why would you have no awareness of it?
Thus, these formations of yours, which do not cease for even a single thought-moment, are called the "subtle darkness," the fourth deluded thought.
This clarifies that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is a subtle and hidden delusion. "Constantly moving" means changing again and again;
"secretly shifting" means a continuous, minute displacement that people do not perceive. Nails grow and hair grows; vital energy wanes and the face wrinkles.
This speaks of how arising and ceasing alternate before one day and night, yet there is not a single person who can perceive it.
The awakened one correctly perceives this subtle shifting. Thus Zhou Xiong said: "The movement and transformation ceaselessly proceed;

heaven and earth shift subtly—who is aware of it? If this *xing-yin* (the aggregate of formation) were merely deluded thought, and not your own substance, how could it cause your nails to grow and your hair to lengthen? If this *xing-yin* were truly you...

Regarding the body, how is it that it undergoes transformation day and night without ever being perceived? One thereby knows that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) changes from moment to moment, yet one does not realize it;
for this reason, it is called "subtle and hidden delusion."
Furthermore, that which you call "perpetually constant"— your brilliant clarity and profound stillness— is not exempt from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing within this body.
If it were truly a refined reality that could not tolerate the habitual presence of delusion, for what reason did you,
upon suddenly beholding a strange object again after many years had passed during which it was neither remembered nor forgotten, find your memory of it perfectly restored?
If there were no loss, then within this refined, lucid, and unwavering state, as thoughts arise moment by moment to receive perfuming, what calculation could there be?

Ānanda, you should know that this stillness is not the True Suchness (*tathatā*). It is like a rushing torrent that appears tranquil at a glance; because the flow is so rapid, it is not seen, yet it is not that there is no flow.
If it were not the source of thought, how could it receive the habitual tendencies of delusion? It is not your six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) that function through mutual opening and closing.
Because this deluded thought can never be extinguished, within your current seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, you have become habituated to it until it becomes clear and pervasive;
yet internally it is a phantom-like void, the fifth inverted, subtle, and refined conception. Ānanda, these five aggregates of clinging are formed by these five deluded conceptions.

This clarifies that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is a subtle and refined perception. "Vital clarity" (*jingming*) refers to the "single vital clarity" mentioned in the preceding text;
"the state of being still and unmoving" (*zhan bu yao chu*), meaning "tranquil like still water," both refer to the eighth consciousness.
As for the term "eternal" (*hengchang*): if you take this vital clarity and state of being still and unmoving to be true eternity, then your entire body does not go beyond it.
If the six faculties were indeed pure and true, they would not be mixed with nor deluded by falsehood; thus, they should not again undergo the perfuming of such mixed and false influences.
For what reason, then, do objects seen many years ago—though long since forgotten—appear exactly as before when seen again?
This is because, although the initial perfuming occurs through the first six consciousnesses, their retention without loss is due to the eighth [consciousness].
The sixth consciousness is like a minister who collects taxes, and the eighth is like a storehouse official;

thus, when one beholds a rare object and recalls it vividly even after many years have passed, this is entirely due to the power of the eighth consciousness’s subtle clarity and unmoving state, which receives perfuming moment by moment. Because it is formless and void, it is perfumed by...
If it is real, it is perfumed by reality; if it is delusory, it is merely delusion. Ānanda, the following analogy clarifies that this is not true reality.
This state of profound stillness and lack of movement is not yet the nature of true, eternal immovability.
It is like a rapid current of water which, at a glance, appears tranquil and serene; this is merely because the flow is so swift that its movement is not perceived. It is not truly [still].
When water flows, one knows the place where it flows; the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is likewise so.

It is not truly unmoving because it serves as the root-source of the four preceding types of false conceptualization, and thus it receives the habitual tendencies of delusion. If it were not the root-source of false conceptualization, how could it receive the mind of the four preceding false habitual tendencies?
However, this source of conceptualization has not yet attained the mutual functioning of the six sense organs, nor has it reached the state of integration and synthesis.
There is no way for cessation to be attained. Why? Because the eighth consciousness and the preceding six sense organs share the same essential nature;
their security and peril are one. If they are identical in terms of the True, they are likewise identical in terms of the deluded.

Therefore, when the six sense organs are worn away, this delusion fundamentally becomes like ice melting in hot water; it should, in an instant, transform into unsurpassed enlightened awareness. Now, as for your present six...

Among the faculties, those that have been habituated through subtle impressions and do not forget their capacities for seeing and hearing do so because they are permeated moment by moment by refined thought (*saṃkalpa*).

Thus, it can see when in the eye and hear when in the ear. Because this refined clarity remains profoundly still and unshaken, yet originally arises from a single thought of ignorance (*avidyā*), it appears to exist while being as if non-existent; it is not truly non-existent, and therefore it is called "non-manifest" (*wang*).
The elephant-like voidness of this consciousness-aggregate (vijñāna-skandha) is therefore called an inverted, subtle, and refined conception.
It is called "inverted" because it arises from the wondrously perfect, truly pure, and sublime mind; it is called "subtle" because its flow is so rapid that it cannot be seen;
and it is called a "refined conception" because both the essence of hearing and the essence of seeing are but this single refined conception. Thus one knows.

Although these five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha) differ in five ways according to their coarseness or subtlety, they are all formed by the five kinds of false conceptualization and do not exist inherently from the beginning.
Therefore, if one perceives the five aggregates as existing, this is the world of sentient beings;
if one realizes the emptiness of the five aggregates, this is the world of ultimate truth; and if one realizes the true mark (lakṣaṇa) of the five aggregates, this is the Middle Way.

The Supreme Truth and Perfect Enlightenment transcend these five aggregates; outside of the three worlds, there is not a single dharma that can be established or posited as either conventional or ultimate.
All the teachings throughout the various periods of the Buddha’s life explain nothing other than this, for there is no other expedient means.
To be deluded regarding this is to be an ordinary being; to awaken to this is to become a Buddha. It is solely this One Mind, which differs only in its opening and closing. Thus it is said.
The preceding response regarding how all five aggregates are termed false conceptualizations is complete.
Now, if you wish to know the depth of the causal realms: only form and emptiness constitute the limit of form; only contact and separation constitute the limit of sensation;
only recollection and forgetting constitute the limit of perception; and only cessation and arising constitute the limit of mental formations.
"That which enters deeply into the profound is the limit of consciousness.
This answers the question of where the first five aggregates reach as their boundary.

"Cause" refers to the five kinds of false conceptualization, and "limit" (or boundary) refers to the demarcation of those five kinds of false conceptualization. "Shallow and deep" refers to these five kinds of false conceptualization.
The former is shallow and the latter is deep. Only form (*rūpa*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) constitute the limits of form:

that which has segmentation is called form, and that which lacks segmentation is called emptiness. Ordinarily, people only know that the segmented physical body is the limit of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), yet they do not realize that emptiness is also the limit of this segmented physical body.

Furthermore, because even in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) there still exists subtle material substance, the contact of sense-faculties (*indriya*) with their objects (*viṣaya*) is called "contact" (*sparśa*), while the non-encounter of faculties and objects is called "separation.
Ordinarily, one understands only the experiencing of the two types of objects—those that are agreeable and those that are disagreeable—as the limit of feeling (*vedanā*).
One does not realize that the non-experiencing of these two types of objects is likewise the limit of feeling. Therefore, the Brahmin [practices] non-appropriation (*apratisaṃkhyāna*).
The World-Honored One questioned him, saying: "Is this view itself received? Therefore, one knows that while reception is indeed reception, even the non-reception of all things is also reception.
To have mindfulness is to record; to lack mindfulness is to forget. People only know that mindfulness of all phenomena constitutes the limit of perception (*saṃjñā-koṭi*);
they do not know that the non-mindfulness of all phenomena is likewise the limit of perception. It is as follows:

The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "Whether thoughts move or thoughts cease, they all return to delusion and confusion. This is precisely it. To transform the non-existent into existence is called arising;

to transform existence into non-existence is called ceasing. People only know that the constant flux of every thought is like a violent torrent, which they take to be conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*).
They do not realize that reaching the state of non-transmigration and transforming into still water is likewise the limit of activity, because [existence] still persists.

Because there are no waves when the wind has ceased, the Sūtra says: "Even reaching the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one is still subject to the flux of the three marks.

To turn back is called "entering," and to merge is called "uniting. People merely know how to divide your profoundly still and perfect enlightened nature (*bodhicitta*) into seeing, hearing, observing, and discerning, causing it to flow away and rush toward forms and sounds; thus they fall into the limits of consciousness.
Not knowing how to reverse the flow and cause it to revolve back into the single, perfectly湛 (zhan) and translucent state remains within the boundaries of consciousness;

for once one seeks the True, that which is already not-True is no longer the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Therefore, know that to know only form as form, while not knowing that emptiness is also form, is shallow;
to know that both emptiness and form are form is deep; this extends even to merely knowing the outflowing stream.
To distinguish the stillness as consciousness and not know how to return the flow to merge with that stillness is a shallow understanding of consciousness;
however, if one knows how to exit the flow and distinguish between the stillness and the returning flow to merge with it, all are seen as the limits of consciousness—
this is the Tathāgata’s elucidation of the five levels of the limits of deluded thought, which may be said to have reached the ultimate boundary of their realm.
These five aggregates originally arise in overlapping succession; their cause of arising is consciousness, and their cessation begins with the elimination of form.

This principle can be suddenly realized, whereby realization and its objects are simultaneously dissolved; yet phenomena are not suddenly eliminated, for they are exhausted only through gradual stages.

I have already shown you how the knots were tied in the *kārpāsa* cloth; what is there that you do not understand that you must inquire about again? You should use this to open up and penetrate the root-source of these deluded thoughts.

This is transmitted to future practitioners of the Dharma-ending age so that they may recognize the profound falsity [of existence], develop deep revulsion toward it, realize the existence of Nirvana by themselves, and no longer cling to the three realms.
This answers the previous question regarding the sudden removal and gradual severance of the five aggregates. As for "arising in layers," this refers to one layer.
These five aggregates arise in successive layers; they evolve from a single moment of non-awakening which turns this awakened mind into the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*).

Because of consciousness there is volitional activity (*saṃskāra*); because of activity there is perception (*saṃjñā*); because of perception there is feeling (*vedanā*); and because of feeling there is form (*rūpa*).
These five aggregates fundamentally arise in this sequential order. Today, in order to dismantle them, one should first extinguish form, and next...
One extinguishes sensation, extinguishes perception, and extinguishes formations before extinguishing consciousness. Birth proceeds from the subtle to the coarse, like putting on clothes;
extinction proceeds from the coarse to the subtle, like taking off clothes.

However, because the principle of the five aggregates fundamentally arises from a single thought of delusive imagination, the ground of the mind opens up with a single word, and one rides upon that single awakening.
Doubt is suddenly dispelled; this is what it means to dissolve my inverted thoughts accumulated over billions of eons.
Since the characteristics of the five aggregates are bound together in successive order, they must likewise be gradually exhausted in that same sequence.
I have previously used the knotting of the cloth to demonstrate the sequential arising of phenomena; now I shall sequentially untie them. Thus, both the dharma and the metaphor are clearly evident.

What is it that you do not understand such that you ask this question again? Therefore, know that the previous six knots and these five aggregates are all produced in succession and must be untied in succession. You should now loosen the final knot and encourage its transmission to others.
"The mind attains opening and penetration" means realizing that the very source of the faculties is entirely the arising of false thoughts, and is not [otherwise].
The nature of things inherently possesses this teaching, which one awakens to by oneself;

it is transmitted and shown to others below to further teach those who have awakened, so as to cause them to recognize what is empty and illusory—meaning that all sentient beings shall thoroughly penetrate the emptiness and illusion of these five aggregates.
To "profoundly loathe their own birth" means that if one penetrates the emptiness and illusion of these five aggregates, one will then profoundly loathe the suffering of this birth. Thus...
