Question: One knows the bliss of *nirvāṇa* and no longer clings to the three realms; what is the meaning of "sudden awakening" and "gradual elimination"? Answer:
It is like the fierce winds of the great ocean ceasing suddenly while the waves subside gradually;

it is like a child’s various faculties being born all at once while their strength is prepared gradually; it is like the light of the sun appearing suddenly while the frost and dew dissipate gradually.

The sudden perfection of the seal-patterns implies a sequence in their realization, as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "At the very moment of first generating the bodhicitta, one attains perfect enlightenment.
Although the three grades of sages and the ten stages of saints realize and certify [this truth] through gradual cultivation, if one practices without awakening, it is not true practice.
This is because there is no way to accord with the True without conduct that flows from the True; how could there be conduct that adorns the True without being derived from it?

The *Zhēnqǐ jīng* (Sutra on True Arising) states: "If one has not heard this Dharma, even after practicing the six perfections and the ten thousand deeds for many kalpas, one will ultimately not realize the Truth.
This refers to the principle of sudden awakening followed by gradual elimination. It is also said that there are those who "suddenly awaken and suddenly practice";

this describes those of the highest grade of intellectual capacity whose aspiration and desire are both superior, who attain awakening upon hearing [the Dharma] once, obtain the Great Total Retention (*mahā-dhāraṇī*), and achieve realization in a single thought-moment.

One does not give rise to the severance of the prior or subsequent limits; if one wishes to sever obstructions, it is like cutting a single strand of silk from a skein—when one is cut, all are severed.
If this is applied to the cultivation of virtue, it is like dyeing a single strand of silk from a skein—when one is dyed, all become that color.
Furthermore, for those of sudden enlightenment, liberation is attained without departing from this very life; just as when a lion cub is first born, it is truly a lion.
When the son practices, he immediately enters the stage of Buddhahood; like a bamboo shoot growing in spring that does not depart from spring, he is equal to his mother.
Why is this? Because the mind is empty. If one eliminates deluded thoughts and forever severs the notions of self and others, one is equal to the Buddha.
As the Sūtra says: "Without destroying the mundane world, one transcends it; without abandoning afflictions, one enters Nirvāṇa."
If one does not cultivate sudden awakening, it is like a jackal following a lion for hundreds of thousands of kalpas; in the end, it can never become a lion.
Therefore, we know that if one does not directly realize one’s own mind, how can sudden awakening be achieved?

Following along with deluded studies will ultimately fail to produce the truth. Thus, the *Song of Realizing the Way* says: "Therefore, in the Chan gate, having brought the mind to an end, one enters suddenly."
By virtue of the power of the knowledge and vision of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna-darśana*), one knows that directly realizing *tathatā* (suchness) is to attain Buddhahood within this very mind;

this is the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuan-dun zong*). If one does not understand this mind but instead falsely engages in cultivation and realization, this is the fruit of the "extinguishing-ashes" (*hui-duan*) of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings (*zang-tong jiao*).

If one relies on this mind yet separately cultivates according to specific practices, this is the Mahayana of the Distinct Teaching (*bie jiao*), which differs from the Perfect Teaching’s [realization] of the mind as such.

Regarding "the complete manifestation": because the stages, practices, and durations of all [gradual] paths increase exponentially over days, kalpas, and eons, it is said that "mind itself is [Buddhahood]"—meaning those who quickly resolve their minds on practice are swift, while others are slow.
This concludes the section on the Correct Teaching (Zhengzongfen).

Ānanda, suppose there were a person who filled all the empty space throughout the ten directions with the seven treasures and offered them to as many Buddhas as there are atoms of dust, serving and making offerings to them with a mind that never faltered. What do you think?
Would this person, by virtue of such an offering to the Buddhas, gain much merit?

This is the section on the dissemination of the teaching. First, it cites an imperial edict to compare [the merit], stating that filling the entirety of the void of the ten directions with inexhaustible seven-jeweled treasures is inexhaustible;
making offerings to fields of merit as numerous as motes of dust is inexhaustible; and having a mind that never fails to deliver others and thoughts that never cease are also inexhaustible.
This edict then commands that the amount of merit obtained by such a person be calculated and compared.

Ānanda replied, “Space is inexhaustible and precious jewels are boundless. In the past, there were sentient beings who offered the Buddha seven coins and, by relinquishing their bodies, still attained the rank of a Wheel-Turning King.
How much more so now, when the entirety of space is filled with Buddha-lands, all of which are offered as precious jewels?
Even if one were to contemplate this for an entire kalpa, it could not be fully grasped. How could there be any limit to such merit?”

This compares and determines the immeasurable [merit]. The first two lines speak simply of the superiority of material wealth. In the passage beginning "Formerly there was... and so forth, the inferior is used to manifest the superior:
giving a single coin to a single Buddha involves both a poor object of merit (*kṣetra*) and poor material wealth, yet it still yields the superior reward of becoming a Wheel-Turning King;

how much more so when one gives to Buddhas who pervade the entirety of space—this is the superiority of the field—and when one gives precious jewels—this is the superiority of the material wealth—throughout the exhaustion of kalpas.
It is already inconceivable that they will obtain such blessings; how much more so when one seeks their ultimate limit?
The Buddha told Ānanda: "The words of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are not false.

If there should be a person who has committed the four grave offenses or the ten pārājika transgressions, and in a mere instant passes through this world and other worlds into the Avīci Hell, until it reaches its very end—"

There is nowhere throughout the ten directions that they do not traverse; they are able to take this Dharma-door with a single thought and reveal it to those who have not yet studied during the final kalpa.
The karmic obstacles of such a person shall be extinguished at that very moment, and the causes for the suffering of hell they were to undergo shall be transformed into a Land of Peace and Bliss.
The merit they attain shall surpass that of the previous donor by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten thousandfold, a hundred millionfold, or even more.
Thus it continues until it reaches that which cannot be fathomed by calculation or analogy. Ānanda,

if there are sentient beings who can recite this sutra and uphold this mantra as I have extensively explained— exhausting an entire kalpa without end— and who act according to my instructions and practice the path as taught,
they will directly attain Bodhi, and no further demonic activities shall arise.
This compares the superiority of the gift of Dharma with the inferiority of the gift of material wealth. "If there should be another person" means that even if there were but one person;

the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*)—namely, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying—and the ten *pārājika* offenses, as described in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, are the most extreme causes of evil.
The ten directions of the Avīci Hell are the most extreme fruits of evil. A single thought-moment...
"One who propagates the sutra" refers specifically to one who was on the verge of falling into hell; "a single thought" means a momentary arousal of the mind rather than a long-term commitment.
This Dharma-gate is a definitive designation for a single door of profound entry into the perfect penetration of Great Samādhi.
"The final kalpa" refers to a time when the sages are distant and demons are powerful; "final-stage learners" refers to those for whom progress is difficult and regression is easy.
For those who have regressed, their karmic obstacles—namely the aforementioned four grave offenses and ten evil deeds—shall be extinguished at the very thought;
that is to say, by a single thought of propagating this sutra, they shall all attain extinction. Furthermore, it transforms what lies below:
not only does it eliminate evil karma, but it can also transform places of suffering into the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Indeed, such a subtle merit of a single thought can [accomplish this].
Those who escape extreme suffering and are born into supreme bliss do so because the myriad phenomena are transformed by the mind alone, whereby delusion becomes awakening.

Regarding the merit obtained, the text below states that one not only extinguishes sins but also acquires blessings surpassing those of a person who previously made offerings of the seven treasures filling the void of space to as many Buddhas as there are atoms; for how could such a thing exist?
When viewed with the Buddha-eye, even the transformation of the great earth into gold is but an ordinary occurrence;
how much more so the wondrous True Suchness-nature, which is the original family treasure, inherently pure and pervading the Dharma-realm—not merely filling empty space, but encompassing all.
If one who bestows all manner of rare treasures upon a Buddha still attains immeasurable merit, how much more so when offering this?
The person who gives the gift of Dharma enables others to obtain all the treasures of their household and to employ them without end;
how could its merit be measured by the mind? Thus, it surpasses the former [merits] by hundreds of thousands of millions of times, such that even analogies cannot reach it.
Furthermore, even a person with the most grievous sins can extinguish their offenses and attain [liberation] through a single thought of propagating this sutra.
If the merit is such even for this, how much more so for those with minor offenses, those without offenses, and even those with merit or great merit?

One may know that the rewards for the profound propagation of the sutra are exceptionally sublime. If even a single thought is thus, how much more so for those who propagate it for a long time, even until the end of their lives;
their rewards can be known to be even greater. Ānanda, the following section reveals the merit of upholding the sutra and reciting mantras without offense.
Virtue is inexhaustible. This is truly because it is only through reciting sutras and upholding mantras that one attains the wisdom born of hearing;

once such merit has been realized, even then it cannot be fully described. Furthermore, if one follows the teachings while reciting mantras, one will proceed directly to the fruit of the Tathāgata’s great Bodhi, with no further demonic activities to cause obstacles. How, then, can such merit be measured? Thus, the Lotus Sutra states:
It is said that if there were anyone who heard the Dharma, not one would fail to become a Buddha. In the past, a mud crab listened to the Dharma and was reborn in heaven;
a stallion elephant heard the sutras and reformed its evil ways; a bhikṣu obtained the fruit of realization through laughter; and a woman attained the realization of emptiness through contemplation.
How much more so for those who hear this Mahāyāna teaching of the Perfect and Sudden—how could they fail to extinguish their transgressions and generate merit?
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās,
and all those in the world— gods, humans, asuras, as well as the bodhisattvas from other directions, the noble ones of the two vehicles, the rishis, the youths,
and the powerful spirits who had first resolved their minds— all rejoiced greatly, paid homage, and departed.

This clarifies the joy and celebration of the Dharma assembly. The "Holy Sage Youth" (Ṛṣikumāra) is one who dwells in the realm of the sages (*ṛṣi-gati*) while practicing the inner teaching, desiring to attain the wondrous fruit of *kumārabhūta* (youthful purity).

Those of "great power in generating the resolve" are those who possess supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), have attained fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*), and having turned their minds to protect the Teaching, dwell beneath the seat of the Tathāgata. "All were greatly rejoiced" refers to those who participated [in the assembly].
Having heard this Great Dharma and attained such great benefit, his joy was beyond compare.
